units.la: VANquam superiorem nostram De uitis Romanorum Pontificum editionem, Brytannicorum scriptorum Catalogo adiunctam, illustrissimi Electoris Comitis Palatini D. Othonis Henrici auspicijs satis munitam uiderem: hanc tamen à magna sciunctâ & auulsam, in munitiorem formâ contractam, accessione uerò non poenitenda locupletatâ, cum nec suis, nec domini uiribus ab unde tueri se posset: alicuius praesidijs ac sub fidijs indigere facile perspexi: atque sic nudam & inermem, nullis fultâ patrocinijs, in manus hominum inimicorum & amicorum emittere dâ temere nullo modo iudicaui. Omnino enim aliquis patronus idoneus erat quaerendus, qui & ingenio, arte, doctrina possit causam desertam agere, & pupillum quasi omnium propè hominum praeiudicijs reum atque damnatum, in fidem ac clientelam uel-
units.tr: Whenever I saw our earlier edition of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, appended to the Catalogue of British writers, sufficiently protected under the auspices of the most illustrious Elector Palatine, Count Otto Henry, I nevertheless saw that it had been torn away from its large companion and was now compressed into a more defensible form and enriched with an addition not to be regretted. Since it could not defend itself by its own strength or by that of its author, I easily perceived that it needed the protection and shelter of someone. So I judged that I should not rashly send it out, bare and unarmed and supported by no patronage, into the hands of men, both enemies and friends. Indeed some suitable patron had to be sought, one who could by his talent, skill and learning plead a deserted cause and take into his faith and clientage a ward who is, by the prejudices of almost all men, accused and condemned, so that he would not, bereft of all the goods of his estate and with no guardian left, perish together with his dying parent.

units.la: lei let recipere: ne omnibus bonorum administraculis orbatus, nullo relicto tutore, simul cum parente moriente intercidat. Itaq; diu multumq; in hac cogitatione occupatus, cum omnes undiq; anxia & attentissima cura circumspiceremus quatuor Ecclesiarum Antistites clarissimi, occurristis primi, in quorum ope tuto acquiescerem: qui saepe in hac causa uersati fuistis, qui longo usu omnes aduersariorum ictus & petitiones didicistis & retudistis: ita ut prior Liber cum Historia nostra coniunctus, fortissimi Principis potentia sat defensus: hic à me posteriore nunc cura aliquanto auctior & recognitus, eruditione & iudicio tatorum virorum probè nixus, liberè serena fronte in medium hostium agmen imperterritus prodire non erubescat. Equidem non sum nescius, unum aliquem uestrum satis ad congrediendum in hoc Theologico certaminis genere ualuisse uiribus: & meam opellam indignam, ut uel uni dedicetur, ingenuè fateor: tamen non quid uos possetis, sed quid ego debeam, confidero: nec domi praesentiam intueor, sed animi in uos omnes ardentissimae uoluntati in dulgeo: qui licet singulos sigillatim ampleCtor, uniuersos tamen uno munusculo, quia pluribus nō possum, demereri cupio: ac una in re omnibus simul, quid animi erga singulos habeam, declarare. Deinde quos una reli-gio,
units.tr: Therefore, occupied for a long time and at length with this thought, while I looked about on every side with anxious and most attentive care, four most distinguished bishops of the Churches presented themselves to me first, and in their help I might rest securely. You have often been engaged in this cause; by long practice you have learned and warded off all the blows and attacks of the adversaries. So it is that the earlier book, joined with our history and sufficiently defended by the power of a most valiant Prince, has here been revised by me and made somewhat fuller in its later care, and, resting securely on the learning and judgment of such men, it need not be ashamed to come forward freely, with a calm brow and undaunted, into the midst of the enemy's ranks. Indeed I am not unaware that any one of you would have been strong enough by himself to engage in this kind of theological contest, and I frankly confess that my little work is unworthy to be dedicated to even one of you. Yet I consider not what you are able to do, but what I owe; and I look not to your presence at home but yield to the most ardent goodwill of your minds towards all of you. Although I might praise each of you individually, I wish to win the favour of you all with one little gift, since I cannot do so with several, and in one matter to declare to all of you together what feeling I hold towards each. Then, since one religion, one faith, one Lord and one baptism join you together, what prevents me from binding you together in one letter? Therefore I trust that you will take my boldness and rashness, if it is any, which springs from your kindness and is born of no ill will, in good and fair part, as you ought and as you are wont to do.

units.la: [?] gio, una fides, unus Dominus, unus bapti-smus iungit: quid vetat, quo minus una copulet epistola? Quare audaciam & temeritatem meam, si quæ sit, ab humanitatis vestræ opinione profectam, & ab animo non malo natam, æqui boniq; consulturos vos, ut debetis ac soletis, confido.
units.tr: Religion, one faith, one Lord, one baptism join you together: what prevents me from binding you together in one letter? Therefore I trust that you will take my boldness and rashness, if it is any, which springs from your kindness and is born of no ill will, in good and fair part, as you ought and as you are wont to do.

units.la: Ut autem causam, quam propugnari ac foveri à vobis cupio, & rogo, intelligatis: animos vestros à gravioribus studiis, & sacris occupationibus paulisper avocate, & ad audiendum, quid sit hic mihi propositum, attentionem vestram mentesq; couertite. Munus quod offero Papale est & pontificale: id est, argumento, non dignitate. & historiam à primo deduxi ad ultimum: initia, cursum, ac totam administrationis tragoediam ostendi: universam illam turbam in treis potissimum libros di-spertiens.
units.tr: So that you may understand the cause which I desire and beg you to defend and support, I ask you to turn your minds away for a little while from your weightier studies and sacred duties, and to direct your attention and thoughts to hear what I have proposed here. The gift I offer is papal and pontifical, that is, in its subject matter, not in its dignity. I have drawn the history from the first to the last: I have shown the beginnings, the course and the whole tragedy of the administration, dividing that whole crowd chiefly into three books.

units.la: Primus, antiquissimos dabit & sanctissimos patres, non pedo, non triplicata mitra insignitos, sed industrios, in vinea Domini excolenda operarios, ad Sylvestrum usque, nimirum ab ipsis inde Apostolis: qui cum vitæ ac sanguinis periculo, plantando & rigando fideliter elaborauerunt. Hi stellæ in dextera Christi permanentes, dici merito potuerunt: Apoc. i. Secundus, mitratos, Archiepiscopos & Patriarchas cotinet, à Sylvestro hoc primo ad Bonifacium tertium, illos quidem non pessimos, nec corruptissimos: qui traditioni bus[?] tamen, aut constitutiunculis humanis, uiā ad Antichristum praestruxerūt. Isti sunt stellae cadentes ad terram: Apoc.6. Tertius habet Papārum farragine, ab hoc Bonifacio ad Paulum quartū, qui nunc uicarius Sathanae, Romae adhuc praesidere dicitur. Fuerunt hi uerē Antichristi, à patris sui uestigijs in omni superbiae, tyrannidis, mendacij, turpitudinisq; genere non recedentes: sidera uideli-cet, ut Apoc.9. describitur, in terram delapsa. Iam & pars haec tertia in quinq; distributa est: nec ineptè ad Ioannis Apocalypsin accommodauimus.
units.tr: The first will give the most ancient and most holy Fathers, not marked with the pallium or the triple mitre, but diligent workers cultivating the vineyard of the Lord, down to Sylvester, namely from the Apostles themselves, who laboured faithfully in planting and watering, at the peril of their lives and blood. These, remaining as stars in the right hand of Christ, could rightly be called so: Rev. 1. The second contains the mitred archbishops and patriarchs, from this first Sylvester to Boniface III: not indeed the worst or most corrupt, yet who, by traditions or petty human constitutions, prepared the way to Antichrist. These are the stars falling to the earth: Rev. 6. The third has a crowd of popes, from this Boniface to Paul IV, who is now said still to preside at Rome as vicar of Satan. These were truly Antichrists, not departing from the footsteps of their father in every kind of pride, tyranny, falsehood and filthiness: stars, clearly, fallen to the earth, as is described in Rev. 9. Now this third part too is divided into five, and we have not inappropriately fitted it to the Apocalypse of John.

units.la: Primum locum occupabit hic merito suo Bonifacius, quem nominauimus, ad Ioannem octauū, meretricem mulierem: in quam partem quadraginta Papas coniecimus, Regnumq;[?] magnae bestiae uocauimus, quod etiam tum Sodoma tum Ægyptus dicitur: Apo. 11. A Ioanne consequenter ad Syluestrū secundū, qui Magus diabolicus erat, & se, obtinendi Papatus causa, Satanae deuouit ac tradidit: quadraginta Papas coplectitur. regnum meretricis magnae, quae sedet super bestiam: Apoc.17. A Syluestro illo, qui tertio loco uenit, ad Innocentium quartum, nocentissimum Christi seruatoris hostem: qui tamen per antiphrasin sic erat dictus, & quatuor Mendicantium monachorum ordines recenter natos firmauit ac roborauit, ut strenuè & pacra nice pro afferendo Antichristi dominatu pugnarent: Regnū draconis manet, qui est diabolus ac Satanas, Apoc.20. & in eo Papæ quadraginta collocātur. Ab illo Innocētio ad Iuliū secundū, qui formidabilissimus bellator extitit, & immitissimus hominū Christianorū peremptor, enumerantur etiā quadraginta Papæ: &Regnum locustarū id erat sub Abaddone, qui perditor nominatur, Apo.9. Iulius autē in huius regni fine, proiectis S.Petri clauibus in Tyberis flumen, rubiginoso Pauli gladio accinctus, in pugnam aduersus Gallū & alios principes Christianos prodijt. Et ita quintus Ordo, capit omnes ab hoc Iulio, usq; ad Pauli quarti finem, per octo Papas, omnium̄sq; posterorum tempora usq; ad Christi iudicis ultionem: & est occasus regni Papistici, sine ui, sine manibus, solo Dei uerbo & flatu diuini spiritus. 2. Thessa. 2. & Dan. 8. In summa, ita historiam hanc totam digessi, ut omnes Romanos episcopos, quatuor equis in Reuelatione Ioannis comparauerim: simplices & candidos, albo equo : Archiepiscopos ac Patriarchas, rufo : Papas & Antichristos ad Syluեstrum secundum, nigro: & ab illo ad Iulium secundum, ac deinceps, cum suis monachorum, fraterculorum & missatorum agminibus, qui ad Papalis regni defensionem, liuore & maleuolētia suffusi, omnibus opibus ac uiribus incūbunt, pallido cōsrens. rens. Hunc ego scopum & Methodum in hoc libello proposui: in quo praeter colligendi, de scribendi, & distribuendi laborem, nihil mi-hi fere uedico. Nam traditum hoc magna ex parte ab aliis scio: ut à Damaso, Carsulano, Platina, Stella, Vuicelio, & alijs: at saepe dissimulanter & obscurè, aliquando falsè, auribus seruiendo: demum à compluribus nostrae & superioris aetatis scriptoribus diligentissimis & fidissimis. Quos cum omnes quot quot reperire potui, diurna nocturnaq; lectione peragrassem, sparsos & nonnunquam dissentientes in unum corpus coegi: ut quod in multis disiectum, lectoribus ad inuestigandū esset difficilius, id comportatū in uno loco ac libello constipatum, & ob oculos expositum, facilius inuenirent. Quod praestitum à quouis alio maluissem quàm à me, & domestica quàm aliena libentius curassem, quoniam in his aetatem consumpsi: hanc uero infinitam Romanae historiae sententiam[?] non mouissem, cui exhauriendae uix duo Hercules pares esse possent.
units.tr: The first place will be rightly occupied by this Boniface, whom we have named, down to John VIII, the harlot woman; into this part we have put forty popes, and we have called it the kingdom of the great beast, which is also called Sodom and Egypt: Rev. 11. Next from John to the second Sylvester, who was a diabolical magician and who, to obtain the papacy, devoted and handed himself over to Satan, it takes in forty popes: the kingdom of the great harlot who sits upon the beast: Rev. 17. From that Sylvester, who came third, to Innocent IV, the most harmful enemy of Christ the Saviour, who nevertheless by antiphrasis was so called, and who strengthened and confirmed the four orders of mendicant monks lately born, so that they might vigorously and sedulously fight to assert the lordship of Antichrist: the kingdom of the dragon remains, who is the devil and Satan, Rev. 20, and in it forty popes are placed. From that Innocent to Julius II, who was a most formidable warrior and the most merciless destroyer of Christian men, forty popes are likewise counted: and it was the kingdom of the locusts under Abaddon, who is called the destroyer, Rev. 9. Julius, moreover, at the end of this kingdom, having cast the keys of St Peter into the river Tiber and girded himself with the rusty sword of Paul, came forth into battle against the French and the other Christian princes. And so the fifth order takes in all from this Julius to the end of Paul IV, through eight popes, and the times of all posterity until the vengeance of the Judge of Christ; and it is the setting of the Papist kingdom, without force, without hands, by the Word of God alone and the breath of the divine Spirit: 2 Thess. 2 and Dan. 8. In sum, I have so arranged this whole history that I have compared all the Roman bishops to the four horses in the Revelation of John: the simple and pure ones, on the white horse, the archbishops and patriarchs, on the red; the popes and Antichrists down to the second Sylvester, on the black; and from him to Julius II and afterwards, with their crowds of monks, friars and couriers, who, suffused with spite and malice, throw themselves with all their resources into the defence of the papal kingdom, on the pale horse. This is the aim and method I have set before myself in this little book. In it, apart from the labour of gathering, writing and arranging, I claim almost nothing for myself. For I know that this material has largely been handed down by others, such as Damasus, Carsulanus, Platina, Stella, Wicel and others; but often covertly and obscurely, sometimes falsely, serving the ears of the powerful; and lastly by many very diligent and faithful writers of our own and the earlier age. When I had gone through all of these whom I could find, by day and by night of reading, I brought together into one body what was scattered and sometimes disagreeing, so that what, dispersed among many places, would be more difficult for readers to track down, they might more easily find gathered together in one place and one book, set before their eyes. I would rather that this had been done by anyone else than by me, and I would more willingly have attended to what is domestic than to what is foreign, since I have spent my life on these matters; but I would not have undertaken this endless opinion of Roman history, which even two Herculeses could scarcely have exhausted.

units.la: Caeterùm quae causae impulerint, accipite. Primùm cohortationes amicorum, huc me, alioqui reluctantem, traxerunt: quòd alterum opus Brytannicum, Anglis proprium, & paucis notum, exteris hominibus parum profuturum iudicarent: hoc adiunctum, bonum fore publicum, ad omnium utilitatem com-modius modius,& ad reliquas res prouidentius. deinde ingressus, perrexi alacrius:&licet alios ad hoc aptiores,& ab eloquentia instructiores, aggredi istuc desiderarem: tamen mihi quoque talenti rationem reddendam censui,& balbutire profecto malui, quàm ut tanta Antichristi nequitia, crudelitas, libido, magis ac magis erumpens, ac fœtore suo omnia opplens, ab omnibus præterita, à paucis aut nullis apertè & plenè detecta uideatur.
units.tr: But hear what moved me. First, the urging of my friends drew me into this work, though I was otherwise reluctant. They judged that the other book, the British one, belonged to the English alone and was known to few, and would be of little use to foreigners. Joined to it, this work would be a common good, more convenient for everyone's use and more useful for the rest of the matter. Then, once I had begun, I went on more eagerly. Although I wished that others, better suited to the task and better equipped in eloquence, had undertaken it, I still thought I must render an account of the talent entrusted to me. I preferred to stammer rather than let such great wickedness, cruelty and lust of Antichrist, breaking out more and more and filling everything with its stench, be passed over by all, and seem to be openly and fully laid bare by few or none.

units.la: Et si eui liberè nimis dicere uidear,cogitet non ab affectus æstu,sed ex conscientiæ scientia proficisci: qui non audita aut lecta tàtum affero,sed comperta:qui ante uiginti quatuor annos, in ea secta uixi, interfui & præfui, Papæ miles non minimus:ubi quid his oculis non uidi? quid his auribus non hausi, indignum Christo, Christianis, Monachis, imò hominibus? A quorum superstitionibus alienus tum non fui, à turpitudine flagitijsq; etiam tum abhorrui. Itaq; quo tum plura sen-si quæ offenderunt, eo nunc cogor esse in scrutando diligentior, in redarguendo acrior, cum non resipiscant. Cum hæc à grege isto facta sint & fuerint, in Italia, Sicilia, Hispania, Gallia, Anglia: quis dubitet oues suum pastorem, uel sues subulcum potius suum fuisse sequutos? An non ex prole sæpe parentem, ex unguibus leonem æstimabimus? Cum claustra his fœditatibus plena sint, Curiam Romanam uacuam existimabimus? Multa in latebris ac tenebris latére potuerunt, quæ sol non uidit: tempus iam ueritatis mater, diru-tis in Anglia monasterijs, loqui didicit & pro-dere. Exemplo sunt Regiarum uisitationum registra, uel, ut illi uocant, Compendia com-pertorum in ipsis Papistarum cœnobijs & collegijs: quæ cum horrore tunc uidi, nunc autem habeo, atq; ad eorum ignominiam ser-uo: quorum aliqua in sequenti ad Lectorem epistola exhibui. Si Ezechiel modò perfode-ret parietem, introductusq; in uestibula, a-tria & cubicula istorum abscondita, esset: nō ibi Israelitas plangentes Thamnur, sed castra tos cœlibes, sanctitatis professione spectabi-les, Baal Peor, Baccho, Veneri litantes cerne-ret. Hæc ego cum explorata habeam, non e-ruerem: non orbi perspicua ac testata facerē? Homo nimirum, inquiunt, ortus à toto diuisis orbe Brytannis, nouit scilicet quæ Romæ geruntur in Papæ ac cardinalium conclaui-bus. Quæ libri loquuntur, quæ testes oculati scriptis mandarunt, quæ non secreta cubicu-la, sed aula Romana, quę nō anguli, sed platee clamāt pro certis non reserā? Sed nec ipsi ne-gāt, sed defendunt, etiā mõstrosis lingua sua editis libellis, quæ me pudor Christianus haud finit eloqui. Veritas ergo euolare de-bet, non personis aut laruis obtecta, sed spe-cia sua exposita: non pallio aut uelo obscura-ta,
units.tr: And if I seem to speak too freely, let the reader consider that I do not speak from the heat of feeling but from the knowledge of my own conscience. I bring forward not only things heard or read but things I have learned by experience. For twenty-four years before now I lived in that sect, took part in it and held office in it, no small soldier of the Pope. What did I not see with these eyes? What did I not hear with these ears, unworthy of Christ, of Christians, of monks, indeed of men? I was not then a stranger to their superstitions, and I shrank even then from their baseness and disgraceful conduct. Therefore, the more I then perceived many things that offended me, the more I am now forced to be careful in searching them out and sharper in rebuking them, since they do not repent. Since these things have been and are done by that flock in Italy, Sicily, Spain, France and England, who would doubt that the sheep followed their shepherd, or rather that the swine followed their swineherd? Shall we not judge the parent often by the offspring, the lion by his claws? When the cloisters are full of these foul deeds, shall we think the Roman Curia is free of them? Many things may have lain hidden in lurking places and darkness, which the sun has not seen. Now the time has come, the mother of truth, since the monasteries in England have been torn down, and she has learned to speak and to reveal. The registers of the royal visitations are an example, or, as they call them, the Compendia of the findings in the very monasteries and colleges of the Papists. I saw these then with horror, and now I possess them, and I keep them for their shame; I have displayed some of them in the following epistle to the Reader. If Ezekiel were only to dig through the wall and be brought into the porches, the inner rooms and the hidden chambers of these men, he would see there not Israelites weeping for Tammuz, but celibates, conspicuous for their profession of holiness, sacrificing to Baal-Peor, to Bacchus and to Venus. Since I have these things well established, should I not dig them out and make them plain and attested to the whole world? "A man," they say, "born in Britain, cut off from the whole world, of course knows what goes on in Rome in the conclaves of the Pope and the cardinals." But what the books say, what eyewitnesses have committed to writing, what the Roman court proclaims, not in secret chambers but in the palace, what the streets cry out, not the corners, as certain facts that cannot be denied? Yet they do not deny them but defend them, even with monstrous little books published in their own tongue, which Christian modesty does not allow me to name. Truth therefore ought to fly forth, not hidden under masks or veils, but with its own features set out: not obscured by a cloak or a veil, but shown with its natural face and colour.

units.la: [?] Reading uncertain in several places: "diuisis" (line 20, word split across lines), "platee", "exposita", "tos". ta, sed facie & colore suo natiuo exhibita. Crassa enim sunt, palpari manibus possunt: Et tamē adhuc stupor hominum tantus est, ut in luce plus quàm meridiana oculos non habeant, sed noctem in oculis circumferant in sole clarissimo.
units.tr: For these things are thick and can be felt with the hands. And yet the stupidity of men is still so great that, in a light brighter than noon, they have no eyes, but carry night in their eyes in the brightest sun.

units.la: Exemplum huius rei, nimirum familiare ac intestinum, est Anglia nostra misera: cuius etiam causa ad scribendum accessi libentius, ut Angli mei uideant, nunc saltem, quale bel luam in Rempublicam adduxerint, quam uiperam in sinu foueat: cuius ante sibilum ferre non poterat, ab eo nunc tributis pungi, & morderi exactionibus, ac ueneno idololatrico intoxicari se patiutur. Cui tot reges, maiores nobilissimi, non semel restiterunt: quem Vuicleuus primus ac pijssimus, ut Antichristu, sui seculi hominibus, scriptis reuelauit: quem Rex Henricus Octauus expulit, quem Eduuardus Sextus diuinus Rex cum omnibus reliquijs ac tota sece Papismi eiecit: hunc Regina Maria subito recepit, intrusore Polo: multis parum uidentibus, pluribus connivientibus, omnibus prope ferentibus, uel saltem affectione uaria turpiter applaudētibus. Miseret me patriae, quae sic defectione sua Deum optimum max. offendit, uiolatis etiā iuramentis Regibus antea factis: ut nutui & imperio nouo, monstrofo, crudelissimo scelestissimi Antichristi, iusto Dei iudicio, seruire cogatur & subiacere: sub quo, idolomanico iugo premi, superstitione & hoc Satanico Patu occæcari,in bello turpiter quouis leuissimo hostiū appulsa cadere mereatur. Quam tamen stante & florente religione, occidente & emarcescente Papismo, nec manus Dei magnopere afflixit, nec hominum externa uis, uel oppugnare ausa est: uel si oppugnarit, expugnare non potuit. Hæc cum dolore dico, Reuerendissimi Patres eoç[?] magis,quod causam harum plagarum, uerbi diuini contemptum & Romanarum sordium illuuiem esse interpretor:quod Christo profligato,Papam hunc totius mundi fascinum & Circen,non seruum seruorum, sed dominum omnium dominorum,non Christi uicarium,sed diaboli ministrum,nostro capiti & ceruicibus insultare maluerimus, quam Christi suauc[?] iugū, onus leue,iucundissimā crucem exosculari. Et hæc apud uos hoc tempore queror, sanctissimi uiri :ut præsentem hanc calamitatem,non leuem causam, quæ me ad hoc incitaret, fuisse intelligatis: utcunque per uiscera misericordiæ in Christo Iesu uos obtestor,ut quod facitis,pergatis facere: pro Anglia,quæ pro se orare non potest,orare uelitis:quo Papa hic ex animis Christianorum, Italorum,Hispanorum,Gallorum,Anglorū, omnium exemptus, è regnis & Ecclesijs deturbatus, rumpatur medius, & pereat. O-rate, sate,ut cæci uideant, surdi audiant, sedentes in tenebris ac umbra mortis ad lucem & agnitionem ueritatis emergant. Plus.n. apud De-um efficient ueftrę preces, quàm omnium Paparum benedictiones aut maledictiones.
units.tr: An example of this, familiar and close to home, is our wretched England. I have come more willingly to write about her cause, so that my fellow Englishmen may now at least see what a beast they have brought into the commonwealth, what a viper they have nursed in their bosom. Before, they could not bear its hissing; now they suffer themselves to be stung by its taxes, bitten by its exactions, and poisoned with its idolatrous venom. Many kings and the noblest of our ancestors have resisted it more than once. Wycliffe, the first and most pious, revealed it in his writings to the men of his age as Antichrist. King Henry VIII drove it out. Edward VI, the godly king, cast it out together with all its remnants and the whole brood of Popery. Queen Mary suddenly took it back again, with Pole as the intruder. Many looked on with little sight, more with connivance, nearly all bore it, or at least shamefully applauded it, each with their own varied affections. I pity my country, which has so offended God, the best and greatest, by its defection, even breaking the oaths previously sworn to its kings, that by the just judgment of God it is compelled to serve and submit to the new, monstrous and most cruel rule of the most wicked Antichrist, under an idolatrous yoke, blinded by superstition and by this Satanic fog, and deserves to fall shamefully in war to the slightest blow of its enemies. Yet while religion stood and flourished, and Popery was dying and withering, neither did the hand of God greatly afflict it, nor did the external force of men dare to attack it, or if it did attack, it could not overcome it. I say these things with grief, most reverend Fathers, and all the more because I judge the cause of these blows to be the contempt of the divine Word and the filth of Roman foulness. Because Christ has been put to flight, we have preferred that this Pope, the bewitcher and Circe of the whole world, who is not the servant of servants but the lord of lords, not the vicar of Christ but the minister of the devil, should trample upon our head and necks, rather than embrace the sweet yoke of Christ, his light burden and most pleasant cross. I make this complaint before you now, most holy men, so that you may understand that this present calamity was not a slight cause that stirred me to this task. Still, I beseech you by the bowels of mercy in Christ Jesus, that you continue what you are doing, and that you be willing to pray for England, which cannot pray for itself. Let this Pope, freed from the minds of Christians, Italians, Spaniards, French and English, all of them, be cast down from the kingdoms and churches, be torn asunder and perish. Pray, speak, so that the blind may see, the deaf hear, and those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death may rise to the light and knowledge of the truth. For your prayers will accomplish more with God than all the blessings or curses of all the Popes.

units.la: Ex his credo uos intelligere, uiri præstantissimi, quid potissimum in manus sumpserim, & quibus de causis. Permouit enim primum amicorum uoluntas, tum conscientia mea huc currentem incitauit: ut quæ uel auditione, uel oculis hausissem, in hoc ætatis decursu communicarem. Postremò uocauit huc luctuosa rerum Anglicarum facies: ut pro pietate, qua deuinctus sum fratribus, opem afferam: ut lectis & cognitis Romanæ tyrannidis initijs, & origine, tum singulorum Paparum singulari turpitudine, meliorem uiam quærant: tum ad dignitatem Reipublicæ amissam recuperandam, tum ad Ecclesiæ restaurationem, & Christi unici in terris supremi capitis gloriam.
units.tr: From these things I believe you understand, most excellent men, what I have chiefly taken in hand and for what reasons. First, the wish of my friends moved me, and then my own conscience urged me, running hither, to share in the course of my life what I had heard or seen. Finally, the sorrowful state of English affairs called me here, so that by the devotion with which I am bound to my brothers I might bring help: so that, once the beginnings and origin of Roman tyranny have been read and understood, and then the singular baseness of each individual Pope, they might seek a better way, both to recover the lost dignity of the commonwealth and to restore the Church and the glory of Christ, the only supreme head on earth.

units.la: Vobis autem non fine causa offero, nostræ ætatis principibus, & Christianæ fidei defensoribus: qui idem onus laboriosum & odiosum sustinetis, & eandem ob causam eodem inuidiæ conflagratis incendio. Equidem loquor quod sentio, & quod credo: & quia credo, non possum non loqui. Si Vuitembergæ Lutherus, Christianæ doctrinæ Atlas; Tiguri Zuinglius, inuictus purę ueritatis pro[?] pugnator,& ad sanguinem ufq; professor:Ba-ileq[?] Oecolampadius, in domo Dei lumen & lampas, uiuos scripturæ fontes non aperuis-sent,apertos à Philistinorum audacia non tu-tati fuissent: si alij illis temporibus in his lo-cis uestris,humeris suis religionem nostram non fulciuissent, si uos succenturiari & suc-currere noluissetis, si uobis Dominus semen ueritatis in Ecclesijs,quibus uos & uicini ue-stri præsidetis,non reliquisset:nullum habe-ret in terris nidum Christus,ubi caput recli-naret: nullus esset Christi exulibus portus, quo profugerent:nullum domicilium Chri-stiana pietas haberet,in quo confirmari iasta ta,& consistere agitata posset.Et q; ad me nūc attinet,à uestris ecclesijs & scriptoribus fere didici,quod hic doceo:itaq; par fuerit,si fru-ctus aliqua pars ad eos cum fœnore aliquo redeat,unde acceperim. Nec solum Ecclesias uestras colo & ueneror,ut fontes purę religi-onis, qui occultis meatibus ad omnes orbis angulos,ad nos etiam ultra Oceanū emana-runt:sed uobis quoq;,humanissimi uiri,seorsim Angli omnes peregrini,uestris summis in nosbeneficijs,sumus deuinctissimi.Quod ego omnium meorum nomine, arrepta hac occasione pluribus ostederem[?]:nisi apud uos, quibus obligamur, agerem:nihil tamen dicere, & silentio præterire omnia, profecto non potero.Itaq; date uenia,& affectui meo igno-scat. siat & sedat modestia uestra, dum ex omni-bus pauca decerpo, quo reliqui intelligant, an iusta causa nobis fuerit hoc Opus quale-cunq;, uobis prae caeteris inscribendi. Quod dum breuiter narro, ut locorū situs & ordo monet:ita quemcq; uestrûm in orationem uo-cabo, non dignitatis uestrae rationem ha-bens, sed imbecillitati memoriae meę & per-spicuitati rei seruiens.
units.tr: I offer this to you, not without cause, as leaders of our age and defenders of the Christian faith. You bear the same laborious and hateful burden, and for the same reason you burn in the same fire of ill will. Indeed I speak what I feel and what I believe, and because I believe, I cannot but speak. If Luther at Wittenberg, the Atlas of Christian doctrine; Zwingli at Zurich, the unconquered champion of pure truth and a confessor even unto blood; and Oecolampadius at Basel, the light and lamp in the house of God, had not opened the living fountains of Scripture, and if, having been opened, they had not been protected against the audacity of the Philistines; if others in those times in these your places had not supported our religion on their shoulders; if you had not been unwilling to be reserves and to come to help; if the Lord had not left in your churches, over which you and your neighbours preside, the seed of truth: Christ would have no nest on earth where he might lay his head; there would be no harbour for exiled Christians to flee to; Christian piety would have no dwelling in which it could be confirmed in what it has received and in which it could stand when shaken. And as far as I am concerned now, I have learned from your churches and writers nearly all that I teach here. So it would be fitting, if some part of the fruit returns to those from whom I received it, with some interest added. Nor do I only honour and revere your churches as fountains of pure religion, which by hidden channels have flowed to every corner of the world, even to us beyond the Ocean. I am also most deeply bound to you, most kind men, and all we Englishmen as strangers are bound by your great kindnesses toward us. I would gladly show this to many more, seizing this occasion, on behalf of all of mine. Yet unless I spoke to you, to whom we are obligated, I could not, indeed, say nothing and pass over everything in silence. So pardon me, and let your modesty excuse my feeling. I shall pick out only a few things from all, so that the rest may understand whether there was a just cause for us to dedicate this work, of whatever quality it is, to you before others. While I speak of this briefly, as the order and arrangement of the places advises, so I shall call each of you into the discourse, not taking account of your dignity, but serving the weakness of my memory and the clarity of the matter.

units.la: Vt ergo a primo ordiar, & a remotissimis ad uiciniora ascendam, quantum Vuitem-bergae, pulcherrimae omnium bonarum ar-tium mercaturae debeamus, non dissimulas hi, qui eō se uisendi & studendi gratia contu-lerunt. Quorum magnificis laudibus multi commoti, frequentes uenirent, si ad tantam itineris longinquitatem emetiendam, ut uo-luntas, sic facultas suppeteret. Nam cum reli-quos doctos nō fine grata multorum erga se meritorū testificatione collaudant: tum Phi-lippe, tuam comitatem singularem, facilita-tem miram, obuiā & paratissimam bene me rendi uoluntatem praedicant. Nec id abs re. Nam & domi omni humanitatis genere pro sequeris, & foris etiam praedicatione tua li-teris amantissimis luctates saepe & fluctuā-tes subleuas. Non enim obscurū est, quid a-pud Vuefalienfem senatum Anglorum no-mine egeris. Qui cum eos religionis ergo la-borare, & hominum quorundam contrā sententium iniustis vociferationibus non- nihil exagitari intelligeres: causam disceptationibus ventilandam, non clamoribus & si- bilis explodendam censuisti: homines reti- nendos & releuandos, non asperiori aliqua sententia affligendos aut vexados iudicasti. In hanc sententiam etiam ad Francofortenses ma- gistratus scripsisti, ut ex literis tuis, quasmihi videre contigit, subodoratus sum: ubi nostros omnibus articulis Christianæ confessionis pure sentientes, & in controuersijs aliquot zeli feruore & natura quadam sua, opinionem suam tuentes: docendos, non opprimendos: colloquio admonendos, non vi extur- bandos, cum res dubiæ obscuris verbis ab aduersario parte tractatę sint, existimasti. Nec dubito, quin cæterę quoq; ciuitates finitimę, Argentina, Basilea, Arouia, Tigurum, Gene- ua, Emdona, tam illustri testimonio tuo ex- citatæ, suo nos fauore magis dignentur: & ue- risimile est, ad earum in nos propensionem, vel commendatione tua tanta, vel aperta hæc comprobatione, cumulum non minimum accessisse.
units.tr: So that I may begin at the beginning and climb from the most distant things to those nearer at hand: how much we owe to Wittenberg, the finest marketplace of all the good arts, is no secret to those who have gone there to see and to study. Many, moved by its glowing praises, would come there often, if their ability matched their will to travel so great a distance. For while they commend the other learned men, not without the grateful testimony of many to their merits, they proclaim your singular courtesy, Philip, your wonderful readiness, and your eagerness to do good to whoever meets you. Nor without reason. For at home you show every kind of kindness, and abroad too, by your advocacy, you often relieve those who struggle and waver amid the most bitter controversies. It is no secret what you did on behalf of the English before the Westphalian senate. When you understood that they were suffering for religion and were somewhat harassed by the unjust clamours of certain men who held other views, you judged that the cause should be aired in debate, not driven off by shouting and hissing; that men should be kept and raised up, not afflicted or harassed by some harsher sentence. You wrote to the magistrates of Frankfurt to the same effect, as I have gathered from your letter, which I chanced to see. There you judged that our men, who hold pure views on every article of the Christian confession, but who in some disputed points, through the heat of zeal and a certain nature of their own, defend their opinion, should be taught, not crushed; should be admonished by conference, not driven out by force, since the matters in doubt had been handled by the opposing side in obscure words. I do not doubt that the other neighbouring cities, Strasbourg, Basel, Aarau, Zurich, Geneva, and Emden, stirred by your so illustrious testimony, will think us more worthy of their favour; and it is likely that to their goodwill towards us a not small addition has come, either from your so great recommendation or from this open approval.

units.la: Cæterum relicta Vuitemberga, Basileam migrabo, ubi parcior ero: non quod non habeam quod laudem copiosissimè, sed quod pars sim eorum qui senatus, ministrorum & populi totius benevolentiam, & sensi hactenus, & indies sentio: hæc non tam gratus laudator,
units.tr: But having left Wittenberg, I shall move on to Basel, where I shall be more sparing. Not that I lack things to praise at length, but because I am one of those who have felt, and do feel daily, the goodwill of the whole senate, the ministers and the people; and so I fear I may seem less a grateful praiser

units.la: dator, quàm blandus adulator esse videar. Nihil itaque hoc tempore de te dicam, Sulcere, humanissime & eruditissime uir: nihil de D. Vuolfgango Vuissenburgio, theologo ual de eximio, et Academiæ rectore clarissimo: nihil de Martino Borrhao, professore tecu theologiæ dignissimo: nihil de optimo & doctissimo Domino Ioanne Iunio, symmista & colega tuo meritissimo: Marco Berfio, Iacobo Truckenbroto, Conrado Lycosthene amico suauissimo, Huldricho Coccio, Thoma Gyrenfalcko, Ioanne Ibelhardo, Sebastiano Leupusculo, Seuerino Erimontano, Ioanne Maxdero, & Ioanne Brandmillero, aliisq; diuini uerbi ministris, quorum officijs quotidianis afficimur: molestias, quas nō sine labore, aut sine dolore & murmure uestro promptissimè fertis, prætermitto. Hoc tantum dicam, multitudinis atq; magistratuum studia, pro se quidem satis accensa: conciionibus tamen uestris & crebris interpellationibus magis inflammari, ut ferè quicquid ab illis in nos benignitatis profectum est, uestro rogatu & impulsu magna ex parte ortum natumq; uideatur. Sed hic, ut dixi, breuitati studeo: quia ex illis sum qui experiuntur, & in aliena cau sa uersor lubentius. Tiguri & Geneuæ diutius hærebo.
units.tr: than a fawning flatterer. So at this time I will say nothing of you, Sulzer, most kind and learned man; nothing of Doctor Wolfgang Wissenburg, a truly outstanding theologian and most distinguished rector of the Academy; nothing of Martin Borrhaus, a professor of theology most worthy to be ranked with you; nothing of the excellent and learned Johann Jung, your deserving colleague and fellow-worker; nothing of Marcus Berus, Jacob Truckenbrot, Conrad Lycosthenes, my most agreeable friend, Ulrich Coccius, Thomas Gyrenfalck, Johann Ibelhardt, Sebastian Leupuscul, Severin Erimontanus, Johann Maxder, and Johann Brandmiller, and the other ministers of the divine Word, by whose daily services we are affected. The troubles which you bear readily, and not without labour, or without pain and grumbling on your part, I pass over. I will say only this: the zeal of the crowd and of the magistrates, though already sufficiently kindled on their own account, is rather inflamed by your sermons and your frequent intercessions, so that nearly whatever kindness has come to us from them seems, for the most part, to have arisen and been born at your request and prompting. But here, as I said, I aim at brevity, since I am one of those who have had experience of such things, and I dwell more willingly on another's cause. I shall linger longer at Zurich and Geneva.

units.la: Tigurum enim omnium semper profugorum tegumentum, & doctissimorum Theologorum logorum Academia quędam pulcherrima, & schola celebratissima, latissimum mihi campum aperit, in quo mea expacietur & excurrat oratio, siue communia omnium getium cōmoda spectare uelim, siue Anglorum propria. Quod enim ibi orbis Christiani uelut oraculum? qualis doctissimorum hominum chorus? Nam ut de te, Bullingēre, taceam: quē tot monumenta librorum pietate rara, doctrina multiplici, rerumq; omnium uarietate, ueterumq; scriptorum sententijs uelut stellis ornatorum, satis catholicæ Ecclesiæ, me silente, iam diu commendarunt. ut reliquos Tiguri indigenas & alumnos prætereeam: Bibliandrum illum, Hippiam omniscium: Rodolphum Gualtherum, concionatorem facundissimum, & scriptorem politissimum: Conradum Gesnerum, quandam uelut omnium disciplinarum bibliothecam, amicum meum singularem: Iosiam Simlerum, & Ioannem Vuolphium, uiros etiam doctissimos & amicos candidissimos, reliquosq; profesores aliarum artium insignes prætermittam: Deum immortalem quales illi duo senes peregrini, quos in urbem uestram recepistis, D. Petrus Martyr, & Bernardinus Ochinus? quæ duo lumina? Quorum alterutrum si aliæ haberent Ecclesiæ, magno thesauro & ornamento ditatæ & beatæ uiderentur. Fœlix Anglia, dum hæc paria [?]ia habuit: misera, quæ amisit. Huius Eccle-siæ antistes cum sis, doctissime vir, merito te patronum elegi, cuius authoritate Romana curia labefieri, mea descriptio stabiliri possit. qui si hos duces nobilissimos, milites fortissimos, cum copijs instructissimis in acies puluereműq; velis euocare: cohortes ac tur-mas Papæ universas facile primo quoque tempore, legitimo congressu fuderis. Sed hęc ut communia, & nota, aliis committo: quæ in nostros Anglos contulerit Tigurum, cum hoc meo instituto proprium fit, illud alie-num: illud relinquam, hoc attingam, sed breuius. Cū enim apud vos essem, & tuam, Bul-lingere, hospitalitatem, aliorumq; humanitatem degustassem: intellexi, quo studio nostros, qui vobiscum sunt & fuerunt, complectamini. Commemorauit vir optimus, & meliori fortuna dignior, Ioannes Park-hurstus, quot nominibus tibi, Domino Gualtero, ac universæ ciuitati debeat. Commemo-rant & hic qui mecum quotidie sunt Basi-leæ; curam, solicitudinem, & paternum erga se affectum tuum, dum apud vos coniun-ctim unis in ædibus sub vestrę ciuitatis um-braculo, contra persecutionis æstum prote-sti, magno cum consensu & amore ciuium, degerent. Commemorant & magistratu-um incredibilem munificentiam: qui per te subsidia vitæ, & frumēti & vini, quantū tredę aut quatuordecim sustentandis satis esset, liberalissimè obtulerunt: & cum accipere recusassent, gratificandi opportunitatem defuisse doluerunt.
units.tr: For Zurich, the shelter of all exiles and a most beautiful academy of most learned theologians, and a most celebrated school, opens to me a very broad field, in which my discourse may range and run freely, whether I wish to regard the common advantages of all nations or the particular ones of the English. For what oracle of the Christian world is there, and what a chorus of most learned men! To say nothing of you, Bullinger, whom so many monuments of books, rare in piety, manifold in learning, varied in all matters, and adorned with the opinions of the ancient writers as with stars, have long since, even in my silence, commended well enough to the Catholic Church. I pass over the other natives and pupils of Zurich: that Bibliander, a Hippias in universal knowledge; Rudolf Gwalther, a most eloquent preacher and most polished writer; Conrad Gesner, as it were a library of all the disciplines, my singular friend; Josias Simler and Johann Wolf, also most learned men and most candid friends; and the remaining distinguished professors of the other arts. Good God, what manner of men were those two old pilgrims whom you received into your city, Doctor Peter Martyr and Bernardino Ochino? What two lights! If other churches had either of them, they would seem enriched and blessed with a great treasure and ornament. Happy England, while she had these equals; wretched, since she has lost them. Since you are the bishop of this Church, learned man, I have rightly chosen you as my patron, by whose authority the Roman curia might be overthrown and my account be established. If you were willing to summon these most noble leaders and most brave soldiers, with their most fully equipped forces, into the battle line and the dust, you could easily rout all the cohorts and squadrons of the Pope in a lawful engagement at the first opportunity. But these things, being common and well known, I leave to others. What Zurich has contributed to our English men, since it belongs to my own undertaking, while the other is foreign to it: that I shall leave aside, though I shall touch upon it, but more briefly. For when I was with you, Bullinger, and had tasted your hospitality and that of the others, I understood with what zeal you embrace our people who are and have been with you. The excellent man John Parkhurst, more worthy of a better fortune, recalled how many debts he owes to you, to Master Gwalther, and to the whole city. Those who are with me daily at Basel also recall your care, concern, and paternal affection towards them, while they lived together with you under one roof, sheltered in the shade of your city against the heat of persecution, with great goodwill and love from the citizens. They also recall the incredible generosity of the magistrates, who through you most liberally offered the means of living, of grain and wine, enough to sustain thirteen or fourteen men; and when they refused to accept, they grieved that the opportunity to show kindness had been lacking.

units.la: Verum nunc Geneuam propero: de qua si longam oratione sumerem, cum omnia dixissem, vix dimidiam tamen partem eorum quæ dici possunt, videbor assequutus. Admiror in ea eximiam Dei nostri providentiam, qui civium & magistratuum animos sic excitaverit, ut tot peregrinorum millia in urbis suæ non ita lata pomœria, non vereantur recipere: rursus ita corda peregrinorum flexerit, ut cum numero plures sint & superiores, potestate tamen ut inferiores se gerere voluerint, ut se nō cives & dominos, sed privatos & peregrinos agnoscant.
units.tr: But now I hasten to Geneva. If I were to take up a long discourse about it, though I had said everything, I would seem to have reached scarcely half of what can be said. I marvel there at the remarkable providence of our God, who has so stirred the minds of the citizens and magistrates that they do not hesitate to receive so many thousands of strangers within the not so wide boundaries of their city; and again has so bent the hearts of the strangers that, though they are more and superior in number, they have wished to conduct themselves as inferiors in power, acknowledging themselves not as citizens and masters, but as private persons and strangers.

units.la: Fingant alii alia miracula, mihi sanè Geneva mundi miraculum videtur miraculosissimum: tot undiq; et huc tanquā ad asylum concurrere, non ut ditescant, sed ut egeant: non ut saturentur, sed ut esuriant: non ut fœliciores, sed ut miseri fiant: non ut bona servent, sed ut amittant. Multi ad lucra mercatores confluunt, ad prædas milites, ad commoda comparanda omnes: sed ad famem à saturitate, ad laborem à quiete, à splendore fortunarum ad ignominiosam mundo paupertatem confugere, monstri ac prodigii simile videri debet. Hæc nova Lu-tetia, aut Londinum, novum negotiationis emporium,nouū sanè Francofortū:ad quod conuolant,nō ad quæstum faciendū, non ad merces emendas,aut ad cauponandū: sed ad patiendū,ad perdendū, ad cōmutandum cœ-lestia nimirū cū terrenis,ut pro humanis the-sauris,diuinos sibi in cœlo reponant. Consules ab aratro ad fasces peruenisse legimus: sed à florente fortuna, à summis opib. & di-gnitatib. ad rastros,ad fodinas,artes, muros, id est,ab equis ad asinos,à tribunali(quod a-iunt)ad remos, uidentes & uolentes descen-dere, nonne miraculū est ? Nonne miraculū est, Hispanos,Italos, Scotos, Anglos, Gallos, Germanos,tot nationes domi moribus,lin-gua,uestitu,animis dispares : nimirum oues & lupos, tauros & ursos,uno Christi iugo co-pulatos, amantissimè & coniunctissimè ui-uere? Monachos,laicos & Monachas,uitæ se-stæq; professione ac titulis dissentientes,quāsi unum cœnobiu spirituale & Christianū, sensibus cōgruentibus, inhabitare? una regu-gula, unis claustris uti & ceremonijs ? An nō miraculū est, tot hostibus potentissimis un-dequaq; imminentibus & inhiantibus,Sata-na, Papa, mundo infrementibus : tot omniū odio laborantes,nō tutos modò esse, sed etiā securos tanto tempore? Gratiæ itaq; Deo op-timo maximo habendæ sunt, qui te Caluine huius dissipati gregis pastorem,exulum du-cem, caput calamitosorū, eo loco constituit: tuius moderatione, consilio, prudentia, tanta populorum frequentia, non diuersa solū, sed contraria, amabili charitatis vinculo coaluerit: ut jam nihil illis inimicis amantius, nihil illa dissimilitudine similius, nihil deniq; illis miseris beatius inveniri uspiam aut cōspici posit. Gratias etiam hoc scripto meo tibi agere volui, communi omnium causa: cum domi in patria, nostri Deum colere pu-rè, ut vellent, nequeant: per te Ecclesiam aperire liceat, cœtumq; celebrare, in quo Patrem suum libertate summa in vocent, sacramenta syncerè administrarent, cæterisq; ritibus tam quam cives priuilegio quodam & summo fa uore magistratuum defungantur. O beatum populum cui hęc sunt, & cui talis contigit Episcopus, qui dispersos congreget, fractos & contusos consoletur, teneris & recentibus ad huc exulibus indulgeat, & infirmiores exemplo doctrinaq; confirmet.
units.tr: Let others invent other miracles; to me Geneva certainly seems the most miraculous miracle of the world: that so many from everywhere should run together here, as to a refuge, not to grow rich but to be needy, not to be filled but to hunger, not to become happier but to become wretched, not to keep their goods but to lose them. Many merchants flock together for gain, soldiers for plunder, all for the acquiring of advantages; but to flee from plenty to hunger, from labour to rest, from the splendour of fortune to a poverty shameful in the eyes of the world, must seem like a monster or a portent. Is this a new Paris, or London, a new mart of trade, a new Frankfurt indeed, to which they flock, not to make a profit, not to buy goods or to trade, but to suffer, to lose, and to exchange, namely heavenly things for earthly ones, so that in exchange for human treasures they may lay up divine ones for themselves in heaven? We read that consuls came from the plough to the fasces; but to go down, from flourishing fortune, from the highest wealth and dignities, to the rake, the mines, the crafts, the walls, that is, from horses to asses, from the tribunal, as they say, to the oars, seeing and willingly, is this not a miracle? Is it not a miracle that Spaniards, Italians, Scots, English, French, and Germans, so many nations differing at home in customs, language, dress, and temper, lambs and wolves, bulls and bears, yoked together under the one yoke of Christ, should live most lovingly and most closely united? That monks, laymen, and nuns, differing in the profession of life, in sex, and in titles, should dwell as if in one spiritual and Christian monastery, with agreeing minds, using one rule, one cloister, and one set of ceremonies? Is it not a miracle that, with so many most powerful enemies pressing and gaping at them from every side, Satan, the Pope, and the world raging against them, and labouring under the hatred of all, they have been not only safe but even secure for so long a time? Therefore thanks must be given to God, best and greatest, who has placed you, Calvin, in that position as the minister of this scattered flock, the leader of the exiles, the head of the afflicted; through whose moderation, counsel, and prudence such a crowd of peoples, not only different but opposed, has been joined together by the lovely bond of charity, so that nothing can be found or seen anywhere more loving to those enemies, more like to them in their unlikeness, and finally more blessed for those wretched people. I also wished to give thanks to you in this my writing, on behalf of the common cause of us all: since at home in our country our people cannot worship God purely as they wish; I would that through you it were permitted to open a church and gather an assembly, in which they might call upon their Father with the greatest freedom, administer the sacraments sincerely, and discharge the other rites like citizens, by a certain privilege and the greatest favour of the magistrates. O happy people, to whom these things belong, and to whom such a bishop has fallen, who gathers the scattered, comforts the broken and bruised, shows indulgence to the tender and recent exiles, and strengthens the weaker by example and teaching!

units.la: Cæterum nimis multa ad te fortasis, imò ad vos omnes, humanissimi viri: qui & gravioribus rebus impediti estis, quàm ut istas laudes vacet legere: & animo eo ac modestia præditi, ut vix velitis attendere. Sed ferte me, dum officium meum facio: dum non vos, sed dona Dei in vobis prædico: dum Ecclesiarū vestrarum statum beatissimum omnibus commendo fidelibus: ut gratias agere & admirari discant, & imitari. Ostendere volui causas, quibus adductus, hanc nouę Romę Papalem historiam uestro nomini inscripserim: partim ut gratam animi significationem de tot uestris in nostram gentem, imò omnes bene ficijs ederem: partim ut eam doctrinam à uobis, his temporibus propagatam, uestro patrocinio tuendam iterum atq; iterum commendarem. Dominus IESVS CHRISTVS, pastorum princeps, omnis ueritatis magister, & Antichristi hostis, Spiritus sancti fortitudine uos reliquos-q; cooperarios roboret ac confirmet, & uitam ad multos annos incolumem conseruet, ad gregis Christiani consolationem & salutem, ad Antichristianorum euersionem, & ad sui nominis amplificationem,
units.tr: Perhaps there is too much here for you, most gentle gentlemen, or rather for all of you: you are burdened with weightier matters than to find time to read these praises, and you are of such a mind and modesty that you would scarcely wish to pay them any heed. But bear with me while I do my duty, while I proclaim not you but the gifts of God in you, while I commend the most blessed state of your churches to all the faithful, so that they may learn to give thanks, to wonder, and to imitate. I wished to set out the reasons that led me to dedicate this Papal history of the new Rome to your name: partly to make a grateful acknowledgement of so many of your benefits toward our nation, indeed toward all people, and partly to commend again and again to your protection the doctrine that has been spread by you in these times. May the Lord Jesus Christ, chief Shepherd, teacher of all truth, and foe of Antichrist, strengthen and confirm you and the rest of our fellow workers by the power of the Holy Spirit, and preserve your lives unharmed for many years, for the comfort and salvation of the Christian flock, for the overthrow of the Antichristians, and for the enlargement of his own name,
Amen.
Psal. 136.

units.la: Filia Babylonis miseră: beatus qui retribuet tibi retributionem tuam, quam retribuisti nobis. Beatus qui tenebit, & allidet paruulos tuos ad petram.
units.tr: Daughter of Babylon, wretched one: blessed is he who shall repay you the recompense you have paid to us. Blessed is he who shall take and dash your little ones against the rock.
Apoc. 18.

units.la: In una die uenient plagæ eius, mors & luctus, & fames, & igne comburetur: quia fortis est Dominus Deus, qui iudicabit illam.
units.tr: In one day her plagues shall come, death and mourning and famine, and she shall be burned with fire: for the Lord God is strong, who shall judge her.
Baptista Mantuanus, in the third book of the Alphonsus.

units.la: Quicquid apud superos thalami sine teste siletꝝ[?] Deliquere, patet: nec habent uelamina culpæ. Cuncta aperit secreta dies: ex tempore uerum Nascitur, & ueniens ætas abscondita pandit.
units.tr: Whatever sins are committed in the bridal chamber without a witness lie open before the gods above, and they have no veil of guilt. Day uncovers all secrets; the truth is born with time, and the coming age brings hidden things to light.
Matth. 10.
Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed.
JOHN BALE to the Reader

units.la: ROGO te, Christiane lector, quisquis es cui Christi gloria aduersus Antichristi malignitates cordi sit, & hortor in Dño:ut omnia, etiā quæ acerbius in tā immane Bestiam dicta uideantur, in meliorem partem interpretari uelis, nō calumnijs interuertere; quemadmodū iam in Opere, de Scriptoribus Brytanniæ nuper edito, fieri à quibusdam intellexi. Quorum aliquos non pudet mentiri, me iniquiorem esse quibusdam mundi principibus, qui regna Christiana nunc administrent: alios autem, contumeliose dicere, & præter omnem modestiam Christianam, Anglorum reginæ Mariæ me obtrectare, qui alicubi Iesabelem in Anglia regnare, & sese martyrum sanguine ingurgitare scripserim: quum ego tamen ex nomine non Mariam, sed Romanam tyrannidé, quæ nunc ualde miserè in Anglia grassatur, intellexerim. lœrim[?]. Loci enim in Nicolao Grimoalda, Traherone[?], Turnero Medico, Hopero, Rid-laeo, Rogero, Bradfordo, Filpoto & aliis, sc satis explicant, de magno Antichristo & eius tortoribus mitratis ac rasis haec omnia dici. Illam synagogam Romanam, piorum homi-num peremptricem, à Spiritu sancto edo-ctus, Iesabelem impiam, Bestiam cornutam, Draconis prolem, diaboli filiam, satanę spon-sam, blasphemias loquentem, Belluam cocci-neam, Babylonem mysticam, Meretrice ma-gnam cum qua scortati sunt reges terrae om-nes qui de prostitutionis suae vino biberunt: Mulierem circundatam purpura, coccino, au-ro, gemmis & margaritis, habetem poculum aureum omnibus mundi turpitudinibus ac stupris refertum: Matrem fornicationum, & ebriam de sanguine sanctissimorum marty-rum Iesu habitationem daemoniorum, & cu-stodiam omnis immundi spiritus & uolu-cris odibilis, vocaui.
units.tr: I beg you, Christian reader, whoever you are, for whom the glory of Christ against the malice of Antichrist is dear, and I urge you in the Lord: be willing to interpret everything in the better sense, even what may seem too harshly said against so monstrous a Beast, and do not twist it with slanders. Some have already done this with my work on the writers of Britain, recently published, as I have learned. Some of them are not ashamed to lie, claiming that I am more unjust than certain princes of the world who now govern Christian kingdoms. Others say insultingly, and contrary to all Christian moderation, that I slander Mary, Queen of the English, because I have written somewhere that Jezebel reigns in England and gorges herself on the blood of the martyrs. Yet from the name I understood that I was not speaking of Mary but of the Roman tyranny, which now rages so wretchedly in England. The passages in Nicholas Grimoald, Tarbone, Turner the physician, Hooper, Ridley, Roger, Bradford, Philpot and others sufficiently explain that all these things are said of the great Antichrist and his mitred and shaven torturers. Taught by the Holy Spirit, I have called that Roman synagogue, the destroyer of pious men, the impious Jezebel, the horned Beast, the offspring of the Dragon, the daughter of the devil, the spouse of Satan, speaking blasphemies, the scarlet Beast, the mystical Babylon, the great Harlot with whom all the kings of the earth have committed fornication and who have drunk of the wine of her prostitution; the Woman clothed in purple, scarlet, gold, jewels and pearls, holding a golden cup filled with all the filthiness and fornications of the world; the Mother of fornications, drunk with the blood of the most holy martyrs of Jesus; the habitation of demons, the prison of every unclean spirit and hateful bird.

units.la: Occasionem, quę primum me mouit, hanc accipe. Anno Domini 1554. post vigesimum suae liberationis per Dei misericordiam an-num, Anglia nostra, ut canis ad vomitum, sa-crosanctum Christi Euangelium, quod ro-bur ac virtus Dei est in salutem omni credenti, contemptibiliter reliquit: & magno Dei aduersario, Romano diabolo & Antichristo, nouam professionem fecit: de quo execrabili facto, inter Appendices in huius Operis calce, plura reperies. partim etiam me provocabant horrenda uitia, quæ secum trahit tam horridum monstrum: quorum est expertus prudentissimus rex Henricus octauus, dum Cucullígerorum cœnobia & Sacrificorum collegia, per uenerabiles legu doctores, Thomam Laeum, Ricardum Laytonum, Thomam Bedillum archidiaconum Cornubiensem, Thomam Bartheletum notarium publicu, & alios, uisitari in suo regno fecisset ante expremam eorum dissolutionem, quæ fiebat anno a Christi natiuitate 1538. In quibus tanto numero reperti sunt scortatores, cinædi, ganeones, pædicones, puerarij, pæderastæ, Sodomitæ, Ganymedes, uotarij tamen ac cœlibes omnes: ut in unoquoq; eorum credideris nouam adesse Gomorrham. Liber eorum uocatur Breuiarium compertorum in monasterijs, conuentibus, collegijs, &c. Ex quo libro, unum & alterum ad gustum insipidum, pro exemplo locum monstrabo. In monasterio Bellensi, quod alio nomine Batell uocatur, Cicestriensis dioecesis, hi sunt Sodomitæ in ipsa uisitatione reperti: Joannes abbas, Ricardus Salchurst, Thomas Cuthbert, Guilhelmus Marche, Joannes Haftinge, Gregorius Champion, Clemens Vueftfelde, Joannes Crosse, Thomas Crambroke, Thomas Basyll, Joannes Hamfelde, Joan-
units.tr: Let me tell you what first moved me to this. In the year of our Lord 1554, in the twentieth year of its deliverance by God's mercy, our England, like a dog returning to its vomit, shamefully abandoned the most holy Gospel of Christ, which is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, and made a new profession to that great adversary of God, the Roman devil and Antichrist. You will find more about this loathsome act among the Appendices at the end of this work. I was also driven by the horrible vices that such a dreadful monster brings with it. The most prudent king Henry VIII had experience of them, when, before their final dissolution, which took place in the year of Christ's birth 1538, he had the monasteries of the hooded friars and the colleges of priests in his kingdom visited by the venerable doctors of law, Thomas Layton, Richard Layton, Thomas Bedyll, archdeacon of Cornwall, Thomas Bartlet, public notary, and others. Among them such a number of fornicators, sodomites, gluttons, pederasts, pimps, boy-lovers, catamites, Sodomites, Ganymedes was found, all of them vowed and celibate, that you would have believed a new Gomorrah was present in each one of them. Their book is called the Breviary of the discoveries made in the monasteries, convents, colleges, etc. From this book I will point out one or two passages, as a sample, to give a taste, though it is insipid. In the monastery of Battle, which is also called Bello, in the diocese of Chichester, these were found to be Sodomites at the visitation itself: John the abbot, Richard Salchurst, Thomas Cuthbert, William Marche, John Haftinge, Gregory Champion, Clement Westfield, John Crosse, Thomas Crambroke, Thomas Basyll, John Hamfelde, John

units.la: Ioannes Hierom, Clemens Grigge, Ricardus Touye, & Ioannes Auftyp. Incontinentes, Thomas Lyuet cum una maritata, & alia soluta: Thomas Crambroke cum eisdem ac pluribus, & cætera Casta Papæ religio.
units.tr: John Hierom, Clement Grigge, Richard Touye, and John Austyp. Incontinent: Thomas Lyuet, with one married woman and another unmarried; Thomas Crambroke with the same woman and several others; and the rest of the chaste religion of the Pope.

units.la: In Ecclesia CHRISTI Cantuariæ, inter monachos etiam Benedictinos, hi quoque reperiebantur Sodomitæ: Ricardus Godmersham, Guilhelmus Lichefelde, Christophorus Iamys, Ioannes Goldmyston, Nicolaus Clement, Guilhelmus Cauuston, Ioannes Ambrose, Thomas Farlegh, & Thomas Morton. Incontinentes, Christophorus Iamys prædictus, cum tribus coniugatis, & Nicolaus Clement cum una soluta. In monasterio Sancti Augustini (Anglorum Apostoli) eiusdem urbis & ordinis, incontinentes isti inuenie-bantur: Ioannes abbas cum una tantum, Ioannes Langdon cum duabus, Ioannes Langport cum una, Ricardus Compton cum una, Guilhelmus Reynesforth cum una, Guilhelmus Godmerston cum duabus, Dauid Frankes cum una, Robertus Saltuuo-de cum una, Laurentius Goldston cum una, Guilhelmus Holingborne cum una, Guilhelmus Mylton cum una, Ioannes Shreuue-bery cum una, & Thomas Barham Sodomi-ta. In Bathonien-si monasterio inter alios plures; Ricardus Lyncombe septem meretri-ces habebat, quatuor solutas & tres coniuga-tas, eratq; Sodomita. Guilhelmus Beuushon undecim scorta quoqʒ habebat, praeter Sodo-mitici[?] uariū genus. In Monkenfarlegensi cœ-nobio Sarisburiensis dioecesis, Ludouicus prior nouem habuit meretrices, & conuentus adhuc plures. Ricardus prior de Mayde Brad-ley, quinq; meretrices & sex spurios habuit. Guilhelmus abbas Bristollensis, quatuor me-retrices habuit, tres solutas, & unam coniuga-tam. Thomas abbas Abindonensis, praeter so-rorem naturalem, ex qua duas procreauit so-boles, tres alias meretrices habuit: & hic pa-ter multorum Sodomitarum fuit. In cœno-bio de Shulbrede Cicestriensis dioecesis, Ge-orgius Vualden prior, septem meretrices ha-buit, Ioannes Standney septem, Nicolaus Du-ke quinq; Henricus Seluuode duas, praeter reliquos & reliquas. Ioânes Blanke prior de Bermondsey, uiginti meretrices habuit.
units.tr: In the Church of Christ at Canterbury, among the Benedictine monks also, these men too were found to be Sodomites: Richard Godmersham, William Lichefield, Christopher James, John Goldmyston, Nicholas Clement, William Cauuston, John Ambrose, Thomas Farlegh, and Thomas Morton. Incontinent: the aforesaid Christopher James with three married women, and Nicholas Clement with one unmarried woman. In the monastery of St Augustine (the Apostle of the English) of the same city and order, these incontinent men were found: John the abbot with only one woman; John Langdon with two; John Langport with one; Richard Compton with one; William Reynesforth with one; William Godmerston with two; David Frankes with one; Robert Saltwood with one; Laurence Goldston with one; William Holingborne with one; William Mylton with one; John Shrewsbury with one; and Thomas Barham, a Sodomite. In the monastery of Bath, among many others: Richard Lyncombe kept seven harlots, four unmarried and three married, and he was a Sodomite. William Beaushon also kept eleven whores, besides a variety of Sodomitical practices. In the monastery of Monkton Farleigh in the diocese of Salisbury, Lewis the prior had nine harlots, and the convent had even more. Richard, prior of Maiden Bradley, had five harlots and six bastards. William, abbot of Bristol, kept four harlots, three unmarried and one married. Thomas, abbot of Abingdon, besides his natural sister, by whom he begot two children, kept three other harlots; and this father was the father of many Sodomites. In the monastery of Shulbred in the diocese of Chichester, George Walden the prior kept seven harlots, John Standney seven, Nicholas Duke five, Henry Selwood two, besides the other men and women. John Blanke, prior of Bermondsey, kept twenty harlots.

units.la: Vt ad sacrificulorum collegia ueniamus: In castro de Vuindesora, Hericus Vuoduuar de succentor, plures meretrices habuit: Nico-laus Vulhyde quatuor, Georgius Vuhitethor-ne quinq, Nicolaus Spoke quinq, Robertus Hune quinq, Simon Todde unam, Nicolaus Vualker, duas, Guilhelmus Vuafe unam, Ro-bertus Dauyson sex, Petrus Bough multas, & alij alias. In ecclesia cathedrali Cicestriæ:
units.tr: To come to the colleges of priests: in the castle of Windsor, Henry Woodward, the precentor, kept many harlots; Nicholas Wilhyde four, George Whitethorne five, Nicholas Spoke five, Robert Hune five, Simon Todd one, Nicholas Walker two, William Wase one, Robert Dawson six, Peter Bough many, and others others. In the cathedral church of Chichester:
PREFACE.

units.la: Ioannes Champion præbendarius de Vual-tam duas meretrices habuit, Guilhelmus Crosse maritatam unam, Thomas Parcker duas solutas, Ricardus Busselde solutam u-nam, de qua suscitauit sobolem: Bartholo-mæus Cokisley solutam unam, Robertus Hunt plures: Thomas Gosse duas coniuga-tas, Ioannes Hylle tredecim meretrices, Ro-bertus More plures, Rogerus Barham plu-res, Ioannes Bedselde plures, & alij alias: in-ter quos etiam prædicti Rogerus Barham & Ioannes Champion reperti sunt Sodomi-tæ. Hæc ex prædicto libro. Vide qualia por-tenta in monasterijs & collegijs, & in suo co-libatu, Papatus per Angliam nutriuit. Nónnę[?] merito sunt pulsi, cum sordidissimo Roma-nensium omnium idolo Papa? In alijs quoq; omnibus, tam collegijs quàm conuentibus, similia sunt perpetrata ac reperta, quæ per-longum esset per omnia referre, imò turpis-simum: contracta simul, ob eandem Papæ reli-gionem, multis in locis, scabie Gallica, uel morbo Hispanico. Quoniam erant in Anglia plus q quadringenta diuersi generis mona-chorum & monialium cœnobia, præter fratrum Mendicatium sceleratissimos nidos, quorum etiam fuerunt ferè duceta. Quibus aptissimè conuenit hoc distichon:
units.tr: John Champion, prebendary of Waltham, kept two whores; William Crosse kept one married woman; Thomas Parcker two unmarried women; Richard Busselde one unmarried woman, by whom he begot offspring; Bartholomew Cokisley one unmarried woman; Robert Hunt several; Thomas Gosse two married women; John Hylle thirteen whores; Robert More several; Roger Barham several; John Bedselde several, and others other things. Among these, the aforesaid Roger Barham and John Champion were also found to be sodomites. These things are from the aforesaid book. See what monstrous things the Papacy nurtured in monasteries and colleges, and in its own celibacy throughout England. Were they not rightly driven out, along with the most filthy idol of all the Romanists, the Pope? In all the other colleges and convents alike, similar things were committed and discovered, which would take too long to report in every detail, and indeed would be most shameful; at the same time, on account of the same Papist religion, they caught the French itch, or the Spanish disease, in many places. For there were in England more than four hundred monasteries of monks and nuns of various kinds, besides the most wicked nests of the mendicant friars, of which there were also nearly two hundred. The following couplet fits them very well:

units.la: Non male sunt Monachis grata indita nomina patrum, Cum numerent natos hic & ubiq; suos.
units.tr: Not ill-suited to monks are the names given to their fathers, since here and everywhere they count their own sons.

units.la: Est adhuc unum tertium, quod me accendebat: atq; his uisis & cognitis, uehementer ad scribendum incitabat: præceptum uideli cet Christi in ipsa Apocalypsi Ioannis, cap. 18. Vox enim é cœlis ipsis est, à diuini patris dextera & æterno Christi throno, quæ magno cum impetu auribus nostris insonuit: Migra te ex ea mi populus (inquit) ne participes si-tis delictorum eius, neq; de plagis eius accipiatis: Quoniam peruenerunt eius peccata usque ad cœlum, & recordatus est Dominus iniquitatum eius. Sequitur q; mandatum nobis exhibitum, aduersus Bestiam illam septi-cipitem: Reddite illi, sicuti & ipsa reddidit uobis: & duplicate illi duplicia, secundum opera eius. In poculo quo miscuit, miscete ei duplum. Quantum glorificauit se, & in delicijs fuit, tantum miscete illi tormentum & luctum. Sententia Dei ac Christi Domini hæc est, nobis ideo prolata tam hic quàm Hier. 50. ut pereat demum hæc hydra, ac nostris conatibus intereat. Sed inter hæc omnia non sum Paulini loci oblitus, honore prosequendos esse principes omnes, etiam malos & inutiles reipublicæ, quòd à Deo positi sint: nec illis esse maledicendum, satis ex scripturis ipsis memini. Neque supernæ Dei prouidentiæ contra eius uerbum, uel mutire quidem audeo, uermis, puluis ac cinis.
units.tr: There is yet a third reason, which spurred me on, and when I had seen and learned these things, it urged me strongly to write: the command of Christ in the very Apocalypse of John, chapter 18. For a voice from heaven itself, from the right hand of the divine Father and the eternal throne of Christ, has sounded loudly in our ears: "Come out of her, my people," it says, "that you may not be partakers of her sins, nor receive of her plagues. For her sins have reached up to heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities." Then follows the command given to us against that sevenfold-headed Beast: "Render to her as she also rendered to you, and double to her double according to her works. In the cup which she mixed, mix double for her. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her." This is the sentence of God and of the Lord Christ, set forth here as much as in Jeremiah 50, so that at last this hydra may perish and be undone by our efforts. But amid all these things I have not forgotten the words of Paul, that all princes are to be honoured, even the wicked and those useless to the commonwealth, because they have been set in place by God; and I remember well enough from the Scriptures themselves that they are not to be cursed. Nor, as a worm, dust and ashes, do I dare to murmur against the higher providence of God or against his word.

units.la: Ex intimo corde igitur, Christum Dominum ac redemptorem deprecor, ut omnium potestatum, regum atque regnorum misereatur: & ita gentes omnes gubernandae curet, ut omnia tendant ad nominis sui gloriam: cuius uindicandae gratia potissimum, me quoq; in hac mea senecta perfortiter concitauit, nullius tamen Christiani principis honori derogandi aut detrahendi studio. Sed iam Romanam Bestiam, Satanae synagogam, cum fessore Antichristo atq; eius ductore diabolo, scripturis & eruditissimorum virorum testimonijs adorior.
units.tr: Therefore from the depths of my heart I beseech Christ the Lord and Redeemer that he may have mercy on all powers, kings and kingdoms, and that he may so care to govern all nations that everything tends toward the glory of his name. It was chiefly for the vindication of this that he stirred me up so vigorously in my old age; yet with no intention of diminishing or detracting from the honour of any Christian prince. But now I attack the Roman Beast, the synagogue of Satan, together with its abettor Antichrist and its leader the devil, with the testimonies of Scripture and of the most learned men.

units.la: Si acerbiora in hoc & altero meo opere sint dicta (pie lector) quam uelles, consideras immanissimam esse eius monstri in hac mundi uespera tyrannidem, eiusq; iuxta diuinas promissiones exitium in foribus esse. Concidet Babylon magna, quae gentes seduxit, & in interitum ibit, mirantibus cunctis qui terram inhabitant. Si offendit styli uehementia: contemplare eximium illum spiritus uigorem in Dauide propheta ac rege sanctissimo, qui in Domini causa perfortiter clamabat: Odivi ecclesiam malignantium, Psal. 25. Et iterum: Iniquos odio habui, quod legem tuam dilexerim, Psal. 118. Alibi quoq; Nonne qui oderunt te Domine, oderā, & super inimicos tuos tabescebam? Perfecto odio oderā illos, Psal. 128[?]. Promittit deinde per Prophetas suos Deus, se demoliturum lupanar[?] illud ac prostibulum. Ezech. 16. Oftendā (inquit) gen-tibus nuditatem tuam, & regnis ignominiam tuam. Nahū 2. Reuelabitur tuū propudium ac dedecus, & opprobrium tuum uidebitur; ultione capiā, & non resistet mihi homo. Esa. 47. Ve regibus illis, quotquot adorauerint be[?] suam illam, quotquot suas illi uires tradiderint, aut potestate ab ea acceperint, uel cū ea fornicati fuerint, quotquot illi seruierint, aut foedus cum ea inierint aduersus Agnum, & cum eo bella illius causa gesserint: quoniam non sunt eorum nomina scripta in libro uitae à mundi constitutione. Et Agnus eos tandem uincet, utpote dominorum Dominus ac regum rex: & cum Belua illa in interitum & damnationem similiter ibunt. Apo. 17. Deus igitur Opt. Max. det in corda Christianorum Principum, quos decem cornua adumbrat, ut hanc eius sententiam atq; hoc eius iudicium fideliter exequantur: scilicet, ut Meretricem illam odio prosequantur, ut desolatam faciat, ut nudam relinquant, ut carnem eius comedant, atq; ut ipsam igne comburat: hoc est, ut ultimum supplicium de ea sumat, propter effusum tot sanctissimorum Christi testium innoxium sanguinem. Fiat, fiat.
units.tr: If the things said in this work and in my other one are harsher than you would wish, gentle reader, consider that the tyranny of that most monstrous beast is at its greatest in this evening of the world, and that its destruction is at the door according to the divine promises. "Babylon the great shall fall, she who seduced the nations, and shall go to destruction, while all who dwell on the earth marvel." If the vehemence of my pen offends you, look at the remarkable vigour of spirit in David the prophet and most holy king, who in the cause of the Lord cried out so boldly: "I have hated the assembly of the wicked," Psal. 25. And again: "I have hated the wicked, because I have loved your law," Psal. 118. Elsewhere too: "Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them," Psal. 128[?]. God then promises through his prophets that he will tear down that brothel and harlot's house. Ezekiel 16: "I will show your nakedness to the nations, and your shame to the kingdoms." Nahum 2: "Your disgrace and shame shall be uncovered, and your reproach shall be seen; I will take vengeance, and no man shall resist me." Isaiah 47: "Woe to those kings, all who have worshipped her beast, all who have given their power to it, or received authority from it, or have committed fornication with it, all who have served it, or made a covenant with it against the Lamb, and have waged war for its sake against him; for their names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. And the Lamb shall at last overcome them, as Lord of lords and King of kings; and they shall go likewise with that Beast to destruction and damnation." Apocalypse 17. May God, then, the best and greatest, put it into the hearts of the Christian princes, whom the ten horns represent, to carry out faithfully his judgment and sentence: namely, that they pursue that harlot with hatred, so that they make her desolate, leave her naked, eat her flesh, and burn her with fire; that is, that they take the final punishment upon her for the innocent blood of so many most holy witnesses of Christ that she has shed. So be it, so be it.
AMEN.
