Roma rues, quondam uerae pietatis asylum, Musarum portus perfugiumq; choro. Roma uetus quondam multorum uecta per ora, Quam celebri Paulus prædicat elogio: Nunc sceleru sedes, nunc nunc erroris & ahtrū[?]. Degener ah nimium Roma nefanda rues. Roma rues, uirgo quondam, purissima uirgo, Cuius casta fides, integra religio, (tis, Intemerata thoro, thalamis non cognita mui[?] Vni sed sponso sponsa dicata Deo: Impia nunc Christo Domino diuortia scribens, Ac effrons meretrix, perfida Roma rues. Roma rues, mundi lux olim, stellaq; terræ: Nunc tenebræ, ac alto stella caduca polo. Cuius ad astra decus quondam sublime uolaq; Corruit, ac terræ est Tartarus Italia. (bat, Roma caput mundi, iam toto uertice calua, Capta tuis membris Roma misella rues. Ille cruore perit, qui fundit Roma cruorem[?])
units.tr: Proud Rome though you are, judge and avenger of the godly, yet learn the judgment of Christ the Lord. Though you are hard, and iron and stone can be softened, Rome, you will break. Hear this, O prince of Sodom and all Gomorrah, and whoever you are of the Roman flock; you who are deaf and blind, look upon your ruins. Read this so that you may not perish, or read it often, lest you perish. Rome, you will fall, once the refuge of true piety, the harbour of the Muses and the shelter of their chorus. Rome of old, carried on the lips of many and proclaimed with famous praise by Paul: now you are the seat of crimes, now of error and ... Degenerate Rome, alas, too much, you will fall, accursed. Rome, you will fall, once a virgin, most pure virgin, whose faith was chaste and whose religion was whole, unspoiled in the marriage bed and unknown to any bridal chamber, a bride dedicated to the one spouse, God. Now you write impious divorces from Christ the Lord, and as a shameless harlot, faithless Rome, you will fall. Rome, once the light of the world and the star of the earth: now darkness, and a star fallen from the high heavens. Your glory, once lofty and soaring to the stars, has collapsed, and Italy has become a Tartarus on earth. Rome, head of the world, now bald on the whole crown, seized in your members, wretched Rome, you will fall. He perishes by blood who sheds Rome's blood.

units.tr: Proud Rome, though you are judge and avenger of the pious, learn the judgment of Christ the Lord. Though you are hard, though you are iron and stone, you will be broken, Rome. Hear, prince of Sodom and all Gomorrah, whoever you are of the Roman flock. Hear, you deaf and blind, and behold your ruins. Read this so that you may not perish, or read it often, lest you perish. Rome, you are falling, once the refuge of true piety, the harbour of the Muses and the sanctuary of their choir. Old Rome, once carried on many lips, whom Paul proclaims with famous praise, you are now the seat of crimes, now of error and darkness. Degenerate Rome, unspeakable, alas, you are falling far too far. Rome, you are falling, once a virgin, most pure virgin, whose faith was chaste and whose religion was whole, undefiled in marriage, unknown to many bridal chambers, but a bride pledged to one spouse, God. Now you write impious divorce from Christ the Lord, and shameless harlot, faithless Rome, you are falling. Rome, once the light of the world and the star of the earth, now darkness, a star fallen from the high sky. Your glory once soared sublime to the stars; it has collapsed, and Italy is a Tartarus on earth. Rome, head of the world, now bald on the whole crown, captive in your limbs, poor Rome, you are falling. He perishes by blood who sheds the blood of Rome.

Calcandus fastus, frangeda superbia: cedrus Alta ruit, sic tu Roma superba rues. Roma rues, mercesq; tuæ, thesaurus & ingës: Gemmas & coccum, thuraq; nullus emet, Et peris & perdes, occidis & occidis ipsa, Idq; malo merito uipera sæuo tuo. Roma rues, regnumq; tuū: uanescet & aurū, Nomē, apex, sceptrū, fulmia, mitra, thronꝰ Et cur Roma rues? prudēsq; uidēsq; peribis? Ergo uolens tibimet tu paris exitium? Dū fallis, falsa es: tua iam spelunca retecta est, Occulti coitus, frausq; Venusq; patent. Ergo tuas labes, & fœdas aspice sordes: Vitaq; nota alijs, sit quoq; nota tibi. Plurima Lutherus patefecit, Platina multa, Quædam Vergerius, cuncta Baleus habet. Ille tuam mouit Camerinam, motaq; foetet, Pandoræ Latiæ pyxis aperta uolat. Ille tuos cæcos uidit, prodituq; recessus: Furtiuos memorat, Roma petulca, thoros. Aulam lustrauit, rimas perspexit & omnes,
units.tr: He who delights in blood dies bloody, as the wolf pursues the lamb, Cain Abel, Esau Jacob, and the bastard the legitimate. You, founded in blood, now with pious blood... So I will conclude: bloody Rome, you are falling. Rome, you are falling, since you swell with the victor's laurel, teeming and fruitful with your ancient spoils, carried about in gilded chariots, and presiding over the satraps and princes of the world. Pride must be trampled and arrogance broken; the tall cedar falls, and so you, proud Rome, will fall. Rome, your merchandise and vast treasure are falling: no one will buy gems, scarlet or incense. You perish and destroy, you slay and are slain yourself, and this by your own deserved fault, savage viper. Rome, your kingdom is falling; gold will vanish, and name, mitre, crown, sceptre, thunderbolts and throne. And why are you falling, Rome? Will you perish knowing and seeing it? Do you, of your own will, prepare your own ruin? While you deceive, you are false: your cave is now uncovered, and secret couplings, fraud and lust lie open. So look upon your stains and foul filth, and let your life, known to others, be known to you as well. Luther has laid open very much, Platina much, Vergerius certain things, and Bale has everything. He stirred your Camerina, and once stirred it stinks; the opened box of Latin Pandora flies abroad. He saw your hidden recesses and secret places; he records your stolen beds, wanton Rome. He searched the court and looked into every crack,

units.la: Ingreditur lectos, concubitusq; tuos: Secretum nihil est, tenebrosa cubilia pandit. Nox nihil inuoluet, nulla latebra teget. Huc ergo uenias, speculū uideasq; malorū, Hic & auos, proauos, hic atauosq; uide. Nunc uocat & reuocat pansis[?] Deus optimus Sancta flens urbe te cupit esse sua. (alis, Roma quidem ῥώμη[?] dicta est, sed noie uerso, Dici Roma potest improbitatis amor. Ah pigeat, pudeat: mores cum nomine muta: Roma ueni, ad Dnm uertere, Roma ueni. Si nil frontis habet meretrix, si stercora nolis Scire sciens: cogor dicere, Roma rues.
units.tr: he enters your beds and your couplings. Nothing is secret; he opens your dark chambers. No night will wrap them up, no hiding place will cover them. Come here, then, and see the mirror of your evils; here see your grandfathers, great-grandfathers and ancestors. Now the best God calls and recalls, with wings spread, and weeping, wishes you to be his holy city. Rome is indeed called strength [ῥώμη], but with the name reversed, Rome can be called the love of wickedness. Alas, let it grieve you and shame you: change your manners along with your name. Come, Rome, turn to the Lord; come, Rome. If the harlot has no shame, and if you, knowing, do not want to know the filth, I am compelled to say: Rome, you are falling.

units.tr: Who could believe (it is even shameful to say) that Rome has had popes, and for so long? (Priapus, not Phoebus' sister, nor Vesta, dwells in that shrine any longer. How do you prove it? Learned Baleus portrays unspeakable debaucheries with such gravity, and he has the nose of a rhinoceros. Whoever, then, is loyal to the wild beasts with lofty head, take care lest you stagger now; the Martian crowd is wise. You have no tunic to cover the part that needs covering. You cannot cover up an impure harlot any more than that. The true word will burst from me, though it sticks in your throat: Rome's chair is no more the chair of holy Peter. But I admit someone sits there. Who? Paul? I deny it. Who, then? The Lampsacene, offspring worthy of Venus and of the god, (you?), who, when he was driven far from the city of Lampsacus,)

He holds bare names, with no traces of Christ; shameful things lie hidden beneath a fair name. Everyone cries out that the Papists are catamites. The Pope is a sodomite. I keep silent about the rest. Yet I will add this much, though only briefly. And it will be permitted to you, if you write "pa" and "po" in the same way, that "Pa-pa" is "Pope" (pa is pa). Venus is called Paphian, and her offspring too: This evil is an egg of an evil crow [ὦον τοῦτο κακὸν τοῦδε κακοῦ κόρακος]. But spare my modest ears, you who bear foul things; spare my verses, I beg you. Coarse things suit coarse men, and the most foul names suit the most foul matters. What I believe, I say. For it will not harm to have said that "Pa", a mark of stench, will be doubled if it is repeated. Know this too: unless you placate God, who rules the stars, the names Papa will bring you to ruin.

units.tr: He must be the husband of one wife, a bishop, as is plainly set out in your writings, Paul. The bishop must be the husband of no wife, which the sacrilegious Popes teach everywhere. But is it not a fine thing that the most wicked crowd of catamites condemns sacred doctrines with its own decrees?

units.la: EXORDIENS Romanorum pontificum acta, seu latinae Ecclesiae ministrorum Catalogum, à primis incipiam, qui pauperes erant, & in verbi ministerio ad mortem usque solliciti. Inde pergam ad eos, qui finitis per-secutionibus, in otio Ecclesiae, ad archiepiscopatus ac patriarchatus fastigia ascendebant: donec ad illos pervenero, qui de Papatu gloriantes, introdu-xerunt perditionis sectas: & eū qui ipsos redemit, juxta D. Petri propheticam vocem, Deum nega-runt, superinducentes celerem sibi perditionem.{2} Pet.2. Constat enim, Apostolos post Christi ascensionem 14. annis, per Iudæam, Samariam, & Palæstinam, Euangelium regni Dei prædicasse primum. Inde post concilium Hierosolymæ anno Christi 48. congregatu, discipuli ex dispersione ad gentes pro perabant[?], et ut in historiarum floribus reperio, anno sequenti Romam peruenerunt. Vbi quum Ecclesiam illam Hierosolymæ prius ab Apostolis ipsis optime institutam, piis concionibus plantassent: à Lino, qui primus eius episcopus erat, usq; ad Syluestrum, & Cæsarem Constantinum magnum, genere quidem Britannum, per ducentos & septuaginta annos, in magnis persecutionibus illam gubernabant. Nam & Constantinus ille, anno à Christi seruatoris incarnatione 319. Christianorum Ecclesiis, profligatis tyrannis, pacem dedit. A Petro quidem cæterorum historiographorum more hoc opus inciperem: sed obstant argumenta quædam, ac sacrarum scripturarum autoritates, quæ id fieri non sinunt, quum Petrum nunquam fuisse Romæ, perspicue commonstrent. Damasum pontificem, Martinum Carsulanum, Ioannem Rufum Anglum, Vincentiū, Antoninū, Platinam, Blondum, Volaterranum, Stellam, Vuicelium[?], ac similes paparū adulatores, in hoc opere per omnia nō sequor: sed in plerisq; Irenæum, Eusebium, Huldricum Augustanum, Luithprandum Ticinensem, Bennonem, Lambertū SchafSchafnaburgensem, Sarifburium, Petrarcham, Petrum Premonstratensem, Capgrauum, Crätzium, Nauclerum, Baptistam Mantuanum: & inter neo-tericos Robertum Barnum, Bibliandrum, Gassarū, Funccium, Pantaleonem, Lycosthenem, Vergeriū, Sleidanum, Matthiam Flacium Illyricum, & alios autores multo fideliores ac veriores.
units.tr: Beginning the acts of the Roman pontiffs, or the catalogue of the ministers of the Latin Church, I will start with the first, who were poor and anxious in the ministry of the Word even unto death. From there I will proceed to those who, once the persecutions had ended and the Church was at rest, rose to the heights of archbishoprics and patriarchates, until I come to those who, boasting of the Papacy, introduced sects of perdition, and who, in line with the prophetic voice of St Peter, denied the Lord who bought them, bringing on themselves swift destruction. [2 Pet. 2.] For it is established that the Apostles preached the gospel of the kingdom of God first in Judea, Samaria and Palestine, for fourteen years after Christ's ascension. Then, after the council of Jerusalem, which was held in the year of Christ 48, the disciples, scattered abroad, spread out among the Gentiles, and, as I find in the flowers of the histories, arrived at Rome the following year. There, having planted that Church, which had earlier been very well founded at Jerusalem by the Apostles themselves, with pious sermons, they governed it through great persecutions for two hundred and seventy years, from Linus, who was its first bishop, down to Silvester and Caesar Constantine the Great, a Briton by birth. For in the year 319 from the incarnation of our Saviour, Constantine, once the tyrants had been overthrown, gave peace to the churches of the Christians. I would indeed begin this work with Peter, as other historians do, but certain arguments and the authority of the sacred Scriptures stand in the way and do not allow it, since they clearly show that Peter was never at Rome. I do not follow Pope Damasus, Martin of Carsula, John Rous the Englishman, Vincent, Antoninus, Platina, Biondo, Volaterranus, Stella, Wicelius, and similar flatterers of the popes in this work in every respect; but for the most part I follow Irenaeus, Eusebius, Ulrich of Augsburg, Liutprand of Cremona, Benno, Lambert of Schafnaburg, Sarisburiensis, Petrarch, Peter of Premontré, Capgrave, Krantz, Nauclerus, Baptista Mantuanus; and among the more recent writers, Robert Barnes, Bibliander, Gassarus, Funck, Pantaleon, Lycosthenes, Vergerius, Sleidan, Matthias Flacius Illyricus, and other authors far more faithful and truthful.
On the Apostle Peter.

units.la: PEtrus autem, cum ex Christi Domini iussu ac praecepto, circumcisionis Apostolus fuerit, aequum profecto non erat, ut relicto Iudaeorum grege, 25.annis (ut somniant Papistæ) apud Gentes incircumcisas Romæ sederet, aut illic gentilium regum more imperaret. In Iudæa ergo, ac finitimis regionibus, Christi mandato obstrictus permansit, praedicans in maritimis urbibus Evangelium regni Dei: quod & ipsa testantur miracula, quæ per illum Deus operabatur. Nam Lyddæ paralyticum Æneam sanitati restituit, Tabitham Ioppæ a mortuis excitauit. In Cæsarea centurione Cornelium baptizauit, atque alibi alia plura fecit. Quæ omnia declarant, illum nec sedisse, nec mortem obiisse Romæ. Unde Baptista Mantuanus in sexto Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Peter, however, since by the command and precept of the Lord Christ he was the Apostle of the circumcision, was certainly not right to abandon the flock of the Jews and sit at Rome for 25 years (as the Papists dream) among the uncircumcised Gentiles, or to rule there in the manner of the kings of the nations. He therefore remained in Judea and the neighbouring regions, bound by Christ's command, preaching the gospel of the kingdom of God in the coastal cities; and this the miracles that God worked through him also attest. For at Lydda he restored Aeneas the paralytic to health, and at Joppa he raised Tabitha from the dead. In Caesarea he baptized Cornelius the centurion, and elsewhere he did many other things. All of which declare that he neither sat at Rome nor died there. Hence Baptista Mantuanus, in the sixth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Urbibus Assyrijs Christi post funera, postq̄In cælum reditus, bis septem dicitur annos Impendisse, graui vexans mala numina bello; Mox maria ingressus, longaq; ambage viarum Circumlatus, iter vertit Bithynica versus Littora: Cappadoces, Galatas, Pōtūq; peragrans, Quotquot erant illis Judæa ab origine regnis, Edocuit Christum, ueteriq; retraxit ab usu.
units.tr: "After Christ's death and his return into heaven, he is said to have spent fourteen years in the Assyrian cities, troubling the wicked powers with grievous war; then, entering the seas, and carried about by a long winding of journeys, he turned his course towards the Bithynian shores; traversing Cappadocia, Galatia and Pontus, he taught Christ to as many as were in those kingdoms from Judea's beginning, and drew them back from their old practice."

units.la: Hieronymus etiam, atq; Lyranus, super illa Christi verba, Ecce ego mitto ad vos prophetas ac sapientes &c. asserunt, Petrum fuisse à Judæis Hierosolymæ crucifixum: quod & illis verbis aptissimè respondet.
units.tr: Jerome also, and Lyra, on those words of Christ, "Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men," etc., assert that Peter was crucified at Jerusalem by the Jews; and this answers aptly to those words.

units.la: SEQuitur prima Romanorū Episcoporum classis, ab Apostolis ad Sylvestrum. Qui om-nes fuere pastores absq; mitris, simplices, et in Evangelij messe ad martyrium usq; laborantes.
units.tr: There follows the first class of the Roman bishops, from the Apostles down to Sylvester. All of them were plain ministers without mitres, laboring in the harvest of the gospel even unto martyrdom.
1. LINUS of Tuscany.

units.la: LINVM verò Thuscum, Apostolicum virum, ac vitæ sanctitate conspicuum, Romanum episcopum, & omnium primum fuisse, non nego: qui Cæsaris Vespasiani tempore, ob Evangelij prædicationem, sub Saturnino consule, anno Christi 82. martyrij pœnam subijt. Sed quod constitue-rit ex mortui Petri mandato, ne qua mulier, nisi operto capite templum ingrederetur, insigne men-dacium est, quamuis id Platina dicat: cum ante Constantini imperium templa Romæ non habuesint[?] Christiani. Paulus etiam Corinthiis similia proponens, de templo non loquitur. Vnde in pri-mo Fastorum praedicti Mantuani:
units.tr: I do not deny that Linus, a Tuscan, an Apostolic man, conspicuous for the holiness of his life, was the Roman bishop and the first of them all. In the time of Caesar Vespasian, on account of his preaching of the gospel, under the consul Saturninus, in the year of Christ 82, he underwent the penalty of martyrdom. But that he laid down, by the command of the dead Peter, that no woman should enter the church unless her head was covered, is a notorious lie, although Platina says so: since before Constantine's reign the Christians had no churches at Rome. Paul too, when proposing similar things to the Corinthians, does not speak of a church building. Hence in the first book of the Fasti of the aforementioned Mantuan:

units.la: Nam cum Cæsarei, gens sanguinolenta, tyranni Prædarentur oues Christi, nullasq; liceret Christigenis habitare urbes impune, ferarum Confortes facti, fines tenuere supremas Orbis, & ardentes Cancri feruentis arenas.
units.tr: "For when the Caesarean tyrants, a bloodthirsty race, were plundering the sheep of Christ, and the Christians were not permitted to dwell in the cities with impunity, they became companions of the wild beasts and held the furthest borders of the world, and the burning sands of the scorching Cancer."
2. ANACLETUS of Athens.

units.la: ANacletus Atheniensis, quem Irenæus post Linum ponit, doctrina & spiritu eximius, uerāq;[?] Ecclesiæ plantator assiduus, usq; ad Domitiani tyranni tempora uixit: cuius mandato, anno salutis nostræ 94. martyrio coronatus fuit. Epistolæ ac de-creta, quæ illi assignantur, de Episcoporum ordinatione ac primatu, horribilibus mendacijs scatet: quoniam, ut est apud Mantuanum, Per spelæa diu traxit syluatica uitam.
units.tr: Anacletus of Athens, whom Irenaeus places after Linus, outstanding in learning and spirit and a diligent planter of the true Church, lived until the time of the tyrant Domitian, by whose command he was crowned with martyrdom in the year of our salvation 94. The letters and decrees assigned to him, concerning the ordination of bishops and their primacy, are full of horrible lies, since, as Mantuan says, "For a long time he drew out his life in the woodland caves."
3. CLEMENT the Roman.

units.la: Clemens Romanus, uir longè doctissimus, Ana-cleto succedens, religionem Christianam, non leges condendo, ut somniant Papicolæ: sed Euan-gelium prædicando, ac uirtutes operando, adauxit plurimum. Qualiter enim ille Rom. urbis regiones in Ecclesiis distribueret, qui uix domunculâ in ea-dem habuerit, non intelligo. Aut quo modo puerorum confirmationes, missas, vestes ac Papistica sacra disponeret: qui & ipse à Cæsare Traiano, ad marmora secanda in exilium erat pulsus, & ancora ad collum eius appensa anno Domini 102. in mare tandem præcipitatus: certè non video. O diabolici Christianorum derisores Papistæ. Mantuanus enim in 11. Fastorum libro sic habet:
units.tr: Clement of Rome, a man by far the most learned, succeeded Anacletus. He greatly advanced the Christian religion, not by framing laws, as the Papicolae dream, but by preaching the Gospel and working miracles. I do not understand how he could have divided the regions of the city of Rome among the churches when he scarcely had a little house in it. Nor can I see how he could have arranged the confirmation of children, the masses, the vestments and the other Papistical rites, when he was himself banished by the emperor Trajan to cut marble, and at last, with an anchor tied to his neck, was thrown into the sea in the year of the Lord 102. Oh, you Papists, diabolical mockers of Christians! For Mantuan says in the eleventh book of the Fasti:

units.la: Hic quia Faustinam magni de sanguine Neruæ, Sisiniumq; virum illustrem cum coniuge Christo Subdiderat, Roma procul ablegatus ab urbe, Hellespontiacæ petiit confinia terræ, Peruenitq; Paron, lapides ubi multa secabant Millia Christigenum Parios, quibus alta theatra, Templa deum, regumq; domos ornare solebant.
units.tr: Because he had brought Faustina, of the great blood of Nerva, and Sisinnius, an illustrious man, with his wife, under Christ, he was banished far from the city of Rome and made for the borders of the Hellespont, and came to Paros, where many thousands of Christian Parian stones were cut, with which they used to adorn high theatres, temples of the gods and palaces of kings.
4. EVARISTUS the Greek.

units.la: Varistus Græcus, Dei gratia præfulgens, fide-l[?]ium Christianorum Ecclesiam concionibus sacris auxit, tempore persecutionum: donec esset anno Christi iio. sub dicto Traiano etiam martyrio sublatus.
units.tr: Evaristus the Greek, outstanding by the grace of God, increased the Christian faithful's Church by holy sermons in a time of persecutions, until in the year 110 of Christ he too was taken off by martyrdom under Trajan.
5. ALEXANDER the Roman.

units.la: Alexander Romanus Ecclesiam Romanam prædicado, & baptizando, in primis uuit[?]: qui Christiani nominis gratia, sub præside Aureliano sup-plicia gravissima, anno Domini 121. ad mortem us-que passus est.
units.tr: Alexander the Roman, preaching and baptizing, chiefly served the Roman Church. For the sake of the Christian name he suffered the most severe torments under the governor Aurelian, and endured death, in the year of the Lord 121.
6. SIXTUS the Roman.

units.la: Sixtus quoq; Romanus, in sermone & opere uir potens: Ecclesiam ipsam pijs quibusdam fictis ornauit, pro Dei grege solliciitus semper. Ob fidem Christianam, hic terrenam vitam amisit, anno Domini 129. ut longe in cœlis meliorem inueniret. His itidem tribus Episcopis, Euaristo, Alexandro, & Sixto, iisque tribuuntur decreta Papistica, De ordinatione cleri, aqua lustrali, ac uasibus sacris: cum de illis atq; aliis eius temporis Episcopis proferatur hoc monoflichon, Vrbibus antiq; patres fugere relictis.
units.tr: Sixtus, also a Roman, was a man powerful in word and deed. He adorned the Church itself with certain pious fabrications, always anxious for the flock of God. For the Christian faith he lost his earthly life in the year of the Lord 129, so that he might find a far better life in heaven. To these three bishops, Evaristus, Alexander and Sixtus, the Papistical decrees are likewise ascribed, concerning the ordination of the clergy, lustral water and sacred vessels; yet of them and the other bishops of that time this single line is quoted: "Having left the cities, the ancient fathers fled."
7. TELESPHORUS the Greek.

units.la: Telesphorus Græcus, eruditione ac pietate uir insignis: sub Antonino Cæsare, tam ore quam sanguine, fidelis Iesu Christi testis fuit, anno Domini 140. Qui non tres Missas in Christi natali, ut Papistæ nugantur, celebrari iussit: quia nondum erat per meretricem Babylonicam concepta, nec per ipsum Satanam genita, Missa illa diabolica: nec contra ipsius D. Pauli doctrinam, Galat. 4. superstitiose adhuc obseruabant dies, menses, & annos. Sed cuiusq; eorum hæc erant exercitia quotidiana, ut est apud Mantuanum: Tunc ubi iam primæ laudes exsoluerat horæ, Ad ruris transfibat opus, ne lenta nocentes, Ocia nutrirent curas, deducere riuos,
units.tr: Telesphorus the Greek, a man distinguished for learning and piety, bore faithful witness to Jesus Christ under Caesar Antoninus, both by his voice and by his blood, in the year of the Lord 140. He did not order three Masses to be celebrated at Christmas, as the Papists trifle. That diabolical Mass had not yet been conceived by the Babylonish harlot nor begotten by Satan himself. Nor, contrary to the teaching of St Paul himself (Gal. 4), did they yet observe days, months and years superstitiously. Their daily occupations were of this kind, as Mantuan has it: "When the first hour had already finished its morning praises, they turned to the work of the countryside, lest idle leisure, which breeds harmful cares, should take hold of them. They drew channels to water the flourishing garden with irrigation ditches, turned the soil, committed seeds to the furrows, tilled the ground, and set out tender young plants. This was their care, and they spent the whole daylight sweating over it. Fleeing sloth, the shepherd practised every kind of work. He could not then pour wine to God or break bread; fortune was cruel to outstanding men."

units.la: Florentem riguus adaquare canalibus hortum, Vertere tellurem, committere semina sulcis, Exercere solum, tenerás depangere plantas, Cura erat, & totam sudando absumere lucem. Segnitiem fugiens, exercuit omnia pastor: Non vinum libare Deo, non frangere panem, Tunc poterat: fortuna viris praestantibus atrox.
units.tr: Then, if Telesphorus advised fasts for Christians, they were devout and voluntary, and were not kept by observing days, nor in superstition, nor as compulsory or tyrannical rules.

units.la: Si ieiunia Christianis tunc suaserit: religiosa ac libera erant, & non cum obseruatione dierum, aut in superstitione, coacticia vel tyrannica. Nam tales ieiuniorum leges, non Telesphorus, sed Montanus haereticus imposuit primum: qui & nuptias solvere, liberum permisit.
units.tr: For such laws of fasting were first imposed not by Telesphorus but by the heretic Montanus, who also permitted marriages to be dissolved at will.
8. HYGINUS of Athens.

units.la: Higinus Atheniensis, ex philosopho Christiano Episcopus factus, officia boni pastoris in ecclesiastici operatoris in messe Domini perfecit[?]: ac morte non incruenta tandem, anno Christi 144. sub mundi tyrannis vitae finem accepit. Epistolam hic scripsisse fertur ex antro seu latibulo, de Deo ac de filij Dei incarnatione. Nam & talis juxta Mantuanum erat, Ut nemoris vasti latebras habitaret, & umbram.
units.tr: Hyginus of Athens, made bishop from a Christian philosopher, carried out the duties of a good shepherd and of a church worker in the Lord's harvest. At last, by a death not bloodless, in the year of Christ 144, under the tyrants of the world, he reached the end of his life. He is said to have written a letter here from a cave or hiding place, concerning God and the incarnation of the Son of God. For such a man, according to Mantuan, was he: "that he might dwell in the hidden recesses and shade of a vast wood."
9. PIUS of Aquileia.

units.la: Pius Aquileiensis, sub Antonino Vero, multa verae pietatis opera, in agro Christianae ecclesiae fecisse[?] ficisse perhibetur: martyrij gloriam anno Domini 159. in sui sanguinis effusione tum demum adeptus.
units.tr: Pius of Aquileia, under Antoninus Verus, is said to have done many works of true piety in the field of the Christian Church; at last, in the year of the Lord 159, he gained the glory of martyrdom by the shedding of his own blood.
10. ANICETUS the Syrian.

units.la: Anicetus Syrus, Romanæ Ecclesiæ in verbi minis-terio sacro, laboriose præfuit: & anno nati Ser-vatoris 169. in magna Christianæ fidei constantia, pro Dei veritate sanguinem postremò fudit.
units.tr: Anicetus the Syrian laboured diligently over the Roman Church in the sacred ministry of the Word, and in the year of the Saviour's birth 169, in great constancy of the Christian faith, at last shed his blood for the truth of God.
11. SOTER of Campania.

units.la: Sother Campanus, in armis spiritualibus Christo fideliter militauit, sub Antonino Commodo: hoc unum agens præcipuè, ut animas per baptismum Christo dicatas, doctrina & exemplo illi suo spon[?]so salvandas adduceret. Mortemq; sui corporis anno Domini 177. pro Christi ipsius testimonio pertulit.
units.tr: Soter of Campania faithfully served as a soldier of Christ in spiritual armour under Antoninus Commodus, doing chiefly this one thing: that he might lead souls dedicated to Christ through baptism to be saved by the teaching and example of their bridegroom. And he suffered the death of his body in the year of the Lord 177, for the testimony of Christ himself.
12. Eleutherius the Greek.

units.la: Eleutherius Græcus, ut bonus paterfamilias, de thesauro suo nova cum veteribus proferens, effecit, ut confirmatis & consolidatis Britannis in suscepta prius ab Apostolis doctrina, totum illud regnum in eius fidei verba iuraret. Quibus temporibus, tyrannorum persecutio paulisper conquievit: multiq; scriptores pii, contra pravorum dogmatum disseminatores fortiter dimicarunt: ipso etiam Eleutherio adversus Tatianum, nullum usua-lis victus reiiciendum esse genus decernente. At quamuis ille tunc vidcrit[?] tempora paululum tran-quilliora, quòd multi ex Romana nobilitate jā Christo crediderant[?]: defunctum tamē anno Domini 191. capitis obtruncatione, Massæus affirmat.
units.tr: Eleutherius the Greek, like a good householder, brought forth from his store new things alongside old, and so effected that the Britons, having been confirmed and strengthened in the doctrine received earlier from the Apostles, swore allegiance to the words of that faith throughout the whole kingdom. In his times the persecution by tyrants subsided for a little while, and many godly writers fought bravely against the disseminators of wicked doctrines, Eleutherius himself also decreeing against Tatian that no kind of food should be rejected. Yet although in his time he saw the times somewhat calmer, since many of the Roman nobility had now believed in Christ, nevertheless he died in the year of the Lord 191 by beheading, as Massaeus affirms.
13. Victor of Africa.

units.la: Victor Aphricanus, post Eleutherium, sub Aelio Pertinace, Ecclesiæ curam à seculo diuisus ges-sit. Hic aliquantulum sedata persecutionum procella, primus fuit, qui autoritate in externos usurpata, in messem alienam, falcem misit. In prædi-[?] Aliis[?] pontificibus (inquit Vuicelius) abundabat spi-ritus, sed in posterioribus malesuada caro. Victore hunc increpare ausi sunt Polycrates Ephesiorum episcopus, & Irenæus Lugdunensis, ut qui fratres in Asia communione priuauerat, quòd in Pascha-tis observatione, morem à Romana consuetudine diuersam sequerentur: ita ut Ecclesia tunc patere-tur naufragium, ob eius pertinaciam. Non potuit nihilominus hic pontifex, anno Domini 203. euita-re mortis supplicium.
units.tr: Victor of Africa, after Eleutherius, under Aelius Pertinax, held the care of the Church, separated from the world. He, when the storm of persecutions had been somewhat calmed, was the first who, usurping authority over foreigners, sent his sickle into another's harvest. Among the earlier bishops (says Wicelius) there was an abundance of spirit, but among the later ones a malicious flesh. Polycrates, bishop of the Ephesians, and Irenaeus of Lyons dared to rebuke Victor, as one who had deprived the brothers in Asia of communion because they followed a custom of observing Easter different from the Roman practice; so that the Church was then in danger of shipwreck because of his obstinacy. Nevertheless this bishop could not escape the punishment of death in the year of the Lord 203.
14. Zephyrinus the Roman.

units.la: Zepherinus Romanus, rei diuinæ magis quàm huma-næ intentus, ut scribunt autores, vitreos calices pro ligneis ordinauit: & anno Domini 220. Aurelij temporibus martyrio coronatus est. Sub hoc episcopo Artemonitæ, per Aristotelem ac Theo-phrastum, phrastu, scripturas sacras corrupisse, atq; in quaestiones omnia, nostri temporis Sophistarum more, posuisse dicuntur.
units.tr: Zephyrinus the Roman, more intent on divine things than on human ones, as the authors write, ordained glass chalices in place of wooden ones; and in the year of the Lord 220, in the times of Aurelius, he was crowned with martyrdom. Under this bishop the Artemonites are said to have corrupted the holy Scriptures by Aristotle and Theophrastus, and to have put everything into questions, after the manner of the Sophists of our own time.
15. Callistus of Ravenna.

units.la: Calixtus Rauennas, feruente rursus persecutione, constans evangelij testis in ecclesiae ministerio perseuerans: in quodam loco secreto trans Tyberim, cum multis Christianis latitabat. Ea tempe-state (inquit Platina) ob crebras persecutiones occulta erant omnia: etiam ipsa sacella, potius abdita, & plerunq; subterranea fuerunt, quàm publicis in locis aperta. Calixtus demum, Alexandri Severi Caesaris jussu, anno Domini 226. capitur, fustibus caeditur, in carcerem recluditur, è fenestra præci-pitatur, corpusq; ejus in puteum profundum demer-gitur. Quòd ille per quatuor temporum jejunia, Dei populum denuò judaizare fecerit: fabulam esse credo.
units.tr: Callistus of Ravenna, when persecution was raging again, a steadfast witness of the gospel, persevering in the ministry of the Church, was hiding with many Christians in a certain secret place across the Tiber. In that time (says Platina), because of frequent persecutions, everything was hidden: even their shrines were rather concealed, and mostly underground, than open in public places. Callistus at last, by the command of Alexander Severus Caesar, was taken in the year of the Lord 226, was beaten with clubs, was shut up in prison, was thrown headlong from a window, and his body was sunk in a deep well. That he caused the people of God to Judaize again by fasting during the four seasons, I believe to be a fable.
16. Urban the Roman.

units.la: Urbanus Romanus, sub libidinosissima bestia Heliogabalo Caesare vixit, vitaq; sanctitate & doctrina singulari multos undiquaq; mortales ad evangelium traxit. Hic saepenumero pro fide Christiana ab urbe proscribebatur: sed à fidelibus iterum clàm revocatus, martyrij coronam anno Domini 233 imperante Severo, tandem accepit.
units.tr: Urban the Roman lived under the most lustful beast, the emperor Heliogabalus, and by his holiness of life and singular teaching he drew many mortals from every quarter to the gospel. Often he was banished from the city on account of the Christian faith, but being secretly recalled again by the faithful, he at last received the crown of martyrdom in the year of the Lord 233, while Severus was emperor.

units.la: De quo Mantuanus in quinto Fastorum libro sic habet: Magnus hic ille Dei cultor, qui conditus antro, Appia Campanos quà se uia flectit in agros, Cæciliam duxit: duxit cum fratre maritum, Patricios iuuenes. Demum iam grandior æuo, Principe Alexandro, liuentis uerbera plumbi Pertulit: & iußus Marti dare thura, deorum Expuit in facies, conflatáq; polluit æra. Moxsecta ceruice, solum mutauit Olympo.
units.tr: Of him Mantuan says in the fifth book of the Fasti: This great worshipper of God, who, hidden in a cave where the Appian Way bends toward the Campanian fields, led Caecilia in marriage, and led her husband with her brother, young men of patrician rank. At last, now grown old, under the emperor Alexander, he bore the lashes of the livid lead, and, ordered to offer incense to Mars, he spat in the faces of the gods and defiled the brazen images; soon, his neck cut, he exchanged the soil for Olympus.
17. Pontianus the Roman.

units.la: Pontianus Romanus, prædicti Alexandri Seueri Imperatoris tempore, Christi minister, ac dispensator mysteriorum Dei: exilium & supplicia pro Euangelio, procq; Ecclesia passus est. Cum enim pro Dei uerbo, ad illum concursus fieret: mandato principis, idolorum sacrificulis instigantibus, ab urbe Roma in Sardiniam insulam deportabatur. In qua post multas calamitates, & grauia tormenta, anno Domini 239. pro Christi fide, martyrij pœnam subijt.
units.tr: Pontianus the Roman, in the time of the aforesaid emperor Alexander Severus, was a minister of Christ and a dispenser of the mysteries of God; he suffered exile and torments for the gospel and for the Church. For when people flocked to him on account of the word of God, by the emperor's command, at the instigation of the priests of idols, he was deported from the city of Rome to the island of Sardinia. There, after many calamities and grievous torments, in the year of the Lord 239 he underwent the penalty of martyrdom for the faith of Christ.
18. Antherus the Greek.

units.la: Antheros Græcus, uir Dei, si quis alius: sub Maximini Imperatoris tyrannide, Christum constanter docuit. Hic pontifex omnium primus curauit, ut Martyrum res gestæ diligenter & accuratè notarijs ... notariis scriberentur: ne una cum vitis, fortissimorum Dei militum memoria aboleretur. Quae utinam (inquit Crantzius) diligentius conscriptae legerentur. Decorauit autem hic Antheros, anno Domini 243. Ecclesiam suo sanguine, quam antea paucarat verbo: in via Appia sepultus.
units.tr: Antherus the Greek, a man of God if ever there was one, taught Christ steadfastly under the tyranny of the emperor Maximinus. This bishop was the first of all to take care that the deeds of the martyrs be recorded by notaries ... written down by notaries carefully and accurately, lest together with their lives the memory of the bravest soldiers of God be obliterated. Would that (says Crantzius) they had been written down more diligently and were read! Antherus adorned the Church with his blood in the year of the Lord 243, whom he had before served with the word: he was buried on the Appian Way.
19. Fabian the Roman.

units.la: Fabianus Romanus, cum ex agris, Eusebio teste, reuerteretur, & una cum suis conciuibus adesset pro nouo eligendo pontifice: uisa est columba eius insidere capiti, et subito, quod non expectabat, Ecclesiae pastor est creatus. Viuens ipse uigilauit quoq;, ut conscriberentur martyrologia, martyrium-busq; cœmiteria pararentur. Qui & sub Decio postea saeuiente in fratres, capitis obtruncatione, anno Domini 250. vitam gloriosa morte consummauit. Sub eo laborauit adhuc Origenes in vinea Domini, theologiae professor: q; contra Celsum scribes, multis rationibus docet, tepla [?] Christianis ad verum Dei cultum, veramq; religionem nihil convenire.
units.tr: Fabian the Roman, when, as Eusebius testifies, he was returning from the fields and was present with his fellow citizens to choose a new bishop, a dove was seen to settle on his head, and suddenly, which he did not expect, he was made minister of the Church. Living, he also took care that martyrologies should be written and cemeteries prepared for the martyrs. He also, later, under Decius, who raged against the brothers, completed his life by a glorious death, beheaded in the year of the Lord 250. Under him Origen still laboured in the vineyard of the Lord, a professor of theology, who, writing against Celsus, teaches by many arguments that nothing is suited to Christians for the true worship of God and the true religion.
20. CORNELIUS of Rome.

units.la: Cornelius Romanus, sub persecutore Decio, quem septimum hostem Christi et Ecclesiae numerant, de salute proximorum pie sollicitus: quotquot in tormentis Christum negauerant, ubi facti sui paenitere cognovit, benigne suscepit, Ecclesiaeq; restituit.O Spiritum Christi in hoc pontifice magnum, & euangelio dignum ministrum. Caeterum homo Dei Cornelius, licet in exilium deportatus, regno tamen Christi minime unquam defuit. Quin optimus eius athleta, in veritatis assertione anno Domini 253. Decii mucroni ceruicem, ut ouis mansueta, praebuit. Unde Mantuanus: Incidit in rigidos praesul Cornelius enses.
units.tr: Cornelius of Rome, under the persecutor Decius, whom they count the seventh enemy of Christ and the Church, was devoutly anxious for the salvation of his neighbours. When he learned that those who had denied Christ under torture regretted what they had done, he received them kindly and restored them to the Church. Here is a great spirit of Christ in this bishop, and a minister worthy of the gospel. Yet although the man of God Cornelius was carried off into exile, he was never at any time absent from the kingdom of Christ. Indeed, this excellent athlete, in the defence of the truth, in the year of the Lord 253, offered his neck to the sword of Decius like a gentle sheep. Hence Mantuanus: "The bishop Cornelius fell upon the harsh swords."
21. LUCIUS of Rome.

units.la: Lucius Romanus, fidelis in domo Domini seruus, ab infectatore Christiani nominis Gallo Hostiliano in exilium actus, a sancto Cypriano per literas confortabatur. Tandemque eo mortuo, per uoluntatem Dei, Romam reuersus, Ecclesiam salutari doctrina locupletauit, ac paradisum caelestem anno Domini 255. a Valeriano occidi iussus, & in sanguine agni dealbatus, penetrauit.
units.tr: Lucius of Rome, a faithful servant in the house of the Lord, was driven into exile by Gallus Hostilianus, the enemy of the Christian name, and was comforted by letters from Cyprian the saint. When he died, by the will of God, he returned to Rome, enriched the Church with wholesome teaching, and in the year of the Lord 255, having been ordered to be put to death by Valerian, he entered heavenly paradise, made white in the blood of the Lamb.
22. STEPHEN of Rome.

units.la: Stephanus Romanus, vir per omnia rectus & bonus, atque ecclesiae ministerio dignus habebatur.
units.tr: Stephen of Rome, a man upright and good in every respect, was regarded as worthy of the ministry of the Church.

units.la: Unde optima (inquit Vuicelius) pontificum exempla, nobis ecclesia proposuit, quamdiu uel nominantur tantum Romanae urbis Episcopi. Furente, Galleno iniquo Caesare, Stephanus anno Domini 257. cum multos gentilium ad Christi fidem convertisset, capite mulctatus, cum plerisque aliis, fit ui stima
units.tr: Hence (says Vuicelius) the Church has set before us the best examples of bishops, so long as the bishops of the city of Rome are named only. While the wicked emperor Gallienus raged, Stephen, in the year of the Lord 257, after he had converted many of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ, was beheaded together with many others, a sacrifice

units.la: Stima [?]ima Deo, accepta iustitiae corona. Additq; Mantuanus:
units.tr: most acceptable to God, having received the crown of righteousness. Mantuanus adds:

units.la: Et quia tunc regnabat adhuc antiqua deorum Impietas, multi nostrum diuersa ferebant Supplicia, exilium, gladios, ignemq; ferasq;, Vincla, famem, Plutone truces agitante tyrannos.
units.tr: And since the ancient impiety of the gods still reigned at that time, many of us bore diverse punishments: exile, swords, fire and wild beasts, chains, famine, cruel tyrants driven on by Pluto.
23. SIXTUS the Second.

units.la: Sixtus secundus, natione Graecus, patria Atheniensis, ex mundi philosopho Christi discipulus, & e terreno caelestis oeconomus factus, Christiani gregis decus, atq; imitandum exemplar effulsit. Islum[?] absumpsit quoq; una cum tot martyrum chiliadi-bus, Deciana atq; Valeriana persecutio, salutare Dei uerbū populo proponente, anno Domini 267.
units.tr: Sixtus the Second, a Greek by nation, an Athenian by birth, a disciple of Christ from the philosophy of the world, and made a steward of heavenly things from earthly ones, shone forth as the glory of the Christian flock and an example to be imitated. The persecution of Decius and Valerian, setting forth the saving word of God to the people, carried him off too, together with thousands of martyrs, in the year of the Lord 267.

units.la: Hic sancto Episcopo, sanctus diaconus Laurentius inseparabiliter adhaesit, usq; ad ultima uita supplicia. Quorum alter gladio, alter igne, terris eximebatur. De quibus Mantuanus in 8. Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Upon this holy bishop the holy deacon Laurence clung inseparably, even to the last torments of life. One of them was taken from the earth by the sword, the other by fire. Of them Mantuanus, in the eighth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Hos Decius sanctis florentes moribus, inter Christigenas iussit vinclis & carcere claudi.
units.tr: "Decius shut these men, flourishing in holy character, among the Christians in chains and prison."

units.la: Sub hoc pontifice, circa annum Christi 260, immani tyrannorum persecutione perterritus, Paulus primus eremita, solitaria loca petijt.
units.tr: Under this bishop, about the year of Christ 260, Paul the first hermit, terrified by the cruel persecution of tyrants, sought out lonely places.

units.la: Nam multi eo tempore Christiani, Eusebio teste, mortis metu fidem abnegabant: sicut nunc apud Anglos sub regina Maria. Hinc Monochatus originem sumpsit, ut Hieronymus refert in ui-ta eiusdem Pauli: & post eum Baptista Mantua-nus, in primo libro de vita Blasij.
units.tr: For at that time many Christians, as Eusebius testifies, denied their faith through fear of death, just as now among the English under Queen Mary. Hence monastic life took its origin, as Jerome relates in the life of this same Paul, and after him Baptista Mantuanus in the first book of the life of Blasius.

units.la: Tum pleriq; patres sancti, cum tale uiderent Excidium, fugere urbes, & more ferarum Per deserta uagi, caecis latuere cauernis.
units.tr: Then many holy fathers, seeing such destruction, fled the cities, and, like wild beasts, wandered through the deserts and hid in dark caves.

units.la: Ista ego crediderim per noxia tempora, Paulum Niligenam sole ardentem qui primus eremum Incoluit, liquisse urbes patriosq; penates, Et didicisse togas textus componere palmis.
units.tr: These things, I would believe, in those harmful times, Paul the Egyptian, scorched by the sun, who first dwelt in the desert, left cities and his ancestral household, and learned to weave cloth with his palms.
24. DIONYSIUS the Greek.

units.la: Dionysius Graecus, à Damaso pontifice Monachus, & à Nicolaio Harlemensi in Chronico temporum, Carmeli solitudinis incola nuncupatus: fidei documentis sub Claudio secundo clarus effulsit, & Christianæ Ecclesiæ amplificator insignis. Nec illi defuerunt aliæ ecclesiæ, quæ subor-tis tunc hæresibus, veritatis doctrina succurrere, ut patet de Antiochena: quæ congregata synodo anno Domini 273. Paulum Samosatenum erroris conuicit, cum ille tamen præ senio interesse non posset. Cyrillam Decij Cæsaris filiam, cum Tri-phonia matre, & 46. militibus, ad Christi fidem Dionysius conuertit: & cum eisdem tum demum, atque aliis nonnullis, anno Domini 277. martyrij palmam ad Salariæ portā suscepit. De quo Matuanus:
units.tr: Dionysius the Greek, called a monk by Pope Damasus, and by Nicolaus of Harlem in his Chronicle of Times, an inhabitant of the solitude of Carmel, shone forth clearly under Claudius the Second by the teachings of the faith, and was a notable enlarger of the Christian Church. Nor did other churches fail him, which, when heresies then arose, came to the aid of the doctrine of truth, as is clear from the Antiochene church, which, gathered in synod in the year of the Lord 273, convicted Paul of Samosata of error, although he could not attend because of his old age. Dionysius converted to the faith of Christ Cyrilla, daughter of Decius Caesar, with Triphonia her mother and forty-six soldiers; and with these at last, and some others, in the year of the Lord 277, he received the palm of martyrdom at the Salarian gate. Of him Mantuanus:

units.la: Hic erat occultus Christi de gente sacerdos / Graius enim, dudum Carmelo à monte profectus, / Vertice Carpathijs alto qui prominet undis.
units.tr: "Here was a hidden priest of Christ of the Greek race, for he had come long ago from the mountain of Carmel, which rises with its high peak above the Carpathian waves."
25[?]. FELIX of Rome.

units.la: Foelix Romanus, saeuiente in fratres imperatore Aureliano, uir integer ac bonus in uerbi ministerio[?] floruit. Quo homicida infœlicissimo tyrannidem exercente, Fœlix anno Domini 282 inter alios martyres ad Christum, hoc est à morte ad uitā fœ-licis[?] me transfiit[?]. Quod martyrum gloriæ consules, statuerit templa fieri, & sacrificia in eorum nomine quotannis celebrari, aperta blasphemia est. Quis enim crederet pios Ecclesiæ primitiuæ patres, lapides, ligna, aut mortuorum ossa, tam anxiè curare, inter tot persecutiones & haereses? ac si nihil aliud agendum tunc esset? Sed talia sunt Romanistarum[?] commenta, ut eorum idolatriæ approbarentur.
units.tr: Felix of Rome, while the emperor Aurelian raged against the brethren, flourished as a man upright and good in the ministry of the Word. When that most unhappy murderer exercised his tyranny, Felix, in the year of the Lord 282, among the other martyrs passed from death to life, that is, to Christ, to a happy life. That he, mindful of the glory of the martyrs, decreed that temples be built and sacrifices be celebrated every year in their name, is open blasphemy. For who would believe that the pious fathers of the primitive Church cared so anxiously for stones, wood, or the bones of the dead, amid so many persecutions and heresies, as if nothing else then needed to be done? But such are the inventions of the Papists, that their idolatry might be approved.
26. Eutychianus the Tuscan.

units.la: Eutychianus Thuscus, uir Deo deditissimus, à doctrinā & uirtutibus Ecclesiæ commendatus, diuini uerbi prædicatione, salutem multis attulit populus. Hic trecentos & 42 martyres sepelisse prius manibus dicitur, & constitutionem fecisse de ritu tumulandorum martyrum, martyr & ipse anno Christi 283. Domino tandem consecratus. Istum, se nihil fecisse pro confirmandis hypocritarum insanijs[?] videretur: fabas atq; vvas benedixisse in alta ri fabulantur Papistæ, & in collobijs purpuratis mortuos sepelisse. Officium certe Christi martyre dignum. Sed tales sunt Papicularum nugæ.
units.tr: Eutychianus the Tuscan, a man most devoted to God, was commended for his teaching and virtues. Through the preaching of the divine word he brought salvation to many people. It is said that he first buried with his own hands three hundred and forty-two martyrs, and that he laid down a regulation on the rite of burying martyrs. He himself was made a martyr in the year of Christ 283, and at last was consecrated to the Lord. The Papists fable that this man, as though he had done nothing to confirm the madness of hypocrites, blessed beans and grapes on the altar, and buried the dead in purple cloaks. Surely a duty worthy of a martyr of Christ. But such are the trifles of the little Papists.
27. Caius the Dalmatian.

units.la: Caius Dalmata, Cæsari Diocletiano cognatus, præpositus domus Dei in Ecclesia Romana pro batisimus, Eutychiano in salutaris verbi sacro ministerio successit. Hunc referunt ex suo Damaso, Paparum adulatores Carsulanus & Platina, cleri dignitates mirum in modum auxisse per varias ordinum distinctiones, ut per certos gradus ascensus fieret ad episcopatus apicem. Obganniunt etiam infulsissimi Papicolæ, vetuisse illum, sacris initiatos a profanis hominibus, paganis, & hæreticis, in ius vocari: si tam fatuus quispiam sit, qui credat tantam tunc fuisse Rom. pontificum autoritatem, regnantibus ipsis paganis ac politica iura administrantibus. Peruenit Gaius ad imperij tempora Diocletiani prædicti, sub quo continuata fuit sævissima persecutio: ita ut in cryptis & terræ cavernis, non in Papali palatio, aut templo magnifico, latuerit diu: atq; inde eductus anno Domini 295. una cum Gabinio fratre, presbytero coniugato, sub gladio vitam finiuerit. De Gaio atq; eius successore Marcellino, sic habet Mantuanus in vita Blasij,
units.tr: Caius the Dalmatian, a kinsman of the emperor Diocletian, was placed over the household of God in the Roman Church as its first baptizer, and succeeded Eutychianus in the saving ministry of the Word. Carsulanus and Platina, flatterers of the popes, report on the authority of his Damasus that he greatly increased the dignity of the clergy by various distinctions of orders, so that there might be an ascent by fixed steps to the summit of the episcopate. The utterly foolish Papists also babble that he forbade those initiated into the sacred rites to be summoned before the courts by profane men, pagans and heretics. Anyone would be a fool who believed that the authority of the Roman pontiffs was so great at that time, when the pagans themselves reigned and administered the civil laws. Caius lived into the time of the aforesaid Diocletian, under whom the most savage persecution continued, so that he lay hidden for a long time in crypts and caves of the earth, not in a papal palace or a magnificent temple. From there he was led out and, in the year of the Lord 295, together with his brother Gabinius, a married presbyter, he ended his life by the sword. Concerning Caius and his successor Marcellinus, Mantuanus says as follows in his life of Blasius:

units.la: Tum Gaius, qui praesul erat Romanus, in altis Delituit cryptis. Tunc Marcellinus et ipse, Romulidum pastor, uictus formidine Christum Prodidit, et plena Marti libauit acerra.
units.tr: Then Caius, who was the Roman prelate, hid himself in deep crypts. Then Marcellinus too, shepherd of the Romulidae, overcome by fear, betrayed Christ and poured incense onto the full altar of Mars.
28. Marcellinus the Roman.

units.la: Marcellinus Romanus, decima persecutione post Neronem, cum grauissime sub Diocletiano et Maximiano, a tortoribus urgeretur, poenarum timore correptus, thuris granum idolis adoleuit. Erant tuno sacrae scripturae (inquit noster Gildas) quaecunque inueniri poterant, in publicis plateis exustae: et electi sacerdotes gregis Domini, cum innocentissimis ouibus trucidati. Sed in se statim reuersus Marcellinus, agnito errore, Diocletianum ipsum redarguit, et ad necem pro Christi veritate seipsum lubens obtulit, anno Domini 303. fortissimeque pugnans uicit, accepta martyrij laurea. His astipulatur praedictus Mantuanus, in suo Bla-fio[?]:
units.tr: Marcellinus the Roman, in the tenth persecution after Nero, when he was most grievously pressed by the torturers under Diocletian and Maximian, seized by fear of punishments, offered a grain of incense to the idols. At that time, says our Gildas, all the holy Scriptures that could be found were burned in the public squares, and the chosen priests of the Lord's flock were slaughtered along with the most innocent sheep. But Marcellinus, returning to himself at once, acknowledged his error, rebuked Diocletian himself, and gladly offered himself to death for the truth of Christ, in the year of the Lord 303. Fighting most bravely he conquered, and received the laurel of martyrdom. The aforesaid Mantuanus agrees with this in his Blasius:

units.la: At scelus id mox erubuit, sensuque recepto, Incepit damnare Deos, extollere Christum: Nec mors horribilis uisa est, sed sponte cucurrit In medios hostes, iugulumque tetendit ad ensem. Fortior in pugnam post signa amissa reuersus Victor, et ornatus uiridi discessit oliua.
units.tr: But that crime he soon blushed at, and when he came to his senses he began to condemn the gods and extol Christ. Nor did he see death as dreadful, but ran of his own accord into the midst of the enemy and offered his throat to the sword. Returning bravely to battle after losing his standards, the victor departed crowned with green olive.
29. Marcellus the Roman.

units.la: Marcellus Romanus, pastor erat, Ecclesiam pa-scens prudentia & doctrina: ac vir secundum cor Dei, ut cum propheta loquar, & plenus operi-bus Christianis. Hic Maximianum Augustum pie admonuit, atque avertere nitebatur à persecutione sanctorum. Augustus autem magis induratus, ipsum flagellis [?] cædi iussit, & urbe expelli. Intravit ergo Lucinæ viduæ domum, ibiq; ecclesiam occultam tenuit, quod audiens tyrannus, ex eadem domo iumentorum stabulum fecit, & curam eius episcopo Marcello commisit. Epistolis inde, sine alio verbi ministerio ecclesiam gubernauit, ad sordida officia damnatus. Et in pœdore atq; immunditiis quotidie cruciatus, anno Domini 308. spiritum Servatori Christo reddidit tandem.
units.tr: Marcellus the Roman was a minister, feeding the Church with prudence and learning; a man after God's own heart, to speak with the prophet, and full of Christian works. He piously admonished the Augustus Maximian and strove to turn him from the persecution of the saints. But the emperor, hardened the more, ordered him to be beaten with whips and expelled from the city. He therefore entered the house of the widow Lucina, and there kept a hidden church. When the tyrant heard of this, he made a stable for beasts of burden out of the same house, and committed its care to the bishop Marcellus. Thereafter he governed the church by letters, without any other ministry of the Word, condemned to filthy offices. Tormented daily in filth and squalor, in the year of the Lord 308 he at last rendered his spirit back to Christ the Saviour.
30. Eusebius the Greek.

units.la: Eusebius Græcus, homo piissimus, Romanæ Eccle-siæ in magna persecutionum procella, Christianorum doctor ac magister, præfuit. In verbo Domi-ni tam Romæ, quàm alibi per patriam, fortiter ille laborabat, sub Maxentio horribili tyranno: donec esset, Maffæo [?] teste, martyrio & ipse, anno Domini 309. consumptus. Unde Angelus ad Blasium, ex Mantuano:
units.tr: Eusebius the Greek, a most pious man, presided over the Roman Church in the great storm of persecutions, as teacher and master of the Christians. He laboured bravely in the Word of the Lord both at Rome and elsewhere throughout the country, under Maxentius, a horrible tyrant, until, as Maffeus testifies, he too was consumed by martyrdom in the year of the Lord 309. Whence the angel to Blasius, from Mantuanus:

units.la: (quant[?] Quod mihi scire datur, fabor [?] tibi. Læta propin-
units.tr: (What has been granted me to know, I will tell you. Joyful

units.la: Tempora: principibus lex est imposita cruentis, Ne possint seuire diu. Quod sanguine gaudet, Hoc crudele genus, paucis abolebitur annis. Roma suos omnes mersos in sanguine uidit Pontifices, posthac tres est uisura cruentos. Illic finis erit: lugubria secula claudet Melchiades: pax est illo uentura sepulto.
units.tr: The times: a law has been imposed on the bloody princes, that they may not rage for long. This bloody race, which rejoices in blood, will be wiped out in a few years. Rome will see all her pontiffs drowned in blood, and afterwards she will see three more bloody ones. There will be the end; Melchiades will close the mournful ages; peace is to come when he is buried.
31. Melchiades the African.

units.la: Melchiades Apher, uir admodum religiosus, & gregis Dominici ductor, Euangelicae religionis ministerio, ac diuinae ueritatis negotio, usq; ad sui sanguinis effusionem, sub Maximiano Galerio processit: & anno Domini 314. in eiusde ueritatis confessione uitam finiuit. Legatur hoc loco Eusebij Caesariensis episcopi historia Ecclesiastica, de tot, deq; tam inusitatis & acerbissimis sanctorum eius temporis moribus.
units.tr: Melchiades the African, a man most devout and a leader of the Lord's flock, in the ministry of the Gospel religion and the business of divine truth, advanced under Maximian Galerius even to the shedding of his blood, and in the year of the Lord 314 he ended his life in the confession of that same truth. Let the ecclesiastical history of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, be read at this point, concerning so many and such unusual and bitter deaths of the saints of his time.

units.la: Plaustra decretorum ac mendaciorum, Carsulanus, Platina, Stella, & alij Paparū adulatores, his Christi martyribus, sed falso, tribuunt: ut suarum caeremoniarum, ne dicam blasphemiarum, institutio diabolica, eorum auctoritate, comprobetur. Non enim sunt ueritis spurcissimi nebulones Papicolae, pul cherrimam hanc ecclesiae primitiuae faciem, ac suo capiti Christo ex assidua persecutione similem, ad sui Abadonis folium erigendum, impijs his stercoribus fœdare, martyrumq; sanctorum polluere sanguine. Sed quis sapiens putaret, simplices uerbi mi-nistros & pastores, quales tunc erant Romani pontifices omnes, in latibulis, cryptis, ac specubus habitantes, & nihil sub tyrannis præter mortem indies expectantes, de statu pontificio, ædificiis, aut ordi-nationibus Papisticis cogitare, quum nec templa, nec certas ædes haberent? Nō adhuc erat ecclesiæ pax data: nondū fruebantur inutili ocio, ac summis mundi deliciis: nec fuit ipsi lesabeli, quæ se dicebat esse prophetam, Apocal.2. paratus adhuc lectum. Talia veruntamen erant pseudoprophetarum pro suo ven-tre commenta: atq; sic est Papistica synagoga il-la, insplendidis mendaciis fundata. Sed ridiculis his ac Satanæ nugis ad sacrificulorum quæstum confi-ctis, superioris sæculi more credere, stultissimū cer-te esset. Potius forent hoc loco spiritus explorandi, ut Ioannes iubet, num sint ex Deo,1. Ioan.4.quum multi pseudovates prodicerint in mundum. Huc usq; stellæ pastores erant, in ecclesiæ firmamento, tam doctrina quam exemplo coruscantes: in eiusq; fer-vatæ dextra manu, qui in septem candelabrorum deambulabat medio, Apocal.1. Huc usq; habebantur Angeli, æternam Dei optimi maximi volunta-tem, sine figmentis hominum pure nunciantes. Imo huc usq; per equum albū in ministerio figurantur, qui Christum uictorem, tam corde quàm corpore, tam ore quàm opere, fideliter serebant, Apocal.6.
units.tr: Carsulanus, Platina, Stella, and the other flatterers of the popes ascribe to these martyrs of Christ, but falsely, carts full of decrees and lies, so that by their authority the diabolical origin of their ceremonies, not to say their blasphemies, may be approved. For the most filthy scoundrel Papists, who are not ashamed of the truth, do not hesitate to defile this most beautiful face of the primitive Church, which resembled Christ its head through constant persecution, with these impious dung-heaps, and to pollute it with the blood of holy martyrs, in order to raise up the throne of their Abaddon. But what wise man would think that simple ministers and pastors, such as all the Roman pontiffs were at that time, living in hiding places, crypts and caves, and expecting nothing day by day under tyrants but death, thought about the papal state, buildings, or Papistical ordinations, since they had neither temples nor fixed dwellings? Peace had not yet been given to the Church; they did not yet enjoy idle leisure and the highest delights of the world; nor was there yet for Jezebel, who called herself a prophetess, a bed prepared (Apoc. 2). Yet such were the inventions of the false prophets for the sake of their bellies; and thus that Papistical synagogue is founded on shining lies. But to believe these ridiculous fabrications, devised by Satan for the profit of the little priests, in the manner of the previous age, would certainly be the most stupid thing. Rather, here the spirits ought to be tested, as John commands, whether they are of God (1 John 4), since many false prophets have gone out into the world. Up to this point the pastors were stars, shining in the firmament of the Church both by teaching and by example, and in the right hand of him who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands (Apoc. 1). Up to this point they were regarded as angels, purely announcing God's eternal will, without the fictions of men. Indeed, up to this point they are signified through the white horse in the ministry, who faithfully bore Christ the conqueror, in heart as in body, in mouth as in work (Apoc. 6).
SYLVESTER I, a Roman.

units.la: Sylvester primus, Romanus, prædicto Melchiadi in uerbi ministerio succedens, adhuc in Soracte monte ob mortis metum, more suorum prædecessorum, solitarius latitabat. Qui tamen, quiescente tum demum ab affligendis Christianorum ecclesiis tartareo dracone, Apocal.12. cassanteq; sub Cæsare Constantino, tyrannorum sæuitia, Romam redijt: desiitq; in illo, Romanorum episcoporum persecutio. De quibus omnibus, Baptista Mantuanus in 12 Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Sylvester the First, a Roman, succeeded the aforesaid Melchiades in the ministry of the Word. Like his predecessors, he hid himself as a solitary on Mount Soracte for fear of death. Yet when the Tartarean dragon, who afflicted the churches of Christians (Rev. 12), had at last ceased, and under Caesar Constantine the savagery of the tyrants had been broken, he returned to Rome. With him the persecution of the Roman bishops came to an end. Concerning all these things, Baptista Mantuanus writes in the twelfth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Multa sub atroci, uitæ discrimina passus Tarquino præfecto urbis secessit: & altum Se in Soracte tulit, sub quo delabitur amnis Albula, & in tacito fugit mala tempora saltu.
units.tr: Having suffered many dangers of life under the cruel Tarquin, the city prefect, he withdrew and took himself to high Soracte, beneath which the river Albula slides, and in a quiet hiding-place he fled from evil times.
On the reign of Constantine.

units.la: At postquam soboles Helenæ sanctissima, Cæsar Constantinus, apud diuos hominesq; fauorem Nactus, in excelso uidit crucis aere formam: In terrena Deus fecit descendere pacem Regna, cruentatos prohibens regnare tyrannos.
units.tr: But after the most holy offspring of Helena, Caesar Constantine, having gained the favour of gods and men, saw in the sky the form of the cross, God made the kingdoms of the earth descend to peace, forbidding bloodthirsty tyrants to reign.
On Sylvester's return.

units.la: Tum redijt tandem Romam, Soracte relicto, Atq; sub Augusto magnos sortitus honores, Credidit è Stygijs umbris se in sidera tolli.
units.tr: Then at last he returned to Rome, having left Soracte. And under Augustus, having obtained great honours, he believed that he was lifted from the Stygian shades to the stars.
On the Synod of Nicaea.

units.la: Tunc Synodus Nicæna fuit celebrata subipso Cæsare, & impietas Arrij damnata, volentis Partiri naturam unam natiq; patriq;.
units.tr: Then the Synod of Nicaea was celebrated under Caesar himself, and the impiety of Arius was condemned, who wished to divide the one nature of Son and Father.
On the churches of the Christians.

units.la: Cæsar hic in nostram gestars pia pectora gentem, Maxima templa Deo, diuisq; eduxit in auras. Immensas donauit opes, uasa aurea, fundos, Vnde sacerdotes magnis proventibus aucti.
units.tr: This Caesar, who bore our nation in his pious breast, raised the greatest temples to God and the saints into the air. He bestowed immense wealth: golden vessels and estates, whereby the priests were enriched with great revenues.

units.la: Huius Syluestri permulta struntur instituta de chrismate consecrando, ordinibus dandis, pueris confirmandis, templis prnandis [?], altaribus tegendis, missatoribus constituendis, ungendis, uestiendis [?]: hostijsq; (ut uocant) deificandis, adorandis, feruandis. Item de Dalmaticis, cappis, corporalibus, aliis, mitris, pallijs, pannis, peplis, sindonibus, sacrificijs, cæremonijs, asylis, extremis unctionibus, aliisq; ritibus, non solum Iudaicis, sed & ethnicis, superstitiosis [?], ac diabolicis, ab Apostolo Paulo atq; ipso Christo damnatis.
units.tr: Many institutions of this Sylvester are laid down concerning the consecration of chrism, the conferring of orders, the confirmation of boys, the preparing of temples, the covering of altars, the appointing of messengers, anointing, vesting, and the deifying, adoring and keeping of hosts (as they call them). Likewise concerning dalmatics, copes, corporals, mitres, palls, cloths, veils, linen, sacrifices, ceremonies, sanctuaries, extreme unctions, and other rites, not only Jewish but also heathen, superstitious and diabolical, condemned by the Apostle Paul and by Christ himself.

units.la: Dicitur quoq; à Polydoro, Platina, & aliis Romanistarum scriptoribus, ethnicorum dierum nomina, Solis, Lunæ, Martis, Mercurij, Iouis, Veneris, & Saturni, ad Christianorum vsum, in Iudæorum feriis commutasse, ac Phrygiam mitram aurei diadematis loco occupasse. De eius vero miraculis sic scribit prædictus Mantuanus: Magna quidem memorant alij miracula abipso Edita Syluestro: sed nullus idoneus autor, Nec tejis[?] productus adhuc: ideoq; relinquam Talia, quæ possunt quædam figmenta uideri. Nostra etenim nugas deliramentaq; damnat Religio, nec dat linguis mendacibus aures.
units.tr: It is also said by Polydore, Platina and other Romanist writers that Sylvester transferred to Christian use the names of the heathen days (Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn) in place of the Jewish feast-days, and that he put the Phrygian mitre in place of the golden diadem. Concerning his miracles, the aforesaid Mantuanus writes thus: "Other men indeed recount great miracles performed by Sylvester himself, but no trustworthy authority has yet been produced for them. Therefore I shall leave out such things, which may seem to be fictions. For our religion condemns trifles and lies, nor gives ears to lying tongues."
Sylvester died as a confessor in the year of the Lord 324[?].

units.la: Baptista Mantuanus, in secundo libro de uita diui Blasij, adducit angelum ad eundem Blasium inter alia sic loquetem, de prædicti Cæsaris Constantini magni imperio, deq; su uro ecclesiæ statu pacis tempore, de Cleri & populi uitijs, ac tandē plagis.
units.tr: Baptista Mantuanus, in the second book on the life of St Blaise, brings in an angel speaking to the same Blaise, among other things, thus: concerning the empire of the aforesaid Caesar Constantine the Great, concerning the state of the Church in time of peace, concerning the vices of clergy and people, and finally concerning the plagues.
On the empire of Constantine.

units.la: Nunc bonus, expulsis Romana in regna tyrannis, Adueniet Princeps, sub quo pacabitur orbis: Et sinem accipi ueterum cultura deorum.
units.tr: Now the good prince will arrive, having expelled the tyrants from the Roman kingdoms, and under him the world will be pacified; and the worship of the ancient gods will be brought to an end.

units.la: Constantinus apud Thraces, qua Bosphorus æquor Thracius Euxinis Ægeum ingurgitat undis, Constituet sedem imperij: Latiumq; relinquet Christo, et Romuleam septem cum collibus urbem. Tunc insigne crucis, quondam damnabile, surget Ex humili in sublime loco: præcedet honore Romanos sasces, & regia signa, coronas. Tunc inter superos unà lætabimur ambo: Utq;[?] ab excelsa mundi speculabimur arce.
units.tr: Constantine will set up the seat of his empire among the Thracians, where the Bosphorus pours the Thracian sea into the Aegean with Euxine waves. He will leave Latium and the city of Romulus with its seven hills to Christ. Then the sign of the cross, once damnable, will rise from a lowly place to a lofty one; it will go before, with honour, the Roman fasces, the royal standards and the crowns. Then we both shall rejoice together among the heavenly ones, and look down from the high citadel of the world.
On the harms to the Church from peace.

units.la: Hac tamen, ô Blasi, de tempestate quietis Pacificæ, clades heu deploranda sequetur: Et graue manabit dulci de melle venenum. Vox est blanda quies, pax delectabile nomen. Plura tamen de pace fluent, opprobria, damna, Dedecora, ærumnæ: quàm de crudelibus armis. Degenerabit enim virtus antiqua, voluptas Inter opes & delicias delumbia reddet Corpora: et amittet mens eneruata vigorem, O studia, ô mores, ô tempora sordida. Cerno Oblitos Christum populos, incredula corda, Conculcare fidem, scelus omne incurrere facto Agmine certatim, fieriq; animantia bruta, Et Romam in caulas, atq; in magalia versam.
units.tr: Yet, O Blaise, from this tempest of peaceful quiet a lamentable disaster will follow, alas, and a grievous poison will flow from sweet honey. Quiet is a soothing voice, peace a delightful name. Yet more reproach, loss, dishonour and distress will flow from peace than from cruel arms. For ancient virtue will degenerate, and pleasure amid riches and luxuries will render bodies flabby; the enervated mind will lose its vigour, its studies, its manners, and its times become sordid. I see peoples forgetting Christ, unbelieving hearts trampling on the faith, every crime rushing in with a crowd, each vying with the other, men becoming brute beasts, and Rome turned into sheepfolds and huts.
On the plagues that follow.

units.la: Cælicolæ, in gentes malè tunc animabimur illas, Atq; sua superi, quando impia sæcula cernent: Destituent ope terrigenas, caua tartara olentes, Irascente Deo, coitum mala sidera in unum Conuenient, tristes in humum iaculantia flammas. Atq; viam cœlum inveniet[?], qua conterat illud Infidum crudumq; genus. Solventur ab Arcto Terribiles hominum vultus, animiq; feroces: Sauromatæ, sine diuina sine lege humana Viventes, Hunni, Alani, Turci, atq; Agathirsi.
units.tr: Then the dwellers of heaven will be angered against those nations, when the impious ages behold their own ruin. The higher powers will abandon the earth-born men, who stink of the hollow pit of Tartarus, with God angered. Evil stars will come together into one, hurling sad flames to the ground. And heaven will find a way to crush that faithless and cruel race. From the North will be loosed the terrible faces of men and their fierce spirits: the Sarmatians, living without divine or human law, the Huns, the Alani, the Turks, and the Agathyrsi.

units.la: Adde, quòd inter se Christi intestina, nepotes Mutua more canum rabidorum in ulnera uersi, Bella gerent: Graecis Itali, Gallis Alemani, Certabunt odijs plusquam capitalibus: utq; Se extirpent, parcent Turcis, parcent Agarenis.
units.tr: Add that the intestines of Christ, his grandchildren, turned against each other's wounds like mad dogs, will wage war: Italians against Greeks, Germans against Gauls. They will fight with hatreds more than deadly, and in exterminating themselves they will spare the Turks, they will spare the Agarenes.

units.la: Non incommodum duxi, adjicere hoc loco, Ioannis Sleidani verba ex secundo libro de quatuor imperijs. Tunc primum (inquit) episcopi Romani coeperunt esse in tuto: nam hucusq; plerique omnes fuerant affecti supplicijs. Numerantur autem inde à Petro, quem ipsi primum fuisse volunt, ad hoc usq; tempus, triginta tres. Horum decreta sunt in libris inserta consiliorum: sed ex his pleraq; tam sunt leuiucula, tam nugatoria, tam aliena prorsus à sacris literis: ut credibile fit, ab aliis longo post tempore fuisse conficta. Sin autem vera sunt, & ab illis emanarunt, tunc sane, quod vaticinando Paulus dicebat, filium illum perditum, hominemq; peccati iam operari coepisse mysterium iniquitatis, rectissime videtur hanc etiam ad partem accommodari posse. Anacleto qui ponitur quartus à Petro, tribuitur, & extat decretum, quo statuit ecclesiam Romanam esse mandatu & constitutione Christi, caput aliarum Ecclesiarum: alteri post eum Alexandro, decretu ascribitur, quo mandat, ut aqua cū sale cõsecretur, ad expurgandum populum et amoliendū insidias. insidiæ diaboli. Quæso, quantum ista differunt ab Apostolorum illa maiestate, quantum autem à Johannis Euangelistæ scriptis, qui prope ad hoc usque tempus ætatem produxit? Hæc duo posui solum, ut de reliquis iudicium fieri possit. Nam fere sunt eius generis, & ambitionem apertè præ se ferunt. Et ut sermo est illatus, ita quoque res ipsa nihil habet satis, quem in ecclesiæ ministris Paulus requirit. Hæc etiam pertinet illud Constantini Cæsaris edictum, quod suis libris inseruerunt, ipsorum potentiæ videlicet fundamentum atque robur, & cætera.
units.tr: It seemed not inappropriate to add here the words of John Sleidan from the second book of the four empires. "For the first time," he says, "the Roman bishops began to be safe; for until then most of them had been subjected to punishments. Counting from Peter, whom they themselves wish to have been first, to this time there are thirty-three. Their decrees are inserted in the books of the councils: but many of these are so trivial, so trifling, so utterly alien to the sacred letters, that it is credible they were fabricated by others long afterwards. But if they are true and emanated from them, then indeed it seems most rightly that what Paul prophesied can be applied to this part too: that the son of perdition, the man of sin, had already begun to work the mystery of iniquity. To Anacletus, who is placed fourth from Peter, is attributed a decree in which he states that the Roman church, by the command and constitution of Christ, is the head of the other churches. To his successor Alexander a decree is ascribed, in which he orders that water be consecrated with salt, to purge the people and to drive away the snares of the devil. How far do these differ, I ask, from that majesty of the Apostles, and how far from the writings of the Evangelist John, who lived almost to this time? I have set forth these two only, so that a judgement may be made about the rest. For they are nearly of that kind, and openly display ambition. And as the style is, so the matter itself has nothing sufficient of what Paul requires in the ministers of the Church. To this also pertains that edict of Caesar Constantine which they have inserted in their books, the very foundation and strength of their power, and the rest.

units.la: LIBER SECVNDVS. SECVNDA Romanorum Episcoporum classis, à Sylvestro ad Bonifacium tertium: in qua mitrati Pontifices erant, canonibus ac decretis suis, Antichristo magno sedem parantes.
units.tr: BOOK II. The second class of Roman bishops, from Sylvester to Boniface III: in which mitred pontiffs prepared a seat for the great Antichrist by their canons and decrees.
Roman pontiffs or archbishops.
1. Marcus, Roman.

units.la: Marcus Romanus, Hostiensem episcopum, qui Rom. pontificem præ cæteris consecraret, pallio donavit: & symbolum Nicænum, in diebus Dominicis post lectum Euangelium, à clero & populo decantari præcepit. Templa cōstruxit, ac varijs donis ornavit: & anno Domini 335. confessor demum obijt.
units.tr: Marcus, a Roman, gave the pallium to the bishop of Ostia, who was to consecrate the Roman pontiff in preference to others. He also ordered that the Nicene Creed be sung by the clergy and people after the Gospel was read on Sundays. He built churches and adorned them with various gifts, and he died a confessor in the year of the Lord 335.
2. Julius I, Roman.

units.la: Julius primus, Romanus, constituit, ne sacerdos alibi. alibi, quàm apud Ecclesiasticum iudicem, causam diceret: & orientales episcopos reprehendit, quòd sine sua autoritate concilia celebrassent. Cœmeteria fieri fecit, atq; in pace tandem anno Domini 351. confessor mortuus est.
units.tr: Julius I, a Roman, decreed that a priest should not bring his case anywhere other than before the ecclesiastical judge. He rebuked the eastern bishops because they had held councils without his authority. He had cemeteries made, and at last he died a confessor in peace in the year of the Lord 351.
3. Liberius, Roman.

units.la: Liberius Romanus, ambitionis gratia in Arriana haeresim, Hieronymo teste, prolapsus, à fidei integritate recessit, & dictis Arrianis subscripsit. Qui anno Domini 366. moritur & ille confessor.
