units.tr: Liberius, a Roman, out of desire for position, fell into the Arian heresy, as Jerome testifies, departed from the integrity of the faith, and subscribed to the Arian formulas. He too died a confessor in the year of the Lord 366.
4. Felix II, Roman.

units.la: Foelix secundus, Romanus, pulso Liberio, ab Arrianis praeficiebatur, sperantibus quòd cum illis in doctrina sentiret. Qui secundo sui pontificatus anno, Liberio iterum restituto, sede sua depellitur: & anno Domini 359. cum quibusdam presbyteris in quodam tumultu occiditur. Hic, teste Isidoro, leges pro cleri defensione composuit.
units.tr: Felix II, a Roman, was set up by the Arians when Liberius was driven out, in the hope that he would agree with them in doctrine. In the second year of his pontificate, after Liberius was restored again, he was deposed from his see. In the year of the Lord 359 he was killed in a tumult together with some presbyters. According to Isidore, this man drew up laws for the defence of the clergy.
5. Damasus, Spaniard.

units.la: Damasus Hispanus, in quadam contentione pontifex factus, & de adulterio vehementer accusatus, Liberij facta damnauit, templa construxit, ac muneribus ornauit, fundos & balneas clero dedit, cultus peregrinos auxit, Missae confessionem addidit, Psalmorum cantiones instituit, & Hieronymi translationem approbauit. Ambitio enim pontificum animos impensius tunc subire coepit. Postea Damasus, diligens temporum supputator, vitas & statuta suorum praedecessorum Romanorum pontificum, quamuis non sine apertissimis mendacis, succincte digessit: atq; anno Domini 384. confessor in pace quievit.
units.tr: Damasus, a Spaniard, was made pontiff amid a contest, and was vehemently accused of adultery. He condemned the acts of Liberius, built churches and adorned them with gifts, gave farms and baths to the clergy, increased the pilgrim cults, added the confession to the Mass, instituted the chanting of the Psalms, and approved Jerome's translation. For at that time the ambition of the pontiffs began to take hold of their minds more strongly. Afterwards Damasus, a careful reckoner of the times, briefly set out the lives and decrees of his predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, although not without very obvious lies. In the year of the Lord 384 he rested in peace as a confessor.
6. Siricius, Roman.

units.la: Syricius Romanus, multa constituens, bigamos à Missæ ministeriis submovit, & Monachos primus ad ordines, ob coelibatus fucum admisit: qui prius nec inter clericos habebantur. Antiphonas Psalmis admiscuit, Missæ memoriam adjunxit, ordines per interualla dandos sanciuit, & anno Domini 399. confessor occubuit.
units.tr: Siricius, a Roman, made many regulations. He removed men who had married twice from the ministry of the Mass, and he was the first to admit monks to orders, as a cover for celibacy; before this they were not even counted among the clergy. He mixed antiphons into the Psalms, added a commemoration to the Mass, decreed that orders be conferred at set intervals, and in the year of the Lord 399 he died as a confessor.
7. Anastasius, Roman.

units.la: Anastasius Romanus, ordinavit, ut stantes, & non sedentes, Evangelij lectionem audirent. Mancos vero, debiles, & morbosos, à ministerio reiecit: atque in pace confessor anno Domini 404. cum patribus obdormivit.
units.tr: Anastasius, a Roman, ordained that people should hear the reading of the Gospel standing, not sitting. He rejected from the ministry those who were maimed, feeble or diseased, and in the year of the Lord 404 he fell asleep in peace as a confessor, with his fathers.
8. Innocent, of Alba.

units.la: Innocentius Albanus sedem Romanam omnibus aliis praetulit, ac nullius judicio subjiciendam esse censuit. Sabbati jejunium fidelibus indixit, ut Christum eo ipso die tumulatum, cum Magdalena dolerent. Ut pax in Missa daretur ordinavit: ac templum[?] semel consecratum (res magni momenti) non amplius esse consecrandum decreuit. De Iudæis, paganis, & Monachis regulas quasdam tulit, & ex infirmorum unctione sacramentum fecit: interq; mortuos confessores anno Domini 416. numera-tur.
units.tr: Innocent of Alba held the Roman see above all others, and judged that it was subject to no one's judgment. He appointed a fast on the Sabbath for the faithful, so that they might mourn with Mary Magdalene that Christ had been buried on that very day. He ordained that the peace be given during the Mass, and decreed that a church, once consecrated (a matter of great importance), should not be consecrated again. He issued certain rules concerning Jews, pagans and monks, and he made a sacrament of the anointing of the sick. Among the dead confessors he is counted in the year of the Lord 416.
9. Zosimus, a Greek.

units.la: Sozimus Græcus constituit, ut cereus sabbato sancto benediceretur, & ut in celebrationibus, diaconi læuas lynostimis tectas haberent. Vetuit etiā ut clerici in publico biberent, aut tabernas fouerent[?], ac ne serui in clerum reciperentur. Et anno Domini 420. rebus humanis confessor excessit.
units.tr: Zosimus, a Greek, decreed that the Paschal candle be blessed on Holy Saturday, and that deacons have their left hands covered with cloths during the celebrations. He also forbade clerics to drink in public or to frequent taverns, and forbade that slaves be received into the clergy. In the year of the Lord 420 he departed from human affairs as a confessor.
10. Boniface, Roman.

units.la: Bonifacius Romanus, sacerdotis lucundi filius, in magna cleri seditione electus, ualde necessarias (si diis placet) constitutiones fecit, scilicet, ne mulier, quamuis velata monacha, altaris palam aut uasa attingat sacra, neque incensum adoleat: nec ante tricesimum ætatis annum sacerdos quisquam ordinetur. Hic anno Domini 426. post institutas sanctorum uigilias, confessor occubuit.
units.tr: Boniface, a Roman, son of a priest named Lucundus, was elected amid a great disturbance of the clergy, and made very necessary (so help me the gods) constitutions, namely that a woman, even if she is a veiled nun, must not touch the altar or the sacred vessels openly, nor burn incense; and that no priest be ordained before the thirtieth year of his age. He died a confessor in the year of the Lord 426, after establishing the vigils of the saints.
11. Celestine, Campanian.

units.la: Coelestinus Campanus, introitum, graduale, re-sponsorium, tractum, & offertorium, ut propria mueta[?], Papistica Missæ inseruit: atq; ut sacerdotes pontificum canones jcirent, arcte praecepit Germanum in Britanniam, Palladium in Scotiam, & Patricium cum quodam Segetio in Hyberniam, ut Pelagianas haereses extirparet, episcopos misit. Obijt anno 435. confessorum numero adscriptus.
units.tr: Celestine, a Campanian, inserted into the Papistical Mass the introit, gradual, responsory, tract and offertory, as its own proper additions. He strictly ordered that priests should learn the canons of the pontiffs. He sent bishops: Germanus to Britain, Palladius to Scotland, and Patrick with a certain Segetius to Ireland, to root out the Pelagian heresies. He died in 435 and was counted among the confessors.
12. Sixtus the Third, a Roman.

units.la: Sixtus tertius, Romanus, Ecclesiarum ditator nominatus: ecclesiam Mariae maioris post miraculum nivis extruxit, ac magnis muneribus ditauit, argento & auro basilicas decorauit. Eudoxiae mulieris adhortationibus, Petri catenas consecrauit, & eisdem annuale festum fieri confirmauit. Obijt confessor, anno Domini 440. in urbe sepultus. De templo Mantuanus:
units.tr: Sixtus the Third, a Roman, was named the enricher of the churches. After the miracle of the snow he built the church of St Mary Major and enriched it with great gifts, and he adorned the basilicas with silver and gold. At the urging of the woman Eudoxia, he consecrated the chains of Peter and confirmed that an annual feast should be kept for them. He died as a confessor in the year of the Lord 440 and was buried in the city. Mantuan, on the temple:

units.la: Hoc Mariae templum dixit maioris, & ipso In frontispicio templi niuis albicat imber.
units.tr: This temple, he said, is of Mary the Greater, and on its very front the snowy shower gleams white.
And on the feast of the chains.

units.la: Sic quoq; decretum est, petro debere Calendas Esse sacras poribac, & dici ad uincula festum.
units.tr: So too it was decreed that the Kalends should be sacred to Peter, and that the feast be called "At the Chains."
13. Leo I, the Tuscan.

units.la: Leo primus, Thuscus, in canone Missae, Sanctum sacrificium, immaculatam hostiam, & hanc igitur oblationem non sine magna Dei blasphemia addidit. In Cornelij episcopi honorem (idolatria) basilicam erexit, & Apostolorum sepulchris clericos custodes adiunxit, Statuis mortuorum tuorum reuerentiam exhiberi decreuit, ac Missæ sacrificium approbauit. Hic pontifex Leo, anno Domini 462. confessor occubuit. Mantuanus:
units.tr: Leo I, a Tuscan, added to the canon of the Mass the phrases "holy sacrifice," "immaculate victim," and "this therefore oblation," and not without great blasphemy against God. In honour of Bishop Cornelius he erected a basilica (an idolatry), and he attached clerks as guardians to the tombs of the Apostles. He decreed that reverence be shown to the statues of the dead, and he approved the sacrifice of the Mass. This pontiff Leo died a confessor in the year of the Lord 462. Mantuan:

units.la: At Leo bis denâ cum iam regnasset & unam Tandem hiemes, obijt curis oppressus & ævo.
units.tr: But Leo, when he had already reigned twice ten years and one, at last died, worn down by cares and by the years.
14. Hilary, a Sardinian.

units.la: Hilarius Sardus, in extruendis & ornandis tem-plis, vir valde assiduus erat. Ille crucis Domini-cæ lignum auro ac gemmis adornauit: decreta synodalia fecit, & per universum mundum servanda publicauit. Minis-trum omnem, qui viduam aut re-pudiatam, & non virginem in uxorem duxerit, à sacerdotali officio repellendum curauit: confes-sorq;, anno Domini 469. tum demum ex hac vita migrauit. Eius tempore Mamertus Claudius, episcopus Viennensis, triduanas ante Ascensionem li-taneas seu processiones instituit. De quibus Mantuanus in quarto Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Hilary the Sardinian was a man very diligent in building and adorning churches. He adorned the wood of the Lord's cross with gold and gems; he made synodal decrees and published them to be observed throughout the whole world. He saw to it that any minister who had married a widow or a divorced woman, and not a virgin, was to be removed from the priestly office. He died a confessor in the year of the Lord 469, and only then departed from this life. In his time Mamertus Claudianus, bishop of Vienne, instituted the litanies or processions on the three days before the Ascension. Of these Mantuan writes in the fourth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Vrbs sedet ad Rhodanum, Galli dixere Viennam Quæ tulit aduersos casus, pastore Mamerto; Et longum vexata fuit. Nam fulmine crebro Arsit, & horrificis terrarum motibus arua Scissa debiscebant, rimis penetrantibus usq; Ad Stygios amnes, ubi sunt Iouis antra profundi, Adde lupos: qui, tartareis agitantibus umbris, In furias acti, nedum iumenta per agros,
units.tr: The city of Vienne sits on the Rhone; the Gauls called it Vienne. Under its shepherd Mamertus it bore adverse calamities, and it was afflicted for a long time. For it burned with frequent lightning, and with dreadful earthquakes the fields were split and gaped open, the cracks penetrating down to the Stygian streams, where lie the caves of deep Jove. Add the wolves, who, stirred up by Tartarean shades and driven to frenzy, dared to tear not only the beasts in the fields but men too, even in the cities themselves.

units.la: Audebant laniare homines & in urbibus ipsis. Casibus his perculsi omnes, diuina coacti Quaerere subsidia, & diuos excire precando. Hinc traxit litanea ortum: transiuit in omnes Relligio similis paruo post tempore gentes.
units.tr: Struck down by these calamities, all were compelled to seek divine help and to summon the gods by prayer. Hence the litany took its origin, and a similar rite passed to all nations after a short time.
15. Simplicius of Tibur.

units.la: Simplicius Tiburtinus, basilicas dedicauit, urbem in quinq; regiones presbyteris diuisit, & sacrifi-culis hebdomadas assignauit. Ecclesiarum omnium primam, Romanam declarauit: in Rauennatenses tyrannice ius usurpauit, Ecclesiasticumq; benefici-um, ne a laico clericus recognoscat, praecepit. Con-fessor & ipse, anno Domini 484. hunc mundum deseruit.
units.tr: Simplicius of Tibur dedicated basilicas, divided the city into five regions among the presbyters, and assigned the lesser clergy their weekly duties. He declared the Roman church first of all churches; he tyrannically usurped rights over the church of Ravenna, and he ordered that an ecclesiastical benefice must not be held by a cleric from a layman. He too died a confessor in the year of the Lord 484 and departed from this world.
16. Felix III, the Roman.

units.la: Foelix tertius, Romanus, Fœlicis sacerdotis fili-us, statuit ut episcopi tantum, non minores sacerdotes, templa dedicarent: festumq; dedicationis eorum approbauit. Agapeti basilicam consecrauit, re-sponsionis inducias clericis accusatis dari censuit: & anno Domini 494. confessor in pace quieuit.
units.tr: Felix III, a Roman, son of the priest Felix, decreed that only bishops, and not lesser priests, should dedicate churches, and he approved the feast of their dedication. He consecrated the basilica of Agapetus, and he ruled that clerks who were accused should be given a respite in which to answer. In the year of the Lord 494 he rested in peace as a confessor.
17. Gelasius Apber.

units.la: Gelasius Apber, episcopi Valerij filius, Mani-chæorum codices combusit: hymnos, praefationes, gradualia, collectas, & orationes perscripsit: ab authenticis libris discreuit apocryphos: ac biga mos suam habentes dispensationem, ad sacerdoti-um admisit. Clerum auxit, basilicas dedicauit, & clericorum ordines quater in anno dari praecepit, precum clausulas, Vere dignum, ac, Te igitur, mis-se adiecit: tandemq; se ac successores suos a nemine iudicandos asseruit: & anno Domini 497. confessor est defunctus.
units.tr: Gelasius Apber, son of the bishop Valerius, burned the Manichaean books; he wrote out hymns, prefaces, graduals, collects, and prayers; he separated the apocryphal books from the authentic ones; and he admitted to the priesthood bigamists, who have their own dispensation. He increased the clergy, dedicated basilicas, and ordered that orders of clergy be conferred four times a year. He added to the Mass the closing clauses "Vere dignum" and "Te igitur." Finally he asserted that he and his successors were to be judged by no one. He died a confessor in the year of the Lord 497.
18. Anastasius II, the Roman.

units.la: Anastasius secundus, Romanus, Eutychianis ac Nestorianis fauit, haereticis communicauit, Caesarem excommunicauit: atq; anno Domini 499. dum ventrem exonerareret, ut Volaterranus habet, intestina in latrinam emittens, confessor obiit.
units.tr: Anastasius II, a Roman, favoured the Eutychians and the Nestorians, communicated with heretics, and excommunicated the emperor. In the year of the Lord 499, while he was emptying his bowels, sending his intestines out into the latrine (as Volaterranus reports), he died a confessor.
19. Symmachus, the Sardinian.

units.la: Symmachus Sardus, magna cleri discordia creatus est pontifex. Qui statuit, ut virgines uel ui-duae continentiam professae, ulterius non nubant: & ne clericus quisquam cum muliere, nisi sanguine iuncta, habitet. Basilicas multas a fundamentis erexit, missam in formam redegit: in natalicijs mortuorum sanctorum, Gloria in excelsis, cani[?] praecepit: & si Gregorij dialogis adhibenda sit fides, Paschasij diaconi animam pertinacem, purgatorio post mortem deputauit, anno autem Domini[?] 514. confessor & iste à mundo demigrauit.
units.tr: Symmachus, a Sardinian, was created pontiff amid great discord among the clergy. He decreed that virgins, or widows who had professed continence, should not marry again, and that no cleric should live with a woman unless she was joined to him by blood. He erected many basilicas from the foundations and reduced the Mass to a fixed form. On the anniversaries of the dead saints he ordered the Gloria in excelsis to be sung. And if Gregory's Dialogues deserve belief, he assigned the soul of the obstinate deacon Paschasius to purgatory after death. In the year of the Lord 514 this man too, a confessor, departed from the world.
20. Hormisdas of Campania.

units.la: Hormisda Campanus clerum composuit, Psalmos alternatim cantari ordinauit, conciliorum decreta seruanda proposuit, ad templorum ornatum pluraq; contulit, trabem argenteam mille & 40. librarum in diui Petri templo reliquit: & ne altaria sine praesulis assensu erigerentur, mandauit: nuptijs publicis caeremonijs addidit: ac Cæsarem Anastasium excommunicauit, quia dicebat, Imperatoris proprium esse imperare, non imperata pontificis accipere. tantum tunc ualuit Antichristi spiritus. Ex archiepiscopo, ut author est Isidorus, pa-triarcham Romanum Iustinus Imperator hunc fecit: qui anno Domini 523. confessor in fata concessit. Hucusq; a Syluestro per ducentos annos, archiepiscopi fuerunt, ab anno scilicet Domini 320 usq; ad annum 520 in quo primum a Cæsare Iustino, ut di-ctum est, effecti sunt patriarchae. Atque eo diligen-tius haec retuli, ut sciret industrius lector, quibus gradibus pontifices Romani, ad ipsum peruenerint Papatum: & quibus artibus diabolus in ipsis sit usus, antequam magnus ille Antichristus aduenerit, & ad plenum reueletur.
units.tr: Hormisdas of Campania arranged the clergy, ordered the psalms to be sung alternately, proposed that the decrees of the councils be observed, and contributed much to the adornment of churches. He left a silver beam weighing 1,040 pounds in the temple of St Peter. He ordered that altars not be erected without the bishop's consent, added public ceremonies to weddings, and excommunicated the emperor Anastasius, because he said it was the emperor's own business to command, not to receive commands from the pontiff. So much did the spirit of Antichrist prevail at that time. As Isidore reports, the emperor Justin made him patriarch of Rome from archbishop. He died a confessor in the year of the Lord 523 and passed away. Up to this point, from Sylvester for two hundred years, they were archbishops, namely from the year of the Lord 320 until 520, in which year they were first made patriarchs by the emperor Justin, as has been said. I have related these things the more carefully so that the diligent reader may know by what steps the Roman pontiffs attained the papacy, and by what arts the devil used them before that great Antichrist comes and is fully revealed.
21. John I.

units.la: Ioannes primus, Thuscus, quem Theodoricus Italiae Rex, ad Iustinum Caesarem, cum quibusdam aliis, suum oratorem misit (subiecti principibus tunc erant) dignissimus omnium huius posterioris classis pontifex, patientia immeritae mortis, uitae sanctitatem testatus est. Constituit ille, & pie quidem, ut spoliatus quisque in integrum restitueretur. Sed quod tria coemeteria restituerit, templa donis locupletauerit, aut altaria auro, argento & gemmis ornauerit, apud Platinam & alios, ne nihil ad Antichristi regnum fecisse uideretur, fabulam esse credo.
units.tr: John I, a Tuscan, whom King Theodoric of Italy sent with certain others as his envoy to the Emperor Justin (at that time they were subject to princes), was the most worthy pope of this later class. He attested the holiness of his life by his patience in an undeserved death. He ordered, and indeed piously, that each person who had been despoiled be restored to his full property. But I believe it is a fable, as Platina and others report, that he restored three cemeteries, enriched the churches with gifts, or adorned the altars with gold, silver and jewels, lest he seem to have done nothing toward the kingdom of Antichrist.

units.la: Extat eius ad Episcopos Italiae, epistola quaedam consolationis plena, qua monet eos, quam praedictus rex Theodoricus, haeresi pollutus Arriana, uastitatem ipsis & toti minitaretur Italiae: ne tamen ab instituto desistant, sed fortiter agant. Apud Rauennam igitur anno Domini 527. tyrannico iussu dicti Theodorici, pedore, situ, & in edia, in carcere martyr periit,
units.tr: There survives a letter of his to the bishops of Italy, full of consolation, in which he warns them that King Theodoric, polluted with the Arian heresy, was threatening them and all Italy with devastation, yet they should not desist from their purpose but act bravely. Therefore at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord 527, by the tyrannical command of the said Theodoric, he died a martyr in prison, of foul disease, squalor and hunger.
Mantuan writes thus about Arius: Mantuanus:

units.la: Arrius humani generis letale uenenum, Legis in excidium natus, fideiq; ruinam, Polluerat gentes, totumq; infecerat orbem.
units.tr: Arius, the deadly poison of the human race, born for the destruction of the law and the ruin of the faith, had polluted the nations and infected the whole world.
22. Felix IV.

units.la: Foelix quartus, Samnita, in cura pastorali ut valde solicitus: reiecto praedicationis officio, Cosmae et Damiani fanum exaedificauit, Saturnini templum restituit, aliaque mortuorum hominum templa refecit. Missas in locis consecratis tantum fieri praecepit, clerum a populo in Ecclesiis discreuit, patriarcham Constantinopolitanum de haeresi notatum excommunicauit, defunctis sacrificulis successores post biduum dari statuit: et ut morientes ungerentur adiurato oleo distinctius madauit (pontificalia certe officia) cōfessōrq; anno Domini 530. demum decessit.
units.tr: Felix IV, a Samnite, was very anxious about the pastoral care. Having rejected the office of preaching, he built a shrine to Cosmas and Damian and restored the temple of Saturn, and he repaired other temples of dead men. He ordered that masses be celebrated only in consecrated places, he separated the clergy from the people in the churches, he excommunicated the patriarch of Constantinople, who had been marked as a heretic, and he decreed that successors be appointed for deceased priests after two days. He also instructed more precisely that dying people be anointed with exorcised oil (surely pontifical functions). He died in the year of the Lord 530, a confessor.
23. Boniface II.

units.la: Bonifacius secundus, Romanus, clericis inter se dissentientibus, non sine acri contentione creatus pontifex: canones quosdam edidit, praecipue, ut tertio die in demortui pontificis locum alius surrogaretur, ordinauit. Populum a clero, Foelicem secutum, in sacris audiendis diuisit, duplici cautela: ut eos in electione pontificum, suis vocibus ac locis tandem priuaret: et ne cuiquam eorum liceret, in ciuili uel criminali causa, Episcopum aut clericum ad secularem iudicem uocare. Sed uide quid miseris illis (meo quidem iudicio) ex hac arrogantia euenerit, dum per capita rasa, digitos unctos, et fa-cella cella disiuncta, caeteris sanctiores, cum ipsis Pharisaeis haberi voluerint, à Christi sanguine redemptis fidelibus se separantes, atrium illud ingrediuntur, quod calamo non metiri, sed eijci foras, Apocalypseos 11. Dominus iusserit. Timendum est ipsis, ne inde fiant haedi, ab agnis in ultimo examine segregandi, Matthaei 25. tanquam ad mysticum Christi corpus impertinentes. Facile est iudicare, quantum isti ab apostolo Petro discrepent, quem tantopere iactitant: cui fas non erat, Cornelium gentilem, Actorum 10. laicum vel profanum statuere. Bonifacius anno Domini 532. confessor decubuit.
units.tr: Boniface II, a Roman, was created pope not without fierce contention, the clergy being divided among themselves. He issued certain canons, chiefly ordering that on the third day another be substituted in the place of the deceased pope. He divided the people, who had followed Felix, from the clergy in the hearing of sacred services, with a double precaution: that in the election of popes they be deprived of their voices and places; and that none of them be allowed, in a civil or criminal case, to summon a bishop or cleric before a secular judge. But see what, in my judgment, has come of this arrogance for those wretched men, while, distinguished by shaven heads, anointed fingers and separate cells, wishing to be held holier than the others, indeed with the Pharisees themselves, they separate themselves from the faithful redeemed by Christ's blood, and enter that court which the Lord ordered not to be measured with a reed but cast out, Apocalypse 11. They ought to fear lest they become goats from which the sheep are to be separated at the last judgment, Matthew 25, as having no part in the mystical body of Christ. It is easy to judge how far these men differ from the apostle Peter, whom they boast of so much: for it was not lawful for him to make Cornelius, a Gentile, a layman or profane person, Acts 10. Boniface, a confessor, lay down in the year of the Lord 532.
24. John II.

units.la: Ioannes secundus, Romanus, qui alio nomine propter eloquentiam, Mercurius seu Iouis nuncius dicebatur. Huic Iustinianus Caesar scyphum aureum gemmis ornatum, librarum sex, duos argenteos scyphos librarum septem, & calices duos argenteos librarum 15. ex Constantinopoli dono misit, postquam Anthemium patriarcham haeresos damnasset. Iusitq; idem imperator, Crantzio teste, suos Episcopos eius nomine, cum benedictione amicissime convenire pontificem. De vita confessor, anno Domini 534. hic pontifex demigravit, & iuxta Vuicelium, nihil eximium gessisse dicitur.
units.tr: John II, a Roman, who on account of his eloquence was also called by another name, Mercury, or messenger of Jupiter. The Emperor Justinian sent him from Constantinople a golden cup adorned with jewels, weighing six pounds, two silver cups weighing seven pounds, and two silver chalices weighing fifteen pounds, after he had condemned the patriarch Anthemius for heresy. The same emperor, as Crantzius bears witness, ordered his bishops to meet the pope most amicably in his name, with blessing. As for his life, he was a confessor; he departed in the year of the Lord 534, and according to Wicelius he is said to have done nothing outstanding.
25. Agapetus I.

units.la: AGapetus primus.Romanus, Presbyteri Cardinalis Gordiani filius, à Theodato Gothorum rege orator missus erat ad Iustinianum placandum, super crudeli interitu Amalasiunthae, optimae reginæ, mulierisq; doctissimæ: cuius claras virtutes magnificiebat idem Caesar: qui & eius procurabat pacem, consumptis sancti Petri thesauris. Constituit ille diebus Dominicus processiones in Ecclesiis fieri, ut Papismum augeret, & anno Domini 535. a-nimam confessor edidit.
units.tr: Agapetus I, a Roman, son of the presbyter and cardinal Gordianus, had been sent as envoy by the Gothic king Theodahad to appease Justinian over the cruel death of Amalasuntha, an excellent queen and a most learned woman, whose famous virtues the same Caesar extolled; and he also procured peace for them, using up the treasures of St Peter. He decreed that processions be held in the churches on Sundays, so as to increase Papism, and in the year of the Lord 535 he gave up his soul, a confessor.
26. Silverius of Campania.

units.la: Sylverius Campanus, Hormisdæ Romani Pontifi-cis filius, post Agapeti in itinere mortem, iuben-te Gothorum rege Theodato prædicto, in eius lo-cum sine Imperatoris consensu assumebatur. Insti-gante igitur Vigilio diacono, eumq; fortiter accu-sante, quòd Romam Gothis prodere voluisset, in exilium à Theodora Augusta & Antonina Belisa-rij ducis uxore, in Pontum insulam relegatus fuit.
units.tr: Silverius of Campania, son of the Roman pope Hormisdas, after Agapetus died on his journey, was taken up into his place without the consent of the Emperor, by command of the aforementioned Gothic king Theodahad. Then, at the urging of the deacon Vigilius, who vigorously accused him of having wished to betray Rome to the Goths, he was relegated into exile on the island Pontus by Theodora the Augusta and Antonina, wife of the general Belisarius.

units.la: Res parui, ut apparet, momenti, Papatus Romanus tunc erat: cum inferiorum principum iussu ac mandato, pontifices eius nuncij mitterentur, & à fœminis exautorari aut loco amoueri possint. Sylverius anno Domini 537. in eo exilio, confessor cu-llatus, miserè demum periit.
units.tr: It was evidently a matter of little importance, then, the Roman papacy: when popes were sent as envoys by the command and order of lesser princes, and could be deposed or removed from their office by women. Silverius, a confessor shut up in that exile, at last miserably perished in the year of the Lord 537.
27. VIGILIUS, Roman.

units.la: Vigilius Romanus, iam dicti Syluerij accusator ajlutus[?], & fraude pontificatum ambiens, à præ-fatis mulieribus in eius est suffictus[?] locum. Sic duo simul Romæ tunc pontifices erant: alter à Gothis, alter à Græcis, seu potius à mulierculis admissi: & male, at non indigne, ab illis tractabantur. Vterq; enim suæ temeritatis meritas luit pœnas. Nā hic dolo, ille ui, Pontificatum est adeptus: ambo tamen sunt à Papicolis, sanctus martyribus adnumerati. Vigilium Theodora in ius uocauit, quòd promissis non staret. Et Constantinopolim adductum, contumeliisq; ac uerberibus affectum, fune[?] in eius collum iniecto, per urbis plateas illum trahi fecit, & tum demum in exilium pelli. Hic proprias le-ctiones diebus festis aptauit, Romanam ecclesiam aliarum matrem haberi uoluit: candelarum festum instituit, & ut Missa celebretur uersus Orientem. In Sicilia tandem anno Domini 554. mortem & ipse confessor obiit. Horum temporibus Maurus in Gallijs monasticam hypocrisin docuit.
units.tr: Vigilius, a Roman, the helper of the accuser of the aforesaid Silverius, and eager for the papacy by fraud, was installed in the place of the same Silverius by the aforementioned women. So at that time there were two popes at Rome at once: one admitted by the Goths, the other by the Greeks, or rather by silly women. Both were treated badly, but not undeservedly, by those men. Each paid the due penalty for his rashness: the one obtained the papacy by trickery, the other by force. Yet both are counted by the Papists among the holy martyrs. Theodora summoned Vigilius to court, because he did not keep his promises. Brought to Constantinople and treated with insults and blows, with a rope put around his neck, she had him dragged through the streets of the city, and at last driven into exile. He adapted the proper lessons to the festival days and wished the Roman church to be called the mother of the others. He instituted the feast of candles and ordered that Mass be celebrated facing the East. At last he died in Sicily in the year of the Lord 554, a confessor himself. In his times Maurus taught monastic hypocrisy in Gaul.
28. PELAGIUS, Roman.

units.la: Pelagius Romanus, dum Totila tyrannus, Dei flagellum dictus, Italiam omnem inuaderet, magno Gothorum, quorum rex erat, applausu, ut author est Procopius, pontificij culmen suscepit. Qui, ut eidem Totilæ atq; suis placeret, Principis authoritatem ac populi consensum in ordinandis pontificibus, necessariam esse, per constitutionem publicavit. In perturbationum eius ætatis medio, Papismum præ Christianismo respiciens, constitu-it ut clerici quotidie canonicas horas septies mur-murarent, abbates regulariter eligerentur, hære-tici per singularem magistratum punirentur, ut quadragesimali tempore hora nona sacrificulus mis-sare liceret, atq; ut unaquæq; provincia duodecim vel ad minus decem civitates continere deberet.
units.tr: Pelagius, a Roman, while Totila, the tyrant called the scourge of God, was overrunning all Italy, took up the papal dignity with the great applause of the Goths, whose king he was, as Procopius reports. In order to please Totila himself and his followers, he published by decree that the authority of the prince and the consent of the people were necessary in ordaining popes. In the midst of the disturbances of that age, looking to Papism rather than Christianity, he ordained that clerics should mutter the canonical hours seven times a day, that abbots should be chosen by rule, that heretics should be punished by a special magistrate, that a priest might say Mass at the ninth hour during Lent, and that each province should contain twelve or at least ten cities.

units.la: Primatum ecclesiæ Romanæ, non à synodis, aut ab hominibus, sed ab ipso Christo prouenisse primus asseruit, Dist 21. Offa protomartyris Stephani cum Diui Laurentij cadauere una collocavit, mortuorum memorias approbavit, ac lucri gratia missis adiecit: & accusatorios libellos ob id non audiendos curavit, quod ipse olim accusatus esset, quod opprimendi ac molestandi prædecessorem Vigilium, occasionem dedisset: à quo vituperio, crucis osculo atq; iuramento se purgasse scribitur. Dura-vit hic duro Romanæ obsidionis tempore, & anno Domini 566[?]. confessor demigravit.
units.tr: He was the first to assert that the primacy of the Roman church came not from synods or from men but from Christ himself (Dist. 21). He placed the bones of Stephen, the protomartyr, together with the body of St Laurence, approved the memorials of the dead, and added them to Masses for the sake of profit. He also saw to it that accusing petitions were not to be heard on this ground: that he himself had once been accused of giving occasion for the oppression and harassment of his predecessor Vigilius. It is written that he cleared himself of this reproach by kissing the cross and by an oath. He held out during the harsh siege of Rome, and in the year of the Lord 566 he departed as a confessor.
29. JOHN the Third.

units.la: Ioannes tertius, Romanus, Narseti Eunucho, Ita-lia rectori, superatis Gothis, amicissimus fuit: ut qui ei irato Romam reconciliauit, atq; Consu-latum impetrauit. Nam Romæ tunc omnis fere po-testas penes Pontificem erat. Contra prædecesso-rem Pelagium iste fanciuit, nullum dici debere sum-mum sacerdotem, aut uniuersalem Episcopū, Dist. 99. Nullus. Ille etiam Episcoporum vicarijs, ma-nuum impositionem auferens, Episcopis tantum, I-sidoro teste, attribuit. Postea ad fabricas conuer-sus, Ecclesiam Philippi & Iacobi, à Vigilio incho-atam, absoluit: ac sanctorum cæmeteria in urbe re-stituit. Deniq; ob tempestates quasdam prodigio-sas, perturbationum ac dolorum plenus, ætate q; grandæuus, anno Christi 577. Romæ confessor, vi-ta decessit. Huius tempore Armeni Christi fidem receperunt.
units.tr: John the Third, a Roman, was a very close friend of Narses the eunuch, the ruler of Italy, once the Goths had been defeated. As one who was angry with him, he brought about a reconciliation with Rome and obtained the consulship for him. For at Rome almost all power then lay with the Pope. Against his predecessor Pelagius he decreed that no one should be called chief priest or universal bishop (Dist. 99, Nullus). He also took away from the vicars of bishops the laying on of hands, and, as Isidore testifies, assigned it to bishops alone. Afterwards he turned to building and completed the church of Philip and James, begun by Vigilius, and restored the cemeteries of the saints in the city. Finally, full of disturbances and sorrows, and aged, he died at Rome as a confessor in the year of Christ 577, amid certain prodigious storms. In his time the Armenians received the faith of Christ.
30. BENEDICT the First.

units.la: Benedictus primus, Romanus, pontificatum ges-sit, cum Longobardi per Italiam seuirent. Et bo-nus pontifex erat, quod nihil memoria dignum fecerit, ut de eo Barnus ac Funccius scribunt. Ve-tuit nihilominus religionis causa (res nempe præ-clara)cruces marmoreas, lapideas, aut ligneas, pe-dibus conculcari: & Romæ atq; in Italia, fame la-borantibus, ipse, uel saltem eius loco Tiberius Au-gustus, granis ex Aegypto allatis, subuenit, nul-la mentione facta super Euangelij semine. Inter tot Vrbis calamitates, anno Domini 582. dolore animi confessor occubuit.
units.tr: Benedict the First, a Roman, held the papacy while the Lombards were raging through Italy. He was a good pope in this sense, that he did nothing worthy of mention, as Barnus and Funccius write about him. Nevertheless, for the sake of religion (a splendid matter indeed), he forbade marble, stone or wooden crosses to be trampled underfoot. And at Rome and in Italy, when people were suffering from famine, he himself, or at least in his place Tiberius Augustus, gave relief with grain brought from Egypt, with no mention made of the seed of the gospel. Amid so many calamities of the City, he died in grief of mind as a confessor in the year of the Lord 582.
31. PELAGIUS the Second.

units.la: Pelagius secundus, Romanus, in Vrbis obsidione, absq; Principis jussu praeter consuetudinem, pontifex creabatur. Quare Gregorium monachum, pro imperatore placando Constantinopolim misit: postea Hermetis martyris cœmeterium fecit, & D. Laurentij basilicam à fundamentis erexit. Pro ho-ris dicendis statutum renovavit, & subdiaconos aut uxores aut Ecclesiæ officia dimittere jussit, nō nemq;[?] præfationes[?] ante canonem in missa canen-das dedit. Pestis inguinaria, ex magnis tempesta-tibus atq; aeris infectione contracta, anno Domini 591 hunc inter alios multos confessorem abstulit. Quæ pestis multarum superstitionum causa fuit. Tum enim primò, septiformi letania per Gregori-um instituta, iram Dei cæremoniis placandam censuerunt.
units.tr: Pelagius the Second, a Roman, was created pope during the siege of the City, contrary to custom and without the prince's command. For this reason he sent Gregory, a monk, to Constantinople to appease the emperor. Afterwards he made the cemetery of the martyr Hermes and built the basilica of St Laurence from its foundations. He renewed the rule for saying the hours, and ordered subdeacons either to give up their wives or to give up their church offices. He also allowed some prefaces to be sung before the canon in Mass. An inguinal plague, contracted from great storms and the infection of the air, carried him off in the year of the Lord 591, a confessor among many others. This plague was the cause of many superstitions. For then, for the first time, a sevenfold litany instituted by Gregory was approved, as a means of appeasing the anger of God by ceremonies.
32. GREGORY the Great.

units.la: Gregorius Magnus, Romanus, ex monacho ac dia-cono pontifex factus: omnium pontificum, seu ut dictum est, patriarcharum Romanorum, d:strima[?] & vita præstantissimus: reluctans, invitus, ac de-mum coactus, Pelagio praedicto successit. Cæremo-niis plusquam Judaicis mirum in modum, quia monachus[?] erat, Ecclesiam ac religionem Dei, præ cae-teris omnibus oneravit, vir alioqui doctus & bonus. Parentum domos in monasteria vertit, & primum eorum Andreæ Apostolo dedicavit. Scholas cantorum instituit, & Ambrosii more Ecclesiasticas cantiones, quas Græce dicimus Antiphonas, composuit. Officiarium Ecclesiæ fecit, antiphonarium nocturnum & diurnum disposuit, sacrorum normas digesit, missarum ritus complanavit, & eius canonem consarcinavit. Introitus missarum cum Psalmorum particulis cantari fecit, nonies Kyrieleyson recitari iussit, Alleluia per totum annum extra quadragesimam vociferari post Gradale curavit, & pro tempore Paschali offertoriis & post communibus idemq; Alleluia adiunxit. Tres postulationes canoni missali adiecit, scilicet: Dies-q; nostros in tua pace, & cæt. orationem Dominicam super Eucharistiæ panem in altum dici aut cani præcepit, super Apostolorum mortua cadavera missas celebrari mandavit, et Deus in adiutorium, cum Gloria patri, horis canonicis addidit. Letanias & processiones excogitavit, atq; in septem ordines, scilicet, clericorum, Monachorum, Monialium, puerorum, Laicorum, viduarum, ac mulierum coniugatarum, distribuit. Imaginem diuæ virginis circumferri permisit, Angelis (ut asserunt Pa-pistæ pistæ)psallentibus, Regina cœli letare, Alleluiæ[?] & Angelum minantem (commentum impudens) cruentum[?] gladium in uaginam reponere coegit. Stationes quasdam in urbe, seu peregrinationes adstatuas, pro plebis deuotione per indulgentias confirmauit. Purificationis Mariæ festum cereis illustratum, & palmarum diem solennem, processionibus honorauit. Quadragesimali ieiunio quatuor dies addidit, & eius initium cinerum aspergine sacrauit. Vsum carnis, lacticiniis, casei, butyri, atq; uorum (quod carnem sapiant) ieiunantibus interdixit: & pisciculis solum, non grandioribus illis piscibus, ut sci permisit. Vnde Mantuanus in 2 Fast. lib. Non tamen illicitum, pisces adhibere minutos. Gregorius grandes prohibet, sed longior usus Obstitit, & ponti pecuaria magna per omnes Iam uolitant procerum mensas, & prandia regum. Sordida Gregorij leges obseruat egestas, Quæ tenues scrutatur aquas & flumina summa, Grande ac pingue pecus fundo uersatur in imo At sacri proceres, qui lina capacia Petri Altius immergunt, laqueant genus omne natantu. Templis lumina Gregorius dedit, modum chori cum psalmodijs, canticis, odis, hymnis atq; aliis gentilium cæremoniis, ornauit. Sex monasteria proprijs impensis in Sicilia condidit, & Agathæ fanum dedicauit. Mulieres Monachorum cœnobia subire uetuit: & Monachos monialium tecta. Monachos etiam baptizare non uolebat, nec moniales baptizatorum commatres fieri. Ne bigamus fiat presbyter, prohibuit: & ut sacerdotes vitæ innocentiam per iuramenta probarent, sanciuit. Veniarum assertor, non uenditor tamen: indulgentias certis diebus, & templa uisitantibus primus concessit. Xenodochia fundauit, peregrinos ad mensam inuitauit, monachis Hi-erosolymitanis necessaria misit, ac ter mille ancillas stipendijs pauit. Prima concilia quinque, decreto approbauit: ne imagines sanctorum con-fringantur, ne clericus mandato Cæsareo mili-tet, & ne in eadem prouincia duo sint metropo-litani, inhibuit. Episcopum semel duntaxat con-secrandum esse statuit, atq; ultimas morientium uoluntates ab omnibus ratas haberi uoluit. Dialogorum libros quatuor pro fulciendo purgato-rio fecit: cinerum consecrationes, pedum lotio-nes, crucis adorationes, ac missas pro mortuis ad-misit: & Traiani imperatoris animam (horribile papistarum mendacium) ab inferis liberauit. Anglos per Augustinum monachum contemptis Brytannis, ad ritus Romanos uocauit: ur-bem Londinensem Archiepiscopatus iure pri-uauit[?], uauit, atq; ad Cantuariam per eundem Augustiñ num translulit. Hæc omnia ut patriarcha Romanus, Gregorius fecit: atque anno Domini 604. confessor & ipse obiit.
units.tr: Gregory the Great, a Roman, was made pope from being a monk and a deacon. He was the most outstanding of all the popes, or, as has been said, of the Roman patriarchs, in dignity and in life. Reluctant, unwilling, and finally compelled, he succeeded the aforesaid Pelagius. Because he was a monk, he burdened the Church and the religion of God, more than all others, with ceremonies more than Jewish in a remarkable manner, although in other respects he was a learned and good man. He turned the homes of parents into monasteries, and dedicated the first of them to the apostle Andrew. He instituted schools of singers, and after the manner of Ambrose he composed ecclesiastical chants, which we call in Greek antiphons. He made the Church's Office book, arranged the nocturnal and diurnal antiphonaries, digested the norms of the sacred rites, smoothed out the ritual of the Masses, and patched together its canon. He had the introits of the Masses sung with portions of the Psalms, ordered the Kyrie eleison to be recited nine times, and saw to it that the Alleluia was shouted through the whole year except Lent, after the gradual; and for the Paschal season he added it to the offertories and communions. He added three petitions to the canon of the Mass, namely "Grant our days in your peace," and so on. He ordered the Lord's Prayer to be said or sung aloud over the Eucharistic bread on the altar. He commanded Masses to be celebrated over the dead bodies of the apostles, and added "God, come to my aid," with "Glory be to the Father," to the canonical hours. He devised litanies and processions, and divided them into seven orders: of clerics, monks, nuns, boys, laymen, widows, and married women. He allowed the image of the blessed Virgin to be carried about, with Angels singing (as the Papists assert), "Rejoice, Queen of Heaven," and "Alleluia"; and he compelled an Angel, threatening (a shameless fiction), to return a bloody sword to its scabbard. He confirmed certain stations in the city, or pilgrimages to statues, for the devotion of the people, by indulgences. He honoured the feast of Mary's Purification, which was made bright with candles, and the day of Palms, with processions. He added four days to the Lenten fast, and consecrated its beginning with the sprinkling of ashes. He forbade those fasting the use of meat, of milk products, of cheese, of butter, and of eggs (because they taste of meat), and permitted only small fish, not the larger ones, as they say. Hence Mantuanus in the second book of the Fasti: "It is not however unlawful to use small fish. Gregory forbids the large ones, but a longer custom has stood in the way, and great herds of the sea fly now through all the tables of nobles and the feasts of kings. Poverty keeps the squalid laws of Gregory, which search the thin waters and the surface of rivers; the large and fat flock is turned over in the deep bottom; but the holy nobles, who plunge the wide nets of Peter deeper, snare every kind of swimming thing." He gave lights to the churches, and adorned the manner of the choir with psalmody, canticles, odes, hymns and other ceremonies of the heathen. He founded six monasteries at his own expense in Sicily, and dedicated a shrine to Agatha. He forbade women to enter monks' convents, and monks to enter nuns' houses. He also did not want monks to baptize, nor nuns to become godmothers of the baptized. He prohibited a bigamist from becoming a priest, and decreed that priests should prove the innocence of their lives by oaths. A champion of pardons, but not a seller of them, he was the first to grant indulgences for certain days to those visiting churches. He founded hospices, invited pilgrims to his table, sent necessities to the monks of Jerusalem, and fed three thousand maidservants from stipends. He approved five first councils by decree, and forbade the images of the saints to be broken, a cleric to serve as a soldier by Caesar's command, and two metropolitans to be in the same province. He decreed that a bishop should be consecrated only once, and he wished the last wills of the dying to be held valid by all. He made four books of Dialogues to support purgatory. He admitted the consecration of ashes, the washing of feet, the adoration of the cross, and Masses for the dead; and he freed the soul of the emperor Trajan from the underworld (a horrible lie of the Papists). Having despised the Britons, he called the English to Roman rites through the monk Augustine. He stripped the city of London of its archiepiscopal right, and through the same Augustine transferred it to Canterbury. Gregory did all these things as Roman patriarch, and in the year of the Lord 604 he too died as a confessor.
33. Sabinianus the Tuscan.

units.la: Sabinianus Thuscus, nullius momenti pontifex, Gregorij prædecessoris odio, institit post editas in illum detrectationes in quas, ut eius exureren- tur libri. Hic ultimus ex Romanorum patriarchis constituit, ut horæ diei per campanarum pulsum propter officia Ecclesiastica distinguerentur: & ut lampades accensæ, in templis perpetuò seruarentur. Horrendo quodam noctis uisu, obstupesactus demum, anno Domini 606. confessor infami mor te concidit.
units.tr: Sabinianus the Tuscan, a pontiff of no account, out of hatred for his predecessor Gregory, pursued him after the disparaging writings published against Gregory, for which Gregory's books were burned. He was the last of the Roman patriarchs. He ordered that the hours of the day be marked by the ringing of bells for ecclesiastical duties, and that lamps, once lit, be kept burning continually in the churches. Finally, stupefied by a dreadful vision in the night, he died an infamous death in the year of the Lord 606, a confessor.
On Gregory's Christian deeds.

units.la: Vt autem de prædicti pontificis Gregorij dictis & factis Christianis aliquid dicam: uehementer ille pugnauit contra Papistici regni primatum, in ipso Papatus limine, ac durissimis conuiciis ipsius proscidit uniuersalis patriarchæ titulum, diuinitus esse Antichristi præcursorem, hypocrisis tyrannum, ac diuinitatis usurpatorem Lucifer um. Miranda operis statuas plures in Tiberi im præcipitari iussit, ne religio illis corrumpe- retur. Propeste sedanda preces & ieiunia mandauit. dauit. Gothos, relicti[?] Arrianis, ad Ecclesiae unitatem reduxit. Homeliarum libros dulci sermone, Augustinum Hipponensem imitatus, scripsit. Sacros Bibliorum libros plures exposuit. Vniuersalis episcopi nomen publico decreto derogauit: seruorum Dei seruum scriptis profitebatur: ut inde uideretur ab omni ambitione ac dominandi libidine alienissimus. Quem quoq; titulum et posteri retinuerunt: sed more Chanaan, atq; filiorum eius, Gen 9. qui mundi imperium ad se rapuerunt, ac tyrannice fideles fratres oppresserunt, tanquam totius terrarum orbis domini. Vlulandi in Ecclesiis consuetudinem tantum inualuisse, neglecto Euangelicae praedicationis officio, plurimum tandem doluit. Ecce (inter cetera inquit) mundus sacerdotibus est plenus: in messe tamen Dei rarus inuenitur operarius. Officium quidem accipimus, sed opus officij non implemus. Nullum puto, fratres, ab alijs maius praeiudicium, quam id quod a sacerdotibus tolerat Deus. Plerunque enim, si quos humiliter, si quos continenter uiuere conspiciunt, irridٍent. Considerate ergo, quid de gregibus agatur, quando lupi pastores fiunt. Hi custodiam gregis suscipiunt, qui insidiari gregi Dominica non metuunt, sed susceptae benedictionis ministerium uertunt ad ambitionis augmentum. Dei causa relinquimus, ad terrena negocia festinamus: locum sanctitatis accipimus, & terrenis actibus implicamur, &c. Ita ut Baptista Mantuanus de illo dicat in 3. Fastorum libro:
units.tr: To say something about the Christian sayings and deeds of the aforesaid pontiff Gregory: he fought vigorously against the primacy of the Papal kingdom, right at the threshold of the Papacy, and with the harshest insults he tore apart the title of universal patriarch, declaring it to be divinely the forerunner of Antichrist, the tyrant of hypocrisy, and a Lucifer who usurped divinity. He ordered several statues of wondrous workmanship to be thrown into the Tiber, lest religion be corrupted by them. To quell the pestilence he ordered prayers and fasts. He brought the Goths, who had been left to the Arians, back to the unity of the Church. Imitating Augustine of Hippo, he wrote books of homilies in a sweet style. He expounded several books of the sacred Scriptures. He repudiated the name of universal bishop by public decree, and in his writings he professed himself the servant of the servants of God, so that he would appear most free from all ambition and lust for domination. Later popes retained this title too, but after the manner of Canaan and his sons (Gen. 9), who seized the empire of the world for themselves and tyrannically oppressed their faithful brothers as if they were lords of the whole globe. He grieved greatly that the custom of howling in the churches had gained such strength, while the office of evangelical preaching was neglected. "Behold," he says among other things, "the world is full of priests, yet in God's harvest workers are rare. We take up the office, but we do not perform the work of the office. I think, brothers, there is no greater prejudice to others than that which God tolerates in priests. For very often, if they see some living humbly or continently, they mock them. Consider then what becomes of the flocks when wolves become shepherds. Those take up the guardianship of the flock who are not afraid to lie in wait for the Lord's flock, but turn the ministry of the blessing they received to the increase of their ambition. We leave for God's sake, and hasten to earthly business; we receive the place of holiness, and are entangled in earthly actions, etc." So Baptista Mantuanus says of him in the third book of the Fasti:

units.la: Ore manu facundus erat, monumenta supersunt Plurima: fatur adhuc, nec fari desinet unquam. Hic docuit cantare choros, melicisq; animauit Verba notis, sacrisq; dedit formamq; modumq. Composuit mores hominum, sua secula fecit Celsa: sacerdoti decus usq; in sidera misit.
units.tr: He was eloquent in voice and hand; many monuments remain. He still speaks, and will never cease to speak. He taught choirs to sing, and gave words life with melodic notes; he gave sacred things their form and measure. He shaped the morals of men and raised his ages high; he sent the glory of the priest up to the stars.

units.la: Mirabilem de hoc pontifice refert historiam Huldricus Augustanus Episcopus, in Epistola sua ad Nicolaum primum. Cuius summa est, quod iste Gregorius primò sacerdotibus mandauerit cœli-batum: sed posteà comperto, quod clam libidines exercerentur, indeq; multi concepti fœtus trucidarentur, id nmandatum[?] abrogauit: dixitq; melius esse nubere, quàm cædibus causam præbere. Nam cum aliquando in piscinam quandam piscatum misisset, inuenta sunt in eadem 6000. submerso-rum infantium capita. Quod uidens ex violento cælibatu[?] prodijsse, ex imo pectore dolens ac inge-miscens, edictum illud protinus reuocauit. Non tantum enim à uirginibus & coniugatis sibi non abstinuerunt, sed etiam cum consanguineis, cum ma-sculi, atq; adeò pariter cum brutis (dictu horren-dum). dum)fœdè sese commiscuerunt, ut idem Huldricus docet. Post huius Gregorii tèpora, secutæ sunt ma-iores tenebræ quàm prius. Deperiit doctrinæ puri-tas, Ecclesiaq; humanis traditionibus mirum in no-dum obscurata fuit. Nam monachatus cum mul-tiplicibus superstitionibus uehementer auctus est. Ac creuit inde cum missarum nundinatione, mortuo-rum inuocatio: & Eucharistiæ mysterium pro nor-tuis offerri cœpit. Episcopi quoq; per spiritum, uel potiùs diabolorum, apparitiones decepti, à doctrina fidei ad operum fiduciam, & humanas sa-tisfactiones defecerunt, id quod palàm constat à prædicto Gregorio. Qui in Dialogis ad Theodo-lindam, multæ superstitionis fœminam, mortuos apparuisse, & suffragia postulasse recenset. Laben-te ita Christianismo ad cæremonias, irrepere mox aggreditur per monachismum superstitio cæca. Misit Gregorius, ut dictum est, Augustinum mo-nachum Romanum cum socijs ad Anglos, anno Domini 596. non ut Christum, cuius doctrinam purio-rem Brytanni priùs habebant à Iosepho & Asia-norum Ecclesijs, illic doceret: sed ut Romanam re-ligionem, hominum mandatis & traditionibus re-sertam intruderet. Erant semper apud Brytannos ueritatis prædicatio, doctrina syncerißima, uiui-ficatrix fides, & cultus tales, quales ab ipsis Ap [?]stolis n[illegible, ~2 letters]ndato diuino traditi erant Christianorum Ecclesi[?]æ. Vnde Galfridus Monumetensis, lib 8. cap.4 Brytannorum gestis: In patria Britonum (inquit) adhuc vigebat Christianitas: quæ ab Apostolorum tempore nunquam inter eos defecerat. Postquam autem venit Augustinus, inuenit in eorum provincia septem Episcopatus & Archiepiscopatum unum, religiosissimis præsulibus munitos, & abbatias complures, suarum manuum labore viventes: in quibus grex Domini restum[?] ormem[?] tenebat, &c. Apparet etiam, pastores apud eos fuisse diligentes in retinenda doctrinæ puritate, per Dionotum Auonium & socios, qui in ea fortiter ad mortem usq; perstiterunt, contemptu Romanistarum cæremoniis, ne dicam idolo-manijs atq; comminationibus. Intrabat Augustinus, non cum Euangelio pacis Christianæ[?], sed cum Apostolatus sui vexillo, cruce argentea, letania, processione, iconibus, simulachris depictis, reliquijs, canticis, ac ritualibus libris. Cum vero ad eius colloquium, in occidentali Anglorum patria, Brytannorum Episcopos & doctores anno Domini 602. regis authoritate convocaret, ut Romanis ritibus communicantes, seipsos ei subijcerent: illi ad synodum ituri, solitarium quendam ac prudentem virum prius consulerunt, an eius mandata se quisuasq; à patribus sumptas traditione reseruare licerent? Si homo Dei est, (inquit) sequatur illum. Et, unde id probabimus: interrogant. Scitis? {r}Dominum praecepisse: Tollite iugum meum super vos, & discite à me, quia mitis sum & humilis corde. Si talis ergo fit Augustinus ille, credibile est, quod Christi iugum & ipse portet, ac vobis portandum offerat. Si autem superbus aut immitis fuerit, constat quia non est à Deo, neque vobis est eius sermo curandus. Et unde id sciemus? inquiunt. Permitti-te, ait, ut ipse prior cum suis ad synodi locum veniat. Et si aduentantibus assurrexerit, scitote quia Christi seruus est, & obtemperate illi. At si vos spreuerit, aut parui æstimauerit, & nullum beni-gnitatis signum ostenderit in vultu, cum numero plures sitis, spernatur à vobis & ipse. Cum ergo venissent, & Augustinum in sella ambitiose se-dentem, nec eis amicitiæ signum aliquod præben-tem vidissent, in iram mox conuersi, eumq; super-bię notantes, cunctis quæ illis proposuit, contra-dicebant. Improperabat enim eis, quod universa-lis Ecclesiæ consuetudini contraria in multis ge-rerent, præsertim in Paschalis festi celebratione in ministerio baptismi, & in prædicationis officio, & quod hominum traditiones non curarent: man-dabatq; ut in his atque aliis, Romanæ Ecclesiæ mores & ritus obseruarent. At illi nihil horum se facturos, neq; illum pro archiepiscopo habituros esse respondebant. Quibus ipse futura bella pro-misit, ac mortis ultionem, quæ mox sequuta est, fe-rociter minitabatur. Vide Bedam in Ecclesiastica historia gentis Anglorum lib. 2.cap 2. ac prædictū Galfridum. Veruntamen de hoc Augustini atroci facto non satis admirari cogor. Cum Gregorius antea disseruerit, & ad illum scripserit, non esse necessariam cæremoniarum in omnibus Ecclesijs similitudinem: sed unamquamq; sibi optimas eligere debere. Sed talis esse solet hypocritarum tyrannis.
units.tr: A wondrous story about this pontiff is related by Huldrych, bishop of Augsburg, in his letter to Nicholas I. Its gist is this: Gregory first commanded priests to live in celibacy, but afterwards, having discovered that lusts were being practised in secret and that many resulting offspring were being slaughtered, he revoked that command, saying it was better to marry than to give cause for murders. For once, when he had sent fishermen to a certain pool, the heads of 6000 drowned infants were found in it. Seeing that this had come from forced celibacy, he grieved from the bottom of his heart, groaning, and immediately revoked that edict. For they did not abstain only from virgins and married women, but also mingled foully with blood relations, males with males, and even with beasts (horrible to say), as the same Huldrych teaches. After the times of this Gregory, greater darkness followed than before. The purity of doctrine perished, and the Church was wonderfully obscured by human traditions. For monasticism grew greatly, with many superstitions. And from this grew, along with the trafficking in masses, the invocation of the dead; and the mystery of the Eucharist began to be offered for the dead. Bishops too, deceived by apparitions of a spirit, or rather of devils, fell away from the doctrine of faith to confidence in works and human satisfactions, as is plain from the aforesaid Gregory. In his Dialogues, addressed to Theodolinda, a woman of great superstition, he recounts that the dead appeared and asked for intercessions. With Christianity thus slipping into ceremonies, blind superstition soon began to creep in through monasticism. Gregory sent, as has been said, the Roman monk Augustine with companions to the English in the year of the Lord 596, not to teach them Christ, whose purer doctrine the Britons had earlier received from Joseph and the churches of Asia, but to thrust in the Roman religion, crammed with human commands and traditions. Among the Britons there had always been the preaching of truth, most sincere doctrine, life-giving faith, and such worship as had been handed down to the churches of Christians by divine command from the Apostles. Hence Geoffrey of Monmouth, book 8, chapter 4, of the Deeds of the Britons: "In the land of the Britons," he says, "Christianity was still flourishing, which had never failed among them since the time of the Apostles. But when Augustine came, he found in their province seven bishoprics and one archbishopric, fortified by most religious prelates, and several abbeys, living by the labour of their hands, in which the flock of the Lord kept ... etc." It also appears that their ministers were diligent in keeping the purity of doctrine, as Dionotus of Avonia and his companions did, who steadfastly persisted in it even unto death, despising the ceremonies of the Romanists, not to say their idolatries and threats. Augustine came in not with the gospel of Christian peace, but with the banner of his apostolate, a silver cross, litanies, processions, images, painted statues, relics, canticles, and ritual books. When he summoned the British bishops and teachers to a conference with him in the western part of England, in the year of the Lord 602, by the authority of the king, so that they would share in the Roman rites and submit themselves to him, they, about to go to the synod, first consulted a certain solitary and prudent man, asking whether they might keep his commands, or each keep the tradition received from the fathers. "If he is a man of God," he said, "let them follow him." "And how shall we prove it?" they asked. "You know that the Lord commanded: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. If then Augustine is such a man, it is credible that he too bears Christ's yoke, and offers it to you to bear. But if he is proud or harsh, it is clear that he is not from God, and his word is not to be heeded by you." "And how shall we know this?" they said. "Allow him," he replied, "to come to the place of the synod first with his men. And if he rises when you arrive, know that he is a servant of Christ, and obey him. But if he despises you, or sets little store by you, and shows no sign of kindness in his face, although you are more in number, let him be despised by you as well." When they came and saw Augustine sitting ambitiously on a chair, showing them no sign of friendship, they were quickly turned to anger, and noting his pride, they contradicted everything he proposed to them. For he reproached them that in many things they acted contrary to the custom of the universal Church, especially in the celebration of the Paschal feast, in the ministry of baptism, and in the office of preaching, and that they did not heed human traditions; and he commanded that in these and other matters they observe the customs and rites of the Roman Church. But they answered that they would do none of these things, and that they would not regard him as archbishop. To them he promised future wars, and fiercely threatened the vengeance of death, which soon followed. See Bede in the Ecclesiastical History of the English people, book 2, chapter 2, and the aforesaid Geoffrey. Yet I am compelled not to marvel enough at this savage deed of Augustine's. For Gregory had earlier discussed the matter and written to him that uniformity of ceremonies was not necessary in all churches, but that each should choose what was best for itself. But such is usually the tyranny of hypocrites.
Of these matters Mantuan writes in his Fasti:

units.la: Adde, quod & patres ausi taxare Latinos: Causabantur eos, stulte, imprudenter, & æquo Durius, ad ritum Romæ voluisse Brytannos Cogere: & antiquum tam præcipitanter amorem Tam stolido temerasse ausu. Concedere Roma Debuit, aiebant, potius, quàm rumpere pacem: Humani quæ iuris erant: modò salua maneret Lex diuina, fides Christi, doctrina, senatus Quam primus tulit ore suo, quæ tradita ab ipso Christo erat, humanæ doctore & lumine vitæ.
units.tr: Add that the Fathers dared to censure the Latins, saying that they were foolish and imprudent, and, more harshly than is fair, that they had tried to force the Britons to the Roman rite and had so rashly violated an ancient love with such a stupid act. Rome ought rather to have yielded, they said, than break the peace, provided that the human matters remained, while the divine law, the faith of Christ and the teaching which the first senate delivered from his own mouth, the teaching handed down by Christ himself, the teacher and light of human life, stayed intact.

units.la: Ut paucis absoluam, stellæ adhuc Romani pontifices erant, sed ex Christi dextera cadentes ad terram: à quibus cælum recessit[?], Apoc.6. & per eaquum rursum mystice adumbrantur: cuius sessori datum est, pacem de terra sumere, & inuicem intersicere. Unde sicut in prima classe, Romani pontifices sub episcoporum nomine, per incorruptum uerbi ministerium & fidei constantiam, stellae in Christi dextera manentes fuerunt, Apoc.1. Ita in hac secunda, sub Archiepiscoporum & Patriarcharum appellatione, per eiusdem uerbi neglectionem ac terrenas affectiones, stellae cadentes ad terram ceciderant, Apoc.6. In tertia uero, quae statim sequetur, sub Papatum & Antichristorum uocabulo, per plenam à Christo defectionem & apertas idololatrias, sidera in terram delapsa erunt, Apoc.9.
units.tr: To be brief: the Roman bishops were still stars, but falling to the earth from Christ's right hand, and from them the sky has withdrawn, Rev. 6. Through the horse they are again mystically shadowed, to whose rider it was given to take peace from the earth and to slay one another. Hence, just as in the first class the Roman bishops, under the name of bishops, remained stars in Christ's right hand through the uncorrupted ministry of the Word and constancy of faith, Rev. 1., so in this second class, under the appellation of archbishops and patriarchs, through neglect of the same Word and earthly affections, the stars fell to the earth, Rev. 6. In the third class, however, which follows immediately, under the title of Papacy and Antichrists, through complete defection from Christ and open idolatries, the stars will fall to the earth, Rev. 9.
The Third Class.

units.la: Tertia & ultima Rom. episcoporum classis, à Bonifacio tertio ad Paulum quartum: in qua ipsissimos esse Antichristos, in carnis superbia gloriantes, atq; in tyrannide Satanam imitantes, aperte se ostendunt.
units.tr: The third and last class of Roman bishops, from Boniface III to Paul IV, in which they openly show themselves to be the very Antichrists, glorying in the pride of the flesh and imitating Satan in tyranny.
Abaddon, or the Latin Antichrist.

units.la: Anno ab incarnatione Domini 604. Phocas tyrannus peremit suum Dominum, Caesarem Mauritium, una cum uxore, fratre, ac liberis, multisq; proceribus. Ad hunc annum, additis adhuc duobus annis, usq; ad Papatus initium per eundem Phocam, sunt 666. anni, à consulatu Marci Tullij Ciceronis & Antonij:ut aptissime colligunt, Bi-bliander, Funccius, & alij: quando Judaei libertatem amiserunt, pontificibus eorum de primatu al-tercantibus. Christus enim in sua revelatione (ut colligit Bibliander) quam per Joannem dilectissi-mum Apostolum, Ecclesiae tradidit, dominatum quendam tyrannicum praedicit afflicturum esse il-lam Ecclesiam Dei veram: sicut olim fecit Nero, Domitianus, & alij. Et vocat bestiam habentem duo cornua agni similia, utique Christi aemulam: quae tamen loquatur ut draco, ut cacodaemon, & sae-viat nihilo clementius quam fecit prior bestia, quae Petrum, Paulum, & agmina ingentia sanctorum prostravit. Quae quidem portentosis operibus in eum stuporem convertat mundum, ut nemo possit emere aut vendere, nisi habeat characterem aut nomen bestiae. Nomen autem notis literarum. χ§ s[?] mysticos profert, & ad indagandum excitat, dicens: Hic est sapientia. Qui habet intellectum, computet numerum bestiae. Numerus enim hominis est, & numerus eius 666. Apoc. 13 Quid sibi autem volunt notae, nisi ut tempus investigemus, quo bellua ista prodeat e terra & abysso, ac vastet Rempublicam Christianam? Quomodo autem ap-tabis, nisi certum tempus habeas, quo Pompeius sceptrum Judaeis eripuit, juxta celeberrimum vati-cinium. [?]inum patriarchæ Iacob, & ingressus templum, adytum ipsum etiam profanauit? Id uero factum scribitur sub Ciceronis consulatu, ut dictum est, Iosepho etiam teste, anno ante Seruatorem natum 60. Illu 60. annis si adiungas 606. usq; post mortem Gregorii Magni, qui uaticinatus est illum fore Antichristum, qui uniuersalis episcopus haberi vellet, aut omnium Ecclesiarum caput. Circumspi-ce igitur oculis uigilantibus, qualia tempora fuerint anno 666. à capta Hierosolyma per Romanos, duce Pompeio: & stupenda quædam occurrent temporibus Phocæ huius Imperatoris. De quo Guilhelmus Stantphurdius in sua Farragine:
units.tr: In the year of the Lord's incarnation 604, the tyrant Phocas killed his lord, the Emperor Maurice, together with his wife, brother and children, and many nobles. To this year, with two more years added, up to the beginning of the Papacy under the same Phocas, there are 666 years from the consulship of Marcus Tullius Cicero and Antony, as Bibliander, Funck and others most aptly reckon, when the Jews lost their liberty while their priests quarrelled over primacy. For Christ, in his revelation (as Bibliander gathers), which he handed down to the Church through the most beloved apostle John, foretells that a certain tyrannical lordship would afflict that true Church of God, just as Nero and Domitian and others once did. And he calls it a beast having two horns like a lamb, that is, a rival of Christ, which nevertheless speaks like a dragon, like a demon, and rages no less cruelly than the earlier beast, which laid low Peter, Paul and vast crowds of saints. This beast, by its portentous works, will turn the world into such stupor that no one can buy or sell unless he has the mark or the name of the beast. Its name, however, it gives in mystical letters, and it stirs us to investigate, saying: "Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding count the number of the beast. For it is the number of a man, and his number is 666," Rev. 13. But what do these marks mean, except that we should search out the time when this monster comes up out of the earth and the abyss and lays waste the Christian commonwealth? How will you apply them unless you have a certain time at which Pompey took the sceptre from the Jews, according to the most famous prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, and entered the temple and even profaned the inner sanctuary? This indeed is written as having happened in the consulship of Cicero, as was said, Josephus also being witness, in the year 60 before our Saviour's birth. If you add 606 years to those 60, up to after the death of Gregory the Great, who prophesied that he would be the Antichrist who wished to be held universal bishop, or head of all Churches, look carefully with watchful eyes at what the times were in the year 666 from the capture of Jerusalem by the Romans under the leadership of Pompey, and remarkable things will meet you in the times of this Emperor Phocas. Concerning him William Stanhurst writes in his Farrago:

units.la: Suffocat imperium Phocæ, stabilitq; Papatum, Impia per regni, mittendo diplomata fines: Primatum Latij quibus antitheiq; draconis, Fortiter ad cunctam confirmet posteritatem: Et bona quod facies fieri cupit illico præsul: Eduntur toto bullata diplomata regno.
units.tr: Phocas' empire is choked, and the Papacy is established, sending out edicts through the kingdom's bounds, impious ones: by these he firmly confirms for all posterity the primacy of Latium and the anti-Christ dragon. And the bishop wishes these good things to be done at once: the sealed edicts are published throughout the whole realm.

units.la: Deinde numerum istum mysticum, plenum sapientia quadam singulari, apta natali Christi, aptæ passioni Dominicæ, apta ei tempori quo Titus cuertit urbem: aut Domitiani 15. anno, quando Apocalypsis scripta est, & semper aliquid monstrorum in Ecclesia offendes. Et ut ad res Angli-cas reuertar, anno Domini 593. Anglorum Heptarchiam, Colmannus, Hardingus, & Fabianus caepisse referunt: qua post annos 1735. à Bryti primi eorum regis initio, regia dignitas apud Brytan-nos cessauit. Nam Brytanni, ut Paulus Diaconus scribit, pro adiutoribus hostes impugnato-resq; acerrimos, Anglos infideles, arma crudelia in eos conuertentes, senserunt. Anno Domini 596. Augustinus praedictus, à Gregorio missus, in An-gliam uenit: non improbans, sed confirmans ipso-rum Anglorum impiissimas proditiones, horribi-lia furta, & homicidia pluquam Neroniana. An-no Domini 600. Archiepiscopale pallium Augu-stino Gregorius dedit: Londino, ut dictum est, suo iure indecenter spoliato, ad utriusq; & Reipubli-ca & religionis perniciem, atq; tandem imperij Brytannici uastationem, indeq; eriguntur templa magnifica. Brytanni prius Ecclesias suas aeterno Patri Deo, atq; eius filio Christo Seruatori dedi-catas habebant: sed Angli deinceps statuis ac mor-tuis sanctis sua templa consecrabant. Anno Domi-ni 604. occiso Mauricio, Christiano Imperatore, Phocas adulter & homicida imperabat: cecidit&q; [?] in ipso, cum nobilissimo Graecorum imperio, Caesa-rea maiestas: Romanaq; per Papatum ab eo con-cessum ac stabilitum diminuta est, & ad nihilum tum demum redacta. Anno Domini 606. in Nouembri[?] ac Decembri, ut Paulus Diaconus 18. libro indicat, cometes mirae magnitudinis, oriente ipso Pa patu, apparuit :uisiones prodigiosae fiebant, ac monstra quaedam marina ad terrorem multorum sese ostendebant. Sub dicto igitur Phoca tyranno ac Caesaricida (quod in Papis mysterio non uacat) Papismus & Mahumetismus simul sunt exorti qui multis in regionibus, doctrinam de Dei filio corruperunt, obscurarunt, labefactarunt. Nam altero eiusdem Phocae Caesaris anno, penes Bibliandrum, Mahumetes Alcoranum recitauit: ita ut simul(inquit) expergefiant tria capita Aquilae, iuxta diuinum somnium ex quarto Esdrae libro: scilicet, Phocas ipse, Papa Bonifacius, & Mahumet Arabs. Sequitur nunc tertia classis de Papis Rom. quae diuiditur in quinq; sectiones.
units.tr: Then this mystical number, full of a certain singular wisdom, is suited to Christ's birth, suited to the Lord's passion, suited to the time when Titus overthrew the city, or to the fifteenth year of Domitian, when the Apocalypse was written; and you will always stumble upon some monstrosity in the Church. And to return to English affairs: in the year of the Lord 593, Colman, Harding and Fabian report that the English heptarchy began. Some 1735 years after the beginning of their first king Brutus, the royal dignity ceased among the Britons. For the Britons, as Paul the Deacon writes, took the Angles, unbelievers, as allies and then as most bitter enemies, and felt cruel weapons turned against them. In the year of the Lord 596, the aforementioned Augustine, sent by Gregory, came to England, not disapproving but confirming the most impious treacheries, horrible thefts and murders more than Neronian of those same Angles. In the year of the Lord 600, Gregory gave Augustine the archiepiscopal pallium, London, as was said, having been shamefully stripped of its rightful status, to the ruin of both the commonwealth and religion, and at last to the devastation of the British empire; and from this magnificent temples were erected. The Britons had previously held their churches dedicated to the eternal Father God and to his Son Christ the Saviour, but the Angles thereafter consecrated their temples to statues and dead saints. In the year of the Lord 604, when Maurice, a Christian emperor, had been killed, Phocas, an adulterer and murderer, reigned; and in him, together with the most noble Greek empire, the imperial majesty fell, and the Roman power, diminished by the Papacy conceded and established by him, was then at last reduced to nothing. In the year of the Lord 606, in November and December, as Paul the Deacon indicates in book 18, a comet of wondrous size appeared, the Papacy itself rising; prodigious visions occurred, and certain sea monsters showed themselves to the terror of many. Under the aforesaid tyrant and Caesar-killer Phocas (which is not without meaning in the mystery of the Papists), Papism and Mahometism arose at the same time, which in many regions corrupted, obscured and undermined the doctrine of the Son of God. For in the second year of this same Emperor Phocas, according to Bibliander, Mahomet recited the Koran, so that, as he says, at the same time the three heads of the eagle awoke, according to the divine dream in the fourth book of Esdras: namely Phocas himself, Pope Boniface, and Mahomet the Arab. Now follows the third class concerning the Roman Popes, which is divided into five sections.
LIBER TERTIUS.

units.la: HVIVS tertiae classis sectio prima, de Papis vel Romanis Antichristis, in regno magnae bestiae: quod dicitur tum Sodoma, tum Aegyptus, Apoc. 11, usq; ad Ioannem octavum.
units.tr: The first section of this third class, concerning the Popes or Roman Antichrists, in the kingdom of the great beast, which is called both Sodom and Egypt, Rev. 11, down to John VIII.
THE POPES, OR ROMAN ANTICHRISTS.
1. BONIFACE III.

units.la: Bonifacius tertius, Romanus, ambitiosa bestia, à Phoca Imperatore, adultero, parricida ac tyranno, in maximo hominum tumultu, anno Domini 607. reclamantibus plurimis tum Episcopis tum Ecclesiis, in Papatu sublimatur[?], confirmatur, adoratur, & omnium Episcoporum dominus & princeps acclamatur. Hic ardenti petitione, sed largitione multo fortiori, obtinuit, ut Romana sedes omnium Ecclesiarum diceretur caput, adductis his friuolis rationibus: quòd Imperium à Roma primùm habuerit suum nomen, & quòd Petrus suis successoribus (mendacium ac blasphemia) Romae tradiderit claves. Ad hunc modum consita-bilita[?] est huius Antichristi authoritas maligna, in omni uirtute sui fundatoris, scilicet adulterio, parricidio, ac tyrannide ita ut non Christi, sed Phocae sceleftissimi proditoris vicarius: non Apostoli Petri, sed apostatae Iudae, atq; ipsius Sathanae successor haberetur. Quàm splendidum fit hoc huius monstri tam execrabilis initium, quod se tam arroganter Ecclesiae Christianae caput iactitat, lectorem hoc loco meminisse operaepretium erit. Super mendacio & apertissimis nugis, non supra petram Christum fundatus est hic principatus, seu potius pompatica tyrannis. Os rugientis leonis accepit haec bestia Bonifacius, & loquebatur ut draco, A-poc.13. dum his verbis authoritatem firmaret, iu[?]ta Platinam atq; alios scriptores: Volumus ac mandamus, statuimus ac praecipimus: dumq; esset, non Ecclesiae, sed aquilae alterum caput, penes vaticinale somnium Esdrae. Sic propter populi peccata, hypocritam regnare fecit Deus, Iob 34. Constituit in sua superbia post Phocam, ut Rom. sedes ceteris omnibus deinceps anteferretur, habita Episcoporum synodo: & ne quis sub anathematis poena, in locum demortui pontificis surrogaretur, nisi tertia saltem post obitum eius die: & ne largitione aut gratia quis Pontificatum ambiret, quā vis ipse prius id fecerit. Voluit item pontificis electionem a clero pariter & populo fieri: sed id non diu durauit, interposita hac clausula, Volumus & iubemus. Ab hoc tempore caelestis doctrinae puritas in Ecclesia euanuit, ac valde est crescentibus superstitionibus obscurata. 2 Thes 2. Bonifacius iste anno Domini 607. nondum expleto Pontificatus anno, rebus humanis excessit.
