units.tr: Boniface III, a Roman, an ambitious beast, was raised to the papacy by the emperor Phocas, an adulterer, parricide and tyrant, in the greatest tumult of men, in the year of the Lord 607, while very many, both bishops and churches, protested. He was confirmed, worshipped, and acclaimed lord and prince of all bishops. By an eager petition, but by a much stronger largess, he obtained that the Roman see should be called the head of all churches, on these frivolous grounds: that the Empire first had its name from Rome, and that Peter handed the keys to his successors at Rome (a lie and a blasphemy). In this way the wicked authority of this Antichrist was established, having in it every vice of its founder, namely adultery, parricide and tyranny; so that he was regarded not as the vicar of Christ but of Phocas, the most wicked traitor; not the successor of the apostle Peter but of the apostate Judas, and of Satan himself. How splendid is the beginning of this so execrable monster, who boasts so arrogantly that he is the head of the Christian Church, it will be worth the reader's while to remember at this point. This principate, or rather pompous tyranny, was founded on a lie and most obvious trifles, not upon the rock Christ. This beast Boniface received the mouth of the roaring lion, and spoke like a dragon (Rev. 13), while by these words he confirmed his authority, according to Platina and other writers: "We will and command, we decree and order." And while he was the other head of the eagle, not of the Church, according to the prophetic dream of Esdras. Thus, because of the sins of the people, God made a hypocrite reign (Job 34). After Phocas he set up in his pride, by a synod of bishops, that the Roman see should be preferred to all others from then on; and that no one should be substituted, under penalty of anathema, in the place of a dead pope unless at least on the third day after his death; and that no one should seek the papacy by largess or favour, although he himself had previously done so. He also wished the election of the pope to be made by clergy and people alike; but this did not last long, a clause being inserted: "We will and command." From this time the purity of heavenly doctrine vanished from the Church, and it was greatly obscured as superstitions grew. (2 Thess. 2.) This Boniface died in the year of the Lord 607, before his first year of papacy was complete.
2. BONIFACE IV.

units.la: Bonifacius quartus, è Valeria Marforum urbe, Pantheon fœdissimum falsorum deorum templum, à Cæsare Phoca impetrauit, ut in eo, Cybelis spurcissimæ deorum matris loco, Maria Christi seruatoris mater, cum martyribus sanctis colerentur, Horrenda certè mutatio, & cum D. Pauli do strina tanquam ex diametro pugnans, ut quod idolis dedicatum fit, verteretur Christianis in usum sacrum, si sacer sit usus ille. Vuicelius tamen id sa-ctum laudat, & in pietatis usum conversum esse fatetur: adeo pro ventre delirare norunt ingenio-si pontificiorum sophistæ. Sed Phocas horum & similium flagitiorum meritas tandem pœnas luit: ab Heraclio successore imperio & vita privatus, atque amputatis manibus ac pedibus, in mare proiectus.Antea in eodem templo, ut Petrus Præ-monstratensis refert, multoties, erant à dæmonibus percussi Christiani homines: sed postea non, fortasse quod essent ex hac mutatione amici eo-rum facti, & eiusdem professionis cum primis cul-toribus. Instituit Bonifacius omnium sanctorum festum: & ut maiorem Missam eo die papa sem-per celebraret, ordinauit. Decreuit quoq;, ut ni-tidus pannus seu corporale, ad sacerdotis usum dum consecraret (ornamentum valde sacrum) in altari sterneretur. Ex paterna domo monaste-rium fecit, monachis fundos dedit: quibus etiam prædicandi, baptizandi, & absoluendi potestatem tribuit. Atq; ita sunt in tribum Levitica assumpti. Et anno Domini 614. extremum di-em obijt. De Pantheon templo, sic habet Man-tuanus: Pantheon hoc templum, Phoca donante recepit Romulidum pastor Bonifacius: atq; fugatis Inde simul cum matre deis, solenniter omnes Transtulit ad superos, &c.
units.tr: Boniface IV, from the city of Valeria Marsorum, obtained from the emperor Phocas the Pantheon, that most foul temple of false gods, so that in it, in place of Cybele, the most filthy mother of the gods, Mary the mother of Christ the Saviour was worshipped together with holy martyrs. A dreadful change indeed, and one that fights directly against the teaching of St. Paul, so that what was dedicated to idols should be turned to sacred use by Christians, if that use is sacred. Yet Vuicelius praises the deed and admits that it was turned to the use of piety; so well do the clever sophists of the Papists know how to rave for their bellies. But Phocas at last paid the deserved penalty for these and similar crimes: he was deprived of empire and life by his successor Heraclius, and, with his hands and feet cut off, was thrown into the sea. Earlier, in the same temple, as Peter of Premontré reports, Christians were often struck by demons; but afterwards not, perhaps because their friends had become friends of theirs through this change, and of the same profession as the first worshippers. Boniface instituted the feast of All Saints, and ordained that the pope should always celebrate the greater Mass on that day. He also decreed that a shining cloth, or corporal, a very sacred ornament, should be spread on the altar while the priest consecrated. He made a monastery out of his father's house and gave estates to the monks, to whom he also granted the power of preaching, baptizing and absolving. And so they were taken into the tribe of Levi. He died in the year of the Lord 614. Concerning the temple of the Pantheon, Mantuanus says thus: "This temple, the Pantheon, was received by the shepherd of the Romulids, Boniface, Phocas giving it; and the gods, having been driven out along with their mother, were solemnly transferred thence to the heavenly ones," etc.
3. THEODATUS I.

units.la: Theodatus primus, seu Deus dedit, Romanus, spiritualem cognationem ex testibus in paruulorum baptismo, ne nihil in Papistico regno fieri uideretur, primus adinuenit. Constituit autem, ne patrinus patrinam, aut filius patrini, puellam e sacro fonte a patre leuatam, in uxorem ducere posset. Quod equidem non paruum Antichristi indicium fuit, legitimas ac liberas a Deo permissas Christianis hominibus nuptias, cum Taciano, Montano, & aliis haereticis prohibere. Hinc illa spiritualis (ut uocant) cognatio, suam traxit originem: de qua non in Bibliis scriptis, sed in pontificiorum decretis profanis fit mentio. Verbuit illa aetate perniciosus morbus, lepra aut elephantia proximus: qui adeo deformatus in facie homines, ut uix internoscerentur. Moritur Theodatus anno Domini 618. post tertium sui pontificatus annum. Hic obseruare licebit, quod nullus Paparum ex hoc tempore, non egregii aliquid pro Romana sedis tyrannide constituens, diu superuixit.
units.tr: Theodatus I, or God-given, a Roman, first devised the spiritual kinship arising from sponsors at the baptism of infants, so that nothing should seem to be lacking in the Papist kingdom. He decreed, moreover, that a godfather might not marry the godmother, nor a godson the girl raised from the sacred font by his father. This was indeed no small sign of Antichrist, to forbid, along with Tatian, Montanus and other heretics, lawful and free marriages permitted to Christians by God. From this came that spiritual (as they call it) kinship, which drew its origin from it; a thing mentioned not in the written Bible but in the profane decrees of the Papists. In his time a pernicious disease broke out, close to leprosy or elephantiasis, which so deformed men's faces that they could scarcely be recognised. Theodatus died in the year of the Lord 618, after the third year of his papacy. Here it may be observed that none of the Popes from this time, who did not establish something outstanding for the tyranny of the Roman see, lived long.
4. BONIFACE the Fifth.

units.la: Bonifacius quintus, Campanus, liberam suis de-cretis alendorum furum atq; homicidarum in locis sacris potestatem concessit. Idemq; constituit, ne latrones aut sicarij ad templa, cœmiteria, & aras, tanquam ad asyla confugientes (afferetes tamen amant) uiolentia aut fortitudine ulla inde trahe-rentur. Acolitos prohibuit (res magni periculi)ne martyrum offa uel reliquias attrectarent. Sacri-legos in quouis loco (nam auferentes odiunt) ana-themate feriri mandauit. Testamentum iussu principis factum, ubiq; ualere uoluit. Quod tamen po-stea eius successores ad se traxerunt: ita ut nisi ip-si comprobassent, diuitum testamenta ualere nequi-bant. Cœmiteria extruxit ac dedicauit, qui & an-no Domini 623. ex uita demigrauit.
units.tr: Boniface the Fifth, a Campanian, by his decrees granted free licence to the feeding of thieves and murderers in sacred places. He also laid down that robbers and assassins who fled to temples, cemeteries and altars as to places of sanctuary (though they love to bring things in) should not be dragged out from there by any violence or force. He forbade the acolytes (a matter of great danger) to handle the bones or relics of the martyrs. He ordered that sacrilegious persons be struck with anathema in any place (for they hate those who carry things off). He wished a will made by order of the prince to be valid everywhere. His successors afterwards drew this power to themselves, so that the wills of the rich could not stand unless they themselves had approved them. He built and dedicated cemeteries, and in the year of the Lord 623 he departed from this life.
5. HONORIUS the First.

units.la: Honorius primus, Campanus, Vuicelio teste, bo-nus Papa fuit: sed ut apparet, negligens pastor, cleri reformator in seruandis cæremonijs, non ta-men in ministerio diuini uerbi: quonia[?] ad mores, nō doctrinam: ad templorū ædificia, non ad obseruationem præceptorum Dei, hæc facta sunt. Templorum enim tā extructor quàm reparator erat: sed nō animarum per Euangelij laborem ædificator, quod ipsi legimus. Basilicam D. Petri, tegulis æneis a Ioue Capitolino seu Romuli[?] templo, Heraclij Caesaris permissu ablatis opperuit: & urbem nouis tem-plis, de pauperum substantia locupletauit. Aedes Pancratij & Agnetis restituit: ac cœmeterium Marcellini & Petri ad pristinum usum reuocauit. Templa Anastasij, Seuerini, Cyriaci, Hadriani, Sylvestri, & quatuor Coronatorum, magnificentissimo opere erexit, auro & argento ac porphyreticis lapidibus ornauit: Festum exaltationis S. crucis instituit, inuocationes sanctorum mortuorum (impo-stor) Gregorij letaniis addidit, & ut processio sabbatis fieret ordinauit. Hinc circuitiones in Ecclesijs originem habere uidentur. Anno Domini 634. Honorius hic fato concessit: sub quo Mahumetes caput extulit.
units.tr: Honorius the First, a Campanian, was, according to Wycliffe, a good pope; but, as it appears, he was a negligent minister and a reformer of the clergy in keeping ceremonies, yet not in the ministry of the divine Word, since these things were done for morals, not doctrine, and for the buildings of temples, not for the observance of the precepts of God. For he was as much a builder and repairer of temples as he was not a builder of souls through the labour of the Gospel, which we read of him. He covered the basilica of St Peter with bronze tiles taken from the Capitoline Jupiter or the temple of Romulus, with the permission of the Emperor Heraclius, and he enriched the city with new temples out of the substance of the poor. He restored the churches of Pancras and Agnes, and recalled the cemetery of Marcellinus and Peter to its former use. He built, with most magnificent work, the churches of Anastasius, Severinus, Cyriacus, Hadrian, Sylvester and the Four Crowned Martyrs, and adorned them with gold, silver and porphyry stones. He instituted the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, added the invocations of dead saints (an imposture) to the litanies of Gregory, and ordained that a procession be made on Saturdays. From this, it seems, the circuits in churches take their origin. In the year of the Lord 634 this Honorius yielded to fate, under whom Mahomet raised his head.
6. SEVERINUS the Second.

units.la: Seuerinus, uel Zepherinus secundus, Romanus, Heraclij Imperatoris nomine, per Isacium Italiæ exarchum (inanis enim tum uidebatur plebis electio) in papam erat confirmatus. Qui etiam uel[?] de studiosus fuit in extruendis mortuorum sanctorum templis: at in uiuificantis Euangelij ministerio nihil. Inde igitur ablatus est ingens Ecclesiæ thesaurus, per dictum[?] Isacium: qui indignabatur tantum eos in thesauris habere, nec quicquam in usus bellicos conferre, præsertim cum milites magnæ[?] rerum inopia laborarent. Nam Saraceni Damascum, Arabiam, Phoeniciam, Aegyptum, & alia mundi regna (diuina plane ultione) Romanis tunc ademerunt: & Sisebutus Gothus Hispaniam, ad imperij detrimentum non modicum. Non excommunicationis fulmine tamen contriuit Papa Seuerinus tam impudentem sacrilegum, qualis fuit Isacius ille, quoniam adhuc ferenda crux erat. Sed aliam posteri uiam inuenerunt, qua & dominos & cruces eiusmodi omnes abijcere ualuerunt, ut in sequentibus eorum factis clarebit. Scotos super Paschae celebratione per Epistolam redarguit: & anno Domini 636. tandem decessit.
units.tr: Severinus, or Zephyrinus the Second, a Roman, was confirmed as pope in the name of the Emperor Heraclius through Isaac, exarch of Italy (for the election by the people then seemed empty). He also was rather keen on building churches for the holy dead, but on the ministry of the life-giving Gospel, nothing. Therefore the great treasure of the Church was taken away by the said Isaac, who was indignant that they kept such riches in their treasuries and contributed nothing to warlike uses, especially since the soldiers were suffering from a great scarcity of goods. For the Saracens then took from the Romans Damascus, Arabia, Phoenicia, Egypt and other kingdoms of the world (clearly by divine vengeance), and the Gothic Sisebut took Spain, to no small loss of the empire. Yet Pope Severinus did not crush so shameless a sacrilegious man, such as that Isaac, with the thunderbolt of excommunication, since the cross still had to be borne. But later generations found another way, by which they were able to cast off both lords and all such crosses, as will be clear in their deeds that follow. He rebuked the Scots by letter concerning the celebration of Easter, and at last died in the year of the Lord 636.
7. JOHN the Fourth.

units.la: Ioannes quartus, Dalmata, ex damnis prædecessori nuper illatis, prudentior factus, Istrios & Dalmatas, conterraneos suos, à Longobardis bello captos, thesauris ab Isacio Laterani relictis, à captiuitate redemit. Et statim post sui pontifica-tus initium, ne deinceps similia fierent, constituit, ut res Ecclesiasticæ tam temeriter ablatæ, in qua-druplum restituerentur: quod nescio an ab omnibus approbatum sit. Ad Anglos ille scripsit, pro Paschate celebrando, & contra Pelagianam hæ-resin[?], quæ & apud eos tunc reuiuiscebat, ut Bedas[?] refert in libro de ratione temporum. Vincentij & Anastasij, duorum martyrum corpora, ex Dalmatia Romam transferri fecit, ut à barbarorum manibus seruarentur, ad futuram idololatriam fouendam, quæ maior est adhuc barbaries. Hic anno Domini 638 nec dum expletis duobus annis in ipsa Papatu, emigrauit. Eius tempore Rothari Longobardorum rex, sectā Arrianus, sed ut Platina scribit, iustitia ac pietate insignis, in singulis sui regni ciuitatibus, duos episcopos pari potestate præesse permisit, unum Arrianum, alterum Catholicum.
units.tr: John the Fourth, a Dalmatian, having become wiser from the recent losses inflicted on his predecessor, redeemed from captivity the Istrians and Dalmatians, his fellow countrymen, who had been taken captive by the Lombards in war, using the treasures left by Isaac of the Lateran. And immediately after the beginning of his pontificate, lest similar things should happen henceforth, he decreed that ecclesiastical goods so rashly taken away should be restored fourfold; whether this was approved by all, I do not know. He wrote to the English about celebrating Easter, and against the Pelagian heresy, which was then reviving among them, as Bede reports in his book on the reckoning of time. He had the bodies of Vincent and Anastasius, two martyrs, transferred from Dalmatia to Rome, so that they might be preserved from the hands of barbarians, in order to foster future idolatry, which is still a greater barbarism. He departed this life in the year of the Lord 638, before two full years in the papacy itself. In his time Rothari, king of the Lombards, an Arian by sect but, as Platina writes, distinguished for justice and piety, permitted two bishops with equal authority to preside in each city of his kingdom, one an Arian, the other a Catholic.

units.la: Quod utinam in Britannia nunc fieret cum Christianis & Papistis. At non potest, cum illic sub regina Maria & Cardinale Polo Papista dominetur, omnib. paganis, haereticis, ac tyrannis truculentiores.
units.tr: Would that this were done now in Britain with Christians and Papists! But it cannot be, since under Queen Mary and Cardinal Pole, a Papist, they rule there, more savage than all pagans, heretics and tyrants.
8. THEODORE the First.

units.la: Theodorus primus, Græcus, Hierosolymorum episcopi Theodori filius: constituit in Paschae vigilia, paschalem cereum consecrari. Templa Romae plura instaurauit, oratoria à fundamentis construxit, Pyrrhum patriarcham Constantinopolitanum ob haeresim exautorauit, quorundam sanctorum corpora thecis ac tumbis ornauit, reliquias martyrum in sacris aedibus collocauit, adhibitis ornamentis aureis atq; argenteis: & contracta post simplex votum matrimonia, diuini uetuit[?] ... Quibus peractis, anno Domini 646. hic Papa defunctus est.
units.tr: Theodore the First, a Greek, son of Theodore, bishop of Jerusalem, decreed that the paschal candle be consecrated on the vigil of Easter. He restored several churches in Rome, built oratories from the foundations, deposed Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople, for heresy, adorned the bodies of certain saints with cases and tombs, placed the relics of martyrs in sacred buildings, using gold and silver ornaments, and forbade, ... marriages contracted after a simple vow. When these things were done, this pope died in the year of the Lord 646.
9. Martin I.

units.la: Martinus primus, patria Tudertinus: sanctus à Papistis habetur, quod otiosus pastor & idolum, nihil memoria dignum fecerit. In Romana synodo, leges quasdam de festis diebus ac templis orandis, quas ipsi idolorum cultores antea seruabant, constituit: & ut sacrificuli comas raderent, arctè praecepit. Episcopis mandauit, ut chrisma, quod uocant sacrum, singulis annis conficerent, & ad omnes suarum diœcesium Ecclesias mitterent. Votum cœlibatus, conscientiarum carnifex, pro Sodoma confouenda, clericis imposuit: & post initum matrimonium, ante carnalem copulam, sponsum ac sponsam à sacerdote benedici iussit, tanquam sine eorum praestigijs non sufficeret Dei benedictio, Gen. 1. Vehemens in festas: (inquit Vuicelius) illas excommunicabat, quas tamen debuerat per scripturas admonere. Paulum patriarcham Constantinopolitanum deposuit: non cum Apostolo, post unam & alteram correptionem declinauit, Tit. 3. Propterea cathenis vinctus, & Constantinopolim perductus, in exilium à Caesare Constantio pellitur: ubi anno Domini 653. miserè deuium moritur.
units.tr: Martin I, a native of Todi, is regarded as a saint by the Papists, because as an idle pastor and an idol he did nothing worth remembering. In the Roman synod he issued certain laws about feast days and about praying in temples, which the worshippers of idols had kept before him. He strictly ordered that the little priests shave their hair. He commanded bishops to make each year the chrism they call holy and send it to all the churches of their dioceses. He imposed the vow of celibacy on the clergy, the executioner of consciences, to foster Sodom. After marriage had been entered into, and before carnal union, he ordered the bridegroom and bride to be blessed by a priest, as if God's blessing would not suffice without their juggling. Gen. 1. Vehement against feasts, he (says Vuicelius) excommunicated those whom he ought to have admonished from the Scriptures. He deposed Paul, patriarch of Constantinople. He did not, as the Apostle bids, avoid him after one or two rebukes. Tit. 3. For this he was bound in chains and taken to Constantinople, and was driven into exile by the Emperor Constans, where in the year of the Lord 653 he died miserably in exile.
10. Eugenius I.

units.la: Evgenius primus, Romanus, laudatus à moribus Papa, Vuicelio teste, nihil eximium fecit. Ille tamen iussit, ut episcopi, carceres haberent propter puniendis, non idololatris, adulteris, aut paederastis, quorum apud eos ingens erat numerus: sed haereticis, ut Christum pure confitentes appellare solent. Ita sensim ad se traxerunt potestatem civilis gladij, tyrannidemq; plusquam Nimrodicam exercuerunt. Monachis praecepit, ne exirent coenobia sine superioris consensu, ut occulta manerent omnia: & ut sacrificulorum domicilia iuxta Ecclesias extruerentur, sanciuit. Romae etiam in conuentu statuit, episcopis non licere, Ecclesiae bona in proprios usus conuertere. Ad extremum anno Domini 656. animam efflauit.
units.tr: Eugenius I, a Roman, praised as a pope for his morals according to Vuicelius, did nothing outstanding. Yet he ordered that bishops have prisons for punishing, not idolaters, adulterers or pederasts, of whom there was a huge number among them, but heretics, who are in the habit of calling themselves those who confess Christ purely. Thus little by little they drew the power of the civil sword to themselves and exercised a tyranny more than Nimrodic. He instructed monks not to leave their monasteries without the consent of their superior, so that everything would remain hidden; and he decreed that the dwellings of the little priests be built beside the churches. At Rome, in a council, he also laid down that bishops were not permitted to turn church goods to their own uses. Finally, in the year of the Lord 656, he breathed out his soul.
11. Vitellianus of Segni.

units.la: Vitellianus, patria Signinus uel Campanus, musicus insignis, Ecclesiasticam regulam scripsit, tantum in templis ordinauit, & organa per consonantias humanis uocibus adhibuit: iuxta illud Baptistae Mantuani, in quarto Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Vitellianus, a native of Segni or Campania, a notable musician, wrote a church rule, and ordained organs for use only in temples, and had them accompany human voices in consonance, according to that line of Baptista Mantuanus in the fourth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Signius adiunxit, molli conflata metallo Organa, quae festis resonant ad sacra diebus.
units.tr: Signius added organs, cast from soft metal, which resound on sacred days of festival.

units.la: Hic Ioannem quendam, cuidam Ecclesiae inseruientem mientem[?] in Creta insula: apud eius loci Epifco-pum (iniusta conscientia hypocrita) per literas accusavit, quod uxorem haberet. Oratores monachos in Angliam misit, Theodorum quendam Græcum & Hadrianum Aphrum, circa annum Domini 666. qui à Christo nato numerus est nominis bestiæ: ut fluctuantes in suscepta fide papistica confirmarent, & ut Antichristi characterem credentes suos signarent, Apoc.13. Horas Latinas, cantiones Latinas, cæremonias, missas & idololatrias Latinas, aliasque manes nugas & circulationes omnes in templis, Latinè fieri disposuit, iuxta Græcam dictionem Λατινὸς, quæ per literas numerales prædictum Bestiæ numerum perfecit. Tonsuras mandauit, unctiones præcepit, & sub illis authoritatem emendi & vendendi, in nundinationibus papisticis concessit, Apoc.13. Vitelianus autem, anno Christi 671. post varias impostaturas, vitæ suæ finem est sortitus. In hac plena ætate Bestiæ, fucata monachorum sanctitas in magno precio erat, coram excæcato in tantis superstitionibus mundo. Triaq; miracula valde magna fiebant. Monachorum cænobia erigebantur, reges in monachos tondebantur, & quotidiana scor-tatio statim erat in sanctam canonizata.
units.tr: He accused a certain John, serving a church (?) in the island of Crete, by letter before the bishop of that place (an unjust conscience, a hypocrite), because he had a wife. He sent monks as envoys into England, Theodorus, a certain Greek, and Hadrian the African, about the year of the Lord 666, which is the number of the name of the beast from the birth of Christ, to confirm the wavering in the faith of the Papists which they had embraced, and to mark their believers with the character of Antichrist, Rev. 13. He arranged that the Latin hours, Latin chants, ceremonies, Latin masses and idolatries, and all other vain trifles and processions in the temples, be performed in Latin, according to the Greek word Latinos [Λατινὸς], which by its numerical letters makes up the aforesaid number of the Beast. He ordered tonsures, and commanded anointings, and under these granted authority to buy and sell at the Papistical fairs, Rev. 13. Vitellianus, however, in the year of Christ 671, after various impostures, reached the end of his life. In this full age of the Beast, the painted sanctity of the monks was held in great esteem, before a world blinded by such great superstitions. And very great miracles were happening. Monasteries of monks were being erected, kings were shaved into monks, and daily whoring was at once canonized as holiness.
12. Theodatus II.

units.la: Theodatus secundus, aliàs à Deo datus, patria Romanus, ex monacho pontifex factus, cœnobium D. Erasmi in Cælio monte, ex quo olim prodierat, sumptuosius auxit: & Benedicti Nursini, sui ordinis patriarchæ corpus, unà cū sorore Scholastica, à monte Casino ad Floriacum in Galliis per monachos transferri permisit. Templum D. Petri in via Portuensi iuxta Meruli pontem tum instauravit, tum dedicavit: ac supplicationes pro abolendis prodigijs quæ suo tempore contigerunt, frequentes fieri iussit. In fata Theodatus concessit anno Domini 675. post quartum sui pontificatus annum. Quo tempore iris cœlestis apparuit, & contremuit terra mirum in modum. Per pluvias & tonitrua coculcatæ[?] sunt segetes omnes, sed iterum postea sunt renatæ.
units.tr: Theodatus II, otherwise called Given by God, a native of Rome, made pope from being a monk, enlarged more sumptuously the monastery of St Erasmus on the Caelian hill, from which he had formerly come forth. He allowed the body of Benedict of Nursia, patriarch of his order, to be carried by monks from Monte Cassino to Fleury in Gaul, together with his sister Scholastica. He both restored and dedicated the church of St Peter on the Portuan road near the Milvian bridge. He ordered frequent supplications to be made for the averting of the portents which occurred in his time. Theodatus departed this life in the year of the Lord 675, after the fourth year of his pontificate. At that time a rainbow appeared, and the earth trembled in a wonderful manner. Through rains and thunderstorms all the crops were beaten down, but they were afterwards reborn.
13. Donus I.

units.la: Donus primus, patria Romanus, papatum iniens, durissimis temporibus nactus est: in quibus agri & segetes fulminibus atq; imbribus emarcuerunt. Vestibulum fani D. Petri, quod Paradisum vocant, columnis (Papale studium) primus exornavit: & quosdam Nestorianæ factionis monachos, Romæ repertos, in diversa Latinorum monasteria post castigationes misit. Instaurauit pretea[?] praeterea, & restitutas dedicauit, Ecclesiam ii.[?] Apostolorum in uia Hostiensi, & Ecclesiam D. Euphemiae in uia Appia sitam. Clerum in uarios distinxit ordines, atq; honoribus ualde auxit. Rauennatum Ecclesiam, hactenus Alliocephalim dictam, blandicijs pontificijs, Theodoro suo archiepiscopo consentiente, Romanae synagogae subiectam post lites demum reddidit. Post alia quaedam eius generis facta, anno Domini 679. Donus defunctus occubuit.
units.tr: Donus I, a native of Rome, on entering the papacy obtained it in the hardest of times, when fields and crops withered from lightnings and showers. He was the first to adorn, with columns (a papal zeal), the vestibule of the temple of St Peter, which they call Paradise. After rebukes he sent some monks of the Nestorian faction, found at Rome, to various Latin monasteries. He also restored and dedicated the church of the Apostles on the Ostian road, and the church of St Euphemia situated on the Appian way. He divided the clergy into various orders and greatly increased their honours. The church of Ravenna, hitherto called autocephalous, was at last, after lawsuits, made subject to the Roman synagogue, through the flatteries of the popes, with Theodore, his archbishop, consenting. After certain other deeds of this kind, Donus died in the year of the Lord 679.
14. Agatho the First.

units.la: AGathon primus, Siculus ac Monachus: Papali authoritate usus, Romanorum pontificum sanctiones, tanquam Apostolicas & diuina uoce firmatas, à Christianis omnibus recipi iussit, ut Gratianus scribit, Dist. 19. cap. Sic. Approbabat ille missam Latinam à multis papis confutam, & instar Aesopicae cornicula, emendicatis aliunde plumis ornatam: & à Deo instituta in Latinorum ministris coniugia, scelerosus impostor damnabat. Ad Angliam anno Domini 679. Ioannem monachum, archicantorem Romanum & abbatem D. Martini desinabat, ut ritum in templis legendi, canendi, ac caeremonizandi, illic doceret, atq; ut celebrationum & sacrificiorum usum traderet: sicut Bedae testatur lib. 4. & cap. 18. de gestis Anglorum. rum. Oratores suos Ioannem Portuensem Episcopum, et Ioannem Rom.Ecclesiae diaconum, ad jextam synodum Constantinopolim, contra Monothelitas etiam Agathon misit. In qua, ut dictum est, Graecis sacerdotibus uxores sunt permissae, Latinis vero ademptae. In eadem quoq; his atq; aliis gestis, in octava Paschae anno Domini 681. idem Ioannes Portuensis, coram principe ac patriar-cha, populoq; Constantinopolitano, in Basilica S. Sophiae, Latinam missam primus celebrauit publice, approbantibus omnibus, qui tum aderant, illam novitatem, aut nuperrime inventum prodigium. Quae hinc authoritatem sumens, non a Dei verbo, sed hominum placitis impijs, omnes inde Eccle-sias Romanum pontificem agnoscentes, idololatrice ad innumerabilium animarum perniciem occuparet. Huius Agathonis tempore, post Lunae ac solis eclipsim, tanta peste anno Domini 682. Romae laboratum est, ut ipsum ea sustulerit. Ces-sauitq; ex hac bene merita Dei ultione papatus, anno uno cum dimidio.
units.tr: Agatho the First, a Sicilian and a monk, exercised papal authority. He ordered that the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, as though they were apostolic and confirmed by a divine voice, be received by all Christians, as Gratian writes in Dist. 19, chapter "Sic." He approved the Latin mass, which many popes had already refuted, and which was adorned with feathers begged from elsewhere, like Aesop's jackdaw. The wicked impostor condemned marriage among the Latin ministers, though it was instituted by God. In the year of the Lord 679 he sent John, a monk, the Roman chief cantor and abbot of St. Martin's, to England, so that he might teach there the manner of reading, singing and performing ceremonies in the churches, and hand on the practice of celebrations and sacrifices. Bede bears witness to this in Book 4, chapter 18, on the deeds of the English. Agatho also sent as his envoys against the Monothelites to the Sixth Council at Constantinople, John, bishop of Porto, and John, deacon of the Roman Church. There, as has been said, wives were permitted to Greek priests but taken away from Latin ones. In the same council, and in these and other doings, in the octave of Easter in the year of the Lord 681, the same John of Porto, before the emperor, the patriarch and the people of Constantinople, first celebrated the Latin mass publicly in the Basilica of St. Sophia. All who were present approved that novelty, or rather that newly invented monstrosity. Taking authority from this, not from the Word of God but from impious human decrees, he began to bring all churches under the Roman pontiff, to the eternal ruin of countless souls. In the time of this Agatho, after an eclipse of the moon and sun, Rome suffered a great plague in the year of the Lord 682, which, it is said, carried him off. And by this just vengeance of God the papacy ceased with him after one year and a half.
15. Leo the Second.

units.la: LEo secundus, monachus, natione Siculus, Gra-ce et Latine aeque sciens, adeo in musicis peritus erat, ut psalmodias et hymnos ad meliorem concentum redigeret. Sextam synodum in Missae gratiam, & quia per illam ademptum fuit sacrifi-culis occidentalibus coniugium, confirmauit: atq; in Latinum sermonem ordinationes eius transfu-lit. Pacis osculum populo dari in missæ ministerio, statuit: quotidie eq[?], si urgeret necessitas (magnum beneficium) baptizare concessit. Electiones Episcoporum valere noluit (ob Rauennates) nisi pri-mi (nota Antichristi cauterium & characterem) accederet Rom. pontificis confirmatio. Sed sine redemptione pallij, inquit Vuicelius, aut pecunia-rum solutione. Porro non tanta tunc audebant, fi-cut post annum à Seruatore nato millesimum. Ante-a Italorum Episcopos, etiam Papam ipsum, Exarchi confirmauerant: postea consentiente Imperatore Constantino quarto, denuo rata erat cleri ac plebis electio. Rauennates tamen archi præ-sules, Exarchorum, quorum fuit apud eos sedes, authoritate Romanæ sedi parere noluerunt, sed æquales illis esse contenderunt. Felix ergo, eorum post Theodorum Archiepiscopus, conatus est Papæ iugum excutere, atque amissam libertatem reparare. Sed illi statim Iustinianus Cæsar, Constantini prædicti filius, à Leone inductus occurrit, & post urbis oppugnationem, candenti ferro ei oculos eruit, atq; Pontum in exilium misit. Leo autem anno Domini 685. uir decem mensi-um sium[?] pontifex, statim moritur. Quo anno lunæ ta- lem eclipsim pertulit, ut per totas noctes sanguineo vultu laboraret.
units.tr: Leo the Second, a monk, a Sicilian by birth, equally skilled in Greek and Latin, was so expert in music that he reduced psalmody and hymns to a better harmony. He confirmed the Sixth Council, for the sake of the mass, and because through it marriage was taken away from the western priests. He also translated its decrees into Latin. He decreed that the kiss of peace be given to the people in the ministry of the mass. He also allowed baptism daily, even, if necessity pressed, (a great benefit). He refused to let the elections of bishops be valid (because of the Ravennates) unless the confirmation of the Roman pontiff, the first, the mark of Antichrist and his branding iron, was added. But, says Wicelius, without payment for the pallium or payment of money. Moreover, at that time they did not dare such things as they did after the thousandth year from the birth of the Saviour. Earlier, the Exarchs had confirmed the Italian bishops, even the Pope himself. Later, with the consent of the Emperor Constantine IV, the election by clergy and people was again ratified. Nevertheless, the archbishops of Ravenna, to whose see the Exarchs had belonged, refused to obey the authority of the Roman see, and strove to be equal to it. Therefore Felix, the archbishop there after Theodore, tried to shake off the yoke of the Pope and recover his lost liberty. But at once Justinian Caesar, son of the aforesaid Constantine, was induced by Leo and came to the rescue. After the siege of the city, he put out Felix's eyes with a red-hot iron and sent him into exile in Pontus. Leo himself died at once in the year of the Lord 685, a pontiff of only ten months. In that year he endured such an eclipse of the moon that for whole nights he was afflicted with a bloody face.
16. Benedict the Second.

units.la: Benedictus secundus, Romanus, ea fuit hypocri-si, quam sanctitatem papistæ vocant, ut Con-stantinus quartus (si non eo mortuo, mentiantur) eius causa decreuerit, ut deinceps Rom. pontifex, absq; consensu imperatoris aut Exarchi, populo præesset: quod tamen postea non diu fuit obserua-tum. Templa D. Petri, Laurentij, Valentini, ac S. Mariæ ad martyres, hic magnis sumptibus restau-rauit. Vasibus aureis & argenteis, inauratis atque holosericis vestibus, aliisq; ornamentis iuxta ritum Iudaicos exornauit. Iste etiam primus Christi (Sa-tanæ potius) habebatur in terris vicarius. Ex Ve-suvio monte Campaniæ tantus ignis tum erupit, ut loca circunquaq; posita, cum hominibus & iu-mentis, exusta sint. Constatq; non multo post, an-no scilicet Domini 686. cædes, incendia, rapinas, ac mortes principum sequi, maxime Benedicti hu-ius, decem mensium Papæ.
units.tr: Benedict the Second, a Roman, was of that hypocrisy which the papists call holiness. Constantine IV (unless they lie, if he was not dead by then) decreed on his account that from then on the Roman pontiff should preside over the people without the consent of the emperor or the Exarch, a rule which, however, was not long observed afterwards. He restored at great expense the temples of St. Peter, Lawrence, Valentine, and St. Mary at the Martyrs. He adorned them with golden and silver vessels, gilded and silk vestments, and other ornaments after the Jewish manner. He was also the first to be regarded as the vicar of Christ (of Satan rather) on earth. At that time such a great fire broke out from Mount Vesuvius in Campania that the places lying all around, with men and beasts, were burned up. And it is established that not long afterwards, in the year of the Lord 686, murders, fires, plunderings and deaths of princes followed, especially in the time of this Benedict, pope for ten months.
17. John the Fifth.

units.la: Ioannes quintus, natione Syrus, patria Antio-chenus, consecrationem à tribus Episcopis, Ho-stiense, Portuense, ac Veliterno, primus accepit quem exinde morem à successoribus seruari decreuit. Et cum ritum posteri eius in hunc usque diem obseruarunt, in Seruatoris ecclesia apud Lateranum, ut ille tunc iusserat, quae & Constantiana à Magno Constantino dicitur. Fuit autem hic Ioannes ante & in papatu ualetudinarius, & inter o-cia papalia scripsit libellum de Archiepiscopali pallij dignitate: opus certe tam languido artifice dignum. Qui & morte praeuentus, anno Domini 688. ampliora pro Romanae sedis honore praestare non ualuit.
units.tr: John the Fifth, a Syrian by birth and an Antiochene by homeland, was the first to receive consecration from three bishops, those of Ostia, Porto and Velletri. He then decreed that his successors keep this custom, and they have observed the rite down to this day, in the church of the Saviour at the Lateran, as he had then ordered, which is also called the Constantinian church after the Great Constantine. This John was sickly before and during his papacy, and among his papal duties he wrote a little book on the dignity of the archiepiscopal pallium, a work certainly worthy of so feeble a craftsman. He was also overtaken by death in the year of the Lord 688, and was not able to render greater services to the honour of the Roman see.
18. CONON the Thracian.

units.la: Conon Thracius, ex presbytero creatus erat pontifex, Petro ac Theodoro competitoribus post longam altercationem repudiatis. Hic sumpto papatu, in ualetudinem, propinato fortasis insipi-do poculo, statim incidit, de qua anno Domini 689. mortuus est, & inter Papas sepultus. Kilianum Scotum, professione monachum, Episcopum hic fe-cit, & cum quibusdam sociis etiam monachis in Germaniam misit, ut Franciae Orientalis populos ad papisticam fidem traduceret, & Antichristi characterē signaret. Qui statim à suis auditoribus occisi sunt, & apud Herbipolim sepulti. Paschalis quidam archipresbyter, & Cononis praedi-cti[?] thesaurarius, Ioannem Platinam Exarchum pe eunuchis[?] eo uiuente folicitabat, ut post eius mortem fieret Papa. Accepit Exarchus pecuniam, sedni-hil præstitit: cum non alio præmio, quam frustra-tione, dignus esset sacerdos auarus, & impiè regnandi cupidus proditor.
units.tr: Conon the Thracian, who had been a presbyter, was made pope after his rivals Peter and Theodore were rejected following a long dispute. Once he had assumed the papacy, he fell ill straight away, perhaps having drunk from a cup of some unpleasant drink, and he died of this illness in the year of the Lord 689 and was buried among the Popes. He made Kilian, a Scot by profession a monk, a bishop, and sent him into Germany with some companions, who were also monks, to bring the peoples of Eastern Franconia over to the papistical faith and to mark them with the character of Antichrist. They were at once killed by their own hearers and buried at Würzburg. A certain Paschalis, archpriest and treasurer of the aforesaid Conon, tried to persuade the exarch John Platyn, through the eunuchs, while he was still alive, that he should become pope after his death. The exarch took the money but did nothing for him, since a greedy priest and a traitor eager to rule by impious means deserved no reward but to be cheated.
19. SERGIUS the first.

units.la: SErgius primus, natione Syrus, & patria Antio-chenus, qui in cantilenis studiosus, per cœmite-ria martyrum missas olim celebrabat, magna in populo per Theodorum & Paschalem prædictum orta diuisione, in Pontificem demum electus fuit.
units.tr: Sergius the first, a Syrian by birth and an Antiochene by origin, who was devoted to singing and in the past used to celebrate masses at the cemeteries of the martyrs, was at last elected pontiff, after a great division had arisen among the people through Theodore and the aforesaid Paschalis.

units.la: In templis ornandis, & idololatriis ampliandis, hic multa fecit. Petri Basilicam ablatis ruderibus, renouatisq; tignis, stillicidiis ac parietibus in antiquam formam restituit, & frontispicium eiusdem basilicæ, opere uermiculato decorauit. Candelabra atque alia templi ornamenta, Iudaico more, ex auro, argento, & pannis preciosis fieri fecit in eadem basilica, ac partem crucis Dominicæ in capsula quadam ænea inuenit. Leonis primi corpus in celebratiori repositum loco, & statuas Apostolorum uetustate exoletas renouauit. Collapsa tem-pla nonnulla restituit, uel noua saltem de integro fecit.
units.tr: In adorning the churches and enlarging the idolatries, he did many things. He restored the basilica of St Peter: having removed the rubble and renewed the beams, gutters and walls, he returned it to its former shape, and he decorated the façade of the same basilica with mosaic work. He had candlesticks and other church ornaments made in the same basilica, in the Jewish manner, of gold, silver and costly cloths, and he found a part of the Lord's cross in a certain bronze casket. He placed the body of Leo the first in a more celebrated spot, and he renewed the statues of the Apostles, which had grown old with age. He restored several collapsed temples, or at least built new ones from the foundations.

units.la: Ter agnus Dei in Missa papistica, sub panis fractionem per sacrificum dici mandauit: & in Annunciationis Mariæ festo letanias cantari iusssit. Aquilegiensem ecclesiam, à papismo parum de-clinantem, revocauit: & Saxones ac Phrysios ad eandem superstitionem per monachos invitauit. Cum vero Aldhelmus Anglus, sui episcopatum ad-missionem Romæ expectaret, Sergium papam, in-fante recens nato, adulterii insimulatum audivit (sic in sanctissimo inclaruit cœhbatu[?]) illumque tan-tæ impietatis clanculum admonuit. Rauennatibus Damianum, Phrysonibus ac Batauis Vuilibror-dum Clementem, & Anglis Brithvualdum, archie-piscopos dedit. Tandenq;[?] anno Domini 701.[?] à præsenti seculo migrauit.
units.tr: He ordered that the Agnus Dei be said three times in the papistical Mass by the priest during the breaking of the bread, and he commanded that litanies be sung on the feast of the Annunciation of Mary. He called back the church of Aquileia, which had moved only slightly away from popery, and through monks he invited the Saxons and Frisians to the same superstition. When Aldhelm the Englishman was awaiting his admission to his bishopric at Rome, he heard that Pope Sergius had been accused of adultery with a newly born infant (so renowned was he for his most holy monastic life), and he secretly warned him about such great impiety. He gave Damian as archbishop to the people of Ravenna, Willibrord Clement to the Frisians and the Batavians, and Berthwald to the English. At last, in the year of the Lord 701, he departed from this present age.
20. JOHN the sixth.

units.la: Ioannes sextus, natione Græcus, ex genitore Pe-tronio, inanium rerum studiosus atque amantissimus, more prædecessorum, templis instaurandis, & divorum aris ornandis, plurimum insudauit. Fa-num D. Petri in primis adornauit: & eius altare summum, ductis columnis dextra lævaq; magnificè decorauit. Basilicam D. Andreæ in Vaticano, & templum D. Marti[?], sarcto tecto restituit. Ex ærario etiam Ecclesiæ, tempore famis & bel-li, multos pauperes pauit (optimus in eo uitæ genere pontifex) & captiuos redemit: Gisulphumq; Beneuentanum ducem, Campaniam tunc uastantem, comminationibus ad sua redire coegit. MarTyrio coronatum pleriq; illum afferunt, quod faci-le crederem: sed causam, & a quibus interfectus sit, non addunt, quum ipsi fortassis tanti facinoris authores fuerint. Mortuus anno Domini 704. ad Catecumbas Sebastianas, in uia Appia sepelitur. Leo quidam hunc Ioannem praecessisse dicitur: ob Sergij stuprum, ut apparet, electus tantum, at non confirmatus, eo iterum restituto: & ideo inter Pa-pas ille non numeratur. Petrus Pramonstraten-sis, propter malum introitum, reiectum fuisse narrat: et propterea in pontificum catalogo non ponit.
units.tr: John the sixth, a Greek by birth, the son of his father Petronius, devoted to empty things and very fond of them, following the custom of his predecessors, worked very hard at restoring temples and adorning the altars of the saints. He first adorned the shrine of St Peter, and he magnificently decorated its high altar with columns on the right and left. He restored the basilica of St Andrew in the Vatican and the temple of St Martin, repairing the roof. He also fed many poor people from the treasury of the Church in a time of famine and war (an excellent pontiff in this kind of life), and he ransomed captives. He also forced Gisulf, duke of Benevento, who was then laying waste Campania, to return to his own land by threats. Many say he was crowned with martyrdom, which I could easily believe; but they do not add the cause, or by whom he was killed, since perhaps they themselves were the authors of so great a crime. He died in the year of the Lord 704 and was buried at the Catacombs of St Sebastian on the Appian Way. It is said that a certain Leo came before this John: elected because of the defilement of Sergius, as it appears, but not confirmed, and then John was restored; and for this reason that Leo is not counted among the Popes. Peter of Prémontré relates that he was rejected because of his wrongful entry, and therefore he does not place him in the catalogue of pontiffs.
21. JOHN the seventh.

units.la: Ioannes septimus, etiam Graecus, ex patre Plato-ne: ut alij praedicessores, aedificandorum, sacran-dorum, atq; ornandorum templorum gratia, & chronographis pariter celebratur. Oratorium e-tenim valde pulchrum, Mariae virgini dedica-tum, in D. Petri templo extruxit: ac S. Eugenia basilicam iam pridem uetustate collapsam, restitu-it. Coemiteria quoq; nonnulla, & praesertim san-ctorum Marcellini, Marci & Damasi pontificum exornauit: aliasq; basilicas picturis ac sanctorum historijs cultiores reddidit. Sed de Euangelij pro-pagatione ad animarum ornatum, inter haec tam splendida aedificia, nulla fit mentio: ac si non in aliis quam in uanissimis his mundi spectaculis, uel quod multo deterius est, idolomaniis Sathanicis sita sit religio. Vita decessit hic papa anno Domi-ni 707. post duos sui regiminis annos, in cratorio præfato sepultus.
units.tr: John the seventh, also a Greek, the son of Plato, is celebrated like his other predecessors for the sake of building, consecrating and adorning temples, and likewise by the chroniclers. For he built, in the temple of St Peter, a very beautiful oratory dedicated to the Virgin Mary, and he restored the basilica of St Eugenia, which had long before collapsed with age. He also adorned several cemeteries, especially those of the saints Marcellinus, Marcus and the popes Damasus, and he made other basilicas more splendid with paintings and scenes from the lives of the saints. But of the spreading of the Gospel for the adornment of souls, there is no mention amid these splendid buildings; as if religion were located in nothing but these most vain spectacles of the world, or, what is much worse, in Satanic idol-worship. This pope departed this life in the year of the Lord 707, after two years of his reign, and was buried in the oratory aforesaid.
22. SISINNIUS the second.

units.la: Sisinnius, uel potius Sozimus secundus, patria Sy-rus: post magnam contentionem, quam cum quo-dam Diofcoro circa pontificatum habebat, papa-lem dignitatem obtinuit. Hic arthetica passione, chiragra ac podagra, ita laborabat, ut nec cibum per se capere posset. Vrbis tamen reparandæ ædi-ficator eximius futurus, solicitam curam gesit, materiamq; sufficientem ad muros instaurandos, paucorum dierum pontifex procurauit. Nam & tota eorum religio, inædificijs ac pictionibus tunc erat. Sed subita morte statim post uicesimum in pa-patu diem correptus, eodem anno quo prædictus Ioannes, & ipse interiit. Sunt qui ueneno illum à Diofcoro sublatum arbitrentur. Vide inter alios Nauclerum.
units.tr: Sisinnius, or rather Sisinnius the second, a Syrian by birth: after a great contention which he had with a certain Diophantus over the pontificate, he obtained the papal dignity. He suffered from arthritic pain, gout in the hands and gout in the feet, so that he could not take food by himself. Yet, as he was going to be an outstanding builder for the repair of the city, he took careful thought and provided, within a few days of his pontificate, enough material to restore the walls. For at that time the whole of their religion consisted in building and painting. But he was seized by sudden death just after the twentieth day of his papacy, and in the same year as the aforesaid John he too perished. Some think he was killed with poison by Diophantus. See among others Naucler.
23. Constantine I

units.la: Constantinus primus, natione Syrus, à Iu-stiniano Imperatore Constantinopolim uo-catus, Cæsari suo Domino pedes osculandos pri-mus exhibuit. Domum reuersus, Philippicum Bardanem eius successorem, idolorum abomi-natio[?] nationes non ferentem, quòd statuas ex Ecclesiis sustulisset, impietatis damnauit. Et ne Imperatoris hæretici (ut ipse pium principem iudicabat) imago reciperetur, siue auro, sine argento insculpta, constituit: omnesq; monetas eius anathemate notauit.
units.tr: Constantine I, a Syrian by birth, was summoned to Constantinople by the emperor Justinian, and was the first to offer his lord the Caesar the honour of kissing his feet. Returning home, he condemned as impious Philip Bardanes, his successor, who could not bear the abominations of idols and had removed statues from the churches. So that the image of a heretical emperor (as he judged that pious prince to be) should not be received, he ordered that it be engraved, whether in gold or in silver, and he marked all of Philip's coins with an anathema.

units.la: Habitaq; Romæ synodo, contra manifestum Dei præceptum, qui iussit non fieri sculptilia, & contra Apostolorum ac Prophetarum testimonia, decreuit ut imagines in templis haberentur, & summa ueneratione colerentur. Moxq; contra Philippicum, Anastasium quendam Arthemium, imaginum defensorem, excitauit: qui captum illum, impe-rio atq; oculus priuauit. Ticinensem episcopum, metropolitano suo Mediolanensi archiepiscopo re-bellem, non ei reconciliauit, sed Romanæ sedi subiecit. Ex quo facto, hoc habuit lucri Ticinensis ecclesia, ut uitans fumum, in insatiabilem ignem seipsam præcipitaret. Kenredum & Offam, duos Anglosaxonum reges, qui peregrinationis gratia, relictis regnis, Romam uenerant, in monachos ver-tit, & alia Antichristi miracula fecit. Qui & demum anno Domini 715. oppetiit mortem.
units.tr: At a synod held in Rome, against the plain command of God, who ordered that no graven images be made, and against the testimony of the Apostles and Prophets, he decreed that images be kept in the temples and worshipped with the highest reverence. Soon afterwards he stirred up against Philip one Anastasius Artemius, a defender of images, who seized Philip and deprived him of his rule and his eyes. He did not reconcile the bishop of Ticinum, who had rebelled against his metropolitan, the archbishop of Milan, but made him subject to the Roman see. From this deed the church of Ticinum gained this advantage: avoiding the smoke, it threw itself into an insatiable fire. He turned Kenred and Offa, two kings of the Anglo-Saxons who had come to Rome on pilgrimage, leaving their kingdoms, into monks, and performed other miracles of Antichrist. He at last died in the year of the Lord 715.
24. Gregory II

units.la: Gregorius secundus, Romanus, qui prius biblio-thecæ præfuerat, mœnia in urbe, ac templa se-nio detrita, instaurauit: & donis tum aureis tum argenteis collocupletauit. Basilicam S. crucis, ob-foletam, ac templum D. Laurentij extra muros re-stituit, & porticus circumquaque positas fornicibus atque tectis auxit. Sufannæ oratorium in Cœlio mon-te à fundamentis erexit: & presbyteram, diaco-nam, monachâm, aut commatrem spiritualem, matrimonio (incestu non) iungi uetuit. Paternam domum, mortua matre, in D. Agathæ cœnobium uertit: atque ut tempore quadragesimali in quintis feriis, ieiunium cum Missarum celebritate in Eccle-siis fieret, ordinauit. Ob res bellicas & portenta quædam in aere uisa, frequentes supplicationes mandauit: ac Germanos ad papismum, per Boni-facium Anglum, monachum ualde superstitiosum, pertraxit. Nullibi quàm in dedicato loco, missa agi uoluit, statuarumq; contemptores ad mortem usq; persecutus est. Luithprandum Italiæ regem, renitentem primo, authoritate sua compulit, A-rithperti donationes iniustas, ad cleri luxum ratas habere, & subditos Imperatoris Leonis Isauri, propter sublatas imagines in apertam rebellionem perduxit. Totam Hisperiam, Aemyliam, Liguri-am, Italiam, & alias terras, ab eius obedientia de-cedere fecit: & uestigalia, quæ solui Christus iu-sit, pessimus latro & Antichristus interdixit. No-luit Imperator idololatrias in Ecclesijs fieri: fideli-um igi[?] tum igitur communione una cum Imperio, proditor[?] ipsum priuauit, additis æterni supplicij minis. Atq; ita sunt Orientis Imperatores, Italiæ regno per sanctissimum diabolum priuati. Nouissimè Gregorius, anno Domini 731 vitam morte commutauit.
units.tr: Gregory II, a Roman, who had previously been over the library, restored the walls of the city and the temples worn out by age, and enriched them with gifts both of silver and of gold. He restored the Basilica of the Holy Cross, which had fallen into disrepair, and the temple of St Lawrence outside the walls, and he enlarged the porticoes placed on every side with arches and roofs. He built from the foundations the oratory of Susanna on the Caelian Hill, and he forbade a presbyter, a deacon, a nun, or a spiritual co-parent to be joined in marriage (not in incest). When his mother died, he turned the family home into a monastery of St Agatha, and he ordered that during Lent, on Fridays, a fast be held in the churches together with the celebration of Mass. On account of wars and certain portents seen in the air, he ordered frequent processions of supplication, and through Boniface, an Englishman, a monk of great superstition, he drew the Germans over to Papism. He wished Mass to be said nowhere but in a consecrated place, and he pursued the despisers of statues even to death. Liutprand, king of Italy, at first resisting, he compelled by his own authority to hold valid the unjust donations of Ariperht, for the luxury of the clergy; and he brought the subjects of the emperor Leo the Isaurian into open rebellion because the images had been removed. He caused all of Hesperia, Aemilia, Liguria, Italy and other lands to fall away from their obedience to the emperor. The most wicked robber and Antichrist forbade the tribute which Christ ordered to be paid. The emperor would not allow idolatries to be practised in the churches; so the traitor deprived him of communion with the faithful, together with the Empire, adding threats of eternal punishment. And thus the emperors of the East were deprived of the kingdom of Italy by the most holy devil. Finally Gregory exchanged life for death in the year of the Lord 731.
25. Gregory III

units.la: GRegorius tertius, patria Syrus, papisimi etiam acerrimus defensor, & occultarum rerum præ-co, Dominum suum Imperatorem Leonem, clero consentiente, excommunicauit, quòd imagines de-strueret: & contra Longobardos Carolum Martellum spurium, Gallorum præfectum, pro Rom. sede tuenda, in auxilium ascivit. Græcos per Longobardos Italia pepulit: illosq; ipsos Longobardos per Francos tum demum oppressit: & arrogans bestia, Italiam ipsam omnem, prædecessorem secutus, Imperatorio sacramento absoluit. Ad exor-randas[?] Ecclesias, ut illi sua templa vocant, ani-mum adiecit, altare S. Petri sex onychinis columnis augustius reddidit, tectum Chrysogoni restituit, hebdomadarios per vices disposuit, & aurea atq; argentea vasa condonauit. Nonnulla templa carie ruinosa reparauit: Centum cellas, neglectum oppidum readificauit, mænia pluribus in locis reficit, nec non monasteria monachis ubiq; repleuit, in Romana synodo Satanicus impostor, contra aper tum Dei verbum & mandatum, imagines mortuorum sanctorum venerandas esse declaravit: & eius statuti violatores excommunicationis senten-tia innodavit. Reliquias divorum in Petri basilica reposuit, & illic quotidie missas celebrari iussit: in quarum canone has clausulas adiunxit, Quorum solennitates hodie in conspectu divinae maie-statis tuae celebrantur, &c. Caballos & equos manducari prohibuit, tutelam Ecclesiae à Graecis ad Gallos transtulit, Apostolorum in templis simula-chra ab aliis distinxit, atque ad Bonifacium Anglum scripsit, sacrificos rasos defunctorum memorias in missis suis facere, ac pro mortuis ipsis orare, offerre & sacrificare debere. Post haec & similia multa, anno Domini 742. diabolicus magus, mundum deseruit.
units.tr: Gregory III, a Syrian by birth, a most fierce defender of the papacy also and a herald of hidden things, excommunicated his lord the emperor Leo, with the clergy consenting, because he destroyed images; and against the Lombards he enlisted in aid, for the defence of the Roman see, Charles Martel, the bastard, prefect of the Gauls. He drove the Greeks out of Italy through the Lombards, and at last the Franks crushed those same Lombards. The arrogant beast, following his predecessor, also absolved all of Italy from its oath of allegiance to the emperor. He took care to adorn the churches, as they call their temples: he made the altar of St Peter more majestic with six onyx columns, restored the roof of Chrysogonus, arranged weekly rotas of canons in turn, and gave gifts of gold and silver vessels. He repaired several temples ruined by decay; he rebuilt a hundred cells and a neglected town, repaired the walls in many places, and filled monasteries everywhere with monks. In a Roman synod, that Satanic impostor, against the plain word and command of God, declared that the images of dead saints were to be venerated, and he bound those who violated this decree with the sentence of excommunication. He placed the relics of the saints in the basilica of St Peter and ordered that Masses be celebrated there every day; to the canon of these he added the clauses: "whose solemnities are today celebrated in the sight of your divine majesty," etc. He forbade the eating of nags and horses; he transferred the protection of the Church from the Greeks to the Gauls; he distinguished the images of the Apostles in the temples from the others; and he wrote to Boniface the Englishman that tonsured priests ought to make memorials of the dead in their Masses, and ought to pray for, offer and sacrifice for the dead. After these and many similar things, in the year of the Lord 742, that diabolical magician departed from the world.
26. Zacharias the Greek.

units.la: Zacharias, natione Graecus, monachus, multa quoque (ut Funccius habet) papalem dignitatem de-centia, eademq; praeclara (scilicet) opera confecit. Basilicas nanq; minitantes ruinam, restituit (oportuit multas Romae fuisse ab antiquo basilicas, quod tot pontifices in his restaurandis laborarint) por-ticum & turrim ante basilicam Lateranensem ex-truxit: in cuius frontispicio totius orbis descriptio-nem poni fecit. Fortasis ut indicaret, Papam totius mundi fore [?], aut esse debere supremum domi-num. Oratoria sanctorum Georgij, Cæciliæ & Sy-ri abbatis condidit: ac uestes auro & gemmis di-stinctas primus in sacrum usum dedit. Bibliothe-cam beati Petri restituit, & Ecclesijs uestigalia, quibus oleum (aliud idololatriæ genus) pro lam-padibus emeretur: & fundos assignauit, unde uiu-uerent [?]. Sacerdotalem habitum adimuenit: & Orien-talem Ecclesiam ab Occidentali seiunxit. Quat-tuor dialogorum libros, à Gregorio primo conscrip-tos, è Latino Græcus in Græcum transtulit; ut contra liberam Christi gratiam, & Græci purga-torium papisticum crederent. Bonifacium An-glum, Maguntinensem archiepiscopum per suas li-teras, episcopatus in Germania fundare permisit: & presbyterorum ordinationem, ad 25. ætatis an-num à tricesimo reduxit. Aunculi mortui uxorem ducere, quamuis à Gregorio tertio permissum, ini-quum declarauit: atq; ut compatres & commatres nullatenus in nuptijs se iungerent, constituit. Magni Gregorij corpus à Laterano ad Velum aureum sui nominis templum transtulit: & epitaphi-um Græcis literis exaratum illius tumulo addidit. Cassinensi cœnobio priuilegia multa contulit: ac Venetis mercatoribus, sub maledictionis pœna prohibuit, (& hoc Christiane quidem) ne lucri cau-sa Chrisa[?] Christianorum filios Saracenis venderent: quod hactenus frequenter faciebant. Divinam quandam potestatem sibi arrogans, ius ponendi & deponendi reges, proteruiter assumpsit, & à fidelitatis iuramento subditos eorum primus absoluit. Nam hunc Zachariam Pipinus pusillus Caroli Martelli spurij filius, Domini sui proditor, per legatos exoravit, ut Franciæ regnum, Childerico rege deturbato, sibi & hæredibus confirmaret. Pontifex accepti prius ex Lombardico bello beneficij memor, speransq; ea ratione contra Orientis Imperatorem se fortiorem futurum, postulatis annuit: principibusq; (ô pessime Antichriste) ut depositò Childerico, & in monasterium detonso, Pipinum à Bonifacio archiepiscopo confirmatum & unctum, regem suum deinceps agnoscant, districtè præcepit. Ad reges sic venit male-dictæ bestiæ character, Apoc. 13. Nam & Lachim Longobardorum regem, Carlomannum, & alios, in monachos etiam transformavit. Fato concessit hoc monstrum anno Domini 752, cum decem annis pestilentiæ sedi præfuisset. Huic successit Stephanus quidam diaconus. Is pontificatus die tertia, somno excitatus, cum res domesticas ordinare instituisset, apoplexiæ morbo corre-ptus interijt. Et propter vitæ brevitatem, in Paparum catalogo non ponitur.
units.tr: Zacharias, a Greek by birth and a monk, also (as Funck reports) carried out many notable works befitting the papal dignity. He restored basilicas that were threatening collapse (there must have been many basilicas in Rome from ancient times, since so many popes laboured to restore them). He built the portico and tower in front of the Lateran basilica, and on its façade had a description of the whole world put up, perhaps to show that the Pope would be, or ought to be, the supreme lord of the whole world. He founded oratories of Saints George, Cecilia and Abbot Syrus. He was the first to give vestments adorned with gold and jewels for sacred use. He restored the library of St Peter and assigned to the churches revenues by which oil (another kind of idolatry) could be bought for the lamps, and he assigned estates from which the clergy might live. He devised the priestly habit and separated the Eastern Church from the Western. He translated the four books of Dialogues, written by Gregory I, from Latin into Greek, so that the Greeks might believe in purgatory of the Papists, against the free grace of Christ. Through his letters he allowed Boniface the Englishman, archbishop of Mainz, to establish bishoprics in Germany. He reduced the ordination of presbyters from the thirtieth year of age to the twenty-fifth. He declared it wicked for a man to marry his dead uncle's wife, although Gregory III had permitted it. He ordained that godparents and godmothers should in no way join in marriage with one another. He transferred the body of Gregory the Great from the Lateran to the temple bearing his name at the Golden Veil, and added to his tomb an epitaph written in Greek letters. He granted many privileges to the monastery of Monte Cassino, and he forbade, on pain of a curse, the Venetian merchants (and this was indeed a Christian act) to sell the sons of Christians to the Saracens for gain, which they had until then frequently done. Arrogating to himself a certain divine power, he shamelessly assumed the right to set up and depose kings, and he was the first to absolve their subjects from the oath of fidelity. For Pippin, the little bastard son of Charles Martel, a traitor to his own lord, begged this Zacharias through envoys to confirm the kingdom of France for himself and his heirs, with Childeric deposed. The Pope, mindful of the favour he had earlier received in the Lombard war, and hoping in this way to become stronger against the Emperor of the East, granted the request, and he strictly ordered the princes (O most wicked Antichrist!) that, once Childeric had been deposed and shorn into a monastery, they should henceforth acknowledge Pippin, confirmed and anointed by Archbishop Boniface, as their king. Thus the mark of the cursed beast, Rev. 13, came upon the kings. For he also transformed Lachim, king of the Lombards, Carloman, and others into monks. This monster yielded to fate in the year of the Lord 752, after he had presided over the see for ten years of pestilence. He was succeeded by a certain Stephen, a deacon. On the third day of his pontificate, roused from sleep, he set about putting his household affairs in order, but was seized by apoplexy and died. And because of the brevity of his life, he is not listed in the catalogue of Popes.
27. Stephen II.

units.la: STephanus secundus, Romanus, prædicto Ste-phano statim suffectus: vir singularis religionis ac prudentiæ à papistis iactatur, ac diligens Chri-stianæ doctrinæ prædicator. Sed mysterium intel-lige. Cum pontificatum ita suscepisset, arte & a-stutia sua, Rauennæ Exarchatum omnem (qui tantum illis displicuerat) & alias complures Ita-liæ terras, Rom. sedi subiecit, ut Italiæ regnum ob-tineret, hoc modo. Contra Aistulphum Longobardorum regem, censum ac vectigal ab eo atq; suis unctis exigentem, auxilium à Pipino ardenter petijt. Ille autem, ut Pontifici rem gratam faceret, ut cui regnum Franciæ acceptum referret, post[?] uarias obsidiones, Exarchatum à Longobardorum armis liberatum, cum omnibus urbibus usque ad stagna Venetorum, ipsi dono dedit: & non alio iure, quam quo ille prius dictum susceperat re-gnum. Atq; hæc est, quam salsissimo titulo, Constantini Magni donationem uocant. Sic Cæsarem[?] Exarchatu illo omnino spoliarunt. Cecidit cum illo (horribile malum) tertia Rom. Imperij dyna-stia. Et destructo per eius amissionem, Orientali imperio, Occidentale mox futurum, uires etiam amisit. Sed Stephanus tanto spolio lætus factus, Pipinum spurium cum duobus filijs, per nouam un-ctionem confirmauit, eiq; ac toti eius progeniei, in magna Dei maledictione, fur furi benedixit, à periurio eum absoluit, immunem fecit, & omnes illi in posterum contradicentes anathematizauit. Childericum uero, hereditario regno spoliatum, detonso capillo, in monasterium iterum trusit. Ad terram se prosternebat Pipinus, Pontificis pedes mox osculabatur, stapedes apprehendit, frenum accepit manu, stratoris officium adimpleuit, ac perpetuam fidelitatem iurauit. Hinc eorum opes, fastus ac tyrannides, radices sumpserunt. Hinc Pa-pa omnium Christianorum principum Deus terre-stris esse cœpit, & mundi monarchas sibi subdi-tos fecit. Et ut pro tam splendido beneficio gratias Deo referret, letanias Romæ per omnes Ecclesias fieri mandauit, Apostolorum caluarias cum aliis sanctorum reliquijs ferri & ostendi iussit: ac se pon-tificaliter in populi medio cum summis triumphis, tanquam alter Alexander, aut Philippus Mace-do, aut Cæsar ipse Iulius, ad Lateranensem basi-licam à perfrarijs[?] se gestari permisit. Quod & à posteris pro magna religione obseruatum est, ut hominum humeris deportarentur. Basilicas ab Aistulpho destructas deinceps restaurauit, Pa-patrum[?] traditiones authoritate firmauit, proditiones principibus factas remisit: de Imperij à Graecis ad Gallos translatione, Graecorum odio, cogitauit: Gallorum Ecclesias cantilenis ornauit: & quicquid erat Imperio uiolenter ademptum, D. Petri patrimonium postea dici uoluit. Sed in horum ac similium conatuum medio, anno Domini 757. Deus illum in sceleris poenam, uita spoliauit.
units.tr: Stephen II, a Roman, was at once made successor to the aforesaid Stephen. The Papists boast of him as a man of singular piety and prudence, and a diligent preacher of Christian doctrine. But understand the mystery. When he had thus assumed the pontificate, by his craft and cunning he subjected to the Roman see the whole Exarchate of Ravenna (which had so greatly displeased them) and several other lands of Italy, so that he might obtain the kingdom of Italy, in this way. Against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, who was demanding tribute and tax from him and from his people, he eagerly sought help from Pippin. Pippin, wishing to do the Pope a favour, since he owed the kingdom of France to him, after various sieges, freed the Exarchate from Lombard arms and gave it to him as a gift, together with all the cities as far as the lagoons of the Venetians, and by no other right than that by which the Pope had earlier received that kingdom. This is what they call, with the most salty title, the Donation of Constantine the Great. Thus they stripped the Emperor entirely of that Exarchate. With it fell (a dreadful evil) the third dynasty of the Roman Empire. And with the destruction of the Eastern Empire brought about by its loss, the Western Empire soon to follow also lost its strength. But Stephen, delighted with so great a spoil, confirmed the bastard Pippin with his two sons by a new anointing, and absolved him from perjury, made him immune, and anathematized all who should in future contradict him, and blessed a thief in the presence of a thief, to the great curse of God on him and all his line. Childeric, stripped of his hereditary kingdom, he again thrust into a monastery, his hair shorn. Pippin prostrated himself on the ground, at once kissed the Pope's feet, took hold of his stirrups, received the bridle in his hand, performed the office of groom, and swore perpetual fidelity. From this their wealth, pride and tyrannies took root. From this the Pope began to be the earthly God of all Christian princes, and he made the monarchs of the world subject to himself. And so that he might render thanks to God for such a splendid benefit, he ordered litanies to be held in all the churches of Rome, had the skulls of the Apostles, along with other relics of the saints, carried and displayed, and allowed himself, with the greatest triumphs in the midst of the people, as a second Alexander, or Philip of Macedon, or Caesar Julius himself, to be borne in a litter to the Lateran basilica, a custom later observed for the sake of great piety, that he should be carried on men's shoulders. He afterwards restored the basilicas destroyed by Aistulf, confirmed the traditions of the Fathers by authority, remitted the treacheries of princes, and thought about transferring the Empire from the Greeks to the Franks out of hatred for the Greeks. He adorned the churches of the Franks with chants, and whatever had been violently taken from the Empire he afterwards wished to be called the patrimony of St Peter. But in the midst of these and similar endeavours, in the year of the Lord 757, God deprived him of life as a punishment for his crimes.
28. Paul the First.

units.la: PAulus primus, Romanus, prædicti Stephani fra-ter, eo mortuo protinus successit: sed non sine contentione, cum alij Theophylactum quendam archidiaconum præferendum censerent. Hic Posquædam, ut ferunt, pietatis opera, ad ueteres prædecessorum pontificum artes conuersus, statuta à Constantino quinto, Imperatore, Byzantij iam denuò abrogatas, fulminationibus nouis restituere laborabat. Sed in sua sententia constans Constantinus, contemptis eius execrationibus ac minis, usque ad uitæ suæ finem execrabilibus idolis bellum intulit. Corpus Petronillæ, filiæ sancti Petri (inquit Vuicelius, adulator papisticus) ualde honorabat hic pontifex, terraq; leuauit. In cuius marmoreo sarcophago, Carsulano teste, clausulam hanc reperit (impudens mendacium) ipsius Petri manu scriptam: Aureæ Petronillæ, dulcissimæ filiæ. Quadragesimale seruitium disposuit: & ante horam sextam officia celebrari constituit. Ecclesias quasdam in urbe ædificijs ampliauit, ac earum dedicationibus nouas cæremonias addidit. Ex æstiuo calore tandem, anno Domini 767. pinguis hic porcus obiit, restitutis quibusdam sanis[?], ruina collabentibus. Vt Petrus Præmonstratensis refert, huius Pauli tempore, stellæ de cœlo in terram cadebant, iuxta id quod scribitur, Apoc.6. & Carolus Magnus statim incepit regnare, qui ædificauit 24. monasteria.
units.tr: Paul the First, a Roman, brother of the Stephen mentioned above, succeeded immediately on his death, but not without contention, since some preferred a certain Theophylact, archdeacon, to be put forward. He, after some works of piety, as they report, turned back to the old arts of his predecessors and laboured to restore by new thunderbolts the decrees of Constantine the Fifth, the Emperor, which had by then been repeatedly abrogated at Byzantium. But Constantine, steadfast in his opinion, despised his curses and threats and waged war on detestable idols until the end of his life. This pontiff greatly honoured the body of Petronilla, daughter of St Peter (says Vuicelius, the papistical flatterer), and raised it from the ground. On its marble sarcophagus, as Carsulanus testifies, he found this inscription (a shameless lie), supposedly written by Peter's own hand: "To Aurea Petronilla, most sweet daughter." He arranged a Lenten service and decreed that the offices be celebrated before the sixth hour. He enlarged some churches in the city with new buildings and added new ceremonies to their dedications. Finally, from the summer heat, in the year of the Lord 767, this fat pig died, some churches having been restored and others collapsing in ruin. As Peter of Praemonstratensis reports, in the time of this Paul the stars fell from heaven to earth, according to what is written in Apoc. 6, and Charles the Great straightway began to reign, the man who built 24 monasteries.
29. Constantine the Second.

units.la: Constantinus fecundus, natione Romanus, Desiderij Longobardorum regis frater, impulsu dicti Desiderij, per Tothonem, Nepesinum ducem, cum plures eandem ambirent sedem, ex laico Papa consecrabatur. Sed temeritas (ut Crantzius scribit) consecrantis Sergii Hostiensis vel Gergii Prænestini, mox paralysi cæditur, quod non effet Constantinus sacris initiatus, tam periculosa res esset, primo Bestiæ characterc non insigniri. Hinc multæ sunt in clero excitatæ discordiæ, inter quas Philippus quidam ab aliis eligebatur, sed statim eo ab officio, armis inferior, se iterum abdicare coactus fuit. Impleuit Constantinus pontificium munus per annum unum: ac pontificalia valde pontificaliter administrauit. Convocato tamen, ex Italorum & Gallorum Episcopis ac monachis, synodali concilio, in magno eorum furore ab Ecclesia eiicitur, & cum contumeliis in monasterium tanquam in perpetuum carcerem damnatur, anno Domini 768. tam oculis quàm Papatu privatus. Suntq; qui istum inter Papas, quod laicus esset, non numerant. Et omnia eius acta irrita fe-cerunt, praeter baptismum & chrisma. Sequenti anno Desiderius rex, sub orationis praetextu Ro-mam veniens, exoculatores fratris sui talione re-taliauit.
units.tr: Constantine the Second, a Roman by birth, brother of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, was made Pope while still a layman, at the instigation of that Desiderius, through Totho, duke of Nepi, when several were striving for the same see. But (as Crantzius writes) the rashness of the consecrators, Sergius of Ostia or Gregory of Praeneste, was soon punished with paralysis, because Constantine had not been initiated into the sacred orders; such a matter would have been dangerous, since he had not first been marked with the character of the Beast. Hence many discords were stirred up among the clergy, and in the course of these a certain Philip was chosen by some, but he was at once forced to abdicate that office, being weaker in arms. Constantine discharged the pontifical office for one year, and administered the pontifical duties most pontifically. Yet, when a synodal council of Italian and Gallic bishops and monks was convened, he was cast out of the Church in their great fury, and was condemned with insults to a monastery as to a perpetual prison, in the year of the Lord 768, deprived of his eyes as well as of the papacy. There are some who do not number him among the Popes, because he was a layman. And they declared all his acts void, except baptism and chrism. In the following year King Desiderius, coming to Rome under the pretext of prayer, repaid with retaliation in kind the men who had gouged out his brother's eyes.
30. Stephen the Third.

units.la: Stephanus tertius, natione Siculus, ac professione monachus, strenuus pontificiae authoritatis & rerum Ecclesiae defensor, à papistis esse scribitur. In Lateranensi enim synodo, acta praedecessoris Constantini solenniter abrogauit: ordinatos ab ipso episcopos, vbi non accessit noua solutio, degra-dauit: & ne quis laicus extra Ecclesiasticos ordines pontifex fieret, sub anathematis poena prohibuit. Constantinopolitanam synodum septimam tanquam haereticam execrauit: statuarum cultum in ea reprobatum iterum approbauit: idololatriae foedissimae revocauit, imagines adorandas esse docuit, earum veneraciones ampliauit: ac thura illis adoleri ethnico ritu praecepit. Ecclesiam Mediolanensem, quae illuc usque extiterat libera, suae subiecit tyrannidi. Desiderium Longobardorum regem, regni sceptro priuari, à Caesare Carolo Magno petijt: canonum transgressoribus anathema proposuit: ut in diebus Dominicis, Gloria in excelsis, super altare S. Petri in missarum solennijs, à septem episcopis Cardinalibus caneretur, constituit, & alia papalia miracula fecit. Periit hic nō inutilis eius Ecclesiae pastor, anno Domini 772. quem, quia nudis pedibus in una processione ad D. Petri templum semel ibat, verum Christi imitatorem atq; ipsius Petri successorem papistae praedicant.
units.tr: Stephen the Third, a Sicilian by birth and a monk by profession, is written of by the papists as a vigorous defender of papal authority and of the affairs of the Church.
