For in the Lateran synod he solemnly abrogated the acts of his predecessor Constantine; those bishops ordained by him, where no new absolution had been granted, he degraded; and he forbade under penalty of anathema that anyone who was not in the ecclesiastical orders should become pope. He cursed the seventh Council of Constantinople as heretical; he again approved the worship of images, which had been condemned in it; he restored the most foul idolatry, taught that images are to be adored, enlarged their veneration, and ordered incense to be burned before them in the heathen manner. He subjected the Church of Milan, which had until then remained free, to his own tyranny. He sought from Charlemagne that King Desiderius of the Lombards be deprived of the sceptre of his kingdom; he proposed anathema to transgressors of the canons; he ordained that on Sundays the Gloria in excelsis be sung at the solemn masses over the altar of St Peter by seven cardinal bishops, and he performed other papal miracles. This not unprofitable minister of that Church died in the year of the Lord 772. Because once, in one procession, he went barefoot to the temple of St Peter, the papists proclaim him a true imitator of Christ and successor of Peter itself.
31. Hadrian the First.

units.la: HAdrianus primus, patria Romanus, vir ad tuendas res Ecclesiasticas impiger, non minore diligentia Papale fastigium auxit, quàm fecerunt antecessores. Corpus S. Pauli argenteis laminis inclusit: Petri fortasis auro circumdaturus, si ad manum reliquiae illius fuissent. Sed ne sine honore abiret, altare eius pallio auro intexto ornauit, atrium S. Pauli vetustate collapsum instauravit, ac marmore strauit, & ad Stephani sanum monachos locauit. Coenobium Anastasij ad aquas Salinas reaedificauit, & portas maiores aereas S.Pe[?]ro dedit. Imagines venerari plus omnibus voluit: de illarum adoratione ac utilitate librum idola-latra composuit: & ut essent laicorum libri, abla-tis scripturis, constituit. Statuarum execratores, Felicem & alios, in synodo damnauit: in officio Ecclesiae offertoria quaedam versibus geminauit, & missarum ritus à magno Gregorio editos, occi-dentalibus Ecclesiis imperauit. Multarum basili-carum in urbe tecta reparauit: aquae ductus, col-lapsas turres, quassatos muros, & similia ad cle-rum pertinentia, magnis expensis restituit, ac pon-tificatum Romanum ab omni externorum prin-cipum molestatione per Carolum magnum libera-uit: Literas Apostolicas, priui legia, ac diploma-ta, ut diuturniora fierent, plumbo primus insigni-uit, infames (ex Euangelij professione fortasis) ad sacerdotium promoueri uetuit, &, ne clericus ex-tra suum forum, in iudicium traheretur, sanciuit.
units.tr: Hadrian the First, a Roman by country, a man vigorous in defending the affairs of the Church, raised the papal dignity with no less diligence than his predecessors had done. He enclosed the body of St Paul in silver plates, intending perhaps to cover Peter's with gold, if his relics had been at hand. But so that Paul should not depart without honour, he adorned his altar with a cloth woven with gold, restored the atrium of St Paul which had collapsed with age, paved it with marble, and set monks at the church of St Stephen. He rebuilt the monastery of Anastasius at the Salvian Waters, and gave the greater bronze doors to St Peter's. He wished images to be venerated above all things; he composed a book in their defence, on their adoration and usefulness, the Idolatry book; and he decreed that, the scriptures having been removed, they should be the books of the laity. He condemned in synod the destroyers of images, Felix and others; in the office of the Church he doubled certain offertories with verses, and he enjoined on the Western churches the rites of the mass as published by the great Gregory. He repaired the roofs of many basilicas in the city; at great expense he restored aqueducts, fallen towers, shaken walls, and similar things pertaining to the clergy; and he freed the Roman pontificate from all molestation by foreign princes through Charles the Great. He was the first to mark apostolic letters, privileges and charters with lead, so that they might last longer; he forbade (perhaps from the profession of the gospel) those infamous men to be promoted to the priesthood; and he enacted that a cleric should not be dragged before a court outside his own jurisdiction.

units.la: Mortuo Carlomanno, Francorum rege & Caroli fratre, Bertha eius vidua cum duobus filijs ad hunc Hadrianum venit, impetratura ut eos confirma-ret, & in paternum regnum inungeret. At pater iste sanctissimus, ne Caroli eorum auunculi ani-mum à se alienaret, pupillos reiecit, causam eo-rum sprevit, in reges ungere recusauit, ac tum de-mum tam matrem quam filios, cum Desiderio Lon gobardorum rege, regno, uxore, atq; liberis, in perpetuam seruitutem dedit. Qui secum omnes in Gallias duxit, & in dolore suum edere panem, ad uitæ finem usq; docuit. Sic Dei in terris uicarium beatissimus, uiduæq; cædusam, atq; orphanorum clamores audiuit. Vt tamen hæc omnia, quodam sanctitatis fuco uestiret, in atrio Lateranensi quotidie centum pauperes ali iußit. Carolus uero tantorum officiorum non malus remunerator, post pedum osculâ, patris Pipini iniquissimam donationem, urbes scilicet omnes ad Rauennatensem Exarchatum pertinentes, illi confirmauit: & Venetiam, Histriam, ducatum Foroiuliensem, ducatum Spoletanum ac Beneuentanum, atq; alias terras Petrinæ possessioni addidit iniquus prædo. Romanæ urbis & Italiæ principem Hadrianum fecit: ac Papatus Imperium, deleto Longobardorum regno, firmauit: fœderaq; inter se & pontificem constituit, communes hostes sibi eos qui alteram partem lacesserent. Hadrianus rursum, Christianissimum regem Carolum uocari iußit, patriciu Rom. fecit, ac ius conferendi patriciatus eidem dedit. Potestates eligendi Papam, & inuestiendi per omnes prouincias episcopos, quæ non diu durabant, astu uulpino concessit: atq; ut solo nomine Rom. Imperator diceretur, ordinauit. Post hæc Hadrianus, anno Domini 796. communi morte sublatus est.
units.tr: When Carloman, king of the Franks and brother of Charles, had died, his widow Bertha came with her two sons to this Hadrian, intending to obtain that he would confirm them and anoint them to their father's kingdom. But that most holy father, lest he alienate the mind of their uncle Charles from himself, rejected the orphans, scorned their cause, refused to anoint them as kings, and at last gave the mother as well as the sons, together with Desiderius, king of the Lombards, his kingdom, his wife and his children, into perpetual servitude. He led them all with him into Gaul, and taught them to eat their own bread in sorrow until the end of their lives. Thus the most blessed vicar of God on earth heard the widow's sorrow and the cries of the orphans. Yet, so that he might dress up all these things with a kind of cosmetic of sanctity, he ordered a hundred poor people to be fed daily in the Lateran atrium. Charles, however, no bad rewarder of such great services, after kissing the feet, confirmed to him his father Pepin's most unjust donation, namely all the cities belonging to the exarchate of Ravenna; and that unjust plunderer added to the Petrine possessions Venice, Istria, the duchy of Friuli, the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, and other lands. He made Hadrian prince of the city of Rome and of Italy, and, with the kingdom of the Lombards destroyed, he confirmed the empire of the Papacy, and he established alliances between them and the pontiff, declaring as common enemies those who should attack either party. Hadrian in turn ordered Charles to be called Most Christian King, made him a patrician of Rome, and gave him the right of conferring the patriciate. He granted, with foxlike cunning, the powers of electing the Pope and of invested bishops throughout all provinces, which did not last long; and he ordained that he be called Roman Emperor in name only. After these things Hadrian was carried off by a common death in the year of the Lord 796.
31. Leo the Third.

units.la: Leo tertius, Romanus genere, cum pontificatum inijsset, statim misit ad Carolum claves S. Petri, urbisque Rom. vexillum, & alia munera: petens, ut populum Rom. fidei sacramento dato, patui subjiceret. Verebatur enim, ne quandoque tyrannidem eius populus excutere vellet. Carolus autem gratiam Leoni facturus, Agilbertum abbatem misit, qui Rom. populum eius iussu, pontifici fidelitatem iurare compulit. Hinc odium populi in Papam ita excitabatur, ut nacti[?] furoris magistros, in quadam processione, equo deiectum, habitu pontificali nudarent, ac multis verberibus caederent.
units.tr: Leo the Third, a Roman by birth, had no sooner entered upon the papacy than he sent to Charles the keys of St Peter, the banner of the city of Rome, and other gifts, asking that Charles would take an oath of loyalty from the Roman people and bring them under the Pope's control. For he feared that the people might at some point want to shake off his tyranny. Charles, wishing to do Leo a favour, sent Abbot Agilbert, who by Charles's command compelled the Roman people to swear fidelity to the pontiff. From this, the people's hatred of the Pope was so stirred up that, having found the ringleaders of their fury, they pulled him from his horse during a procession, stripped him of his pontifical dress, and beat him with many blows.

units.la: In quo tumultu, non oculis privatus, & lingua mutilatus erat, atque (ut papistae tradunt) diuinitus postea restitutus: ut eius authoritatem splendidis mendaciis amplificarent: sed in vincula solum in D. Erasmi coenobio coniectus. Unde Mantuanus in 4. Fastorum libro:
units.tr: In this tumult he was not deprived of his eyes or his tongue was not cut out, as the Papists relate, and he was afterwards restored by divine power, so that they might magnify his authority with splendid lies. Rather, he was only thrown into chains in the monastery of St Erasmus. Whence Mantuan, in the fourth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Ille diu Romanorum foedissima passusIurgia, damna, minas: iter est ingressus ad Alpes,Vt sibi Gallorum regem sociaret: & illoAuspice, terrorem Romanae euaderet irae.
units.tr: For a long time he had suffered the most shameful quarrels, losses and threats of the Romans; then he set out for the Alps, so that he might join the king of the Gauls to himself, and under his auspices escape the terror of Roman wrath.

units.la: Tandem adueniente Carolo, cum cognouissent quo animo ipse esset erga pontificem, conceptum odium eius metu in fauorem uerterunt, obiecta cri-mina probare non ausi. Vno ore ergo, interro-ganti de eius uita, responderunt, sedem Apostoli-cam a nemine laico iudicari debere. Quo respon-so accepto, dum & ipse iureiurando affirmasset se innoxium esse, placatus, Carolus eum absoluit, atq; innocentem declarauit. Pro quibus officijs gratiam relaturus hic pontifex, magna uoce Impe-ratorem eum declarauit, imunxit, ac diademate or-nauit: Romano populo acclamante, Carolo Au-gusto, magno Imperatori, uita & uictoria. Vt a-pud eundem Mantuanum:
units.tr: At last, when Charles arrived, the Romans, having learned what his feelings were towards the pontiff, turned the hatred they had conceived into favour out of fear, not daring to prove the charges they had made. So with one voice, when he asked them about Leo's life, they answered that the apostolic see ought to be judged by no layman. Having received this answer, and when Leo himself had sworn an oath that he was innocent, Charles was appeased, absolved him and declared him innocent. In return for these services, this pontiff, about to repay the favour, proclaimed Charles emperor in a loud voice, anointed him and adorned him with a diadem, while the Roman people acclaimed: "To Charles Augustus, the great emperor, life and victory!" As the same Mantuan has it:

units.la: Imperij tandem Roma applaudente coronamImpofuit Carolo, tantiq; insignia regni.
units.tr: At last Rome, applauding, placed on Charles the crown of empire, and the insignia of so great a kingdom.

units.la: Sic est Imperij nomen Romanis restitutum, ita tamen ut ne Papae authoritas excluderetur, ut in Apoc.cap.17. de octauo dicitur. Hinc mos reman-sit, ut qui imperij sceptrum acciperent, a Papa Rom. inungerentur. Ab illo die, qui fuit anno Domini 801. Romani imperij dignitas, a Grae-cis per Papam ad Gallos est translata, postea a Gallis ad Germanos secundum beneplacita eius. Ita est imperium, quod ante a coelo dari credi-tum fuit, nunc ad Papae manus deuolutum. Et haec translatio ex magnis est Antichristi mira-culis unum, cui draco suam sedem ac potentiam dedit, Apoc.13. Pipinum quoq; Caroli huius filium, illius partis Italiae regem, declarauit hic pontifex: quam nec ipse, nec ullus praedecessorum suorum sibi subiicere poterant. Et hac ratione id fiebat, ut reges Galliae imperatorium titulum habentes, nunquam paterentur eiusmodi maiestatem ab eo tolli. Hinc factum est (inquit Hieronymus Marius) ut per Papam perpetuae inimicitiae differmina[?]e sint inter Orientis & Occidentis imperatores. Unde tot strages, tot incendia, tot regnorum vastationes subsecutae sunt, sed nondum finis. Hac tamen conditione, Imperator ab hoc pontifice factus est, magnus hic Carolus, ut iureiurando pollicere-tur, se perpetuam obedientiam sibi seruaturum. Iure ergo Draconico acquisito & confirmato, iuxta id quod scribitur, Apoc.13 res Ecclesiae curare aggressus est Leo:ac trium dierum supplicationes ante ascensionem Christi, instituit: atq; thuris usum, infidelium Iudaeorum & paganorum more, altaribus primus assignauit. Hospitale amplissimum, pro peregrinis idololatris Romam aduentantibus, aedificauit: & tectum aedis S. Petri restituit. Pontificum decreta, omnium doctorum scriptis praeponenda esse statuit: & sanguinem adulterium, quem e crucifixo quodam ligneo fluxisse impostores dixerant, ut statuarum idololatrias, dii[?] adhuc essent in quaestione, confirmarent, pro vero Christi sanguine (horribile dictu) haberi voluit. Et Mantuam profectus, ubi hucusque servatur, salutatur, adoratur, sic esse sua authoritate approbavit, ac bullis confirmavit, addito illi quotannis, in maximam Christi derogationem, solenni die festo. Ita tunc praevaluit potestas tenebrarum. Unde Baptista Mantuanus, eadem etiam elusione olim deceptus, de eius ad Carolum itinere sic scribit:
units.tr: Thus the name of empire was restored to the Romans, yet in such a way that the authority of the Pope was not excluded, as is said of the eighth in Rev. 17. From this a custom remained that those who received the sceptre of the empire should be anointed by the Pope of Rome. From that day, which was in the year of the Lord 801, the dignity of the Roman empire was transferred by the Pope from the Greeks to the Gauls, and afterwards from the Gauls to the Germans, according to his pleasure. Thus the empire, which was formerly believed to be given from heaven, has now fallen into the hands of the Pope. And this transfer is one of the great and wondrous miracles of Antichrist, to whom the dragon gave his seat and power, Rev. 13. This pontiff also declared Pepin, son of this Charles and king of that part of Italy, which neither he nor any of his predecessors could subject to themselves. And this was done for this reason: that the kings of France, holding the imperial title, would never allow such majesty to be taken from them by him. Hence it came about (says Girolamo Mari) that through the Pope there have been perpetual enmities and quarrels between the emperors of the East and of the West. From this followed so many slaughters, so many fires, so many devastations of kingdoms, and still there is no end. Yet on this condition was Charles, this great emperor, made emperor by this pontiff: that he should promise with an oath that he would keep perpetual obedience to him. Having thus acquired and confirmed the dragon's right, according to what is written in Rev. 13, Leo set about managing the affairs of the Church; he instituted three days of supplications before the ascension of Christ, and he was the first to assign the use of incense to altars, after the manner of the unbelieving Jews and pagans. He built a very large hospice for idolatrous foreigners coming to Rome, and he restored the roof of the church of St Peter. He decreed that the decrees of the pontiffs should be placed above the writings of all teachers, and he wished the blood, which impostors had said flowed from a certain wooden crucifix, to be held (horrible to say) as the true blood of Christ, just as they wished the idolatries of statues to be confirmed, although it was still in question whether they were gods. And when he set out for Mantua, where that blood is kept to this day, is greeted and adored, he approved it by his authority as genuine, and confirmed it with bulls, adding to it a solemn feast day every year, to the very great disparagement of Christ. Thus the power of darkness then prevailed. Whence Baptista Mantuan, once deceived by the same trickery, writes thus of Leo's journey to Charles:

units.la: Dum meat audito ficti rumore cruoris / Nuper adinuenti, gressum convertit ad urbem, / Nomina cui fecit virgo Cadmeia Manto. / Et quae purpureus sanguis faciebat in horas, / Mira opera intuitus, credi debere putavit, / Effusum nostra pro libertate cruorem.
units.tr: As he went, on hearing the rumour of blood lately invented in pretence, he turned his steps to the city to which the Cadmean maiden Manto gave her name; and, gazing at the wonderful works that purple blood made hour after hour, he thought it must be believed to be blood poured out for our liberty.

units.la: Nullus diabolorum fecisset, quae fecit hic Papa diabolicus: non serpens ille qui Euam seduxit, ut hominibus persuaderet, Christum ex ligno, aut lapide suum velle iam glorificatum emittere sanguinem, ut idola gentium sua olim responsa. Quae iniquitas haec est, aut quae blasphemia in servatorem Iesum, atq; eius sanguinem, nostrae redemptionis precium unicum? Semel inquiunt Apostoli, pro nobis effusum? Sed haec vera esse, omnes credebant: tanta tunc erat Christianorum hominum caecitas, & divini verbi ignorantia. Et ita futurum esse praedixit Antichristi adventum Apo-stolus Paulus, secundum operationem Satanae in mendacibus signis ac seductione, ne salui fierent increduli 2. Thes.2. Impostor hic Leo, ac mendaciorum magister, anno Domini 816. cum his ludibrijs tartara penetravit, in sanctum nihilominus à Papistis relatum.
units.tr: No devils would have done what this diabolical Pope did: not that serpent which seduced Eve, to persuade men that Christ wished to send forth from wood or stone his blood, now glorified, as the idols of the nations once gave their responses. What iniquity is this, or what blasphemy against the Saviour Jesus and his blood, the sole price of our redemption? Once, they say, it was poured out for us by the apostles? But all believed these things to be true: so great was then the blindness of Christian men and their ignorance of the divine word. And so the Apostle Paul foretold that the coming of Antichrist would be according to the working of Satan, with lying signs and deception, so that unbelievers would not be saved, 2 Thess. 2. This impostor Leo, master of lies, in the year of the Lord 816, penetrated hell with these mockeries, and was nevertheless reckoned among the saints by the Papists.
33. STEPHEN the Fourth.

units.la: Stephanus quartus, Romanus, Leoni tertio fuc-cessus, tertio mense post initum papatum, in Galliās proficiscebatur, ad Ludovicum Pium Imperatorem, ut se apud illum de sui electione purga-ret. Quoniam inconsulto Imperatore, à clero & populo Rom. contra Hadriani ac Leonis decreta de eligendo pontifice, in Satanae vicarium electus ac confirmatus fuit. Tam fidelis est Romana sedes, suarum legum observatrix, ut in primo suc-cessore eas infringat. Sed ut Ludovicum pro tempore, per hypocrisim adulator ludificaret, Re-gis (non Romæ) coronam pulcherrimam, quàm secum attulerat, eius imposuit capiti, & aliam Hir-mingardi reginæ, Augustam eam nuncupans. Rediens vero, à Cæsare remuneratus, Reatina Ecclesia vacante, Episcopum consecrare Stephanus noluit (astuta vulpes) nisi prius cognosceret, Imperatorem probare eius electionem. Sed perpende sequeiam. Cum Romam iterum uenisset, cogitare mox coepit, ius Carolo ac suis successoribus datum, mali plurimum secum adferre posse. Et Lodouici lenitate audacior factus, ius illud abrogabat: ac pronunciabat, id esse debere penes clerum, senatum, ac populum Rom. ut pontificem ipsum eligerent. At ne Imperatoris iram in se concitaret, hanc interpretationem addidit: Licere scilicet eis, pontificem Rom. sine eius authoritate eligere: sed non licere ipsum consecrare, sine eius aut suorum legatorum praesentia. Atq; ita sunt Imperatores à Papae electione aliquandiu exclusi. Stephanus autem, quoniam octo tantummodo menses sedem illam occupauit, nihil propter temporis breuitatem, quemadmodum se facturum sperabat, imperio suo addere potuit. Sed anno Domini 817[?]. uitam in solita superstitione finiuit.
units.tr: Stephen the Fourth, a Roman, succeeded Leo the Third. Three months after he began the papacy, he set out for Gaul, to Louis the Pious, the Emperor, in order to clear himself before him of his election. The Roman clergy and people had elected and confirmed him without the Emperor's consent, against the decrees of Hadrian and Leo on the election of the pontiff, and so he became the vicar of Satan. So faithful is the Roman see, the keeper of its own laws, that it breaks them in its very first successor. But to fool Louis for the moment, as a hypocritical flatterer, he placed on the Emperor's head a most splendid crown, which he had brought with him from the King (not from Rome), and another on the head of Queen Hermingard, calling her Augusta. On his return he was rewarded by the Emperor. When the church of Rieti became vacant, Stephen (the cunning fox) refused to consecrate a bishop unless he had first learned that the Emperor approved the election. But consider what follows. When he had come to Rome again, he soon began to think that the right granted to Charles and his successors could bring a great deal of harm. Made bolder by Louis's mildness, he abrogated that right and declared that it ought to belong to the clergy, the senate and the Roman people, so that they might elect the pontiff himself. Yet, so as not to stir up the Emperor's anger against himself, he added this interpretation: that they might indeed elect the Roman pontiff without his authority, but that it was not lawful for him to be consecrated without the presence of the Emperor or of his legates. And so for some time the Emperors were excluded from the election of the Pope. Stephen, however, since he held that see for only eight months, could add nothing to his power by way of what he hoped to do, because of the shortness of his time. But in the year of the Lord 817[?] he ended his life in his accustomed superstition.
34. PASCHAL the First.

units.la: PAschalis primus, monachus Romanus, iuxta Stephani praedecessoris glossam, sine Ludouici Imperatoris consensu, à clero & populo Rom. pontifex eligebatur. De qua electione cum Imperator conquereretur, Paschalis, missus ad eum nuncijs & literis, astute se purgauit. Processu temporis, homo callidus, cum Ludouicum, falsa licet religione deceptum, Romanae sedi plurimum deferentem ne misset[?]:periculosum ratus, si in augenda authoritate moram pertraheret, miris artibus eum fuscinauit, ut ius eligendorum pontificum Carolo datum, Romanis relinqueret, & parentum suorum donationes (illicita violentia partas) scriptis confirma-ret. Quod & ille, fallacias eorum ignorans, fecit, atq; obsignauit. Sed postquam Lotharium eius filium, Romae in Augustum, quo id facilius fieret, coronasset: Theodorum primicerium & Leonem nomenclatorem, eius partes, dum ad patrem abiret, fideliter defendentes, oculis ac capitibus priuari, per quosdam seditiosos, latenter ac proditorie fecit. Et cum apud Imperatorem, tam excitatae seditionis, quàm perpetratae caedis accusaretur, coacta praelatorum synodo, iuramento se purgauit. Eorum nihilominus interfectores absoluens, casos reos egit lesae maiestatis, iureq; esse occisos pronunciabat. Atq; hæc est sanctissimorum illorum sanctitas, in eo regno perditionis. Hic pontifex Paschalis, duo milia sanctorum cadauera (si non fit in numero error) in cœmiteriis condita, magnificentiore in urbe sepultura honestauit. Praxedis fanum à fundamentis extruxit, & in eo reposuit Caeciliae, Tiburtij, Valeriani, Maximini, & aliorum martyrum: Urbani verò ac Lucij pontificum corpora. Templa quaedam ruinâ minantia restituit, & oratorium Agnetis folenniter dedicauit. Altaria tem-plis, & altaribus ornamenta preciosa tribuit. Maria templum ad præsepe, uetustate quassum, in melius formam redegit: reliquias q; sanctorum uenerari & coli iussit. Clerici postremo mandauit, ne à laicis (sic arrogantia eorum creuit) beneficia Ecclesiastica acciperent. Sed inter hæc omnia, Euangelij Dei prædicatio, locum non habet. Cum his papalibus factis anno Domini 824. Paschalis hinc abijt, uniuersæ carnis uiam ingressus.
units.tr: Paschal the First, a Roman monk, was chosen pontiff by the Roman clergy and people, without the consent of the Emperor Louis, following the precedent of his predecessor Stephen. When the Emperor complained of this election, Paschal sent him messengers and letters and cleverly cleared himself. As time went on, being a crafty man, and judging it dangerous if he delayed in increasing his authority, he, with Louis (though deceived by a false religion and greatly deferring to the Roman see, lest he should be [?] ...) he by wondrous arts brought him round, so that he left the right of electing pontiffs, which had been granted to Charles, to the Romans, and confirmed in writing the gifts of his parents (acquired by illicit violence). Louis, ignorant of their deceits, did this and sealed it. But after he had crowned Lothair, his son, as Augustus at Rome, so that this might be done more easily, he had Theodore the primicerius and Leo the nomenclator, who faithfully defended his party while he was going off to his father, deprived of their eyes and heads, secretly and treacherously, through certain seditious men. When he was accused before the Emperor both of stirring up such sedition and of committing the murder, he cleared himself by oath before a synod of prelates which he had gathered. Nevertheless, he absolved their killers, and charged the victims with treason, declaring that they had rightly been killed. This is the holiness of those most holy men, in that kingdom of destruction. This pontiff Paschal honoured with a more magnificent burial in the city the two thousand bodies of saints (if there is no error in the number) which had been laid in the cemeteries. He built the church of Praxedes from its foundations, and placed in it the bodies of Cecilia, Tiburtius, Valerian, Maximinus and other martyrs, and the bodies of the pontiffs Urban and Lucius. He restored some churches threatening ruin, and solemnly dedicated an oratory to Agnes. He gave precious ornaments to the churches and to the altars. He reduced the church of Mary by the manger, shaken by age, to a better form, and ordered the relics of the saints to be venerated and worshipped. Lastly, he commanded clerics not to accept ecclesiastical benefices from laymen (so greatly had their arrogance grown). But amid all these things there is no place for the preaching of the Gospel of God. With these papal deeds done, in the year of the Lord 824, Paschal departed hence, entering the way of all flesh.
35. EUGENIUS the Second.

units.la: Evgenius secundus, patria Romanus, pontifica-tum Paschale mortuo, sed non sine eligentium patrum discordia, suscepit: nam & suffragia ad eam dignitatem Zinzimus quidam habuit. Sed composito tandem dissidio, tum propter affabilitatem (ut dicunt) tum eloquentiam, Eugenius omnium consensu, papatum obtinuit. Dum esset ille Cardinalis S. Sabinæ, ut Præmonstratensis habet, argenteo ciborio & pictura folenni (opera ualde Christiana) eandem Ecclesiam decorauit. Nunc autem in pontificatu, rem frumentariam adeo ipsum curasse ferunt, ut multis uideretur pascendis hominibus natus. Quid interim egerit in pastu uinifici Dei uerbi, certe nihil adhuc legimus. Aliqui tamen scribunt, quod fit à Romanis ciuibus, alij [?] ab aduersarijs sacrificulis, oculis ac uita priuatus. Lotharius Imperator, & Italiae rex, huius Papae tempore magistratus per Italiam constituit, qui Rom. populo dicerent: eo quod libertate, qua sub Carolo Magno ac Ludouico usi erant, nimis abu-terentur. Quod factum, ut multi coniiciunt, Eugenii cedem maturauit. Michael Imperator Constantinopolitanus, legatos ad Ludouicum Caesarem misit, rogans iudicium de imaginibus, an essent abrogandae, uel colendae? Ludouicus ad Eugenium eos remisit, ut illius audirent sententiam, cum nihil auderet in ea causa, aut fortasse, quod eius esset ignarus. Sed papae responsum non retulerunt scripto res. Quatuor annos in pontificatu peregit, & anno Domini 827. ad patres suos perrexit.
units.tr: Eugenius the Second, a Roman by birth, took up the papacy after Paschal died, not without discord among the electing fathers; for a certain Zinzimus also had votes for that dignity. But when the dispute was finally settled, Eugenius obtained the papacy with the consent of all, both for his affability (as they say) and his eloquence. While he was cardinal of St Sabina, as the Praemonstratensian writer records, he adorned that church with a silver ciborium and a solemn painting (a very Christian work). Now, in the pontificate, they say he took such care of the grain supply that he seemed born to feed many people. Meanwhile, what he did in feeding the vine of God's Word, we have certainly not yet read. Some write, however, that he was deprived of his eyes and his life by the Roman citizens, others by the adversary sacrificing priests. Lothair, Emperor and King of Italy, in the time of this Pope set up magistrates throughout Italy, who would tell the Roman people this, because they abused too much the liberty they had enjoyed under Charlemagne and Louis. Many conjecture that this act hastened the death of Eugenius. Michael, the Emperor of Constantinople, sent envoys to the Emperor Louis, asking for a judgement on images: whether they were to be abolished or worshipped. Louis sent them back to Eugenius, that they might hear his opinion, since he did not dare to decide that matter himself, or perhaps because he was ignorant of it. But the envoys did not bring back the Pope's answer in writing. He spent four years in the pontificate, and in the year of the Lord 827 he went to his fathers.
36. Valentinus the First.

units.la: VAlentinus primus, natione Romanus, ex dia-cono nondum presbyter factus, in papam pa-liter assumebatur. A tenera aetate in Romano-rum scholis enutritus, sub Paschale & Eugenio pontificias virtutes didicit, ac non secus (inquiunt) in pontificatu quam in priuata uita se habuit. Fuit in homine ingenij dexteritas, qua posset suadere uel dissuadere quod uellet: nil tamen quod non placeret, pacificum pastor proposuit. Tanta nihilominus in eo erat, ut quidam scriptores indi-cant, felicioris gubernationis expectatio, ut sibi timerent patres a consueta eorum sanctitate. Vitae brevitas, ne quid pro Republica Romana aut Antichristi monarchia faceret, vehementer impediuit. Quadragesimo enim sui pontificatus die deficiens, eodem anno quo Eugenius prædictus, venenata sorsan potione, ex hac vita migrauit.
units.tr: Valentinus the First, a Roman by birth, was hastily raised to the papacy while still a deacon and not yet a presbyter. Brought up from tender years in the Roman schools, he learned papal virtues under Paschal and Eugenius, and, as they say, he was no different in the pontificate than he had been in private life. He had a man's cleverness, by which he could persuade or dissuade as he wished, yet the minister proposed nothing that did not please, peacefully. Nevertheless, some writers indicate that there was so much expectation of a happier government from him that the Fathers feared for their customary holiness. The brevity of his life greatly hindered him from doing anything for the Roman commonwealth or the monarchy of Antichrist. For he died on the fortieth day of his pontificate, in the same year in which Eugenius had died, perhaps from a poisoned draught.
37. Gregory the Fourth.

units.la: Gregorius quartus, etiam Romanus, Valentino prædecessori statim suffectus, Papatum inire noluit (futura pericula timens) donec Imperator eius approbasset electionem. Atq; per istum ad tempus, Imperatoribus ius confirmandi Papæ statutum fuit. Sub hoc pontifice anno Domini 830. conuentus episcoporum, Ludouici Cæsaris iussu, Aquisgrani celebrabatur. In quo Gregorio præsidente, statutum erat, ut unaquaeq; Ecclesia suos proventus possideret, unde sacrifici viverent: ne cogerentur, desertis officijs, quaestuosis artibus se dare. Sancitumq; fuit, ne ullius gradus clerici, pretiosis aut coccinei coloris vestibus uterentur: neq; in digitis gemmas gestarent, nisi quando præsules (gemmea certe exceptio) missas vel exorcismos ficerent[?], Ne prælati nimis magnam haberent fa-[?] miliam[?], ne equos, aleas, & scorta nutrirent, ac ne monachi gula aut crapula (paederastia negligitur) mensuram excederent. Ne aurum quoq; uel argentum clerici, uncti, uel rasi, in calceis, crepidis, aut baltheis, instar Heliogabali, ferrent. Tantus eo tempore fuit eorum luxus. Anno Domini 835. Gregorius, iubente Ludouico, festum omnium sanctorum à 13. die Maij, ad Calendas Nouembris transtulit: sacrumq; esse, dicti Cæsaris authoritate, mandauit: quoniam teste Vincentio, eius in ea re confirmationem rogauerat. Et illud festum Germani atque Galli, primum celebrare coeperunt. Causam translationis huius festi sic tradit Mantuanus: Nam modo collectæ fruges, & in horrea missæ, Ocia parturiunt: iam transfuere labores. Cessauere operæ: tempus geniale propinquat. Bruma uenit, glacialis hyems apparet in altis Montibus: & canis albet iuga summa capillis, &c.
units.tr: Gregory the Fourth, also a Roman, was immediately appointed successor to his predecessor Valentinus, but he was unwilling to enter the papacy (fearing the dangers to come) until the Emperor had approved his election. Through him, for a time, it was established that the Emperors should confirm the Pope. Under this pontiff, in the year of the Lord 830, a gathering of bishops was held at Aachen by the order of Louis the Emperor. At this gathering, with Gregory presiding, it was decreed that each church should possess its own revenues, from which the clergy might live, so that they would not be compelled, having abandoned their duties, to turn to profitable trades. It was also decreed that clerics of no rank should wear precious garments or garments of scarlet colour, nor should they wear gems on their fingers, unless the prelates (a jewelled exception, certainly) were celebrating masses or exorcisms[?], that prelates should not keep too large a household[?] miliam[?]; nor should they feed horses, dice and whores, and that monks should not exceed the measure in gluttony or drunkenness (sodomy being overlooked). Nor should clerics, anointed or shaven, carry gold or silver on their shoes, sandals or belts, in the manner of Heliogabalus. So great was their luxury at that time. In the year of the Lord 835, Gregory, at the command of Louis, moved the feast of All Saints from the thirteenth day of May to the Kalends of November, and by the authority of the said Emperor he ordered that it be observed as holy, since, according to Vincentius, he had asked the Emperor to confirm this matter. And the Germans and the Gauls were the first to begin to celebrate that feast. Mantuan gives this reason for the transfer of the feast: "For now the crops are gathered and sent into the barns, and leisure is brought forth; now the labours have passed over. The works have ceased; the genial season draws near. Winter comes, and icy winter appears on the high mountains, and the hoary ridges whiten with snow," and so on.

units.la: Templa collapsa Gregorius, antecessorum exemplo restituit: & cadauera sanctorum, Fabiani, Gregorij, & aliorum, à loco in locum transtulit. Fanum Martini in montibus, nouis fabricis extruxit: festa Bartholomei, Sebastiani, atq; Gregorij, cerebrari præcepit, & illis altaria dedit.
units.tr: Gregory restored the collapsed churches, following the example of his predecessors, and he moved the bodies of saints, Fabian, Gregory and others, from place to place. He built a shrine of Martin on the mountains with new structures; he ordered the feasts of Bartholomew, Sebastian and Gregory to be celebrated, and he gave altars to them.

units.la: Mauros, iuuante Cæsare, Italia profligauit: Hamburgensem archiepiscopum Ansgarium confirmauit:decimas ac proventus Ecclesiis procurauit: & sepulchrorum erectiones solennes excogitauit. Ro-mani, ut apparet, catholicam fidem antea satis erant docti, nec opus tunc habebant Evangelica doctrina. Quoniam inter haec omnia, nulla fit eius mentio. Obiit Gregorius anno Domini 843. & ad suos patres positus est.
units.tr: With the help of the Emperor, he overthrew the Moors in Italy; he confirmed Ansgar as archbishop of Hamburg; he provided tithes and revenues for the churches; and he devised solemn ceremonies for the erection of tombs. The Romans, it seems, had already been sufficiently taught the Catholic faith and then had no need of evangelical doctrine, since among all these things there is no mention of it. Gregory died in the year of the Lord 843 and was laid to rest with his fathers.
38. Sergius the Second.

units.la: Sergius fecundus, patria Romanus, os porci antea vocatus, defuncto Gregorio, papatum statim iniit, & mutandorum nominum initium successoribus dedit. Ad cuius confirmationem Lotharius Imperator, cum authoritate Caesarea, suum primogenitum Ludovicum, multis nobilibus comitatum, Romam misit. Quod genus confirmationis fere omnes expectabant, donec Hadrianus tertius populo Romano retulit, in creando pontifice, consensum Imperatoris expectandum non esse. Sergius iste primus fuit, qui nomen Christo datum, & in ipso baptismate suscepto, propria voluntate abnegauit. Mysterium intellige. Istum enim, & alij sequentes, baptismi sui gratiam aperte ac manifestè respuerunt: honorificentius aestimantes (ut Funccius habet) nomen in unctione, à miseris hominibus excogitata, susceptum: quàm quod in baptismo, à Christo servatore instituto, acceperunt.
units.tr: Sergius the Second, a Roman by birth, formerly called Pig's Mouth, took up the papacy immediately upon the death of Gregory, and he gave successors the beginning of changing names. For his confirmation, the Emperor Lothar, with imperial authority, sent his firstborn son Louis, accompanied by many nobles, to Rome. Almost everyone expected this kind of confirmation, until Hadrian the Third reported to the Roman people that in creating a pontiff the consent of the Emperor was not to be awaited. Sergius was the first who renounced, of his own will, the name given to him in Christ and received at his very baptism. Understand the mystery. For he and the other successors who followed him openly and plainly rejected the grace of their baptism, judging it more honourable (as Funccius has it) to receive a name at anointing, devised by wretched men, than the one they had received at baptism, instituted by Christ the Saviour.

units.la: Sed manifesta est hæc Antichristi facies: & ita fieri, ut à fidelibus nosceretur, Deus certè voluit. Quidam ab hac nominis mutatione, ad septimum annum Iulij secundi, qui assumpto Pauli gladio, Petri clauem in Tiberim proiecit: Bestiæ numerum, ob quædam tunc reuelata mysteria, supputant. Sed hæc suo tempore manifestiora reddam: ad Sergium ipsum redeo. Lotharium Imperatorem ille coronauit, & ornandis templis animum applicauit. Sylvestri & Martini basilicas ampliauit, ac monasterium earum lateribus adiunxit. Diuorum tumulos ibidem euexit, & multorum sanctorum cadavera in ipsis collocauit. Agnus Dei in missa ter dici constituit, & hostiam (ut uocant) interim in tres partes diuidi mandauit. Sed de Euangelio ad Dei gloriam promulgando nihil ipse curauit. Post hæc & eiusmodi papalia facta, anno Domini 846, animam moriens exhalauit.
units.tr: But this face of Antichrist is plain, and God certainly willed that it should be recognised by the faithful and so come about. Some reckon from this change of name to the seventh year of Julius the Second, who, taking up the sword of Paul, threw the key of Peter into the Tiber, the number of the beast, because of certain mysteries then revealed. But I will set these out more clearly in their proper time; now I return to Sergius himself. He crowned the Emperor Lothar, and he applied his mind to adorning the churches. He enlarged the basilicas of Sylvester and Martin and joined a monastery to their sides. He raised the tombs of the divine men there, and he placed the bodies of many saints within them. He ordered that the Lamb of God be said three times in the mass, and he commanded that the host (as they call it) be divided meanwhile into three parts. But he himself took no care to spread the Gospel to the glory of God. After these and similar papal deeds, he breathed out his soul in dying in the year of the Lord 846.
39. Leo the Fourth.

units.la: Leo quartus, monachus Romanus, sub Imperatore Lothario papatum accepit, & urbem Romanam multis munitionibus, templaq; ornamentis ditauit. Turrim namq; in Vaticano apud sanctum Petrum, magno sumptu extruxit: urbis mænia & portas uetustate lapsas restituit: ac propugnacula quindecim à fundamentis eisdem adiecit. Quorum duo ad exitum Tiberis commodissimè collocata fuerunt, ad retundendam uim hostium, qui nauibus ad urbem diripiendam sæpius aduecti erant. Vaticanum muro cinxit, atq; in urbis formam redegit, quam ex suo nomine Leoninam uocauit. Templum S. Mariæ nouæ fabricauit: & quatuor coronatorum martyrum ossibus altare dedit. Arcem S. Angeli reædificauit, atq; in uestibulo atrij Lateranensis ex marmore sedilia fecit. Solarium à Leone tertio inchoatum absoluit: & tribus portis insculpsit tres precationes ad Deum pro Roma conseruanda, scilicet, Deus qui Apostolo, Deus qui ab ipso, & Præsta quæsumus. Hactenus ædilem curulem egit: nunc fit miles ac dux exercitus. Nam cum Saraceni Italiam incursionibus undiq; vexarent, regnum cælesti pro sua fede pugnantibus primus promisit. Conuocataq; Romana militia, facto crucis signo, illis occurrit, & cum hac oratione, Deus cuius dextra, ad Hostiæ Portam eos hostes fugauit ac uicit. Hinc dicitur, quod suo fla-tu tubasiliscum[?] expulerit: sed atrociorem bestiam (papatum) in urbe ipsa fuit. De hoc certamine sic scribit Mantuanus:
units.tr: Leo the Fourth, a Roman monk, received the papacy under the emperor Lothair. He enriched the city of Rome with many fortifications and the churches with ornaments. He built, at great expense, a tower in the Vatican beside St Peter's. He restored the city walls and gates, which had collapsed with age, and added fifteen bulwarks from the foundations. Two of these were placed most conveniently at the mouth of the Tiber, to check the force of the enemy, who had often come up to the city by ship to plunder it. He walled in the Vatican and reshaped it into a city, which he called Leonine after his own name. He built the new church of St Mary and gave an altar made from the bones of the four crowned martyrs. He rebuilt the citadel of St Angelo, and in the vestibule of the Lateran atrium he made seats of marble. He completed the solarium that Leo the Third had begun, and on its three gates he carved three prayers for the preservation of Rome: "God, who to the Apostle...", "God, who by him...", and "Grant, we beseech thee." Hitherto he had acted as an aedile; now he becomes a soldier and commander of an army. For when the Saracens were harassing Italy with raids on every side, he was the first to promise the kingdom of heaven to those who fought for his faith. Having summoned the Roman militia, and making the sign of the cross, he met them with this prayer, "O God, whose right hand...", and at the Gate of Hostia he put those enemies to flight and conquered them. Hence it is said that by his breath he drove out the basilisk; but a more savage beast, the papacy, remained in the city itself. Concerning this battle Mantuanus writes thus:

units.la: Ismaelitarum prope Tibridis ostia quartus fregit mille rates: traxit nova mœnia ab arce Pontis, ad aduersi delubra ingentia Petri. Tandem ipse Papam egit. Synodum quadra-gintaseptem Episcoporum congregauit: in quâ Athanasium quendam S. Marcelli presbyterum Cardinalem, de multis criminibus convictum, damnauit, censuit tamen postea, non nisi 72. testibus Episcopum esse condemnandum. Sed illi fortasse hic summè displicuit. Crucem papalem, contra Aquisgranensis concilii[?] statuta, gemmis primus exornauit, & ante se ferri præcepit. Pedes populo deosculandos præbuit, & contra terræ motum supplicationes instituit, horasq; vespertinas in D. Pauli natalicijs dici. Decreuit ut nullus laicorum, dum missæ fierent, in presbyterio vel choro adesset, nisi altaribus ministrans: & ut octauæ assumptionis Mariæ passim celebrarentur. Super multis criminibus accusatus, præsertim quòd concilium iniisset de transferendo Imperio iterum à Gallis ad Constantinopolitanos: sed consueto pontificum more, iuramento se purgauit. Cum his atq; aliis papalibus factis, anno Domini 854. ad vitæ finem peruenit. Huius Leonis tempore, anno Domini 847. Ethelwolphus per eius dispensationem, ex cœlibe ac monacho Anglorum rex factus, provinciam suam Rom. synagogæ tributariam fecit, constitu-ens ex qualibet domo nummum angenteum quo-tannis dari. Sic tota Anglia (ut non minus verè quàm Hodie [?] Ioannes Funccius scribit) Romanæ bea-stiæ fuit subiugata, ut impleretur quod dicitur de decem regibus, Apoc. 17. Hi unum consilium habent, & virtutem ac potestatem suam bestiæ transdent. Sed Henricus octauus eius nominis rex, illud iugum feliciter excussit, ut suo loco dicetur.
units.tr: Near the mouths of the Tiber, Leo the Fourth shattered a thousand Ishmaelite ships; he extended new walls from the citadel of the Bridge to the great temple of Peter opposite. At last he himself played the Pope. He gathered a synod of forty-seven bishops, in which he condemned a certain Athanasius, a cardinal priest of St Marcellus, convicted of many crimes; yet he later judged that a bishop should not be condemned except on the testimony of seventy-two witnesses. But perhaps this (decision) displeased him greatly. Contrary to the decrees of the Council of Aachen, he was the first to adorn the papal cross with jewels, and he ordered it carried before him. He offered his feet for the people to kiss, and he instituted supplications against earthquakes, and ordered the evening hours to be said on the feast of St Paul. He decreed that no layman, while masses were being celebrated, should be present in the presbytery or choir, unless ministering at the altars, and that the octave of the Assumption of Mary be celebrated everywhere. Accused of many crimes, especially of having undertaken a council to transfer the empire again from the Franks to the Constantinopolitans, he cleared himself by oath, in the customary manner of the popes. With these and other papal deeds, he came to the end of his life in the year of the Lord 854. In the time of this Leo, in the year of the Lord 847, Ethelwolphus, through his dispensation, was made king of the English, though he was a celibate monk, and he made his province tributary to the Roman synagogue, establishing that a silver penny be paid yearly from every house. Thus all England (as John Funck writes, no less truly than today?) was subjected to the Roman beast, so that what is said of the ten kings in Revelation 17 was fulfilled: "These have one mind, and they give their power and authority to the beast." But Henry the Eighth, king of that name, happily shook off that yoke, as will be told in its place.
BOOK FOUR.

units.la: TERTIAE classis sectio secunda, de Papis vel Romanis Antichristis, in regno meretricis magnæ, quæ sedet super Bestiam, Apoc. 17. usque ad Sylvestrum secundum.
units.tr: THE SECOND SECTION OF THE THIRD CLASS, concerning the Popes or Roman Antichrists, in the kingdom of the great harlot who sits upon the beast, Rev. 17, down to Sylvester II.

units.la: A Cæsare Phoca per 247. annos, hucusque tanquam bestia regnauit Antichristus in Ecclesiis Christianorum, sine omni iudicio aut ratione spiritus diuini. Oculos ad terrena toto hoc tempore, conuertebant Rom. pontifices, usque ad quadragesimum papam, æterni Dei testamenti immemores, ac si solummodo cutes & uentres, non animas curarent. In nouis traditionibus, cæremoniis, ædificijs, illecebris, pompis, bellis, proditionibus, ac regnorum translationibus, totum eorum studium fuit, ut ex præcedentibus liquet, ut cum hoc mundo in gloria, non in contemptu cum Christo, hic regnarent. Ita ut Ecclesia sub eorum regimine [?], fit tunc demum Babylonica meretrix facta: iuxta Id quod passim in ipsa Ioannis Apocalypsi scribi-tur. Cuius veritatem, in sequenti pontifice, Ioanne octavo, qui mulier et meretrix erat, Dominus Deus in apertissima luce, toti mundo manifestavit, ut omnes mysterium à Christo revelatum intelligant.
units.tr: From Caesar Phocas, for 247 years to this point, Antichrist has reigned like a beast over the churches of Christians, without any judgement or any reason of the divine Spirit. During all this time the Roman popes turned their eyes to earthly things, forgetful of the eternal covenant of God, as if they cared only for skins and bellies and not for souls, until the fortieth pope. As the preceding account makes clear, their whole zeal was for new traditions, ceremonies, buildings, enticements, pomps, wars, betrayals, and transfers of kingdoms, so that they might reign here with this world in glory, not in contempt, with Christ. Thus the Church under their rule was at last made the Babylonian harlot, just as is written everywhere in John's own Apocalypse. The truth of this was shown plainly to the whole world by the Lord God in the next pope, John VIII, who was a woman and a harlot, so that all might understand the mystery revealed by Christ.
THE POPES, OR ROMAN ANTICHRISTS.
40. JOHN VIII.

units.la: Ioannes octavus, qui ab Anglo quodam Fuldensis cœnobij monacho, quem apprimè dilexit, Anglici cognomentum acceperat, officio Papae, sed sexu fœmina: Romae duobus annis ac mensibus sex, in pontificali cathedra pontificaliter sedit. Hæc genere Germana, & Maguntina puella, Gilberta primùm dicta, virilem mentita sexum, sumpto adolescentis habitu, Athenas cum suo amatore monacho perrexit. Ubi cum excellenter in omnibus artibus profecisset, eo tandem mortuo, Romam ipsa rediit, sed dissimulato semper muliebri sexu. Cum .n. ex acutissimo ingenio & promptissima lingua, in disceptationib. ac lecturis publicè ornatissimè loqueretur, multiq; vehementer admirarentur sup eius doctrina, adeò in se conuertit omnium animos, ut mortuo Leone, in pontificem ab ipsis eligeretur, tur. In quo officio, aliorum pontificum mores, con-tulit sacros ordines, presbyteros ac diaconos fecit, Episcopos promovit, abbates ordinavit, missas celebravit, altaria & templa consecravit, sacramenta ministravit, pedes osculandos praebuit, caeteraq; Rom. pontificum exercuit munera: & facta eius in Ecclesia non fuerunt tunc irrita. Sub huius mulieris papatu, Lotharius Imperator senex, Monachum induit, & Ludovicus secundus, Romani profectus, Imperii sceptrum atque coronam, ab eius manu cum Petri benedictione suscepit. In quo facto tam potentem se ostendit Babylonica meretrix, ut subjiceret sibi reges, Apoc. 17. Sub eo etiam Ethelwolphus Anglorum rex, decimam sui regni partem, pro anima sua clericis ac monachis muliebriter dedit, ut tradit Houedenus, & filius eius Ethelbaldus, defuncti patris viduam, suamq; novercam Juditham, in uxorem duxit. In pontificatu vero, a quodam suo familiari capellano, Cardinale, eius sexum cognoscente, compressa, praegnans efficiebatur. Et in quadam processione solenni ad Lateranensem Ecclesiam, inter Colosseum & Clementis fanum, puerum ex forma-tione conceptu, in media Roma, in ipsa platea, in via publica, coram omni populo peperit: eoq; loci ex partu obijt, anno Domini 857. Ac propter hoc
units.tr: John VIII, who had received the surname "the Englishman" from an Englishman, a monk of the monastery of Fulda whom he dearly loved, held the office of pope, though he was a woman by sex. For two years and six months he sat on the papal throne as pope. She was by birth a German, a girl from Mainz, first called Gilberta. Pretending to be a man, she took on the dress of a youth and set off for Athens with her lover, a monk. There she advanced excellently in all the arts, and when he died she returned to Rome, always hiding her female sex. For with her very keen mind and ready tongue, she spoke most ornately in public disputations and lectures, and many greatly admired her teaching. So she won over the minds of all, so that when Leo died she was chosen pope by them. In this office she compared the morals of the other popes, conferred holy orders, made presbyters and deacons, promoted bishops, ordained abbots, celebrated masses, consecrated altars and churches, administered the sacraments, offered her feet to be kissed, and performed the other duties of the Roman popes; and her acts in the Church were not then void. Under this woman's papacy, the aged Emperor Lothair put on a monk's habit, and Louis II, when he came to Rome, received the imperial sceptre and crown from her hand, together with Peter's blessing. In this act the Babylonian harlot showed herself so powerful that she subjected kings to herself, Rev. 17. Under her also Ethelwulf, king of the English, gave the tenth part of his kingdom to clerks and monks for the sake of his soul, in a womanish way, as Hoveden relates; and his son Ethelbald took to wife his father's widow and his own stepmother, Judith. In the papacy she was violated by a certain chaplain of hers, a cardinal who knew her sex, and she became pregnant. And in a solemn procession to the Lateran church, between the Colosseum and the shrine of Clement, in the middle of Rome, in the very square, on the public street, before the whole people, she gave birth to a child, having conceived it in the course of the procession, and she died there from the delivery, in the year of the Lord 857. And because of this crime of the public birth, she, stripped of all papal honour, was buried without papal pomp. Mantuan mentions her in book 3, describing hell:

units.la: Scelus publici partus, omni honore pontificio spoliata, sine pompa papali sepulta erat. Cuius in Alphonso[?] mentionem Mantuanus lib. 3. facit, inferos describens:
units.tr: There she still hung, a woman who had feigned the male sex, whom the peak of a Phrygian mitre with its triple diadem was lifting up, and who was an adulterer as pope.

units.la: Hic pendebat adhuc, sexum mentita uirilem Fœminae, cui triplici Phrygiam diademate mitram Extollebat[?] apex, & pontificalis adulter.
units.tr: There she still hung...

units.la: In hoc poteris uidere, pie lector, qualiter Ecclesia Romana post missam de spiritu sancto, non potuit errare. Hoc factum reuera, meretricis magnae sedem, & omnium fornicationum matrem, ipsam clarius esse demonstrat, quam ullus unquam Apelles coloribus depingere queat.
units.tr: In this, pious reader, you can see how the Roman Church, after the mass about the Holy Spirit, could not err. This deed truly shows more clearly than any Apelles could ever paint with colours that this is the seat of the great harlot and the mother of all fornications.

units.la: Vt vero pontifices & uncti patres, id facimus detestari uideantur, ab ea platea declinant, tanquam a loco de malo omine ualde suspecto.
units.tr: But in order that the popes and the anointed fathers may appear to detest this deed, they avoid that square, as a place of very suspicious ill omen.

units.la: Functius[?] non dubitat, quin diuinitus fit permissum, ut haec fœmina fieret pontifex, & eadem meretrix, cum eo tempore subderet sibi reges (quales in Anglia Ethelwuolphus & Alphredus erant) ut Antichristum regem agnosceret.
units.tr: Functius does not doubt that it was permitted by divine decree that this woman should become pope and at the same time the harlot, since at that time she subjected kings to herself (such as Ethelwulf and Alfred were in England), so that they might acknowledge Antichrist as king.

units.la: Voluit namque tunc Deus in Papa meretrice, Babylonicum fornicum, de quo praedixerat Spiritus sanctus Apoc. 17, mundo manifestare, ut ab illo electi cauerent.
units.tr: For God then wished, in the harlot pope, to reveal to the world the Babylonian fornicator, of whom the Holy Spirit had foretold in Rev. 17, so that the elect might be on their guard against him.

units.la: Sed ne in posterum, in similem casum inciderent patres, ordinauerunt, ut electi pontifices genitalia per sedem perforatam a diacono attrectarentur. starentur, quo scirent esse mares. Nunc autem ad te ipsum Papatum, in Cardinalatu tot spurios generant, ut nemo dubitet esse mares, nec tam sancta observatione fit opus. De qua Ioannes Pannonius:
units.tr: But so that the fathers in future would not fall into a similar case, they ordained that elected popes should be felt by a deacon through the perforated seat, so that they might know they were males. But now, in the papacy itself, they produce so many bastards among the cardinals that no one doubts they are males, and such a holy observance is no longer needed. Concerning this, John Pannonius:

units.la: Non poterat quisquam referentes æthera claues
units.tr: No one could take up the keys that reach to heaven
without first examining the testicles.

units.la: Cur igitur nostro mos hic iam tempore cessat?
units.tr: Why, then, has this custom now ceased in our time?

units.la: Ante probat sese quilibet esse marem.
units.tr: Before, each man used to prove himself a male.
41. Benedict III.

units.la: Benedictus tertius, Romanus, post meretricem eā lectus in ipsa meretricia sede successit: sed tactis prius prudenti cautela virilibus, ne forte ut antea in Ioanne deciperentur. Miserabiliter (inquit Masseus) deplorabat, se fuisse[?] promotum ad onus illud, indignum se nociferans honore tanto, quod in eius sedis pontifice rarissimum est. Sed ex magna hypocrisi id provenisse affirmant quidam, quod pedes, ut Platina testis est, præbuerit osculandos, ac se tanquam patrem sanctissimum, uel potius terrenum idolum, adorari permiserit. Legati deinde a Ludouico Cæsare missi, Romam uenere, qui electionem cleri & populi sua authoritate confirmarent. Confirmatus autem, multas Ecclesias collabentes instaurauit, & in earundem sacraria, dona[?] preciosa reposuit. Instituit quoq;, ut Papa cum-dero[?], funus defuncti Episcopi, presbyteri, uel dia[?]oni, ornaret sua praesentia. Item ut vicissim totus clerus in funere pontificis adesset: et ut, Dirige, pro mortuis diceretur, primus, ut fertur, ordinavit. Iussit etiam, ut clerici honestè et ordinatè incederent: et moriens anno Domini 859. corpus jum[?] ante fores Ecclesiae S. Petri sepeliri mandavit.
units.tr: Benedict III, a Roman, was elected after that harlot and succeeded to the very seat of the harlot, but only after his male parts had been carefully examined with prudent caution, lest they should be deceived as before with John. (So Masseus says.) He lamented miserably that he had been promoted to that burden, declaring himself unworthy of so great an honour, a thing very rare in a pontiff of that see. But some affirm that this came from great hypocrisy, since, as Platina testifies, he offered his feet to be kissed and allowed himself to be adored as a most holy father, or rather as an earthly idol. Then envoys were sent from the Emperor Louis, and came to Rome to confirm by his authority the election made by the clergy and people. Once confirmed, he restored many churches that were falling into ruin and placed precious gifts in their sacristies. He also instituted that the Pope should adorn with his presence the funeral of a deceased bishop, presbyter or deacon, and, in turn, that the whole clergy should attend the funeral of a pontiff, and that the Dirige should be said for the dead; he is said to have been the first to ordain this. He also ordered that the clergy should walk honourably and in good order. Dying in the year of the Lord 859, he commanded that his body be buried in front of the doors of the Church of St Peter.

units.la: Huius tempore, in urbe Moguntinensi, daemonium quoddam, sub cuiusdam presbyteri cappa, dum aquam lustralem spargeret, quasi ipsi familiaris esset, latitans, illum accusabat, quod ea nocte cum filia procuratoris concubuisset, ut Sigebertus atque Vincentius referunt.
units.tr: In his time, in the city of Mainz, a certain demon, hiding under the cowl of a priest while he was sprinkling holy water, as if he were familiar with him, accused him of having slept the previous night with the daughter of a procurator, as Sigebert and Vincent report.
42. Nicholas I.

units.la: Nicolaus primus, Romanus, pontificatum init, praesente Imperatore Ludovico secundo, qui Lothario patri in imperio successit. Quo Italiae-gresso, quae ad augendam pontificiam potestatem facerent (quam tamen astutè prius fugerat, ut ab ipso Caesare sanctius crederetur) circumspiciebat. Ioannem Rauenne archiepiscopum, pristinam sue sedis libertatem afferentem, dignitate privavit: eandemq; Ecclesiam in perpetuam servitutem redegit. Multas constitutiones ille fecit: quae et frequentes in Papalibus decretis sunt. Statuit enim, ne princeps ullus secularis, nec imperator ipse (impudens latro) concilijs[?] clericorum interesse au deret,nisi de fide ageretur, ut quos fuasanctitas hæreticos esse iudicaret, ille statim vel proscribe-ret, vel occideret. Sanciuit quoq;, ne laici de cleri-corum vita iudicent (mirum bestiæ artificium) nec super pontificis potestate quicquam disputent. Ni-hil iuris in præsulem, magistratus Christianos ha-bere decreuit(ita se exaltabat Antichristus, diui-nam ordinationem conculcans pedibus ) eo quod pontifex, inquit, appelletur Deus. Anton.tit. 16. Præcepit ne Episcopi aut clerici bella gererent, sed orationi incumberent: ocio & luxui potius Re-diuinam Latino sermone celebrari iterum iussit: Sclauis tamen & Polonis, per dispensationem, in sua lingua fieri permisit. Sequentias in missa (can-tus puellares) primus approbauit: Gloria in excel-sis in cœnæ Dominicæ festo ad missam cantari man-dauit: & Romanorum pontificum decretis autho-ritatem Apostolicam addidit. Nuptias in publico celebrari præcepit, basilicam Mariæ nouæ repara-uit: D. Clementis corpus transtulit, & Bremen-sem Ecclesiam Hamburgensi coniunxit. A malis ministris sacramenta suscipi voluit: non tamen presbytero uxorem habente, quam hypocrita con-cubinam vocat. Per hanc immanem bestiam, sacer-dotes ad cœlibatum cogi primum cœperunt, sed ab Huldrico[?] episcopo Augustano, viro sanctissimo, per epistolam, est eius impietas acerrime impugnata. His gestis, anno Domini 867. Nicolaus fato concessit, quem sanctitatis titulo, omnibus post Gregorium Magnum, papistae praeferunt.
units.tr: Nicholas I, a Roman, entered upon the pontificate while the Emperor Louis II, who succeeded his father Lothair in the empire, was present. When he came into Italy, he looked around for whatever would serve to increase papal power (which he had nevertheless cunningly shunned before, so that he might be more holily believed by the Emperor himself). He deprived John, archbishop of Ravenna, of his dignity, because he was claiming the former liberty of his see; and he reduced that Church to perpetual servitude. He made many constitutions, which are frequent in the papal decrees. For he decreed that no secular prince, nor even the emperor himself (shameless robber), should presume to attend the councils of the clergy unless matters of faith were being treated, so that those whom his holiness judged to be heretics should at once be banished or killed. He also decreed that laymen should not judge the life of the clergy (a marvellous trick of the beast), nor dispute anything about the power of the pontiff. He ruled that Christian magistrates have no right over the prelate, so exalting himself was this Antichrist, trampling underfoot the divine ordinance, because, he says, the pontiff is called God. (Anton. tit. 16.) He commanded that bishops and clergy should not wage war but devote themselves to prayer, rather than to idleness and luxury. He again ordered the divine service to be celebrated in Latin, but by dispensation he allowed it to be done in their own language for the Slavs and Poles. He was the first to approve sequences in the Mass (girls' songs). He ordered the Gloria in excelsis to be sung at Mass on the feast of the Lord's Supper, and he added apostolic authority to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. He ordered weddings to be celebrated in public, he repaired the basilica of the New Mary, transferred the body of St Clement, and joined the Church of Bremen to that of Hamburg. He wished the sacraments to be received from wicked ministers, yet not from a presbyter who had a wife, whom this hypocrite calls a concubine. Through this monstrous beast, priests first began to be forced to celibacy, but his impiety was most sharply attacked by Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, a most holy man, in a letter. After these things were done, Nicholas departed this life in the year of the Lord 867, whom the Papists prefer to all others since Gregory the Great, with the title of holiness.
43. Hadrian II.

units.la: Hadrianus secundus, natione Romanus, Talari episcopi filius, exploratis uerendis (quod in ipsis tunc penderet religionis summa) a populo et clero sedi papali impositus fuit, priusquam Imperatoris legati illuc peruenire possent. Vi etenim eligendi pontificis potestatem, ad se tunc rapiebat Romani. Quod cum aegre ferrent legati, tale responsum acceperunt: non potuisse multitudinis uoluntatem in tanto tumultu moderari: eos tamen auspicato egisse, quod tam bonum uirum ordinassent. Legati uero necessitate coacti, cum dictam electionem frustrari nequirent, Hadrianum inuiti salutabant pontificem. Confirmatus ergo, multa pauperibus tribuisse scribitur: alienorum bonorum munificus dator. Quod ad Papalem cathedram illis diebus nolentes et inuiti traherentur, Benedictus, Nicolaus, et hic Hadrianus, insignis fuit impositura, ut eo simplicitatis colore, Caesares dementarent. Vt papali artificio Bulgaros et Dalmatas, in suum rete a Nicolao pertractos, reuincteret, misit tres legatos Episcopos, Syluestrum,
units.tr: Hadrian II, a Roman by birth and son of Talarus the bishop, was placed on the papal see by the people and clergy after the usual scrutiny (since at that time the chief point of religion depended on it), before the emperor's legates could arrive there. For the Romans at that time seized the power of choosing the pontiff for themselves by force. When the legates took this badly, they received this answer: the people's will could not be controlled in such a great tumult, but they had nevertheless acted auspiciously in ordaining so good a man. The legates, compelled by necessity, since they could not frustrate the said election, reluctantly greeted Hadrian as pope. Once confirmed, he is written to have given much to the poor, a generous giver of other people's goods. That Benedict, Nicholas, and this Hadrian were, in those days, unwilling and reluctant men dragged to the papal chair, was a notable imposture, so that under this colour of simplicity they might beguile the emperors. To bind the Bulgarians and Dalmatians, whom Nicholas had drawn into his net, to himself by papal craft, he sent three legates, the bishops Sylvester,

units.la: H Leopardum, & Dominicum, in sua culina natos ac nutritos, qui omnia in Ecclesiis ex eius senten-tia constituerent. Sed eius tyrannidem experti Bul-gari, Latinos sacerdotes expulerunt, retentis presbyteris Graecis. Quæ res multorum malorum incendia, inter Graecos & Latinos, suscitauit. Vita decessit Hadrianus anno Domini 873. ante cuius mortem, Brixiae tribus diebus sanguinem pluit: & locustae Galliæ[?] magnis agminibus miserè affixe-runt. Ab hoc pontifice Alphredus Anglorum rex, anno Domini 872 unctionem et coronam Anglorū primus accepit: Rom. papæ adoptivus filius inde dictus. Et ab eo anno usq; ad annum Domini 1538. sunt anni 666. qui faciunt plenum Bestiæ numerū. In quo Henricus octauus, qui tyrannicum pontificū iugum excusserat, omnes monachorum sectas[?] à suo regno deleuit, cænobiaq; ob paederastiam & hypo-crisin euertit.
units.tr: Leopardus and Dominicus, born and reared in his own kitchen, who were to set up everything in the churches according to his opinion. But the Bulgarians, having experienced his tyranny, expelled the Latin priests, while keeping the Greek presbyters. This matter stirred up many fires of evils between the Greeks and the Latins. Hadrian died in the year of the Lord 873. Before his death, at Brescia, it rained blood for three days, and locusts in great swarms fell dead in Gaul[?]. Under this pontiff, Alfred, king of the English, in the year of the Lord 872, first received the anointing and crown of the English; he was therefore called the adopted son of the Roman pope. And from that year until the year of the Lord 1538 there are 666 years, which make up the full number of the Beast. In that year Henry VIII, who had shaken off the tyrannical yoke of the pontiffs, destroyed all the monastic sects in his kingdom and overthrew the monasteries on account of paederasty and hypocrisy.
44. John the Ninth.

units.la: Ioannes nonus, patria Romanus, Græce ac Latine doctissimus, non sine magna bellorum occasione, tres Imperatores, Carolum Caluum, Ludovicum Balbum, & Carolum Crassum, sub suo pontificatu coronauit. Caluus, ut acceperat, Cæsarem esse mortuum, Romam ad Ioannem pontificem contendebat: quem muneribus in suam pertraxit sen[?]entiam, atq; ab eo imperiali corona infignieba-tur. Sed ille uenenata potione, per Sedechiam Iu-daeum medicum ac praestigiatorem, Mantuae post annum periit. Ioannes uero, audita eius morte, om-nes intendit uires, ut Balbus patri succederet, sed obsistentes Romani proceres, Crasso imperium decernunt. Pontifex in sententia persistens, nec fle-sti uolens, a ciuibus capitur, & in carcerem conii-citur. Amicorum tamen opera elapsus, in Galliam sufugit, ac Balbum imperij corona donatum, Au-gustum saluta. Interea Crassus, urbe Romana po-titus, Ioannem e Gallijs terrore reuocat. Qui Ro-mam rediens, ut tuto sibi liceret illic agere, eun-dem Carolum Crassum inungit, Cæsarem pronun-ciat, & imperij diademate adornat. Dum in Gal-lijs profugus adhuc esset Ioannes, concilium apud Trecas coegit: in quo contentiones quorundã com-posuit, ac pro Papistico regno plura constituit. Ad Ludouicum Balbum inde scripsit, Rom. Ecclesiæ priuilegia auferri non posse, nisi præscriptione centum annorum: & Flandris primum Episcopum dedit. Omnes item qui non sacrum de sacro, uel sacrum de non sacro, raperent, sacrilegij puni-uit: & homicidam nunquam debere in sacerdotem ordinari, statuit. Sacrilegij reos excommunicauit, pecuniarum multam transgressoribus præfixit ac reliquias sanctorum multis dono contulit. Li-bertatem Ecclesiarum, camiteriorum[?], clericorū, Ecclesiasticorum bonorum, atq; monasteriorum confirmauit. In Saracenos exercitum parauit, & eos Italia ac Sicilia depulit. E Graeco sermone plura transtulit: & magni Gregorij vitam quatuor libris explicuit. Caeterum anno Demini[?] 883. vita functus decubuit. Atq; hoc ipso tempore, imperium pror-sus est, per Carolum Crassum, ad Germanos trans-latum.
units.tr: John the Ninth, a Roman by birth and very learned in Greek and Latin, crowned three emperors during his pontificate, Charles the Bald, Louis the Stammerer and Charles the Fat, not without great occasion for wars. When Charles the Bald heard that the emperor had died, he hurried to Rome to see Pope John. The pope won him over to his opinion with gifts and was honoured by him with the imperial crown. But Charles was later poisoned at Mantua, a year afterwards, by a Jewish physician and charlatan named Sedechias. When John heard of his death, he exerted every effort to make Louis the Stammerer succeed his father. But the Roman nobles opposed this and decreed the empire to Charles the Fat. The pope, holding to his view and unwilling to yield, was seized by the citizens and thrown into prison. Through the efforts of friends, however, he escaped and fled into Gaul, and he greeted Louis, who had been given the crown of the empire, as Augustus. Meanwhile Charles the Fat, having made himself master of the city of Rome, recalled John from Gaul by means of terror. When John returned to Rome, so that he might be safe there, he anointed that same Charles the Fat, declared him emperor and adorned him with the imperial diadem. While John was still a fugitive in Gaul, he held a council at Troyes, in which he settled certain disputes and laid down several measures for the Papistical kingdom. From there he wrote to Louis the Stammerer that the privileges of the Roman Church could not be taken away except by prescription of a hundred years. He also gave Flanders its first bishop. He likewise decreed that those who should carry off what was sacred from the sacred, or what was sacred from what was not sacred, were to be punished as sacrilegious, and he ruled that a murderer must never be ordained a priest. He excommunicated the guilty of sacrilege, set a fine of money on transgressors and gave relics of the saints as gifts to many. He confirmed the liberty of the churches, cemeteries, clergy, ecclesiastical goods and monasteries. He prepared an army against the Saracens and drove them out of Italy and Sicily. He translated several works from Greek, and he wrote out the life of Gregory the Great in four books. He died in the year of our Lord 883. At this very time the empire was entirely transferred to the Germans, through Charles the Fat.
45. Martin the Second.

units.la: Martinus secundus, natione Gallus, patre Palumbo necromantico (ut ferunt) sacrificulo, fraude potius, ac malis artibus, quam honesta ele-ctione, probatis masculinis, ad papatum venit. Hu-ius concitatione subdola contigisse scribunt, ut Ioannes prædictus à Romanis proceribus capere-tur, & in vincula coniiceretur: adeò, ut necesse illi fuerit, pro vita seruanda, auxiliantibus amicis in Galliam aufugere. In huius Martini confirmatio-ne, non expectabatur Cæsaris authoritas, nec quarebatur[?] eius admissio: tam superbus atq; arrogans fuit. Ita paulatim sese pontifices Imperatorum potestate exuerunt, ut facilius eos tum demum conterent pedibus. Sed eo felicius prouenit Ecclesiæ & urbi, quòd in tam male acquisito Papatu, diudiutius non durauerit. Nam post annum unum & aliquot menses defecit, anno scilicet Domini 884. cum nihil memoria dignum suis reliquisset papa colis.
units.tr: Martin the Second, a Frenchman by nation, whose father Palumbus was (as they say) a necromancer and a sacrificing priest, came to the papacy by fraud and wicked arts rather than by an honest election, with his manhood proven. They write that by the crafty stirring up of this man it came about that the aforementioned John was seized by the Roman nobles and thrown into chains, so that he had to flee into Gaul to save his life, with his friends helping him. In this Martin's confirmation the authority of the emperor was not awaited, nor was his consent sought, so proud and arrogant was he. In this way the popes gradually stripped themselves of the power of the emperors, so that at last they could trample them under foot more easily. But it turned out the more happily for the Church and the city that his papacy, so badly acquired, did not last for long. For after one year and a few months he died, in the year of our Lord 884, leaving behind nothing worth remembering for his Papal worshippers.
46. Hadrian the Third.

units.la: HAdrianus tertius, patria Romanus, tantæ au-daciæ ac superciliï fuit, ut mox adepto Papatu, decretum faceret, ut in creando pontifice, non amplius expectaretur Imperatoris authoritas: sed ut Romæ libera semper essent & cleri & populi suf-fragia. Erat tunc Imperator, bella gerens contra Normannos pietatis hostes. Sic ausi sunt pontifi-ces (inquit Crantzius) ac Romanorum improbi-tas, Imperatores suos contemnere, dum imperii virtus elangueret. Unde, quod antecessores sui multis iam annis parturierant, ipse uno fœtu e-dito, in lucem protulit. Porro hanc rem tentauit prior Nicolaus primus: sed ad effectum, ut ipsi lo-quuntur, non perduxit. Atqui hic perpende, pie le-ctor, quomodo per hoc decretum, ius Imperatori-bus omne, quod in pontificem atque urbem Roma-nam habuere, fit ademptum. Ita ut in hoc fœtu, pontifices magno cum triumpho, superiores ac victores euaserint. Videbis eos adhuc maiora ten-tare, & non cessare, donec sese extulerint super omne quod dicitur Deus, aut quod colitur 2. Thes. 2. ut dicant eius adoratores: Quis similis bestiæ aut quis poterit pugnare cum eâ? Apoc.13. Sed nec diu superstes mansit hic Hadrianus post depressam authoritatem Cæsaream. Anno enim Domini 886. ex hac vita repente migravit, cum magnam de ipsa sobolem concepissent papicolæ.
units.tr: Hadrian the Third, a Roman by birth, was of such boldness and haughtiness that, as soon as he had obtained the papacy, he made a decree that in choosing a pope the authority of the emperor should no longer be awaited, but that the votes of the clergy and people should always be free in Rome. At that time the emperor was waging war against the Normans, enemies of piety. Thus, says Crantzius, the popes and the wickedness of the Romans dared to despise their emperors, while the strength of the empire was failing. Hence what his predecessors had been labouring under for many years, he alone brought forth into the light, having produced one offspring. Earlier, Nicholas the First had attempted this matter, but he did not bring it to fulfilment, as they themselves put it. Yet here, pious reader, consider how by this decree every right that the emperors had over the pope and the city of Rome was taken away. So in this offspring the popes emerged as superior and victors, with great triumph. You will see them attempting still greater things, and not ceasing until they have exalted themselves above everything that is called God or is worshipped (2 Thess. 2), so that their worshippers may say: Who is like the beast, or who can make war with it? (Rev. 13). But this Hadrian did not remain alive for long after the Caesarean authority had been suppressed. For in the year of our Lord 886 he suddenly departed from this life, after the papist worshippers had conceived a great brood from him.
47. Stephen the Fifth.

units.la: STephanus quintus, patria quoque Romanus, eo tempore papatum iniit, quo Gallia Normannis, Anglia Dacis, Pannonia Hunnis, & Italia Saracenis collustabantur. Vixit multa perturbatione & animi tædio, toto Papatus sui tempore (pœ-na certe tantæ temeritati debita) quoniam Itali inquieta fuit, & Romani non satis parebant. Fecit tamen quod potuit, ut sua synagoga, scortum impudens, in malis de die in diem proficeret, & ut eius iuribus nihil detraheretur. Nam ut Gratia-nus scribit, dist. 19. Erimuero[?]. Statuta Romana Ecclesiæ omnibus necessario obseruanda, primum esse decreuit. Idem pontifex (inquit) iudicium can-dentis ferri & feruentis aquæ (quod tum in usu e-rat) Christianis inhibuit. cau.2.q.4. Permisit hic D. Martini corpus in Gallia, tempore incursionis Normannorum, à Turonis Altissiodorum depor-tari, litigantibus utrinq; propter oblationes mo-nachis.
