Celebratur etiam ab Antonino papistico scriptore, ab unico tantum consilio, quod Mogun-tinensi archiepiscopo dederit. Quomodo uideli-cet cum illis agendum sit parentibus, qui proles inscij[?] in lectum sumptas, aut suffocant, aut oppressione necant. Post haec & similia, anno Domini 892[?]. animam edidit.
units.tr: Stephen the Fifth, also a Roman by birth, entered the papacy at a time when Gaul was being ravaged by the Normans, England by the Danes, Pannonia by the Huns, and Italy by the Saracens. He lived throughout the whole time of his papacy in great disturbance and weariness of mind (certainly a punishment due to such recklessness), since Italy was restless and the Romans did not sufficiently obey him. Nevertheless he did what he could, so that his synagogue, a shameless harlot, might advance from day to day in evils, and that nothing might be taken from its rights. For, as Gratian writes, dist. 19, he first decreed that the statutes of the Roman Church were to be observed by all of necessity. The same pope (he says) forbade Christians the trial by cold iron and boiling water, which was then in use (C. 2, q. 4). He also permitted the body of St Martin to be carried in Gaul, at the time of the Norman incursion, from Tours to Auxerre, the parties on both sides contending over the offerings for the monks. He is also praised by the papist writer Antoninus, on the strength of a single piece of advice which he gave to the archbishop of Mainz: namely, how those parents must be dealt with who, when unwanted children have been placed in bed, either smother them or kill them by pressing them down. After these and similar things, he gave up his soul in the year of our Lord 892.
48. FORMOSUS the first.

units.la: Formosus primus, etiam Romanus, cum Portu-ensis episcopus esset, Ioannis noni seueritatem meritus, urbem dimisit, quod conscius crederetur vinculorum eiusdem Ioannis. Nomen (inquit Cranzius) assumptum in pontificatu, insinuat hominem insolentem. Episcopatum & urbem abiurauit: ergo Formosus in profanum ordinem actus (quo sciri datur, ex Episcopo laicum fieri posse, charactere illo indelebili non obstante) sed sequens Marinus[?] illum pro pecuniis, a iuramento Ioanni præ-stito, absoluit ac restituit. Post Stephani prædicti mortem, Formosus, muneribus datis, papatum est consecutus, sed non sine grandi dissensione, Sergio quodam diacono eandem sedem ambiente. Pro cuius remedio Arnulphum Carlomanni fili-um, in urbem accitum, Imperatorem fecit: qui pro tali officio gratias relaturus, præcipuos eius adversarios capite truncauit. Nihil operis aut constitutionis Formosus fecit, nisi quod basilicam Petri, leui (ut Platina scribit) pictura exornauit. Papa tum vero in sextum annum pertraxit, & anno Domini 896. mundum deseruit: demumq; à Sergio tertio proiectum est eius cadaver in Tiberim.
units.tr: Formosus the first, also a Roman, when he was bishop of Porto, earned the severity of John the ninth and left the city, because he was thought to be privy to John's imprisonment. The name he took on in the papacy (says Cranzius) indicates an insolent man. He abjured the bishopric and the city; so Formosus was driven into the profane order (by which it is made known that a bishop can become a layman, the indelible character notwithstanding). But Marinus, who followed, absolved him from the oath he had sworn to John, for money, and restored him. After the death of the aforementioned Stephen, Formosus, having given bribes, obtained the papacy, but not without great dissension, since a certain deacon Sergius was also seeking the same see. To remedy this, he summoned Arnulf, son of Carloman, into the city and made him Emperor; who, about to repay him for such an office, beheaded his chief adversaries. Formosus did nothing of note in works or ordinances, except that he adorned the basilica of Peter with a crude painting (as Platina writes). The pope then dragged on into his sixth year, and in the year of the Lord 896 he left the world; and afterwards his corpse was thrown into the Tiber by Sergius the third.
49. BONIFACE the sixth.

units.la: Bonifacius sextus, patria Thuscus, in demortui Formosi locum suffectus, peractis[?] de more cæremoniis, paucis diebus præfuit in papatu. Nihil igitur magni, in tam angusta temporis brevitate, in illo Babylonicæ meretricis regno efficere potuit: nec cuius effet factionis, in tanta Cardinalium ac Romanæ multitudinis divisione offendere. Tantum enim 25. diebus in papatu vixisse dicitur: sola electione pacifica memorandus (inquit Valerius Anselmus) & vitæ brevitate felix. Corruptum atq; confusum illud seculum, corruptamq; & confusam historiam, corruptus hic pontifex reliquit: eodem anno mortuus, quo prædictus Formosus.
units.tr: Boniface the sixth, a Tuscan by birth, was installed in the place of the dead Formosus, and after the customary ceremonies he presided over the papacy for a few days. In such a short span of time he could therefore achieve nothing great in that kingdom of the Babylonian harlot, nor could he give offence by which faction he belonged to, amid such a great division of the cardinals and the Roman multitude. For he is said to have lived only 25 days in the papacy: memorable only for his peaceful election (says Valerius Anselmus) and fortunate in the brevity of his life. This corrupt pontiff left behind that corrupt and confused age and a corrupt and confused history; he died in the same year as the aforementioned Formosus.
50. STEPHEN the sixth.

units.la: Stephanus sextus, patria Romanus, papalem gloriam post Bonifacium adeptus, tanto odio Formosi nomen persecutus est, ut statim eius decreta abrogaverit, acres gestas resciderit. Neq; ipsum beneficiorum memoria, quae in illum Formosus contulerat, dum Anagniae episcopum creasset, à diro incepto revocare potuit. Sed quia ab eodem antea, quo minus optata hac sede potiretur, ac scorta nutriret, impeditus fuerat: tanta in mortuum quoq; rabie defeuijt, ut habita synodo, eius e tumulo corpus tractum, pontificali habitu spoliatum, indutumq; (ut uocant) seculari, sepulturæ laicorum mandauerit, abscissis ante duobus dextræ manus digitis, & in Tiberim proiectis. Exemplum hoc longe omnium immanissimum erat, & tyran-nis hæc plusquam Neronica. Post unum uero annum papalis functionis, anno Domini 897. carnem & ille exuit.
units.tr: Stephen the sixth, a Roman by birth, obtained the papal glory after Boniface, and pursued the name of Formosus with such hatred that at once he annulled his decrees and rescinded his acts. Nor could the memory of the benefices that Formosus had conferred on him, when he had made him bishop of Anagni, call him back from his dreadful undertaking. But since he had earlier been prevented by Formosus from gaining this coveted see, and from supporting prostitutes, he raged so fiercely even against the dead man that, after holding a synod, he had the body dragged from its tomb, stripped of its pontifical vestments, clothed in what they call secular dress, and handed over to burial among laymen, after two fingers of its right hand had first been cut off and thrown into the Tiber. This example was by far the most savage of all, and this was more than Neronian tyranny. But after one year only of papal office, in the year of the Lord 897, he too put off the flesh.
§1[?]. ROMANUS the first.

units.la: Romanus primus, nomine ac patria Romanus (sunt tamen qui Hispanum fuisse tradant) in hac pestilentiæ cathedra succedens, nihil in papatu memoria dignum gessit. Cum tamen Formosi partibus fuisset, illius causam approbauit: Stephani uero prædecessoris decreta & acta statim improbauit ac sustulit. Atq; ultra fortasis processisset in eo negotio, si uita fuisset illi longior: ad declarandam suam factionem seu sectam, quibus tunc turpissime pontifices laborant. Sed hominem schismaticum, qui scandala scandalis addidit, non permisit Dominus diutius uiuere. Nam post tertium mensem initi pontificatus, anno Domini 898. de-moriebatur.
units.tr: Romanus the first, a Roman in name and birth (yet there are those who hand down that he was a Spaniard), succeeding in this seat of pestilence, did nothing worthy of memory in the papacy. Although he had been on the side of Formosus, he approved his cause; but he at once disapproved of and annulled the decrees and acts of his predecessor Stephen. And perhaps he would have gone further in that business, if his life had been longer: to declare his faction or sect, with which the pontiffs of that time were most shamefully afflicted. But the Lord did not permit this schismatic man, who added scandals to scandals, to live longer. For after the third month of his pontificate, in the year of the Lord 898, he died.
52. THEODORE the second.

units.la: Theodorus secundus, & ipse Romanus in papatu mox constitutus, prædicti Romani vestigijs inhæsit, nihilo melior suis antecessoribus factus. De isto quoque propter temporis brevitatem, in tali horribili functione, nihil à scriptoribus traditur, nisi quòd creatus pontifex (ut Stella Venetus scribit) in seditiosorum pontificum vijs & ipse ambu-lauerit. Qui nulla virtute præditus, postposito Dei timore & honore, Formosi facta restituit, eiusq; sectatores in precio plurimum habuit. Sed non potuit infra tam paucos dies edere multa. Vicesimo nanq; suscepti papatus die, anno Domini 899. vitæ suæ finem miser accepit[?].
units.tr: Theodore the second, also a Roman, was set up in the papacy soon after, and clung to the footsteps of the aforementioned Romanus, made no better than his predecessors. Nothing is handed down by the writers about him either, on account of the brevity of his time in such a dreadful office, except that, once made pontiff (as Stella the Venetian writes), he himself walked in the ways of the seditious pontiffs. Endowed with no virtue, and with the fear and honour of God set aside, he restored the acts of Formosus and held his followers in the highest esteem. But he could not accomplish much in so few days. For on the twentieth day of his undertaken papacy, in the year of the Lord 899, he met the end of his wretched life.
53. JOHN the tenth.

units.la: Ioannes decimus, patria Romanus, Theodoro successit: qui pontificatus sui tempore, seditiones propemodum sopitas resuscitauit, ac res turbatas exulcerauit magis. Causam Formosi (inquit Barnus) in integrum restituere volens Ioannes, repugnante maxima Romani populi parte, dissidium ingens excitauit. Quod cum videret in apertum bellum euasurum, contulit se Rauennam. Coactaq; ibidem 74. Episcoporum synodo, omnia eiusdem Formosi decreta ad plenum restituit. Stephani vero sexti acta, coram omnibus damnauit, quod tantum in eius mortuum cadauer fecisset contumeliam: & omnia quae ex ipsius synodo contra Formosum erant scripta, combusit. Sunt qui refe-rant, Eudonem Francorum regem cum archiepis-copis Galliae, huic interfuisse synodo. Sed ne Ioan-nes ultra procederet, vita etiam breuis effecit. Se-cundo enim pontificatus sui anno, à Christi scilicet incarnatione 901. mortuus, successori reliquit lo-cum.
units.tr: John the tenth, a Roman by birth, succeeded Theodore; during his pontificate he revived the seditions that were almost quelled and inflamed the troubled affairs even more. Wishing to restore the cause of Formosus to its former state (says Barnes), John stirred up a huge quarrel, the greater part of the Roman people resisting. When he saw that it would break out into open war, he betook himself to Ravenna. And there, a synod of 74 bishops having been gathered, he fully restored all the decrees of this same Formosus. But the acts of Stephen the sixth he condemned in the presence of all, because he had done such an insult to his dead corpse; and he burned all the writings against Formosus that had come from that synod of his. Some report that Eudes, king of the Franks, with the archbishops of Gaul, took part in this synod. But a brief life also prevented John from going further; for in the second year of his pontificate, in the year 901 from the incarnation of Christ, he died and left his place to a successor.
54. Benedict IV.

units.la: Benedictus quartus, etiam Romanus, in hac ma-ximorum scelerum sede collocatus, nihil ponti-fice dignum, in tantis tumultibus ac rerum turbi-nibus fecisse scribitur. Acciderat illi aetati (inquit Stella) quod omnis uirtus, tam in capite (Papam intelligit, qui Apoc.17.ex septem Bestiae capitibus unum est) quàm in membris, ex hominum ignavia consumpta fuerit. Et Platina: Vbi cum ipsis opinibus, lasciuire cœpit Ecclesia, nullo principe clericorum flagitia coercente, peccandi mox licentia nobis haec monstra ac portenta peperit, à quibus ambitione & largitione haec sedes occupatur. Obiit Benedictus anno Domini 904. statim post tertium sui pontificatus annum.
units.tr: Benedict IV, also a Roman, placed in this seat of the greatest crimes, is recorded to have done nothing worthy of a pontiff amid such great tumults and upheavals. That age, says Stella, had come to the point where all virtue was consumed by the sloth of men, both in the head (he means the Pope, who is one of the seven heads of the Beast in Apoc. 17) and in the members. And Platina: when the Church began to run wild along with the opinions themselves, and no prince of the clergy restrained the crimes, the license to sin soon brought forth these monsters and portents to us, by whom this see is occupied through ambition and bribery. Benedict died in the year of the Lord 904, straight after the third year of his pontificate.
55. Leo V.

units.la: Leo quintus, Antonino teste, patria Aretinus fuit, qui pontificatum adeptus, à Christophoro quādam presbytero, suo domestico, Papatus fastigium ambiente, quem domi nutriuerat, manu uiolenta apprehendebatur, & in carcerem coniiciebatur. Quod quidem (ut inquit Platina) non poterat fieri sine magna seditione, & multorum interitu: tam ardenter sunt sanctissimi patres, illius meretriciae sedis cupidi. Quantae quoque authori-tatis papatus ille tum esset, regnantibus scortis, ut mox dicetur, ex hoc uel maxime sciri poterit, quòd à uiro priuato, tam breui momento, quadragesimo scilicet die, fit occupatus. Videns autem Leo, honore se spoliatu, et à suo familiari, cui multa contulerat beneficia, animi dolore paulo post interijt.
units.tr: Leo V, according to Antoninus, was a native of Arezzo. When he had obtained the papacy, he was seized by violent hands and thrown into prison by Christopher, a certain presbyter, his household servant, whom he had reared at home and who coveted the summit of the papacy. As Platina says, this could not be done without great sedition and the death of many, so eagerly were those "most holy fathers" desirous of that harlot's see. How great the authority of that papacy then was, while harlots reigned, as will soon be told, can be known chiefly from this: it was seized by a private man in so brief a moment, namely in forty days. Leo, seeing himself stripped of honour and betrayed by his own familiar, to whom he had given many benefits, died of grief of mind a little later.
56. Christopher I.

units.la: Christophorus primus, cuius patria atq; cognomentum ob ignobilitatem ignorantur, deiecto Leone, ut iam dictum est, scortis adminiculatibus, papatum uiolenter inuasit. Sed quia malis artibus atq; immani scelere sedem illam acquisiuerat, per Sergium quendam Marozīæ splendidæ meretriciæ mafium, eandē uehementer affectante, turpiter ipsam & ille am'fit[?]. Ita mensurā (inquit Ioannes Stella) quam Leoni domino suo mensus fuerat, & ipse recepit. Quia septimo mense papatu deiectus, monasticam vitam (unicum miserorum refugium) obire cogebatur. Et non multo post, per dictum Sergium successorem suum, e monasterio extra-ctus, atque in arctissimum carcerem coniectus, anno Domini 905. in magna miseria tandem vitae cursum compleuit.
units.tr: Christopher I, whose native place and surname are unknown because of his obscurity, after Leo had been cast down, as has already been said, violently seized the papacy with the support of harlots. But because he had gained that seat by wicked arts and monstrous crime, he himself was shamefully deprived of it by Sergius, a certain son of the splendid harlot Marozia, who was eagerly coveting it. "So the measure which he had meted out to his lord Leo," says John Stella, "he himself also received." For in the seventh month, deposed from the papacy, he was compelled to enter the monastic life, the one refuge of the wretched. Not long after, through that same Sergius, his successor, he was dragged from the monastery, thrown into a very narrow prison, and in the year of the Lord 905 finished his course of life in great misery.
57. Sergius III.

units.la: Sergius tertius, natione Romanus, dum esset solum diaconus, ad pontificatum aspiras, una cum Formoso, in quodam Romanorum tumultu electus fuit, sed repulsam tunc passus, in Galliam aufugit. Nunc vero occasionem nactus, Caroli Simplicis, Francorum regis, & Adelberti Thuscorum Marchionis auxilio, iterum latenter in urbem redijt. Christophorum ille, ut dictum est, sede deiectus, cæpit, incarcerauit: ac papalem cathedram violenter[?] invasit. Caeterum in abominationis sede collocatus, tyrannide Antiochum exprimens, prae-dicti Formosi cadaver, post octo annos à sepultura denuò è terra extrahi fecit, & sedi papali impositum, capitali supplicio, tanquam viveret, affecit. Tres quoque digitos, ex altera mutilatione relictos, amputauit: & corpus ipsum, cum his omnibus, in Tiberim proiici iussit, tanquam communi Christianorum hominum sepultura indignum. Ne-que hanc quidem ignominiam homini mortuo in-tulisse tulisse contentus, omnia eius acta exprobravit, irritavit, damnauit[?], ita ut tunc denuo ad eorum ordines necesse fuerit illos admittere, quos ipse vi-vus, sacerdotali officio dignos censuerat: compu-litaq; Romanos timore regis Galliae, haec omnia confirmare & ipsis subscribere. Hic Sergius Ecclesiam Lateranensem, Stephani sexti tempore fere collapsam, instaurauit: & candelas in D. Mariae purificatione ferendas ordinauit. Ex impudentissima meretrice Marozia, nothum, Joannem 12. papam, spurcissimus adulter genuit, ut habet Liutprandus Ticinensis, lib 3 cap.12. de imperatorum gestis: & alia miracula cum scortis & lenonibus in ipso pa-patu fecit. Quo tandem anno Domini 913. morien-tes, faces in aere discurrentes, magni prodigii loco visae.
units.tr: Sergius III, a Roman by nation, while he was still only a deacon, aspired to the papacy. He was elected along with Formosus in a certain tumult of the Romans, but then suffered rejection and fled into Gaul. Now, having got his opportunity with the help of Charles the Simple, king of the Franks, and Adalbert, Marquis of Tuscany, he slipped back into the city secretly. Christopher, as has been said, he deposed from the see, seized, and imprisoned, and he violently invaded the papal chair. Moreover, placed in this seat of abomination and imitating Antiochus in tyranny, he had the corpse of the aforesaid Formosus, eight years after its burial, dug up again from the earth, placed on the papal seat, and subjected it to capital punishment as if it were alive. He also cut off the three fingers left from the earlier mutilation, and ordered the body itself, with all these parts, thrown into the Tiber, as unworthy of common Christian burial. Not content with inflicting this disgrace on a dead man, he reviled and annulled all his acts and condemned them, so that afterwards it was again necessary to admit to their orders those whom he himself, while alive, had judged fit for the priestly office. He also compelled the Romans, through fear of the king of France, to confirm all these things and to subscribe to them. This Sergius restored the Lateran church, which had nearly collapsed in the time of Stephen VI, and he ordained that candles be carried at the Purification of the Blessed Mary. By the most shameless harlot Marozia he begot an illegitimate son, John XII, a most filthy adulterer, as Liutprand of Pavia has it in book 3, chapter 12, on the deeds of the emperors. And he performed other wonders with harlots and pimps in the papacy itself. At last, in the year of the Lord 913, when they died, torches running about in the air were seen as a great portent.
58. Anastasius III.

units.la: ANastasius tertius, patria Romanus, post Ser-gij mortem, peractis de more caeremoniis: omnem, ut Apocalypsis habet, prioris Bestiae potestatem, in eo regno perditionis accepit. De illo tamen historici tradunt, quod in pontificatu, nec boni nec mali quicquam praestiterit: & eo ipso, plu-ribus aliis redditur ab eis commendabilior. Sed cū ipsis est suam ex eo facto recepturus mercedem: qui aliis laborantibus, tota die stabat ociosi, Matth.
units.tr: Anastasius III, a Roman by birth, after the death of Sergius, with the customary ceremonies performed, received, as the Apocalypse has it, all the power of the former Beast in that kingdom of perdition. Yet historians hand down that in the papacy he achieved neither good nor evil, and by that very fact he is rendered more commendable than many others by them. But with them he will receive his wage for that very thing, like those who stood idle all day while others laboured, Matth. 20, when the lord of the vineyard is about to render to each according to his works.

units.la: 20. 20. quum uinea dominus unicuiq; redditurus fit iu- xta opera sua. Huius tempore, Formosi pontificis corpus, in Tiberis aqua à piscatoribus repertum scriptores referunt: & quòd fit, dum celebrare- tur funus in D. Petri basilica, ab imaginibus (idolum ab idolis) venerabiliter salutatum. Quod est impudens papistarum commentum, et insignis Dei blasphemia, licet in tanta hominum caecitate, ac diuinae ueritatis ignorantia, Diabolus ille statuae mouere coram idololatris potuit, qui olim per illas fuerit locutus. Anastasius autem anno Domini 915. communi fato decubuit.
units.tr: In his time, writers report, the body of Pope Formosus was found by fishermen in the waters of the Tiber, and that, while the funeral was being celebrated in the basilica of St Peter, it was reverently greeted by the images (an idol by idols). This is an impudent fiction of the Papists and a notable blasphemy against God. Yet in such blindness of men and ignorance of divine truth, it is no wonder that that devil could move statues before idolaters, he who once spoke through them. Anastasius died in the year of the Lord 915, by the common fate.
59. Lando the First.

units.la: LAndo primus, patria etiam Romanus, prolificus pontifex, à Petro Præmonstratensi, longè ante te initum papatum, Ioannem undecimum, nefario adulterio generasse scribitur. Huius namq; uita, ipso Platina teste, tam obscura fuit, ut etiam sint, qui inter pontifices illum non numerent: potissi- mum Vincentius ille Beluacensis historicus. Inter meretrices (ut appáret) maiorem uitæ suæ partem, unctorum eius ætatis more cœlibum, consumpsit: consumptus & ille tum demum ab ipsis anno Domini 916. quum non septem mensibus papatum tenuisset. Theodora enim, Romanæ urbis tum gubernatrix ac scortum inuerecundissimum,non poterat suo amatore (huius papæ filiō notho) Ioanne Archiepiscopo Rauennate, diutius carere. Ducentorum milliariorum interpositio-ne (ut Liuthprandus habet) à Roma Rauenna distabat: qua, rarissimo potita concubitu, ea fede re-licta, Romanum papatum, inuitis patribus, ufur-pare illum coegit. Tam periti erant in eo artifi-cio, infulati heroes, magnæ meretricis aluni. Quaeritur nunc (inquit Funccius) quis horum pontifi-cum, qui omnes sanctissimi sunt dicti, & capita universalis Ecclesiæ appellati, à uero aberrauit? Respondete mihi, uos defensores pontificiæ se-dis.
units.tr: Lando the First, also a Roman by birth and a prolific pontiff, is recorded by Peter the Premonstratensian, writing long before the papacy you now hold, to have fathered John XI by a wicked adultery. For his life, as Platina himself testifies, was so obscure that some do not count him among the popes, above all that Vincent of Beauvais, the historian. He spent most of his life, as it seems, among prostitutes, as was the custom of the unmarried anointed men of that age. He too was finally consumed by them in the year 916, after holding the papacy for less than seven months. For Theodora, then ruler of the city of Rome and a most shameless whore, could not do without her lover, John, archbishop of Ravenna, the bastard son of this pope, for long. Ravenna was two hundred miles from Rome (as Liutprand has it). Having enjoyed his rare embrace, she left that see behind and forced him, against the will of the fathers, to seize the Roman papacy. So skilled were these mitred heroes, nurslings of a great whore, in that trickery. Which of these popes, all called most holy and heads of the universal Church, has now strayed from the truth, asks Funccius? Answer me, you defenders of the papal see.
60. John the Eleventh.

units.la: Ioannes undecimus, patria atq; cognomento Rauennas, Papæ prædecessoris Landonis, ex adulterio filius, ut Petrus Præmonstratensis refert, papatum quasi hæreditario iure, sed per scortationes, obtinuit. Liuthprandus enim Ticinensis, in 2. lib. & cap. 13. de Imperatoribus, sic scribit: Theodora scortum impudens, & Romanæ urbis domina, Veneris calore succensa, tam vehementer in huius Ioannis Romam aduenientis, speciei decorem exarsit, ut eum non solum secum scortari voluerit, verum etiam compulerit. Quem postea ob mutuas scortationes, Bononiensem episcopum primò, Rauenæ archiepiscopum secundò, & tertiò (ut sic insano eius amore commodius frueretur) Romanum Papam fecit. Ita erat his diebus, sanctissima mater Ecclesia Romana, meretrici subiecta, ut per illam tota regeretur: sitq; meretrix facta iuxta propheticum scriptum, Apoc.17. Ioannes iste spiritus militares induens, militem potius quàm Episcopum se esse ostendit: ut qui Saracenos, Calabriam, Apuliam, & Italiam deuastantes, sumptis armis, ac multis eorum occisis, his terris expulerit. De cuius fine iterum Liuthprandus, lib.3. cap. 12. sic loquitur: Guido interea, Thusciæ provinciæ Marchio, cum Marozia uxore (prædi-ctæ Theodoræ filia) de Ioannis Papæ deiectione coepit vehementer tractare. Habebat Guido milites multos, Romæ congregatos, qui in Lateranensi palatio anno Domini 928. comprehendentes Papam, custodiæ manciparunt, & cervicale super os eius iniecto, suffocatum illum miserrimè occiderunt. Quo mortuo, prædictum Marozie filium, Ioannem 12. quem ex Sergio Papa meretrix ipsa genuerat, Papam constituerunt. Sic meretricis matris Theodoræ amasium, meretrix Marozia filia, pro filio spurio sublimando, per mariti Guidonis milites peremit. Sed quia Romani, clerus scilicet ac populus, in eius electionem non consenserant, eodem anno est iterum depositus, & in ma-ximo ciuium tumultu, Leo sextus in eius locum suf-sectus. Et hic ille Ioannes est, quem ui surrogatum, ac loco mox deiectum, Carsulanus, Platina, Stel-la, ac alij scriptores commemorant: ignorantes ue-ram eius temporis historiam, à Liuthprando de-scriptam. Cuius ignoratio magnam confusionem parit. Nam aliqui scriptores, hos duos Ioannes pro uno Ioanne capiunt, aliqui unum eorum pro altero assumunt, & aliqui unum tertium eliciunt ex ac-tis principum eius temporis, confusum chaos faci-entes.
units.tr: John XI, a Ravennese by birth and by surname, son by adultery of the preceding pope Lando, as Peter the Premonstratensian reports, obtained the papacy as if by hereditary right, but through whoring. For Liutprand of Ticino, in book 2, chapter 13, On the Emperors, writes thus: Theodora, a shameless whore and mistress of the city of Rome, burning with the heat of Venus, was so vehemently inflamed by the beauty of this John, when he came to Rome, that she wanted him not only to whore with her but also compelled him to do so. Afterwards, because of their mutual whoring, she made him bishop of Bologna first, archbishop of Ravenna second, and third (so that she might enjoy his mad love more conveniently) pope of Rome. Thus in those days the most holy mother Church of Rome was subject to a whore, and was governed entirely through her, and she became a whore according to the prophetic writing, Rev. 17. This John, putting on military spirits, showed himself to be a soldier rather than a bishop: when the Saracens were laying waste Calabria, Apulia and Italy, he took up arms, killed many of them, and drove them from these lands. Concerning his end, Liutprand again speaks thus, in book 3, chapter 12: Meanwhile Guido, marquis of the province of Tuscany, with his wife Marozia (daughter of the aforesaid Theodora), began vigorously to plan the deposition of Pope John. Guido had many soldiers gathered at Rome, who in the year 928, in the Lateran palace, seized the pope, put him in custody, and, pressing a pillow over his face, suffocated him most cruelly. When he was dead, they set up as pope the aforesaid son of Marozia, John XII, whom the whore herself had borne by Pope Sergius. Thus the whore Marozia, to raise her bastard son, had her husband Guido's soldiers kill the lover of her mother, the whore Theodora. But because the Romans, that is the clergy and people, had not agreed to his election, he was deposed again the same year, and amid the greatest tumult of the citizens, Leo VI was substituted in his place. And this is the John whom Carsulanus, Platina, Stella and other writers record as having been put in by force and soon deposed from his place, ignorant of the true history of that time, as described by Liutprand. Their ignorance produces great confusion. For some writers take these two Johns for one John, some take one of them for the other, and some draw a third from the acts of the princes of that time, making a confused chaos.
61. Leo the Sixth.

units.la: LEo sextus, patria Romanus, deiecto (ut suprà dictum est) Ioanne 12. Sergij pontificis & Ma-rozia meretricis filio notho, cleri ac populi Ro-mani suffragijs in maximo tumultu, papalem se-dem ascendit. De isto scribunt Paparum adulato-res, quòd Italiam pacauerit, lites composuerit, ex-ternos hostes excluserit, & in melius omnia re-formauerit. Sed incredibilia haec sunt cordatis ho-minibus. In tanta temporis breuitate (inquit Ioan-nes Funccius) nihil scitu dignum fecit, nisi quòd pa-cis & concordiae studiosum fuisse tradunt. Quia quae rebat fortassis in sabelis mollicie, Apoc.2. ui-tam amoenam ducere, at superuenit interitus quem ignos[?] ignorabat. Statim post septimum sui regiminis men-sem, anno Domini 930. veneno sublatus a Marozia sertur, ut spurio locum daret.
units.tr: Leo VI, a Roman by birth, after John XII, the illegitimate son of Pope Sergius and the whore Marozia, had been deposed (as said above), ascended the papal see by the votes of the clergy and people of Rome amid the greatest tumult. Flatterers of the popes write of him that he pacified Italy, settled quarrels, drove out foreign enemies, and reformed everything for the better. But these things are incredible to sensible men. In so short a time, says John Funccius, he did nothing worth knowing, unless they report that he was zealous for peace and concord. Perhaps, as he lived in the softness of his couch, he thought he was leading a pleasant life (cf. Rev. 2), but there came a destruction that he did not know. Within seven months of his reign, in the year 930, he is said to have been removed by poison at the hands of Marozia, so as to make room for her bastard.
62. Stephen the Seventh.

units.la: Stephanus septimus, patria quoq; Romanus, qui in rebus gestis Leoni prædecessori similis inveniatur: eo tempore papatum (ut pleriq; scribunt) ad-ministrauit, quo Hungari Alemaniam & Saxoniam depopulati sint. Ipse autem (inquit Crantzius) dum Italiæ prospicit, dum urbem Romanam componit, maiora meditatus, medio vitæ cursu subtra-hitur. Nam post duos annos imiti[?] pontificatus, cum in pace secura, ac libertate carnis, quiescere videretur, mundum habens in tenebris ignorantiæ ac magna Dei obliuione sibi obtemperantem, an-no Domini 932. vitam cum morte, per venenatum poculum (ut fertur) commutauit. Mirum est (teste eodem Crantzio) de tot paucorum men-sium pon-tificibus, non enim carebant hæc tempora confusa veneni suspicione.
units.tr: Stephen VII, also a Roman by birth, who is found in his deeds to be like his predecessor Leo, held the papacy (as most write) at the time when the Hungarians laid waste Germany and Saxony. He himself (says Crantz), while he looked after Italy and set the city of Rome in order, meditating greater things, was taken away in the middle course of his life. For after two years of his pontificate, when he seemed to rest in secure peace and freedom of the flesh, having a world obeying him in the darkness of ignorance and great forgetfulness of God, in the year 932 he exchanged life for death, by a poisoned cup (as it is said). Remarkable it is (on the testimony of the same Crantz) that of so many popes of a few months, these times were not free from suspicion of poison.
63. JOHN the Twelfth.

units.la: Ioannes duodecimus, natione Romanus, Sergij tertij Papæ ac Marozia famosæ meretricis (ut dictum est) ex horrido stupro filius, iterum post seditiones, Leone & Stephano sublatis, papatum in assuetis sordibus papaliter administrauit. Eo tempore Genuæ fons sanguinis largissimè effluxit, præmonstrans[?] breui affuturam Dei vindictā; sicut in effectu contigit, Aphricanis, Saracenis, & Hungaris omnia, trucidata etiam populi multitudine, diripientibus.
units.tr: John XII, a Roman by birth, son of Pope Sergius III and of the notorious prostitute Marozia (as has been said), born of a dreadful debauchery. After the seditions again, with Leo and Stephen removed, he administered the papacy in his customary filth, in the papal manner. At that time a fountain of blood flowed very copiously at Genoa, foreshadowing that God's vengeance would soon come. This came to pass in fact, as the Africans, Saracens and Hungarians plundered everything and also slaughtered a multitude of the people.

units.la: Sunt inter scriptores, ut dixi, qui ex hoc Ioanne duos faciunt: unum, qui Leonem & Stephanum præcessit, quem à pontificum albo secludunt, & hunc de quo nunc agimus, Stephano surrogatum, de quo nihil esse ab historicis scriptum referunt. Sunt & alij, qui ex hoc Roma-no & altero Rauennate, unum quoque constituant.
units.tr: There are among the writers, as I have said, some who make two Johns out of this John: one who preceded Leo and Stephen, whom they exclude from the list of popes, and this one, of whom we are now speaking, who was substituted for Stephen and about whom the historians report nothing written. There are also others who make one John out of this Roman and the other from Ravenna.

units.la: Ex quorum numero Platina, utrunque dicit esse Sergij pontificis filium. Valerius Anselmus scribit, unum eorum fuisse alterius fratrem, ex eiusdem Platinæ errore deceptus. Sunt etiam adhuc alij, qui illum à prædictis duobus separant, & omnino diuersum fuisse credant: dicentes esse scriptoribus ignotum, ac nihil fecisse memoria dignum. Sed ad Liuthprandum reuertamur, qui in lib 3 cap.12. de huius Ioannis matre sic scribit: Marozia scortum impudens, & Ioannis pontificis mater, post Guidonis mariti mortem, Hugonem eius fratrem, Italiæ regem, patria Burgundum, per nuncios inuitat ut ad se veniat, & ab ea Romam nobilissimam urbem sumat. Quod aliter fieri non posse scribit, nisi ipsam in uxorem accipiat. In cuius libidinem
units.tr: Among their number, Platina says that both were sons of Pope Sergius. Valerius Anselmus writes that one of them was the brother of the other, deceived by the same error of Platina. There are still others who separate him from the two mentioned and believe he was altogether a different man, saying that he is unknown to writers and did nothing worth remembering. But let us return to Liutprand, who in book 3, chapter 12, writes thus of this John's mother: "Marozia, shameless harlot and mother of Pope John, after the death of her husband Guido, invites by messengers Hugh, his brother, king of Italy and a Burgundian by birth, to come to her and take Rome, the most noble city, from her. She let it be known that this could not be done unless he took her as his wife." Liutprand inveighs against her lust thus:

units.la: Liuthprandus sic invebitur: Quid Veneris facibus compulsa, Marozia, sæuis? Coniugis ecce tui spectas tu suauia fratris, Nubere germanis satagens Herodia binis. Immemor aspiceris præcepti cæca Ioannis, Qui fratri vetuit, fratris violare maritam. Hæc tibi Moyseos non præstant carmina vatis, Qui fratri sobolem fratris de nomine iussit Edere, si primus nequeat sibi gignere natum. Nostra tuo peperisse viro te secula norunt. Respondes; scio, tu: Nihil hoc Venus ebria curat. Aduenit optatus, ceu bos tibi ductus ad aram Rex Hugo, Romanam potius commotus ad urbem. Quid iuvat o scelerata virum sic perdere magnū? Crimine dum tanto satagis regina videri, Amittis magnam Domino tu iudice Romam. Rex ergo, relicto longe exercitu, Romam ad-venit. Qui decenter a Romanis suscep-tus, in Ha-driani molem, seu castrum S. Angeli, fortissimam munitionem, ad meretricis Marozia thalamum declinavit. Cuius incesto concubitu dum esset po-titus, Romanos, quasi iam securus, despicere cœpit. Habuerat tunc Marozia filium Albericum, Ioannis pontificis fratrem: quem tamen ex Albe-rico Marchione genuerat. Qui dum matris hor-tatu, Hugoni aquam funderet, ubi manus ablueret, ab eo pro correctione, in faciem cæsus est, quod non moderate & prudenter id fecisset. Is vero, ut illatam sibi posset ulcisci iniuriam, congregatis in unum Romanus, eiusmodi eos sermone convenit: Romanæ urbis dignitas ad tantam est stultitiâ ducta, ut meretricum etiam imperio pareat. Quid enim fœdius, quidve turpius, quàm ut unius mulieris incestu, Romana civitas pereat? Romanorum aliquando servi Burgundiones Romanis imperent? Si meam priuigni fui faciem cecidit, quum præsertim novus habeatur hospes: quid vobis iam inveteratum, facturum creditis? An Burgundionum superbiam ignoratis? &c. Nec mora, his auditis, Hugonem regem omnes deserunt, atque eundem Albericum sibi dominum eligunt. Tanto igitur ter-rore coactus, Romanam urbem deseruit rex Hugo, atque ad suos, relicta Marozia confugit. Albericus ergo, cum Marozia matre, Romanæ urbis monarchiam solus tenuit, Ioanne eius fratre papatui præsidente. Qui post papalia facta, anno Domini 937. & quinto anno sui pontificatus, naturæ cessit, dum meretrix mater, Romæ tam regnum quàm Ecclesiam adhuc regeret.
units.tr: "Why, Marozia, driven by the torches of Venus, so cruelly? Behold, you gaze upon the kisses of your husband's brother, eager to marry two brothers like Herodias. Blind John, heedless of the precept, you are looked upon, who forbade a brother to violate his brother's wife. The verses of Moses' prophet do not favour you, who commanded that offspring be raised in a brother's name if the first could not beget a son for himself. The ages know that you bore children to your husband. You answer: I know it; but drunken Venus cares nothing for this. King Hugh has arrived, the one you desired, like an ox led to the altar for you, moved rather toward the Roman city. Why does it help, O wicked woman, to ruin so great a man? While by so great a crime you strive to seem a queen, you lose great Rome, the Lord being judge." Then the king, leaving his army far behind, came to Rome. Received fittingly by the Romans, he turned aside to the mole of Hadrian, or the castle of St Angelo, a very strong fortress, to the bed of the prostitute Marozia. While he was enjoying her incestuous embrace, he began, as if now secure, to despise the Romans. Marozia then had a son, Alberic, brother of Pope John, whom she had however borne to the Marquis Alberic. While he, at his mother's urging, was pouring water for Hugh to wash his hands, he was struck in the face by him as a correction, because he had not done it with moderation and prudence. Alberic, in order to avenge the injury done to him, gathered the Romans together and addressed them with such words: "The dignity of the Roman city has been brought to such folly that it obeys the command of harlots. For what is more foul, or more shameful, than that the Roman state should perish through the incest of one woman? Shall the Burgundians, slaves once of the Romans, now rule over the Romans? If he has struck the face of my stepson, since he is regarded as a new guest, what do you believe he will do to you, who are now long established? Or are you ignorant of the pride of the Burgundians? &c." Without delay, having heard this, all deserted King Hugh and chose this same Alberic as their lord. Under such terror King Hugh was compelled to abandon the city of Rome and fled to his people, leaving Marozia behind. Alberic therefore, together with his mother Marozia, held the sovereignty of the Roman city alone, with his brother John presiding over the papacy. Who, after his papal acts, in the year of the Lord 937 and the fifth year of his pontificate, yielded to nature, while his prostitute mother still ruled Rome, both kingdom and Church.
64. LEO the Seventh.

units.la: LEo septimus, patria Romanus, Ioanni succedens, assumpto papatu, cum suæ studeret quieti, nullis se rebus implicuit, sed remissus uir (ut insinuat Stella) nihil recordatione dignum post se reliquit. Eius tempore (ut Liutbprandus habet) praedictus rex Hugo, contempta uxore Berta, in tres concubinas prae ceteris, Bezolam, Rosam et Stephanam, turpissimo ardebat amore. Et illis tribus, ob artes impudicas et spurca lenocinia trium dearum nomina tribuit: Bezolam Venerem, Rozam Iunonem, et Stephanam Semelem appellans. Ex Bezola Bozonem genuit, quem in Placentinū episcopum ordinauit: ex Stephana Theobaldum Mediolanensis Ecclesiae archidiaconum, et ex Ro-sa alium magnum Ecclesiae praelatum, ac filiam pulcherrimam. E sole per plures dies, manare tum[?] sanguinem in Italia multi uiderunt, ut Maffeus scribit: et secuta est hominum mortalitas maxima. Quibus[?] Leo anno Domini 941, post tertium sui pontificatus annum, cum nihil boni fecisset.
units.tr: Leo VII, a Roman by birth, succeeding John, when he had assumed the papacy, devoted himself to his own quiet and involved himself in no affairs; a slack man (as Stella hints), he left nothing worth remembering after him. In his time (as Liutprand has it) the aforesaid King Hugh, scorning his wife Bertha, burned with the most shameful love for three concubines above the rest: Bezola, Rosa and Stephana. On account of their immodest arts and filthy procuring, he gave these three the names of goddesses, calling Bezola Venus, Rosa Juno, and Stephana Semele. By Bezola he begot Boso, whom he made bishop of Piacenza; by Stephana, Theobald, archdeacon of the Church of Milan; and by Rosa another great prelate of the Church, and a very beautiful daughter. Many saw blood flowing from the sun for several days in Italy, as Maffei writes, and there followed a very great mortality of men. In these times Leo, in the year of the Lord 941, after the third year of his pontificate, died, having done nothing good.
Stephen the Eighth.

units.la: Stephanus octauus, natione Germanus, hanc pestilentiae cathedram post Leonem suscepit: mirum tamen multis uidetur, quomodo id fieri potuerit, cū nullus ex Germania Imperator urgeret. Qui nihilominus accepto papatu, ita ciuilibus Romanorū seditionibus uexatus erat, ut nil memoriae dignum ab eo geri potuerit. In populari tumultu tam turpiter uulneratus erat, ac cicatricum defor-mitate signatus, ut puduerit eum postea in publi-cum prodire. Adeo sancti tunc temporis Papæ e-rant, ut eorum oues nulla sanctitatis aut beatitu-dinis ipsorum habita ratione, eos uulneribus assi-cerent. Huius tempore Guilla, Berengarij Italici mar-chionis uxor, presbyterulum capellanum, nomine dominicum, statura breuem ac deformem amauit. Qui cum nocte quadam, solito more, ad domini cu-bile in eius absentia accederet, canis latratu at morsu impeditus, capitur, nudatur, ac uirilibus pri-uatur: uocifferantibus illis qui ipsum castrabant, quod merito diligebatur à domina, cum arma pri-peia[?] illum portare constaret Liuthprandus, lib.5. cap. 15. Tales tunc multi erant papistici cæliba-tus custodes, at non donati eodem munere. Stepha-nus autem anno Domini 944. moriens, alteri reli-quit locum.
units.tr: Stephen VIII, a German by birth, took up this seat of pestilence after Leo. Yet it seems strange to many how this could happen, when no emperor from Germany was pressing for it. Although he had accepted the papacy, he was so harassed by the civil factions of the Romans that nothing worthy of memory was done by him. In a popular uprising he was so shamefully wounded, and marked with the disfigurement of scars, that he was later ashamed to appear in public. So holy were the popes of that time that their sheep, taking no account of their sanctity or blessedness, wounded them. In his time Guilla, the wife of Berengar, marquis of Italy, fell in love with a little priest and chaplain named Dominic, a man short and ill-favoured. One night, when he was going as usual to the lady's bed in her absence, he was held up by a dog's barking and biting, was seized, stripped, and deprived of his manhood, while those who castrated him shouted that he was rightly loved by the lady, since it was well known that he carried weapons. Liuthprandus, lib. 5. cap. 15. There were many such guardians of papistical celibacy at that time, but they were not given the same gift. Stephen died in the year of the Lord 944 and left his place to another.
66. MARTIN the Third.

units.la: MArtinus tertius, patria Romanus, post consue-tas cæremonias papatum adeptus, respexit ad officium, quod neglecta Euangelij functione, admul[?] torum perniciem, in magna superbia, tunc gerebat. Istum dicunt templa restaurasse lapidibus & lig-nis, sed non à superstitione seruasse: pauperes alu-isse[?] cibarijs, quæ cum uentre pereant, at non uti-uificit[?] vificis animarum pabulis: pietatem coluisse, sed in humanis traditiunculis, quae potius impietas est: ac mores reformasse, sed non in Dei verbo, ad verum eius cultum. Nam ad forenses causas, pro ventre ac marsupio, totum scribitur intuitum vertisse. Hu-ius anno primo, cometa mirae magnitudinis in Italia uidebatur: quem, teste Vrspergio, secuta est fames ualidissima. Rursum (inquit Masseus) sol[?] ter-ribilem se ostendit, quae res futuram Dei vindictam minabatur. Martinus anno Domini 947, adueniente fato, papatum ac vitam amisit.
units.tr: Martin III, a Roman by birth, obtained the papacy after the customary ceremonies. He turned his attention to the office which, with the function of the Gospel neglected, he then carried on to the ruin of many, in great pride. They say this man restored temples with stones and wood, but did not preserve them from superstition; that he fed the poor with food which perishes with the belly, but not with the living food of souls; that he cultivated piety, but in human traditions, which is rather impiety; and that he reformed morals, but not by God's word, toward his true worship. For it is written that he turned his whole attention to lawsuits in the courts, for the sake of his belly and purse. In the first year of his reign a comet of remarkable size appeared in Italy, and, according to Urspergensis, it was followed by a very severe famine. Again (says Masseus) the sun showed itself terrible, a thing which threatened future vengeance from God. Martin, when fate drew near, lost both the papacy and his life in the year of the Lord 947.
67. AGAPETUS the Second.

units.la: Agapetus secundus, natione et ipse Romanus, pontificatum Romae papaliter tenuit, in diebus praedicti Berengarii: qui ultimus eius nominis, prius capitatum in Italia post Hugonem gerebat. Monachorum plurimos, qui ociose viventes, in habitu monastico, seculi voluptates sequerentur, claustris suis eiecisse scribitur Berengarius ille. Quem cum intractabilem in his atq; aliis aeque spiritualibus cerneret, et non ad sui ac suorum nutum regnare, Othonem primum Germaniae regem in Italiam vocabat, et Romanorum regnum illi promisit, ut cum eo conflictaret: turbabatq; Sabellico teste, eius terra[?] statum. Ita dexteram maxillam percutienti, alteram praebuit Euangelicus pastor: nihilq; aliud, quod memoriæ proditum fit, in ipso papatu egit. Synodus istis temporibus, in Ingelheim habita est: sed quàm ob causam, nullus prodit. Tanta fuit eius seculi scriptorum negligentia. Agapetus anno Domini 954. in fata concessit.
units.tr: Agapetus II, also a Roman by birth, held the papacy at Rome in the manner of a pope, in the days of the aforesaid Berengar, who, the last of that name, had previously held the leadership in Italy after Hugh. It is written that this Berengar drove out of their cloisters many monks who, living idly in monastic dress, pursued the pleasures of the world. When Agapetus saw that Berengar was unmanageable in these matters and in others equally spiritual, and that he did not rule at his and his followers' nod, he called Otto I, king of Germany, into Italy and promised him the kingdom of the Romans, so that he might fight with Berengar. According to Sabellicus, this disturbed the state of his land. Thus the Gospel pastor, having the right cheek struck, offered the left as well, and in his papacy he did nothing else that has been handed down to memory. A synod was held at Ingelheim in those times, but for what reason no one records. So great was the carelessness of the writers of that age. Agapetus departed to his fate in the year of the Lord 954.
68. JOHN the thirteenth.

units.la: Ioannes decimustertius, etiam patria Romanus, de uia lata, Alberici supradicti MarozIæ nati, ac Romani principis filius, Octauianus antea dictus, patris fui partim muneribus partim minis, papatum occupabat. In eo namque officio, nempe paliter, sed generaliter & hiftrionice uixit ille: omni uoluptatum generi, scilicet stupris, adulteriis, incestis, libidinibus, uenationibus, ludicris, ludis, rapinis, incendiis, homicidiis, periuriis, aleis, armis, sacrilegiis, aliisque flagitiis, ab ipsa adolescentia incumbens. Ex suis Cardinalibus, quosdam oculis, quosdam linguis, quosdam digitis, manibus, naribus & testiculis priuauit. In ipsa enim synodo coram Cæsare Othone primo, hæc sibi erant obiecta crimina, ut author est Liuthprandus, in lib. 6. ferè per totum: quòd matutinas & horas non dixerit, quòd missam celebrans non communicauerit, quòd in equorum stabulo diaconos ordinauerit, quòd cum duabus sororibus incestum commiserit, quòd in alearum ludo dæmones in auxilio lia uocauerit, quòd pueros pro nummis aureis in episcopos constituerit, uirgines & peregrinas uio-lauerit, Lateranense palatium sacrum, lupanar ac prostibulum fecerit, quòd Stephanam patris sui concubinam, Raimeram uiduam, & Annam alium adhuc uiduam cum sua nepte constuprauerit, Benedictum patrem spiritualem luminibus priuauerit, uenationes publicas exercuerit, arma portauerit, incendia procurauerit, fores & fenestras nocte fregerit, diabolo uinum praebiberit, & se crucis signo nunquam muniuerit, cum multis aliis. Vnde ab ipso Cæsare consentientibus praelatis, depositus fuit, & Leo octauus in eius locum suffectus. Sed post eius decessum, mulieres meretrices illæ, cum quibus commercium habuerat, nobiles Romanos concitauerunt, promissis Ecclesiarum thesauris, ut Ioannem rursus in urbem susciperent. Quod & ipsi statim fecerunt, deiecto Leone, quem Cæsar creauerat. Constituit hic Papa, ut imperator Augustus, semper posthac a papa Romæ coronaretur. Dum uero quadam nocte extra Romam, anno decimo sui pontificatus, & anno Domini 964. cum cuiusdam strenui uiri uxore se oblectaret: ita est ab eo, pugione confossus, ut infra octiduum ex uulneribus moreretur, dignas scelera tissimæ uitæ das pœnas: ut et uitæ morib.exi tus iusto Dei iudicio responderet. Vnde Mantua-nus:
units.tr: John the thirteenth, also a Roman by birth, of the broad way, son of the aforesaid Alberic born of Marozia and a Roman prince, previously called Octavian, seized the papacy, partly by his father's gifts and partly by threats. In that office he lived in a merely nominal but general and theatrical manner, giving himself over from his earliest youth to every kind of pleasure: fornication, adulteries, incest, lusts, hunting, games, sports, robberies, arson, murders, perjuries, dice, arms, sacrilege, and other shameful deeds. Some of his cardinals he deprived of eyes, some of tongues, some of fingers, hands, noses and testicles. For in that very synod, held before the Emperor Otto I, these crimes were laid against him, as the author Liutprand reports, in book 6, nearly throughout: that he did not say matins and the hours; that when celebrating mass he did not communicate; that in the stable of horses he ordained deacons; that he committed incest with two sisters; that at the game of dice he called on demons for help; that he made boys bishops for gold coins; that he violated virgins and pilgrims; that he made the Lateran palace a sacred brothel and stew; that he debauched Stephana, his father's concubine, Raimera a widow, and Anna, another widow, together with his niece; that he deprived his spiritual father Benedict of his eyes; that he held public hunts, carried arms, procured arson, broke doors and windows at night, drank wine to the devil, and never fortified himself with the sign of the cross; with many other things. Whereupon, with the Emperor himself and the prelates agreeing, he was deposed, and Leo the eighth was installed in his place. But after his death, those harlots with whom he had had dealings stirred up the Roman nobles, with promises of the treasures of the churches, to take John back into the city. This they did at once, Leo whom the Emperor had created being thrown out. This Pope established that the emperor Augustus should always afterwards be crowned at Rome by the pope. Then indeed, on a certain night outside Rome, in the tenth year of his pontificate and in the year of the Lord 964, while he was amusing himself with the wife of a certain vigorous man, he was stabbed by him with a dagger, so that within eight days he died of his wounds, paying the worthy penalty for his most wicked life, so that the manner of his death answered to the just judgment of God on his life and conduct. Whence Mantuan:

units.la: Ad Romam conuerte oculos, luxumq; fluentem Aspice, & indignos Christi propagine mores. Tota in capreolos it uinea: tota comantem Effluit in syluam, foliis spargentibus umbram Pestiferam scegeti[?]: dulces neq; parturit uuas. Hos steriles ramos, nemus istud inutile, trunca.
units.tr: Turn your eyes to Rome and behold her flowing luxury, and manners unworthy of the offspring of Christ. The whole vineyard runs to wild tendrils; the whole runs out into the leafy wood, its foliage spreading a baneful shade; it bears no sweet grapes. Lop off these barren branches, this useless grove.

units.la: Ab hoc Satanæ uicario, Ioanne 12[?]. Dunstanus monachus necromanticus, Archiepiscopus Cantua-riensis in Anglia, confirmationem, ac metropolis suæ pallium Romæ suscepit, anno Domini 960. Multa etiam pecuniæ summa, ab eodem obtinuit diabolo, magnæ authoritatis diploma: quo posset ministrorum Ecclesiæ coniugia damnare, & adpellere[?] pistici cœlibatus uotum compellere, aut omni prop-sus Ecclesiastico proventu exuere. Vide Ioannem Capgrauum in Catalogo sanctorum Angliæ, ac Po-lydorum Vergilium, lib. 6. Anglicæ historiæ. Inde Satanicus impostor, Edgari regis authoritate fre-tus, anno sequente, adiunctis sibi in eadem commis-sione, Osuualdo Eboracensi, atq; Ethelwaldo Vuintoniensi Episcopis, & similium artium mona-chis, sacerdotes omnes (quos uasa fornicationum hypocrita uocabat) cum non uellent uxores re-linquere, à cathedralibus Ecclesijs una cum ipsis [?]uxoribus uiolenter exclusit. Et monachos sub castitatis fuco, cum omni Sodomia ac pederastia in illas introduxit: quas usque ad Henrici octaui tempora tenuerunt. Sed erant tunc multi, praecipue Scotus unus, qui horribilibus his monstris fortiter restiterunt. De quibus Baptista Mantuanus in primo Fastorum libro: Romulidum leges, quae sunt connubia contra, Esse malat quidam perhibent. Prudentia patrum Non satis aduertit, dicunt: quid ferre recusef, Quid ualeat natura pati. Ceruicibus, aiunt, Hoc insuaue iugum, nostris imponere Christus Noluit. Istud onus, quod adhuc quamplurima mona- secit, ab audaci, dicunt, pietate repertum. [?](strá Tutius esse uolunt, quae lex diuina sinebat Isse uia, ueterumque sequi uestigia patrum, Quorum uita fuit melior cum coniuge, quam nunc Nostra fit, exclusis thalamis, & coniugis usu.
units.tr: From this vicar of Satan, John the twelfth [?], Dunstan, a monk and necromancer, archbishop of Canterbury in England, received his confirmation and the pallium for his metropolis at Rome, in the year of the Lord 960. He also obtained from the same devil, for a large sum of money, a diploma of great authority by which he could condemn the marriages of the ministers of the Church, compel the vow of fleshly celibacy, or strip them of all ecclesiastical revenue. See John Capgrave in the Catalogue of the Saints of England, and Polydore Vergil, book 6 of the English history. Then the Satanic impostor, relying on the authority of King Edgar, the following year, with Oswald, bishop of York, and Ethelwold, bishop of Winchester, joined to him in the same commission, and with monks of similar arts, violently expelled from the cathedral churches, together with their wives, all the priests (whom this hypocrite called vessels of fornication) because they would not leave their wives. And he introduced monks into those churches under the cloak of chastity, with all sodomy and pederasty; these they held until the time of Henry the Eighth. But there were then many, especially one Scot, who strongly resisted these horrible monsters. Of them Baptista Mantuan, in the first book of the Fasti: Some say he prefers the laws of the sons of Romulus, which are against marriage. They say the wisdom of the fathers did not sufficiently consider what nature can refuse to bear and what it can endure. "On our necks," they say, "Christ did not wish to place this unpleasant yoke. This burden, which very many monks still bear, was devised by bold piety." They want it to be safer to follow the way which divine law allowed, and the footsteps of the ancient fathers, whose life with a wife was better than ours is now, with bedchambers shut and no use of a wife.
69. BENEDICT the fifth.

units.la: Benedictus quintus, natione Romanus, declinante cum suo exercitu Othone Imperatore, deturbatoque a Romanis Leone, ex diacono Cardinale ab amicis Ioannis, in odioso plebis tumultu, pontifex efficiebatur. Non tamen est passus Otho praedicti Leonis a se ordinati pontificis iniuriam: sed exercitu urbi iterum admoto, Romanos ciues multis tis[?] incommodis adegit, ut Benedictum in eius potestatem traderent, Leonem autem papatui denuò restituerent. Benedictum ergo post duos menses referatis portis, Imperatori dediderunt: & Leonem antea electum receperunt, folenniq; more in pontificiam sedem reposuerunt. Et cum Otho ipse in Germaniam rediret, Benedictum papali dignitate priuatum, Hamburgam ad suum cancellarium Adaldagum, archiepiscopum Hamburgensem, in exilium misit. Vbi anno Domini 964. ex animi mærore defunctus, in Ecclesia cathedrali sepultus iacet.
units.tr: Benedict the fifth, a Roman by birth, was made pope from deacon and cardinal, by the friends of John, amid the hated tumult of the people, while Emperor Otto was withdrawing with his army and Leo had been driven out by the Romans. Yet Otto did not suffer the wrong done to Leo, the pontiff he had ordained. Bringing the army back up to the city, he compelled the Roman citizens, by many hardships, to hand Benedict over into his power and to restore Leo to the papacy again. So after two months, with the gates unbarred, they surrendered Benedict to the Emperor, and they received Leo, who had been elected before, and placed him back on the papal see with the customary solemnity. And when Otto himself returned to Germany, he sent Benedict, deprived of papal dignity, into exile at Hamburg, to his chancellor Adaldag, archbishop of Hamburg. There, having died of grief of mind in the year of the Lord 964, he lies buried in the cathedral church.
70. LEO THE EIGHTH.

units.la: LEo octauus, ciuis Romanus, & Lateranensis Ecclesiae protoscriniarius, deposito ob vitae turpitudinem Ioanne, pontifex in illius locum ab Othone Imperatore constituebatur. Qui in papatu confirmatus, exauctoratus, ut dictum est, Benedicto, cum Romanorum nequitias non ignoraret, quòd minus, largitionibus, ac malis artibus, suos passim intruderent: Othonem ipsum coronauit, & universale Augustum declarauit. Postea omnem eligendi pontificis potestatem à Carolo Magno datam, ut Gratianus refert, à clero & populo Romano abstulit, ac synodali decreto in illum Othonem transtulit: quo vitarentur seditiones, quæ in electionibus exoriri solea[?] folebant. Otho autem hanc concessionem grato suscipiens animo, ut se vicissim erga sedem Romanam beneficum exhiberet, restituit omnia quae vel Constatinus donasse fingitur: vel quae Pipinus & Carolus Magnus, Longobardis erepta, concesserint. Restituit ea, inquit Barnus[?], quae neque possedit, neque unquam tueri potuit. Verum in papatu Leo nō diu vixit, sed anno Domini 966. post annū et tres menses obiit.
units.tr: Leo the Eighth, a Roman citizen and chief notary of the Church of the Lateran, was set up as pope in place of John, who had been deposed for the foulness of his life, by the Emperor Otho. Once confirmed in the papacy, he had Benedict deposed as said above. Knowing the wickedness of the Romans, and that they kept thrusting their own men in everywhere through bribery and dishonest dealings, he crowned Otho himself and declared him Augustus over the whole empire. Afterwards he took from the clergy and people of Rome the whole power of electing the pope, which Gratian reports had been granted by Charlemagne, and by a synodal decree transferred it to Otho, so that the seditions which usually arose at elections might be avoided. Otho, gladly accepting this concession, in turn showed himself a benefactor to the Roman see: he restored all that Constantine is feigned to have given, and whatever Pepin and Charlemagne granted after taking it from the Lombards. "He restored," says Baronius, "things which he neither possessed nor could ever defend." But Leo did not live long in the papacy; he died in the year of the Lord 966, after one year and three months.
JOHN THE FOURTEENTH.

units.la: Ioannes decimusquartus, natione Italus, ex Narnia civitate natus, & eiusdem sedis Episcopus, to[?] annis Episcopi (vel ut aliqui volunt, papae eiusdem nominis duodecimi) filius, quasi iure paterno, Ro[?] sedi praesiciebatur. In hunc pontificem, summa tranquillitate (quod rarum est) confirmatum, Petrus Romanae urbis praefectus, duo consules, & 12. senatores cum aliis nobilibus conspirabant, quòd Cafari faveret: & in Ecclesia Lateranensi eum captiebant, carceriq; ad Hadriani molem u.[?] fere mensibus mancipabant. Quibus auditis, Imperator Otho, contractis copiis, Romam cum exercitu festinabat[?], & in seditionis reos graviter animadvertebat: quosdam exilio, alios fortunis, & alios patibulis plectens. Petrum vero, eius voluntati commissum, Papa carnifici tradidit: qui illius mandato nasibus[?] exutum, rasaq; barba, ad integrum item capillis eum suspendit. Postea impositum da sino, uultu ad eius posteriora uerso, manibus q; sub asini cauda ligatis, ut omnibus esset spectaculo, per urbem praecepit circumduci, uirgis cædi, ac tum demum in Germaniam exulatum misit. Ita is mitatus est Christum sanctissimus pater, qui Lucæ 6. dicebat: Diligite inimicos uestros, &c. Ea in suos hostes crudelitate usus est, ut immanissimis potius tyrannis, Phalaridi, Dionysio, Neroni, & horum similibus, quàm Christi vicario conferri meretur: errare tamen Papa non potest. Ipse Ioannes Othonem secundum, à patre in Italiam uocatum, Romæ in Augustum coronauit: Poloniæ regnum ad papisimum inuitauit: Ægidium Tusculanum Cardinalem illuc misit, ut populum in ea fide confirmaret, diœcesES per regiones distingueret, Episcopos suâ unctione consecraret, atq; ut ipsum pro Ecclesiarum omnium capite agnoscerent. Post hæc & alia papalia facta, Ioannes anno Domini 973. præsenti ualedixit seculo. Ab hoc tempore cœperunt campanis baptizatis peculiaria dari nomina. Quoniam ipse Lateranensis Ecclesiæ maiori campanæ post prædicti Othonis coronationem (mirigra res) suum tribuit nomen.
units.tr: John the Fourteenth, an Italian by birth, born in the city of Narni, and bishop of the same see, the son (as some will have it, of the twelfth pope of that name) of a bishop, was set over the Roman see as if by paternal right. When this pope had been confirmed in the most peaceful manner (which is rare), Peter, prefect of the city of Rome, together with two consuls, twelve senators and other nobles, conspired to favour the Emperor. They seized him in the Lateran church and cast him into prison at the Mole of Hadrian for nearly five months. When this was heard, the Emperor Otho gathered his forces and hurried to Rome with an army, and punished the authors of the sedition severely: some he sent into exile, others he stripped of their property, and others he hanged on the gibbet. But Peter, whom he had handed over to his will, the pope gave to the executioner. By the executioner's order Peter was stripped of his nose, shaved of his beard and, likewise, of his hair entirely, and then hanged. Afterwards he was placed on a donkey with his face turned towards the donkey's rump, and with his hands tied beneath the donkey's tail. The pope ordered him to be led through the city so that everyone might see him, to be beaten with rods, and only then sent into exile in Germany. Thus did the most holy father imitate Christ, who said in Luke 6: "Love your enemies," etc. He used such cruelty against his enemies that he deserves to be compared with the most savage tyrants, Phalaris, Dionysius, Nero and their like, rather than with the vicar of Christ. Yet the pope cannot err. This same John crowned Otho the Second, summoned to Italy by his father, as Augustus at Rome. He invited the kingdom of Poland to the papacy, and sent Cardinal Giles of Tusculum there so that he might confirm the people in that faith, divide the dioceses by regions, consecrate bishops with his anointing, and make them acknowledge him as head of all churches. After these and other papal deeds, John bade farewell to this present age in the year of the Lord 973. From this time onward bells began to be given special names when they had been baptized. For the largest bell of the Lateran church, after the coronation of the aforesaid Otho (a remarkable thing), took its name from him.
72. BENEDICT THE SIXTH.

units.la: Benedictus sextus, patria Romanus, teste Volaterrano, terrano, Joanni in Pontificatu & calamitatibus magnis successit. A Cynthio enim Romano cive, & quidem potente, ob quasdam nequitias captus, in Hadriani molem, quam S. Angeli castrum nunc vocant, noxiorum custodiam, includebatur. Eodemq; in carcere, non multo post, laqueo miserabiliter, ne ex Germania, praedecessorum more, Cæsarem evocaret, strangulabatur, vel ut scriptores volunt, qui eius favebant nomini, inedia ac fame moriebatur. De tanta ipsi illata iniuria, nullam ei se sumptam vindictam, vel à civibus Romanis adversae factionis, vel ab O bone Imperatore, non possum ego (inquit Platina) non satis admirari, praesertim cum Otho ipse vir optimus fit habitus, & Ecclesiae Romanae acerrimus defensor. Sed verear (ait) ne talia fuerint Benedicti merita, quale praemium à Cynthio consecutus est. Nemo eius necem vindicavit: quod multis suspicionem fecit, anno Domini 974. suis esse meritis interfectum.
units.tr: Benedict the Sixth, a Roman by birth according to Volaterranus, succeeded John in the papacy amid great calamities. He was seized by Cynthius, a Roman citizen and a powerful man, on account of some wickedness, and shut up in the Mole of Hadrian, now called the Castle of St Angelo, the prison of criminals. In that prison, not long after, he was miserably strangled with a noose, so that he might not summon the Emperor from Germany as his predecessors had done; or, as some writers who favoured his name relate, he died of starvation and hunger. "I cannot (says Platina) sufficiently wonder that no vengeance was taken for so great an injury done to him, either by the citizens of the Roman faction opposed to him, or by the Emperor Otho, especially since Otho himself was held to be an excellent man and a most zealous defender of the Roman Church. But I fear," he says, "that Benedict's merits were such as the reward he received from Cynthius shows." No one avenged his death, which made many suspect that he was killed in the year of the Lord 974 for his own deserts.
73. DONUS THE SECOND.

units.la: Donus secundus, natione quoq; Romanus, in sede papali post Benedictum locatus, tam prudens & cautus ex periculis alienis factus est, ut nihil ageret in pontificatu historia dignum. Hoc solum de ipso à scriptoribus narratur, quòd Polonis per legatos regni coronam petentibus, postu-lata negauerit. Nihil fortasse ad culmen attule-runt: nec adhuc cōuentum erat (sicut cum Anglis) super Petri denario ex omnibus caminis. Suorum tamen ciuium uoluntatibus non adeò refragatus est, quin pacem & concordiam, quandiu, cum ipsa mæchetur Iesabele, quæ se dicit esse prophetam, & Ecclesiam sanctam, cum illis habuerit, Ecclesiastica ( inquit Crantzius ) administrauit mediocriter, neq; laudem magnam, neq; reprehensionem meritus. Quiete sua pertransiuit tempora, per annū & 6 menses: atq; anno Domini 975. in eiusdem Iesabelis pace quieuit.
units.tr: Donus the Second, also a Roman by birth, was placed in the papal see after Benedict. He became so prudent and cautious, learning from the dangers of others, that he did nothing in his pontificate worthy of record. Only this is related of him by the writers: when the Poles sent envoys asking for the crown of their kingdom, he refused their request. Perhaps they brought nothing to his advancement, nor had the question of the penny of St Peter from all the chimneys yet been agreed upon (as it had with the English). Yet he did not so far resist the wishes of his own citizens that, for as long as he kept company with that Jezebel who calls herself a prophetess, and the holy Church, he maintained peace and concord with them. He administered the Church, says Crantzius, moderately, deserving neither great praise nor great blame. He passed his time in quiet for one year and six months, and in the year of the Lord 975 he rested in the peace of that same Jezebel.
74. Boniface VII.

units.la: Bonifacius septimus, cuius ob ignobilitatem, & cognomen & patria reticetur, malis artibus adeptus pontificatum, malè etiam, & merito, tandem amisit. Nam inito eo magistratu, conspirantibus in eum ciuibus simul, seipsum occultare & coactus est. Et cum uideret, sibi non esse tutum amplius manere Romæ, ex D. Petri Basilica preciosissimos thesauros clam & furtim surripuit, ac Constantinopolim aufugit. Vbi post menses aliquot, diuenditis omnibus, ingentem uim auri collegit, Romamq; redijt, pecunia ratus cuncta expugnari posse. Interea temporis dum abesset, Romani in eiu locum, Ioannem decimumquintum, patria Papiensem, pontificem fecerunt. Sed ille reuersus, ciues auro illectat, & pessimos quosq; pecunia corrumpit. Ioannem ergo paratis praesidiis caepit, oculis priuauit, carcere inclusit, fame necauit, occupauitq; rursus pontificiam sedem.
units.tr: Boniface VII, whose lowly birth is passed over in silence, both his surname and his homeland, obtained the papacy by wicked arts and lost it in the end, and deservedly so. For at the start of his tenure, when the citizens conspired against him, he was forced to go into hiding. Seeing that it was no longer safe for him to remain in Rome, he secretly and furtively stole the most precious treasures from the Basilica of St Peter and fled to Constantinople. There, after some months, he sold everything off, gathered a huge sum of gold, and returned to Rome, thinking that everything could be won over with money. Meanwhile, during his absence, the Romans made John XIV, a native of Pavia, pope in his place. But when Boniface returned, he won the citizens over with gold and bribed all the worst men with money. He therefore seized John with ready guards, blinded him, shut him in prison, and starved him to death, and then again seized the papal see.

units.la: In qua non multo post, anno Domini 976, subita morte (apoplexia scilicet) turpiter cum luda[?] perijt, ut qui pauperum bona furto abstulerit. Unde cadauer eius, fune ad pedes alligato, per plateas tractum, ac lanceis & contis opprobriose confossum, tandem à clericis populari sepulturae demandabatur.
units.tr: In that same office, not long after, in the year of the Lord 976, he died a sudden death (namely by apoplexy), shamefully, as a man who had stolen the goods of the poor by theft. His corpse was then dragged through the streets with a rope tied to its feet, and was stabbed with lances and poles in an insulting manner; at last the clergy handed it over for a common burial.
75. John XV.

units.la: Joannes decimusquintus, natione Lombardus, patria Ticinus uel Papiensis, à ciuibus & clero pontifex constituebatur, dum Bonifacius praedictus, surreptis Ecclesiae thesauris, ad Constantinopolim clam fugerat. Unde Platina de Bonifacio: Sacra ipsa (inquit) furto abstulit, & tanti sacrilegij factum est author, qui & uindicare sacrilegia debuerat. Sed hoc in quauis republica contingere consueuit, quando plus malorum ambitio ualet, quàm bonorum uirtus aut grauitas. Ioannes iste ante papatum, diaconus Cardinalis, & magnae authoritatis uir erat: qui Bonifacij incaeptis non fauebat, sed cum honestis aliquot ciuibus (ut idem Platina refert) conatibus eius serio obstitit. Eo igitur absente, unanimi consensu illum pontificem creabant. Quo demum audito, Bonifacius aere alieno onustus, Romam, ut dictum est, repetiit: & conductis largitione sicariis, ac ex pessimo hominum genere ciuibus multis, Ioannem captum atque oculis priuatum, in Hadriani molem coniecit. Vbi anno Domini 976. post octo fui papatus menses, tam diu paedore carceris, inedia, & animi molestia macerabatur, donec uitam turpiter & ille finiret, in Vaticano sepultus. Sunt tamen qui dicant, interemptum fuisse à Ferrucio Bonifacii parente, magnae potentiae viro, quód filio in pontificatu aduersatus esset. Nam & ferro discerptum Valerium Anselmus tradit.
units.tr: John XV, a Lombard by nation and a native of Ticino or Pavia, was made pope by the citizens and the clergy, while the aforesaid Boniface had secretly fled to Constantinople after carrying off the treasures of the Church. Hence Platina says of Boniface: "He stole sacred things by theft, and became the author of such sacrilege, when he ought to have avenged sacrilege. But this is wont to happen in any commonwealth whenever the ambition of the wicked prevails over the virtue or seriousness of the good." This John, before his papacy, was a cardinal deacon and a man of great authority; he did not favour Boniface's undertakings but, as Platina again relates, with some honest citizens he firmly opposed his attempts. Therefore, while Boniface was away, they created John pope by unanimous consent. When Boniface heard of this, weighed down with debt, he returned to Rome, as has been said, and, with assassins hired by largesse and many citizens drawn from the worst sort of men, he seized John, blinded him, and threw him into the Mole of Hadrian. There, in the year of the Lord 976, after eight months of his papacy, he was worn down by the stench of the prison, by hunger and mental distress, until he too ended his life shamefully; he was buried in the Vatican. Yet there are some who say that he was killed by Ferrucius, the father of Boniface, a man of great power, because he had opposed his son's pontificate. For Anselmus also reports that Valerius was torn apart with a sword.
76. Benedict VII.

units.la: Benedictus septimus, patria Romanus, post Bonifacium ac Ioannem, pontifex à clero & ciuibus constitutus: annuente imperatore Othone secundo, seniorem eius filium Othonem tertium, in Ecclesia Lateranensi cum Theophania coniuge coronauit. Indeq; multos, adminiculante eodem imperatore, Romanae urbis, seditiosos cives illic capit. Et compertis quibusdam conspirationibus, cum grauiter deliquissent, carceraria poena atque bor-[?]rido rido [?] uinculorum supplicio damnauit. Synodum etiam Remis contra Francorum regem Lotharium celebrauit: in qua Arnulphum archiepiscopum uiolenter electum, restituit: & Gilbertum Floriacensem monachum, necromantem, pecuniis & artibus malis ab eodem rege intrusum, depositit, ac haereseos damnauit. Qui tamen postea obtinuit ab Imperatore Othone tertio, quem suam artem docuerat, ut esset archiepiscopus Rauennae: ac à Diabolo huius seculi principe, ut tum demum fieret Papa Romanus. Vnde Polydorus Vergilius in 6. Anglicae historiae libro: Monachi & sacerdotes, hoc tempore à maiorum vestigiis aberrantes, ubiq; gentium, veluti iure suo immodicas opes comparare, malis artibus honores ambire, & tyrannidem exercere coeperunt. Benedictus verò, suis praedecessoribus non multo sanctior, anno Domini 984. ad nonum sui pontificatus annum peruenit, & obiit.
units.tr: Benedict VII, a Roman by birth, was made pope after Boniface and John by the clergy and citizens. With the consent of the emperor Otto II, he crowned Otto III, the elder son of Otto, together with his wife Theophania, in the Lateran Church. Then, with the same emperor's assistance, he seized many seditious citizens of the city of Rome there. And when certain conspiracies had been discovered and they had grievously offended, he condemned them to imprisonment and a horrible punishment of chains. He also held a synod at Rheims against Lothair, king of the Franks, in which he restored Arnulf, the archbishop who had been violently elected, and deposed Gilbert, a monk of Fleury and a necromancer, who had been thrust into the see by the same king through bribes and wicked arts, and condemned him for heresy. Yet Gilbert afterwards obtained from the emperor Otto III, whom he had taught his art, that he should become archbishop of Ravenna, and from the Devil, the prince of this age, that he should at last become Roman pope. Hence Polydore Vergil in the sixth book of his English history: "The monks and priests, at this time straying from the footsteps of their ancestors, everywhere began to acquire immoderate riches as if by their own right, to seek honours by wicked arts, and to exercise tyranny." Benedict, however, not much holier than his predecessors, reached the ninth year of his pontificate in the year of the Lord 984, and died.
77. John XVI.

units.la: Ioannes decimusextus, patria & ipse Romanus, uncti cuiusdam sacrifici Leonis filius, eregione Gallinae albae, pontifici Benedicto, praelatorum atq; plebis electione successit. Qui suscepto papatu, miro statim odio in clericos exarsit: ita ut non ipsis modò, verumetiam omni populo exosus inde fuerit: maxime autem, quod omnia cognatis & affinibus (scortis ac spurijs) postposito Romane sedis honore, fit elargitus. Quem certe errorem (inquiunt Platina & Stella) ad nostra usque tempora, pessimo posteritatis exemplo, peruenisse cernimus. Qua quidem consuetudine nil perniciosius dici potest: cum non ob religionem, & Dei cultum, appetere pontificatum nostri sacerdotes uideantur, sed ut uel nepotum, uel familiarium (non thorum ac meretricum) ingluuiem atq; auaritiam expleant. Haec illi. Quae non omnino praeterijt Baptista Mantuanus, in 3. libro de suorum temporum calamitatibus:
units.tr: John XVI, himself also a Roman by birth, the son of a certain anointed priest named Leo, opposite the White Hen, succeeded Benedict in the papacy by the election of the prelates and the people.
