As soon as he took up the papacy, he flared up with a remarkable hatred against the clergy, so that he became hateful not only to them but to the whole people; and especially because, setting aside the honour of the Roman see, he lavished everything on his relatives and kin (prostitutes and bastards). Platina and Stella say that this error, by a most harmful example for posterity, has come down to our own times. Nothing more pernicious can be said of this custom, since our priests seem to seek the papacy not for religion and the worship of God, but in order to satisfy the gluttony and greed of their nephews or household servants (not of their wives and whores). Thus they. Baptista Mantuanus, in the third book of his work on the calamities of his times, did not wholly pass over these things:

units.la: Sanctus ager scurris, uenerabilis ara cinaedis / Seruit: honorandae diuum Ganymedibus aedes.
units.tr: The holy field serves buffoons, the venerable altar serves catamites; the temples dedicated to the gods serve Ganymedes.

units.la: Apparuisse cometem tum ferunt, futurae calamitatis indicium. Nam & fame & peste diu laboratum est: & terraemotu Beneuentum ac Capua concussa sunt: eaq; mala ob superbiam, luxuriam, & rapacitatem pontificum, contemptum Dei & hominum accidisse, putatum est. Octauo papatus sui mense defecit iste Ioannes, a clero non amatus: anno Domini 985. potione mortifera fortasse sublatus. Sed in Petri Basilica sepelitur, quod esset [?]sapistici sa-cerdotis filius.
units.tr: A comet is said to have appeared then, as a sign of the calamity to come. For there was long suffering from both famine and plague, and Benevento and Capua were shaken by an earthquake; and it was thought that these evils came about because of the pride, luxury and rapacity of the popes, and the contempt of God and men. In the eighth month of his papacy this John died, not loved by the clergy, in the year of the Lord 985, perhaps carried off by a deadly drink. But he was buried in the Basilica of St Peter, since he was the son of a priest.
78. John XVII.

units.la: Ioannes decimusseptimus, etiam patria Romanus, in re militari exercitatissimus: cleri ac populi sui fauore papatum iniit, Othone tertio imperante, sed nondum ornato imperij diademate. Fuit autem Ioannes vir tantæ doctrinæ, vt multa eleganter ediderit: quemadmodum Carsulanus, & post illum Præmonstratius scriptis testantur. Agitatus ipse seditionibus, à Crescentio consule Romano, Imperium urbis sibi vendicante, cupiditati hominis cessit, & in Hetruriam exulatum abijt. At vero Crescentius, cognita Ioannis indignatione, quâ percitus, Othonem contra se cum exercitu in Italiam vocabat, ipsius pontificis cognatos & amicos, qui in urbe remanserant, ad hominem mittit rogatum, vt omissa accersendi Othonis cura, ad urbem cum potestate redeat: pollicenturq; se ei rebus in omnibus obtemperaturum. Precibus suorum motus Ioannes, veritus etiam (callida vulpes) ne, si Otho cum exercitu Italiam intraret, plus mali quàm boni, sibi ac suis, secum afferret: prodeunte obuiam Crescentio cum suis magistratibus, & vrbana multitudine, in ædes Lateranenses magno comitatu introducitur. Quarum vestibulo, eius pedes Crescētius, & omnes seditiōis authores, petita veniâ, exosculati sunt: atq; ita in concordiam reda sti, vitam simul Herodes & Pilatus traxere. His temporibus, in Ecclesijs Anglorum, schisma gra-vissimum erat, inter sacerdotes & monachos, quòd Edgarus rex, eorum collegia illis dedisset. Sed mo-nachi mendacibus signis et doctrinis dæmoniorum superiores semper evaserunt. Joannes autem anno Domini 995, post papalia facta, vitæ suæ finem accepit.
units.tr: John XVII, also a Roman by birth and very experienced in military affairs, entered the papacy with the goodwill of his clergy and people, while Otto III was emperor, though Otto had not yet received the imperial diadem. John was a man of such learning that he published many elegant works, as Carsulanus and, after him, the Premonstratensian attest. Harassed by civil strife, he yielded to the ambition of Crescentius, the Roman consul, who was claiming sovereignty over the city, and went into exile in Etruria. Crescentius, however, learned of John's indignation, and in his anger he summoned Otto with an army into Italy against Crescentius himself. He sent to the pope the pope's own relatives and friends who had remained in the city, asking him to abandon his plan of bringing Otto and to return to the city with his authority, and promising that they would obey him in all things. Moved by the entreaties of his people, and also fearing (the crafty fox that he was) that if Otto entered Italy with an army he would bring more harm than good to himself and his followers, John was led with a great retinue into the Lateran palace, as Crescentius came out to meet him with his magistrates and the city crowd. In the vestibule of the palace, Crescentius and all the authors of the sedition kissed his feet and asked his pardon; and so they were reconciled, and, like Herod and Pilate, they lived together as friends. In those times there was a very serious schism in the churches of the English between the priests and the monks, because King Edgar had given the colleges of the clergy to the monks. But the monks always came out on top, through lying signs and the teachings of demons. John died in the year of the Lord 995, after his papal acts.
79. Gregory V.

units.la: Gregorius quintus, origine Germanus, patria Suevus vel Saxo, antea Bruno vocatus, Othonis tertij authoritate, post schismata & lites, pontifex ob affinitatem creabatur. Verum, Othone in Germaniam regresso, Romanus populus, novarum rerum cupidus, Crescentium ad consularem potestatem trahebant, & res Romanas eius fidei commiserunt. Crescentius vero, ac populus urbis, aegre ferebant Gregorium natione Germanum, authoritate Imperatoris ordinatum esse Papam: ideo illum papali sede deijciebant. Populusq; & clerus Romanus, Joannem eius nominis decimum octauum, prius episcopum Placentinum, natione Graecum, hominem eruditum & pecuniosum, in eius locum substituerunt. Gregorius autem, in Hetruriam primò, mox ad Imperatorem in Germaniam se contulit, de summa iniuria conquesturus. Imperator indignè ferens eam contumeliam, in Italiam cum exercitu redijt, urbem oppugnauit, Crescentium consulem & Ioannem nouum pontificem cepit. Quorum Ioannes, effossis prius oculis, pontificatu simul & vita privabatur. Crescentius vili iumento imponebatur, et vultu ad caudam uersò, nasoque cum auribus abscisso, ut spectaculo esset omnibus, per plateas circumducebatur, ac truncatis membris ante urbis moenia patibulo suspendebatur. Punitis ergo aduersarijs, Gregorius pristinam sedem recuperauit. Qui uidens circa imperium varios esse fortunæ euentus, ex principum ambitione & Episcoporum philargyria, grauissimis bellis inde sequentibus, congregata Romæ synodo, de Imperatoris electione sanctionem tulit. Constituit enim, ut ius eligendi Cæsaris, apud Germaniæ principes deinceps maneret: scilicet, Moguntinensem, Treuerensem, & Coloniensem archiepiscopos: comitem Palatinum Rheni, ducem Saxoniæ, ac Marchionem Brandenburgensem. His præterea Bohemiæ principem adiunxit, ad dirimendas discordias, in paribus suffragijs. Quam sanctionem anno Domini 1002. Otho Imperator approbauit. At Galliarum reges iniquissimè ferebant, eligendi Cæsaris potestatem, Germanis esse concessam: sed aperto bello id illis eripere non audebat. Gregorius iste finitis, anno Domini 998. mundum dereliquit, 3. sui pontificatus anno.
units.tr: Gregory V, a German by origin, a Swabian or Saxon by country, formerly called Bruno, was made pope through the authority of Otto III, after schisms and disputes, because of his kinship with the emperor. But when Otto had returned to Germany, the Roman people, eager for revolution, raised Crescentius to the consular power and entrusted the affairs of Rome to his good faith. Crescentius and the people of the city, however, resented that Gregory, a German by nation, had been appointed pope by the emperor's authority; so they drove him from the papal see. The Roman people and clergy then put in his place John, the eighteenth of that name, formerly bishop of Piacenza, a Greek by nation, a learned man and a rich one. Gregory, however, first withdrew into Etruria and soon afterwards went to the emperor in Germany, to complain of the great wrong done to him. The emperor, taking that insult badly, returned to Italy with an army, attacked the city, and captured the consul Crescentius and the new pontiff John. Of these, John was first deprived of his eyes, and so of both the papacy and his life. Crescentius was set on a worthless beast of burden, with his face turned to the tail, and his nose and ears cut off, so that he might be a spectacle to all; he was led around through the squares and, with his limbs mutilated, was hanged on a gallows before the city walls. So, with his enemies punished, Gregory recovered his former see. Seeing that fortune's outcomes in the empire were various, arising from the ambition of princes and the greed of bishops, and that very grave wars followed from them, he called a synod at Rome and issued a decree on the election of the emperor. For he established that the right of electing the Caesar should thereafter remain with the princes of Germany: namely, the archbishops of Mainz, Trier and Cologne; the Count Palatine of the Rhine; the Duke of Saxony; and the Margrave of Brandenburg. Besides these he added the prince of Bohemia, to settle disputes when the votes were equal. Otto III approved this decree in the year of the Lord 1002. But the kings of Gaul took it very badly that the power of electing the emperor had been granted to the Germans; yet they did not dare to snatch it from them by open war. Gregory died in the year of the Lord 998, in the third year of his papacy.
80. John XVIII.

units.la: Ioannes decimusoctauus natione Græcus (de quo in prædicto Gregorio dictum est) hanc diabolicā Romanæ tyrannidis sedem, muneribus, tumultu, ac seditione, aliorum pontificum more ambiuit. Hic antea Placentinus episcopus erat, senex quidem doctus & diues, sed insatiabili mentis ardore papatum exoptans: quod illi exitium, diuina ultio- ne, perhorridum postea peperit. Tantum enim pecuniarum ex Constantinopoli secum Romam detulit, ut non solum prodentes, sed & constantes, suis largitionibus, ad maleficia impellere posset. Unde Crescentij Romani consulis potentia fretus, quem immensa pecunia corrupisse scribitur, Gregorio iniuriarum multarum, quod Germanus esset, incommodis profligato, per factionem pecuniæ conductam, papatum occupabat. De illis vero, quæ in illo ipso papatu cum suis sequacibus, mercatui exposuerit, Baptista Mantuanus in tertio Calamitatum libro, sic loquitur: Pernices mercantur equos. Venalia Romæ, Templa, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, coronæ, Ignes, thura, preces, cœlum est venale, Deus q;
units.tr: John XVIII, a Greek by nation (of whom we have spoken under the aforementioned Gregory), sought this devilish seat of Roman tyranny by bribes, tumult and sedition, after the manner of the other popes. He had previously been bishop of Piacenza, an old man indeed, learned and rich, but longing for the papacy with an insatiable burning of mind; and this later brought him, by divine vengeance, a most dreadful end. For he brought so much money with him to Rome from Constantinople that he could drive not only the informers but even the steadfast to wickedness by his largesse. So, relying on the power of Crescentius the Roman consul, who is said to have been corrupted by immense sums, he seized the papacy by a faction bought with money, Gregory having been ruined by many injuries because he was a German. Baptista Mantuanus, in the third book of his Calamities, speaks thus of the things which this John, in that very papacy, put up for sale with his followers: "Partridges buy horses. Things for sale at Rome are temples, priests, altars, sacred things, crowns, fires, incense, prayers; heaven is for sale, and God too."

units.la: Miror ego (inquit Platina) historicos, Ioannem istum inter pontifices numerasse: cum, uiuen- te adhuc Gregorio, sedem occupasset: nisi forte in conscribendis pontificum uitiis, ita faciendum cen- seant, ut in perpetua historiâ fit. Nam & tyran- norum peruerse factâ, optimorum principum re- bus gestis annumerantur: ut quantum inter se mâ- li & boni dissideant, à legentibus cognosci possit: quo malorum exemplo à uitiis deterreantur, & bonorum exemplo ad uirtutes impulsi, uitam in terris beatam ducant. Qui quidem beatitudine Ioannes iste caruit, fur certè in pontificatu & la- tro. Hæc Platina. Cum ignominiâ tandem, anno Domini 997. hic Ioannes cum suo Crefcentio pe- riit, oculis effossis, & toto corpore lacerato: Gre- gorius ad papatum restituebatur. Adducam hoc loco Rodolphi Gualtheri, Tigurinæ Ecclesiæ mi- nistri, uiri doctissimi, uerba, ex Homelia tertia de Antichristo: & hanc secundam tertiæ classis sectio- nem, cum illis perficiam. Iam ergo (inquit) penes cordatum quemuis iudicium esto, num merito de pontificum tyrannide & iniquitate conquesti sint optimi quique: cum tot, quos modo commemoraui- mus, nebulones, tyrannos, sures, raptores, latro- nes, seditiosos, adulteros, & palam sacrilegos, in- tra tam paucos annos, sedes illa gestauerit. Et quis sedes ceu sanctâ ueneretur, q tot pestes sustinere potuit? Nondum tamen impletus fatis fuit impiissimorum hominum catalogus, &c. ut mox sequetur. In huius etiam sectionis fine, ex praeteritis historiis claret, quod sidera[?] in terram collapsa, Apoc. 9. sint hi pontifices octoginta, quos papas nominauimus, per plenam a Christo defectionem et apertas idolomanias. Quoniam data est eis clavis putei tartari, de cuius fumo prodierunt in terram locustae. A Bonifacio enim tertio, qui fuit ambitiosa bestia, usque ad Ioannem octauum, in prima sectione per annos 247, eadem Romae in Ecclesia fecerunt, ad idolorum cultum, editis templis et ceremoniis, quae perniciosissimi tyranni in sua Babylone. Et a dicto Ioanne octauo, qui fuit vulpina meretrix ac scortum impudens, usque ad Sylvestrum secundum, magnum diabolicum, in hac secunda sectione per annos 146, eadem sunt foeditates ad Sathanae beneplacitum operati, in sacratissimo eorum caelibatu, quae impiissima gens Abrahami tempore, in Sodoma et Gomorra, et adhuc maiores. Ita ut sint per equum nigrum designati, Apoc. 6. cuius sessor diabolus, habebat malarum interpretationum [illegible, ~12 letters] stateram in mas[?] [illegible, ~10 letters] nu sua.
units.tr: I wonder (says Platina) that the historians have counted this John among the popes, since, while Gregory was still alive, he had seized the see; unless perhaps they think it should be done in writing about the popes' vices as is done in a continuous history. For the deeds of tyrants done wickedly are also counted among the accomplishments of the best princes, so that from the reading one may know how far the good and the bad differ; so that by the example of the wicked they may be deterred from vices, and by the example of the good they may be driven to virtues and lead a blessed life on earth. John indeed lacked that blessedness; certainly as pope he was a thief and a robber. Thus Platina. At last, in the year of the Lord 997, this John perished with his Crescentius, with his eyes put out and his whole body torn to pieces in disgrace, and Gregory was restored to the papacy. I will here add the words of Rudolph Gualther, minister of the Church of Zurich, a most learned man, from his third homily on Antichrist, and I will complete this second section of the third class with them. "Now then," he says, "let it be left to the judgment of any sensible person whether the best men have justly complained of the tyranny and wickedness of the popes, when that see, within so few years as we have just mentioned, bore so many scoundrels, tyrants, thieves, robbers, brigands, seditious men, adulterers, and openly sacrilegious men. And who could venerate such a see as holy, which could endure so many pests? Yet the catalogue of the most impious men was not yet complete, etc., as will follow soon." At the end of this section too, it is clear from past histories that the stars fallen to earth, Rev. 9, are these eighty popes whom we have named papas, through complete defection from Christ and open idolatries. For "the key of the bottomless pit was given to them, and out of its smoke came locusts upon the earth." For from Boniface III, who was an ambitious beast, down to John VIII, in the first section, over 247 years, they did the same things in the Church at Rome for the worship of idols, by publishing temples and ceremonies, such as the most pernicious tyrants did in their Babylon. And from the said John VIII, who was a foxlike harlot and a shameless whore, down to Sylvester II, the great devil, in this second section, over 146 years, the same foulnesses were committed to the pleasure of Satan, in their most sacred celibacy, as that most impious nation did in the time of Abraham, in Sodom and Gomorrah, and even greater ones. So that they are designated by the black horse, Rev. 6, whose rider is the devil, having a balance of evil interpretations [illegible] in his hand [illegible].
Book Five.

units.la: TERTIAE classis sectio tertia, de Papis, vel Romanis Antichristis, in regno Draconis magni, qui est Diabolus & Satanas, Apoc. 20. usque ad Innocentium quartum.
units.tr: THE THIRD SECTION OF THE THIRD CLASS, concerning the Popes, or Roman Antichrists, in the kingdom of the great Dragon, who is the Devil and Satan (Rev. 20), down to Innocent IV.

units.la: A Ioanne octavo, qui meretrix erat, per centum & 46. annos, ad annum hunc usque à Christi nativitate millesimum, tanquam meretrix in Romana Ecclesia Antichristus regnavit, licet interea purissimum caelibatum tactitaverint Sodomitae. In omni carnalium foeditatum genere, toto hoc tempore pontifices diffluebant, ad octogesimum primum Papam usque, iuxta illud Danielis 11. de Antichristo: Et erit in concupiscentiis foeminarum. Ac Hiere. 5[?]. In domo meretricis luxuriabantur, & amatores in foeminas, equi facti sunt emissarii. In lasciviis enim, luxuriis, impudicitiis, paederastiis, scortationibus, prolificationibus, arrogantiis, pedum osculis, sacrilegiis, dissidiis, necromantiis, veneficiis, homicidiis, & aliis impudentiis, totum exercitium eorum erat, ut ex praedictis historiis claret: ita ut rectius ex Esaia, Sodomorum principes, quàm Ecclesiae proceres vocari merentur. Consequenter, post millesimum nati servatoris annum, soluto Satana, magni Draconis regnum mox merito dicetur: consentientibus mirum in modum per ea tempora pontificum actis: in Sylvestro secundo, qui suis necromantijs Satanam de abysso soluit, ac super habendo papatu, cum eo pactus est: in Benedicto nono, qui in sylvis & montibus sacrificia daemonibus fecit: in Hildebrando seu Gregorio septimo, qui malignos spiritus in consilia vocabat, atque in aliis qui diabolicis artibus sunt usi. Ut verissimum videatur, quod Apoc 20. ab Evangelista Joanne scribitur.
units.tr: From John VIII, who was a harlot, for 146 years, down to this year 1000 after the birth of Christ, Antichrist reigned as a harlot in the Roman Church, although meanwhile the Sodomites professed the purest celibacy. The popes wallowed in every kind of carnal filth throughout this whole time, down to the eighty-first Pope, according to that of Daniel 11 about Antichrist: "And he shall regard the desire of women." And Jeremiah 5: "In the house of the harlot they revelled, and lovers of women; they became like stallions sent out." For their whole practice was wantonness, lusts, impurities, sodomy, fornication, begetting children, arrogance, kissing of feet, sacrilege, dissensions, necromancy, poisonings, murders and other shameless acts, as the histories cited above make clear. So they deserve to be called princes of Sodom, as in Isaiah, rather than leaders of the Church. Consequently, after the thousandth year of the birth of the Saviour, when Satan was loosed, the kingdom of the great Dragon may rightly be said to have begun at once, and the deeds of the popes of those times agree remarkably with this: in Sylvester II, who by his necromancies loosed Satan from the abyss and made a pact with him about holding the papacy; in Benedict IX, who offered sacrifices to demons in woods and on mountains; in Hildebrand or Gregory VII, who summoned evil spirits to his councils; and in others who used diabolical arts. So it seems most true what the Evangelist John writes in Rev. 20.
81. Sylvester II.

units.la: Sylvester secundus, natione Gallus, ac professione monachus, Gilbertus primum appellatus, in Floriacensi cœnobio Benedicti regulam adolescens profitebatur: & artibus diabolicis intentus, totum se satanæ mancipabat. Monasterio demum relicto, in Hispaniam se contulit, profanarum artium studio struens[?]: & ad philosophum Saracenum magiæ peritum, Hispalim pervenit. Apud quem, non eruditione solum, sed & ambitione crevit: cogitavitq; quo pacto sibi viam inveniret, ad altiora honoris & opum fastigia: putavitq; nihil ad eam rem conducibilius esse, quàm ut magicis artibus se addiceret. Viderat ante apud Magum hospitem, librum necromanticum, eumq; ut ei surriperet, operam operam dedit. Cum uero codicem religiosus ille seruaret, quàm à Gilberto surripi posset: perfua-sit filiæ, quam domi habuerat Magus, cum qua si-bi intercessit domestica familiaritas, ut patris li-brum secreto tolleret, daretq; sibi perlegendum. Puella morem gessit, sitq; ille uoti compos. Libro accepto, clàm parat abitionem: metuens tamen, ne ex furto illo, sibi uitæ periculum imminret. Sa-tanæ igitur iureiurando se tradidit, ea lege, ut eius præsidio tutus in Galliam ueniret, & conse-queretur non uulgares dignitatum gradus. Venit in Galliam, scholas cum quibusdam aliis aperuit: liberales artes non sine auditorum admiratione docuit. Vnde plures habuit in prædicta arte discipulos, Constantinum scilicet, abbatem D. Maximi-ni prope Aurelianum, Lotharium archiepiscopum Senonensem, Adelboldum Episcopum Vuirtzen-burgensem, Othonem Imperatoris filium, Roberum Franciæ regem, Theophylactum, Laurentium, Malfitanum, Brazutum, Ioannem Gratianum, sa-cerdotes Romanos, atque alios multos. Horum ope-ra & largitionibus fiebat primum Episcopus Rhe-mensis, ut dictum est: deinde malis artibus adep-tus est archiepiscopatum Rauennæ, postremo dia-boli ope adiutus, Romani papatus fede accepit: e-ius uicarius factus, quem è puteo tartareo suis præstigijs[?] ac necromantijs soluit, Apoc. 20. Nam & Petrus Præmonstratensis cum quibusdam aliis scriptoribus, refert illum in anno à Christi natiuitate millesimo, assumpfisse[?] papalem cathedram. In quo anno, terræmotus magnus & mirabilis (teste Masfeo) contigit, & cometes horribilis visus erat 14. die Decembris. Magicas artes in papatu celabat: & necessitudinem illam, quam cum ipso habuit dis-simulabat. Caput ueruntamen æneum in abdito quodam loco seruabat: à quo, cum quicquam peteret à maligno spiritu illo, responsa semper accepit. Tandem sibi pulchre placens in papali stigio, sciscitabatur ex suo congerrone diabolo, quamdiu potiturus esset pontificatu? Diabolus ambigue respondit: non moriturum illum, prius-quam in Hierusalem missam celebrauerit. De uita ergo diuturnitate, bona spe accepta, omnino capit esse securus, quòd sciret se posse cauere, ne Hierosolymam (Palæstinæ urbem intelligens) proficisceretur. Mos uero fuit, ut pontifex in quadam quadragesimalis stationis die, Romæ sacra face-ret, in basilica S. crucis, quæ Hierusalem uocabatur. Vnde Syluefter de sua uita securus, cum tamen in cauendis Satanæ insidiis non satis circumspectus esset, missam ex more, in eo templo peregit. Quì statim graui correptus sebre, ex strepisu dæmonum (inquit Petrus Præmonstratensis) sen[?] fit sibi mortem adesse, pensumq; Satanæ redden-dum. Scelus magici erroris publice plorans, inde confitebatur, miserabili & horrendo hoc interitu præuentus. Et inter ipsius mortis angustias suppli-cat (inquit Benno) manus & linguæ abscindi(sunt qui addant genitalia) per quas in ipso cælibatu sa-crificando dæmonibus, Deum ipsum blasphemas-sit. Atq; ita anno Domini 1003 dignum jus mer-ritis exitum invenit. Sed eius discipulos mors hæc teterrimi, ab idololatriæ studiis non absterruit, ut statim sequitur: quibus etiam non desuit diuina ultio. Et quis non hinc intelligit, quale nam istud munus sit, qualis dignitas, quale officium, quod dia-bolus suis conferre novit, quodq; Satanicis & ne-pharijs artibus adipisci possunt homines perdi-tissimi? Quale sit etiam missæ sacrificium, quod vivis & mortuis prodesse tam crebro factitatur[?]: cum diabolus tantam tragœdiam adversus sanctis-simum Petri successorem & socium (Simonem Ma-gum potius) sub eo excitauerit, atq; ad lacum tar-tareum secum tandem traxerit. Huius Sylustri sepulchrum, ofium collißione & sudore emisso, ab eo tempore dicitur semper pontificum mor-tem prænunciasse. Dubio procul ideo, ut diabo-lus significet, cum pontificibus successoribus, eamdem necessitudinem sibi esse, quæ cum Syluestro si[?] it: quem etiam suæ mortis ante obitum admonuit.
units.tr: Sylvester II, a Frenchman by birth and a monk by profession, was called Gilbert at first. As a young man he professed the Rule of Benedict in the monastery of Fleury, but, intent on diabolical arts, he gave himself wholly over to Satan. At last he left the monastery and went to Spain to devote himself to the study of forbidden arts, and he came to Seville to a Saracen philosopher skilled in magic. There he grew in learning, but also in ambition. He pondered how he might find a way to the higher pinnacles of honour and wealth, and he thought nothing would serve this purpose better than to devote himself to magic arts. He had earlier seen a book of necromancy in the house of his host, a magician, and took pains to steal it. But since that religious man kept the codex carefully, Gilbert could not steal it, so he persuaded the magician's daughter, with whom he had become a close familiar in the house, to take her father's book secretly and give it to him to read. The girl complied, and he got what he wanted. Having received the book, he secretly prepared to leave, fearing however that danger to his life would threaten him because of that theft. So he gave himself over to Satan by an oath, on the condition that under his protection he would come safely into France and attain no ordinary steps of dignity. He came to France, opened schools with some others, and taught the liberal arts to the no small admiration of his hearers. From this he had many pupils in that art, namely Constantine, abbot of St Maximin near Orléans; Lothair, archbishop of Sens; Adalbold, bishop of Würzburg; Otto, son of the Emperor; Robert, king of France; Theophylact, Lawrence, of Malfi, Brazutus, John Gratian, Roman priests, and many others. By their work and gifts he first became bishop of Reims, as has been said; then by evil arts he obtained the archbishopric of Ravenna; and at last, aided by the Devil's help, he received the see of the Roman papacy. He became the vicar of him whom he freed from the Tartarean pit by his tricks and necromancies (Rev. 20). For Peter of Premonstré and certain other writers also report that in the year 1000 after the birth of Christ he assumed the papal chair. In that year, according to Matthew (Masfeo), a great and wonderful earthquake occurred, and a horrible comet was seen on the 14th day of December. In the papacy he concealed his magic arts and disguised the intimate relationship he had with the Devil. He kept a bronze head in a hidden place, from which, whenever he asked anything of that evil spirit, he always received answers. At last, pleasing himself splendidly on the papal throne, he asked his fellow-conspirator, the Devil, how long he would hold the pontificate. The Devil answered ambiguously: that he would not die until he had celebrated Mass in Jerusalem. So, having received good hope about the length of his life, he became altogether secure, because he knew he could take care not to go to Jerusalem (understanding it to be the city in Palestine). Now it was the custom that on a certain day of Lent the pope should perform the sacred rites at Rome in the basilica of the Holy Cross, which was called Jerusalem. Therefore Sylvester, secure about his life, yet not sufficiently watchful in guarding against Satan's snares, performed Mass as usual in that church. He was at once seized by a severe fever, and from the uproar of demons (says Peter of Premonstré) he perceived that death was at hand and that his debt to Satan had to be paid. Publicly bewailing the crime of his magic error, he then confessed, overtaken by this wretched and horrible end. And in the agonies of his death (says Benno) his hands and tongue were cut off (some add his genitals), with which, in sacrificing to demons in his very celibacy, he had blasphemed God himself. And so in the year of the Lord 1003 he found an end fitting his deserts. But this most foul death did not turn his disciples away from their devotion to idolatry, as follows at once; nor did divine vengeance fail them. And who does not understand from this what kind of gift, what dignity, what office it is that the Devil knows how to confer on his own, and which the most depraved men can obtain by Satanic and nefarious arts? What is also the sacrifice of the Mass, which is so often practised for the benefit of the living and the dead, when the Devil stirred up so great a tragedy under this man against the most holy successor and partner of Peter (Simon Magus rather), and at last dragged him with him into the Tartarean lake? It is said that the tomb of this Sylvester, from which, when it was broken open, sweat and blood issued, has from that time always foretold the death of the popes. Doubtless this is so that the Devil may signify to the successor popes that he has the same familiarity with them as he had with Sylvester, whom he also warned of his death before he died.

units.la: Quid autem de his magis dicere attinet? cum uul-go constet tam magiæ quàm aliarum artium, di-uinis legibus prohibitarum, peritissimos doctores & magistros suisse semper, uel sacrificulos uel mo-nachos, huius bestiæ characterē insignes: qui hoc modo artis & sectæ suæ authorem studiis suis pro-dere consueuerunt.
units.tr: But why is it worth saying more about these things? Since it is common knowledge that teachers and masters of magic, and of other arts forbidden by divine laws, have always been most skilled, whether they were sacrificing priests or monks, distinguished marks of this beast, who in this way have been accustomed to reveal by their pursuits the author of their art and sect.
82. JOHN the Nineteenth.

units.la: Ioannes decimusnonus, cognomine Siccus, ut Blondus author est, ac natione Italus, adiutore diabo-lo, cuius tum erat papatum dare, Syluestro mago ac Satanico monstro successit in eadem sede. Certamen suit (inquit Benno) inter ipsius Syluestri discipulos necromantas, dum quisq; ambelaret ad rapiendum sibi papatum. Nihil egit hic Ioannes (ut Barnus scribit) modico tempore quo in papa-tu uixerat, pontificia fede indignum: sed omnia ad eius uoluntatem fecit, cuius erat vicarius. Cleri sui persuasione, Romanum populum pontificis ele-ctione priuauit, adiectis his clausulis: Docendum est populus, non sequendus. Maior est dignitas le-gis, quæ regitur Spiritu sancto, quàm legis secula-ris. Vnde per hæc Deum ipsum, traditionum sua-rum diabolicarum statuerunt authorem, ac leges imperata[?] Imperatorias nihil esse ducebant. De his mentione facit Ioannes Baconthorpius, in prologo quarti Sententiarum, quaest. 10 Festum animarum, ab Odilone abbate Cluniacensi excogitatum et institutum, Ioannes iste acceptauit, approbauit, atque confirmauit: et ut post Festum Omnium sanctorum ab omnibus Ecclesiis obseruaretur, districte praecepit.
units.tr: John the Nineteenth, surnamed Siccus, as Blondus is the authority, and an Italian by birth, succeeded Sylvester, a magician and satanic monster, in the same see, with the devil as his helper, whose business it then was to bestow the papacy. There was a contest (says Benno) among Sylvester's own disciples, who were necromancers, each of them canvassing to snatch the papacy for himself. This John, as Barnus writes, did nothing in the short time he held the papacy that was worthy of the papal see; rather, he did everything according to the will of him whose vicar he was. At the urging of his clergy, he deprived the Roman people of the election of the pontiff, adding these clauses: the people must be taught, not obeyed; the authority of the law that is governed by the Holy Spirit is greater than that of the secular law. From these, they made God himself the author of their diabolical traditions, and they considered the imperial laws to be nothing. John Baconthorpius makes mention of these things in the prologue to the fourth book of the Sentences, question 10. This John accepted, approved and confirmed the Feast of Souls, devised and instituted by Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and he strictly ordered that it be observed by all churches after the Feast of All Saints.

units.la: Ex Aetna enim Siciliae monte, qui perpetuis ignibus ardet, quod Siculus esset Odilo, purgatorium esse didicerat: atque ex Gregorij dialogis, cum non suppeditarent scripturæ, illud probauit. Per missas papisticas, defunctorum animas ab eo liberari somniauit: dicebatque impostor ille monachus, diras se daemonum plangentium ac lugentium voces audiuisse, dum per missas et exequias funerales, eriperentur sibi animæ. Sedit Ioannes post Sylvestrum (ut dictus Benno refert) et quinto mense, anno scilicet Domini 1004, veneno suffocatus a suis dicitur. Eius tempore, Cardinalium nomen in precio esse coepit, iuxta praefatum Baconthorpium: et visa sunt inaudita prodigia, magnam mutationem praesagientia, ac terraemotus mirabiles.
units.tr: For Odilo was a Sicilian, and so he had learned that there is a purgatory from Mount Etna in Sicily, which burns with perpetual fires; and he proved it from the Dialogues of Gregory, since Scripture did not supply it. He dreamed that souls were freed from it by the Papist masses for the dead, and that impostor monk used to say that he had heard the dreadful voices of demons wailing and lamenting while souls were being snatched from them through masses and funeral rites. John sat after Sylvester (as the said Benno reports) and, in the fifth month, in the year of the Lord 1004, he is said to have been suffocated with poison by his own people. In his time the name of cardinal began to be held in esteem, according to the aforementioned Baconthorpius; and unheard-of portents appeared, foretelling a great change, and remarkable earthquakes.
83. JOHN the Twentieth.

units.la: Ioannes uicesimus, cognomento Fafanus, patria Romanensis, in ea natus regione, quæ Metropolitana porta dicitur, Ioanne prædecessore uenenata potione, ut dictum est, sublato, prodigiosis artibus Satanici papatus sellam[?] occupavit. A præ dicto enim Sylvestro, qui Magus diabolicus erat, usque ad Gregorium septimum, celeratissimum nebulonem ac præstigiatorem miquissimum (ut author est Benno in vita eiusdem) famosi fuerunt incantatores Romani pontifices omnes, lamnem ac lambrem Ægyptios magos maleficijs longe superantes. Ita ut verum fit, quod Baptista Mantuanus ad iulium scripserit.
units.tr: John the Twentieth, surnamed Fafanus, a native of Rome, born in that district which is called the Metropolitan Gate, after his predecessor John had been removed by a poisoned drink, as has been said, occupied the seat of the satanic papacy by means of prodigious arts. For from the aforementioned Sylvester, who was a diabolical magician, down to Gregory the Seventh, the most wicked scoundrel and most villainous trickster (as Benno writes in his life), all the Roman pontiffs were notorious enchanters, far surpassing in their wicked arts the Egyptian magicians Jannes and Jambres. So it is true what Baptista Mantuanus wrote to Julius:

units.la: Sicut enim tunc regna rapax laceraverit hostis Improbitas: sic et sanctos Atherontigenarum Laruarum impietas, et perniciosa libido Corrupit mores: quibus illa antiqua parentum Semideorum ætas totum condiverat orbem, &c.
units.tr: For just as the rapacious enemy then tore apart the kingdoms, so also the impiety of the Atherontigenous Larvae and a destructive lust corrupted the holy morals, by which that ancient age of the semi-gods had seasoned the whole world, etc.

units.la: Quicquid externo habitu pollicebantur, religio eorum nihil aliud erat quam fucus, ac mire simulata hypocrisis. Dei zelum, Ecclesiæ causam, et animarum curam, prætendebant: cum non alio tamen quam priuati commodi studio tenerentur.
units.tr: Whatever they promised by their outward appearance, their religion was nothing other than a mask and a wonderfully feigned hypocrisy. They pretended zeal for God, the cause of the Church and care for souls, although they were in truth held by nothing but a desire for private gain.

units.la: Spirituum circa sepulchra apparitiones, querelas, gemitus, eiulatus, lachrymas, formas igneas, speciesque horribiles, quas mortuorum animas esse, simplex crediderat vulgus: et alias per exorcismos excitabant tragœdias. Per sacrificulos et monachos, adiurati illi spiritus, de mortuorum quorundam rundam animas se esse simul[?]abant: dolores increa-dibiles, quos in purgatorij flamma sustinerent, ex-ponentes. De poenarum carnificina queritantes, ab heredibus opem flebiliter, per suffragia, pre-ces meritorias, & missas mortuorum postulabant. Atq; horum omnium actor erat diabolus. Et ut ad Ioannem reuertamur, ad otium conuersus (ut ait Platina) nihil memoria dignum gefit. Paucis se rebus implicuit (inquit Crantzius) memor, quibus se priores difficultatibus innoluissent. Solummo-do suis commodis ac templorum quieti, ad volu-ptatem indulsit: & praeter dictas hydromantias nihil fecit. Post quatuor annos Satanici regiminis, anno Domini 1009. non fine veneni suspicione exspirauit.
units.tr: The apparitions of spirits about the tombs, their complaints, groans, wailings, tears, fiery forms and dreadful shapes, which the simple crowd had believed to be the souls of the dead; and these they also stirred up as other tragedies by exorcisms. Through priests and monks those spirits, being adjured, pretended that they were the souls of certain dead men, describing the incredible pains that they endured in the flames of purgatory. Complaining about the butchery of their punishments, they tearfully begged their heirs for help through intercessions, meritorious prayers and masses for the dead. And the author of all these things was the devil. And to return to John: having turned to leisure (as Platina says), he did nothing worth remembering. He involved himself in few affairs (says Crantzius), mindful of those difficulties in which his predecessors had entangled themselves. He indulged only his own convenience and the quiet of the temples, for pleasure; and apart from the aforementioned hydromancies he did nothing. After four years of satanic rule, in the year of the Lord 1009, he expired, not without suspicion of poison.
§4. SERGIUS the Fourth.

units.la: Sergius quartus, patria & ipse Romanus, post horribilia haec, authore diabolo, perpetrata in ipso papatu facinora, Ioanni succedens, non aliis medius quàm sui praedecessores, pontificale consendit fastigium. A magna sanctitate, multisque virtutibus, cum tamen iuxta chronographos nihil egerit historia dignum, à suis commendatur. Ita solent adulatores papistae, nigros in albos vertere, ac fallaces operarios in lucis angelos transforma-re. Nec magnum est (inquit Apostolus) si Satanae minifiri sic transfigurentur, ut sint tanquam minifiri iufticiæ, dum modò dignus eorum factis exitus maneat.2, Cor. 11. Platina, Stella, & alij eius fari-næ scriptores, uirum sanctissimæ uitæ, gratæq; consuetudinis uocant, cuius & tantam fuisse prudentiam garriunt, ut toto suo pontificatu nihil commissum sit, quod merito reprehendi possit. Quàm impudens hoc sit mendacium, cum cæteris quæ apud eos illic sequuntur, ipsi norunt, qui eius temporis naturam ex diuina Ioannis Apocalypsi norunt. Sol enim factus est niger, tanquam saccus cilicinus, & luna tota facta est sicut sanguis, Apoc.6. In quibus significantur purae doctrinae defectum, & Antichristi in Ecclesia tyrannis. Filius hominis veniet (inquit Christus) putas inueniet fidem in terra? Luc.18. Et quomodo potest omnem mentem in Deum conuertere, ut ipsi blaterant, qui verbi ministerium non neglexit modò, uerumetiam suppressit, contempsit, damnauit, quod tamen in Ecclesiis pr aliis functionibus florere debebat. Integre gubernare ille non valet, qui Christi sermone non utitur. Quòd inter amicos & familiares iucundus fuerit, uerum esse credo, quum apud sceleftiffimos eorum id fieri soleat. Obijt Sergius anno Domini ioi2. dum in Italia regnarent fames ac pestis, & esset in Lo-thoringia fons quidam in sanguinem uersus.
units.tr: Sergius the Fourth, himself also a Roman by birth, succeeding John after these horrible crimes perpetrated in the papacy by the devil's authority, ascended the pontifical throne no differently from his predecessors. He is commended by his own people for great holiness and many virtues, although according to the chronographers he did nothing worthy of record in history. Thus the Papist flatterers are wont to turn black into white and to transform deceitful workers into angels of light. "Nor is it great," says the Apostle, "if the ministers of Satan are so transformed that they appear as ministers of righteousness, provided that their end is worthy of their deeds." 2 Cor. 11. Platina, Stella and the other writers of that stripe call him a man of most holy life and pleasant company, and they babble that he had such prudence that nothing was committed during his whole pontificate that could rightly be blamed. How shameless this lie is, they themselves know, along with the other things that follow there among them, who know the nature of that time from the divine Apocalypse of John. For "the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood," Apoc. 6. By these things are signified the lack of pure doctrine and the tyranny of Antichrist in the Church. "When the Son of Man comes," says Christ, "do you think he will find faith on earth?" Luke 18. And how can he turn every mind to God, as they prattle, who has not only neglected the ministry of the Word but has also suppressed, despised and condemned it, although it ought to have flourished in the Churches above other functions? He cannot govern well who does not use the words of Christ. That he was pleasant among friends and family I believe to be true, since among the most wicked of them this is usually the case. Sergius died in the year of the Lord 1012, while famine and pestilence were raging in Italy, and there was a certain spring in Lorraine that turned into blood.
85. Benedict VIII.

units.la: BEnedictus octauus, patria Tusculanus, ex genitore Gregorio Portuensi episcopo, Alberici ac Ioannis frater, & conditione laicus: per magicas operationes Theophylacti nepotis sui ministerio, qui Syluestri secundi discipulus olim fuerat, papatum obtinuit. Quamdiu etenim uixit Henricus Bauarus, quem imperiali corona donauerat, in rebus omnibus illo defensore semper est usus. Sed eo tandem mortuo, ab æmulis Cardinalibus è Satanæ sede pellebatur, & alius eius loco surrogabatur: factumq;[?] inde fuit schisma[?] grauissimum. Postea tamen, inita per aureos nummos cum aduersarijs concordia, pulsoq; adulterino pontifice, in urbem cum pristina pompa ac dignitate redijt, in sedemq; restituebatur. Hunc Benedictum rogauit Henricus prædictus (Barno teste) ut templi[?], quod Bamberge erexerat, in cathedralem Ecclesiam consecraret. Quod ita factum se promisit, sed hac lege, quòd ea Ecclesia quotannis Rom. pontifici census nomine centum marcas argenti numeraret, cum albo ac phalerato equo. Ad annum undecimum sui papatus peruenit ille, & anno Domini 1023. ex hac uita decessit. Refert Petrus Damianus, Cardinalis Hostiensis, istum Benedictum post mortem cuidam Episcopo sibi olim familiari appaapparuisse, nigro insidentem equo (uide quàm sint concordes scripturæ, Apoc 6. cum historijs) qui ea territus visione, dicebat: Nonne tu es papa Benedictus, quem nunc defunctum nouimus? Ego sum ille (inquit) infelix Benedictus. Et quomodo tecum est pater? alter interrogauit. Graviter torquetor, ipse respondit: sed iuuari possum. Vade ergo (ait) & dic Ioanni fratri meo, qui sedem nunc occupat, ut thesaurum tali in loco reconditum, thecamq; ac locum nominabat, det pauperibus. Ipsiq; Ioanni apparuit dicens: Liberandum me spero. Atq; utinam Odilo Cluniacensis, pro me rogaret. Sic ea ætate lusit Satan, ut idolomanijs, purgatorijs & missis, suum constabiliret regnum. Ab isto nebulone, Hungariæ ac Poloniæ reges, sceptra, coronas, atq; authoritates, neglecta Dei authoritate accepisse, ab historicis traduntur.
units.tr: Benedict VIII, a native of Tusculum, was the son of Gregory, bishop of Porto, and brother of Alberic and John. He was a layman by status. Through magical operations, and with the help of his nephew Theophylact, who had once been a pupil of Sylvester II, he obtained the papacy. As long as Henry of Bavaria lived, whom he had crowned with the imperial crown, Benedict always used him as his defender in all matters. But when Henry died, rival cardinals drove Benedict out of the Satanic seat and put another in his place, and a very grievous schism arose. Afterwards, however, having made peace with his opponents through gold coins and expelled the adulterous pontiff, he returned to the city with his former pomp and dignity and was restored to the seat. Henry said above asked this Benedict (as Barnus testifies) to consecrate as a cathedral church the church he had built at Bamberg. Benedict promised to do so, but on this condition: that the church would pay the Roman pontiff a yearly tribute of a hundred marks of silver, together with a white, decorated horse. Benedict reached the eleventh year of his papacy and died in the year of the Lord 1023. Peter Damian, cardinal of Ostia, reports that after Benedict's death he appeared to a bishop who had once been close to him, mounted on a black horse (see how well Scripture agrees with the histories, Rev. 6). Terrified by the vision, the bishop said: "Are you not Pope Benedict, whom we now know to be dead?" "I am," he replied, "the unhappy Benedict." "And how is it with you, Father?" the other asked. "I am tormented grievously," he answered, "but I can be helped. Go, then," he said, "and tell my brother John, who now occupies the seat, to give to the poor a treasure hidden in such a place," and he named the chest and the place. He also appeared to John himself, saying: "I hope to be set free. And would that Odilo of Cluny might pray for me." So in that age Satan played his game, establishing his kingdom through idolatries, purgatories and masses. Historians hand down that from this scoundrel the kings of Hungary and Poland received their sceptres, crowns and authorities, neglecting the authority of God.
86. John XXI.

units.la: Ioannes vicesimus primus, cognomento Neophytus, & patria Tusculanus, ut author est Benno, ex patre Gregorio prædicto Portuensi episcopo genitus, post Benedictum fratrem, Theophylacti nepotis arte nepharia, nullis adhuc initiatus sacris, pontificatum est assecutus. Huius Theophylacti, Ioannis Gratiani, Laurentij, Malfitani, Brazuti, & aliorum pseudosacrificulorum maleficijs, sijs[?], in tantamentis, atq; operationibus geomanti-cus, omnia tunc Romæ ad Satanæ nutum regebantur. Theophylactus enim, sacrificiis dæmoniorum in syluis & montibus deditus, mulieres post se curare faciebat (inquit Benno) quas magicis artibus ad sui amorem coegerat. Testantur hoc etiam libelli ipsius, in eius inuenti cubiculo, postquam vitam male finiuerat. Ita ut vera videantur hæc Mantuani ad Iulium dicta:
units.tr: John XXI, surnamed Neophytus and a native of Tusculum, as Benno reports, was the son of the aforesaid Gregory, bishop of Porto, and was born after his brother Benedict. Through the nefarious art of his nephew Theophylact, and though not yet initiated into any sacred orders, he obtained the papacy. Through the wicked deeds of this Theophylact, of John Gratian, Laurence, Malfitanus, Brazutus and other pseudo-priests, and through their enchantments and geomantic operations, everything at Rome was then ruled at Satan's nod. For Theophylact, given over to sacrifices to demons in woods and on mountains, had women cured after him (Benno says), whom he had compelled by magic arts to love him. His own little books, found in his bedroom after he had ended his wicked life, also bear witness to this. So the words of Mantuan to Julius seem true:

units.la: Hæc morum iactura nocet. nam dissipat omne Imperium Christi, toto iam cognita mundo.
units.tr: This loss of morals does harm, for it scatters the whole empire of Christ, now known throughout the whole world.

units.la: Mendacem fecit[?] esse Deum, qui dixit Auernum, Imperiis non posse suis inferre ruinam.
units.tr: He made God a liar, who said that Avernus could not bring ruin upon his empires.

units.la: Ecce ruunt, charitas fr get[?], spes pallida languet: Aegra fides fragili vix sustentata bacillo, Ex procerum tectis fugit, & gurgustia quærit.
units.tr: Behold, they fall: charity grows cold, hope languishes pale, and faith, sick and scarcely upheld by a fragile staff, flees from the houses of the great and seeks a hovel.

units.la: Ioannes iste, ut Volateranus habet, Conradum Imperatorem Imperij diademate redimiuit: & à Romanorum violentiis, qui illum diu vexaverant, per eundem Conradum, defendebatur. Intermina-tus enim excidium illis erat, si quicquam deinceps in pontificem molirentur: illiusq; patrocinio per-mansit in pontificatu, in annum usq; undecimum. Eius vitam nihilominus, mirifice à Romanis lau-datam esse, Platina demonstrat: sed non addita virtutum ac beneficiorum ratione, cum nulla fur-tassit[?]
units.tr: This John, as Volateranus has it, crowned the Emperor Conrad with the imperial diadem, and was defended by the same Conrad against the violence of the Romans, who had long harassed him; for Conrad threatened them with destruction if they should ever plot anything against the pontiff. John remained in the papacy under his protection until his eleventh year. Platina nevertheless shows that the Romans praised his life greatly, but no account of his virtues and benefits is added, since there were none.

units.la: tas[?]is fuerint. Ab isto multa feruntur institu-ta, in-dicta enim principibus sunt solennes eleemosynæ, sacerdotibus missæ, populoq; ieiunia. Tum quoq; D. Ioannis Baptistæ, & D. Laurentij per Christi-anum misimum ieiunia, cum magna superstitione sunt su-scepta. Ex Tribunensi[?] synodo, anno Domini 1030, surrexit in Galliis ieiunantium secta: qui dicebat, sibi fuisse cœlitus reuelatum, quòd feriæ sextæ ieiu-nium in pane & aqua, hominibus sufficeret (dia-bolica illusio) ad remissionem omnium peccato-rum, modo sese iuramento ad id constrinxerint. Sed hanc blasphemiam Gerardus Cameracensis e-piscopus non minimâ curâ aboleuit, ut Christi me-rita pessundantem. Mortem obiit Ioannes anno Domini 1034, successori relinquens locum. Eius tempore, per quosdam in Saxonia saltantes, ad missantis sacrificuli imprecationem, idololatriâ & abhominatio papistica missæ uehementer sunt confirmatæ. Tam impudenter & aperte regna-bat tum Satan, ut & morionicis nugis mundum se-ducerent.
units.tr: Many institutions are reported from him: solemn alms were enjoined on princes, masses on priests, and fasts on the people. Then too, fasts in honour of St John the Baptist and St Laurence were undertaken by the wretched Christians with great superstition. After the synod of Tribur, in the year of the Lord 1030, a sect of fasters arose in Gaul. It claimed that it had been revealed to them from heaven that a Friday fast on bread and water was enough for men (a diabolical illusion) for the remission of all sins, provided they bound themselves to it by oath. But Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, abolished this blasphemy with no small care, since it overthrew the merits of Christ. John died in the year of the Lord 1034, leaving his place to a successor. In his time, through certain dancers in Saxony, at the curse of a sacrificing little priest saying mass, idolatry and the abominable papistical mass were vehemently confirmed. Satan then reigned so shamelessly and openly that they seduced the world even with the foolish jests of buffoons.
87. Benedict the Ninth.

units.la: Benedictus nonus, patria Tusculanus, ex patre Alberico, Benedicti & Ioannis, ut dictum est, nepos, ac Theophylactus antea uocatus, sedem Satanicis artibus ac magicis præstigijs obtinuit. LaurenLaurentium & Ioannem Gratianum, tunc Archi-presbyteros vel Cardinales, suos condiscipulos atque incantatores diabolicos, prae caeteris omnibus intimos, & secretorum conscios semper habuit. In quibusdam memoribus ac sylvis ante papatu complicibus his sociatus, per nefariae curiositatis ritus atque caeremonias, spiritus malignos invocare solebat, & feminas quasdam volebat necromanticis operationibus in foedos amplexus trahere. Talis est Romani caelibatus sanctitas. Dum vero semel (ait Benno) de sylvarum secretis ad Ecclesiam cum bis socijs rediret, convenientibus multis, subito audita est avicula, quae vulgo passer dicitur, dulces voces iterare. Et interrogatus Laurentius maleficiorum princeps, qui & augur erat, quae avis illa caneret, statim respondit: Avicula iubet (inquit) alias aves ad portam maiorem convenire, ubi nunc fractus est cuiusdam rustici currus, & effusum milium, quod super illo ferebatur. Invitat autem frequenti cantu, ut illuc cito veniant ac fa-turentur. Quo audito, aflantium[?] plures, concito cursu ad eam portam alius alium certatim praevenerunt, & sicut dixerat, invenerunt. Augurijs illud sciebant[?] quid esset factum in Oriente & Occidente, in Meridie, in Septetrione, aut in extremis terrarum partibus, sive de bellis, sive de morte principum. Et multi studiose eorum magisterio adhaerebant (studium Apostolicum) atq; imbuebantur illorum artibus, praesertim Hildebrandus, Qui monasterio relicto, in schola tantae peruersitatis, arte & usu edoctus, tantorum maleficiorum fidus minister, & pessimis magistris peior est fictus discipulus. Quod ex fructibus perfidiae ipsius postmodum percepit Ecclesia. Haec Benno. Benedictus post d[?]fun-stum Caesarem Conradum, habito consilio cum su-is familiaribus, molitus est filium eius Henricum tertium successione priuare, & illius loco Petrum Hungariae regem, Augustum constituere. Missiq; Imperij coronam cum hoc versiculo:
units.tr: Benedict the Ninth, a native of Tusculum, the grandson, as has been said, of Alberic through his father, the nephew of Benedict and John, and formerly called Theophylact, obtained the see by Satanic arts and magical tricks. He always kept Laurentius and John Gratianus, then archpriests or cardinals, as his fellow pupils and diabolical enchanters, and as the closest of all others and sharers in his secrets. Joined with these men in certain groves and woods before he held the papacy, he used to invoke evil spirits through the rites and ceremonies of unholy curiosity, and he wanted to draw certain women into foul embraces by necromantic workings. Such is the holiness of Roman celibacy. Once, however (says Benno), when he was returning to the Church from the secrets of the woods with his two companions, and many had gathered, a little bird, commonly called a sparrow, was suddenly heard repeating sweet notes. Laurentius, the prince of sorcerers, who was also an augur, was asked what that bird was singing, and at once he replied: "The little bird (he says) bids the other birds gather at the greater gate, where a peasant's cart has just overturned and millet has been spilled that was being carried on it. It invites them with frequent song to come there quickly and feed." When this was heard, several of the attendants raced eagerly to that gate, each trying to get ahead of the others, and, just as he had said, they found it so. By augury they knew what had happened in the East and the West, in the South and the North, or in the farthest parts of the earth, whether of wars or of the deaths of princes. And many devotedly clung to their teaching (an Apostolic zeal) and were steeped in their arts, especially Hildebrand, who, having left the monastery, was schooled in such perversity, trained and practised in the art, a loyal minister of such great evils, and a worse feigned disciple of the worst masters. The Church later perceived this from the fruits of his treachery. So Benno. After the death of the Emperor Conrad, Benedict, having taken counsel with his intimates, planned to deprive Conrad's son Henry the Third of the succession and to set up in his place Peter, king of Hungary, as Augustus. And he sent the imperial crown with this little verse:

units.la: Petra dedit Romam Petro, tibi Papa coronam.
units.tr: The Rock gave Rome to Peter; the crown to you, Pope.

units.la: Sed Henricus primo conflictu Petrum cepit, Romamq; uenire disposuit. Quo audito, Benedi-ctus timore perterritus, papatum complici suo Ioanni Gratiano uendidit, acceptis ab eo libris mille quingentis, qui postea dictus est Gregorius sextus. Sed interim deposito ob ignauiam Benedicto, anno Domini 1045. Ioannem Sabinensem episcopum Romani in eius locum substituerunt, Syluestrum tertium appellantes. Ob hanc uendi-tionem (inquit Platina) ab omnibus accusatus erat Benedictus, ac iudicio diuino damna-tus, Et cur non magis ob fornicationes, idolola-triae[?], {ō}riat, necromanticas artes, incantationes, exorcismos, invocationes daemonum, & id genus alia diabolorum portenta? Mysterium est. Solum hoc damnabile uitium reputatur, caetera omnia in pa-tu uirtutes sunt. Sed tandem est in syluis circa annum a nato Seruatore 1056. meritum sortitus finem, a quodam daemone suffocatus. Referunt historici Benedictum istum, seu Theophylactum, pro pe molendinum a quodam heremita horrenda imagine uisum. Erat enim corpore urso, cauda atq; capite asino simili. Et cum interrogaretur ab eo, unde incidisset in eam metamorphosin, respondisse fertur: Haec species oberro, quia in pontificatu, sine ratione, sine lege, sine Deo uixi, & omnibus probris Rom. sedem inquinaui. Huius tempore, Cardinalium nomen ex paruis initijs ad maiora creuit.
units.tr: But Henry, in the first encounter, captured Peter and resolved to come to Rome. When this was heard, Benedict, terrified with fear, sold the papacy to his accomplice John Gratian for fifteen hundred pounds, which he received from him; this man was afterwards called Gregory the Sixth. Meanwhile, Benedict having been deposed for cowardice in the year of the Lord 1045, they put John, bishop of Sabina, in his place, calling him Sylvester the Third. For this sale (says Platina) Benedict was accused by all and condemned by divine judgment, but why not rather for his fornications, idolatry, necromantic arts, incantations, exorcisms, invocations of demons, and other such monstrous acts of the devils? It is a mystery. This one damnable vice alone is counted, while all the rest are virtues in the papacy. But at last, about the year 1056 after the birth of the Saviour, he ended his wicked life in the woods, suffocated by a demon. Historians report that this Benedict, or Theophylact, was seen near a mill by a hermit in a dreadful shape. For he had the body of a bear, with a tail and head like an ass. And when he was asked by the hermit how he had fallen into that metamorphosis, he is said to have answered: "I wander in this form because in the papacy I lived without reason, without law, without God, and I defiled the Roman see with every disgrace." In his time the name of cardinal grew from small beginnings to greater things.
88. Sylvester the Third.

units.la: Syluester tertius, patria Romanus, Ioannes Sabinensis episcopus antea dictus, largitionibus ac per tumultum, ut aliqui uolunt, in pulsi Benedicti locum a suis ciuibus surrogatus erat. Ego tamen id potius fieri opinor, prædicti Laurentij, qui (teste Platina) genitor eius fuit, magicis impostiris: quoniam hoc addit Benno Cardinalis, post eiectum Benedictum atque uenditum pontificatum. Eisdem diebus (inquit) superpositus est in papatum præ-dicto archipresbytero Ioanni Gratiano, Ioannes Sabinensis episcopus, qui mutato nomine dictus est Syluester tertius: & factum est, ut Romana Eccle-sia in partes diuersas scindi uideretur. Graui schis-mate, feralibus bellis, & immensis caedibus his au-thoribus, laniata est ipsa Ecclesia: ac sub colore melliis ueneno propinato, haeresibus nefandissimis propemodum suffocata. Haec ille. Ac non diu, ait Platina, in pontificatu Syluester mansit. Nono e-nim & quadragesimo die, factione suorum, Bene-dictus restitueba-tur. Sic in perfidia, unus impostor alium superauit, ac Satanas Satanam pepulit. Eò (inquit) tum pontificatus deuenerat, ut qui plu-ris largitione & ambitione, non dico sanctitate uitae & doctrina, ualeret: iis tantummodo dignitatis gra-dum, bonis oppressis & reiectis, obtineret. Quem morem, ait, utinam aliquando non retinuissent no-stra tempora. Sed hoc parum est, peiora, ni Deus auertat, uisuri aliquando sumus. Sic Platina. Ad Syluestrum redeo, quem Caesar Henricus, relicto Papatu, ad propriam sedem anno Domini 1045 redire compulit: in qua permansit, ut prius, Sa-binensis Cardinalis & episcopus. Sub praesulato Be-nedicto, anno Domini 1039. sexta die Aprilis, magna trabes ardere in caelo uisa est, iuxta Mas-seum, saeum[?], lib.16. Cazimirum, Cluniacensem monachū ac diaconum, idem Benedictus, anno Domini 1041. in regem Polonis dedit, hac lege, ut suis successori-bus, pontificibus Romanis, de quolibet capite usuā[?] lem[?] nummum singulis annis soluerent: deinde ut comam capitis non nutrirent. Meminissentq; semper, se Romanæ sedi subditos esse, quòd ipsis è monasterio[?] dedisset regem.
units.tr: Sylvester the Third, a native of Rome, formerly called John, bishop of Sabina, was put in the place of the expelled Benedict by his fellow citizens, by bribery and, as some want, by a riot. I, however, think rather that this came about through the magical trickery of the aforesaid Laurentius, who (according to Platina) was his father. For Benno the cardinal adds this, that after Benedict was driven out and the papacy sold, "in those same days John Gratian, the archpriest just mentioned, was raised to the papacy over the top of him, and John, bishop of Sabina, who changed his name and was called Sylvester the Third. And it came about that the Roman Church seemed to be split into different parts. The Church itself was torn apart by a grievous schism, deadly wars and immense slaughters, caused by these authors; and, with the poison of honey poured out, it was almost suffocated by the most abominable heresies." So he. And not for long, says Platina, did Sylvester remain in the papacy. For on the forty-ninth day, by the faction of his supporters, Benedict was restored. Thus in perfidy one impostor overcame another, and Satan drove out Satan. By then (he says) the papacy had reached such a state that whoever was stronger by bribery and ambition, I do not say by holiness of life and learning, obtained the rank of dignity, the good being crushed and rejected. "I wish," he says, "that our times had never retained this custom. But this is too little; worse things, unless God averts them, we shall one day see." So Platina. To return to Sylvester: Emperor Henry, having set aside the papacy, compelled him in the year of the Lord 1045 to return to his own see, where he remained, as before, cardinal and bishop of Sabina. Under the pontificate of Benedict, in the year of the Lord 1039, on the sixth day of April, a great beam was seen burning in the sky, near Masseus, lib. 16. The same Benedict, in the year of the Lord 1041, gave Casimir, a Cluniac monk and deacon, as king to the Poles, on this condition: that they should pay to his successors, the Roman pontiffs, a customary coin from each head every year, and that they should not let the hair of their heads grow; and that they should always remember that they were subject to the Roman see, because he had given them a king from the monastery.
89. Gregory VI.

units.la: Gregorius sextus, natione Italus, à Sylvestro fe-cundo magicas artes olim edoctus, & Ioannes Gratianus vocatus: archipresbyter seu Cardinalis S.Ioannis ad portam Latinam, papatum à Benedicto nono suo propinquo, ut diximus, emit, ac tan-dem accepit. Pontifex autem post schismata & seditiones factas, cum videret, ut Petrus Praemonstrâ[?] tensis narrat, quòd Ecclesiae bona à praedonibus tollerentur, peregrini ubiq; spoliarentur, & oblationes violenter auferrentur (ad aurum cor habuit) admonuit illos primò, excommunicavit postea, ac tum demum in contemptores arma suscitavit. Unde Ecclesiae bona non solum recuperavit, sed etiam mirum in modum auxit: occisis oblationum D.Pe-tri raptoribus omnibus. Cuius sæuitia moti Car-dinales, simoniacum, homicidam, & humani san-guinis appetentissimum (necromanticum magum addiaddidissent)ipsum uocabant: & cum ægrotaret se-mel, indignum affirmabant Ecclesiæ sepultura. Quibus ille inter cætera respondit: Bellum aliis indixi, ut ciuium damno, gloriam emerem cleri-corum, & hæc rependitis. Ac statim reualuit. Ot-tho Frisingensis, Godfridus Viterbiensis, & alij authores, tragicam turbationem rerum pontifici-arum eius temporis, in hunc modum descripserut[?]: Benedicto nono (inquiunt) in pontificatu sedente, Sylvester tertius, ac non multo post Gregorius se-xtus, eandem sedem inuaserunt. Et anno septimo Imperij Henrici tertij, tres pontifices, tres sedes Romæ, sibi constituerunt. Unde schisma horren-dum introduxerunt: dabantq; operam singuli, ne alter alteri, seditione, impietate & fugitijs esse inferior. Benedictus in palatio Lateranensi resi-debat. Ex aliis, unus ad S. Petrum, alter ad S. Ma-riam maiorem, pontificiam sedem collocauerat. Tribus ergo pontificibus, urbem totius reipublicæ periculo sic occupantibus, Ioannes Gratianus presby-ter eos adijt, cuiq; persuadens, numerata pecu-nia, ut papatum abdicarent: quod & factum est. Hinc Romani Gratianum tanquam urbis liberatorem, pontificem creabant. Henricus imperator, hisce motibus auditis, Romam propere uenit, sy-nodum celebrabat. In qua damnabantur tres illi pi iificuli, Benedictus, Sylvester & Gregorius (tria teterrima monstra) quartusq; constituebatur, Clemens secundus. His addit Benno: Theophylactum (inquit) in fugam coegit, Gregorium in custodiam reclusit, quem postea cum Hildebrando in exilium in Germaniam damnavit: ac Sabinensem Episcopum ad sedem propriam redire compulit, cum tamen debuisset tantos idololatras, simoniacos & haereticos, aeterno carcere ab[?] omni hominum societate separare. Defunctus est igitur Gregorius in exilio apud Germanos circa annum Domini 1049. & non Romae apud suos, ut aperte mentiuntur pa-pistæ cum suo Platina. Qui dicit illum nebulonem scelestissimum, resilientibus divino quodam flatu templi repagulis, in D. Petri basilica, non sine magnæ sanctitatis nota, sepeliri. Accedit etiam Vi-celius eiusdem impudentis mendacij confirmator. Alij laudant (inquit) alij secus: sed miraculo corpo-ris eius tumulati probatur, non fuisse hominem ma-lum. Vide hoc loco, qualis sit papicularum[?] sancti-tatis, & quae eorum miracula. Huius perfidiae (ait Benno) simul & pecuniae, Hildebrandus heres ex-titit: Romam post eius mortem reversus.
units.tr: Gregory VI, an Italian by birth, who had once been taught the magic arts by Sylvester II and was called John Gratian, was archpriest, or cardinal, of St John at the Latin Gate. As we have said, he bought the papacy from his kinsman Benedict IX and then received it. When the schisms and seditions were over, he saw, as Peter of Praemonstratensis reports, that the goods of the Church were being seized by robbers, that pilgrims were being plundered everywhere, and that the offerings were being taken by force. Since he had a heart set on gold, he first admonished these men, then excommunicated them, and only at last took up arms against the scorners. As a result he not only recovered the goods of the Church but also increased them remarkably, after all the plunderers of St Peter's offerings had been killed. Moved by his cruelty, the cardinals called him a simoniac, a murderer, and a man greedy for human blood (they added that he was a necromancer and a magician). When he once fell ill, they declared him unworthy of burial in the Church. To these charges he replied, among other things: "I declared war on others so that I might buy the glory of the clergy at the cost of the citizens, and you repay me with this!" He then recovered at once. Otto of Freising, Godfrey of Viterbo and other authors describe the tragic disorder of the pontificate of that time in this way. "While Benedict IX (they say) was seated in the papacy, Sylvester III and, not long after, Gregory VI invaded the same see. And in the seventh year of Henry III's reign, three popes set up three seats for themselves at Rome. From this they introduced a dreadful schism, and each of them took pains not to be inferior to the others in sedition, impiety and desertion. Benedict was residing in the Lateran palace; of the others, one had established his papal seat at St Peter's and the other at St Mary Major." While these three popes were thus holding the city to the peril of the whole commonwealth, John Gratian, a priest, approached them and, having persuaded them with money paid down, got them to abdicate the papacy, and this was done. Thereupon the Romans made Gratian pope, as the liberator of the city. When the Emperor Henry heard of these disturbances, he came to Rome in haste and held a synod. In it those three little pontiffs, Benedict, Sylvester and Gregory (three most foul monsters), were condemned, and a fourth, Clement II, was set up. Benno adds to this: "He (he says) drove Theophylact into flight and shut Gregory up in prison, and afterwards condemned him to exile in Germany along with Hildebrand. He also compelled the bishop of Sabina to return to his own see, although he ought to have separated such idolaters, simoniacs and heretics from all human society in eternal prison." Gregory therefore died in exile among the Germans, about the year of the Lord 1049, and not at Rome among his own people, as the papists falsely claim, with their Platina. Platina calls him a most wicked scoundrel, and says that, when the bars of the temple sprang open by some divine breath, he was buried in the basilica of St Peter, not without a mark of great holiness. Vitellius also joins in confirming this same shameless lie. "Some praise him (he says), others otherwise; but by the miracle of his body, once entombed, it is proved that he was not a bad man." See here what the sanctity of these little Papists is, and what their miracles are worth. Hildebrand, (says Benno) became heir to this treachery and to the money, when he returned to Rome after Gregory's death.
90. Clement II.

units.la: Clemens secundus, natione Germanus, Bambergensis Episcopus, & Sindigerus antea dictus, in synodo Romæ, iubente Imperatore Henrico ter-tio, uiuentibusq; adhuc tribus aliis pontificibus, potifex & ipse creabatur. Iste eundem Henricum coronauit, coegit Romanos iureiurando renunciare suo iuri de eligendo pontifice: ut schismata & simultates, quæ ex pontificum electionibus nasci consueuerant, hoc modo uitarentur. Sunt tamen qui asserunt dictum Imperatorem, iuramentum hoc à Romanis accepisse, quod non deberent in futurum sibi arrogare quicquam in pontificis electione. A-bcunte itaq; in Germaniam imperatore: Romani iurisiurandi immemores, ut moris est ipsis, pontificem absq; suis suffragijs creatum, anno Domini 1048 post nouem menses veneno necabant. Quod venenum miscuisse scribitur Stephanus, qui impontificatu successit: cui deinde Damasus secundus nomen fuit. Sed Benno, Gerhardum Brazutum, Theophylacti atq; Hildebrandi amicum, incomparabilibus maleficijs assuctum, tam nefandi sceleris authorem facit. Inauditæ contentiones bis diebus erant circa missæ uel altaris, ut uocant, sacramentum: multaeq; uisiones & miracula operante Satana, fiebant. Pluresq; doctorum, longè aliter loqui de Eucharistia uoluerunt quam Papa iussit: nisi metu fuissent territi, ut eorum implicita & nimis anxia scripta testantur.
units.tr: Clement II, a German by birth, formerly called Suidger and bishop of Bamberg, was himself made pope at a synod at Rome, by order of the Emperor Henry III, while three other popes were still living. He crowned that same Henry, and he compelled the Romans by oath to renounce their right to elect the pope, so that the schisms and quarrels which used to arise from papal elections might be avoided in this way. Some, however, assert that the Emperor received this oath from the Romans, namely that they should not claim for themselves any right in the election of a pope in future. So when the Emperor had gone back into Germany, the Romans, forgetting their oath, as is their custom, poisoned the pope, who had been created without their votes, after nine months, in the year of the Lord 1048. It is written that Stephen, who succeeded him in the papacy and was afterwards called Damasus II, mixed the poison. But Benno makes Gerhard Brazutus, a friend of Theophylact and Hildebrand, accustomed to incomparable crimes, the author of so wicked a deed. Unheard-of contentions were then going on twice a day about the sacrament of the mass, or altar, as they call it, and many visions and miracles were being wrought by Satan. And many teachers wished to speak about the Eucharist quite differently from what the Pope ordered, had they not been terrified by fear, as their entangled and overanxious writings bear witness.
91. Damasus II.

units.la: DAmafus fecundus, patria Bauarus, Stephanus Bagniarius antea uocatus, imperante Henrica tertio, pontificatum, nullo cleri aut populi con- sensu, per uim occupauit. Adeo enim Romae mos imoleuerat ille, sicut Platina refert, ut cuiq; tunc ambitioso liceret Petri sedem, sic uocant Satanae sellam & omnium scelerum sententiam, uiolenter inuadere, sed tam ambitioso dominatu non diu la- tatus est. Vigefimo tertio namq; die pontificatus fui, uenenato etiam poculo, per eundem Brazu- tum, anno Domini 1049 sublatus est. Praedecef- foris fui Clementis cancellarius hic erat: & do- minum suum, ambitione accensus ueneno petisse dicitur. Sed infamiam esse Crantzius credidit, ab illius artis magistris ipsi impositam, quo tam ini- quum facinus a fe deriuarent. Et Benno: Theophy- lactus inquit, magister Hildebrandi, post fugam, tunc Romam reuersus, cum familiare suo Lauren- tio, multis maleficijs sedem illam uexabat, & per literas eiusdem Hildebrandi, regum praditor fuit, ea quae in palatio Imperatoris gerebantur, perpe- tuo sciebat. Eo ergo immaniter illos nexante, ite- rum Romani consilio Cardinalium, legatos ad Im- peratorem ipsum dirigut, & ut aliquem in Papam eligendum, Romam mittat, exposcunt. Bruno igitur, qui & Leo, ex consilio Cardinalium, Romam inuitus & coactus dirigebatur. In cuius comitatu, nimia Imperatoris indulgentia, permissum est reuerti Hildebrandus; sacerdotium pariter & regnum, sub specie religionis euersurus, ac iuramenta Imperatori praestita, non diu seruaturus. Haec Benno,
units.tr: Damasus II, a Bavarian by birth, formerly called Stephen Bagnarius, seized the papacy by force in the reign of Henry III, with no consent of clergy or people. For at Rome, as Platina reports, custom had so prevailed that whoever was then ambitious might violently invade the seat of Peter (which they call Satan's seat and the sentence of all wickedness). But he did not long enjoy such an ambitious lordship. For on the twenty-third day of his pontificate, he was carried off, in the year of the Lord 1049, by a poisoned cup, again through the same Brazutus. He had been chancellor to his predecessor Clement, and he is said, inflamed with ambition, to have sought his lord's life by poison. But Crantz believed the infamy was imposed on him by the masters of that art, so that they might divert so iniquitous a crime from themselves. And Benno says: "Theophylact, the master of Hildebrand, after his flight, returned to Rome, and with his familiar Laurence he troubled that see with many crimes, and through letters of the same Hildebrand, who was a betrayer of kings, he knew continually what was going on in the Emperor's palace. Therefore, while these men were tormenting them so savagely, the Romans again, by the counsel of the cardinals, sent envoys to the Emperor himself and asked him to send someone to Rome to be elected pope. So Bruno, who was also called Leo, was sent to Rome, unwillingly and under compulsion, by the counsel of the cardinals. In his train, through the Emperor's excessive indulgence, Hildebrand was allowed to return, about to overturn the priesthood and the kingdom alike under the appearance of religion, and not long to keep the oaths he had sworn to the Emperor." So Benno.
92. Leo the Ninth.

units.la: Leo nonus, natione Germanus, patria Alsatius, ex comitibus de Dagsburg, comes & ille de E-tisheim, atq; episcopus Tullensis: Pontificatum (ut referunt authores) hac ratione iniit. Romani pertaesi seditionum, quas excitauerant papatus in uasores[?], legatos ad Henricum miserunt, rogantes, ut pontificem ipsis daret. Alterna inuidia magis (inquit Crantzius) quam honore regio moti, id Imperatori deferebant. Vnde obtulit eis Imperator, Tullensem episcopum Brunonem (iderat ei nomen) simplicem ingenio virum: cum inter Episcopos Germaniae alius non esset, qui uenefi-cijs Romanis praefici uellet. Is pontificali habitu cum illis proficiscens, abbatem Cluniacensem & Hildebrandum monachum, multarum calamitatum auctorem, in itinere obuios habuit. Qui uidentes eum pontificijs ornatum insignijs, apostaseos crimen illi odiose impingebant, quod ab Imperatore authoritatem suscepisset: cum prius debuisset cum prædecessore Sylvestro secundo, Draconem ado-rare, Apoc.13. & ab eo uires ac potentiam fume-re. Persuadebant ergo illi, ut deposito habitu ponti-ficio, Romam consueto cultu peteret, dicentes: Imperatori non esse concessum ius eligendi Papam (egregie mentita est sibi iniquitas) sed clero ac Romano populo, tam bene memores iuramenti sui boni patres erant. Bruno admonentibus morem gef-fit, ac in habitu priuato Romam uenit. Fatebatur delictum coram patribus, Hildebrando persuaso-re: & eo libentius pontificem eum creabant, quod confiteretur pontificis electionem ad clerum per-tinere, non ad Cæsarem: & propterea Leonem illum appellabant, cum merus esset asinus. Inde Hil-debrandum ipsum Cardinalem fecit, ac pontificij muneris confortem, committens ei curam Ecclesiæ S. Petri. De quibus sic habet Benno: Vt Romam uenit, à Leone obtinuit, ut fieret unus de custodi-bus altaris S. Petri. Et breui loculos impleuit: atque ut pecuniam illam ad quotidianum lucrum ad-licui committeret, cuiusdam Iudæi filium, nouiter baptizatum, sed nummulariorum mores adhuc re-timentem, familiarem sibi fecit. Et iam diu sibi con-ciliauerat alium quendam (ut dictum est) in com-parabilibus maleficijs assuetum, Gerhardum Bra-
units.tr: Leo IX, German by nation, Alsatian by birth, of the counts of Dagsburg, count also of Egisheim, and bishop of Toul. He came to the papacy (as the authors report) in this way. The Romans, weary of the factions that their papacy had stirred up among themselves, sent envoys to Henry asking him to give them a pope. Moved more by mutual hatred (says Crantzius) than by any royal honour, they handed the matter over to the emperor.
