The emperor then offered them Bruno, bishop of Toul (that was his name), a man simple in nature, since among the bishops of Germany there was none other whom he wished to set over those Roman poisoners. Setting out for Rome with them in papal vestments, Bruno met on the way the abbot of Cluny and Hildebrand, a monk, the author of many calamities. Seeing him adorned with the papal insignia, they hurled at him the charge of apostasy, because he had received his authority from the emperor, whereas he should first have adored the dragon with his predecessor Sylvester II (Rev. 13) and drawn his power and strength from him. They therefore persuaded him to lay aside the papal dress and seek Rome in the customary garb, saying that the emperor had no right to elect the pope (iniquity has lied to itself splendidly), but that this belonged to the clergy and the Roman people, whose good fathers were so mindful of their oath. Bruno complied with their admonition and came to Rome in private dress. He confessed his offence before the fathers, Hildebrand persuading them; and they created him pope all the more willingly because he confessed that the election of the pope belonged to the clergy and not to Caesar. For this reason they called him Leo, though he was a mere donkey. Then Hildebrand made him a cardinal and a partner in the papal office, committing to him the care of the church of St Peter. Of these matters Benno writes thus: "When he came to Rome, he obtained from Leo that he be made one of the guardians of the altar of St Peter. And soon he filled the coffers; and so that he might entrust that money to a daily profit, he made a friend of a certain Jew's son, newly baptized, but still retaining the habits of money-changers. And for a long time he had already won over another (as said), accustomed to comparable crimes, Gerhard Bra-

units.la: Notes: the marginal and footnote lines of this page are not printed in the scan. zutum Theophylacti amicum, qui subdola familiaritate, sex dicitur Romanos pontifices, intra spatium tredecim annorum veneno suffocasse. Quo-rum hæc sunt nomina: Clemens secundus, Damasus secundus, Leo nonus, Victor secundus, Stephanus nonus, & Nicolaus secundus. Et ipsum postea Theophylactum, antiquum dominum suum ac magistrum, pœnitentiam magnam simulantem, idem Hildebrandus Leoni Papæ in dolo reconciliauit, ita ut eius etiam consilio in pluribus duceretur. Hæc ille. Henricus Imperator Beneuentum urbem Leoni dono dedit, & illi vicissim Bambergensis Ecclesiæ tributum remisit, palliumque Episcopo concessit. Vercellis concilium Leo coegit, Berengarij do-ctrinam[?] de sacramento damnans, quod nollet Eu-charisticum panem Dei loco adorari. Moguntiæ quoque synodum habuit: in qua pro sacrificulis ac monachis statuta quædam fecit, ne canes vel aves alerent, aut profana tractarent. Sacerdotum coniugium, sanctissimum Dei institutum, impulsore Hildebrando, in perpetuum hypocrita illic damnauit, & Ecclesiastica beneficia à laicis dari, prosi-moniaca hæresi deinceps impostor decreuit. Cantus de sanctis aliquot, Sigeberto teste, composuit: & clericorum domos, ut casti fierent, prope templum extruendas esse statuit. Cum autem Norman ni potenter in Apulia regnarent, Hildebrando ac Theophylacto, quorum non intellexerat dolos(ut Benno testatur) infligantibus, exercitum in eos duxit. Sed quia Theophylactus, inquit, manifeste eum ledere non audebat, simulato obsequio cum illo manens, & ingressus atque egressus ipsius explorans, singula per secretos nuncios intimabat Normannis, ac in eorum manus, Hildebrando di-ante[?], ipsum Papam tradidit. De quorum manibus vix Papa, interfectis per proditionem suis Teutonicis, desolatus evasit. Qui tamen Romam reversus, anno Domini 1054. hausto p[?] Brazutum veneno, diem protinus post quinq; papatus annos, clausit extremum.
units.tr: zutus, friend of Theophylact, who by treacherous familiarity is said to have suffocated six Roman popes with poison within the space of thirteen years. Their names are these: Clement II, Damasus II, Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, and Nicholas II. And Hildebrand later reconciled to Pope Leo, by deceit, Theophylact himself, his old lord and master, who pretended great penitence, so that Leo was led in many things by his counsel." So far he. The emperor Henry gave the city of Benevento to Leo as a gift, and in return remitted to him the tribute of the church of Bamberg and granted the bishop the pallium. Leo held a council at Vercelli, condemning Berengar's teaching on the sacrament, because Berengar would not have the Eucharistic bread adored as God. He also held a synod at Mainz, in which he made certain rules for sacrificing priests and monks: that they should not keep dogs or birds or handle profane things. At the instigation of Hildebrand, he there condemned for ever, the hypocrite, the marriage of priests, a most holy institution of God; and he decreed, as the impostor that he was, that church benefices should no longer be given by laymen, which he called the heresy of simony. He composed chants about some saints, according to Sigebert's testimony, and decreed that houses for the clergy should be built near the church, so that they might become chaste. When the Normans reigned powerfully in Apulia, he led an army against them at the urging of Hildebrand and Theophylact, whose treachery, as Benno testifies, he had not understood. But because Theophylact, he says, did not dare to harm him openly, he remained with him in feigned compliance, spying on his comings and goings, and by secret messengers reported every detail to the Normans, and, with Hildebrand guiding them, handed the pope himself into their hands. From their clutches the pope barely escaped, after his Germans had been killed through treachery, and he was left desolate. Yet on returning to Rome, in the year of the Lord 1054, having drunk poison administered through Brazutus, he closed his last day right after five years of the papacy.
93. Victor II.

units.la: Victor secundus, natione Germanus, patria Bauarus, Gebehardus antea dictus, episcopus Eistetensis, ex Henrici tertij Imperatoris sententia, post Leonis mortem, pontifex hoc modo declaratur. Accipe prædicti Bennonis testimonium. Leone (inquit) post modicum defuncto, Theophylactus, de parentum potentia præsumens, Romanam ecclesiam, quam prius toties vexaverat, iterum vexare non destitit. Interim Hildebrandus, novus Proteus, novis tergiversationib. præsumens: de Roma ad Imperatorem, et de Imperatore ad Romam, absq; Romanæ Ecclesiæ consilio discurrebat. Et si quis alius interea in papatum eligeretur, quàm ipse:prædictus mox aderat Brazutus, familiaris eius, qui breui illum veneno suffocaret. Tantum ille. Romani timentes Henrici potentiam, de ordinando pontifice non audebant noui aliquid attentare, contra iusiurandum dicto Imperatori sub Clemente secundo prius datum. Mittunt ideo pro eligendo pontifice ad ipsum Imperatorem, nuncium Hildebrandum: qui tum filium eius Henricum iuniorem, authoritate suæ legationis fretus, imperij successorem designauit. Victor inde pontifex eligebatur, non tam liberis suffragijs, quàm ut Henrico gratificaretur, in eligendo pontifice Germanio. Hic Victor magnam synodum Florentiæ congregauit: in qua complures episcopos, de Symonia, hoc est, quod à secularibus dominis, & non ab eius sanctitate honores ac dignitates pro lucro susce-perant: & fornicatione (uxoratos fortasse Romanorum Sodomitarum more pro fornicarijs habebat) suis decretis, non Dei verbo, convictos, episcopatu ac functione priuauit. Propositq; clericis grauissimas pœnas, ne in his quæ ad illum pertinebant, delinquerent. In pontificatu hic Victor, parum excessit biennium: & anno Domini 1057. prædicti Brazuti ministerio, ad Hildebrandi nutum, venenæ absumebatur.
units.tr: Victor the Second, a German by birth, a Bavarian by country, formerly called Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, was declared pope in this way, by the decision of the Emperor Henry III, after the death of Leo. Take the testimony of the Benno mentioned above. "Leo (he says) having died after a short time, Theophylactus, presuming on the power of his parents, did not cease to trouble the Roman Church, which he had so often troubled before. Meanwhile Hildebrand, a new Proteus, relying on new evasions, ran back and forth from Rome to the Emperor and from the Emperor to Rome, without the counsel of the Roman Church. And if anyone else at that time were chosen to the papacy instead of himself, the aforesaid Bruzutus, his familiar, was at once at hand, who would soon smother that man with poison." So much for him. The Romans, fearing the power of Henry, did not dare to attempt anything new in ordaining a pope, against the oath previously given to the said Emperor under Clement II. They therefore sent Hildebrand as their envoy to the Emperor himself to choose a pope; and he, relying on the authority of his embassy, designated the Emperor's younger son Henry as successor to the empire. Victor was then elected pope, not so much by free votes as in order to please Henry, in choosing a German pope. This Victor gathered a great synod at Florence, in which he deprived of their bishoprics and offices several bishops who, by his decrees (not by the word of God), were convicted of simony, that is, of having received honours and dignities for gain from secular lords and not from his holiness, and of fornication (he regarded married men as fornicators, perhaps after the manner of the Sodomites of Rome). He laid the most severe penalties before the clergy, so that they should not offend in those matters which pertained to him. In the papacy this Victor lasted barely two years; and in the year of the Lord 1057, through the ministry of the aforesaid Bruzutus, at the nod of Hildebrand, he was carried off by poison.
94. STEPHEN the Ninth.

units.la: Stephanus nonus, patria Lotharingus, ac ducis frater, Casimensis abbas, & Fridericus antea nuncupatus, Victore papa mortuo, omnium suffragio ad pontificatum sine Cæsaris, ut apparet, consensu assumebatur. Qui statim curavit, ut Mediolanensis Ecclesia, quæ à Romana Babylone ducentis fere annis se subtraxerat, nunc demum eidem obtemperaret, ac matrem, totius impudicitiæ monstrum potius, agnosceret. Henricum quoq; imperatorem, ante papatum hærefos accusasse diciturdelirans hypocrita, quod Romanæ sedis authoritatem, nova hæresis, aliquantulum imminueret. Audiens etiam, simoniaca contagione, ut ipsi definierant, Ecclesias passim per Italiam ac Burgundiam infectas esse: Hildebrandum illuc misit, ut suo nomine eam tolleret labem, nisi se magnis redimerent precis. Symoniacam hæresin tunc bestiæ ac indocti asini vocabant, ut superius dixi-mus, si quisquam à laico, & non ab ipsis, Ecclesiasticum acciperet beneficium. Hildebrandus legationem diligenter suscepit, iussaque strenuè exequebatur, cumulatis undiq; nummis. Stephanus interim, Florentiæ synodum convocavit, prædictos simoniacos ac fornicarios sacerdotes, ut coniugatos vocabant pæderastas, expugnaturus: & super pluralitate ralitate beneficiorum adturus non pauca. Sed Bruzuti[?] pharmaco Hildebrandi impulsu tactus, anno Domini 1058. decimo sui pontificatus mense, in eadem urbe statim occubuit: in cathedrali Ecclesia ibidem sepultus. Romam ergo Hildebrandus, omni celeritate reuersus, omnem ordinis clericos adesse iussit: praesentesque sacramento adegit, ne quenquam patiantur in pontificem eligi, nisi sit ille omnium consensu designatus pontifex.
units.tr: Stephen the Ninth, a Lotharingian by birth, brother of the duke, abbot of Casino, previously called Frederick, was raised to the papacy on the death of Pope Victor by the vote of all, apparently without the emperor's consent. He at once took care that the Church of Milan, which had withdrawn from the Roman Babylon nearly two hundred years before, should now at last submit to it and acknowledge as its mother the monster of utter impudence. This raving hypocrite is also said to have accused Emperor Henry, before he became pope, of lessening somewhat the authority of the Roman see, a new heresy. Hearing that, by simoniacal contagion, as they themselves had defined, the churches throughout Italy and Burgundy were everywhere infected, he sent Hildebrand there to wipe out that stain in his name, unless they bought themselves off with large sums. The beasts and ignorant asses then called it simoniacal heresy, as I said above, if anyone received an ecclesiastical benefice from a layman and not from them. Hildebrand undertook the legation diligently and carried out his orders vigorously, with money heaped up on every side. Meanwhile Stephen convened a synod at Florence, intending to attack the aforesaid simoniacal and fornicating priests, whom they called married pederasts, and of benefices he was about to bring not a few charges. But, touched by the poison of Brazutus, at Hildebrand's urging, he died in that same city in the tenth month of his pontificate, in the year 1058, and was buried in the cathedral church there. Hildebrand hurried back to Rome and ordered all the clergy of the order to be present, and bound them by oath that they would not allow anyone to be elected pontiff unless he had been designated by the consent of all.
95. BENEDICT the Tenth.

units.la: Benedictus decimus, patria Campanus, Mincius prius appellatus, et Veliternus seu Veltrensis episcopus: cum Romani tumultuarentur, pontificem ex sua gente poscentes, pontifex acclamabatur, et clamore populari pro pontifice habebatur. Iniit autem ille pontificatum, sub imperatore Henrico quarto, quando mater eius Agnes pro eo quinquennium puero regnare caeperat: qui et ipse inuitis Antichristis, quinquaginta annis imperauit. Hildebrando abeunte uersus Florentiam, clerici dabant fidem, se papam non electuros, ante eius in urbem reditum. Seditione ciuium nihilominus moti, absente Hildebrando, hunc papam creabant. At Hildebrandus indigne ferens electionem factam, Benedicto eiecto, quod ut ac largitione (ut ipse dicebat) pontificatum inuasisset, instituit apud clerum, ut Gerhardus episcopus Florentinus, quem secum adduxerat, in papam eligeretur, se præsente, quemadmodum data fide promiserant sibi abituro. Cum uero non esset tutum Romæ, aliud eligere, contulerunt se Senas, ibiq; elegerunt prædictum Gerhardum, quem & Nicolaum secundum nominabant. Qui simul ac pontificatum suscepisset, synodum Sutrij indixit contra Benedictum: eoq; uocauit Godfridum Italiæ ducem, Mathildis Comitisse maritum, & Guibertum eiusdem Italiæ administratorem, atq; episcopos Lombardiæ, Hetruriæ, ac Romandiolæ. Quod cum intelligeret Benedictus, & in se conspirasse illos duce Hildebrando comperisset, anno Domini 1059. uel tras abiit exulatum, homo quietis amans post no- uem menses, ac uitam duxit priuatam. Hic non uenno[?], ut ceteri (inquit Benno) sed ui ac dolis Hil- debrandi eiectus fuit. Anno eodem, non procul a Tornaco multitudo colubrorum prælio concertan- tes, non ante cessauerunt, quàm industria populi, circumstructo igne comburerentur, ut libro 16. Christianus Massæus refert.
units.tr: Benedict the Tenth, a Campanian by birth, previously called Mincius, and bishop of Velletri or Veletri: when the Romans were rioting and demanding a pope from their own people, he was acclaimed pope and was held to be pope by popular shout. He entered upon the pontificate under the emperor Henry the Fourth, when his mother Agnes had begun to reign for him, a boy of five years; he too, though the Antichrists were unwilling, ruled for fifty years. Hildebrand, on his departure toward Florence, the clergy gave their pledge that they would not elect a pope before his return to the city. Nevertheless, moved by civil sedition in Hildebrand's absence, they created this man pope. But Hildebrand, taking it ill that the election had been made, expelled Benedict, on the ground (as he himself said) that he had seized the papacy by bribery and largesse, and arranged with the clergy that Gerhard, bishop of Florence, whom he had brought with him, should be elected pope in his presence, as they had promised him by pledge when he was about to leave. But since it was not safe to elect another at Rome, they betook themselves to Siena, and there elected the aforesaid Gerhard, whom they also called Nicholas the Second. As soon as he had taken up the pontificate, he called a synod at Sutri against Benedict, and summoned to it Godfrey, duke of Italy, husband of the Countess Matilda, and Guibert, administrator of the same Italy, and the bishops of Lombardy, Tuscany and Romagna. When Benedict learned of this, and found that they had conspired against him with Hildebrand as leader, in the year 1059, or thereabouts, he went into exile, a man who loved quiet, after nine months, and led a private life. Benno says that he was driven out not by bribery, as the others were, but by the force and tricks of Hildebrand. In the same year, not far from Tournai, a multitude of snakes fighting in battle did not cease until, by the industry of the people, they were burned with a fire built around them, as Christian Massaeus reports in book 16.
96. NICHOLAS the Second.

units.la: Nicolaus secundus, patria Allobrox uel Sabaudus, Florentinus Episcopus, & Gerhardus antea uocatus, Senis, cum Romae non liceret per[?] tumultum, Hildebrandi astutia, sine Cæsaris consensu pontifex creabatur. Hic peracta aduersus Benedictum, Sutrensi synodo, Romam illinc uenientes, apud Lateranum aliud concilium conuocauit: in quo hanc legem tulit, ut non apostolicus, sed apostaticus censeretur, qui sedem Petri, Satanae potius, obtineret, uel pecunia uel fauore, uide artem Hildebrandi, sine unanimi consensu Cardinalium. Dediq; potestatem Cardinalibus, clericis ac laicis, talem pontificem anathemate ferire, & quoties loco, si Romae non liceret, synodum aduersus illum conuocare, ac sede propellere. In eo etiam concilio Berengarius Andegauensis archidiaconus, opinionem suam de Eucharistia, coactus est reuocare. In qua asseuerabat, Christum non esse in pane & uino naturaliter, sed sacramentaliter, & tanquam in ministerio, signo, figura aut sacramento. Romanæ terræ capitaneos Nicolaus iste constituit: & Robertum Guiscardum, iuratum mancipium (quod Imperatoris erat) Apuliæ, Calabriæ ac Siciliæ ducem decernebat, uexilloque donabat propter initum cum eo fœdus. Sic fur furem, & latro latronem iuuabat iuxta ueterem Rom. pontificum morem. De fictis[?] diris, dolis, mendaciis, insanis, & arrogantiis, quibus in suarum excommunicationum fulminibus utebatur, ut mundo formidabilis effet, sumpto leonis exuuio, Cumanum asinum referens. Vide Baronium[?] in Pontificum vitis. Bennonis cardinalis de isto Nicolao testimonium, hoc loco praeterire non potui. Postquam sedit Nicolaus (inquit) Hildebrandus, quia papatum adipisci non potuit, ad archidiaconatum quoquo modo inuadendum se convertit. Et Mincium tunc archidiaconum Rom. Ecclesiæ multis iniuriis afflixit ac circumvenit. Qui victus contumeliis & dolis, atque eius Hildebrandi pecunia deceptus, ad ultimum concessit, ut illius vice archidiaconatu fungeretur. Hac concessione arrepta, Hildebrandus papam Nicolaum ex improviso aggressus, coegit inverecundis precibus, & militum minis, quos pecunia collegerat, metum mortis etiam quibusdam terribilibus significationibus incutiendo, ut eum archidiaconum ordinaret atque constitueret. Et post paucos dies, anno scilicet Domini 1062. ipse Nicolaus defunctus est, veneno (ut dicitur) a Brazuto Hildebrandi complice suffocatus. Cardinales autem, Hildebrandi ambitionem non ignorantes, Imperatorem multis precibus coegerunt, ut eis in electo suo Parmensi episcopo Cadolo favorem & auxilium praestaret. Quod factum, cor Hildebrandi altius percussit, & manifeste ste factum est ex illo die Imperatoris inimicus. Om-nia jurata fidelitatis vincula disrupit: et facta con-spiratione cum inimicis Imperatoris, & cum Nor-mannis, ut quem Cadolo à Cardinalibus electo op-poneret, Anselmum Lucensem episcopum dece-pit, & eum in Papam eligi à quibusdam Roma-nis fecit: ipsumque mutato nomine, Alexandrum se-cundum vocavit. Anselmum igitur, quem sub do-lo Romani elegerant, pariter & Parmensem epi-scopum Cadolum, quibus poterat artibus Hilde-brandus vexavit: qui utriq; succedere anhelabat.
units.tr: Nicholas the Second, a Savoyard or Allobrogian by birth, bishop of Florence, previously called Gerhard, was created pope at Siena, since it was not permitted at Rome because of the tumult, by the cunning of Hildebrand, without the emperor's consent. After the Sutri synod against Benedict was completed, he came from there to Rome and called another council at the Lateran, in which he passed this law: that the one who held the see of Peter, by money or favour, that is, by the art of Hildebrand, without the unanimous consent of the cardinals, should be judged not apostolic but apostate, and rather a holder of Satan's see. He gave power to the cardinals, clergy and laymen to strike such a pontiff with anathema, and, wherever it was not allowed at Rome, to call a synod against him and drive him from the see. In that same council, Berengar, archdeacon of Angers, was compelled to retract his opinion concerning the Eucharist, in which he maintained that Christ is not in the bread and wine naturally, but sacramentally, and as it were in the ministry, sign, figure or sacrament. Nicholas appointed captains for the Roman land, and he decreed Robert Guiscard, a sworn bondsman (who belonged to the emperor), duke of Apulia, Calabria and Sicily, and gave him a banner on account of the covenant made with him. Thus, after the ancient custom of the Roman pontiffs, thief helped thief and robber helped robber. Of the feigned curses, tricks, lies, madnesses and arrogances with which he used the thunderbolts of his excommunications, so that he might be formidable to the world, he put on the lion's skin, imitating the Cuman ass. See Baronius in the Lives of the Popes. I could not pass over here the testimony of Cardinal Benno about this Nicholas. After Nicholas sat (he says), Hildebrand, because he could not obtain the papacy, turned himself to seizing the archdeaconship by whatever means. And he harassed and circumvented Mincius, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, with many injuries. He, overcome by insults and tricks, and deceived by Hildebrand's money, at last yielded, so that Hildebrand might act as archdeacon in his place. Seizing on this concession, Hildebrand suddenly attacked Pope Nicholas, and, by shameless entreaties and the threats of soldiers whom he had gathered with money, and by striking fear of death into some with terrible signs, forced him to ordain and appoint him archdeacon. And a few days later, in the year 1062, Nicholas himself died, suffocated by poison (as it is said) by Brazutus, Hildebrand's accomplice. But the cardinals, not unaware of Hildebrand's ambition, with many prayers compelled the emperor to grant them his favour and aid for their elected man, Cadalus, bishop of Parma. When this was done, Hildebrand's heart was pierced more deeply, and from that day he manifestly became the emperor's enemy. He broke all the sworn bonds of fidelity, and, with a conspiracy formed with the emperor's enemies and with the Normans, in order to set against Cadalus the man elected by the cardinals, he deceived Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and caused him to be elected pope by certain Romans, and, changing his name, called him Alexander the Second. Hildebrand harassed Anselm, whom the Romans had chosen by trickery, and likewise Cadalus, bishop of Parma, by whatever arts he could, since he longed to succeed each of them.
Thus Benno.
97. ALEXANDER the Second.

units.la: ALexander secundus, patria Mediolanensis, episcopus Lucensis, & Anselmus antea dictus, vulpina[?] Hildebrandi calliditate, ut sibi ipsi adpa-patum viam sterneret, Romæ absens electus fuit in pontificem, Imperatore neq; salutato, neq; consulto. Huic Longobardi, ex Imperatoris consensu, alium oppo-suerunt pontificem: quem ipsi Basilea in comitijs eo præsente elegerant, Cadolum nomine (ut dictum est) episcopum Parmensem. Qui magno cum exercitu Romam obsedit: comissoq;[?] prælio uno atq; altero, cum suis est fugatus. Henricus vero Imperator, ut schisma tolleretur, Othonem Colonienfem archiepiscopum cum sua authoritate illus[?] illuc misit. Qui Romam ueniens, multis egit de Im-peratoris iure in eligendo pontifice: & Alexan-drum, qui sine eius consensu electus esset, graviter incusabat. Tunc Hildebrandus, ad hominum per-niciem natus, & propter uictoriâ nuperrimè par-tam elatior factus, orationem archiepiscopi inter-rumpit, acriterq; tuetur pontificis partes, electi-onem eius afferens esse apud clerum. Otho plus foe-ditatis[?] in ea re pontifici quàm Imperatori deferens, facile cedit: petitq; ut synodus pro sedando schis-mate Mantuae congregaretur. In qua constituit Alexander, non esse missam audiendam à sacerdo-te concubinario factam, quod nunc obsoletum uide-tur: alioqui nemo missas audiret sub toto fere papa-tu. Deinde maritos episcopos, presbyteros ac dia-conos, beneficijs priuandos esse uoluit. Filios tamen sacerdotum, sacris initiari licere permisit, inter-posita pontificis authoritate. Papam à solis Car-dinalibus eligi decreuit, & alia plura pro clericis ac monachis fecit. Alleluia quoq; à septuagesima usq; ad pascha suspendi præcepit. His temporibus, episcopi plusquam principes, regibus imperare ac leges præscribere conantur: decimasq; magna auste-ritate extorquent. Hæc quoq; fuit eorum vicario-rum Christi religio, ut quo uentri luxuiq; suo satis facerent, non sint ueriti totas nationes bellis immi-scere. fcere. Accedit nunc Bennonis Cardinalis de Alexandro pipa [?] testimonium. Vbi Alexander (inquit) tandem intellexit, se dolis & arte ab Hildebrando & inimicis Imperatoris electum atq; intronizatu[?], die quodam cum intra missarum solennia sermonem haberet ad populum, praedicauit se nolle sedere in sede Apostolica, abjq; licentia Imperatoris. Et publice dixit, se literas huius rei gratia missurum ipsi Imperatori. Quo audito, Hildebrandus multa murmurando [?], vix manus, donec missa compleretur, abstinuit. Missa vero expleta, ipsum Alexandrum cum militari manu ab altari duxit in cameram: & non dum exutum pontificalibus indumentis, pugnis dure colaphizauit, increpans & improperans, quod vellet inquirere gratiam Imperatoris. Et statuit Hildebrandus, ut ex eo die non darentur ei amplius quam quinque solidi Lucensium denariorum. Et ex tunc Hildebrandus omnes redditus Rom. Ecclesiae sibi retinuit (Alexandro in vincula coniecto [?]) & immensam pecuniam congregauit. Alexandro igitur sub miserabili iugo Hildebrandi, anno Domini 1074. quodam vespere (non sine toxico fortassis [?]) defuncto, eadem hora Hildebrandus a suis militibus, sine assensu cleri & populi est intronizatus, timens ne alius per moram eligeretur. In cuius electione, nullus Cardinalium subscripsit. Ad qua eum ueniret abbas Cassinensis, ait ipse Hildebran-dus: Frater nimium tardasti. Respondit abbas: Et tu Hildebrande nimium festinasti, qui nondum sepulto Domino tuo Papa, sedem Apostolicam contra Canones usurpasti. Hoc modo intbronizatus Hildebrandus, qualiter uixerit, qualiter a se Cardinales, qui testes uitae & doctrinae eius esse debuerant, remouerit: quam miserabiliter uexauerit, quantis haeresibus mundum corruperit, quanta per iuria, quam immensas proditiones consecrauerit, nix a multis describi potest. Clamat tamen altius sanguis Christianorum eo authore & incentore, miserabiliter effusus. Haec Benno,
units.tr: Alexander the Second, a native of Milan, bishop of Lucca, formerly called Anselm, was elected pope in Rome in his absence. By the foxlike cunning of Hildebrand, who thus paved his own way to the papacy, he was chosen without the Emperor being greeted or consulted. The Lombards, with the Emperor's consent, set another pope against him: Cadalus, as already said, bishop of Parma, whom they had elected at Basel in an assembly held in his presence. He besieged Rome with a large army, but after one or two battles he was put to flight with his men. So that the schism might be ended, the Emperor Henry sent Otto, archbishop of Cologne, to Rome with his authority. On arriving there, Otto argued at length about the Emperor's right to elect a pope, and sharply blamed Alexander, who had been elected without the Emperor's consent. Then Hildebrand, born for the ruin of men and made more arrogant by his recent victory, interrupted the archbishop's speech and vigorously defended the pope's position, asserting that his election belonged to the clergy. Otto, granting more of the matter to the pope than to the Emperor, gave way easily and asked that a synod be gathered at Mantua to settle the schism. In that synod Alexander decreed that a mass said by a concubinary priest was not to be heard. This now seems obsolete; otherwise almost nobody would have heard mass under the whole papacy. Next he wished married bishops, presbyters and deacons to be deprived of their benefices. He did allow the sons of priests to be initiated into holy orders, with the pope's authority interposed. He decreed that the pope should be chosen by the Cardinals alone, and did many other things concerning clerics and monks. He also ordered that the Alleluia be suspended from Septuagesima until Easter. In these times bishops, more than princes, try to rule kings and prescribe laws, and they extort tithes with great harshness. This too was the religion of these vicars of Christ: to satisfy their belly and their luxury, they did not hesitate to plunge whole nations into wars. Now there follows the testimony of Cardinal Benno concerning Pope Alexander. "When Alexander (he says) at last understood that he had been elected and enthroned by deceit and craft by Hildebrand and the enemies of the Emperor, one day, while he was preaching to the people during the solemnities of the mass, he declared that he would not sit in the Apostolic see without the Emperor's permission. And he publicly said that he would send letters to the Emperor himself about this matter. Hearing this, Hildebrand, muttering much, could scarcely keep his hands off him until the mass was finished. When the mass was over, he led Alexander himself from the altar into a chamber with an armed band, and before he had been stripped of his pontifical vestments, struck him hard with his fists, scolding and reproaching him for wanting to seek the Emperor's favour. Hildebrand then decreed that from that day he should be given no more than five shillings of Lucca money. From then on Hildebrand kept all the revenues of the Roman Church for himself, with Alexander thrown into chains, and gathered immense sums of money. So Alexander, under the wretched yoke of Hildebrand, died one evening in the year of the Lord 1074, perhaps not without poison. At that same hour Hildebrand was enthroned by his soldiers, without the assent of clergy and people, fearing that another would be chosen if there were delay. In his election no Cardinal signed. When the abbot of Monte Cassino came to him, Hildebrand said: "Brother, you have been too slow." The abbot replied: "And you, Hildebrand, have been too hasty, who, before your lord the pope was even buried, seized the Apostolic see contrary to the canons." Having been enthroned in this way, how Hildebrand lived, how he removed from himself the Cardinals who ought to have been witnesses of his life and teaching, how wretchedly he harassed the Church, with what heresies he corrupted the world, what great wrongs and immense betrayals he sanctioned, can hardly be described by many. Yet the blood of Christians, wretchedly poured out under his authority and instigation, cries out all the more loudly. Thus Benno.
98. GREGORY the Seventh.

units.la: GRegorius septimus, natione Hetruscus, patria Senensis, secta uero Cluniacensis monachus, & Hildebrandus antea uocatus impostor, incantator ac praestigiator diabolicus, maudita (ut diZum est) tyrannide, papatum inuasit. Relicto hic olim coenobio professus Romam, Laurentio archipresbytero se insinuauit, a quo magicas artes ac necromantiam didicit. Quas artes & ipse Laurentius adhuc iuuenis, a Syluestro papa secunda eius nominis, Sathanico monstro, inter alios baufit. Erat quidem peculiaris necessitudo inter illum Laurentium, Theophylactum, Ioannem Gratianum, atq; Hildebrandū, archipresbyteros seu Cardinales Romanæ synagogæ. Vnde apud eundem Theophylactum, dum esset in papatu officio sub nomine Benedicti noni, sua astutia Hildebrandus omnia egit: imo nihil erat actum usq; ad eius pontificatum sub aliis pontificibus, quod ab illius uo-tis alienum fuerat.
units.tr: Gregory the Seventh, Tuscan by nation and a native of Siena, was a Cluniac monk, called Hildebrand before. An impostor, enchanter and diabolical trickster, he seized the papacy by his accursed tyranny, as has been said. Having once professed in a monastery, he left it and came to Rome, where he insinuated himself with the archpriest Laurence, from whom he learned magic arts and necromancy. Laurence himself had learned these arts while still a young man from Pope Sylvester the Second, that Satanic monster, among others. There was indeed a peculiar close tie between that Laurence, Theophylact, John Gratian and Hildebrand, archpriests or Cardinals of the Roman synagogue. Hence, while Theophylact held office in the papacy under the name of Benedict the Ninth, Hildebrand by his cunning managed everything. Indeed, nothing had been done under other popes, up to his pontificate, that was foreign to his wishes.

units.la: Hic cum uellet, teste Benzone[?], manicas suas discutiebat, & in modum scintillarum ignis dissiliebat: atq; his miraculis simplicium oculos, uelut sanctitatis signo, ludificabat. Et quia diabolus (inquit) per paganos ipsos, Christum publicè persequi non poterat, per pseudomonachum, sub specie religionis, nomen eius fraudulenter subuertere disponebat.
units.tr: When he wished, as Benzo testifies, he would shake his sleeves, and sparks of fire would leap out like sparks from a flame; and by these miracles he deluded the eyes of simple people, as if they were a sign of holiness. And because the devil (he says) could not openly persecute Christ through the pagans themselves, he set about fraudulently subverting Christ's name through a pseudo-monk, under the appearance of religion.

units.la: Scribunt authores, per hunc Hildebrandum sex aut octo pontifices, Gerardi Brazuti ministerio, venenis enecatos esse: ut ita sterneretur ei ad papatum uia. Ille tamen in istis turbis callide sic omnia egit, ut suspicionem optatae sedis declinaret.
units.tr: Writers relate that through this Hildebrand six or eight popes were killed with poison by the ministry of Gerard Brazutus, so that a way to the papacy would be cleared for him. Yet in these disturbances he acted so cleverly in everything that he avoided suspicion of the see he desired.

units.la: Et cum nomine non esset pontifex, re ipsa tamen fuit ordinati pontificis & impiarum eius inventionum organum unicum: paulatimq; sub aliis pontificibus machinabatur, quod sub suo pontificatu reddidit effectum.
units.tr: And although he was not pope in name, in fact he was the sole instrument of the ordained pope and of his impious inventions. Little by little, under other popes, he was plotting what he brought to effect under his own papacy.

units.la: Infignū hy-pocrita, prætextu canonum & pietatis, iniustissima & impiissima quaeq; effecit. Alexandrum secundum, dominum ac magistrum suum, præsidia Cæsaris quærentem contra suos æmulos, accusa-sit[?], dicens: Non esse æquum, ut is iuxta canones pontificia dignitate gaudeat, qui contra canones auxilia peteret à profano principe. Et exautora-tum in vincula coniecit, ac latenter occidit: statim usurpans pontificiam sedem, in ipsius defuncti exequiis. Brazuto ac Judaeo quidam[?] familiaribus suis (ut refert Benno) pecuniam suam atq; cofilia[?] comunicauit: & per eos venales multorum linguas sibi comparauit. Qui altis clamabant vocibus, Alexandro nondum sepulto, Petrus Apostolus clegit Hildebrandum: atq; illum sub Gregorii septimi nomine in pontificiam sedem collocabant. Et hoc fiebat anno millesimo post excidium Hierusalem: in quo anno hi Satanae vicarii palam cæperunt si-bi vendicare Dei nomen, & officium atq; virtu-tes Christi veri Dei ac veri hominis. Nam in hu-ius Gregorii declaratione vel ordinatione, eodem anno proclamatum fuit, verum Christi vicarium esse creatum. Ipse quoque Gregorius aptauit si-bi, quæ psalmo 2. scripta sunt de Christo. Et mu-tauit leges Christi & Dei omnipotentis patris, prohibendo matrimonium sacerdotibus, & reges deturbando e foliis suis. Qui belli Gog & Magog, Apoc. 20. quo nullum unquam fuit vel perniciosius vel scelleratius, femina sparsit[?]: quæ & familiaris ipsius, Vrbanus secundus executus est. Sequentem historiam narrat Benno. Die quadam (inquit) cum de Albano Romam ueniret Gregorius, oblitus est ferre secum familiarem sibi librum Necromantiæ artis, sine quo nusquam aut raro incedebat. Quod cum in itinere ei ad memoriam redijset, in introitu portæ Lateranensis, sestinanter uocauit duos de familiaribus suis, assuetos et fidos ministros scelerum suorum. Et ut eundem librum citissime sibi afferrent, præcepit: ac terribiliter interminatus est, ne librum in uia aperire præsumerent, nec ulla curiositate secreta eius inuestigarent. Sed quanto amplius inhibuit, tanto uehementius eorum curiositatem ad inuestiganda eiusdem libri arcana accendit. Igitur dum in reditu librum referassent, et diabolicæ artis præcepta curiose legerent, subito affuerunt angeli Sathanæ, quorum multitudine & horrore duo illi iuuenes prope essi amentes, uix ad se reuersi sunt. Et (ut ipsi re-tulerunt) maligni spiritus instabant, dicentes: Ad quid nos uocastis? quare fatigastis? Cito præcipite, quod nos agere ultus, alioquin insurgemus in uos, si nos diutius tenueritis. Ad hoc alter iuuenum, sestinanter (inquit) muros illos deiicite. Et hæc dicens, manu ostendit muros altos uicinos Romæ, quos in momento maligni spiritus deiecerunt. Et juvenes sanctæ crucis signo se signantes, tanto terrore exterriti, trementes & palpitantes, vix Romam ad dominum suum pervenerunt. Hæc Binno[?].
units.tr: A remarkable hypocrite, under the pretext of the canons and of piety, he carried out every most unjust and most impious deed. He accused Alexander the Second, his lord and master, who was seeking the protection of Caesar against his rivals, saying it was not right that he should enjoy papal dignity according to the canons who sought help against the canons from a profane prince. Having deposed him, he cast him into chains and secretly killed him, at once seizing the papal see during the funeral rites of the dead man. As Benno relates, he shared his money and his plans with Brazutus and with a certain Jew who were his familiars, and through them bought for himself the tongues of many as if they were for sale. These men shouted loudly, while Alexander was not yet buried, that the Apostle Peter had chosen Hildebrand, and they set him in the papal see under the name of Gregory the Seventh. This happened in the thousandth year after the destruction of Jerusalem. In that year these vicars of Satan openly began to claim for themselves the name of God and the office and virtues of Christ, the true God and true man. For at the declaration or ordination of this Gregory, it was proclaimed in the same year that the true vicar of Christ had been created. Gregory himself applied to himself what is written of Christ in Psalm 2. He also changed the laws of Christ and of God the almighty Father, forbidding marriage to priests and deposing kings from their thrones. He scattered the seed of the war of Gog and Magog, Rev. 20, than which there never was anything more pernicious or wicked; and Urban the Second, his familiar, carried it out. Benno narrates the following story. "One day (he says), when Gregory was coming to Rome from Albano, he forgot to bring with him a book of the art of necromancy, which he always or almost always carried with him. When this came to his mind on the road, at the entrance of the Lateran gate, he hastily called two of his familiars, servants faithful and accustomed to his crimes, and ordered them to bring the same book to him as quickly as possible. He sternly forbade them to open the book on the way or to investigate its secrets by any curiosity. But the more he forbade it, the more violently he kindled their curiosity to investigate the mysteries of that book. So when they had brought the book back, and were reading the precepts of the diabolical art with curiosity, suddenly the angels of Satan were present, and the two young men, nearly out of their minds from their multitude and horror, could scarcely come to themselves. And (as they themselves reported) the evil spirits pressed upon them, saying: 'Why have you summoned us? Why have you wearied us? Quickly command what you want us to do, otherwise we will rise against you if you keep us any longer.' To this one of the young men said: 'Quickly, throw down those walls.' And saying this, he pointed with his hand to the high walls near Rome, which the evil spirits threw down in an instant." And the young men, signing themselves with the sign of the holy cross, trembling and quivering with such terror, scarcely reached Rome and their lord. Thus Benno.

units.la: Inito igitur pontificatu, statim cœpit urgere Canones antecessorum pontificum, de Simonia ac cœlibatu, quos fecerant, eius usi astuto consilio: non ob id, ut beneficiorum Ecclesiasticorum impiam nundinationem tolleret, sed ut aliqua ratione honesti, principibus eriperet potestatem conferendi Ecclesiastica officia. Et ut sic redigerentur sub seruitutem Romanæ sedis omnes episcopi, qui propter inuestituræ ius principibus erant magis obnoxij, quam pontifici Romano. Atq; cum omnium principum summus esset Imperator Henricus, ab ipso sibi faciendum esse exordium Simoniacæ tra-gœdiæ, arrogans nebulo censuit. Concilium Romæ apud Lateranum, super his ille conuocauit; sed bellis occupatus Cæsar, synodalibus contentionibus vacare non potuit. Tam erat cordi nihilo-minus res ea pontifici, ut eius gratia nec prodi-tionibus nec cædibus parceret: quin multis in lo-cis bella quoq; intestina, & omne calamitatum genus concitaret.
units.tr: So, at the beginning of his pontificate, he at once began to press the canons of his predecessors on simony and celibacy, which they had enacted, and he used them with cunning design. He did this not to remove the impious trafficking in ecclesiastical benefices, but so that, under a pretence of honesty, he could strip the princes of the power of conferring ecclesiastical offices. In this way all bishops would be brought under the servitude of the Roman see, since through the right of investiture they were more bound to the princes than to the Roman pontiff. And since the Emperor Henry was the highest of all the princes, that arrogant scoundrel judged that the tragedy of simony must begin with him. He summoned a council on these matters at Rome, at the Lateran; but the Emperor, occupied with wars, could not attend to synodal disputes. Nevertheless the pontiff cared so much for this matter that for its sake he spared neither treachery nor murder, and indeed in many places he stirred up civil wars and every kind of calamity.

units.la: Primo enim Imperatoris vitæ in-sidias struens, variis modis eundem tollere conatus est, adeo ut in ipso quoq; templo, inter preces illum perdere voluerit. Historiam sic recitat Cardinalis Benno. Imperator (inquit) solitus erat frequenter ire ad orationem, ad Ecclesiam S. Mariae, quae est in monte Aventino. Hildebrandus autem cum per exploratores suos omnia eius opera diligenter inquireret, locum in quo frequentius Imperator, vel stans vel prostratus, orabat, notari fecit. Et quendam promissa pecunia ad hoc induxit, ut supra trabes Ecclesiae (sanctum Papae consilii) occulte lapides magnos collocaret: et ita aptaret, ut de alto super caput orantis Imperatoris demitteret, et ipsum contereret. Quod minister tanti sceleris cum festinaret implere, et lapidem magni ponderis super trabes aptare vellet, lapis pondere suo eum traxit, ac fracta sub trabibus tabula, et lapis et ille miser homo, Dei iudicio, in pavimentum Ecclesiae cecidit, et eodem lapide contritus penitus est. Huius rei gestae ordinem postquam Romani cognoverunt, pedem illius miseri fune ligaverunt, et triduo per plateas urbis, ad exemplum trahi fecerunt. Imperator autem solita clementia iussit eum sepeliri. Idem Benno. Ioannes Portuensis episcopus, qui Hildebrando intimus a secretis erat, in Ecclesia S. Petri suggestum ascendens, inter cetera multa, audiente clero et populo, dicebat: Tale quid fecit Hildebrandus et nos, unde deberemus vivi incendi: significans de sacramento mento corporis Domini. Ut quod Hildebrandus, rè sponsa divina quaerens (atq; olim pagani à suis idolis) contra Imperatorem: fertur iniecisse igni, cum non responderet, contradicentibus Cardinalibus, qui assistebant ei. Dictumq; Imperatorem, sine legitima accusatione, sine Canonica vocatione, sine iudiciario ordine, obedientem etiam excommunicavit, regni sui principes ab eo separavit, et per occultos proditores perdere paravit: sed Deus illum custodivit. O nova proditio, procedens de sanctua-rio, imò de eo qui videbatur ut summus sacerdos Ecclesiam regere, ac senioribus iudicibus praeesse.
units.tr: First, plotting the emperor's life, he tried in various ways to remove him, so that he even wished to destroy him in the church itself, while he was at prayer. Cardinal Benno recounts the story thus: "The emperor," he says, "was accustomed often to go to prayer at the church of St Mary on the Aventine Hill. Hildebrand, however, having carefully inquired through his spies into all his habits, had the place noted where the emperor prayed most often, either standing or prostrate. He then induced a man, for a promised sum of money, to secretly place great stones on the beams of the church (the holy counsel of the pope), and to arrange them so that they would fall from above onto the head of the praying emperor and crush him. When the minister of so great a crime hastened to carry this out, and wished to fix a stone of great weight upon the beams, the stone dragged him down with its weight; the board beneath the beams broke, and the stone and that wretched man fell by God's judgement onto the pavement of the church, and he was utterly crushed by that same stone. When the Romans learned the order of this deed, they tied a rope to the foot of that wretch and had him dragged through the streets of the city for three days, as an example. The emperor, however, in his customary clemency, ordered him to be buried." The same Benno says: "John, bishop of Porto, who was Hildebrand's closest secretary, climbed into the pulpit of St Peter's and, among many other things, said in the hearing of clergy and people: 'Hildebrand and we have done such a thing that we ought to be burned alive,' meaning the sacrament of the body of the Lord." Hildebrand, seeking a divine bride, as the pagans once did with their idols, is said to have thrown the (Eucharistic) bread into the fire, against the emperor, when he did not answer, while the cardinals who stood by him objected. And he excommunicated the emperor, who was obedient, without lawful accusation, without canonical summons, without judicial process; he separated the princes of his realm from him and prepared to destroy him through secret traitors; but God protected him. O new treachery, proceeding from the sanctuary, indeed from him who seemed to rule the Church as chief priest and preside over the elders as judge!

units.la: Ab episcopis etiam cum terrore ac minis sacra-mentum exegit, ne eius causam defenderent, aut ei in aliquo fauerent, scripturis violenter intortis in adiutorium falsitatis. Ut primum veruntamen (in-quit Benno) ad excommunicandum Cæsarè, de se-de surrexit, sedes ipsa nouiter lignis fortissimis cõposita, subitò, Dei nutu terribiliter scissa est in plures partes: ut manifestè daretur intelligi, quòd tam praesumptuosa excommunicatione, sessor ille terribilia schismata contra Christi ecclesiam seminaret. Hæc Benno. Cum verò insidias minus succedere videret, aperte vi et inimicitijs uti cœpit: ac Herico excommunicato, omnes à fidelitatis (ut ipsi vocât) sacramento absoluês, imperij coronam Rodolpho Su. uorum duci,hoc barbaro uersu exornata transmisit:
units.tr: He also extracted an oath from the bishops, with terror and threats, that they would not defend his cause or favour him in anything, the Scriptures being violently twisted to support falsehood. "But as soon as," says Benno, "he rose from his seat to excommunicate the Caesar, that seat, lately made of the strongest timbers, was suddenly and terribly split into many pieces by the will of God, so that it might be clearly understood that that occupant of the seat, by so presumptuous an excommunication, was sowing terrible schisms against the Church of Christ." Thus Benno. When he saw that his plots were less successful, he began to use open force and hostility; and, absolving all from the oath of fidelity (as they call it) to Henry, the excommunicated man, he sent the imperial crown to Rodolph, duke of the Suevians, adorned with this barbarous verse:
The rock gave to Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rodolph.

units.la: Eam ob rem non parum turbatus Henricus, de positis ornamentis regalibus, cum uxore ac filio paruulo, in asperrima hyeme Canusium periculo-sissimo itinere ad illum uenit. In laneis uestibus, pe-dibus nudis spectaculum angelorum & hominum factus (inquit Benno) ante portas ciuitatis, a ma-ne usq; ad uesperam ieiunus uenia supplex petijt, Hildebrandi ludibria inter meretrices & mona-chos in lach ymabili afflictione triduo pertulit, cupiens ad illum intromitti, sed ingressus denega-batur: petenti in tantum per totum triduum, respondebatur (O pessime Antichriste) pontifici non esse adhuc otium colloquendi cum eo. Henricus eo quo animo ferens, se non intromitti in urbem, mansit in suburbio non sine magna incommoditate. Hyems nanq; solito crudelior erat, & cuncta ri-gescebant. Indesinenter tamen, ne quicquam offenderet, toto triduo permansit, petens sibi veniam dari. Tandemq; quarta scilicet die, rogantibus Mathilda comitissa, quae nimium (inquit historia) amabat Pontificem: & Cluniacen-sium mona-chorum abbate, Sabaudiaq; comite Adellao, ad pontificem intromittebatur. Postulanti vero ut[?]iam, iam[?], & eius potestati coronam offerenti, ponti-sex neq; uenianm[?] dare, neq; ab excommunicatione illum absoluere uoluit, nisi prius sponderet, se iu-acta sua decreta uelle culpam, quæ nulla erat, in sy-nodo expiare cum aliis conditionibus illicitis. Quæ omnia promisit, ac scripto confirmauit, non ta-men erat in regnum restitutus. Ea re cognita (in-quit Sleidanus lib. 3. de Monarchiis) quòd Cæsar Henricus cum Hildebrando in gratiam redijsset, proceres Italiæ uehementer offensi erant, quòd tã fœdè, tamq; indigné se submississet illi, qui p[illegible, ~4 letters] artibus papatum inuasisset, qui cædibus & adul-teriis omnia polluisset, &c. Pontifex inde cum Car-dinalibus non parum superbiens, quòd illum sub iugum misisset, maiora præsumere audebat: sed hæc omnia armis ille statim, monente Dei spiritu, uindicabat. Et post bella grauiter gesta, Rodol-phum prælio superauit. Qui Rodolphus, manu de-xtera mutilatus, iussit ad se accersiri episcopos & primores suæ conspirationis. Quibus præsentibus, allata ad se dextera, sic ait: Rectè mecum factum esse fateor. Hæc est manus, qua fidem ac iurifu-randi sacramentum præstiti domino meo Henri-co. Vobis autem urgentibus, toties tam infœlici-ter pugnaui contra illum, fidem q; uiolaui: idea sendignam accepi periurij mercedem. Videte an recta uia me duxeritis. Ite ergo & implete regi-uestro[?] primam fidem. Nam ego ad patres ibo. Sta timq; Rodolphus obijt. Eo sublato, alium pontifi-cis iussu creabant Imperatorem, Hermannum Saxo-nem, Lucelburgi comitem. Qui non ab, & Domini uoluntate, dum castellum quoddam in Germania oppugnaret, à fœmina, quae ex arce grande saxum deuoluit, occisus fuit. Nec adhuc coherceri potes-rat immanissimi huius tyranni malitia, quin ter-tium contra piissimum principem proditorem ex-citaret, nempe Egbertum quendam Marchio-nem, illius consanguineum. Sed & hic in incolen-dino quodam deprehensus, ab ipsis Caesarianis mi-ferè trucidatus fuit. Sic tutatus est Dominus fer-uum suum aduersus malignantis Satanae vicarium Papam: dum interim indiuidua comes Mathilda comitissa, spreto marito Azone Marchione Esten-si, eius lateri meretrix adhaereret, S. Petri filia di-cta. Unde factum est (scribit Lambertus Hirfuel[?] densis) quod omnes incesti amoris eos insimulaue-rint, dixerintq; passim, Mathildam frui fartiuis[?] co-plexibus Pontificis Romani: & consuetudinem il-licitam habere cum eo:qui & sacerdotibus bone-stum coniugium ademit. Abbas Vrspergensis, Con-radus à Lichtenau, haec addit in suo Chronico: Constat Hildebrandum non à Deo electum, sed a feipseipso, fraude ac pecunia intrufum. Qui Eccle-siasticum subuertit ordinem, Christiani imperij turbauit regnum, pacifico regi intendit mortem, per-iuros defendit, lites fouit, discordias seminauit, scan-dala suscitauit, diuortia fecit: & quicquid interpie-tiuentes recte stare uidebatur, concussit, &c. Pri-mus hic fuit (insignis hypocrita) qui per excommu-nicationes, Ecclesiae ministros uxoribus priuauit, ac innumerabilibus paederastijs mundum imple-uit. Ita ut illa ciuitas magna, quae uocatur spiritua-liter, Apoc. 11. Romana scilicet Ecclesia, sit deinceps ex praepostera uenere, atq; idolorum cultu, ipsissima Sodoma & Aegyptus. Mirabilesq; tragediae per Italiam, Galliam, Germaniam & Angliam fiebant, quas longum esset hoc loco narrare: & multis eius temporis doctis hominibus, hoc institutum displicuit. In Germania enim & Gallia 24. & adhuc plures episcopi fuerunt, qui una cum clero suarum diaecesium, coniugati fuerant, coniugiumq; suum constanter defenderant: ut de Anglia & Italia nihil dicam. Haec erant huius Satanici monstri acta pontificalia. Caelibatus uotum clericis praecepit, sub excommunicationis poena, monachis omnibus carnis usum uetuit, sabbati ieiunium Christianis imposuit, oblationes in missarum solennijs fieri decreuit, Liberium Arria-num num, haereticus haereticum, canonizauit, eius fi-stum (ut habet Benno) celebrari sanciuit[?], fideli-um ministrorum coniugia perpetuò profl gauit[?], su-is sacrificiis decimas jolui mandauit, & coronam per interdictum Poloniae regi ademit. Berenga-rij sanctissimi viri opinionem de sacramento dam-nauit, ac transsubstantiationem primus, ut fertur, praesticauit. Laicum decimas possidentem, sacri-legij investituras dantem, haereticos: & a laico re-cipientem, idololatriae censuris confirmixit. Sic plumbeum tandem pontificis gladium, adeò fir-tem reddidit, ut eius vi ferream imperij vim deim-ceps obtuderit. Haec & alia plura referunt papi-sta. Opposuit sese tum demum, iniquis Hildebran-di conatibus, imperator Henricus: & anno Do-mini 1083. in Brixiensi synodo, ubi obiectus eius crimimibus, pontificia sede illum merito deiecit, & alium pontificem, quem Clementem tertium vocabat, eius loco substituit. Copiasq; Romam ad eum expellendum misit, in D. Petri templum cum pontificali habitu Clementem introducens: ac ur-bem ad eam redegit inopiam, ut cogerentur pete-re pacem. Hildebrandus vero cum in conspectum Caesaris venire nollet, à Romanis desertus & re-iectus, Salernum fugit anno Domini 1086 ubi & vi-ta in exilio miser finiuit, qui tot gladio, fame, uen nis[?], atq; aliis mortium generibus peremerat. Illud tamen Satanæ organum, iactitant Papico[?] æ, multa tua post mortem clarere miraculis: postq; iam facere dos quidam in Saxonia moriens, Sigeberto teste, in inferno illum cruciari vidisset. Referunt Antoninus ac Vincentius, Hildebrandum ipsum in ultimo vitæ suæ articulo ad se vocasse Cardinalem quendam, ac esse professum, se graviter offendisse, quod suadente diabolo, simultates, inimicitias, odia et bella inter multos excitaverit, iussu[?] q; illum adire Imperatorem Henricum, et ab eo admissorum fa-cinorum veniam petere. Contra hunc Hildebrandum scripserunt Hugo Candidus cardinalis Præ-positus, Vualramus episcopus Niemburgensis, Ve-ricus Vercellensis episcopus, Rolandus Parmensis sacerdos, Sigebertus Gemblacensis, atq; alij multi. Et Benno 13 Cardinales enumerat, qui illum acriter impugnabant.
units.tr: For this reason Henry, not a little troubled, put off the royal insignia and, with his wife and small son, came to him at Canossa, by a most perilous journey in the harshest winter. Dressed in woollen garments, with bare feet, made a spectacle to angels and men (as Benno says), he sought pardon as a suppliant before the gates of the city, fasting from morning until evening. For three days he endured Hildebrand's mockeries among prostitutes and monks in a pitiable affliction, desiring to be admitted to him, but he was refused entry; and to his request, throughout the whole three days, the answer was given (O most wicked Antichrist) that the pontiff did not yet have leisure to speak with him. Henry, bearing this with what spirit he could, since he was not admitted into the city, remained in the suburb, not without great discomfort. For the winter was harsher than usual, and everything was stiff with cold. Yet, so as not to give offence in anything, he remained for the whole three days without ceasing, asking that pardon be granted him. Finally, on the fourth day, at the request of Matilda the countess, who (as the history says) loved the pontiff too much, and of the abbot of Cluny, and of Count Adelao of Savoy, he was admitted to the pontiff. When he asked for pardon and offered him the crown and his authority, the pontiff would neither grant pardon nor absolve him from excommunication, unless he first promised that he would atone, in a synod, for his acts, which were not sinful, by his own decrees, along with other unlawful conditions. All these things he promised and confirmed in writing, yet he was not restored to his kingdom. When this became known (says Sleidanus, book 3 of De Monarchiis), because the emperor Henry had returned to favour with Hildebrand, the princes of Italy were greatly offended that he had submitted himself so shamefully and so indignantly to one who had invaded the papacy by wicked arts, who had polluted everything with murders and adulteries, and so on. The pontiff, then not a little proud with his cardinals because he had sent him under the yoke, dared to presume greater things; but the emperor at once avenged all these things by arms, the Spirit of God prompting him. And after serious wars, he overcame Rodolph in battle. Rodolph, mutilated in his right hand, ordered the bishops and chief men of his conspiracy to be summoned to him. When they were present, he had his right hand brought to him and said: "I confess I have been justly treated by me. This is the hand with which I pledged faith and the sacred oath to my lord Henry. But at your urging I have so often fought against him so unhappily, and have violated my faith; therefore I have received the worthy reward of perjury. See whether you have led me on the right path. Go then, and restore to your king his first faith. For I go to my fathers." And Rodolph died at once. With him removed, they created another emperor by the pontiff's command, Hermann the Saxon, count of Luxemburg. He, not by the will of the Lord, while he was besieging a certain castle in Germany, was killed by a woman who rolled a great stone down from the citadel. Nor could the malice of this most savage tyrant yet be restrained, but he stirred up a third traitor against that most pious prince, namely a certain Marquis Egbert, his kinsman. But he too, caught in a certain village, was wretchedly slaughtered by the Caesarians themselves. Thus the Lord protected his servant against the vicar of Satan, the Pope who fights against him; meanwhile the countess Matilda, having scorned her husband Azo, Marquis of Este, clung to his side as a prostitute, called the daughter of St Peter. Whence it came about (writes Lambert Hirsfeld) that all accused them of an incestuous love, and said everywhere that Matilda enjoyed the secret embraces of the Roman pontiff and had an unlawful relationship with him, who also took away the honourable marriage of priests. The abbot of Ursperg, Conrad of Lichtenau, adds this in his chronicle: "It is established that Hildebrand was not chosen by God, but thrust himself in by fraud and money. He overthrew the ecclesiastical order, disturbed the kingdom of the Christian empire, plotted the death of a peaceful king, defended perjurers, fostered quarrels, sowed discords, stirred up scandals, brought about divorces, and shook whatever seemed to stand rightly among the pious, etc." He was the first (the notable hypocrite) who, through excommunications, deprived the ministers of the Church of their wives, and filled the world with countless acts of sodomy. So that great city, which is called spiritually in Revelation 11, namely the Roman Church, became thereafter, through perverse lust and the worship of idols, Sodom and Egypt itself. Wonderful tragedies were occurring throughout Italy, France, Germany and England, which would take too long to narrate here; and this institution displeased many learned men of that time. For in Germany and France there were twenty-four and even more bishops who, together with the clergy of their dioceses, had been married and had steadfastly defended their marriages, not to mention England and Italy. These were the pontifical acts of this satanic monster. He commanded celibacy for the clergy under penalty of excommunication, forbade all monks the use of flesh, imposed the Sabbath fast on Christians, decreed that offerings be made at the solemn celebrations of the Mass, canonized Liberius the Arian, a heretic canonizing a heretic, decreed that his feast (as Benno has it) be celebrated, sanctioned that the marriages of faithful ministers be perpetually condemned, ordered that tithes be paid for his sacrifices, and by an interdict took the crown from the king of Poland. He condemned the opinion of the most holy man Berengar concerning the sacrament, and was the first, as is reported, to bring in transubstantiation. He confirmed with censures of idolatry the laymen who held tithes, who gave investitures of sacrilege, the heretics, and those who received from a layman. Thus at last he made the leaden sword of the pontiff so strong that by its force it has afterwards blunted the iron power of the empire. These and many other things the papists report. Then at last the emperor Henry set himself against the wicked attempts of Hildebrand; and in the year of the Lord 1083, in the synod of Brixen, where his crimes were laid before him, he justly deposed him from the pontifical see and set in his place another pontiff, whom he called Clement the Third. He also sent troops to Rome to drive him out, and introduced Clement into the temple of St Peter in pontifical dress; and he reduced the city to such want that they were forced to seek peace. But Hildebrand, since he would not come into the presence of Caesar, was deserted and rejected by the Romans, and fled to Salerno in the year of the Lord 1086, where he miserably ended his life in exile, he who had destroyed so many by sword, famine, poison, and other kinds of death. Yet the papists boast that this instrument of Satan performed many miracles after his death; indeed some man in Saxony, dying, is said (as Sigebert testifies) to have seen him tormented in hell. Antoninus and Vincent report that Hildebrand himself, at the last point of his life, called to him a certain cardinal and professed that he had grievously offended, because, at the urging of the devil, he had stirred up enmities, hatreds, and wars among many, and he ordered him to go to the emperor Henry and ask pardon from him for the crimes he had committed. Against this Hildebrand wrote Hugh Candidus, cardinal and provost, Walram bishop of Naumburg, Veric bishop of Vercelli, Roland a priest of Parma, Sigebert of Gembloux, and many others. And Benno enumerates thirteen cardinals who fiercely opposed him.
99. VICTOR the third.

units.la: Victor tertius, natione Italus, Desiderius antea vocatus, abbas Casinensis, et Romanæ curiæ Cardinalis, Papatum iniit, non Cardinalium aut Romani populi suffragijs electus, sed a Matilda meretrice ac suæ factionis Normannis intrusus. Qui assumpto mox papatu, Gregorij successor constitutus, Gregorij ipsius partes, à dicta Matilda eius amatrice edoctus, fortiter tueri coepit, & monachus monachum defendere aduersus Imperatorem & Clementem eius Papam, indignum ratus, ab eiusdem sui praedecessoris diabolicis moribus degenerare. Sed ne illud animi virus, quod odio plus quàm Neroniano in eos conceperat, publica aliqua pernicie expueret, vetuit mors, quæ anno Domini 1088, citius opinione sua, vitam cum Papatu finiuit. Tradunt authores, Hermannus Contractus, Carsulanus, Pramonstratensis, et alii plures, veneno per suum ministrum subdiaconum, dum missaret, in calicem iniecto, periisse illum. Vincentius tamen (ut Platina scribit) longè aliter sentit, quum dysenteria interiisse hominem dicat, quod neque à suspicione dati veneni alienum est. Nam & in dysenteriam, veneno petiti, interdum incidunt, corruptis & labefactatis intestinis. Aliqui Papistarum ab Henrico Cæsare, alij à Clementè pontifice id procuratum esse, maliciose fingunt: cum sit à suo ipsius capellano subdiacono Si-cinus editum. Sunt qui eo tempore multa prodigia apparuisse scribant, quòd & aues domesticæ, utpote gallinæ, anseres, columbæ, pauones, ad lo-ca montana confugerint, sylvestresq; fiunt facta, & pisces tum fluviales tum marini magna expar-te perierint. Terræmotu etiam quædam urbes
units.tr: Victor the third, an Italian by birth, previously called Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and a cardinal of the Roman court, entered upon the papacy. He was not chosen by the votes of the cardinals or the Roman people but was thrust in by Matilda the harlot and by the Normans of his faction. Once he had taken up the papacy, having been made successor to Gregory, he was taught by Matilda, that harlot who was his lover, and he began to defend vigorously the cause of Gregory himself. A monk, he thought it unworthy to defend a monk against the Emperor and his Pope Clement, and he regarded it as degenerate to depart from the devilish ways of his own predecessor. But death, which came in the year of the Lord 1088, sooner than he expected, prevented him from spitting out in some public destruction the poison of his mind, which he had conceived against them with a hatred more than Neronian, and ended his life along with his papacy. Hermann the Lame, the Carsulan, the Premonstratensian, and many others, relate that he perished by poison, which his minister, a subdeacon, poured into the chalice while he was celebrating mass. Vincentius, however (as Platina writes), thinks quite otherwise, since he says the man died of dysentery, which is not foreign to the suspicion of poison given. For those who have been attacked with poison sometimes fall into dysentery as well, when the intestines are corrupted and weakened. Some of the Papists maliciously pretend that the deed was done by Henry the Emperor, others by Pope Clement; yet it was put into effect by Sicinus, his own chaplain and subdeacon. There are those who write that many portents appeared at that time: domestic birds, such as hens, geese, doves and peacocks, fled to mountain places and became wild, and a great part of the fish, both river fish and sea fish, perished. Some cities also were shaken by an earthquake,

units.la: Vrè[?] concussæ sunt, ut Syracusis maior basilica corruens, dum vespera canerentur, omnes qui tum in templo aderant, duobus exceptis, contriverit.
units.tr: as at Syracuse, where the greater basilica collapsed while the evening hymns were being sung, and crushed all who were then present in the temple, except two.
100. URBAN the second.

units.la: VRbanus secundus, patria (ut fertur) Hetruscus, Otho antea dictus, monachus Cluniacensis, & sub Hildebrando cardinalis Hostiensis, per eos in-mito Imperatore ad Papatum venit: Matildam sci-licet meretricem, ac Normannos Apuliae domi-nos, qui & Victorem intruxerant. Is ille est Hilde-brandi discipulus ac pedissequus, quem Benno cardinalis Turbanum cotemptim vocat, caecum, schismaticum, haereticum, & Liberij Arriani socium. Qui, ne venenum, inquit, erroris[?] eorum percipe-retur, quasi mel veneficorum more admiscuit. Scri-pturas enim intentione fallendi mendacijs assutè addidit: & in errore cum suo Hildebrando perse-verans, cum angelis apostatis in abyssum relega-tus est. Vrbanus (inquiunt quidam nostri tempo-ris scriptores) turbator orbis, vel potius turbo & procella urbium, Hildebrando familiaris: permi-ciosa illa rigavit, fovit & produxit feminam, quae ipse jamdudum sparserat. Guibertum Rauenna-te, qui & Clemens tertius dicebatur, quod esset ab imperatore electus, Imperatoremq; ipsum excom-muni[?] municauit: atq; ab eodem Clemente, ut Vincentius refert, & ille uiolissim ex communicatus sit. Disputationibus etiam tam inter clerum quàm populum, cuncta illis diebus apud Germanos & alias nationes turbulentissimè perstrepuerunt. Cum autem Vrbanus neminem vellet absoluere, quem dictus Hildebrandus ligasset, de vitae periculo timens, latenter ab urbe decessit. Et multas ỹ nodos celebrauit: primum in Melphi, secundam Troia in Apulia, tertiam Placentiae, quartam in Clavo monte, anno Domini 1094. & quintam Turonis. In quibus Hildebrandi pestilentissimi nebulosis actis confirmauit, & nouas leges Ecclesiasticas tulit, ne quid de pontificia authoritate ui ut[?] fraude acquisitum deperiret. Sanciit[?], ne à quouis principe beneficiorum inuestituram clericus reciperet. Ecclesiasticos quosdam, cum Caesare Henrico sentientes, aduersarios habuit. Ad Matildam igitur, ueterem Ecclesiae amicam, ac S. Petri filiam, scripsit: & suam synagogam contra illos Christianos, quos haereticos uocat, fortiter suis fraudibus armauit. Archiepiscopo Mediolanensi praeterea pallium dedit, & Cartusiensium ac Cistercensium monachorum sectas confirmauit. Vacantes uxoribus post diaconatus ordinem, officiis suis priuauit: & presbyterorum filios à sacris exclusit officia [?]sijs.Archiepiscopum Toletanum in eius uerba iu-rantem, totius Hispaniæ primatem fecit, ut per eam uiam Hispanias totas sibi subijceret Romana bestia. Principes Christianos ad arma contra Saracenos concitauit, sub recuperandæ Hierosolymæ spe: trecentaq; hominum millia cruce sig nati, dum ille ipse res suas ad diaboli patris sui voluptatem ageret domi. Regem Galatiæ exebrabatur, quòd episcopum incarceraret, & iuramenta ab ordinandis exegit, cum hac clausula: Ita me Deus adiuuet, et hæc sancta Dei Euangelia. Statuta quædam edidit, scilicet ut horæ D. virginis (res valde necessaria) à clericis quotidie dicerentur, eidemq; uirgini Sabbati diem cum Missa dicauit. Neminem ad Papisticos ordines admittendum esse decreuit, nisi sit uirgo: hoc est, inconiugatus, scortator uel Sodomita, uel uterq;, ut acta probant. Sacerdotes uero uxoribus carere oportebat, nō scortis. Episcopos ordinari sine titulis uetuit, atq; idem seruari illis quos Papæ excommunicarent. [?]annem Paganum, Romanum ciuem, timens, in domo cuiusdam Petri Leonis biennio latuit, ubi & decessit anno Domini 1099, cadauerq; eius trans Tyberim, clam metu inimicorum, delatum fuit. Gulbertus etiam, qui & Clemens tertius, eodem anno obijt, cum tres Papas sub se mortuos uidisset,
units.tr: Urban the second, a native (as is said) of Tuscany, previously called Otho, a monk of Cluny, and under Hildebrand a cardinal of Ostia, came to the papacy through those same means, the Emperor being an intruder: namely, through Matilda the harlot and the Normans, lords of Apulia, who had also thrust in Victor. This is that disciple and follower of Hildebrand whom Benno the cardinal scornfully calls "Turbanus," blind, schismatic, heretical, and a companion of Arius Liberius. "So that the poison of their error might not be perceived," he says, "he mixed it in, like honey, after the manner of poisoners." For, with the intention of deceiving, he cunningly added lies to the Scriptures, and persisting in error with his Hildebrand, he was banished into the abyss with the apostate angels. Urban (say certain writers of our time), disturber of the world, or rather whirlwind and storm of cities, a familiar of Hildebrand, watered, nursed and brought forth that pernicious woman who had long before sown those very things. He ordained Guibert of Ravenna, who was also called Clement the third because he had been elected by the Emperor, and he excommunicated the Emperor himself; and, as Vincentius reports, he was himself most violently excommunicated by the same Clement. Disputations also, both among the clergy and among the people, raged most turbulently in those days among the Germans and other nations. But since Urban did not wish to absolve anyone whom the said Hildebrand had bound, and fearing for his life, he secretly left the city. He held many councils: first at Melfi, second at Troia in Apulia, third at Piacenza, fourth on Mount Clermont, in the year of the Lord 1094, and a fifth at Tours. In these he confirmed the cloudy acts of the most pestilent Hildebrand, and passed new ecclesiastical laws, lest anything acquired by force or fraud concerning papal authority should perish. He decreed that no cleric should receive investiture of benefices from any prince. He had some ecclesiastics as opponents, who sided with the Emperor Henry. Therefore he wrote to Matilda, the old friend of the Church and daughter of St Peter, and strongly armed his synagogue with her deceits against those Christians whom he calls heretics. Moreover, he gave the pallium to the archbishop of Milan, and confirmed the sects of the Carthusian and Cistercian monks. He deprived of their offices those who were married after the order of deacon; and he excluded from sacred offices the sons of presbyters. He made the archbishop of Toledo, who swore to his words, primate of all Spain, so that by that way the Roman beast might subject all Spain to itself. He stirred up Christian princes to arms against the Saracens, under the hope of recovering Jerusalem; and three hundred thousand men, marked with the cross, went forth, while he himself, at home, carried on his own affairs for the pleasure of the devil, his father. He railed against the king of Galatia because he had imprisoned a bishop, and he exacted oaths from those being ordained, with this clause: "So may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God." He issued certain statutes, namely that the hours of the Blessed Virgin (a thing very necessary) should be said daily by the clergy, and he dedicated the Saturday to that same Virgin with a mass. He decreed that no one was to be admitted to the Papistical orders unless he were a virgin, that is, unmarried, a fornicator or a sodomite, or both, as the acts prove. But priests indeed ought to be without wives, not without whores. He forbade bishops to be ordained without titles, and he ordained that the same should be observed for those whom the Pope excommunicated. Fearing John Pagan, a Roman citizen, he lay hidden for two years in the house of a certain Peter Leo, where he also died in the year of the Lord 1099; and his corpse, secretly, for fear of his enemies, was carried across the Tiber. Guibert also, who was called Clement the third, died in the same year, after he had seen three popes die under him.

units.la: De prædicto Hildebrando, & hoc Turbano eius discipulo, sic scribit Theodorus Bibliander, Ad omnium ordinum principes: Hildebrandus, inquit, concitando imperatorem Græcum contra Turcas, femina iecit expeditionis Gog & Magog. In quem clamat sanguis Ecclesiæ, gladio linguæ eius miserabili perditione effusus. Quæ lingua ue-ro, aut quis calamus posset exprimere fatis, quantum sanguinis Christiani, & omnium prope nati-onum, profundi curauerit Vrbanus secundus: ut sub prætexu expeditionis pro Christiana religione propaganda, & recuperando sepulchro Domini, in sedem Romanam, oppressa factione Gui-bertina, restitueretur? Nota impostura hanc insignem.
units.tr: Concerning the aforesaid Hildebrand, and this Turbanus his disciple, Theodor Bibliander writes thus, in his address to the princes of all orders: "Hildebrand," he says, "by stirring up the Greek emperor against the Turks, cast forth, through a woman, the expedition of Gog and Magog. Against him cries the blood of the Church, poured out in wretched ruin by the sword of his tongue. But what tongue or what pen could express sufficiently how much Christian blood, and almost of all nations, Urban the second caused to flow deep, so that under the pretext of an expedition to propagate the Christian religion and to recover the sepulchre of the Lord, the Roman see, with the Guibertine faction overthrown, might be restored?" Note this notable imposture.
101. Paschal II.

units.la: Paschalis secundus, natione Italus vel Thuscus, ex Flaminia oriundus, & Raynerus monachus antea dictus: presbyter Cardinalis D. Clementis ab Hildebrando olim præceptore factus, Vrbano secundo in Papatu successit. Hic cum se eligendum cerneret, sellam pontificiam ascendere noluit, superbissimus ne bulo, prius quàm populus ter acclamasset: Sanctus Petrus Raynerum virum optimum elegit. Indutus deinde coccinea chlamyde (iuxta illud Apoc. 17. Et mulier erat circundata pur-pura[?] purâ[?] & coccino,&c. )thiaraq; capiti eius impofi-ta,deducebatur albo equo uectus, in Lateranum, ubi Pontificium sceptrum illi dabatur, ac balthea cingebatur: de quo clauis septem, & totidem fi-gilla dependebant,tàquam Papicæ potestatis symbola(ita se exaltabat magnus ille Dei aduersarius & Antichristus)quibus ius Papæ datum esse signi-ficabat,secundum septiformem S. Spiritus gratiam (abominatio inaudita) Ecclesias claudendi & aperiendi,obsignandi et resignădi.Hoc modo,ait Funeius,equus meretrix,uirilem ætatem nacta, in be-stiam illam decacornem ascendit: quam & usq; ad nostram ætatem magno saltu rexit, ut prædictum est in Apoc, cap.13 & 17. Totum uitæ cursum in bellis gerendis ac seditionibus absoluit hic summum[?] in terris Satanæ uicarius. Et ne ulla in re impijssi-mo Hildebrando haberetur inferior, omnia expe-riebatur,quæ ad amplitudinem Satanicæ sedis per-tinere uidebantur.Episcopos omnes atq; abbates, à Cæsare constitutos, sedibus furiose depositi. Al-bertum quendam, Theodoricum ac Magimulphū, Papatum ambientes,in exilium pepulit. Romæ cū episcopis Italiæ & Galliæ concilium indixit,anno Domini 1101[?] ob Fluctini præsulis de nato Antichri-sto opinione,ut habet Sabellicus.Ipsum namq; dixe-rat tunc esse manifestum,cum uidisset in ecclesijs tot mala fieri: sed multis iniuriis illum repressit. Nu-ptias sacerdotibus, Hildebrandum secutus, iterum probauit[?], Nicolaitarum haeresim appellans: et Romanae Pontificis obedientiam uel censuram negligere, ac sacerdotij inuestitionem à profana manu agnoscere, haereses esse maximas pronunciauit. Statutum renouauit de decimis, subministratoribus dandis, et earum decimarum uenditiones peccata in spiritum esse uoluit. Excommunicationem in Henricum quartum, piissimum principem, in eadem synodo renouabat ac promulgabat. Imo in tantum saeuit huius immanissimi tyranni in illum rabies, ut et eius filium Henricum quintum (dictu certe horrendum) in arma contra patrem excitaret. Quid unquam atrox et crudele, si hoc non fit? Filius, et ut unicus, non aliqua uel priuata uel publica iniuria irritatus, patrem non spernit modo, non deserit, non suo destituit auxilio: sed insuper armis petit, obsidione premit, proditione circumuentum capit, imperio spoliat, et miserum captumq;, triste mortem obire patitur.
