Et haec quidem (inquit Rodolphus Gualterus) nō alicuius barbari tyranni iussu, non Phalaridis alicuius instinctu, sed sanctissimi patris (si diis placet) consilio fiunt. Gaudete, inquit, nunc Caligulae, exultate Nerones, et quotquot unquam crudelitatis nomine [illegible, ~2 letters] fussis[?] celebres. Habetu erim, qui dum uos longo po,t fe r eli qu t spacio, infamia & diri nominis me moria liberat: Romanum uidelicet pontificem, quum in patris uiscera fili gladium stringi praecipit Hec ille. Nec ita conquieuit horribilis monstri,. Papae huius, odium, quum in mortuum eius cadauer rabide saeuierit, exhumari per literas[?] iusserit[?], extra Ecclesiam proiici, a Leodio ad Spiram transRheni[?], & quinquennio carere Christiana sepultura. Sic regem honorabat, 1. Petri 2. sic Dei institutis obeduit, Rom. 13. superbissimus Antichristus. Sed attende quid interim fecerit Deus. Sanguis (teste Vrspergense[?] chronographo) ex panibus fluxit Spirae, in signum pontificiae tyrannidis. Guar-dastalli[?] anno Domini 1106. conuentum principum & episcoporum habuit, cum quibus egit de rebus fidei, ad culmen pertinentibus, utpote de homagijs, studijs, & episcoporum sacramentis, laicis prius exhibitis. Rauennatem quoq; archiepiscopum terris suis spoliauit, sibi ipsi eas adijciens. Cum ue-rò recusaret, episcopos confirmare ab Henrico quinto constitutos, ab eodem Imperatore post pe-dum oscula capitur, & in carcerem truditur: nec inde educitur, donec omnes confirmaret: inuesti-endius[?], Carolo Magno datum, diplomate resti-tuerit, atq; ipsum Imperatorem confirmaret. Dum in cathedra, inquit Massæus, post Missam se con-tineret Pontifex, ecce milites clamantes, Reddi-te quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari: tam ipsum quàm totum clerum inuaserunt & abduxerunt, exuerunt-que vestibus adeo nudos, ut ne femoralia reliquerint eis, atq; ita spoliatos apud montem Soractis custodiæ mancipauerunt, &c. Compositis tandem dissidijs, & Henrico Imperij diademate insignito, Paschali ei renouabat priuilegium de prælatorum inuestituris: & coram tota Ecclesia pronunciabat, omnes anathematis reos, quotquot datum priuilegium irritum duxerint. Cantatumq; est deinde, Gloria in excelsis Deo: quòd pax esset inter Cæsarem & Papam confirmata. Sed eo in Germaniam regressō, singula & omnia quæ magnis iuramentis promiserat, perfidus ac periurus revocauit, afferens se non sponte, sed coactè in Cæsaris uenisse sententiam. Priuilegium inde damnatur, Cæsarq; excommunicatur, & mirabiles tragœdiæ fiunt, quæ per omnia regna mox publicantur. Apud Trecas, in Campania Gallicana, sy-nodum conuocauit, in qua Gallorum sacerdotibus ademit coniugia: sicut ante eius tempora Hilde-brandus Germanis, quibusdam ecclesiarum antisti-tibus e sedibus suis propter ipsa coniugia pulsis. Pontificiam authoritatem amplificare adhuc cu-piens piens[?] , contentionem de dandis episcopatibus re-suscitabat , quae fuerat maximae cladis occasio per uniuersas Europae regiones. Anselmus Anglorum archiepiscopus & monachus , sophisticis perfua-sionibus huius pontificis , sicut & Vrbani praedecessoris , augebat impudentiam : eorum Romae con-sulior[?] , & in Anglia uicarius. Qui Anselmus Henricum primum Anglorum regem, regio iure in ministerijs assignandis, ab Israelitarum regibus, Dauide, Salomone, Iosaphato, Ezechia, Iosia , & aliis Dei authoritate usurpato, tyrannice priuauit , etiam contra illud Christi seruatoris dictum, Luc. 22. Reges gentium dominantur, &c. uos autem non sic. Presbyterorum legitimas nuptias , in Anglia perpetuo, ut dictum est, damnauit, contra sanctissimas utriusque Testamenti leges , & primitiuae Ecclesiae manifesta exempla: ut Satana suggerente, in omni Sodomia, Draconi diabolo, atque eius uicario Antichristo , clerus illic inseruiret. Et alias impostoras fecit. Paschalis autem multarum iniquitatum seminator, anno Domini 1118[?]. carnis indumenta deposuit.
units.tr: Paschal II, an Italian or Tuscan by birth, a native of Flaminia, formerly called the monk Rainer, was made presbyter cardinal of St Clement by his former tutor Hildebrand, and succeeded Urban II in the papacy. When he saw that he was being chosen, the most arrogant knave refused to mount the papal chair until the people had acclaimed three times: "Saint Peter has chosen Rainer, an excellent man." Then, clothed in a scarlet cloak (in accordance with Apoc. 17: "And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet," etc.), with a tiara placed on his head, he was carried on a white horse to the Lateran, where the papal sceptre was given to him and he was girded with a belt. From this hung seven keys and as many seals, as symbols of papal power (so did that great adversary of God and Antichrist exalt himself), signifying that the pope had been given the right, according to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit (an unheard-of abomination), to shut and open churches, to seal and unseal them. In this way, says Funeius, the horse, the harlot, having reached maturity, mounted that ten-horned beast, which she has ridden with a great leap even to our own age, as was foretold in Apoc. chapters 13 and 17. This highest vicar of Satan on earth spent the whole course of his life waging wars and stirring up sedition. And lest he be thought inferior in any respect to the most impious Hildebrand, he tried everything that seemed to pertain to the enlargement of Satan's see. He furiously deposed all the bishops and abbots appointed by the Emperor from their sees, and drove into exile Albert, Theodoric and Magimulf, who were canvassing for the papacy. At Rome, in the year of the Lord 1101 [?], he called a council with the bishops of Italy and Gaul, on account of the opinion of Bishop Fluctinus that Antichrist had been born, as Sabellicus reports. For Fluctinus had then said that it was manifest, since he saw so many evils being done in the churches; but the pope suppressed him with many injuries. Following Hildebrand, he again approved marriage for priests, calling it the heresy of the Nicolaitans. He pronounced it the greatest of heresies to neglect obedience to or the censure of the Roman pontiff, or to acknowledge the investiture of the priesthood from a profane hand. He renewed the statute on giving tithes for the support of ministers, and declared that the sale of those tithes was a sin against the Spirit. In the same synod he renewed and promulgated excommunication against Henry IV, a most pious prince. Indeed, the rage of this most savage tyrant against him ran so high that he also stirred up Henry V, the son, against his father (horrible to say). What could be more atrocious and cruel? The son, an only son, provoked by no injury, private or public, not only scorns his father and does not desert him or withdraw his support, but moreover attacks him with arms, presses him with a siege, captures him surrounded by treachery, strips him of his rule, and allows the wretched captive to meet a sad death. And these things (says Rudolf Walter) are done not at the command of some barbarian tyrant, nor at the instigation of some Phalaris, but at the counsel of the most holy father (if it pleases the gods). "Rejoice now, Caligulas, exult, Neros, and whoever have been celebrated for the name of cruelty: for you have a man who, though long left behind by you in time, frees you from infamy and from the memory of a dreadful name, namely the Roman pontiff, when he orders the sword to be drawn into a son's vitals against his father." So far he. Nor did the pope's hatred of this horrible monster end there: when he raged savagely against the dead body, he ordered it to be exhumed by letter, cast out of the Church, carried from Liège to Speyer across the Rhine, and to go five years without Christian burial. Thus he honoured the king (1 Pet. 2.); thus he opposed the ordinances of God (Rom. 13.), the most arrogant Antichrist. But observe what God meanwhile did: blood (as the chronicler Ursperg attests) flowed from the bread at Speyer, as a sign of papal tyranny. At Guardastalla, in the year of the Lord 1106, he held a meeting of princes and bishops, with whom he dealt with matters of faith pertaining to the highest concerns, namely the homages, the studies, and the sacraments of bishops, previously conferred by laymen. He also stripped the archbishop of Ravenna of his lands, adding them to his own. But when the archbishop refused to confirm bishops appointed by Henry V, he was seized by the same Emperor after kissing his feet and thrown into prison, nor was he released until he had confirmed them all; he restored the investiture granted to Charlemagne by charter, and confirmed the Emperor himself. "While the pontiff was sitting in his chair after Mass," says Masseus, "behold, soldiers shouting, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's,' attacked him and the whole clergy with him, led them away, and stripped them of their clothes so completely that they left them not even their breeches; and so despoiled they were consigned to custody near Mount Soracte," etc. At length, the quarrels being settled and Henry invested with the imperial crown, Paschal renewed for him the privilege concerning the investiture of prelates, and declared before the whole Church that all who regarded the privilege as void were liable to anathema. Then the song "Glory to God in the highest" was sung, because peace had been confirmed between Emperor and Pope. But when the Emperor had returned to Germany, faithless and perjured, he revoked each and every thing he had promised with great oaths, asserting that he had come to the Emperor's sentence not willingly but under compulsion. The privilege was then condemned, the Emperor was excommunicated, and wonderful tragedies occurred, which were soon published throughout all kingdoms. At Troyes in Gallic Champagne he called a synod, in which he took marriage away from the priests of Gaul, just as Hildebrand had earlier done to the Germans, driving some bishops from their sees on account of their marriages. Still wishing to magnify papal authority, he revived the contention over the giving of bishoprics, which had been the occasion of the greatest disaster throughout the regions of Europe. Anselm, archbishop and monk of the English, by the sophistical persuasions of this pope (as also of his predecessor Urban), increased the impudence: he was their adviser at Rome and their vicar in England. This Anselm tyrannically deprived Henry I, king of the English, of his royal right in assigning ministries, a right which the kings of Israel, David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah and others had exercised by the authority of God; he did so also against the saying of Christ the Saviour, Luke 22.: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them," etc., "but you shall not be so." In England he condemned the lawful marriages of presbyters for ever, as has been said, against the most holy laws of both Testaments and the manifest examples of the primitive Church, so that, at Satan's suggestion, throughout all Sodom the clergy there might serve the dragon, the devil, and his vicar Antichrist. And he made other impostures. Paschal, sower of many iniquities, put off the garments of flesh in the year of the Lord 1118.

units.la: Ex Matthaei Parisij chronicorum libro 2. Huius Paschalis tempore , anno Domini 1103[?]. cum Anselmus Cantuariensis archiepiscopus , regem Henricum primum , Romae coram illo accusaret (cui potius ex diuino præcepto obediuisset) quòd quosdam episcopos & abbates ordinasset: Guilhelmus Vuareluuast, procurator atq; cleri- cus ipsius regis, pro eius iure respondens, inter cae- tera constanter dicebat, non velle regem pro regni amissione prælatorum imvestituris privari. Ad hæc Papa: Si, quemadmodum dicis, rex tuus nec pro regni sui periclitatione, donationes Ecclesiarum à se alienari pateretur: scias præcise, coram Deo loquor, quia nec pro sui capitis precio (superbissimus Satan) eas ei impune permitterem. Qui- bus finitis, Anselmus rogabat, ut Papa, contem- pto rege, degradatus manum imponeret. Tunc se- des clementissima, inquit dictus Matthæus, quæ nulli deesse consueuit, dum albi aliquid intercesserit, aut rubei, pristinis restituit dignitatibus. Rex ergo Anselmum privavit omnibus bonis, & archiepiscopatum in fiscum redegit. Et Papæ spiritualem auctoritatem nunquam timebat eruditus rex, sed temporalem potestatem tantum. Anno Domini mo[?]. luna quasi luminis expers, extincta videbatur. Anno frequenti, apud Rauennam & Parmam, in Iulio sanguinem pluit. Anno Domini 1114. in Decembri, cælum repente rubens apparuit, quasi arderet, & luna passa est eclipsim. Tamen Tamesis eodem anno per duos dies exsiccata fuit. Anno Domini 117.[?] tonitrua, grandines, ac uentorum impetus horribiles fiebant, ac terraemotus magni, qui Ecclesias, turres, moenia, aedificia, arbores, & homines contriuerunt. Anno Domini 1118. Templariorum suffecta[?] in cœpit. Hæc Matthæus.
units.tr: From the second book of the Chronicles of Matthew Paris. In the time of this Paschal, in the year of the Lord 1103 [?], when Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, accused King Henry I at Rome in his presence (to whom he ought rather, by divine command, to have obeyed) because he had ordained certain bishops and abbots; William Warelwast, the procurator and clerk of the same king, answering on his behalf, stoutly said among other things that the king did not wish to be deprived of the investiture of prelates even at the cost of losing his kingdom. To this the Pope replied: "If, as you say, your king would not allow the gifts of churches to be alienated from him even at the peril of his realm, know this: I speak before God, I would not, for the price of his own head (most arrogant Satan), permit him to keep them unpunished." When these matters were concluded, Anselm asked that the Pope, with the king despised, should lay hands on the degraded man. Then, says the said Matthew, the most merciful see, which is accustomed to fail no one, restored them to their former dignities, so long as something white or red intervened. So the king deprived Anselm of all his goods and reduced the archbishopric to the royal treasury. And the learned king never feared the spiritual authority of the Pope, but only his temporal power. In the year of the Lord 1100 [?] the moon seemed extinguished, as if without light. In the same year, often, at Ravenna and Parma, blood rained in July. In the year of the Lord 1114, in December, the sky suddenly appeared reddened, as if burning, and the moon suffered an eclipse. Yet the Thames was dried up in the same year for two days. In the year of the Lord 117[?] there were thunders, hailstorms and horrible gusts of wind, and great earthquakes, which shattered churches, towers, walls, buildings, trees and men. In the year of the Lord 1118 the order of the Templars was begun. So far Matthew.
102. GELASIUS the Second.

units.la: Gelasius secundus, patria Campanus, & Ioannes Caietanus antea uocatus, monachus olim Casinensis, ac illustri genere procreatus, mortuo Paschale, in eius est suffectus locum, sed non sine grandi dissensione. Nam cum sine Imperatoris consensu eligeretur, Cincius quidam Fregpanus[?] dictus, patricius urbis potentissimus, illius iniuriam non ferens, ad Palladij monasterium, ubi Cardinales erant congregati, cum satellitibus armatis venit. Et in eos irrumpens, refractis foribus, obuium quemq; percussit: Pontificem, obtorto eius collo, in terram deiectum, calcibus contriuit, in uinculaque protrusit. Cardinales autem fugam parantes, ex multis & equis deiecit: nullumq; genus contumeliae praetermisit, quo affici tantus senatus pos-set. Sed non tulit tantam iniuriam pop. Romanus, quin auxilio Normannorum cum tandem liberauerit, & hostes ad pedum oscula compulerit. Hinc Imperator Henricus exercitum magnum ex Germania Romam misit. Quod timens Gelasius, cum fuit[?] suis Caietam nauigio mox petijt, ibiq; sacerdos factus est, cum solum diaconus ante creatus suis-set pontifex. Henricus Romam ueniens, abiente Gelasio, Mauricium Burdinum Bracharensem archiepiscopum, pontificem creauit, ac Gregorium octauum uocauit, indeq; abijt. Quo audito, Gelasius clam rediit, & sumpto animo prodit in aedem Praxedis, Missam facturus. Vbi ab aduersaria parte ita fuit impetitus, ut aegre fuga suae incolumitati consuleret. Elapsus difficulter e manibus suorum hostium, Pisas nauigauit: atq; inde in Galliam soluit, ad portum S. Aegidij. Et consecratis in uia inter eundum aliquot Ecclesijs, scilicet S. Caeciliae in Stagello, S. Syluestri in Tillano, & S. Stephani in Tornaco (Christum nullibi praedicabat) lapidibus earum terminos notabat. Ab abbate de Cluniacensi peramice exceptus est: ac pleuritisi correptus, anno Domini 1119. post unu fuit pontificatus annum & aliquot dies obijt mortem, in eodem sepultus coenobio. Hic Romanae curiae statum negligentia atq; ignorantia maiorum labefa-statum in meliorem formam & ornatum redegit (magna laus.) Coloniae per legatum Canonem, episcopum Praenestinum, concilium habuit, in quo Caesarem excommunicauit. Successores suos Rom. pontifices a nemine iudicari posse aut debere sta[illegible, ~1 letter]dit,et Templariorum sectam, ut habet Matthæus Parisius, à Hierosolymorum patriarchæ obedien-tia exemit, ita, inquit, ut more Cham maledicti fi-lij Noe, illum contemnerent, qui eos primum fun-dauerat.
units.tr: Gelasius the Second, a native of Campania, formerly called John Caetanus, once a monk of Monte Cassino and born of a noble family, was chosen to succeed Paschal after his death, but not without great dispute. For when he was elected without the consent of the Emperor, a certain Cencius Frangipane, as he was called, the most powerful patrician of the city, could not bear the insult to him. He came with armed henchmen to the monastery of Palladius, where the cardinals had gathered. Bursting in, after breaking down the doors, he struck whoever he met. He seized the Pontiff by the neck, threw him to the ground, trampled him with his feet, and thrust him into chains. He drove the cardinals, who were trying to flee, from their horses, and he left no kind of insult untried by which so great a senate could be humiliated. But the Roman people would not endure such an injury. Aided at last by the Normans, they freed him and forced the enemy to kiss his feet. Thereupon the Emperor Henry sent a large army from Germany to Rome. Gelasius, fearing this, quickly sailed with his people to Gaeta, and there he was made a priest, although before this he had been only a deacon when he became pope. Henry came to Rome while Gelasius was away, created Maurice Burdinus, archbishop of Braga, pope, called him Gregory the Eighth, and then departed. On hearing this, Gelasius returned secretly, and, gathering his courage, came forward into the church of Praxedes to celebrate Mass. There he was attacked by the opposing party in such a way that he could hardly save his own safety by flight. Escaping with difficulty from the hands of his enemies, he sailed to Pisa, and from there put out to Gaul, to the port of St Gilles. On the way, while travelling, he consecrated several churches, namely St Cecilia in Stagello, St Silvester in Tillano, and St Stephen in Tornacum (he preached Christ nowhere), and he marked their boundaries with stones. He was most kindly received by the abbot of Cluny, but, seized by pleurisy, he died in the year of the Lord 1119, after one year and some days of the pontificate, and was buried in the same monastery. This man, through the negligence and ignorance of his predecessors, restored the state of the Roman curia, which had been weakened, to a better form and ornament (great praise). At Cologne, through the legate Cono, bishop of Palestrina, he held a council, in which he excommunicated the Emperor. He established that his successors, the Roman pontiffs, could not and should not be judged by anyone. He also removed the sect of the Templars from obedience to the patriarch of Jerusalem, as Matthew Paris reports, so that, he says, after the manner of Ham, the cursed son of Noah, they should despise the man who had first founded them.
103. CALIXTUS the Second.

units.la: Calixtus secundus, ante Papatum Viennensis episcopus, & Guido Burgundus nuncupatus, qui genus à Francorum & Anglorum regibus duxerat, à Cardinalibus illis, quos Gelasius secum duxerat, Cluniaci in pontificem eo mortuo creabatur. Quidam etiam ex Cardinalibus, qui partim Romæ, partim in Italia agebant, electionem illam Cluniaci factam[?], ratam habuerunt. Romam ergo proficiscebatur, ut pontificatum iniret: atq; à Romanis, obuiam factis, summo cum honore excipie-batur. Qui statim in Germaniam ad Cononem, de quo iam diximus, Gelasij prædecessoris legatum, misit, ut excommunicationem aduersus Henricum continuaret. Quare coactus est Imperator, apud Triburium conuentum episcoporum & principum agere, ut concordia inter ipsum & Papasta-tim procuraretur. Et ne pontificum arte, regno(ut piissimus[?] eius pater) exueretur, conditiones pacis iniquas admisit. Missis Triburium oratori-bus, Calixti huius electionem, ad summum suū decus, confirmauit viuo adhuc Gregorio seu Burchardimo[?], quem ipse pontificem prius fecerat. Et cum perurgerent pontifices legati et episcopi, ut de suo iure inuestiendi praelatos cederet, perijt indu-cias, ut super ea re cum Germaniae principibus deliberare posset. Qui anathematis eius fulmine me-tuentes (erat enim Pontifex b id toti tunc munus formidabilis) ipsi persuadebant, ut in gratiam cum eo rediret. Sic eius tandem Dominus retaliabat proditiones in piissimum patrem fidas. Misit ergo legatos Romam Imperator, suos lanciones[?], episcopum Spirensem et Fuldensem abbatem: qui redeuntes, Pontificis legatos secum adduxerunt, qui et rerum agendarum summam potestatem habebant. Vuormaciae comitia indicebantur Germanis episcopis et principibus. Agebatur de inuestitura episcoporum, utraque parte acriter ius sibi vendicante. Vicit tandem (ut plerumque fit) maior pars meliorem. Imperator autem, fidei ex omnium timore, et episcoporum quorundam filio, qui defectionem futuram praedixerant, persuasus, cogebatur suum ius in episcopis uestiendi deferre. Quo facto, legati eum ab anathemate resoluebant, faciebant quoque copiam ad Ecclesiae con-|sortium redeundi, a quo per Gerlafium[?] videbatur exclusus. Factum hoc ex utraque parte literis committebatur, quarum formulae, in loco spacio-so et campestri iuxta Rhenum, in magna populo-rum frequentia publice relegebantur, maxima pi-colarum congratulatione. Pontificij literas su-per ea concessione ab Henrico datas, in Lateranen-si basilica publice suspenderunt, in triumphale te-stimonium uicti et subacti demum Caesaris. Stabi-lita eo modo cum Imperatore concordia, Calixtus contractis copijs, Gregorium antipapam perse-quebatur: qui ob reconciliationis famam excesse-rat Romā, Sutrijq; commorabatur. Sutrium à Ca-lixto capiebatur, Gregorius uincebatur: et ut in-signiter exponeretur ludibrio, etiam non sine sum-ma Caesaris ignominia, impositus camelo, capite ad caudam uerso, Romam ducebatur, tonsusq; in monasterium exilij causa mittebatur: Carsulanus, Platina, Stella, Vincentius, Antonimus, et alij. Ca-lixtus quietem nactus (ait ipse Platina) Cardina-les 12. creauit, basilicas multas reficit, urbis mœ-nia instauravit, aquam in urbem induxit, arces Ec-clesiæ muniuit, donaria plurima templis diuisit, fundos coemptos S. Petro donauit, et Ecclesiam S. Nicolai in palatio ædificauit. Sed Christi Euan-gelium non prædicauit. Concilium Romæ contra Turcam celebrauit. Genuenses, Venetos, et Pisa-nos in crucis hostes concitauit: Pontificum decreta contra Imperatorem stabilivit, cōfirmationem episcoporum Germanis plané ademit, Ecclesiam Compostellanam in archiepiscopatum sublimavit: de confictis prodigiis S. Jacobi pro idololatria il-lic ampliandā librum fecit, & Præmonstratensium monachorum sectam admisit. Decrevit adulteri-um iudicari, si quis episcopatum vel Ecclesiam vi-vus dimitteret, per illud Pauli, Alligata est uxor legi viri, quamdiu vir eius vivit (Scriptura artifi-ciosè detorta) eo defuncto, soluta est à lege viri, cui vult ergo nubat in Domino: id est, alium eligat, sed regulariter 7.q. 1.cap. Sicut alterius. Eos ex-communicabat, qui vel peregrinos spoliarent, vel alio modo Romipetas impedirent. 24.q.3 cap. Si quis. Quatuor temporum ieiunium instituit, cum antea ter in anno ieiunatum esset, Dist. 76 cap. le-iunium à Romana Ecclesia non licere dissentire edixit: rationem addens, Quia ut filius, inquit, ve-nit, facere voluntatem patris: ita Christianos o-portet facere voluntatem matris (magna ratio) Romanæ Ecclesiæ: Matris scilicet magnæ, scorta-tionum & abhominationū terræ, Apoc.17. Febre demum correptus, ex cuiusdam itineris labore, in [?]no Domini 1125 Romæ ex hac vita decessit.
units.tr: Calixtus the Second, before his papacy bishop of Vienne, and called Guy of Burgundy, who traced his descent from the kings of the Franks and the English, was created pope at Cluny after Gelasius died, by those cardinals whom Gelasius had taken with him. Some of the cardinals too, who were active partly at Rome and partly in Italy, held that election made at Cluny to be valid. He therefore set out for Rome to take up the pontificate, and the Romans, going out to meet him, received him with the highest honour. Straightway he sent to Germany Cono, of whom we have already spoken, the legate of his predecessor Gelasius, to continue the excommunication against Henry. Because of this, the Emperor was forced to hold, at the assembly of Triburium of bishops and princes, negotiations so that concord might be secured between himself and the Pope. And lest, by the cunning of the pontiffs, he be stripped of his kingdom (as his most pious father had been), he accepted unjust conditions of peace. Envoys were sent to Triburium, and he confirmed the election of this Calixtus to his own highest honour, while Gregory, or Burdinus, was still alive, the man whom he himself had earlier made pope. And when the papal legates and bishops pressed hard that he should yield his right of investing prelates, he obtained a truce so that he could deliberate on that matter with the princes of Germany. They, fearing the thunderbolt of his anathema (for the Pontiff was then formidable to all), persuaded him to return to favour with him. Thus at last the Lord repaid him for his treacheries against his most pious father. The Emperor therefore sent envoys to Rome, his men of confidence, the bishop of Speyer and the abbot of Fulda, who, on their return, brought back with them the legates of the Pontiff, who also had full power to conduct the business. A diet was announced at Worms for the German bishops and princes. The question of the investiture of bishops was debated, each side vigorously claiming its right. At last, as usually happens, the greater part prevailed over the better. The Emperor, however, persuaded by the fear of all and by the advice of some bishops who had foretold a coming revolt, was compelled to surrender his right of investing bishops. When this was done, the legates absolved him from the anathema, and also gave him the opportunity of returning to fellowship with the Church, from which he seemed to have been shut out through Gerlaf. This was settled on both sides by written documents, the wording of which was publicly read out in a broad open field beside the Rhine, before a great crowd of people, to the greatest rejoicing of the partisans. The papists publicly hung up in the basilica of the Lateran the letters of concession given by Henry, as a triumphal monument to the conquered and at last subdued Caesar. With concord thus established with the Emperor, Calixtus gathered his forces and pursued the antipope Gregory, who, because of the rumour of reconciliation, had left Rome and was staying at Sutri. Sutri was taken by Calixtus, and Gregory was defeated. And so that he might be conspicuously exposed to ridicule, not without the greatest dishonour to the Emperor as well, he was set on a camel with his face turned to the tail, led to Rome, and, shaven, sent to a monastery as a place of exile. (Carsulanus, Platina, Stella, Vincentius, Antoninus, and others.) Calixtus, having gained quiet (Platina himself says), created twelve cardinals, restored many basilicas, repaired the walls of the city, brought water into the city, fortified the strongholds of the Church, divided many gifts among the temples, gave purchased estates to St Peter, and built the church of St Nicholas in the palace. But he did not preach the Gospel of Christ. He held a council at Rome against the Turk. He stirred up the Genoese, the Venetians, and the Pisans against the enemies of the cross. He established the decrees of the pontiffs against the Emperor, completely took away from the Germans the confirmation of bishops, and raised the church of Compostela to the rank of archbishopric. He wrote a book for the enlargement there of the idolatry of the fabricated miracles of St James, and he admitted the sect of the Premonstratensian monks. He decreed that it should be judged adultery if anyone should leave a bishopric or church while alive, by that saying of Paul, "The wife is bound by law to her husband as long as her husband lives" (Scripture craftily twisted), so that after his death she is free from the husband's law, and "let her marry whom she will in the Lord", that is, let her choose another; but this is a rule, 7. q. 1, cap. Sicut alterius. He excommunicated those who either despoiled pilgrims or hindered those going to Rome, 24. q. 3, cap. Si quis. He instituted the fast of the Four Seasons, whereas before they had fasted three times in the year. Dist. 76, cap. Ieiunium. He enjoined that it was not lawful to dissent from the Roman Church in fasting, adding this reason: "Because, as the Son came to do the will of the Father, so Christians ought to do the will of the mother" (a great reason), namely of the Roman Church, the great mother of harlotries and abominations of the earth, Rev. 17. At last, seized by fever after the toil of a certain journey, he died at Rome in the year of the Lord 1125.

units.la: Simeon Dunelmensis in 2. libro suarum Hi-storiarum de Regibus Anglorum: Anno DomiAn[?] 1119. Calixtus Papa concilium generale tenuit Rhemis in Gallia. In quo inter caetera constituit hoc decretum: Presbyteris, diaconibus & subdiaconibus concubinarum & uxorum contubernia prorsus interdicimus. Si qui autem huiusmodi reperti fuerint, Ecclesiasticis officijs ac beneficijs priventur. Et si neq; has immunditias correxerint, communione careant Christiana. Unde quidam temporis in Anglia scriptor,
units.tr: Simeon of Durham, in the second book of his Histories concerning the Kings of the English: In the year of the Lord 1119, Pope Calixtus held a general council at Reims in Gaul. In it, among other things, he laid down this decree: "We absolutely forbid to priests, deacons and subdeacons the keeping of concubines and wives. If any such are found, let them be deprived of ecclesiastical offices and benefices. And if they do not correct these uncleannesses, let them be cut off from Christian communion." Hence a certain writer of that time in England:

units.la: Obone Calixte, nunc omnis clerus odit te. Quandam presbyteri poterant uxoribus uti: Hoc destruxisti, postquam tu Papa fuisti. Ergo tuum merito nomen habent odio.
units.tr: O Calixtus, now all the clergy hate you. Priests were once allowed to use wives; you destroyed this when you became Pope. Therefore your name rightly holds hatred.

units.la: Matthæus Parisius. Eodem anno Papa Calix-tus in Normanniam venit, ad Henricum primum Anglorum regem, locutusq; est cum eo ad Gisor-tium.
units.tr: Matthew Paris. In the same year Pope Calixtus came into Normandy, to Henry the First, king of the English, and spoke with him at Gisors.
104. HONORIUS the Second.

units.la: Honorius secundus, patria Aemylius, ex agro I-molensi, quod olim Cornelij forum dicebatur, ob-scuro loco oriundus, & Lambertus primum dictus, literarum beneficio fiebat episcopus Hostiensis, & ex episcopo pontifex Romanus. Non adeo laudatur eius ingressus (inquit Platina) cum ambitione quorundam potius quam bonorum virorum con-sensu Papatui iniverit. Magna equidem contentione electus in pontificem ille erat, arte magis & astu-tia Leonis Frangepanus, potentissimi civis, quàm cordatorum hominum suffragijs. Is namq; Leo persuasit Cardinalibus, ne prius eligerent Pontificem, quàm omnes maiorum canones de electione dili-genter observassent. Interea verò dum cunctarentur Cardinales, Leo huius pontificis ambitioni serviturus, quibus poterat versutijs, auxilia ad id callidè procurabat. At Cardinales, comperta Leonis astutia, Theobaldum S. Anastasiæ Cardinalem, Pontificem creabant, Cœlestinumq; appellabant. Populus verò Saxonem S. Stephani Cardinalem, Pontificem efflagitabant. Quod et dictus Leo se velle simulavit, ut Cardinalium electionem irritam faceret. Et quum eam ob rem populum habe-ret aliquantulum æquiorem, effecit paulatim, ut per eundem populum Lambertus crearetur, atq; Honorius diceretur. Qui omnibus eius super-bissimi regni titulis insignitus, ut consilio ac poten-tia suis adversarijs par esset, fecit & ipse Cardinales aliquot. Quorum stipatus auxilio, sedem cum pace obtinuit. Ex huius latere (ut testis est Matthæus Parisius) pro implenda cruentà, legatum e-misit Ioannes Cremensis luxuriosissimus Cardinalis, tituli S. Chrysogoni. Is, inquit, anno Domini 1125[?] de licentia regis in Angliam veniens, per ab-batiâs batias[?] & episcopatus lucris ac delitijs indulgebat. Et tandem metens[?] ubi non seminauerat, cum multis donarijs bene fagimaretur[?], ad natiuitatem S. Mariae, folenne concilium Londini celebrauit. In quo sacerdotum concubinas (uxores intellexit) ac sacerdotes concubinarios damnauit. Tandem uero, sequenti scilicet nocte, in eodem uitio & ipse legatus (impudens scortator) in delicijs crapulatus, cecidit. Et deprehensus atq; compeditus, non minimum in Ecclesia scandalum suscitauit. Pro quo tamen sic scripserat Honorius ad clerum Anglicanum, ut Simeon Dunelmensis in historijs refert: Rogamus uos, & monemus atq; praecipimus, ut hunc Ioannem tanquam S. Petri uicarium (Sardanapali potius) reuerenter suscipiatis, humiliter audiatis, & ad ipsius uocationem synodales cum eo conuentus solenniter celebretis. Quatenus per ipsius & uestram inductriam in regno uestro, quae corrigenda sunt, corrigantur: & quae firmanda sunt, sancto inspirante spiritu, firmentur, &c. Et ad Dauidem Scotorum regem, Roxburgi tunc commorantem: Nobilitati tuae rogando mandamus, ut dilectum filium nostrum (patri valde similem) Ioannem Cardinalem, cui uices nostras in partibus illis commisimus, reuerenter suscipias & honores. Episcopos etiam terrae tuae, cum ab eo nocati fuerint (officium certè regium) ad concilium suum faciás conuenire, &c. Accedit statutum eiusdem Ioannis, ex prædicta Londinensi synodo: Presby-teris, diaconibus, subdiaconibus & canonicis, u-xorum, concubinarum, & omnium omnino fœmi-narum contubernia, authoritate Apostolica inhi-bemus, præter matrem, aut sororem, vel amitam, siue illas mulieres quæ omnino careant suspicione. Et qui decreti huius violator extiterit, confessus vel conuictus, ruinam ordinis patiatur. Inter con-sanguineos, seu affinitate propinquos, usq; ad se-ptimam generationem (impostor diaboliçe) ma-trimonia contrahi prohibemus. Honorius autem inter alias ordinationes Rogerium Normannum Apuliæ ducem fecit, Aquileiensem Patriarcham deposuit: ac Venetorum patriarcham, quòd schis-maticorum sautores essent, dignitate priuauit. Fa-to concessit Honorius, insignis præstigiator, anno Domini 1130. Cuius tempore Arnulphus, pius concionator, Anglus doctissimus, prælatorum Ro-mæ uitia incessens, martyrij coronam nancisceba-tur.
units.tr: Honorius II, by birth Aemylius, from the district of Imola, which was formerly called the Forum of Cornelius, sprang from an obscure place, and was first called Lambert. By the advantage of his letters he was made bishop of Ostia, and from bishop he became Roman pontiff. His entry (says Platina) is not much praised: he came to the papacy by the ambition of certain men rather than with the consent of good men. He was indeed elected pontiff with great contention, by the craft and cunning of Leo Frangipani, a most powerful citizen, rather than by the votes of sensible men. For this Leo persuaded the cardinals not to elect a pontiff until they had carefully observed all the canons of the elders concerning elections. Meanwhile, while the cardinals hesitated, Leo, serving the ambition of this man, cleverly procured support for him by whatever tricks he could. But the cardinals, having discovered Leo's cunning, created Theobald, cardinal of St Anastasia, as pontiff, and called him Celestine. The people, however, demanded Saxo, cardinal of St Stephen, as pontiff. Leo also pretended to want this, so that the cardinals' election would be made void. Since he had the people somewhat more on his side for this purpose, he gradually brought it about that through the same people Lambert was created and named Honorius. Adorned with all the proud titles of his kingdom, so that he might be a match for his adversaries in counsel and power, he also made several cardinals himself, and supported by their help he held the see in peace. From his side (as Matthew Paris attests), to carry out the bloody business, he sent as legate John of Crema, the most dissolute cardinal, of the title of St Chrysogonus. He, it is said, coming into England in the year of the Lord 1125 with the king's permission, indulged himself in the profits and pleasures of abbacies and bishoprics. At last, reaping where he had not sown, and being well fattened with many gifts, he held a solemn council at London at the Nativity of St Mary. In it he condemned the concubines of priests (he meant wives) and the priests who kept concubines. Yet that very night the legate himself, a shameless whoremonger, fell into the same vice, drunk with pleasures, and, caught and fettered, he stirred no small scandal in the Church. Nevertheless, Honorius had written to the English clergy about him in these terms, as Simeon of Durham reports in his histories: "We ask you, admonish you and command you to receive this John reverently as the vicar of St Peter (rather a Sardanapalus), to hear him humbly, and to hold synods solemnly with him at his summons, so that through his and your industry what needs correcting in your kingdom may be corrected, and what needs confirming may be confirmed, the Holy Spirit inspiring, etc." And to David, king of the Scots, then staying at Roxburgh: "We command your nobility by request, that you receive reverently and honour our beloved son John, the Cardinal (very much like his father), to whom we have committed our place in those parts, and that you cause the bishops of your land, when they are summoned by him (certainly a royal office), to come to his council, etc." There is also a statute of the same John from the aforesaid London synod: "By apostolic authority we forbid the cohabitation of wives, concubines, and absolutely all women with priests, deacons, subdeacons and canons, except a mother, sister or aunt, or women who are wholly beyond suspicion. And whoever shall be a violator of this decree, if confessed or convicted, shall suffer the ruin of his order. We also forbid marriages to be contracted between blood relations, or those near by marriage, up to the seventh generation (diabolical impostor)." Honorius, moreover, among other appointments, made Roger the Norman duke of Apulia, deposed the patriarch of Aquileia, and deprived the patriarch of the Venetians of his dignity, because they were supporters of schismatics. Honorius, a notable deceiver, died in the year of the Lord 1130. In his time Arnulf, a pious preacher and a most learned Englishman, who attacked the vices of the prelates at Rome, was winning the crown of martyrdom.
103. INNOCENT II.

units.la: Innocentius secundus, patria Romanus, ex regi-ne trans Tyberim, patre Ioanne, post initum Pa-satum nihil antiquius aut sanctius duxit, quàm Ro-gerium gerium Siciliæ ex Normannis ducem, qui se regem Italiæ dixerat, reprimere. Eduxit suas acies ma-gnanimus Papa, ac profligauit celeriter hostes: sed à superueniente ducis cum exercitu filio, cum suis Cardinalibus mox capiebatur, omniaq; præter re-gni Siciliæ titulū Rogerius impetrauit. Interea Ro-mani, Petri Leonis filium, pontificem creauerant, & Anacletum illum appellauerant. Quo cognito, à captiuitate liberationem rogabat, & obtinuit: Romamq; redire decreuit. Sed cū illic cerneret om-nia turbis ac tumultibus esse plena, Pisas nauigio petiit, & inde Genuam abiit. Postremò Genua reli-ta, in Galliam quàm citissimè proficiscebatur. A-nacletus autem submoto Innocentio, omnium ani-mos qui ei fauere uidebantur, sibi per largitiones conciliare festinabat. Rogerium inde utriusq; Si-ciliæ regem decernebat, ut illius auxilio stipatus tutior in omnibus esset. Innocentius uero de recu-perando Papatu in Gallijs sollicitus, concilium in Claro monte collegit, & Anacletum ut hostem Ec-clesiæ damnauit. Post hæc Aurelianum se contu-lit, ad Philippum Galliæ regem, ubi & Ludoui-cum eius filium coronauit. Hinc Carnotum petijt, ubi & Henricum Anglorum regē, eius nominis pri-mum, obuiam habuit. Cum quo de cōscribendo ex-ercitu contra Saracenos egit, in auxilium ijs quæ terram sanctam obtinuerant. Sed eo sub prætex-tu cupiebat illorum copijs Papatum recuperare.
units.tr: Innocent II, a Roman by birth, from the region across the Tiber, the son of John, after taking up the papacy considered nothing more urgent or more holy than to put down Roger, the Norman duke of Sicily, who had called himself king of Italy. The magnanimous pope led out his armies and quickly routed the enemy. But when Roger's son arrived with an army, the pope was soon captured along with his cardinals, and Roger obtained everything except the title of King of Sicily. Meanwhile the Romans had made Peter Leo's son pontiff and called him Anacletus. When Innocent learned of this, he begged for his release from captivity, obtained it, and resolved to return to Rome. But seeing that everything there was full of disorder and tumult, he sailed to Pisa and from there went on to Genoa. Finally, leaving Genoa, he set out for France as quickly as possible. Anacletus, meanwhile, having removed Innocent, hastened to win over, by largesse, all the men who seemed to favour his rival. He then declared Roger king of both Sicilies, so that with his help he might be safer in every respect. Innocent, anxious to recover the papacy in France, gathered a council at Clermont and condemned Anacletus as an enemy of the Church. After this he went to Orléans, to Philip, king of France, where he also crowned Louis, the king's son. From there he made for Chartres, where he met Henry, king of the English, the first of that name. With him he discussed raising an army against the Saracens, to help those who held the Holy Land. But under this pretext he desired to recover the papacy with their forces.

units.la: Ab Henrico Anglo in Lotharingiam deflexit, conuenturus Lotharium Germaniæ regem, ut illum quoq; sollicitaret de se restituendo. Lotharii sacramento pontifici dato, parabat expeditionem, qua Innocentius Romam tutus reduceretur.
units.tr: From England, Innocent turned aside into Lorraine, intending to meet Lothair, king of Germany, and to persuade him also to restore him. Lothair, having given the pope his oath, was preparing an expedition by which Innocent might be brought back safely to Rome.

units.la: Concilia celebrauit hic pontifex Rhemis, Placentiæ, Pisæ, ac demum Romæ in Laterano, in quibus Genuensibus ac Pisanis archiepiscopos dedit.
units.tr: This pope held councils at Reims, Piacenza, Pisa, and at last at Rome in the Lateran, in which he appointed archbishops for the Genoese and the Pisans.

units.la: Sub hæc Lotharius, magno cum exercitu, Italiam ingrediebatur, ut Innocentium Pontificiæ sedi restitueret. Et Romam veniens, partitis copijs, in urbem irruit, ac profligato Anacleto una cum duce Rogerio, Innocentium tutum in Lateranum reduxit. Innocentius autem, ne uideretur ingratus, Lotharium imperiali diademate coronauit; & comiti Reginaldo Cæsariani exercitus duci, Apuliæ du-catum (non suum) dedit, ac quicquid in Italia Rogerius tenebat. Scribit tamen Otho Frisingensis, magnam inde subortam esse controuersiam inter Cæsarem ipsum & Pontificem, uter haberet ius dandi ducatum. Et cum neuter alteri totum ius cederet, sedata est hac lege controuersia, ut utrque apponeret manum, ad uexillum nouo Apuliæ du-ci tribuendum. Quo declararetur, utriq; ius esse dandi[?] ipsum ducatum. Sed mortuo statim Regi-naldo, Rogerius suum ius repetijt, & aduersa mo-lientem Pontificem cum Cardinalibus iterum ca-pit, securum & incautum. Necillos dimisit, donec omnia quæ vellet, etiam ut diceretur utriusq; Si-cilię rex, impetrasset. Et abeo tempore Siciliæ re-gnum S. Petri patrimonium (insignis impostura) appellatum est. At quia Pontifex, hac etiam regij tituli concessione, Imperatores suo iure spoliauerant, ut quod armis ipsi parauerant, hic ad se solum transferret, magna inde (ut Nauclerus scribit) sunt subortæ malæ. Constituit Innocentius, excommunicandum esse, qui unctum sacrificum aut clericum rapuit, percusserit, nec absoluendum esse, nisi abi-Pso Papa. Caus. 17. quest. 4. Si quis. Et Ecclesiam non esse committendam condustitijs sacrificulis, Cau. 21. quest. 3. Precipimus. Ille quoq; mutando statum Ecclesiæ in Syria pro sua libidine, magnas contentiones inter episcopos ibidem seminauit, iuxta Guilhelmum Tyrium lib. 14. cap. 12. de Bel-lo sacro. Post hæc & alia sacta Papalia, Innocen-tius anno Domini 1143. communis naturæ debi-tum, deposito carnis onere, soluit. Sub hoc Innocen-tio anno Domini 1136. Stephanus Anglorum rex, mœstituras prælatorum iure regio sibi reseruas, sibi Matthæus Parisius author est in 4. suorum
units.tr: Meanwhile Lothair entered Italy with a great army, to restore Innocent to the papal see. Coming to Rome, he divided his forces, burst into the city, and, after routing Anacletus together with Duke Roger, led Innocent back safely to the Lateran. Innocent, however, so as not to seem ungrateful, crowned Lothair with the imperial diadem; and to Count Reginald, commander of the imperial army, he gave the duchy of Apulia (which was not his to give), together with whatever Roger held in Italy. Yet Otto of Freising writes that a great controversy then arose between the emperor himself and the pontiff as to which of them had the right to bestow the duchy. Since neither would yield the whole right to the other, the dispute was settled on this condition: that both should lay their hands on the banner to be given to the new duke of Apulia, so that it might be declared that the right to give the duchy itself belonged to both. But Reginald died at once, Roger took back his own right, and when the pope was plotting against him, he seized the pope and the cardinals again, while they were off their guard and unsuspecting. He did not release them until he had obtained everything he wished, including, as it was said, to be called king of both Sicilies. From that time the kingdom of Sicily was called (an outstanding imposture) the patrimony of St Peter. But because the pontiff, by this grant of royal title as well, had despoiled the emperors of their right, so that what they had won by arms he transferred to himself alone, great evils, as Nauclerus writes, arose from this. Innocent laid down that whoever seized, struck, or laid hands on an anointed priest or clerk should be excommunicated, and should not be absolved except by the pope himself (Causa 17, question 4, "Si quis"). He also decreed that the Church should not be entrusted to hirelings (Causa 21, question 3, "Precipimus"). Moreover, by altering the state of the Church in Syria at his own pleasure, he sowed great contentions among the bishops there, according to William of Tyre, book 14, chapter 12, on the Holy War. After these and other papal deeds, Innocent in the year of the Lord 1143 laid down the burden of the flesh and paid the debt of common nature. Under this Innocent, in the year of the Lord 1136, Stephen, king of the English, as Matthew Paris is the authority in the fourth of his

units.la: Chronia Chronicorum libro. Et Lotharius imperator, ut Nauclerus habet, privilegium Henrico Cæsari ademptum, de prælatorum investitura, repetere cōstituerat: sed ne illud faceret, D. Bernardus dissuasit, qui eo tempore in admiratione fuit.
units.tr: Chronicles in the book of the Chronicles. And Lothair the emperor, as Nauclerus has it, had resolved to recover the privilege over the investiture of prelates that had been taken from the emperor Henry; but Bernard dissuaded him from doing so, who at that time was held in great admiration.
106. CELESTINE II.

units.la: Cœlestinus secundus, natione Thuscus, Typher-ni, in quodam S. Felicitatis castro, D. Marci presbyter Cardinalis, & Guido ante Papatum di[?]ctus, omnium suffragiis, imperante Conrado, post defunctum Innocentium, in Papam assumebatur. Ob vitæ brevitatem nihil potuit hic facere, quo se posteris ex inclytis factis commendaret. Hoc unum tamen legimus, quòd Syriæ Palæstinæ, quam Terram sanctam dicimus, valde sub eo periclita-batur, Tripolitano comite Pontio cum aliis occiso. Legimus etiam apud Matthæum Parisium, quum nulla daretur clericis reverentia, durante quodam in Angliæ schismate inter Stephanum regem & Mathildam imperatricem, Guilhelmus Vvintoniensis (nescio an conscio Cœlestino) Londini concilium celebravit. Vbi statutum fuit, ne aliquis, qui Ecclesiam aut cæmiterium violaverit, vel in clericum aut religiosum manum violenta iniecerit, ab alio quàm ab ipso Papa possit absolui. Et hæc fiebant, inquit, candelis accensis, ac pulo pulsatis campanis. Cum uero ubiq; per Italiam la-boraretur peste, Cœlestinus iste anno Domini 1144. sexto sui Pontificatus mense absumebatur, in Laterano sepultus.
units.tr: Celestine II, a Tuscan by nation, from Tifernum, in a certain castle of St Felicity, cardinal priest of St Mark, and called Guido before he became pope, was chosen pope by the votes of all, under the emperor Conrad, after the death of Innocent. Because of the brevity of his life he could do nothing here by which he might commend himself to posterity through famous deeds. We read only this one thing: that the Syria and Palestine which we call the Holy Land were then in great danger, with Count Pontius of Tripoli slain together with others. We also read in Matthew Paris that, when no reverence was shown to clergy, during a certain schism in England between King Stephen and the empress Matilda, William of Winchester (I do not know whether with Celestine's knowledge) held a council at London. There it was decreed that no one who had violated a church or cemetery, or laid violent hands on a clerk or religious, could be absolved by anyone other than the pope himself. And these things were done, he says, with candles lit and bells rung. But since trouble from plague was then raging throughout Italy, this Celestine died in the year of the Lord 1144, in the sixth month of his pontificate, and was buried in the Lateran.
107. Lucius II.

units.la: Lucius secundus, patria Bononiensis, ex Cardinale presbytero tituli S. Crucis in Hierusalem, post mortuum Cœlestinum, in omni superbia Pontifex creabatur. Qui statim Romanorum magistratum nouum, quem sub Innocentio secundo ad urbis commodum instituerant, demoliri & extirpare conatus est. Nam cum Innocentius ille, consulum electionem ferre non vellet, elegerunt Romani pristino more, Patricium nomine Iordanum. Non enim volebant pontificum violentias diutius ferre. Is urbis regalia, tum intra muros tum extra, repoposcit: aitque ius illud officii nomine ad se pertinere, quod Pontifex, abrogatis patriciis, per Ca-rolum Magnum tempore tam longo usurpauerat. Iussitque (ô magnum hæreticum scilicet, Romanæ curiæ non ferendum) ut Pontifex prædecessorum exemplo, primitijs, decimis & oblationibus con-tentus uiueret. Lucius autem à Romanis propter hæc uehementer exagitatus, supplex per legatos Conradum imperatorem in Italiam uocabat. Sed Conradus aliunde impeditus, illuc uenire nō poterat, nec eius tunc inseruire tyrannidi. Lucius ergo alia uia rem aggrediendam ratus, expectabat donec semel essent senatores omnes cum patricio unà in Capitolium congregati, ut de suis rebus consultarent. Tunc collecto milite, pontifex Capitolium invasit (Papaliter factum) ut senatum illum uel omnino perderet, uel saltem expelleret. Fama statim de Pontificis conatu, per urbem spargebatur. Populus cucurrit ad arma, fiebatq; atrox pugna. Lucius (sanctissimus pater) militia immixtus, ad Capitolium, lapidibus & saxis ita est quassatus, anno Domini 1145. ut breui post ictu illos fit mortuus, primo nondum finito sui pontificatus anno.
units.tr: Lucius II, a native of Bologna, was formerly a cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. After the death of Celestine he was made pope, full of all pride. At once he set about tearing down and rooting out the new magistracy of the Romans, which they had set up under Innocent II for the good of the city. For when that Innocent would not allow the election of consuls, the Romans, following the old custom, chose a patrician named Jordan. They did not want to endure the popes' violence any longer. Jordan demanded the royal rights of the city, both within the walls and outside them, and claimed that the right which the pope had usurped for so long under Charlemagne, by abolishing the patricians, belonged to him by virtue of his office. He ordered (O great heretic, surely, one not to be tolerated by the Roman court!) that the pope, after the example of his predecessors, should live content with firstfruits, tithes and offerings. Lucius, however, was violently harassed by the Romans for this, and he called Emperor Conrad into Italy by means of envoys, begging him to come. But Conrad was hindered elsewhere and could not come there, nor then submit to his tyranny. Lucius, therefore, thinking that the matter must be attacked by another way, waited until all the senators, together with the patrician, had gathered once in the Capitol to deliberate on their affairs. Then, having collected soldiers, the pope attacked the Capitol (done in papal fashion), intending either to destroy that senate utterly or at least to drive it out. The news of the pope's attempt spread at once through the city. The people ran to arms, and a fierce battle followed. Lucius (the most holy father), mingling with the soldiery, was battered with stones and rocks near the Capitol, in the year of the Lord 1145, so that shortly afterwards he died of the blow, in the first year of his pontificate, not yet complete.
108. Eugenius III.

units.la: EVgenius tertius, patria Pisanus, Cisterciensis olim sectæ[?] sub D. Bernardo monachus, eiusq; discipulus, & Romæ ad S. Anastasium abbas, consensu Cardinalium, Lucio prædicto, in Papatu hac ratione successit. Cogitauerant enim Cardinales, in præsenti tunc rerum statu non expedire, ut ex suo collegio quisquam in pontificem eligeretur, cum ita ius libertatis à Romanis ciuibus quæreretur. Bernardi quoq; crebrescentem famam, multum in rem suam facere putabant: atq; si eius discipulum eligerent, præceptoris autoritatem, au silium[?] & consilium nunquam defuturum suis defi-derijs sperabant. Nec eos fefellit spes subdola. Auxit enim Bernardus quantum potuit, Romani pontificis authoritatem, ut in 2. libro Cosiderationum[?] videre licet. Eugenius autem, mox inito Pontificatu, intellexit populum instare uelle, ut suorum senatorum electionem ratam haberet. Noctu igitur cum Cardinalibus in Sabinos, ad Farfense monasterium abijt: ibiq; consecratus, Viterbium perrexit. Vbi Romanos omnes, qui urbis ciues electo patricio Iordano parere coegerant, cum ipso Iordano excommunicauit. Iunctoq; suo exercitu cum Tiburtinorum copijs, antiquis Romanorum hostibus (sanctum Papæ studium) Romanos ad petendam pacem compulit. Quam ea lege demum concessit, ut patriciatus principatum plene abolerent, & suum præfectum pristino loco suo restituerent: & ut in futurum, quos ipse Papali authoritate illis da-rét[?] senatores, solos acciperent. Paceque in hunc modum facta, in urbem regrediebatur. Sed quoniam postea sentiebat subesse dolum, insidias ueritus, Tiburium dilabebatur. Romani mox fugientem, sagittis & armis insequebantur. A Tiburi er-Pisas nauigio appulsus, in Gallias demum peruenit. Et D. Bernardi opera usus, Ludouicum & alios exoraunt reges, ut in Tureas expeditionem paparárent: qui tamen nihil præclari fecerunt. Con-cilium Rhemis habuit, in quo manissima statuta pro monachis edidit, ut hæc sunt. Ne monachus lucri causa cœnobium exiret, ne puerum in baptismo testis leuaret, ne baptizaret, ne pœnitentias daret, ne ægrotos inuiseret, ne mortuorum funeribus adesset, & ne secularem Ecclesiam guberna-ret: cum ille ipse tamen monachus omnium Ecclesiarum monarchiam diabolorum sanctissimus usurparet. Sed ne scortarentur, aut pædicarent (quod sacrificulis ac monachis commune est) nullam tulit legem. Profanarum artium scholas erexit, porticum S. Mariæ ad præsepe extruxit, Gilbertinorum in Anglia sectam confirmauit, Norwegios per Hadrianum Anglum ad Papismum conuertit, & alia quædam prodigia fecit. Romam reuersus, anno Domini 1152. communi fato tum demum occubuit, in basilica Petri sepultus.
units.tr: Eugenius III, a native of Pisa, formerly a monk of the Cistercian order and a disciple of St Bernard, and abbot of St Anastasius at Rome, succeeded Lucius, mentioned above, in the papacy by the following means, with the consent of the cardinals. For the cardinals had thought that, in the state of affairs at that time, it was not expedient for any member of their own college to be elected pope, since the right of liberty was being sought from the Roman citizens in this way. They also thought that the growing fame of Bernard would greatly serve their cause; and if they chose his disciple, they hoped that the authority, help and counsel of his teacher would never be lacking to their desires. Nor did that deceptive hope disappoint them. For Bernard increased the authority of the Roman pontiff as much as he could, as may be seen in the second book of his Considerations. Eugenius, however, soon after entering upon the pontificate, understood that the people were insisting on having their own senators' election ratified. So by night, with the cardinals, he went off into the Sabine country to the monastery of Farfa, and there he was consecrated, and then proceeded to Viterbo. There he excommunicated all the Romans who had forced the citizens of the city to obey the elected patrician Jordan, together with Jordan himself. Then, joining his army to the forces of the Tiburtines, the ancient enemies of the Romans (a holy zeal on the pope's part), he compelled the Romans to seek peace. This he at last granted on the condition that they should utterly abolish the rule of the patriciate and restore their prefect to his former place, and that in future they should accept as senators only those whom he himself, by papal authority, gave them. With peace made in this way, he was returning to the city; but since he afterwards perceived that treachery lay beneath, fearing an ambush, he slipped away to Tivoli. The Romans at once pursued him as he fled, with arrows and weapons. Having been carried by ship from Tivoli to Pisa, he at last reached Gaul. Using the good offices of St Bernard, he urged King Louis and others to undertake an expedition against the Turks, but they achieved nothing notable. At Reims he held a council, in which he issued most excellent regulations for monks, as follows: that a monk should not leave his monastery for the sake of gain; that he should not stand as sponsor for a child at baptism, nor baptize, nor impose penances, nor visit the sick, nor attend funerals of the dead, nor govern a secular church; although that same monk usurped the monarchy of all churches, most holy of the devils. But he passed no law against fornication or sodomy (which is common to priests and monks). He founded schools of the liberal arts, built the portico of St Mary at the Crib, confirmed the sect of the Gilbertines in England, converted the Norwegians to Papism through Hadrian the Englishman, and performed certain other wonders. Returning to Rome, he at last died the common death in the year of the Lord 1152, and was buried in the basilica of St Peter.
109. Anastasius IV.

units.la: Anastasius quartus, patria Romanus, ex patre Benedicto quodam genitus, fuit primum abbas S. Russi in Veliterna diœcesi: postea sub Eugenio Romanæ synagogæ Cardinalis, & ex Cardinale Papa, uel ipsissimus Antichristus. Hic nihil fecit dignum, inquiunt Barnus & Funccius, quod ad posteros referatur, nisi quod calicem magni ponde-ris si Lateranensi templo dederit, & S. Mariæ rotundæ fabricam ædificauerit. Anastasius, ait Platina, pontificatum adeptus, & calicem pulcherrimi operis, magnaq; æstimationis Lateranensi basilicæ condonauit, & ædes egregias apud Pantheon, quod S. Mariam rotundam uocant, breui ædificauit. Plura enim mente destinauerat, tum ad dignitatem Ecclesiæ, tum ad ornatum urbis Romæ pertinentia, si ei aliquandiu uiuere licuisset. Sed fui[?] pontificatus anno secundo, anno scilicet Domini 1154. uitam cum morte commutauit, in Lateranensi templo tumulatus. Per hunc Anastasium, ut Matthæus Parisius refert, defuncto Henrico Mordacho, ambitioso monacho, quem Eugenius eiusdem professionis Papa intruserat, Guilhelmus Eboracensis archiepiscopus suæ sedi restitutus fuit. Qui tamen Guilhelmus, bausto in ipso calice inter sacra veneno, eodem anno Domini 1154. sublatus est, & pro sancto colitur. Sub eo etiam Pontifice, Thamesis fluuius in Anglia memorabilis, ita gelabat, ut rhedæ ac plaustra ferret. Et parum antea eclipses erant tam solis quam lunæ, teste Matthæo: quas secuta sunt fulgura, tonitrua, & pluuiæ tempestas horrida cælum commouit & undas.
units.tr: Anastasius IV, a native of Rome, born of a father named Benedict, was first abbot of St Rufus in the diocese of Velletri; afterwards, under Eugenius, he became a cardinal of the Roman synagogue, and from cardinal, pope, or rather the very Antichrist himself. Barnes and Funck say that this man did nothing worthy of being handed down to posterity, except that he gave a chalice of great weight to the Lateran church, and built the structure of St Mary of the Round. Anastasius, says Platina, on attaining the pontificate, gave a chalice of very beautiful workmanship and great value to the basilica of the Lateran, and soon built splendid buildings near the Pantheon, which they call St Mary the Round. For he had planned many more things, both pertaining to the dignity of the Church and to the adornment of the city of Rome, if he had been allowed to live for some while. But in the second year of his pontificate, that is in the year of the Lord 1154, he exchanged life for death, and was buried in the Lateran church. Under this Anastasius, as Matthew Paris reports, after the death of Henry Murdac, an ambitious monk whom Eugenius, a pope of the same profession, had thrust in, William, archbishop of York, was restored to his see. Yet this William, after a poisoned draught was drunk from that very chalice during the sacred rites, was taken away in the same year of the Lord 1154, and is honoured as a saint. Under this same pontiff the River Thames in England, famous for its memories, froze so hard that it bore carts and wagons. And a little before, there were eclipses of both the sun and the moon, according to Matthew; these were followed by lightning, thunder and rain, and a dreadful storm stirred the sky and the waves.
110. Hadrian IV.

units.la: HAdrianus quartus, natione Anglus, Nicolaus Brekspeare, Latinè Hastefragus, ante Papatum dictus, & Roberti cuiusdam monachi ac sacerdotis ad Albani fanum filius, ex regulari Canonico & episcopo cardinale Romanus fiebat pontifex. Ab Eugenio tertio ad Norwegios hic olim fuerat missus, ut Romanam religionem, omni diabolicarum superstitionum genere refertam, eos doceret. Qui tandem inde rediens, & urgente clero magnus Abadon effectus, noluit in Lateranum ut consecraretur ascendere, nisi prius consentirent, ut Arnoldus Brixiensis episcopus, quem nominabat haereticum, urbe pelleretur. Suaserat ille Romanis, ut amissam libertatem (grande piaculum) eligendi magistratus, & administranda urbis re-peterent. Sed cum populus obstinatæ pontificis petitioni obsisteret, magnæ turbationes sunt excitatæ. Pontifex vero ad arma solita, quibus mūdi monarchas domare consueverant, recurrens, Romanos excommunicationis fulmine feriebat, donec Arnoldum eicerent, et consules abdicare se magistratu cogerent, liberamque suæ sanctitati urbis administrationem relinqueret. Interea Fridericus Imperator, pro subigendis rebellib. collecto exercitu in Italiam movebat, & Roma citatis agminib. perrexit Pontifex cum clero apud Sutrium Imperatori fit obuiam, putans se opportunitatem nactum, ut [?]cifcendi se per illum de suis aduersarijs. Equo re-lito, pedes Imperator Pontificem excepit, ac fi-niftram sellæ strepam descendenti de iumento te-nuit. Quod Papa (fuperbiffimus Satan) ludibrij lo-co duxit, quum (ut ille arroganter petiuerat) de-xtera fuisset contrectanda. Quo nonnihil commo-tus Imperator, paululum subridens respondit: Mi-nimè fe studuisse apprehendendis strepis. Tu pri-mus es, pater, inquit, cui tali officio unquam defer-uiuimus. Et quia loquendo, bilis ei mouebatur ma-gis: Scire uelim abs te, ait, officij genus hoc, ex de-bito ne fit, an beneplacito? Quod fi ex beneuolen-tia descendit, quis causabitur negligentiam in [?]ftpon-taneo? Si non ex debito, parum interesse puta-mus, quo latere acceffert, qui uenerabundus ac-cedit. Seuerius sic collocuti, discedunt utrinq; non fine stomacho. Imperator tamen, homo prudentissimus, dissimulans ea omnia, quæ de portentofo fictu pontificis audierat ac uiderat, die postero Pontificem in sua castra reuocabat. Pontifex au-tem adiuenit. Imperator illi obuiam ibat: atq; ex priore eius obiurgatione doctior factus, dextram felle strepam apprehendit, perduxitq; intus. Consedentibus ipsis, Hadrianus ordiebatur bunc sermonem: Prisca ætatis principes, inquit, qui ad petendam coronam venerant (vide Antichristum in sua natura) solebant insigni aliquo officio Rom. ecclesiæ benevolentiam promereri, ut suo velut officio prævenientes benedictionem, & debitam coronam omnibus præclaro facinore testarentur. Sic Carolus, dum domuit Longobardos: Otho, dum compescuit Berengarios: Lotharius, dum Normannos repressit, coronam Imperij meruere. Quo circa tua serenitas Apuliam, Romanæ ecclesiæ provinciam, iam à Normannis occupatam, nobis ecclesiæq; restituat: deinde quæ nostri officij sunt, facile exequemur. Cum ergo viderent principes pontificem in ea sententia esse, quòd Fridericum coronare nollet, nisi prius Apulia, à Guilhelmo Siculorum rege occupatam, armis & impensis suis restitueret: pollicentur id futurum, collecto novo exercitu ex Germanis militibus, cum præsens exercitus esset detritus, modò vellet Cæsarem coronare: Altera ergo die in D. Petri basilica, à pontifice imperiali diademate insignieb[?]atur. Sacris de more peractis, & plus mille civibus, qui commotiones in urbe fecerant, cæsis, reditum in Germaniam parauit.
units.tr: Hadrian IV, an Englishman by birth, called Nicholas Breakspear before he became pope (in Latin, Hastefragus), was the son of a certain Robert, a monk and priest at the church of St Albans. From a regular canon and cardinal bishop he became Roman pontiff. Earlier Eugenius III had sent him to the Norwegians to teach them the Roman religion, which was stuffed with every kind of diabolical superstition. On returning from there, and at the urging of the clergy, he became a great Abaddon. He refused to ascend to the Lateran to be consecrated unless they first agreed that Arnold of Brescia, a bishop whom he called a heretic, should be driven out of the city. Arnold had persuaded the Romans to seek back their lost liberty (a great sin) of electing their magistrates and managing the affairs of the city. But when the people resisted the pontiff's stubborn demand, great disturbances were stirred up. The pontiff then had recourse to the weapons he was accustomed to, with which the monarchs of the world had usually been subdued, and struck the Romans with the thunderbolt of excommunication. He did this until they expelled Arnold, forced the consuls to give up their magistracy, and left the administration of the city free to his holiness. Meanwhile Emperor Frederick gathered an army and moved into Italy to subdue the rebels. The pontiff set out from Rome with the clergy and mustered troops, and met the emperor at Sutri, thinking he had found an opportunity to climb up over his enemies by means of him. The emperor had left his horse, and on foot he received the pontiff and held the stirrup with his left hand as the pontiff dismounted. The Pope (most proud Satan) took this as a mockery, since, as he had arrogantly demanded, he should have been given his right hand to kiss. The emperor was somewhat moved and, smiling slightly, replied that he had not at all intended to take hold of the stirrups. "You are the first, father," he said, "to whom we have ever paid such service." And because the talk stirred his anger still more, he said: "I should like to know from you whether this kind of service is owed or given freely. If it comes from goodwill, who could be blamed for negligence in what is voluntary? If it is not owed, we think it matters little from which side he approaches who comes with reverence." After speaking rather harshly, they parted on both sides, not without resentment. The emperor, however, a most prudent man, ignored all the things he had heard and seen of the pontiff's monstrous behaviour, and on the next day he called the Pontiff back to his camp. The Pontiff came. The emperor went out to meet him and, made wiser by the earlier rebuke, took hold of the right stirrup and led him inside. When they had sat down, Hadrian began his speech thus: "Princes of old, who came to seek the crown (see Antichrist in his nature), used to earn the goodwill of the Roman Church by some notable service, so that by anticipating their duty, as it were, they might show by a splendid deed that the blessing and the due crown were theirs. So Charles, when he subdued the Lombards; Otto, when he checked the Berengars; Lothair, when he repressed the Normans, earned the imperial crown. Therefore let your serenity restore Apulia, a province of the Roman Church, now occupied by the Normans, to us and to the Church. Then we shall readily carry out what belongs to our office." When the princes saw that the pontiff was of the opinion that he would not crown Frederick unless Apulia, occupied by William, king of the Sicilians, was first restored at the emperor's own arms and expense, they promised that this would be done. A new army would be raised from German soldiers, since the present army was worn out, provided only that the pontiff would crown the Caesar. So on the next day, in the basilica of St Peter, he was adorned with the imperial diadem by the pontiff. When the sacred rites had been performed as usual, and more than a thousand citizens who had caused the disturbances in the city had been slain, he made ready to return to Germany.

units.la: Post imperatoris discessum, eius ope destitutus Papa, ad eas perfidias animum intendit, qui-bus {hu}posset Guilhelmum Apulia priuare. Excom-municabat primùm, nolentem sibi Apuliam cede-re, quam iure succeßionis à patre acceperat: subdi-tosq; eius omni sacramento datæ fidei liberabit, ut eo facilius ab illo deficerent. Sed cum cerneret, hæc parum póteris habere apud Guilhelmū, Gra-corum Imperatorem Emanuelem contra illum euo-cabat, apud quem nouerat esse exitiale odium er-ga patrem eius defunctum. Quod timens Guilhel-mus, pacem à Pontifice per legatos petiit, promit-tens se omnia restituturum. Sed hanc ne Papa con-cederet, quidam dissuaserunt Cardinales, putantes (patres sancti) sibi plus lucri prouenire ex bello, quàm ex pace. Bellum igitur Guilhelmo Papa de-nunciabat. At Guilhelmus rex moram noxiam ra-tus, ex tota Sicilia exercitum contraxit. Apuliam classe petijt, Emanuelem in fugam uertit: Beneuentum urbem, ubi tum Papa cum Cardinalibus ade-rat, ita oppugnauit, ut de uita desperantes, pete-rent pacem. Concessit Guilhelmus, recipiebaturq; in gratiam à Papa, et declarabatur ab eo utriusq; Si-cilia rex: prius tamen iuramento ei dato, quòd non effet amodò ea infestaturus, quæ essent ecclesiæ Ro-manæ. Romam ergo cum summa ignominia Pon-tifex redijt: ubi præter opinionem in contentio-nem ciuilem incidit, consulibus ciuitatem in antia-quam quam libertatem afferere conantibus. Et cum per consueta excommunicationum fulmina nihil profet ad suam voluntatem, Arimimum concessit.
units.tr: After the emperor's departure, the Pope, deprived of his help, turned his mind to those treacheries by which he might strip William of Apulia. First he excommunicated him, since he would not yield Apulia, which he had received from his father by right of succession, and he released his subjects from every oath of faith given, so that they would more easily desert him. But when he saw that these measures had little effect on William, he called in against him the Greek emperor Manuel, knowing that there was a deadly hatred between him and William's late father. William, fearing this, sought peace from the Pope through envoys, promising to restore everything. But some of the cardinals advised the Pope not to grant this, thinking (holy fathers) that more profit would come to them from war than from peace. So the Pope declared war on William. William the king, judging that delay would be harmful, drew an army together from all over Sicily. He sought Apulia by fleet, put Manuel to flight, and attacked the city of Benevento, where the Pope was then staying with the cardinals, so fiercely that they, despairing of their lives, begged for peace. William agreed, and was received back into favour by the Pope, who declared him king of both Sicilies; but first William gave him an oath that he would no longer attack what belonged to the Roman Church. So the Pope returned to Rome in great disgrace, where, contrary to expectation, he fell into civil strife, as the consuls tried to reclaim their ancient liberty. When the usual thunderbolts of excommunication achieved nothing for his purpose, he withdrew to Ariminum.

units.la: Domi consistens Imperator, dum haec gerentur, considerato quòd Papa prius ius investiturae praelatorum Caesaribus praeripuisset, per legatos suos nationes omnes compilasset, & defectionis semina sparsisset per totum imperium, ab omnibus Germaniæ episcopis homagium ac fidelitatis iuramentum exegit. Legatos Pontificis, si in Germaniam venirent (ab ipso Caesare non vocati) excludendos esse mandavit. Et ad Romanam sedem suos appellare vetuit, nomenq; suum in suis literis pontificio praetulit nomini. Quo eius facto, intantum movit superbissimum Papam, ut acerrimis literis ad eum datis, cum ipso graviter de his rebus expostulaverit. Quas libuit adscribere, ut haec melius intelligantur.
units.tr: While these things were happening, the Emperor stayed at home. Considering that the Pope had earlier seized from the Caesars the right of investing prelates, had through his legates plundered all nations, and had sown the seeds of rebellion throughout the empire, he demanded homage and an oath of fidelity from all the bishops of Germany. He ordered that the legates of the Pontiff, if they came into Germany without being summoned by the Caesar himself, should be shut out. He also forbade his subjects to appeal to the Roman see, and in his letters he put his own name before the papal name. Because of this action the most proud Pope was so greatly moved that he wrote a very bitter letter to him and complained seriously to him about these matters. It is worth setting down these letters, so that these things may be better understood.
Letter of Hadrian to the Emperor.

units.la: Hadrianus episcopus, servus servorum Dei, Friderico Imperatori salutem, & Apostolicam benedictionem. Lex divina, sicut parentes honorantibus longaevitatem promittit: ita maledicentibus patri & matri, sententiam mortis intendit. Veritatis voce docemur, quia omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Quapropter dilecte in Domino fili, super prudentiam tuam non mediocriter admira-mur, quòd beato Petro & S. Romanæ Ecclesiæ, non quantam deberes, reuerentiam exhibere uideris. In literis enim ad nos misisti, nomen tuum nostro præponis: in quo insolentiæ, ne dicam arrogantiæ notam incurris. Quid dicam de fidelitate beato Petro & nobis à te promissa & iurata, quo modo eam obseruesi? Cum ab his qui dii sunt, & fi-lii excelsi omnes (episcopis uidelicet) homagium requiris, fidelitatem exigis, & manus eorum sa-cratas manibus tuis innectis, manifestè nobis sa-ctus contrarius? Cardinalibus à latere nostro di-rectis, non solum Ecclesias, sed & ciuitates regni tui claudis. Quid dicam? Resipisce ergo, resipis-ce, tibi consulimus. Quia, dum à nobis consecratio-nem & coronam merueris, dum inconcessa captas, ne concessa perdas, nobilitati tuæ timemus. Vale. Ad has Pontificis literas Imperator ita respon-dit.
units.tr: Hadrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Frederick the Emperor, greeting and apostolic blessing. The divine law promises long life to those who honour their parents, and it threatens death to those who curse father and mother. We are taught by the voice of truth that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. Therefore, dear son in the Lord, we marvel not a little at your prudence, that you seem to show no more reverence than you ought to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church. In your letter to us you have put your own name before ours, and in doing so you incur the mark of insolence, not to say arrogance. What am I to say about the fealty promised and sworn to blessed Peter and to us by you? How do you keep it? You demand homage and fealty from those who are gods and all sons of the Most High (that is, from bishops), and you clasp their consecrated hands in your own; and you clearly act contrary to us. You shut out not only churches but also the cities of your kingdom against the cardinals sent from our side. What shall I say? Come to your senses, then, come to your senses; this is our counsel to you. Since you have received consecration and the crown from us, while you seize what has not been granted so that you do not lose what has been granted, we fear for your nobility. Farewell. To this letter of the Pontiff the Emperor replied as follows.
The Emperor Frederick's reply.

units.la: Fridericus Dei gratia Romanorum Imperator semper Augustus, Hadriano Romanæ ecclesiæ pon-tifici, omnibusq; adhærere volentibus ijs quæ cæ-pit Iesus facere & docere, S. D. Lex iusticiæ uni-q; quod suum est restituit. Non enim parenti-bus nostris derogamus, quibus in hoc regno nostro debitum exhibemus honorem, à quibus (uidelicet progenitoribus nostris) & regni dignitatem suscepimus, & coronam. Nunquam tempore Costantini, Syluester Regalis aliquid habuisse dignoscitur? Sed eius pietatis concessione libertas data est Ecclesiae, pax restituta, & quicquid Regalis Papatus uester[?] habere dignoscitur, largitione principum donatur. Vnde cum Romano pontifici scri[?]simus, iure ex antiquo nomen nostrum praeponimus, & ad iusticiae normam eidem nobis scribenti concedimus. Reuoluite annales: & si lectum neglexistis quod afferimus, illic inuenitur. Ab his autem qui dij sunt per adoptionem, & Regalia nostra tenent, cur Homagium & regalia sacramenta no exigamus? cum ille noster & vester institutor, ab homine regeni-hil accipiens, sed omnia bona omnibus conferens, tamen pro se & Petro censum Cæsari persoluit, & exemplum vobis dedit, ut et vos ita faciatis?
