Do-cet itaque vos, dicens: Discite à me, quia mitis sum, & humilis corde. Aut igitur Regalia nobis dimit-tant: aut si haec sibi utilia iudicauerint, tunc quae Dei, Deo: quae Cæsaris, Cæsari persoluant. Car-dinalibus utiq; vestris clausae sunt Ecclesiae, et non patent ciuitates. Quia non-uidemus eos prædica-tores, sed prædatores: non pacis corroboratores, sed pecunia raptores: non orbis reparatores, sed auri[?] insatiabiles corrafores. Cum autem uideri-mus eos, quales requirit ecclesia, portantes pacē, illuminantes patriam, assistentes causae humilium in æquitate: necessariis stipendiis & commeatu eos sustentare non differemus. Humilitatis autem (quae est custos virtutum) & mansuetudinis uestrae non minimam notam incurritis, cum huiusmodi quaestiones religioni non multum conferentes, singularibus personis proponitis. Prouideat itaque paternitas uestra, ne dum talia mouet quae indignam ducimus, offendiculum ponat illis qui uelut ad imbrem se rotundum ori uestro aures suas arrigere festinant. Non enim non possumus respondere auditis, cum superbiae detestabilem bestiam usque ad sedem Petri reptasse uideamus, paci ecclesiae semper bene prouidentes. Valete.
units.tr: Frederick, by the grace of God Roman Emperor, ever august, to Hadrian, pontiff of the Roman Church, and to all who wish to cling to those things which Jesus began to do and to teach, greeting. Justice renders to each his own. For we do not detract from our forefathers, to whom in this our kingdom we render due honour, and from whom (namely, our ancestors) we received both the dignity of the kingdom and the crown. Is it known that in the time of Constantine, Sylvester possessed anything royal? But by the grant of that piety liberty was given to the Church and peace was restored, and whatever your royal papacy is known to hold is given by the largesse of princes. Hence, when we write to the Roman pontiff, we place our name before his by right of old, and we grant him, writing to us, the same in accordance with the rule of justice. Turn over the annals; if you have neglected to read what we assert, it is found there. But why should we not demand homage and royal oaths from those who are gods by adoption and hold our regalia? Our founder and yours, who received nothing from any man but conferred all good things on all, nevertheless paid tribute to Caesar for himself and for Peter, and gave you an example, that you should do likewise. He teaches you, therefore, saying: Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart. Let them therefore either give up our regalia, or, if they judge these useful to themselves, then let them render what is God's to God, and what is Caesar's to Caesar. Indeed, the churches are shut against your cardinals, and the cities are not open to them, because we do not see in them preachers, but plunderers; not strengtheners of peace, but robbers of money; not restorers of the world, but insatiable gatherers of gold. But when we see them such as the Church requires, bringing peace, enlightening the country, and upholding the cause of the humble in equity, we will not delay to sustain them with the necessary stipends and provisions. Yet you incur no small mark of humility (which is the guardian of the virtues) and of your gentleness, since you put forward such questions, which contribute little to religion, to particular persons. Let your fatherhood therefore take care lest, while it stirs up such matters, which we consider unworthy, it place a stumbling block before those who hasten to prick up their ears to your mouth, as if for a rain shower. For we cannot fail to answer what we have heard, since we see the detestable beast of pride creeping as far as the seat of Peter, always providing well for the peace of the Church. Farewell.

units.la: Potes in his literis (pie lector) uidere stupidam infanctissimo patre cæcitatem: & in ipso Impera-tore insignem Christianae sapientiae cognitionem. Cum prudentissimus Imperator ille, non tantum honorem ambitioso ac superbo Pontifici daret, quantum eius patebat arrogantia, Imperiiq; ius nō segniter defenderet: idem pontifex per suos legatos, defectiones ab illo per Italiam & alias regiones procurabat. Et ut inde haberet promptiorem occasionem rebellandi, certis cæremoniis illū excommunicabat publicè. Fecitq; latenter, ut rebellium conspiratio, legibus his, iuramento etiam præsti-to, firmaretur: Ne quis sine aliorum omnium con-sensu in pacem cum eo rediret. Item si contingeret Hadrianum ipsum mori, alium non eligerent Pa-pam, nisi ex conspirantium Cardinalium numero. Sed non multo post, cum expaciaretur cum suis a-pud Anagniam, tantæ impietatis anno Domini 1159, quinto Pontificatus anno, pœnas dedit. Musça[?] e-nim inuolauit in os: quæ, quia medicorum arte exi-mi non poterat, præclusit illi spiritum, atq; itafuf-focatus obijt. Ioannis Funccij testimonium ex Barno. Hinc Itali doli in Fridericum usi, per morionem si-ticium, mufices peritum, cum sire occidissent, nisi per fenestram se in aquam præterlabentem præci-pitasset Imperator. Morio deprehensus, per ean-dem fenestram præcipitatus gulam fregit. Hinc in toxicatorem Arabem, qui frena, calcaria, annu-los, nolas, & alia id genus inficerat veneno, ut so-lo contactu eum occiderent, subornabant. Sed & is proditus, suspendio mulctabatur. Hadrianus Ro-manam ditionem plurimum auxit: circa lacu Vuul-finum castella erexit, Radicophanum arcibus mu-niit, urbemq; Romanam ædibus ac mœnibus cul-tiorem reddidit, & Hyberniæ dominatum Henrico secundo Anglorum regi concessit.
units.tr: In these letters, dear reader, you can see the stupid blindness of the most unholy father, and in the Emperor himself a notable knowledge of Christian wisdom. For that most prudent Emperor did not give to the ambitious and proud Pontiff as much honour as his arrogance deserved, and he did not sluggishly defend the rights of the Empire. The same pontiff, through his legates, was procuring defections from him in Italy and other regions. And so that he might have a readier occasion for rebelling, he publicly excommunicated him with certain ceremonies. He also secretly arranged that the conspiracy of the rebels be confirmed by these laws, with an oath even sworn, that no one should return to peace with him without the consent of all the others. Likewise, if it happened that Hadrian himself died, they were not to elect another pope except from the number of the conspiring cardinals. But not long after, when he was taking his leisure with his people at Anagni, in the year of the Lord 1159, in the fifth year of his pontificate, he paid the penalty for so great an impiety. For a fly flew into his mouth, and since it could not be removed by the art of physicians, it closed off his breath, and so, suffocated, he died. The testimony of John Funck, from Barnes. Hence the Italians plotted against Frederick: through a Scythian jester, skilled in music, they tried to kill him, but the Emperor threw himself out of a window into the river flowing past. The jester, having been caught, was thrown through the same window and broke his neck. Hence they also hired an Arab poisoner, who had smeared bridles, spurs, rings, bells and other things of that kind with poison, so that they might kill him by mere touch. But he too was betrayed and punished by hanging. Hadrian greatly enlarged the Roman domain: he built castles around the lake Vulsinus, fortified Radicofani with strongholds, and made the city of Rome more elegant with buildings and walls, and he granted the lordship of Ireland to Henry II, king of the English.
Alexan-
III. Alexander III.

units.la: ALexander tertius, natione Hetruscus, patria Senensis, Rolandus cancellarius antea vocatus, Hadriano Anglo musca deglutita, ut dictum est, suffocato, immanior adhuc bestia successit. Sed quia in eius electionem non omnes concordare poterant, nouem Cardinales, qui ab Imperatoris parte steterant, alium constituerunt Pontificem: nempe Octauianum Romanum ciuem, presbyterum Cardinalem titulo S. Clementis, quem Victorem quartum appellabant. Continuato quoq; post hu-ius Victoris mortem schismate, ordine successe-runt, Paschalis, Calixtus & Innocentius, Alexan-dro opponentes, & magnos tumultus in Eccle-sia Romana dederunt: omnesq; perierunt, eo adhuc superstite. Cum autem Imperator Fridericus, ut lites dirimeret, Papiae conuentum indixisset, & utrunq; Pontificem illuc uocasset, ut causa discuteretur, is qui iure diceretur Pontifex, in officio confirmaretur: Alexander, spretis eius nuncijs, superbissime respondebat, Pontificem Romanum a nemine debere iudicari: legatosq; a se contemptos repulit: ac missis per totam Christianitatem literis, Imperatorem ipsum cum Victore pontifice excommunicationis flagello feriebat. Et ut Romanam urbem in fide retineret, literas ad Ioannem Ecclesiæ D. Petri Cardinalem, qui eius illic gerebat uices, statim misit. Qui uicarij munera memor, largitionibus & familiaritate quadam astu-ta, maiorem partem ciuium eo pertraxit, ut ipsi Alexandro fauerent: & eos crearent consules nouos, qui illius essent studiosissimi. Interea Alexander ex Gallijs in Siciliam delatus, mox rediit: ubi per benigne acceptus fuit. Et urbes Italiæ, illius aduentu, in spem libertatis erectæ: contra iusiurandum Imperatori prius datum, ab eo deficiebant, fauen-te eis Philippo Gallorum rege.
units.tr: ALexander III, a Tuscan by birth and from Siena, formerly called Roland the chancellor, succeeded Adrian the Englishman, who had swallowed a gnat and been choked, as was said above; he was an even more savage beast. But since not all agreed on his election, nine cardinals who had taken the Emperor's side appointed another pope, namely Octavian, a Roman citizen and priest-cardinal of the title of St Clement, whom they called Victor IV. After Victor's death the schism continued, and in turn Paschal, Callixtus and Innocent succeeded, setting themselves against Alexander and stirring great tumults in the Roman Church; all of them perished while Alexander was still alive. When the Emperor Frederick, to settle the disputes, called a meeting at Pavia and summoned both popes there, so that the case might be examined and he who rightly should be pope confirmed in office, Alexander, scorning the messages, replied most arrogantly that the Roman pope ought to be judged by no one. He rejected the legates he had despised, and by sending letters throughout all Christendom, he struck the Emperor himself with the scourge of excommunication, together with Victor the pope. And to keep the city of Rome in the faith, he at once sent letters to John, cardinal of the church of St Peter, who was acting there as his vicar. Mindful of his vicarial duties, John, by largesses and a crafty familiarity, drew most of the citizens over, so that they favoured Alexander himself and created new consuls who were most devoted to him. Meanwhile Alexander was carried from France to Sicily, and soon returned, where he was kindly received. The cities of Italy, raised to hope of freedom by his coming, broke away from the oath previously given to the Emperor, with the support of Philip, king of the French.

units.la: Imperator autem cognitis his rebellionibus, & conspirationibus contra se factis, collecto nouo exercitu, rursus in Italiam mouebat. Cum uero Brixiam uenisset, Hartmannus eius loci episcopus (insignis hypocrita) qui Imperatori à secretis fuit, dehortabatur eum à bello. Persuasit ei, consilio Papæ, in Turcas potius Christianæ fidei hostes, inferendum esse bellum, quam in sanctissimum patrem atq; homines Christianos: cum tamen ipsi sint omni Turca deteriores. Addiditq; (prodi-tor) Hierosolymam sanctam, cum tota promissionis terra, quam Conradus eius patruus armis ac sumptibus maximis olim subegerat, nunc rursus à Soldano occupari. Precabatur, ut experiretur bellicæ fortunæ uires in pessimos Agarenos, & ut has terras cum suo exercitu, iam denuo recupe-raret. Pollicebatur quoq; (fraudator ille) effectu-rum se, ut ad expugnandum Soldanum Aegypti regem, rex Galliae auxiliares mitteret copias. Hu-ius oratione Fridericus motus, aduersus Turcas exercitum illum duxit, quem contra pontificem & alios conspirationis socios conscripserat. Per Vngariam iter faciens, Constantinopolim peruenit, transmissisq; copijs, oppida multa Turcis eripuit, inter quas fuere Philomenia & Iconium. Peruenit q; in minorem Armeniam, & expugnabat omnia. Imo tanta fortuna utebatur, ut Soldanus ipse desperaret de toto suo imperio. Tandem monebat Hierosolymam, & data paganis ciuibus vita, ex urbe eos cedere coegit. Potitus tum demum magnis in Iudaea victoriis, rationes Imperator habuit, quo pacto parta seruaret a Turcis: & quae de structa erant, instaurare t.
units.tr: When the Emperor learned of these rebellions and conspiracies against him, he gathered a new army and again moved into Italy. But when he came to Brescia, Hartmann, bishop of that place (a notorious hypocrite), who was the Emperor's secretary, urged him to abandon the war. At the pope's suggestion he persuaded him that war should be waged rather against the Turks, the enemies of the Christian faith, than against the most holy father and Christian men, although these men were worse than any Turk. And the traitor added that the Holy City of Jerusalem, with the whole land of promise, which his uncle Conrad had once subdued with arms and very great expense, was now again held by the Sultan. He begged the Emperor to test the strength of his military fortune against the worst Agarenes, and to recover these lands with his army, now again. That deceiver also promised that he would bring about the sending of auxiliary troops by the king of France to attack the Sultan of Egypt. Frederick, moved by his speech, led against the Turks that army which he had raised against the pope and his other fellow conspirators. Travelling through Hungary, he reached Constantinople, and after the troops had been ferried across, he snatched many towns from the Turks, among them Philomelium and Iconium. He also came into Lesser Armenia and stormed everything. Indeed he enjoyed such good fortune that the Sultan himself despaired of his whole empire. At last he marched on Jerusalem, and, granting the lives of the pagan citizens, forced them to leave the city. Having at last gained great victories in Judaea, the Emperor considered how he might keep what he had won from the Turks, and how to restore what had been destroyed. (text continues below)

units.la: Verum, interea dum esset in Oriente, laboribus his occupatus, Alexander pontifex, iniquissimus proditor, cum suis conspiratoribus, non cessabat sibi ab eo metuere, si victor in Italiam rediret. Operam igitur dedit Alexander omnibus modis, ut illum perderet. Misit pictorem, qui nescien-te Imperatore, coloribus clam eius exprimeret faciem. Iussitq; simulachrum illud sic depictum, Soldano per secretum nuncium dari: literiq; ipsum admonuit, ut si quietus vivere vellet, illu[?] per insidias necaret. Soldanus acceptis his literis, cum expressa boni Imperatoris imagine, studuit ma-ligno huic monstro gratificari, & se ulcisci de adversario. Sed occasio in castris aut conflictu nunquam obtulit se, ad explendam proditionem Pon-tificiam. Cum vero potitus Hierosolyma exercitum reduceret Cæsar, se curus partiebatur copias in suos ordines, ut eo commodius emensum iter remetiri possent. In Armenia autem, cum semel ex calore solis atque itineris difficultate æstuaret ac sudaret nimium, nihil esse periculi in ea nemorum solitudine ratus, cum paucis equitibus & suo fa-cellano ab exercitu discessit. Non admodum procul, equo descendit, vestes parabat exuere, & ut ipse cum facellano in amne lavaret, ad restinguendum[?] æstum corporis, equites iussit ab amne rece-dere. Ibiq; statim benignus Imperator, equitibus i-gnorantibus, cum suo facellano, ab insidiatoribus capiebatur, ac per nemora abducebatur ad Soldanum. Equites frustra expectabant Imperatorem, quærebant diligenter in alterum usq; diem. Rumor ad exercitum venit, eum esse demersum. Ingens omnibus erat tristitia, & ferè ad integrum mensem in eo flumine illum quærebant. Cum autem non reperirent, electis nouis ducibus, domum redierunt.
units.tr: But meanwhile, while the Emperor was in the East occupied with these labours, Pope Alexander, a most wicked traitor, together with his fellow conspirators, did not cease to fear that the Emperor, if victorious, would return to Italy. Alexander therefore took every means to destroy him. He sent a painter who, without the Emperor's knowledge, secretly painted his likeness in colours. And he ordered that the image so depicted be given to the Sultan by a secret messenger, and in a letter he urged him that, if he wished to live in peace, he should kill him by treachery. The Sultan, having received this letter together with the portrait of the good Emperor, was eager to gratify that malignant monster and to avenge himself on his enemy. But no opportunity ever offered itself in the camp or in battle to accomplish the papal treachery. Then, when Caesar, having taken Jerusalem, was leading the army back, he divided the troops into their own companies so that they could more conveniently retrace the route. In Armenia, however, once, when he was overheated and sweating excessively from the heat of the sun and the difficulty of the journey, thinking there was no danger in that lonely wood, he left the army with a few horsemen and his chaplain. Not far off he dismounted and began to take off his clothes, and in order to bathe in the river with his chaplain to cool his body, he ordered the horsemen to withdraw from the river. There, while the horsemen were unaware, the kindly Emperor was at once seized with his chaplain by ambushers and led through the woods to the Sultan. The horsemen waited in vain for the Emperor, and searched diligently until the next day. A rumour reached the army that he had drowned. Great sadness came upon everyone, and for almost a whole month they searched for him in that river. But when they could not find him, they chose new leaders and returned home.

units.la: Imperator ad Soldanum perductus, simulauit se Imperatoris esse officiarium. Soldanus de facie, ex imagine à Pontifice accepta, cognoscens eundem illum esse, iussit simulachrum eius proferri, ac literas à Pontifice missas coram eo legi. Imperator ad istam proditionem obstupefactus, uidensq; negationi non esse locum, fatebatur uerum, & supplex misericordiam petijt. Soldanus autem, postquam de rebus multis cum eo collocutus esset, atque intelligeret ex eius dictis & factis, uirum esse optimum, in quo nullam uirtutem desideraret bono principe dignam, & cuius prudentiam, candorem, fidem & integritatem admiraretur: cogitauit se ex eius dimissione plurimum sibi gloriæ & honoris comparaturum. Eum igitur postea accersiuit, conditiones libertatis proposuit: atq; ut numerata multa, obsides daret, humaniter obtulit. Illumq; tandem ea lege dimisit, ut secum foedera perpetuae pacis sanciret, ac numeraret millies centum ducatos, relinqueretq; obsidis loco suum illic sacellanum usq; ad solutionem. Parabantur inde diplomata, & itineri se accinxit Imperator. Sacellanum itaq; iussit bono esse animo: polliceba-tur se non quieturum, donec missa pecunia eum liberaliberatum ac reducem uideret in Germania. Soldanus ergo Imperatorem muneribus ornauit, uiatico profequit, 34. equis & certis militibus Brixiam usq; deduxit, ibiq; subsistit.
units.tr: The Emperor, led to the Sultan, pretended to be one of the Emperor's officials. The Sultan, recognising from the face, by the image received from the pope, that this was that very man, ordered the portrait to be brought forward and the letter sent by the pope to be read in his presence. The Emperor, astonished at this treachery, and seeing there was no room for denial, confessed the truth and humbly begged for mercy. The Sultan, however, after he had talked with him at length about many matters, and understood from his words and deeds that he was a most excellent man, in whom he found no virtue unworthy of a good prince, and whose prudence, candour, faithfulness and integrity he admired, thought that by his release he would gain for himself much glory and honour. Therefore he afterwards summoned him, proposed the terms of freedom, and kindly offered that he should give hostages as well as a sum of money counted out. Finally he dismissed him on the condition that he should ratify with him the covenants of perpetual peace, and pay a thousand times a hundred ducats, leaving his own chaplain there as a hostage until payment. Then the documents were prepared, and the Emperor girded himself for the journey. He therefore ordered his chaplain to be of good cheer, promising that he would not rest until he saw him freed and returned to Germany once the money had been sent. So the Sultan honoured the Emperor with gifts, sent him on his way with provisions, and escorted him to Brescia with thirty-four horses and certain soldiers, and there he stopped.

units.la: Principes de Imperatoris reditu certiores fiĕi, frequentes eum adibant. Cæsar Soldano suos varijs donis onustos remisit, adiunctis illis qui eos deducerent, usq; ad Imperij fines. Deinde comitia indixit Norimbergæ, & illuc vocabat omnes imperij principes: quibus Alexandri pontificis proditionem aperuit, proditoriam epistolam ab eo ad Soldanum missam legit, & quibus modis liber esset dimissus exposuit. Principes pollicebantur illi auxilium, ut fidem suam apud Soldanum liberaret: indignantes & suppetias spondebant aduersus Alexandrum, Imperij proditorem. Conscribebatur exercitus: per Italiam nemine repugnante, Romam mouebat. Missisq; in urbem legatis suis, à Romano populo postulabat (dissimulata interim priuata iniuria) ut causa utriusq; Pontificis audita, restitueretur concordia ecclesiæ: decerneretur q;Papalis sedes uni ex electis Pontificibus, ut ecclesiasticæ administrationis summa penes unum maneret. Id uero si faceret, promisit se eis non solum pacem concessurum esse, sed etiam omnia reddituram, quæ iure debebantur. Alexander cernens Im
units.tr: When the princes were informed of the Emperor's return, they often came to him. Caesar sent the Sultan's men back, laden with various gifts, with escorts to conduct them to the borders of the empire. Then he called an assembly at Nuremberg and summoned all the princes of the empire. To them he revealed the treachery of Pope Alexander, read the treacherous letter sent by him to the Sultan, and explained by what means he had been released. The princes promised him aid, so that he might free his good faith with the Sultan, and, indignant, they pledged support against Alexander, the traitor to the empire. An army was raised, and, with no one opposing, he moved on Rome through Italy. Sending his envoys into the city, he demanded of the Roman people (his private wrong being for the time set aside) that, after the cause of both popes had been heard, the concord of the Church be restored, and that the papal see be decreed to one of the elected popes, so that the supreme administration of the ecclesiastical office might remain in one man's hands. If they did this, he promised that he would grant them not only peace, but would also restore all that was rightly owed. Alexander, perceiving that the Emperor would obtain his purpose by these plans,

units.la: [The word "perato" at the lower right is the catchword and is not part of the text.] peratorem istis consilijs fui propositi compotem fore, noctu aufugit Caietam, deinde Beneuentum: postremo 17. anno fui pontificatus in ecqui fui habitu Venetias uenit ubi in monasterio delitescens, ortulo praeficiebatur. Et post aliquot menses agnitus, habito senatu, iussu ducis Sebaftiani, maximo honore exceptus, pontificali pompa in templum D. Marci deducebatur. Nauclerus, Barnus, Funccius, & alij.
units.tr: [The word "perato" at the lower right is the catchword and is not part of the text.] by night fled to Gaeta, then to Benevento; finally, in the seventeenth year of his pontificate, he came to Venice in the guise of a common man, where, hiding in a monastery, he was put in charge of a garden. And after some months he was recognised; the senate was convened, and by the command of Doge Sebastiano he was received with the greatest honour and led in pontifical pomp into the temple of St Mark. Naucler, Barnes, Funck, and others.

units.la: Imperator audiens Venetijs esse Papam, a Venetis postulabat, ut suum hostem, hominem reipublicae perniciosum, sibi restituerent. Quod cum Veneti denegarent, Othonem filium suum cum armata classe misit, ad reposcendum Alexandrum: interdicens tamen illi, ne quid armorum attentaret, priusquam ipse ueniret. Otho autem iuuenis prin-ceps, ferues & gloriae cupidus, neglecto patris man-dato, cum Venetis congrediebatur, uictus capiebatur, uinculisq; inclusus Venetias deducebatur. Creuerunt ex ea re cornua Alexandro, qui pacem inire cum Friderico noluit, nisi prius ueniret Venetias, accepturus ab eo praescriptas pacis conditiones. Vnde pater, mala fortunae filij cosulturus, pollicebatur se statuto tempore uenturum. Indicebatur illi dies[?]; adueniit, coueniebantq; de conditionibus pacis.
units.tr: The Emperor, hearing that the Pope was at Venice, demanded that the Venetians hand over to him his enemy, a man harmful to the commonwealth. When the Venetians refused, he sent his son Otto with an armed fleet to demand Alexander back, but forbade him to attempt anything by force before he himself arrived. Otto, however, a young prince, fiery and eager for glory, disregarded his father's order and engaged the Venetians. He was defeated, captured, put in chains and led off to Venice. Alexander's pride grew from this event. He refused to make peace with Frederick unless the Emperor first came to Venice to receive the terms of peace prescribed by him. Thereupon the father, wishing to help his unfortunate son, promised that he would come at the appointed time. A day was set; he arrived, and they met to discuss the terms of peace.

units.la: Sed Papa non prius absoluit Imperatorem a vinculo excommunicationis, quàm templū D. Marci ad cesserat. Quò cum uentum esset, astante uniuerso populo, Alexander iussit Imperatori (ò ipso Turca crudelior Antichriste) ut humi se prosterneret, ac ueniam peteret. Imperator mox iussa fecit. Tum in manus bestia Papa, prostrati Imperatoris (supremi mundi monarchæ) collum pedibus conculcans, ait: Scriptum est, Super aspidem & basiliscu ambulabis, & conculcabis leonem ac draconem. Cæsar indignâ ferens hanc contumeliam, respondit: Noti bi[?]sed Petro. At Papa rursus (impudens Satan) de primens collū principis, ait: Et mihi, & Petro. Cæsar metuens aliquid subesse periculi, obmutuit, sicque tandem est absolutus, et concordia redintegrata.
units.tr: But the Pope did not release the Emperor from the bond of excommunication until they had come into the temple of St Mark. When they had arrived there, with the whole people standing by, Alexander ordered the Emperor (more cruel than the Turk himself, O Antichrist) to prostrate himself on the ground and beg pardon. The Emperor soon did as he was commanded. Then the Pope, setting his foot on the neck of the prostrate Emperor (the supreme monarch of the world), said: "It is written: 'Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and shalt tread down the lion and the dragon.'" The Caesar, bearing this insult with indignation, replied: "Not to you, but to Peter." But the Pope again (the impudent Satan), pressing down on the prince's neck, said: "And to me and to Peter." Caesar, fearing that some danger lay hidden in this, held his tongue, and so at last he was absolved and concord was restored.

units.la: Conditiones pacis hæ erant: Vt Cæsar habe-ret Alexandrum pro uero Papa: & ut restitueret uniuersa Romanæ Ecclesiæ, quæ tempore belli ef-fent ablata. Compositâ sic pace, Cæsar decessit cum filio. Pontifex, ut Venetis aliquam repende-ret gratiam, pro acceptis beneficijs: Sebastiano duci & senatui donaria dedit, pontificia largi-tione non indigna. Primum, funale candidum da-bat, quo foli Romani pontifices uti solebant. De-inde, ut litera eorum plumbo obsignarentur. Ad hæc, duci concessit tertiam sedem in theatro Rom. pontificis. Quarto in ascensione Domini ad tem-plum Plum S. Marci, concesit indulgetias plenarias perpetuo duraturas. Quinto, duci dedit octo uexilla serica, atq; umbellam galero persimilem, &c. Papiensem episcopum pallij & ferendae crucis dignitate Alexander priuauit, quod ex parte Imperatoris stetisset: & Alexandriae urbi nouae, quo celebraretur suum nomen, episcopum dedit. Concilia ab eo habita fuerunt, unum Turonis in Gallia, aliud Romae in Laterano, in quibus multas constitutiones fecit.
units.tr: The conditions of peace were these: that the Emperor should hold Alexander as the true Pope, and restore everything belonging to the Roman Church that had been taken during the war. The peace being thus concluded, the Emperor departed with his son. The pontiff, in order to repay the Venetians for the benefits received, gave Duke Sebastiano and the senate gifts not unworthy of papal generosity. First, he gave a white candle, which only the Roman pontiffs were accustomed to use. Second, that their letters should be sealed with lead. Besides, he granted the duke a third seat in the theatre of the Roman pontiff. Fourth, on the Ascension of the Lord at the temple of St Mark, he granted plenary indulgences, to last forever. Fifth, he gave the duke eight silk banners and an umbrella very like a galero, etc. Alexander deprived the bishop of Pavia of the pallium and the dignity of carrying the cross, because he had taken the Emperor's side; and he gave a bishop to the new city of Alexandria, so that his name might be celebrated there. He held councils, one at Tours in Gaul and another at Rome in the Lateran, in which he made many constitutions.

units.la: Statuit, ne quis archiepiscoporum reciperet pallium, nisi prius obedientiae iuramentum Papae praestitisset: & ne relictam fratris sponsam frater in matrimonio haberet. Ordinandis ad sacerdotium, uotum castitatis imposuit: & illegitimum, episcopum non debere fieri sanxit. Canonizationes sanctorum mortuorum a solo Papa esse decreuit, & illis solis diuinum honorem exhiberi iussit. Bernardum Clareuallensem, ac Thomam Cantuariensem, Anglorum regis ac regni proditorem, Papisticorum deorum adscripsit numero. Henrico secundo Anglorum regi, se excusanti super caede eiusdem Thomae, sub poenitentiae fuco iniunxit, subditos eius liberè ad Romanam curiam appellare posse: et nemo in posterum Angliae rex foret, nisi prius a Rom. pontifice rex esset appellatus. Constituit[?], coniuges ob lepræ contagium non esse separandos: ad manifestus usurarijs interdicendam esse communi-onem & sepulturam ecclesiasticam. Post hæc & alia facta Papistica, anno Domini 1181. ex hac uita migrauit, & illum optimè præfuisse Vuicelius pa-pista scribit.
units.tr: He decreed that no archbishop should receive the pallium unless he had first sworn an oath of obedience to the Pope, and that a brother should not take his dead brother's wife in marriage. He imposed a vow of chastity on those being ordained to the priesthood, and ruled that an illegitimate person should not be made a bishop. He decreed that the canonization of dead saints belonged to the Pope alone, and ordered that divine honour be paid to those saints alone. He enrolled Bernard of Clairvaux and Thomas of Canterbury, a traitor to the king and kingdom of the English, in the number of the Papist gods. To Henry II, king of the English, who excused himself for the slaying of that same Thomas, he imposed, under the cloak of penance, that his subjects might freely appeal to the Roman court, and that no one in future should be king of England unless he had first been named king by the Roman pontiff. He ruled that spouses should not be separated on account of the contagion of leprosy, and that communion and ecclesiastical burial should be forbidden to manifest usurers. After these and other Papistical acts, he departed this life in the year of the Lord 1181, and the papist Vuicelius writes that he presided most excellently.

units.la: Ex Roberti Montensis Chronico: Alexandri Papam, Ludouicus Gallia & Henricus Angliæ re-ges, officio stratoris usi, pedites dextra lœuaq; frenum equi ipsius tenentes, per Totiacum urbem ad Ligerim, magna pompa deduxerunt, iuxta il-lud Apoc. 17. Cum ea fornicati sunt reges terræ.
units.tr: From the Chronicle of Robert of Mont: King Louis of France and King Henry of England, performing the office of grooms, holding the bridle of his horse with the right and left hands as they went on foot, led Pope Alexander with great pomp through the town of Totiacum to the Loire. This fits that saying of Revelation 17: "With her the kings of the earth have committed fornication."

units.la: Sub isto Pontifice, sol eclipsim patiebatur, & ter remotus undiq; fiebant. Dominus etiam his tem-poribus contra pontificum status ac tyrannides, su-scitauit Vualdenses, seu pauperes de Lugduno: ut per contemptos homines, huius mundi sortes ac sa-pientes confunderet, 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: Under this Pope the sun suffered an eclipse, and earthquakes occurred three times on every side. In these times also the Lord, against the states and tyrannies of the pontiffs, raised up the Waldenses, or the Poor Men of Lyons, so that by means of despised men he might confound the wisdom and the lots of this world, 1 Cor. 1.
112. Lucius III

units.la: Lucius tertius, natione Thuscus, patria Lucen-sis, prius Vbaldus appellatus, ex clariore stir-pe oriundus, omnium Cardinalium consensu, post mortuum Alexandrum, Romani pontificatus gu-bernaculâ suscepit. Is urbe proturbabatur, capti-que ex suis multi sunt ab ipsis Romanis ciuibus, quos partim impositos superkasinos, ac mitris or-natos, satos[?], auersis uultibus per urbem ludibrij causa circumduxerunt, partim aliis affecerunt iniurijs. Nonnullis etiam effrenata eorum malicia oculos ademerunt, & alios neci dederunt. Causa praecipua fuit, quod consulum in urbe nomen abolere niteretur Lucius. Accepta autem tam insigni contumelia, pontifex Veronam profectus est: & habito mihi concilio, Romanorum superbiam improbauit, & acta eorum damnauit, atque tum demum ut nostris in Asia pro re Christiana laborantibus (fucata sanctitas in multorum perniciem) fuc curreretur, maxime, inquit Platina, quum seditione nostrorum principum hostes freti, duce Saladino Hierosolymitanum agrum popularentur. Hic pontifex non immemor suae patriae, multis eam munieribus ante mortem ornauit: & ab Imperatore Friderico obtinuit, ne Hetrusci alia quam Lucensi moneta uterentur: quemadmodum Longobardi solam Rapiensem admitterent, Imperatoriam notam signatam. Nam Cisalpinos, iam antea Pontifex Imperatori conciliauerat. Indignum tamen esse, cum pro suis rapis [illegible, ~12 letters] homagia illi praestare, Valerius Anselmus inter alia refert, quod sanctus Pontifex approbauerit [?] scortatorum [?] fa-ctis. Verone moriebatur anno Domini 1185[?] in cathedrali templo illic sepultus. Eius tempore terrae motus ingens aliquot in Asia insignes urbes, & in Sicilia 25000. hominum deleuit. Armeni etiam odio Graecorum, huic pontifici atque eius institutis Papisticis se subiecerunt, ut Ioannes Paleonydorus in 3. suorum Chronicorum libro refert. Ex-tunc, inquit, suasione Cyrilli Carmelitae Graeci, rex Armeniae cum omnibus episcopis & regni subditis, anno Domini 1181. Lucio 3. Papae se subiecit. De qua re sic habet Mantuanus in 3. Fastorum libro:
units.tr: Lucius III, a Tuscan by birth and a native of Lucca, formerly called Ubaldus and of a more distinguished family, was chosen by the consent of all the cardinals after the death of Alexander and took up the government of the papacy. He was driven out of the city of Rome, and many of his people were captured by the Roman citizens themselves. Some of them they set up on asses, decked out in mitres and chasubles, with their faces turned backward, and led them through the city for mockery; others they treated with other outrages. Some of them their unbridled malice even blinded, and others they put to death. The chief cause was that Lucius was striving to abolish the name of the consuls in the city. After receiving such a serious insult, the pontiff went to Verona, and there, having held a council, he condemned the arrogance of the Romans and annulled their acts. And then at last, while our people were labouring in Asia on behalf of the Christian cause, he saw to it that help was sent (a sham holiness, to the ruin of many), especially, as Platina says, because the enemies, relying on the discord of our princes, were laying waste the land of Jerusalem under the leadership of Saladin. This pontiff, not forgetful of his own homeland, adorned it with many gifts before his death, and he obtained from the Emperor Frederick that the Tuscans should use no coinage other than that of Lucca, just as the Lombards admitted only the coin of Pavia bearing the imperial mark. For earlier the pontiff had reconciled the cisalpine regions to the Emperor. Valerius Anselmus, however, reports among other things that it was unworthy that they should render homage to him for their coins, since the holy pontiff had approved the deeds of whoremongers. He died at Verona in the year of the Lord 1185 [?] and was buried there in the cathedral church. In his time a huge earthquake destroyed several notable cities in Asia, and in Sicily 25,000 people. The Armenians also, out of hatred for the Greeks, submitted themselves to this pontiff and his Papist institutions, as John Paleonydorus relates in the third book of his Chronicles. "From that time," he says, "at the persuasion of Cyril the Greek Carmelite, the king of Armenia, with all the bishops and subjects of his kingdom, submitted himself to Pope Lucius III in the year of the Lord 1181." Concerning this matter Mantuan has the following in the third book of his Fasti:

units.la: Tu vero venerande pater, per Medica cum iam Regna, per Armenias urbes, Parthosque ꝑ omnes, Undique sparsisses diuini semina verbi: Attritus gravitate ævi, gravitate laborum, Ad stata perpetuae migrasti gaudia vitæ.
units.tr: You, indeed, venerable father, who had scattered the seeds of the divine word through the realms of the Medes, through the cities of Armenia, and through all the Parthians, on every side, worn down by the burden of age and the burden of labours, have passed on to the appointed joys of everlasting life.
113. Urban III

units.la: Vrbanus tertius, qui & Turbanus, patria Mediolanensis, è gente Cribella, genitore Ioanne, Pontificatum iniens, revocare ad concordiam Christianos principes primo annixus est (rara avis, si ita fit) ne diffidentes à Barbaris opprimerentur.
units.tr: Urban III, also called Turbanus, a native of Milan, of the family of the Cribelli, son of John, on entering the papacy first strove to recall the Christian princes to concord (a rare bird, if it can be so), lest the distrustful be oppressed by the barbarians.

units.la: Sed vide quid sequitur, ex Alberto Crantzio, in chronicis Saxonum: Statuerat hic, inquit, excommunicationis mucronem in Imperatorem stringere, quia suis conatibus sese opponere ausus fuerat. At priusquam id posset opere adimplere, morte præ preventus fuit. Tantum Crantzius, lib.6,cap.52. Sub hoc Pontifice (ut scribit Vuicelius) nil nisi bella Hierosolymitana. Illic ceciderunt nostri. Heu calamitates infandas. Audiuit Vrbanus, indies in Palaestinae fieri deteriores, Saladino ubique triumphante. Audiuit iterum captam esse Hierosolymam, ac regem Guidonem superatum, dum esset in itinere Venetias versus, comparandae classis gratia. Et ex dolore concepto (ut scribunt authores) Ferrariae moriebatur, anno Domini 1187, secundo sui Pontificatus anno. Huius Pontificis tempore, eclipsis solis erat in die Ioannis Baptistae, hora sexta diei, quam secuta est maxima pestis in Polonia, Russia, & aliis terris. Linonia quoque ad fidem Papisticam convertebatur.
units.tr: But see what follows, from Albert Krantz, in his Chronicle of the Saxons: "He had determined," he says, "to draw the sword of excommunication against the Emperor, because he had dared to oppose his undertakings. But before he could carry this out, he was prevented by death." So far Krantz, book 6, chapter 52. Under this pontiff (as Wicelius writes) there was nothing but wars over Jerusalem. There our people fell. Alas, the unspeakable calamities! Urban heard that conditions in Palestine were growing worse every day, with Saladin triumphant everywhere. He heard again that Jerusalem had been taken and King Guy overcome while he was on his way to Venice to gather a fleet. And from the grief he had conceived (as the authors write) he died at Ferrara in the year of the Lord 1187, in the second year of his papacy. In this pontiff's time there was an eclipse of the sun on the feast of John the Baptist, at the sixth hour of the day, and it was followed by a very great plague in Poland, Russia and other lands. Livonia also was converted to the Papist faith.
114. Gregory VIII

units.la: Gregorius octauum, natione Apulus, patria Beneuentanus, purpuratorum patrum suffragijs in unum coeuntibus, Vrbano praefato, ut iam dictum est, moerore defuncto, in hac Satanæ sede successit. Magna fuit illis diebus, pro recuperanda Hierosolyma, Pontificum sollicitudo: non adeo tamen pro Christianæ reipublicæ commodo, ut pro suorum ventrium impinguatione, ut exitus comprobabat. Serverant[?] principum arma, non modico suarum rerum dispendio. Eos ergo ad ulteriores mundi partes transmittebant, astu hoc in specie ualde bone-sto, ut & interim suas artes exercerent domi. Nam & Gregorius hic noster, statim post initum Papa-tum, nuncios ac literas ad regnorum principes mi-sit, eos cohortatus, ut uiribus[?] omnibus, compara-to terra marique[?] exercitu, Hierosolymam perge-rent, captamq; ex hostibus infidelibus urbem re-cuperarent: cum tamen nulli essent illis ipsis infi-deliores. Sed in uia, dum Pisanos ac Genuenses ob illam professionem conciliare niteretur, anno Do-mini 1187. uenenata potione, ut Matthæus Parisi-us scribit, Pisis per diuinam ultionem spiritum ef-flauit, nōdum expletis in ipso papatu duobus men-sibus: atque ibi sepultus est. Massæus tamen refert, quod pro totius Ecclesiæ reformatione multum la-borauerit. Sed qualis sit talium Antichristorum reformatio, communis experientia satis docet.
units.tr: Gregory VIII, a Apulian by birth, a native of Benevento, succeeded in this seat of Satan, when the cardinals had come together in one body by their votes, after Urban, as has been said, died of grief. In those days the popes showed great concern for the recovery of Jerusalem, yet not so much for the good of the Christian commonwealth as for the fattening of their own bellies, as the outcome proved. They urged the arms of princes, not without considerable loss of their own resources. They therefore sent them to the more distant parts of the world, under the very fair-seeming pretext that they might meanwhile carry on their own arts at home. For this Gregory of ours, immediately after entering the papacy, sent envoys and letters to the princes of the kingdoms, exhorting them that, with all their strength, once an army had been raised by land and sea, they should press on to Jerusalem and recover the city captured from the infidel enemies, though there were none more unfaithful than they themselves. But on the way, while he was trying to win over the Pisans and Genoese for that undertaking, he breathed his last at Pisa in the year of the Lord 1187, by a poisoned drink, as Matthew Paris writes, through divine vengeance, with only two months of his papacy completed; and there he was buried. Massaeus, however, reports that he laboured much for the reformation of the whole Church. But what the reformation of such Antichrists is like, common experience teaches well enough.
115. CLEMENT the Third.

units.la: Clemens tertius, genere Romanus, ex patre Io-anne, cognomento Scholaris, post initum Papa-tum, ad eius regni commoda impiger operarius, de bello statim in Seracenos gerendo edictum pro-posuit. Inde moti principes, arma sumpserunt: quo-rum de numero præcipui fuerunt, Friderieus[?] Impe-rator, Philippus rex Franciæ, Ricardus Rex An-glie, glię,& Otho Burgundię dux, sequentibus multis episcopis atq; archiepiscopis, ut qui potius ad pa-cem quàm bella per Euangelij prædicationem eos incitassent. Ex Dania, Frisia, ac Flandria multi ac cesserunt: sed nihil magnum peregerunt. Contigit anno Domini 1188. Guilhelmum Siciliæ regem Pa-normo uita defungi, nullo relicto hærede: cuius nex [?] regnum papa Clemens ad Rom. Ecclesiæ ius trahere conabatur. Sed insulæ proceres, Tancre-dum Rogerij nothum interim substituerunt. Ponti-sex armis repetere ius illud (non suum, iuxta id q; scribitur Luce 22. Vos autem non sic) animo desti-nauit, ex quo rapinis (sanctum Pontificis studium) ac cædibus omnia repleuit. Et cum uideret non sin-gula sibi ad votum succedere, ad religionis studium se conuertit. Cleri mores correxit, sed scortationes interea atq; horribiles Sodomias non semel repre-hendit. Statuit, solum Papam episcopos posse ad alium locum, aut altiorem dignitatem transferre. Eosdé [?] episcopos quoq; (super bissimus nebulo) primi-cipibus dignitate præire decreuit. Talia erant isto-rum Antichristorum bona opera, dum ipsi princi-pes absentes essent. Nonnulla ædificia in urbe re-stituit, claustrum S. Laurentij extra muros con-struxit, & ædes Lateranenses uetustate collaben-tes non mediocri impensa refecit. Azymos panes & vinum lymphatum in Missis haberi mandauit, aliaq; plura constituit. Affert tamē Baptista Mat-tuanus in 6. Fastorum libro, Azyma seu fuerint, sicut dixere Pelasgi, Liba, quibus fecit sacri venerabilis author, Ambiguum celebrare modo laudabile utroq; si nostrae sinerent leges, Romanaq; iura.
units.tr: Clement the Third, a Roman by birth, son of John, surnamed Scholaris, after taking up the papacy, zealously worked for the advantage of his realm and at once issued a proclamation for war against the Saracens. Moved by this, princes took up arms. Among the most prominent were Frederick the Emperor, Philip king of France, Richard king of England, and Otho duke of Burgundy, followed by many bishops and archbishops, who had urged them to this rather by preaching the Gospel of peace than of war. Many came from Denmark, Friesland and Flanders, but they achieved nothing great. In the year of the Lord 1188 it happened that William, king of Sicily, died at Palermo without leaving an heir. Pope Clement tried to draw the kingdom under the right of the Roman Church, but the nobles of the island meanwhile set up Tancred, an illegitimate son of Roger, in his place. The pontiff resolved to reclaim that right by arms (not his own, in keeping with what is written in Luke 22: "But ye shall not be so"), and from this he filled everything with plunder (the holy aim of the Pontiff) and with slaughter. And when he saw that not everything went according to his wishes, he turned to the pursuit of religion. He corrected the morals of the clergy, yet in the meantime he rebuked fornication and horrible sodomies more than once. He decreed that only the Pope could transfer bishops to another see or to a higher dignity. He also decided that bishops (the most arrant knave) should rank above princes in dignity. Such were the good works of these Antichrists, while the princes themselves were absent. He restored some buildings in the city, built the monastery of St Laurence outside the walls, and at no small expense rebuilt the Lateran palace, which was collapsing with age. He ordered that unleavened bread and watered wine be used in the Masses, and he laid down many other things. Baptista Mantuanus, however, in the sixth book of his Fasti, says: "Whether they were unleavened cakes, as the Pelasgians called them, or liba, with which the venerable author of sacred rites made offerings, it is a matter of doubt; to celebrate it in this way is praiseworthy, if our laws and Roman rights allowed it."

units.la: Mortem Clemens anno Domini 1191. operibus his insistens, obiit. In praedicta cleri reformatione, Cardinalem quendam in Poloniam misit, qui corrigens clericorum mores, synodum illic congregauit. In qua caelibatum unctis suis praecepit: & pro recuperanda terra sancta decimas dari monuit. Chron. Pol. lib. 3. cap. 26. Danorum plebs suis sacer dotibus coniugia decernens, ab hoc pontifice excommunicabatur. Saxo Gram. libro 15.
units.tr: Clement died in the year of the Lord 1191, still busy with these works. In this same reform of the clergy he sent a certain cardinal to Poland, who, correcting the morals of the clergy, gathered a synod there. In it he ordered that priests be celibate and urged that tithes be given to recover the Holy Land. (Chronicle of Poland, book 3, chapter 26.) The common people of Denmark, who had decreed marriage for their priests, were excommunicated by this pontiff. (Saxo Grammaticus, book 15.)
116. CELESTINE the Third.

units.la: Coelestinus tertius, natione Romanus, patre Petro Bubonis, & Iacynthus antea dictus: uir senex, in festo Paschae post Clementis mortem, per Cardinales & episcopos inauguratus, sequenti die Imperatorem Henricum sextum coronauit. Qui aegre ferens Tancredum Siciliae regno potiri (ars[?] vere pontificia) eidem Imperatori Constantiam monacham, Rogerij filiam, e monasterio Panormitano eductam[?], uxorem dedit, ea conditione, ut dotis nomine utriusque Siciliæ regnum peteret, pulsoq; Tancredo possideret, reseruato censu (hoc semper debebat fieri) qui Pontifici quotannis feudatario iure soluebatur. Atq; hoc modo Sueuorum duces Siciliæ regnum obtinuerunt: sed inde creuere bella non incruenta. Ex Funccio. Post huius Henrici mortem, ex magno imperij schismate, ortum est tantum per totam Germaniam dissidium (quum Papa Sueuis infensus ob Siciliæ dominationem, quā ipse ambiebat, Othonem cōfirmaret) ut nulla paræcia cum altera consentiret. Vnde Romanæ pontifici non parum fuit lucri ex compositione litium inter spirituales illos. Talia erant sanctissimorum patrum exercitia, dum principes essent circa expugnandam Hierosolymam occupati, ut prius est significatum. De qua litium compositione, Conradus à Lichtenau, Vrspergensis abbas, ita scripsit: quæ ob id hoc loco referenda esse puto, ut sanctitatem Romanam, & qua occasione tantas acquisierit diuitias, pius lector agnoscat. Vix remansit, inquit, aliquis episcopatus, siue dignitas ecclesiastica, uel etiam parochialis ecclesia, quæ non fieret litigiosa, & Romam deduceretur ipsa causa, sed non manu uacua. Caude mater nostra Roma, quoniam aperiuntur cataractæ thesaurorum in terra, ut ad te confluant riui & aggeres nummorum rum in magna copia. Lætare super iniquitate filiorum hominum: quoniam ad recompensationem tantorum malorum datur tibi precium. Iocundare super adiutrice tua discordia, quæ erupit de puteo infernalis abyssi, ut accumulentur tibi multa peccatorum præmia. Habes quod fitifli[?]. Decanta canticum: quia per maliciam hominum, non per pietatem religionem orbem vicisti. Ad te trahit homines, non ipsorum devotio, aut pura conscientia, sed scelerum multiplicium perpetratio, & litium decisio, precio comparata. Hæc abbas ille.
units.tr: Celestine the Third, a Roman by nation, son of Peter Bubonis, previously called Hyacinth, an old man, was installed by the cardinals and bishops on the feast of Easter after the death of Clement, and on the following day he crowned the Emperor Henry the Sixth. Being displeased that Tancred held the kingdom of Sicily (a truly papal trick), he gave the same emperor as wife Constance, a nun and daughter of Roger, brought out of the Palermo monastery, on the condition that he claim the whole kingdom of Sicily under the name of dowry, drive out Tancred and possess it, reserving the tribute (which was always to be paid) that was owed each year to the Pontiff as feudal lord. In this way the dukes of Swabia obtained the kingdom of Sicily, but from this bloody wars arose. From Funccius: after the death of this Henry, from the great schism of the empire there arose such a discord throughout the whole of Germany (since the Pope, hostile to the Swabians because of his own ambition for the rule of Sicily, confirmed Otto) that no parish agreed with another. Hence the Roman pontiff gained not a little profit from the settlement of lawsuits among those spiritual men. Such were the exercises of the most holy fathers, while the princes were occupied with storming Jerusalem, as was said before. Concerning this settlement of lawsuits, Conrad of Lichtenau, abbot of Ursperg, wrote as follows. I think these words should be quoted here, so that the pious reader may recognise the Roman holiness and by what means it acquired such great riches. "Scarcely any bishopric," he says, "or ecclesiastical dignity, or even parish church, was left which did not become a matter of dispute, and the case was brought to Rome, but not empty-handed. Hail, our mother Rome, since the floodgates of treasures are opened on earth, so that streams and heaps of money flow together to you in great abundance. Rejoice over the iniquity of the sons of men, since a price is given you as recompense for so great evils. Be glad over your helper, discord, which has burst out of the pit of the infernal abyss, so that many rewards for sins may be piled up for you. You have what you wanted. Sing a song, for you have conquered the world not by the piety of men but by their malice, not by their devotion or pure conscience but by the commission of manifold crimes and the settling of lawsuits bought for a price." So says that abbot.

units.la: Quæ si quis in Anglia, aut alibi, ubi niget Papatus, aperte nunc diceret, non tantum pro hæretico haberetur, sed & igne comburerentur: quæ tamen monachus ille tunc dicere non abhorruit. Instabat adhuc Cœlestinus (quod magno sibi ac suis tunc esset lucro) ut terram sanctam principes bellis recuperarent. Et interim ipse, inquit Platina, in tantis rerum perturbationibus, tantaq; sumptu bellico, ædes egregias tum apud S. Petrum, tum ad Lateranum ædificavit, quibus recipi Pontifices percommodè possent. Extant adhuc in Lateranō valvæ æneæ egregiæ ad sanctam sanctorum, suo iussu suaq; impensa fabrefactæ. Prætera vero civitatis nomen Viterbio dedit, ecclesiamq; eorum cathedralem fecit: Tuscanensem & Centumcellen-[illegible, ~3 letters] sem ita in eandem transferens, ut unum episcopum omnibus praesset. Praesulem, bigamum ordinan-tem ad ecclesiasticos gradus, potestate priuandum censuit, & iuramentum metu extortum adnihilauit. Peracius[?] his omnibus, Cœlestinus anno Domini 1198. ex hoc seculo reliqua carne migrauit. Vt Stella Venetus scribit: Nihil hic praetermisit (sed ad suum commodum semper) quo minus Hierosolyma recuperaretur. Occupabatur, inquit Vuicelius, & in bellis Palaestinis, sed felicius: homo ecclesiae Romanae perutilis. Non minus apte quam vere, & veritatis aduersario dictum. Huius tempore, Cyrillus praedictus eremita, anno Domini 1192. post decem Papisticae praedicationis annos, ex Armenia ad Carmelum est reuersus, ubi statim oraculum valde prodigiosum inter missandu habuit. De quo Mantuanus in quinto Fastorum libro, eius seculi mysteriis excaecatus, sic scribit:
units.tr: If anyone in England, or elsewhere where the papacy is denied, were to say these things openly now, he would not only be held a heretic but would also be burned with fire; yet that monk did not shrink from saying them then. Celestine, meanwhile (which was then a great gain for himself and his own), kept urging the princes to recover the Holy Land by war. And meanwhile, says Platina, amid such upheavals of affairs and such great expense on war, he built splendid buildings both at St Peter's and at the Lateran, in which the Pontiffs could be most comfortably received. Still today at the Lateran there remain fine bronze doors to the Holy of Holies, made at his command and at his expense. Moreover he gave the name of city to Viterbo and made its church a cathedral, transferring the bishops of Tuscania and Centumcellae into it so that one bishop would preside over them all. He decreed that a bishop who ordained a bigamist to the ecclesiastical grades should be deprived of his power, and he annulled an oath extorted by fear. Having accomplished all these things, Celestine departed from this age, leaving his flesh behind, in the year of the Lord 1198. As Stella of Venice writes: "He left nothing undone here (but always for his own advantage) by which Jerusalem might not be recovered." "He was also occupied in the wars in Palestine," says Wicelius, "but more fortunately; a man very useful to the Roman Church." This was said no less aptly than truly, and by an adversary of the truth. In his time, the aforementioned hermit Cyril, in the year of the Lord 1192, after ten years of Papist preaching, returned from Armenia to Carmel, where he at once had a very prodigious oracle while celebrating Mass. Concerning this Mantuan, in the fifth book of his Fasti, blinded by the mysteries of his age, writes as follows:

units.la: Cyrillus diuinus homo, cum sacra litaret, Mane sub auroram, sacra uestitus abolla (Res miranda) puer fulgenti splendidus ore Astitit ante virum, liquidis suspensus in auris: Argentumq; docens annorum fata sequentum, Protulit, & manibus pronis dimisit in aram, Adijciens: Deus ista tibi secreta reuelat, Sancte pater, tu sic populis ea nota Latinis.
units.tr: Cyril, a divine man, while offering sacrifice at dawn, clad in a sacred cloak (a wonderful thing!), a boy shining with radiant face stood before the man, suspended in the clear air; and, teaching him the fates of the years to come, he brought out a silver plate and laid it on the altar with his hands bowed down, adding: "God reveals these secrets to you, holy father; make them known thus to the Latin peoples."
Cota[?]

units.la: Continuò mutàns Romanis Atticà uerbis Nomina, ad abbatem Siculum transmisit, & ille Coenobitam in Latium, scholijs ad singula iunctis: Quæ superant, & habentur adhuc, passimq; legun tur. Sed huius historiæ veritas, sub Gregorio nono postea reuelabitur. Tria nanq; prodigia, ma gna atque miranda, suscepit illa ætas, ut in magna admiratione mendicantium ordinum sectas tunc mundus haberet, dum operaretur Satan in suo An tichristo plenum iniquitatis mysterium, 2. Thess. scilicet Lateranensis templi corruentis sustenta tionem in uisione Romæ per Dominicum, quinque Francisci uulnera Seraphica in quodam Lauernia monte, & huius Cyrilli cœlestè oraculum dum in Carmeli solitudine misseret. Nicolaus Tolentinus nondum erat natus: postea tamen pro suis Augu stinianis, quarto mendicantium generi, stellam ac piscēs adduxit.
units.tr: Immediately changing the names into Roman words from Attic ones, he sent them to the Sicilian abbot, and that man sent the monk into Latium, with commentaries attached to each item. What remains of them is still extant, and is read everywhere. But the truth of this history was later to be revealed under Gregory the Ninth. For that age received three great and marvellous prodigies, so that the world then held the sects of the mendicant orders in great admiration, while Satan was at work in his Antichrist, the mystery of iniquity (2 Thess.): namely the sustaining of the collapsing Lateran temple, shown in a vision at Rome to Dominic; the five wounds of Francis, a seraphic sign, on a certain mountain of La Verna; and this heavenly oracle of Cyril, given while he was at prayer in the solitude of Carmel. Nicholas of Tolentino was not yet born; afterwards, however, he brought a star and fishes for his Augustinians, the fourth kind of mendicant orders.
117. INNOCENT III.

units.la: Innocentius tertius, natione Campanus, patriâ Anagninus, genitore Trasimundo è familia comi tum natus, concordantibus in eius electione Car dinalibus, in demortui Cœlestini locum sufficieba tur. Contra Philippum Imperatorem, eo quòd à Germaniæ principibus ipso inuito creatus fuisset, tanto odio exarsit, ut in hæc uerba proruperit: Aut pontifex Philippo diadema & regnum(o arrogans bestia)aut Philippm pontifici insigne Apostolicum adimat. Othonem subinde ducem audacem ac temerarium contra Philippum concitabat. Unde huius beatissimi confessoris opera, saevissima & tot bella, & humani sanguinis profusiones innumerae factae fuerunt, donec tandem ab alio quodam Othone sceleratoac nefando homicida, prodi torio animo Philippo occiso, Otho ipse quem Pontifex in Philippum concitauerat, Romam propera-rans, diadema Imperij acceperit ab eodem. At non diu horum impiorum(Papae & Othonis) firmata pax durauit. Nam quum Otho ea recuperare instituereт[?] (quae, quum Imperio subiacerent, per multos tamen annos variis artibus à Pontificibus occupata fuerant) ab ipso Pontifice anathemate per cutiebatur[?], imperialiq; dignitate spoliabatur. Ac principes sacramenti religione, qua Othoni tenebantur, absoluit: prohibebatq;, ne quis sub anathematis poena Othonem, aut habeat aut dicat Imperatorem. Fridericumq; Siciliae regem, à primipibus Imperatorem creari curauit. Hic praeterea Innocentius, in Christi doctrinam blasphemum, lege sanciuit, ut maledicentibus Papae, poena infligeretur. Haec Marius, in Eusebio captiuo, ex Vrspergen[?] sabbate[?]. Innocentius iste, anno Domini 1212. tria ardua moliebatur praedicti Othonis depositionem, pro-vocationem[?] Hierosolymae, & universale concilium. Atq; eodem anno (ut Huldricus Mutius narrat) in Alsatia quidam nobiles hunc Papam impietatis damnabant, quod sacerdotibus uxores non permit-teret, centum que sunt per episcopos uno die combu-sti, nam carnium & matrimonii usum, omni tem-pore Christianis esse licitum docebant. Magna hae-resis, ab ipso etiam Apostolo suffulta, 1. Tim 4. Tales etiam, inquit Nauclerus, Mediolani erant, qui Alsatiis collectas miserunt. Mirabiles in Anglo-rum regem Ioannem tragoedias excitavit hic pon-tifex. Stephanum Cardinalem, cognomento Lan-gtonum, eo invito, in Cantuariensem archiepisco-patum intrusit, & 64. monachi ad varias in il-lum proditiones animum addidit. Eundem regem ecclesiae hostem, cum haec non pateretur, judica-vit, fidelium communione privavit, regnum eius sub interdicto per 6. annos & tres menses posuit, regia administratione illum submovit, sceptrum & coronam abstulit, populum ab illius obedien-tia absoluit, terras eius Francorum regis filio Lu-douico dedit, ut fortunis acuita[?] spoliaretur, ut sit[?], & alias in eum tyrannides fecit. Territus Ioannes, princeps alioqui validus & invitus, quod à suis optimatibus, episcopis ac popularibus destituereretur, inuitus ad eius obedientiam redijt. Christianorum omnium caput, atq; in terris Deum, Antichristum hunc agnouit: ac graui iureiu-rando se obstrinxit, se eius arbitrio staturum, posterosq; reges idipsum facturos, ut se deinceps Romanae pontificis beneficiarios agnoscerent perpetuo. Insignis certè haec erat Christianorum regum contumelia.
units.tr: Innocent III, a Campanian by nation and a native of Anagni, born to the noble Trasimund family of the Conti, was chosen to fill the place of the deceased Celestine, the cardinals agreeing in his election. He was so inflamed with hatred against Philip the Emperor, because the princes of Germany had created him against his will, that he burst out in these words: "Either the pope must take the diadem and kingdom from Philip (you arrogant beast), or Philip must take the apostolic insignia from the pope." He then incited the bold and rash Otto against Philip. As a result of the work of this most blessed confessor, the most savage wars and countless effusions of human blood took place, until at last Philip was treacherously killed by another Otto, a wicked and nefarious murderer. Otto himself, whom the Pontiff had stirred up against Philip, hastened to Rome and received the imperial diadem from the same pontiff. But the peace of these impious men (the Pope and Otto) did not last long. For when Otto set about recovering those things (which, though subject to the Empire, had for many years been seized by the popes by various arts), he was placed under anathema by the Pontiff himself and stripped of his imperial dignity. The Pope also absolved the princes from the sacred oath by which they were bound to Otto, and forbade anyone, under penalty of anathema, to hold or call Otto emperor. He also saw to it that Frederick, king of Sicily, was created emperor by the princes. Moreover, this Innocent enacted a law, blasphemous against the doctrine of Christ, that punishment be inflicted on those who spoke ill of the Pope. These things Marius reports, in Eusebius captive, from Urspergensis. In the year of the Lord 1212 this Innocent was undertaking three arduous projects: the deposition of the aforesaid Otto, the provocation to Jerusalem, and a universal council. And in that same year (as Huldrich Mutius relates) certain nobles in Alsace condemned this Pope as impious, because he did not permit priests to have wives; and a hundred of them were burned in one day by the bishops. For they taught that the use of flesh and marriage was lawful for Christians at all times. This was a great heresy, supported by the Apostle himself, 1. Tim 4. Such people, says Naucler, were also at Milan, and they sent collections to Alsace. This Pontiff stirred up wondrous tragedies against the English king John. Against his will he thrust Stephen the Cardinal, surnamed Langton, into the archbishopric of Canterbury, and he encouraged sixty-four monks to various betrayals of the king. When the king would not tolerate this, the Pope judged him an enemy of the Church. He deprived him of communion with the faithful, placed his kingdom under interdict for six years and three months, removed him from royal administration, took away his sceptre and crown, absolved the people from their obedience to him, gave his lands to Louis, son of the king of France, so that he might be stripped of his fortunes, and inflicted other tyrannies upon him. John, otherwise a powerful prince but unwilling, was terrified because he was deserted by his nobles, bishops and common people, and he returned unwillingly to obedience to him. He acknowledged this Antichrist as the head of all Christians and God on earth, and bound himself by a solemn oath that he would abide by his judgment, and that subsequent kings would do the same, so that they would recognise themselves forever as beneficiaries of the Roman pontiff. Certainly this was a notable insult to Christian kings.

units.la: Idem Innocentius, sub recuperandae Hierosolymae fuco, Lateranense concilium anno Domini 1215. contra Imperatorem celebrauit, ut eum excommunicaret ac deponeret: inuaserat enim urbes S. Petri. In quo concilio, auricularem confessionem à Christianis primus extorsit, ac laicis calicem in Eucharistiae communione primus etiam prohibuit. Almaricum virum eruditum pro haeretico damnauit, atque eius ossa Parisijs cum suis sectatoribus cremari praecepit. Et hoc fecit (inquit Dominicus Soto, in quodam sermone) quod ex templis eijciendas esse imagines docuisset. Ioachimi abbatis doctrinam improbabat, ministrorum coniugia in perpetuum sustulit, & monachorum mendicantium se in suam tutelam suscepit.
units.tr: Under the pretext of recovering Jerusalem, the same Innocent celebrated the Lateran council in the year of the Lord 1215 against the Emperor, in order to excommunicate and depose him, for he had invaded the cities of St Peter. At this council he was the first to extort auricular confession from Christians, and he was also the first to forbid the laity the chalice in the communion of the Eucharist. He condemned Amalric, a learned man, as a heretic, and ordered his bones to be burned at Paris together with his followers. And he did this (says Dominicus Soto, in a certain sermon) because Amalric had taught that images ought to be removed from churches. He disapproved of the teaching of the abbot Joachim, abolished the marriages of ministers for ever, and took the mendicant monks under his protection.

units.la: Omnis utriusque sexus decretalem edidit: pascalem communionem ordinauit, decimas occultas exegit, de Missae officio librum copofuit, & pro Asiatico bello qua-dragesimam omnium reddituum partem postula-uit. Potestatem ordinariam patriarchis, archiepi-scopis & episcopis, in multis rebus ademit: primi-pum discordias, ac discordem Cæsaris electionem Romana pontificis arbitrio subiecit, & uxores in quarto affinitatis aut cognationis gradu posse du-ci permisit. Eucharisticum panem in templis asseruari statuit, & tintinnabulum cum lumine, quum ad ægrotum portaretur, eundem præcedere decre-uit: clericum habentem concubinam, à beneficio suspendendum censuit.
units.tr: He issued the decretal Omnis utriusque sexus. He ordained the Easter communion, exacted secret tithes, composed a book on the office of the Mass, and demanded for the Asian war a fortieth part of all revenues. He took away from patriarchs, archbishops and bishops their ordinary power in many matters. He subjected the primacies and the discord over the election of Caesar to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, and he permitted wives to be taken within the fourth degree of affinity or kinship. He decreed that the Eucharistic bread be kept in churches, and ordered that a bell with a light should go before it when it was carried to the sick. He judged that a cleric keeping a concubine should be suspended from his benefice.

units.la: Missalis canonis verba (iniquus Satan) verbis Evangelicis æqualia fieri iussit: sacerdotem con-sessiones reuelantem, in monasterium adperpetuā poenitentiam includi voluit: & quòd principes ter-rarum corrigere Papa debeat, ac nullū deinceps, quem ille non coronauerit, pro Imperatore debere capi, ordinauit. Vniuersis ecclesiis, uel cuiq; ea-rum quæ Romæ erant, pro conficiendis calicibus, argen-ti libram dedit: basilicam D. Sixti restituit: altare S. Petri plurimum ornauit, & ecclesiam S. Mariæ trans Tyberim solenniter dedicauit. Turrim, quam Comitū dicunt, superfluis sumptibus excitauit: [illegible, ~3 letters]ti Spiritus hospitale Romæ erexit, ac prouentibus auxit, & alia in ea Satanæ sede mirabilia magna [illegible, ~3 letters]fecit. ficit. Dum uero Perusium anno Domini 1216. pro tollendis (sed ingentis lucri gratia) dissidijs inter Genuenses & Pisanos, profectus esset, uitam morte commutauit. Eius tempore Liuonia Papisticam suscepit religionem. Petrus quoq; Arragonū rex, Papistarum praestigijs excaecatus, feudatarium Papæ Romano suum regnum cum omnibus suis ditionibus fecit (Vincentio teste) ut animæ salutem meretur[?] & ita bestiam adorabat, Apoc. 13.
units.tr: He ordered that the words of the canon of the Mass be made equal to the words of the Gospel (wicked Satan). He wished a priest who revealed confessions to be shut up in a monastery for perpetual penance. He ordained that the Pope ought to correct the princes of the earth, and that from then on no one should be taken as emperor whom the Pope had not crowned. He gave a pound of silver to all churches, or to any of those in Rome, for making chalices. He restored the basilica of St Sixtus, greatly adorned the altar of St Peter, and solemnly dedicated the church of St Mary across the Tiber. At great superfluous expense he raised the tower which they call that of the Counts. He erected a hospital of the Holy Spirit at Rome and increased its revenues, and did many other marvellous things in that seat of Satan [illegible]. But when he went to Perugia in the year of the Lord 1216 to settle the quarrels between the Genoese and the Pisans (for the sake of great profit), he exchanged life for death. In his time Livonia adopted the Papist religion. Peter also, king of Aragon, blinded by the deceits of the Papists, made his kingdom with all its dominions a fief of the Roman Pope (as Vincentius testifies), so as to earn the salvation of his soul; and so he worshipped the beast, Rev. 13.

units.la: In Anglia nobilis quidam, audiens sacerdotum coniugia in Lateranensi synodo iterum damnari per istum Innocentium, hunc rhythmum sequente anno Domini, scilicet 1216. cecinit, ut Oxonij in uetustissimo quodam codice Ioannes Pullanus reperit, & ad me misit.
units.tr: In England a certain nobleman, hearing that the marriages of priests had again been condemned by this Innocent at the Lateran synod, sang this rhyme in the following year, 1216. John Pullanus found it in a very ancient codex at Oxford and sent it to me.

units.la: Prisciani regula penitus cassatur, Sacerdos per hic & hæc olim declinatur: Sed per hic solummodo nunc articulatur, Cum per nostrum præsulem hæc amoueatur:
units.tr: The rule of Priscian is utterly cancelled: "sacerdos" was once declined as "hic" and "haec"; but now it is inflected only as "hic", since by our prelate this is removed.

units.la: Ita quidam presbyter cæpit allegare: Peccat criminaliter, qui uult separare, Quod Deus coniunxerat, fœminam amare. Tales dignum duximus, fures appellare.
units.tr: So a certain priest began to argue: he sins criminally who wishes to separate what God had joined, namely to love a woman. Such men we have thought worthy to be called thieves.

units.la: O quàm dolor anxius, quàm tormentum grauè, Nobis est dimittere, quoniam suaue. O Romanæ pontifex, statuisti prauè, Ne in tanto crimine moriaris, caue.
units.tr: O how anxious the grief, how grievous the torment, for us to let go of what is so sweet! O Roman pontiff, you have decided wickedly; take care lest you die in so great a crime.

units.la: Non est Innocentius, immo nocens vere, Qui quod facto docuit, verbo vult delere: Et quod olim iuvenis voluit habere, Modo vetus Pontifex studet prohibere.
units.tr: He is no Innocent, indeed he is truly harmful, who wishes to erase by word what he taught by deed; and what the old pontiff once wished to have as a young man, now he strives to forbid.

units.la: Gignere nos praecipit vetus testamentum: Novum quod non retinet, nusquam est inventum. Praesul qui contrarium donat documentum, Nullum necessarium his dat argumentum.
units.tr: The Old Testament commands us to beget; what the New does not retain is found nowhere. The prelate who gives the contrary document gives no necessary argument for these things.

units.la: Dedit enim Dominus maledictionem, Viro qui non fecerit generationem. Ergo tibi consulo per hanc rationem, Gignere ut habeas benedictionem.
units.tr: For the Lord gave a curse to the man who does not beget offspring. Therefore I counsel you by this reasoning, that you may beget and have the blessing.

units.la: Nonne de militibus milites procedunt? Et reges a regibus, qui sibi succedunt? Per locum a simili, omnes iura laedunt, Clericos qui gignere, crimen esse credunt.
units.tr: Do not soldiers come from soldiers, and kings from the kings who succeed them? By argument from likeness, they all wrong the laws who believe it a crime for clerics to beget children.

units.la: Nobis adhuc praecipit vetus testamentum, Quod nostrae nunc legis est verax fundamentum, Ut mares & feminae sciant instrumentum, Tale per quod habeant prolis incrementum.
units.tr: Still the Old Testament commands us, which is the true foundation of our present law, that males and females should know the instrument by which they may have an increase of offspring.

units.la: Zacharias habuit prolem & uxorem, Per virum quem genuit adeptus honorem. Baptizavit etenim mundi Salvatorem: Pereat qui teneat novum hunc errorem.
units.tr: Zacharias had a son and a wife, and through the son he begot he obtained honour; for he baptized the Saviour of the world. Let him perish who holds this new error.
Paul is caught up to the higher heavens,

units.la: Ubi multas didicit res secretiores. Ad nos tandem redieṅs[?], instruensq; mores, Suas (inquit) habeant quilibet uxores.
units.tr: where he learned many more secret things. Returning at last to us and instructing our morals, he says: let each man have his own wife.

units.la: Propter hæc & alia dogmata doctorum, Reor esse melius, & magis decorum, Quisq; suam habeat, & non proximorum, Ne incurrat odium vel iram eorum.
units.tr: For these and other doctrines of the teachers, I think it better and more fitting that each man should have his own wife, and not his neighbours', lest he incur their hatred or anger.

units.la: Proximorum feminas, filias & neptes, Violare nefas est, quare nil deceptes. Vere tuam habeas, & in hac delectes, Diem ut sic ultimum tutius expectes.
units.tr: It is wicked to violate the wives, daughters and granddaughters of one's neighbours, so do not be deceived. Truly, have your own and take your pleasure in her, so that you may await your last day more safely.

units.la: Ecce iam pro clericis multum allegavi, Nec non pro presbyteris plura comprobavi: Pater noster nunc pro me, quoniam peccavi, Dicat quisq; presbyter, cum sua suavi.
units.tr: Behold, I have now argued much for the clergy and proved many things for the presbyters too. Since I have sinned, let each presbyter now say the Our Father for me, with his sweetheart.
118. HONORIUS the Third.

units.la: Honorius tertius, patria Romanus, Americo ge- nitore, perusij[?] Pontificatum init: quum ciborū subtractione artarentur Cardinales inclusi, electi onem ipsius illic accelerare. Qui quamprimū pro- sectus Romam, quo ad potuit, Asianus[?] bellis consu- it[?], sciens illa nonnihil conducere his quæ[?] tunc mi apud ipsos agebantur. Deligebaturq; statim lo- annes Columna, Cardinalis Romanus, qui legatus ad copostendas[?] cū ipsis copijs proficisceretur, qua Innocentius tertius ad id ante collegerat. Fridericum fecundum, Constantiæ monialis filium, adversus execratum Othonem quartum, Imperij dia-demate coronauit: cui tamen postea, ius suum in Siciliæ & Apuliæ terris legitimè occupanti, sacris interdixit. Et Honorius ille, inquit Marius, adeo castra Fridericum hunc Imperatorem concitatus est, ut ipsius rebelles quosdam, qui in Tuscia contra eius maiestatem arma sumpserat, seditiosè fouerɛt, ut illos Imperator (ut par erat) castigare non possset: baronesq; ab eius fidelitate absoluit. Quæ lis[?] nihilominus, Magistri[?] de Salza Teutonicorum intercessione, ad tempus est composita, ut habet eius ordinis Chronicon. Petrum Altissiodoren-sem comitem, in D. Laurentij basilicâ extra muros, in Græcorum Imperatorem, cum solâ coniuge coronauit. Carmelitas & Augustinianos ante productos, protegendos suscepit. Dominicanos vero et Franciscanum, sub Innocentio generatos, approbauit, confirmauit, & in adoptionis filios admisit, ut ecclesiæ patrimonium, ac panis in Missa papisticâ transubstantiationem, contra nouiter exortos hæreticos Vualdenses & Albianos defenderent. Fixerant enim Dominicani parum ante eius morte, visionem Innocentio tertio factam esse, Lateranensem ecclesiam omnino ruituram, nisi parens eorum Dominicus eâ subleuasset humeris. De quâ visione
units.tr: Honorius the Third, a Roman by birth, son of Americus, entered the papacy at Perugia, where the cardinals were shut in and pressed by a reduction of their food, and were hastening his election there. As soon as he set out for Rome, he settled the wars in Asia as far as he could, knowing that this would somewhat help the affairs then being carried on among them. John Colonna, a Roman cardinal, was at once chosen to set out as legate with the forces that Innocent III had previously gathered for that purpose. He crowned Frederick II, son of the nun Constance, emperor with the diadem of the empire, against the cursed Otto IV. Yet afterwards he forbade him the sacraments, though Frederick was lawfully occupying his right in the lands of Sicily and Apulia. And that Honorius, says Marius, so stirred up this emperor Frederick that he seditiously fostered some of his rebels who had taken up arms in Tuscany against his majesty, so that the emperor could not (as was right) punish them. He also absolved the barons from their allegiance to him.
