Nevertheless this quarrel was settled for a time through the intercession of Hermann of Salza, master of the Teutonic Knights, as that order's chronicle has it. He crowned Peter, count of Auxerre, emperor of the Greeks in the basilica of St Laurence outside the walls, with his wife alone. He took the Carmelites and Augustinians, who had been brought forward earlier, under his protection. The Dominicans and Franciscans, who had been born under Innocent, he approved and confirmed, and admitted them as adopted sons, so that they might defend the patrimony of the Church and the transubstantiation of bread in the papistical Mass against the heretics, the Waldenses and Albigenses, who had lately arisen. For the Dominicans had put it about, shortly before his death, that Innocent III had had a vision that the Lateran church would utterly collapse unless their father Dominic had propped it up on his shoulders. Concerning this vision,

units.la: Mantuanus in 8 Fastorum libro, Satanicis his tunc nugis illusus, sic refert:
units.tr: Mantuan, in the eighth book of the Fasti, deluded by these satanic trifles of that time, reports thus:

units.la: Solicitus demum pro posteritate, penates Venit in Aufonios. Penetrauit limina summi Alta sacerdotis: qui postquam somnia uidit Admiranda, uirum blandas admisit in ulnas, Et genus illius durare in secula iussit.
units.tr: At last, anxious for posterity, the household gods came to the Ausonians. They entered the lofty threshold of the chief priest, who, after he had seen the wondrous dreams, took the man into his coaxing embrace and ordered that his race should endure for ages.

units.la: Viderat in somnis Laterani ingentia templi Tecta ruinosum caput inclinare, uirumq; Supposuisse humero, & sustinuisse ruinam. Taliter admonitus pastor, succurrere sibi Posse hominem fidei rebus, regnoq; labanti: Annuit, & uentis impleuit uela secundis.
units.tr: In his sleep he had seen the huge roof of the Lateran temple bowing its ruinous head, and a man put his shoulder under it and held up the collapse. Thus warned, the pastor agreed that a man could help him in the affairs of faith and in his tottering kingdom, and he filled his sails with favourable winds.

units.la: Pro Franciscanis etiam, ut & illi de suis fictionibus gloriantur, idem Mantuanus, magnae tunc me-retricis poculo inebriatus, in 1o Fastorum libro, fabulosum hoc portentum in sui Francisci gratia adducit:
units.tr: For the Franciscans too, as they boast of their own fictions, the same Mantuan, drunk on the cup of a great harlot, brings in this fabulous portent in the first book of the Fasti for the sake of his Francis:

units.la: Umber erat, coluit Tuscae montana Lauernae, Quae sirum[?] tutelae fuit: pannosus, & ultro Factum inops, missio sua sub uestigia fastu. Mortales longe ante alios mitemq; humilemq; Se exhibuit, Christi ante oculos patientis imago Semper erat. Plagas & uerbera mente ferebat: Et quas mente tulit, Deus apparere figuras Illius in membris uoluit. Nam ulnere pectus, Vulnere signauit palmas, & ulnere plantas. Huius ad exemplum uitæ, se magna uirorum Copia conuertit, numerumq; effluxit in amplum. Posteritas huius patris appellata Minorum Nomine, nodoso lumbos consueta rudente Cingere, & in soleas calces inferre saligras[?].
units.tr: There was an Umbrian who dwelt on the mountains of Tuscan Lauerna, which was a fitting place for him. He was ragged, and of his own accord made poor, his mission beneath the feet of pride. Beyond other mortals he showed himself gentle and humble; the image of the suffering Christ was always before his eyes. Blows and stripes he bore in his mind, and the marks he bore in his mind God willed to appear in his limbs: for he marked his breast with a wound, his palms with a wound, and his feet with a wound. After the example of this life a great crowd of men turned to him, and it flowed out into a large number. The posterity of this father, called by the name of Minors, accustomed to gird their loins with a knotted cord and to put wooden soles on their feet.

units.la: Huius pontificis tempore, dum ista fieret, por-tenta mixtifica militum armatorum in aere sunt ni-fa[?], tanquam acies illa Gog & Magog, Apoc.20. quæ sub Satana gentes seducerent. Hi enim, mendi-cantium scilicet fraterculorum ordines quatuor, adorauerunt bestiam & imaginem eius, habentes illius characterem in frontibus ac manibus. Hi se-duxerunt gentes, quæ sunt supra terræ angulos: & eos congregauit Satan, quorum numerus erat sicut arena maris. Hi ascenderunt super latitudi-nem terræ, & circuierunt castra sanctorum, ac ciuitatem dilectam: ut in sequentibus historijs mul-to lucidius apparebit. Honorius autem, satis a re-bus externis quietus, Christianis principibus pro Hierusalem urbe non sine multorum sanguine di-micantibus, ad templorum structuras se conuertit. Ecclesias S. Laurentij, S. Viuianæ, & ad Sancta sanctorum restituit. Aedes praterea Casemarij co-struxit, semi fornicem & cyborium beati Petri mi-ris fabrefactionibus exornauit. Decretales episto-las edidit, & indoctos ad sacerdotium promoueri non debere decreuit. In Eucharistici panis elevatione, genuflectiones à populo exigebat: & quòd de-centi habitu ac lumine praecedente ad aegrotum de-ferri debeat, constituit. Mulierem illam à marito suo separandam esse statuit, quae post triennium initi coniugij, virum confitetur non habere potentiam eoe-undi. Archiepiscopus intra suas provincias indul-gentias concedere permisit, atq; in Parisiensi aca-demia civile ius legi voluit. Anno Domini 1223. quā Adamus Cathanensis episcopus in Scotia (ut Boe-thius refert) à suis civibus in propria culina crema-tus esset, quòd quosdam eorum propter subtractas decimas excommunicasset: non quieuit hic Papa, donec pro illo uno, quadringenti eorum, castratis etiam liberis, laqueis essent per Alexandrum re-gem suffocati. Immanissima certè haec erat Anti-christi huius Papae tyrannis. In Apulia cum Cesa-re bellum gessit: Raymundum comitem Tolosa-num haereticum declarauit, eius terras Francorum regi dedit, Christianaq; sepultura illum tum de-mum privauit. Post haec & alia facta Papalia, Honorius anno Domini 1227. mundum ipsum defer-uit. De quo sic scribit Matthaeus Parisius in octa-vorum Chronicorum libro: Anno Domini 1226. Papa Honorius per Othonem legatum, praeben-dis àtoto Angliæ regno petijt sibi dari. Debent (inquit Papa) matris inopiam filij naturales fuble- uare. Petijt ab omnibus ecclesijs cathedralibus, du- as prabendas sibi seruari: unam de portione episco- pi, alteram de capitulo. Similiter de cœnobijs, di- uersas petijt portiones. Papa eo tempore, inquit Pa- rifius, hydrope spirituali laborans, euacuauit per suum legatum, clericorum et claustralium loculos, ac mirabilem in eos exercebat tyrannidem. Nam Hugo Lincolnienfis (cognomento Vuellys) pro epi- scopatu recuperando, mille marcas exposuit, ac i- pfi legato centum numerauit. Illius exemplo cæ- lij sunt edocti, eandem sedare sitim. Ea ætate Ro- mæ, per tres dies terram sanguineam pluit. Quo- uis portento, quidam scripsit:
units.tr: In this pope's time, while these things were happening, monstrous portents of armed soldiers were seen in the air, like that army of Gog and Magog in Apoc. 20, which would seduce the nations under Satan. For these, namely the four orders of mendicant friars, worshipped the beast and its image, bearing its mark on their foreheads and hands. They seduced the nations that are at the corners of the earth, and Satan gathered them, whose number was as the sand of the sea. These went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city, as will appear much more clearly in the following histories. Honorius, however, quite at rest from external affairs, while Christian princes were fighting for the city of Jerusalem not without much bloodshed, turned himself to the building of temples. He restored the churches of St Laurence, St Viviana and Sancta Sanctorum. Moreover he built the house of Casemarius, and adorned the semi-dome and ciborium of blessed Peter with wonderful workmanship. He issued decretal letters, and the promotion of the unlearned to the priesthood ought not to be, he decreed. In the elevation of the eucharistic bread he required genuflections from the people, and he laid down that it should be carried to the sick in decent dress and with a light going before. He decreed that a woman who, after three years of marriage, confesses that her husband has no power of intercourse, should be separated from him. He allowed archbishops to grant indulgences within their provinces, and wished civil law to be read in the Paris academy. In the year of the Lord 1223, when Adam, bishop of Caithness in Scotland (as Boethius reports), had been burned in his own kitchen by his citizens, because he had excommunicated some of them on account of withheld tithes, this pope did not rest until four hundred of them, even the free-born children, were strangled by the men of King Alexander for that one man. Truly this was a most savage tyranny of this Antichrist pope. In Apulia he waged war with Caesar. He declared Count Raymond of Toulouse a heretic, gave his lands to the king of the Franks, and at last deprived him of Christian burial. After these and other papal deeds, Honorius departed this world in the year of the Lord 1227. Matthew Paris writes of him thus in the eighth book of his Chronicles: In the year of the Lord 1226, Pope Honorius, through his legate Otto, sought to have prebends given to him from the whole kingdom of England. The pope said that natural sons ought to relieve the poverty of their mother. He asked of all cathedral churches that two prebends be reserved for him, one from the bishop's portion and the other from the chapter's. Similarly from monasteries he sought various portions. The pope at that time, says Paris, labouring under a spiritual dropsy, drained the purses of clergy and monks through his legate, and exercised a remarkable tyranny over them. For Hugh of Lincoln (surnamed Welles), to recover his bishopric, laid out a thousand marks and counted out a hundred to the legate himself. Following his example, the clergy were taught to quench the same thirst. In that age at Rome, for three days, it rained bloody earth. On this portent someone wrote:

units.la: O pater honori, multorum nat e dolori,Est tibi decori uiuere suade mori.
units.tr: O father of honour, born to the sorrow of many, it becomes you to live; I advise you to die.
110.[?] Gregory IX.

units.la: GRegorius nonus, natione Campanus, patria Ana- gninus, e comitum familia, et Innocentij ter- tij nepos (sic solent sanctissimi patres, suos appel- lare spurios) in Septizonio electus, prædecessoris Honorij in Fridericum sententiam probauit. Gregorius iste, ut Marius scribit, crudeliore adhuc animo in Imperatorem defeuijt. Eum namq; accusare incœpit, quoniam Hierosolymitanæ peregrina- tionis votum, quod sub Honorio uouerat, perficere ac absoluere nollet: eumq; hac ex causa non modo non auditum, sed neq; ulla ratione conuicium, anathemate ferit. Imperatorisq; nuncios, honestas ac veras domini sui excusationes afferentes, nun-quam ut ad suae beatitudinis pedes accederet, per-mittere uoluit, ne in cōspectu Cocilij audire. Quis unquam maiorem tyrannidem uidit? Pontificis o-dium nullis artibus unquam mitigari potuit. Sed Ioannem Hierosolymitanum regem, ac comites Thuscie[?] imperatoris rebelles, multosq; alios principes ad eum lacessendum excitauit. Dumq; Imperator diem conuentus, Christianorum principibus quibusdam Rauennæ indixisset, principesq; ut ei pare-rent, illuc properarent, Pontificis iussu iter eorū intercipiebatur: ac milites cruce signati (hi iussu Imperatoris collecti fuerant) ad Hierosolymitanam peregrinationem parati, omni uiatico spoliaban-tur. Quæ omnia imperator uidens, Pontificis rabiem demum delimire curauit. Hierosolymam uersus iter parabat, traiecto mari Cypru peruenit, mox Acon applicuit, multaq; propter Christi fidē mul-to cum sudore ac labore apud Soldanum egit.
units.tr: Gregory IX, a Campanian by birth and of Anagni, of the family of the counts and a nephew of Innocent III (the holy fathers are accustomed to call their bastards nephews), was elected in the Septizonium and confirmed the sentence of his predecessor Honorius against Frederick. This Gregory, as Marius writes, raged against the emperor with an even crueller spirit. He began to accuse him because he would not carry out and complete the vow of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem that he had made under Honorius. For this reason he struck him with anathema, not only without a hearing but without any ground for accusation. He would not even allow the imperial envoys, who brought their lord's honest and true excuses, to approach his holiness's feet, lest they be heard in the presence of the council. Who has ever seen greater tyranny? The pope's hatred could never be softened by any arts. He stirred up John, king of Jerusalem, and the counts of Tuscany, rebels against the emperor, and many other princes to attack him. When the emperor had called a day of assembly at Ravenna for some Christian princes, and the princes were hastening there to obey him, the pope's order intercepted their journey, and the soldiers marked with the cross (who had been gathered by the emperor's order and were ready for the pilgrimage to Jerusalem) were stripped of all their travelling money. Seeing all this, the emperor at last took care to curb the pope's fury. He set out for Jerusalem, crossed the sea, reached Cyprus, and soon landed at Acre, and for the sake of the Christian faith he accomplished much, with great toil and effort, before the Sultan.

units.la: Interim beatissimus Christi uicarius, ob Impe-ratoris absentiam capta occasione, Apuliam ty-rannidi suae (proditor) subegit: cruce signatos mi-lites transfretare prohibuit, eosq; ex Apulia ac
units.tr: Meanwhile the most blessed vicar of Christ, seizing the opportunity of the emperor's absence, reduced Apulia to his own tyranny, as a traitor would. He forbade the soldiers marked with the cross to cross the sea, and drove them out of Apulia and Lombardy, and did many other monstrous and unworthy things.

units.la: Longobardia expulit, multaq; alia portentosa & indigna fecit. Sicq; dum bonus Imperator Christi oues, ne à lupis dilcerperentur, ense defendit: Pon-tifex, qui eas pascere tenebatur, lacerabat ac de-uorabat. Imperator Hierefolymam, Nazareth, Ioppen, à Soldano recuperabat, & cum eo indu-cias decennales paclus fuit: atq; de his omnibus Pō-tificem per literas certiorem fecit, inde ipsius con-gratulationem ac Christianorum publicum gau-dium (ut par erat) expectans. At Pontifex contem-ptis & abiectis literis (magna Hierosolymæ cura) eos qui literas attulerat, ne rei infignitèr gestæ ue-ritatem narrarent, occidi mandauit, & Imperato-rem diem suum obijsse palàm nunciauit. Quis un-quam futurus carnifex Antichristus, si Papa no sit? At qua nam ex causa id fecit? Vt Apuliæ urbes ali-quot, quæ Pontifici se subijcere noluerant, hac ar-te flectere posset. Atq; ne reuerteretur Imperator, ipsecq; pro sua libidine totam Apuliam sibi su-bijceret, Soldanum per literas rogabat, ne terram sanctam Cæsari redderet: (uide nunc eorum erga Hierosolymam zelum) quemadmodum eum redde-re intelligebat. At Imperator, omnibus cum Soldā-no, quæ tum fieri poterant, peractis, in Italiam re-uertebatur. Et ex Apulia pulso Pontifice exercitu, diuino ei fauente auxilio, quæ sibi iniuste ablata fue-rant, rant, breui recuperauit. Pontifex iterum Impera-torem anathemate percussit, & una cum Longo-bardis ac Thuscis contra ipsum coniurationem fe-cit, eo quod cum Soldano fœdus inisset.
units.tr: And so, while the good emperor defended Christ's sheep with the sword lest they be torn apart by wolves, the pope, who was bound to feed them, was tearing them apart and devouring them. The emperor recovered Jerusalem, Nazareth and Joppa from the Sultan, and made a ten-year truce with him, and he informed the pope of all these things by letter, expecting his congratulations and the public joy of the Christians (as was fitting). But the pope, scorning and rejecting the letters (with great concern for Jerusalem), ordered that the men who had brought the letters be killed, lest they report the truth of so notable an achievement, and he announced openly that the emperor had died. What Antichrist would ever be a more savage executioner, if the Pope were not? And why did he do this? So that he might by this trick bend some towns of Apulia which had been unwilling to submit to him. And so that the emperor would not return and subject all Apulia to himself at his own pleasure, he asked the Sultan by letter not to restore the Holy Land to Caesar (see now their zeal for Jerusalem) in the way he understood it was to be restored. But the emperor, having done with the Sultan everything that could then be done, returned to Italy. Having driven the pope's army out of Apulia, with divine help he soon recovered what had been unjustly taken from him. The pope again struck the emperor with anathema, and together with the Lombards and Tuscans he formed a conspiracy against him, because he had made a treaty with the Sultan.

units.la: Postremò, procurantibus principibus multis, ut pius Cæsar cum superbissimo tyranno Pontifice componeretur, absolutionem ipse centum millibus auri uncijs emit. Hinc conijcere licet, quàm carus rerum suarum mercator fit Pontifex factus: qui ta men fatetur, se nullis nummis Christo datis, clauos soluendi ab illo accepisse. Mox Imperator in Germaniam parabat iter, ut quædam Henrici primogeniti sui errata corrigeret. At Pontifex (o inaudità perfidiam) statim Germaniæ principibus per nun-cios mandabat, ne quenquam ex Imperatoris domo in regem Romanorum decernant. Quod cum ei relatum esset, atq; una intellexisset Pontificem cum multis Italiæ principibus contra ipsum con-spirasse, ut prorsus Imperatoria maiestate priuaretur: Italiam inuasit, rebellesq; Longobardos* compescuit: multas Umbriæ, denique ac Hetruriæ urbes expugnauit. Totam Longobardiam, Viterbi-um, Perusium, Faventiam, Cremonam, Vicentiam, Patauiumque, quæ cum Pontifice conspirauerant, Imperio subdidit. Quæ cum Pontifex uidisset, Fridericus rursus Anathemate percutiebatur. Imperator, qui Patauij tunc erat, hoc audiens, & quoniam Romanorum pontificum auaritia, audacia ac tyrannis, amplius ferri non poterant, ideo omnibus Christi fidelibus eas patefacere decreuit, ut illos ab errore ac falsa eorum religione revocaret. Hac ex causa iussit cuidam in sacris literis eruditissimo, ut coram se liberam haberet concionem de anathemate, ac de ecclesia Romana. Contigitq; ut absoluta concione adeo Romanæ ecclesiæ errores detecti sint, Pontificumq; techna atq; pessimæ artes ita patefactæ, ut Imperator Pontifici illi in hæc verba scripserit:
units.tr: Finally, when many princes had arranged for the pious Caesar to be reconciled with the most proud tyrant, the pope, he bought his absolution for a hundred thousand ounces of gold. From this one may conjecture what a dear merchant of his own affairs the pope became, he who nevertheless confesses that he received the keys of loosing from Christ without giving Him any money. Soon the emperor was preparing his journey into Germany, to correct some errors of his firstborn son Henry. But the pope (O unheard-of perfidy) at once sent word through messengers to the princes of Germany not to elect anyone from the emperor's house as king of the Romans. When this had been reported to him, and he had learned at the same time that the pope had conspired with many princes of Italy against him, so that he might be utterly deprived of imperial majesty, he invaded Italy and checked the rebellious Lombards; he took by storm many towns of Umbria, and finally of Tuscany. He subjected to the empire the whole of Lombardy, Viterbo, Perugia, Faenza, Cremona, Vicenza and Padua, which had conspired with the pope. When the pope saw this, Frederick was again struck with anathema. The emperor, who was then at Padua, hearing this, and because the avarice, audacity and tyranny of the Roman pontiffs could no longer be endured, decided to lay them open to all the faithful of Christ, so as to call them back from their error and false religion. For this reason he ordered a man most learned in the sacred letters to hold before him a free sermon on the anathema and on the Roman Church. And it came about that, when the sermon was finished, the errors of the Roman Church were so exposed, and the pontiffs' cunning and wicked arts so laid bare, that the emperor wrote to that pope in these words:

units.la: Roma diu titubans, longis erroribus acta, Corruet, & mundi desinet esse caput.
units.tr: Rome, long wavering, driven by long errors, will fall, and will cease to be the head of the world.

units.la: Interim potior Italiæ pars Imperatori adhæsit, et Gregorius in desperationem rerum ac tyrannidis suæ in posterum exercendæ adductus, anno Domini 1241. animam diabolo reddidit, cuius & opera et consilia dum viueret, secutus est. Hæc Ma[?]rius in Eusebio.
units.tr: Meanwhile the greater part of Italy clung to the emperor, and Gregory, brought to despair of his affairs and of exercising his tyranny in the future, in the year of the Lord 1241 gave up his soul to the devil, whose works and counsels he had followed while he lived. So Marius, in Eusebius.
On other deeds of Gregory IX.

units.la: Gregorius iste, ut Matthæus Parisius illum vocat, sanguisugus & auarus Papa, contra Fridericum Cæsarem, qui Isabellam, Ioannis Anglorum regis filiam, duxerat in uxorem, concilium Romæ celebrauit, ut illum Imperio deiiceret. Ante cuius[?] initium, Apostolorum in processione solenni capita aduersus eum circumtulit, ut eo spectaculo, manu quamuis ipsi terrorem incuteret, ac subdi-torum animos abalienaret: pugnantibusque contra eum, uitam aeternam promisit. Sed ea re cognita, uias omnes terra marique Fridericus praeclusit: ex Cardinalibus plures, atque alios Ecclesiae prae-latos, nauigio uectos, per Pisanos cepit, & in carceres trusit. Cardinalium duos aquis submersit: ali-orum quosdam, episcopos, abbates, & clericos, atque inter illos Papae fratrem, ob insignes prodi-tiones, patibulis suspendit. Prima excommunicatio huic Imperatori contigit, quod periculo pro terra sancta obeundo, iuxta Papae voluntatem, immi-scere se nollet. Papa enim, ut acta probabant, u-triusq; Siciliae regnum, Apuliam & alias terras quaerebat: unde & Imperatorem ipsum, earum terrarum haeredem, libenter extinctum uidisset. Han-nibalem prisca Romanorum libertates optan-tem, senatorio munere deiecit: & Polonos, ut Pru-tenos, eius tunc aduersarios, delerent, instigauit. Guelphorum ac Gibellinorum factiones, quas ne-cess innumerae ac intolerabiles miseriae subsecutae sunt, in Italia excitauit: & Decretalium opus (sententiam stultitiae & impietatis) à Raimundo quodam Hispano ac Dominicano collectum, ad multorum perniciem publicauit. Dominicum, Francif-cum, Antonium de Padua, & Elizabetham Hun-gariæ regis filiam, in sanctos retulit: ut in festis Mendicantium fraterculorum, dum in hypocrisi res eius agerent, sanctitatis opinionem atq; autho-ritatem augeret. Carmelitis, præter asinos mas-culos, & aliquod animalium seu volatilium nutri-mentum, hoc est, lac & ova, anno Domini 1230. ni-hil possessionis admisit, cætera omnia hostiatim pe-tere iussit: ut Paleonydorus refert. Immunitatem Iudæis, in uitis Christianis regibus, pro pecunia cō-cessit: & suos usurarios, uirorum omnium pessi-mos (Parisio teste) pro nummis omni fallacia hau-riendis, in Angliam post legatos misit. Sacerdotia plura uni prohibuit, ut & inde lucrum accresce-ret: & quintam partem in Anglia, ac uicesimam in inferiore Germania, omnium ecclesiæ prouen-tuum per dictos legatos petijt. Ad uirginis Ma-riæ salutationem, & ad antiphonam (Christo ual-de blasphemam) Salue regina, quam in templis can-tari primus instituit, campanæ pulsum addidit, & Eucharistici panis elevationi tintinnabulum. Statuit, ne laici Euangelium prædicent, cuiuscun-que sint conditionis: nec ullam ualere consuetudi-nem, per quam quis inducitur ad peccandum. Dam-nari per hoc statutum deberet Missa Papistica, quæ suis idololatriis tot horribiles in ipsum Deum blasphemias peperit. Multo plura adhuc hic Papa constituens, reparans, & ædificans Romæ (ut dictum est) anno Domini 1241. diem suum obiit. In quo mons quidam in Burgundia[?], magnam populi multitudinem debiscens[?] oppressit.
units.tr: This Gregory, whom Matthew Paris calls a bloodsucking and greedy pope, held a council at Rome against Frederick Caesar, who had married Isabella, daughter of John, king of the English, intending to depose him from the empire. Before it began, he carried the heads of the Apostles in a solemn procession against Frederick, so that by this spectacle he might strike terror into him, though only by hand, and turn the hearts of his subjects away from him. He promised eternal life to those who fought against him. Frederick, learning of this, blocked every route by land and sea. He captured through the Pisans several cardinals and other prelates of the Church who were travelling by ship, and thrust them into prison. He drowned two of the cardinals and hanged others, bishops, abbots and clerics, among them the pope's brother, on the gallows for notorious treasons. The first excommunication fell on this emperor because he would not, as the pope wished, involve himself in the danger of going to the Holy Land. For the pope, as the acts show, was seeking both kingdoms of Sicily, Apulia and other lands, and so would gladly have seen the emperor, the heir of those lands, dead. He deposed Annibaldus, who desired the ancient liberties of the Romans, from his office as senator. He also incited the Poles, and the Prussians, then his enemies, to destroy each other. In Italy he stirred up the factions of the Guelphs and Ghibellines, from which countless and intolerable miseries followed of necessity. He also published, to the great ruin of many, the work of the Decretals (a doctrine of folly and impiety), collected by a certain Raymond, a Spaniard and Dominican. He enrolled Dominic, Francis, Anthony of Padua, and Elizabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary, among the saints, so that in the feasts of the mendicant friars, while they carried on their hypocrisy, he might increase the reputation and authority of their holiness. In the year of the Lord 1230 he allowed the Carmelites no possessions except male donkeys and some sustenance from animals or birds, that is, milk and eggs, and ordered them to beg everything else from door to door, as Paleonydorus reports. He granted immunity to the Jews, against the will of Christian kings, for money, and after this sent his usurers, the worst of all men (according to Paris), into England to suck out money by every trick. He forbade one man to hold several benefices, so that profit might also grow from this. He demanded for himself, through the said legates, a fifth part in England and a twentieth in Lower Germany of all the revenues of the churches. He was the first to institute the addition of a bell at the salutation of the Virgin Mary and at the antiphon Salve Regina (which is very blasphemous against Christ), sung in the temples, and a little bell at the elevation of the eucharistic bread. He decreed that laymen, of whatever rank, should not preach the Gospel, and that no custom should hold good by which anyone is led into sin. By this decree the Papist Mass ought to be condemned, which through its idolatries has brought forth so many horrible blasphemies against God himself. This pope, establishing, repairing and building much more besides at Rome (as has been said), died in the year of the Lord 1241. In the same year a certain mountain in Burgundy, gaping open, overwhelmed a great multitude of people.
On the oracle of Cyril, concerning the Mass.

units.la: Huius Gregorij noni tempore, anno scilicet Domini 1234. Cyrillus Græcus, de quo in Lucio tertio ac Cœlestino tertio dictum est, tertius Carmelita-rum præses generalis, obiisse fertur. Hunc dicunt, tam Mosi quam Ioannis Euangelistæ exemplo, nouam Apocalypsin è cælis circa annum à Christi natiuitate 1192 accepisse, Dei ipsius digito in argenteis tabulis Græcè scriptam, super futuro eccle-siæ statu. Et per hanc nitebantur impostores quidam, priorem illam Ioannis auferre, uel potius in ea sæculi cæcitate funditus delere. Erant enim in Italia, Germania, Francia & Anglia tunc multi, qui per Friderici Cæsaris concionatores, & Vual-densium doctrinam ex priore illa Apocalypsi, qui Romam credebant Babylonem, ac meretricem illam magnam esse, & Papam ipsissimum esse Antichristum. Cuius opinionis, D. Petri Veronensis patrum extitisse, ipsius Legenda ac Temporum fasciculus probant. Oportebat igitur huiusmodi columnis labentem Lateranum (ut in Innocentij uisione) callide his diebus fulciri. Conabantur etiam tunc principes, temporalia, ut uocant, ab Ecclesijs auferre, & panis in Missa transubstantiationem contemnere: atq; alia quaedam facere, quae uentribus & culinis non congruebant. Sed uide quam sint abinuicem diuersa, haec Cyrilli & Ioannis oracula.
units.tr: In the time of this Gregory IX, namely in the year of the Lord 1234, Cyril the Greek, of whom it was said under Lucius III and Celestine III, the third general prior of the Carmelites, is said to have died. They say that, following the example of both Moses and the Evangelist John, he received a new Apocalypse from heaven around the year 1192 after the birth of Christ, written in Greek on silver tablets by the very finger of God, concerning the future state of the Church. And through this some impostors strove to remove that earlier Apocalypse of John, or rather to blot it out utterly in that darkness of the age. For at that time there were many in Italy, Germany, France and England who, through the preachers of Frederick Caesar and the teaching of the Waldensians, used that earlier Apocalypse to believe that Rome was Babylon and that great harlot, and that the pope himself was truly Antichrist. The Legend of Peter of Verona and the Fasciculus Temporum prove that he was the father of this opinion. It was therefore necessary, in these days, to prop up the tottering Lateran with such pillars, as in the vision of Innocent. Princes then also tried to take away the so-called temporal goods from the churches, and to despise the transubstantiation of the bread in the Mass, and to do certain other things which did not suit bellies and kitchens. But see how far apart these oracles of Cyril and John are from one another.

units.la: Primum tradebatur a Deo, dum adhuc fuisset ecclesia in purissimo statu sub apostolis: alterum hoc, ab angelo nescio quo, dum esset ecclesia in statu corruptissimo sub apostatis & Antichristo. Primum in persecutione dura, ac Pathmi exilio, sub calamitate & cruce: alterum in placida mollicie, ac iucunda Carmeli solitudine, sub felicitate atq; otio suaui. Primum erat mundum, lucidum, rectum, ac Dei scripturis & promissionibus consonum: alterum spurcum, tenebrosum, obliquum, atq; ab omni diuinae ueritatis usu alienum. Primum, in luce Euangelij: alterum, in tenebris Papismi. Ioannes diuinitus afflatus, in fide ac spiritu oraculu suscepit: Cyrillus Aaronicis uestibus indutus, in argenteis tabulis suum accepit. Ioannes in contemplatione rerum caelestium, et in die Dominico: Cyrillus in Missa Papistica, atq; in Hilarionis festo. Ille in agro, iste in templo manufacto. Ille uersus cælum, iste uersus altare lapideum. Ioannes pauidus, ac pene mortuus, ut cecidit ad Christi pedes: Cyrillus erecto multa ante altare stetit imperterritus. Ioannis reuelatio nobis attulit Euangelium æternum: Cyrilli reuelatio[?] lucalicem & thuribulum adfert, pro obscuran[da] do Dei cultu ac idololatria [?]sulcienda. Ioannes dicit, quòd in sexta ætate ecclesiæ, in qua nos sumus, sol factus sit niger ut saccus cilicinus, Apoc.6. Cyrillus uero fatetur, oriturum tunc esse solem intra muros periurij. Quod tanquam ex diametro, cum altero pugnare uidetur: quum sol ibi Christum significet. Ioannis prophetia, paracletum interpretem habet: Cyrilli uaticinium, commentatores monachos, Ioachimum abbatem, Gilbertum Cistercien-sem, & Ioannem de Rupe scissa[?]. Vtrunque tamen a-culum Græcè scribitur, ac futurum ecclesiæ statum narrare dicitur. Illud pellucidè & apertè, sed obscure atque confuse. Probate ergo spiritus, si ex Deo sint: 1. Ioan. 4. nam poterit Satan se transformare in angelum lucis: 2. Cor. 11. At anathema sit, qui aliud Euangelium doceat, Gal. 1. quàm ab ipsis Christi Apostolis prædicatum est. Aduentus filij perditi erit in omni iniquitatis seductio ... salui fierent, qui non crediderunt veritati, 2. Thess. 2.
units.tr: The first was delivered by God, while the Church was still in its purest state under the Apostles; the second by I know not what angel, while the Church was in its most corrupt state under apostates and Antichrist. The first came in harsh persecution and the exile of Patmos, under calamity and the cross; the second in soft ease and the pleasant solitude of Carmel, under happiness and sweet leisure. The first was clean, bright, upright, and consonant with God's Scriptures and promises; the second foul, dark, crooked, and alien from all use of divine truth. The first was in the light of the Gospel; the second in the darkness of Papism. John, inspired by God, received his oracle in faith and spirit; Cyril, clothed in Aaronic vestments, received his in silver tablets. John was in contemplation of heavenly things, and on the Lord's day; Cyril in the Papist Mass, and on the feast of Hilarion. The one in the field, the other in a man-made temple. The one turned toward heaven, the other toward a stone altar. John, fearful and nearly dead, fell at Christ's feet; Cyril stood long before the altar, upright and undaunted. John's revelation brought us the everlasting Gospel; Cyril's revelation brings the chalice and the censer, to obscure the worship of God and to prop up idolatry. John says that in the sixth age of the Church, in which we are, the sun has become black as sackcloth of hair, Apoc. 6. But Cyril affirms that the sun will then rise within the walls of perjury. This seems to contradict the other as diametrically opposed, since the sun there signifies Christ. John's prophecy has the Paraclete as its interpreter; Cyril's prophecy has monk commentators: Joachim the abbot, Gilbert the Cistercian, and John of Rupescissa. Yet both oracles are written in Greek, and both are said to tell of the future state of the Church. The one clearly and openly, the other obscurely and confusedly. "Test the spirits whether they are of God," 1 John 4. For Satan can transform himself into an angel of light, 2 Cor. 11. "But let him be accursed who preaches another Gospel," Gal. 1. than that which was preached by Christ's own Apostles. "The coming of the son of perdition will be with all deception of iniquity ... that they might be saved, who did not believe the truth," 2 Thess. 2.
120. Celestine IV.

units.la: Coelestinus quartus, natione Lombardus, patria Mediolanensis, è familia Castilionum, episcopus Sabinensis, doctus, sed senex admodum ac valetudinarius, in locum demortui Gregorij suffectus est. Qui, etsi multa etiam contra praedictum Fridericum, Imperatorem optimum, moliri cogitauerat, ea tamen furibundus pontifex ob uitae breuitatem absoluere non potuit. Nam eodem anno, quo Gregorius, intra primum mensem tantum, transfactis[?] solummodo decem & octo diebus, communi fato concessit, uenenato poculo (ut fertur) absumptus. Et non immerito fortassis. Legitur enim in libro Thomae Ecclestoni, de aduentu Minoritarum ad Angliam, de Roberto quodam Somertono Anglo, Romanae ecclesiae Cardinale, qui, ne Gregorio praedicto succederet in Papatu, sub ipsa electione, uenenò sublatum fuit. Vnde Matthaeus Parisius, in octauo suorum Chronicorum libro sic scribit: Obijt eo tempore, anno scilicet Domini 1241, ad magnam ecclesiae Romanae confusionem, magister Robertus de Somercote, Anglicus, Cardinalis, officio Papali dignissimus, dum de electione Papali tractaretur, qui omnibus se amabilem exhibuerat, &c. Idem Matthaeus, eodem anno delegatorum moribus: Duo, inquit, remanserunt in Anglia[?] Papales nuncij, pro colligendis pecunijs, de quorum extorsionibus, ne aures offendantur, meius est silere, quàm aerem fœdando recitare. Huius Cœlestini commune dictum erat: Difficilius est (ait) in secundis rebus, quàm in aduersis, esse moderatum. Post eius mortem uacauit Romana sella u-no & uiginti fere mensibus: donec à Friderico capti Cardinales, Balduuini Constantinopolitani Imperatoris, & Raymundi comitis Tolosani preci-bus restituerentur. Hos quatuor Pontifices, Inno-centium tertium, Honorium tertium, Gregorium nonum, & Cœlestinum quartum, Georgius Vuiceulius[?], adulator papisticus, ueros esse Ecclesiæ pastores, & senes optimos, atq; officio satis fecisse dicit: cum scelestissimi fuerint proditores.
units.tr: Celestine IV, a Lombard by birth, of Milan, of the family of the Castiliones, bishop of Sabina, learned but very old and infirm, was chosen to succeed the dead Gregory. Although he had devised many schemes against the aforesaid Frederick, the excellent emperor, the furious pontiff could not carry them out, because his life was so short. For in the same year as Gregory, within the first month only, after just eighteen days had passed, he departed by the common fate, carried off by a poisoned cup (as it is said). And perhaps not undeservedly. For it is read in the book of Thomas Eccleston, on the coming of the Minorites to England, that a certain Robert Somerton, an Englishman, cardinal of the Roman church, was removed by poison during the very election, so that he would not succeed Gregory in the papacy. Hence Matthew Paris, in the eighth book of his Chronicles, writes thus: He died at that time, namely in the year of the Lord 1241, to the great confusion of the Roman church, Master Robert de Somercote, an Englishman, cardinal, most worthy of the papal office, while the papal election was being discussed, he who had shown himself lovable to all, etc. The same Matthew, in the same year, on the conduct of the legates: Two, he says, remained in England as papal envoys for collecting money; of whose extortions, lest ears be offended, it is better to be silent than to recite them and foul the air. A common saying of this Celestine was: It is more difficult (he said) to be moderate in prosperity than in adversity. After his death the Roman see stood vacant for nearly twenty-one months, until the cardinals, who had been seized by Frederick, were restored at the prayers of Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, and Raymond, count of Toulouse. George Wicelius, a papist flatterer, says that these four pontiffs, Innocent III, Honorius III, Gregory IX and Celestine IV, were true ministers of the Church and excellent old men, and had done their office well, when they were most wicked traitors.

units.la: LIBER SEXTVS. Tertiæ classis sectio quarta, de Papis vel Romanis Antichristis in regno locustarum sub Abadone, qui perditor est, Apoc. 9. usq; ad lu-lium[?] secundum.
units.tr: BOOK SIX. Section four of the third class, concerning the Popes or Roman Antichrists in the kingdom of the locusts under Abaddon, who is the destroyer, Rev. 9, down to Julius II.

units.la: Ad Syluestro secundo, qui magus diabolicus erat, per 243. annos hucusq; : hoc est, ad annum à Christi natiuitate 1243, tanquam diabolus ipse, aut malignissimus Satan, in Romana ecclesia Antichristus regnauit. In omni enim seductione, tyrannide, ac veritatis oppressione (non addo fœ-ditates plusquam Sodomiticas) sua tempora tran-sigebant Pontifices, ad centesimum & vicesimum primum Papam usque, ita ut Satanæ synagoga & diaboli sedes, Apoc.2 merito tunc Roma dicere-tur: & pro habitatione dæmoniorum, ac omnis im-mundi spiritus custodia haberi potuerit, Apoc.18. Unde dum pergerent ipsi ad Concilia generalia, vel eorum Cardinales atq; à latere Legati ad prō-uinciarum principes & episcopos, sub reformati-onis (ut solent) aut componenda pacis fuco: uide-batur semper à Domini facie egressus Satan, ut ul-cere pessimo lobum percuteret, Iob 2. Nam quic-quid in-uarijs scripturæ locis Satan fecisse scribi-tur: & illi tunc, eius perpetui in terris vicarij, in-fulati, rasi & uncti, in omni crudelitatum genere horribiliter faciebant. Nec potentissimis huius mu-di monarchis, in infernalibus eorum furijs peper-cerunt. Exempla in præcedente libro, & in eo, qui nunc sequitur, clariora sunt, quàm ut egeant probatione: in duobus Henricis, quarto & quinto: in Fridericis quoq;, primo ac secundo: in Henrico septimo, ac Ludouico quarto: in Ioanne Anglorum rege, atq; eius patre Henrico secundo, & in aliis multis Christiani orbis regibus. Posthac autem, ab anno Domini 1243. sub Innocentio quarto aliis 40. Papis, Abadonis, qui rex locustarum ac perditor est, regnum durabit ad Iulium secundum usque. In quo regno per 260 annos locustæ, id est, sectarum Mendicantium fraterculi, per prædi-stum[?] Innocentium constabiliti, ac fortiores facti, omnia per doctrinas sophisticas vorabunt, vastabunt, destruent ac perdent. Quales sunt, Thomas Aquinas, Ioannes Scotus, Gerardus Borceniensis, Ægidius Romanus, & alij sine numero Sententiarij ac Sorbonistæ, hi quicquid ex fide aut Dei veritate viride est, per suas præstigias atrociter deuorabunt. hi fures illi sunt, qui aliunde quàm per ostium in ovile ovium ascendunt: de quibus Christus tam serio nos admonuit, Ioan.10. hi certè non venient, nisi ut furentur & mactent. Attendite à pseudoprophetis illis, & Antichristi apostolis: à pestilentibus autem eorum fructibus sunt statim cognoscendi.
units.tr: From Silvester II, who was a diabolical magician, for 243 years until now, that is, to the year 1243 after the birth of Christ, Antichrist reigned in the Roman Church like the devil himself or the most malignant Satan. For the popes spent their times in every kind of seduction, tyranny and suppression of truth (I do not add their foulness, which was more than Sodomitical), down to the one hundred and twenty-first pope. So Rome could rightly be called the synagogue of Satan and the seat of the devil, Rev. 2, and could be held as a dwelling place of demons and a prison for every unclean spirit, Rev. 18. Hence, whenever they went to general councils, or their cardinals and legates a latere went to the princes and bishops of the provinces under the pretence (as they usually do) of reformation or of arranging peace, Satan seemed always to go out from the presence of the Lord, to strike Job with a most wicked ulcer, Job 2. For whatever is written of Satan's doings in various places of Scripture, those men then, his perpetual vicars on earth, mitred, shaven and anointed, did horribly in every kind of cruelty. Nor did they spare the most powerful monarchs of this world in their infernal fury. The examples in the preceding book, and in the one that follows, are clearer than they need proof: in the two Henries, the fourth and the fifth; also in the two Fredericks, the first and the second; in Henry VII and Louis IV; in John, king of the English, and his father Henry II; and in many other kings of the Christian world. Hereafter, however, from the year of the Lord 1243, under Innocent IV and forty other popes, Abaddon, who is the king and destroyer of the locusts, will hold his kingdom down to Julius II. In this kingdom, for 260 years, the locusts, that is, the little friars of the mendicant orders, established and made stronger by the aforesaid Innocent, will devour, lay waste, destroy and ruin everything by sophistical doctrines. Such are Thomas Aquinas, John Duns Scotus, Gerard of Borgo San Donnino, Giles of Rome, and countless other Sentence-men and Sorbonists; whatever is green in faith or in the truth of God, they will savagely devour by their juggling tricks. They are those thieves who climb into the sheepfold by some other way than the door, about whom Christ warned us so earnestly, John 10. Surely they will not come except to steal and to slaughter. Beware of those false prophets and apostles of Antichrist; they are to be recognised at once by their pestilent fruits.
121. Innocent IV.

units.la: Innocentius quartus, patria Genuensis, Synebal-dus antea dictus, è Flisca familia ac Lauaniæ comitibus natus: à Cardinalibus illis quos Fridericus Cæsar carceribus detinuerat, in libertatem tum redactis, Anagniæ Pontifex creabatur, ut eorum damna vindicaret. Qui ex intimo ciusdem Cæsaris amico, inimicissimus hostis ilico factus (talis esse
units.tr: Innocent IV, a native of Genoa, formerly called Sinibaldo, born of the Fieschi family and counts of Lavagna, was made pope at Anagni by those cardinals whom the Emperor Frederick had held in prison, and who had then been set free, so that he might avenge their losses. Though he had been an intimate friend of the same Caesar, he at once became his most bitter enemy (such is usually the nature of Antichrists), and he troubled the excellent prince more grievously than anyone else. Here it is worth quoting the very clear testimony of Girolamo Marii. This pope, he says, at once summoned a council at Lyons in hatred of Frederick, where Innocent himself, preaching, cited Frederick in person. But Frederick's envoy begged that a suitable time be granted in which he could come to Lyons.

units.la: T solet Antichristorum natura) maioribus molestius quàm alius quisquam, optimum grauabat princi-pem. Lubet hoc loco luculentissimum Hieronymi Marij testimonium assumere. Hic Pontifex, inquit, in Friderici odium, Lugduni concilium statim indi-xit: ubi illemet Innocentius concionabundus, Fridericum ipsum citabat. Friderici uero legatus, tempus opportunum dari precabatur, quo venire Lu-gdunum posset.
units.tr: The pope not only refused this, but, inflamed with anger and fury, branded Frederick with anathema, deprived him of his imperial dignity, released the princes from their oath of fidelity, and urged them to choose another emperor. He brought forward many false charges against the most impious emperor: perjury, sacrilege, the imprisonment of certain clergy, and other things of that sort. Although the emperor had cleared himself most honourably before the princes beforehand, the pope so stirred up the princes and moved them with promises that they chose Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia. When this reached the emperor's ears, he vigorously defended his empire against Innocent and against all other tyrants, until he could no longer escape the pope's snares in Apulia.

units.la: Quod Pontifex non modo non dedit: sed ira ac furore succensus, Fridericum anathe-mate notabat, imperiali dignitate priuabat, à iuramento fidelitatis principes absoluebat: eosq; ut alium eligant Imperatorem, hortabatur. Multa contra impissimum[?] Imperatorem falsa produxit: periurium, sacrilegium, & quorundam clericorum captiuitatem, atq; id genus alia. De quibus omnibus, etsi Imperator honestissimè apud principes antea se purgasset: Pontifex tamen adeò principes sollicitauit, ac pollicitationibus commouit, ut Henricum Landgrauium Thuringiæ elegerint. Quod cùm ad imperatoris aures peruenisset, strenuè aduersus Innocentium, ac alios quoscunq; tyrannos, imperium suum defendit, donec in Apulia Pontificis laqueos effugere nequiuit.
units.tr: For there a certain man, corrupted by papal bribery, gave poison to the holy emperor. When the emperor had fallen seriously ill because of it, he seemed to be recovering; but he was smothered with a cushion by a certain spurious young man, Manfred, who had also been corrupted with money or promises by the pope. These are the things which ought to be related of the most invincible Frederick. Nor in this matter is Blondus, Platina, Stella or Sabellicus to be trusted. Nor is this surprising, for they wrote only those things which were everywhere published throughout Italy by the pope and his flatterers against the emperor, so that they might rouse the whole world against him, if that were possible. But those who wish to know the truth of the matter should read the six books of the Letters of Pietro della Vigna. Thus Marius. When the aforesaid Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, had been elected king of the Romans, Conrad, son of Frederick, gathered an army and made war on him. But Henry was defeated without difficulty, lost many of his men, and a large part of his nobility was captured. Thereafter he began to be despised by those who disliked his election, and was called the clerics' king. Yet the pope sought by envoys to win over all the princes of Germany, so that they should abandon Frederick and Conrad his son and obey the elected Henry. Meanwhile Henry died, and Innocent did not cease to set a new enemy against Frederick. He sent into Germany the cardinal Pietro Capuccio, who, having summoned the electoral princes to Cologne, brought it about that William, Count of Holland, a man keen for arms, should be elected king.

units.la: Nam ibi quidam pontificia largitione corru-ptus, venenum sacro Imperatori exhibuit. Cuiu[?] causa cum imperator graviter laborasset, iam convalescere videbatur: sed à Manfredo quodam adolescente spurio, qui & à Pontifice sibi corruptus erat pecunia, vel promissis, nobiliori iaculo pulmino, suffocatus est, haec sunt, quae de invictissimo Friderico enarrari debent. Nec hac in causa Blondo, Platina, Stella, vel Sabellico fides habenda est. Nec mirum quidem, hi enim tantum ea scripserunt, quae passim à Pontifice, ac eius adulatoribus, contra Imperatorem inivulgabantur per totam Italiam, ut contra eum totum terrarum orbem (si fieri potuisset) concitarent. at, qui rei veritatem agnoscere cupiunt, Petri de Vineis libros sex Epistolarum legant. haec Marius. Cum praedictus Henricus, Thuringiae Landgravius, in Romanorum regem electus esset, Conradus Friderici filius, collecto exercitu bellum ei intulit. Sed sine difficultate victus, multos suorum amisit, ac magna pars nobilitatis suae capta est. Henricus inde ab his qui-bus eius electio displicebat, contemni coepit, & clericorum rex dici. Papa tamen omnes Alemaniae principes, per legatos solicitavit, ut Friderico & Conrado eius filio relictis, Henrico electo parerent. Henricus interea cum finem vivendi fecisset, Innocentius non cessavit Friderico novum hostem opponere. Misitque in Germaniam legatum,
units.tr: For there a certain man, bribed by papal largesse, gave poison to the holy Emperor. When the Emperor had fallen seriously ill from it and seemed to be recovering, he was smothered with a pillow by Manfred, a bastard youth who had also been bought by the Pope with money or promises. These are the things that must be told of the most invincible Frederick. Nor in this matter is credence to be given to Blondus, Platina, Stella or Sabellicus. And no wonder, for they wrote only what was circulated everywhere throughout Italy by the Pope and his flatterers against the Emperor, so that they might stir up the whole world against him, if that could be done. But those who wish to know the truth of the matter should read the six books of Peter de Vinea's Letters. Thus far Marius.

units.la: Petrum Caputium cardinalem: qui vocatis Colo-niam principibus electoribus, effecit, ut Guilhel-mus Holandiæ comes, vir impiger ad arma, rex eligeretur.
units.tr: Peter Capuano, the cardinal, who, having summoned the electoral princes to Cologne, brought it about that William, Count of Holland, a man vigorous in arms, was elected king.

units.la: Fuerunt hoc tempore in Suevia prædicatores, qui contra Romanum pontificem & Cardinales magna dicendi libertate veritatem profiterentur. Hi Friderici secundi & Conradi causam iustificantes, ausi sunt dicere, apud summum Pontificem, Cardinales & episcopos nullam residere authoritatem: quoniam omnes una labe Simoniæ maculati essent, nec quicquam tenere poteßatis à Christo. Et quod sacerdotes in mortali peccato constituti, nec ligarent, nec soluerent, nec consecrarent: quòd nemo in orbe Christiano divinis officijs interdicere posset: quodq; sine discrimine ea audirentur & celebrarentur impunè. Et in fine suarum prædicationum: Indulgentiam (inquiunt) quam annuncia-mus, non à Papa confictam, non à prælatis compositam, sed ex Deo omnipotente vobis annuncia-mus. Conradus rex cum hos tueretur Romanæ sedis adversarios & hæreticos (ita enim veritatis divinæ confessores appellant) in capitis pene peri-culum incidit. Ex Functio similiter sunt hæc desumpta. Regnauit hinc Guilhelmus Holandiæ comes solus, sed duobus annis: sed nihil pro tanta dignitate dignitate memorabile fecit. Post hæc interregnum fuit, sub quod ducibus imperij spes facta est, Alphonso Hispano, et Ricardo Cornubiæ duci, Ioannis Anglorum regis filio, ad magnum Papæ commodum ac rei Christianæ perniciem: sed cum alter metu alterius nihil attentaret, imperium quasi acephalon per id temporis fuit, donec Rodulphus Habsburgi-us eligeretur.
units.tr: At this time there were preachers in Swabia who, with great freedom of speech, professed the truth against the Roman pontiff and the cardinals. Defending the cause of Frederick II and Conrad, they dared to say before the supreme Pontiff, the cardinals and the bishops that no authority resided in them, since they were all stained by the one taint of simony and held no power from Christ. And that priests living in mortal sin neither bound nor loosed nor consecrated; that no one in the Christian world could lay divine offices under interdict; and that those things were heard and celebrated without distinction and with impunity. And at the end of their sermons they said: "The indulgence we proclaim is not devised by the Pope, nor composed by prelates, but we proclaim it to you from almighty God." King Conrad, when he protected these adversaries of the Roman see and heretics (for so they call the confessors of divine truth), fell into danger of his head. From Functio these things are likewise taken. Thereafter William, Count of Holland, reigned alone, but for two years, and did nothing memorable for so great a dignity. After this there was an interregnum, during which hope was held out to the princes of the empire, to Alphonso of Spain and to Richard, Duke of Cornwall, son of John, King of the English, to the great advantage of the Pope and the ruin of the Christian cause. But since each did nothing for fear of the other, the empire was for that time as it were headless, until Rudolf of Habsburg was elected.
For fortifying the kingdom of Abaddon and the locusts.

units.la: In prædicto Lugdunensi concilio, anno Domini 1245. Innocentius pro firmando Abadonis imperio, constituit, ut Cardinales rubris galeris ac pallijs uterentur, & equis phaleratis per urbem veherentur: non ut eo significarent, se paratos esse pro fide catholica ac populi salute, proprium sanguinem fundere, ut Christianus Massæus in Chronologia somniat: sed honestandi ordinis gratia (sic Platina dicit) ut inde pompa insatiabili atq; ambi-tione turgescerent: vel potius, ut meretrici matri, quæ inebratur sanguine sanctorum martyrum, & sedet super bestiam coccineam, purpura & coccino induta, Apoc. 17. per omnia responderent. Apparatum Decretalium scripsit, authenticas com-posuit, de ecclesiastica potestate librum fecit, Clarissis Franciscanorum sororibus regulâ dedit, cru-cem cem contra suos æmulos prædicari iussit, imperatorem à Pontifice deponi posse sanciuit, & octauas Mariæ natiuitatis celebrari mandauit. Et ut de locustis Apocalypticis aliquid dicam: Mendicantium ordinum fratres (inquit Stella) plurimum dilexit, & eos quidem Apostolicis sauoribus & priuilegijs, ac multis beneficijs, quoad uixit, prosequi non desitit. Dominicanos ad prælaturas promouit, ut patet de Hugone Cardinale, Ioanne Bofnensi præsule, & Guilhelmo Anteradensi episcopo. Franciscanos ad suam confessionem uocabat: erat enim ei Nicolaus Anglicus ab animæ secretis. Carmelitas & Augustinianos in adoptionis filios admisit, & ex professis Christianis per nouam for-mationem suas creaturas fecit. Ab eremi[?] adur-bes pertraxit, & in ocio suum mendicare panem docuit. Carmelitarum regulam, ab Alberto Hie-rosolymorum patriarcha prius eis traditam, per Dominicanos correxit, mitigauit, declarauit, at-tum demum cum Apostatica benedictione confirmauit, ut non de solo Saluatore (ut eadem dicat regula) salutem sperarent. Permisit eos cum ceteris Mendicantium ordinibus, diuinum Dei uerbum adulterantes, prædicare, ut Abadonis regnum to[?] citius promoueretur: disputare, & eius aduersarij per Aristotelem confunderentur: & confessiones audire, ut populos omnes audientes haberet. Et o-mnes, quotquot erant sub religiosae medicationis tulo[?], prouidens eorum quieti, ab omni regum iuris ditione & episcoporum authoritate exemit.
units.tr: At the aforesaid Council of Lyons, in the year of the Lord 1245, Innocent, to strengthen the empire of Abaddon, decreed that the cardinals should wear red hats and red copes and be carried through the city on caparisoned horses. He did this not to signify that they were ready to shed their own blood for the Catholic faith and the salvation of the people, as Christianus Massaeus dreams in his Chronology, but for the sake of honouring their order (so Platina says), so that they might swell with insatiable pomp and ambition. Or rather, he did it so that they would match the harlot mother in every respect, who is drunk with the blood of the holy martyrs, sits upon the scarlet beast, and is clothed in purple and scarlet (Rev. 17). He wrote the Apparatus of the Decretals, compiled the authentic texts, and wrote a book on ecclesiastical power. He gave a rule to the Franciscan Clarist sisters, ordered the cross to be preached against his rivals, decreed that an emperor could be deposed by the Pope, and commanded that the octave of the Nativity of Mary be celebrated. To say something more about the Apocalyptic locusts: he loved the friars of the mendicant orders very much (Stella says), and as long as he lived he never ceased to favour them with apostolic favours and privileges and many benefits. He advanced Dominicans to prelacies, as is evident in the case of Hugh the cardinal, John, bishop of Bosnia, and William, bishop of Anteradus. He summoned the Franciscans to his confession, for Nicholas the Englishman was his secretary of secrets. He admitted the Carmelites and Augustinians as adopted sons, and by a new formation he made them his own creatures out of professed Christians. He drew them from the desert into the cities, and taught them in their idleness to beg for bread. He corrected, moderated and clarified the rule of the Carmelites, which Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, had earlier given them, through the Dominicans. At length he confirmed it with an apostate blessing, so that they would not hope for salvation from the Saviour alone (as the same rule says). He permitted them, together with the other mendicant orders, who corrupt the divine Word of God, to preach, so that the kingdom of Abaddon might be advanced more quickly; to dispute, so that its opponents might be confounded through Aristotle; and to hear confessions, so that he might have all the people as listeners. And he, providing for their peace, exempted from the jurisdiction of all kings and the authority of bishops all those who were under the title of religious healing.

units.la: Scripserunt interim hi Papae pugiles, ne inue-nirentur in his suis officijs negligentes, super Sententiis, super Decreta, super Aristotelem, super monachorum regulas, cum repertorijs, summis, tabulis, triuijs, quadriuijs, determinationibus, quaestionibus, quod libetis, mortuorum miraculis, martyrologijs, Marialibus, legendis, perspectiuis, aphorismis, & similibus. Scripserunt concordantias De cretorum[?], institutiones ordinum, de casibus iuris, de arte notariatus, de libellorum formatione, de praeludijs causarum, de actione aduocatorum, de institutione nouitiorum, de substantialibus religionis, de excellentia eucharistiae, de virtute Missae, de professu monachatus, de sex alis Seraphim, de scandalis Apostolorum, de defensorium medicitatis, de subiecto (non substantia) theologiae, & alia, ita ut totus admiraretur mundus, super locustis tarentum puteum egressis, quibus potestas data est, ut scorpionum terrae, Apoc. 9. Nulla tunc erat religio aut doctrina authoritatis, nisi apud Iuris, & horum Mendicantium fraterculos. Iean. Theutonicus, sacerdotis prebendarij ex Friburgo filius, Summam confessorum fecit. Rolan-dinus de Romancijs, iuris utriusq; professor, de or-dine maleficiorum opus edidit. Qui Tritemium & alios legit, ex eius temporis scriptis uidebit, regnasse cum suis locustis Abadonem ipsum Apocalypticum & verum. Magna tunc erat mundi excitatio, veritatis amissio, populi perditio, & animarum periclitatio. Sed hos demum tetigit egregius Dei athleta, Guilhelmus de S. Amore, in libello de nouissim ꝛum temporum periculis, & pseudoprophetantium stigmis. In hos Nicolaum Gallum, fidelis Christi seruus, igneam sagittam, aculeatum opus, emisit, ad eremum iterum reuersus.
units.tr: Meanwhile these champions of the Pope wrote, lest they be found negligent in their offices: on the Sentences, on the Decretals, on Aristotle, on the rules of the monks, with indexes, summaries, tables, trivia, quadrivia, determinations, questions, quodlibets, miracles of the dead, martyrologies, Marian books, legends, perspectives, aphorisms and suchlike. They wrote concordances of the decretals, institutes of the orders, on the cases of law, on the art of the notary, on the forming of petitions, on the preliminaries of lawsuits, on the conduct of advocates, on the instruction of novices, on the essentials of religion, on the excellence of the Eucharist, on the virtue of the Mass, on the profession of monkhood, on the six wings of the seraphim, on the scandals of the apostles, on the defence of the medicine of the mind, on the subject (not the substance) of theology, and other such things. So much so that the whole world marvelled at them, at the locusts that came out of the bottomless pit, to whom power was given as the scorpions of the earth have power (Rev. 9). At that time there was no religion or doctrine of authority except among the lawyers and these little friars of the mendicant orders. John Teutonicus, son of a prebendary priest of Freiburg, made the Summa of confessors. Rolandinus of Romancia, professor of both laws, published a work on the order of crimes. Whoever reads Trithemius and others will see from the writings of that time that Abaddon himself, the Apocalyptic and true one, reigned with his locusts. There was then great stirring in the world, loss of truth, destruction of the people, and peril to souls. But at last the outstanding athlete of God, William of Saint-Amour, touched these men in his little book on the perils of the last times and the brands of false prophets. Against them the faithful servant of Christ, Nicholas Gallus, sent forth a fiery arrow, a stinging work, after returning again to the desert.

units.la: Ad Innocentium quartum nunc regrediamur, Vt consuetis Papārum praestigijs mundum deluderet, ad mortuorum canonizationes se conver-tit. Eadmundum Cantuariensem archiepiscopum, & Stanislaum Cracouiensem praesulem, qui in pia Pontificis causa principibus restiterunt, ac Petrum Veronensem Dominicanum, Christianorum hominum pro hac Satanae fede proditore & martyrem Papisticum, sanctorum adscripsit numero. Ad Tartaros, legatos misit, eiusdem sectae Dominicanae monachos, qui eos ad pacem & fidem Papisticam adhortarentur. Tantam sibi authoritatem apud Barbaros esse putauit hic Papa, ut sperà[?] ritimmanißimos hostes illos, inspectis eius literis, collastatim submissuros bestiae, iussaq; eius sactu- ros. Spurios ille plures habuit, quos religionis gra- tia nepotes nuncupabat: praecipue Guilhelmum quendam, cuius sepulchrum in S. Laurentio extra muros cernebatur.
units.tr: Let us now return to Innocent IV. In order to deceive the world with the customary tricks of the Popes, he turned to the canonisation of the dead. He counted among the saints Edmund, archbishop of Canterbury, and Stanislaus, bishop of Krakow, who resisted princes in the pious cause of the Pope, and Peter of Verona, a Dominican, a traitor to Christian men for this faith of Satan and a Papistical martyr. He sent to the Tartars, as legates, monks of the same Dominican sect, who were to exhort them to peace and the Papistical faith. This Pope thought he had so much authority among the barbarians that, as he hoped, those most savage enemies, once they had inspected his letters, would at once submit to the beast and do his bidding. He had many bastards, whom for the sake of religion he called nephews, above all a certain William, whose tomb could be seen in St Lawrence outside the walls.

units.la: Vsq; ad hunc Innocentium (inquit Bibliander) articulus fidei non fuit, neq; lex ecclesiae, ut homi- nes adorarent panem & vinum in eucharistia. Pa- pigitur creator, nouum deum Mauzim produ- xit per transsubstantiationem, &c. Thomas Can- tipratensis. A procumbentibus, inquit, adoratur et honoratur: sed sub Honorio parabantur taberna- cula. Viriusque Siciliae regnum, Henrico tertio An- glorum regi uendendum obtulit: hic Pontifex, ad- Edmundi filij sui usum, Contadino rege adhuc uiuente: Anglorumq; ecclesias per suos legatos, usurarios & Iudaeos, inauditis exactionibus uexa- bat. Inclero pro nummis aureis omne luxuriarum genus defendebat: & in suis nepotulis ac spurijs ad huc turpiora.
units.tr: From this Innocent onward (says Bibliander) there was no article of faith, nor law of the Church, that men should adore bread and wine in the Eucharist. The Pope ... created a new god, Mauzim, through transubstantiation, etc. (Thomas Cantipratensis). He is adored and honoured, he says, by those who prostrate themselves; but under Honorius tabernacles were being prepared. He offered the kingdom of both Sicilies for sale to Henry III, king of the English, for the use of his son Edmund, while King Conradin was still alive. Through his legates, who were usurers and Jews, he harassed the churches of England with unheard-of exactions. Among the clergy he defended every kind of luxury for gold coins, and in his nephews and bastards, things even more shameful.

units.la: Cum hoc Innocentio quasdam contentiones ha- buit magnus tunc doctor ecclesiae, Robertus Lin- colniensis, cognomine Capito, eius improbans te- terrimos mores, auaritiam, sastum, tyrannides, tam multa quàm scriptis. Noluit ille admittere ad canonicatum Lincolniensem, quendam eius spuri- um, ob inscitiam: sed eius Papae expilationibus re- stitit, Angliam deglubentis. Fuitq; ideo ab illo excommunicatus. Quam excommunicationem tan- ta constantia contempsit, ut & in ea mortuus sit. Disputabat ille, Papam nihil contra iusticiam veri- tatemq; posse: imo cum id attentet, peiorem esse Lucifero & Antichristo. Tandem a Papa ad curiam citatus, & iniuste damnatus, ab eo appellauit ad iudicem Christum. Narratq; Cestriensis lib. 7. quod obeunte Lincolniensi, audita sit nox in curia Papae clamans: Veni miser in iudicium Dei: repertusq; sit sequenti die Papa in lecto xanimis, ac liuida in eo plaga, tanquam si[?] percussus fuisset: Fiebat hoc, anno Domini 1253[?], quum esset Neapoli: arbitratus breui, toto Siciliae regno se potiturum, & ibi in Ecclesia S. Laurentij sepelitur: uocabatq; sella Romanensis annis duobus.
units.tr: With this Innocent there were certain disputes on the part of the great teacher of the Church of that time, Robert of Lincoln, surnamed Capito, who condemned his most wretched morals, his avarice, his pride and his tyrannies, as much in writing as in speech. He refused to admit to the canonry of Lincoln a certain bastard of his, because of his ignorance; and he resisted the plundering of this Pope, who was flaying England. For this he was excommunicated by him. He despised that excommunication with such constancy that he died under it. He used to argue that the Pope could do nothing against justice and truth; indeed, that when he attempted it he was worse than Lucifer and Antichrist. At last he was summoned to the court by the Pope, unjustly condemned, and appealed from him to Christ the judge. Higden of Chester, in book 7, relates that when the bishop of Lincoln died, a voice was heard in the Pope's court at night crying: "Come, wretch, to the judgement of God." And the next day the Pope was found lifeless in his bed, with a livid wound on him, as if he had been struck. This happened in the year of the Lord 1253, while he was at Naples, thinking that he would soon possess the whole kingdom of Sicily; and he is buried there in the church of St Lawrence. He held the Roman see for two years.
122. ALEXANDER the Fourth.

units.la: Alexander quartus, natione Campanus, patria Anagninus, ex cardinale Hostiensi, in Innocentij locum, Papa Neapoli surrogatus: Ecclesiam de Runcano, & Manfredum Siciliae regem, Pontificum hostes, persecutus est: Haec erant huius [?]ritualissimi patris prima exercitia: non cura Christiana siani[?] gregis non animarum zelus, non diuinae ue-ritatis promulgatio. Admonuit nihilominus primum callidissima vulpes, paratis interim adver-sus illos militaribus copiis, ne contra Ecclesiae di-gnitatem quicquam molirentur: hoc est, ne Siciliae regnum, quod ille affectauerat, sibi ac suis Cardi-nalibus auferrent. Qui tamen heroicos gerentes animos, accersitis e Nuceria Saracenis atq; aliis, copiae[?] Papales, nihil tale metuentes, apud fossam aggressi, partim ceperunt, partim trucidarunt. In-terea Alexander, excommunicato Manfredo, Anagniam profectus, Octavianum Vbaldina gentâ[?] ortum; Ecclesiae Romanæ Cardinalem, Neapolim misit: qui Neapolitanos contra eundem Manfre-dum in fide confirmaret, pollicitus se breui Cam-panis omnibus ac Neapolitanis auxilium allatu-rum. Sed Manfredus non contentus Neapolitanos solum vexare, in Hetruria quoq; factiones move-bat, maxim-vero Florentiæ, ubi placuit Guelphos reducere, qui Gibellinorum conatibus resisterent. Sic est Italia tota, grauibus odiis ac maximis tu-multibus & bellis horribiliter exagitata. Manfredus autem, qui Conradum Siciliae regem veneno extinxerat, Panormi rex declaratus, conducto mi-litum[?] legatum Apostolicum magnis cladibus attri-buit, [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Alexander the Fourth, a Campanian by birth and from Anagni, was installed at Naples as Pope in place of Innocent, having been a cardinal of Ostia. He pursued the Church of Runcano and Manfred, king of Sicily, the enemies of the Popes. These were the first exercises of this most ritualistic father. There was no Christian care for the flock, no zeal for souls, no proclamation of divine truth. Yet this most crafty fox first gave warning, while in the meantime he prepared military forces against them, so that they should not plot anything against the dignity of the Church; that is, so that they should not take from him and his cardinals the kingdom of Sicily, which he had coveted. Nevertheless they, bearing heroic spirits, summoned Saracens and others from Nocera, and attacked the Papal forces at a ditch, where those forces feared nothing of the kind; some they captured and some they slaughtered. Meanwhile Alexander, having excommunicated Manfred, set out for Anagni and sent Octavian, a native of the Ubaldini family and a cardinal of the Roman Church, to Naples, to confirm the Neapolitans in the faith against that same Manfred, promising that he would soon bring help to all the Campanians and the Neapolitans. But Manfred, not content to harass only the Neapolitans, was also stirring up factions in Tuscany, above all at Florence, where he saw fit to restore the Guelphs to resist the attempts of the Ghibellines. Thus all of Italy was dreadfully agitated with grievous hatreds, the greatest tumults and wars. Manfred, however, who had poisoned Conrad, king of Sicily, was declared king at Palermo, and, by hiring soldiers, inflicted great defeats on the Apostolic legate [illegible, ~20 letters].

units.la: Eo tempore, theologi quidam Franciscanorum sectæ, Brixiam à Pontifice missi (non pacis, sed belli exuscitatores) eò prædicando ciuitatem dedu-xere, ut & Guelphos extorres reciperent, & partes synagogæ Papisticæ sequerentur. Beneficium erat Alexander, ac liberalis erga hos & similes, optimè de Abadonis religione per prædicationis officium meritos: eò tunc per tales hypocritas deductum est officium tam sanctum. Nam libellos quosdam contra fictam eorum paupertatem editos ab erudito uiro Guilhelmo de S. Amore, perpetuo edicto aboleuit. Affirmabat enim uir ille bonus, pauperes hos, ociosos nebulones potius (no-ta locustas) de eleemosynis viuentes, non esse in statu salutis. Combusit etiam (teste Platina) uidente ipsa curia Romana, libellum pestiferum, à fraterculis editum, quo asserebant, statum gratiæ non à lege Euangelij (ò Dei proditores) sed à lege suorum spirituum procedere: ne ex illo homini-bus apparet, suorum amicorum, fraterculorum scilicet, damnabile furtum. Quæ opinio ex Ioachi-mi abbatis & Cyrilli Carmelitæ uisionibus sumpta, declarabatur. Et liber ille à suis sectatoribus Euangelium æternum dicebatur. Ex uisione, quà beatum Augustinum in somnio se uidisse credebat Alexander, fra[?]trum Eremitarum ipsius Au[?]ustini undonem, à suo prædecessore inchoatam, ardenter perfecit: ordinemq; ipsum, sicut & antea Carmelitas Innocentius, relictis eremis, urbes petere & incolere ubiq; coegit: ut & ipsi doctrinis impostricibus, & confessionum auditione, fructus eo genere dignos afferre possent. In eodem statu(inquit Stella Venetus) eundem ordinem confirmavit, quo alios Mendicantium ordines: multaq; privilegia, exemptiones & indulgentias ipsis contulit. Et eorum primus generalis præses, Lanfrancus Mediolanensis ponitur.
units.tr: At that time certain theologians of the Franciscan sect, sent to Brescia by the Pontiff (not as bringers of peace but as stirrers up of war), by preaching there led the city to receive the Guelphs in exile and to follow the party of the Papist synagogue. Alexander was a benefactor and generous towards these men and others like them, who had deserved well of Abaddon's religion by the office of preaching; so at that time such a holy office was led astray by such hypocrites. For he abolished by a perpetual edict certain books published against their feigned poverty by the learned man William of Saint-Amour. That good man affirmed that these poor men were idle scoundrels, rather locusts, living on alms, and were not in a state of salvation. He also burned (according to Platina, in the sight of the Roman curia itself) a pestilent little book, put out by these little brothers, in which they asserted that the state of grace proceeds not from the law of the Gospel (O betrayers of God) but from the law of their spirits, so that from it there might appear to men the damnable theft of their friends, namely the little brothers. This opinion, taken from the visions of the abbot Joachim and of Cyril the Carmelite, was being proclaimed; and that book was called the Eternal Gospel by its followers. From the vision in which Alexander believed he had seen blessed Augustine in a dream, he zealously completed the union of the hermits of Augustine himself, which had been begun by his predecessor; and, just as Innocent had earlier compelled the Carmelites, he forced this order too, having left the deserts, to seek and inhabit cities everywhere, so that they might bring fruit of that kind worthy of their deceitful teachings and of hearing confessions. In the same condition (says Stella of Venice) he confirmed that order, just as the other orders of Mendicants; and he conferred on them many privileges, exemptions and indulgences. And Lanfranc of Milan is named as their first general superior.

units.la: Huius Alexandri legatus Rustandus, anno Domini 1255 in Angliam venit, ut decimas in Angliâ, Scotiâ & Hybernia contra Manfredum colligeret. Et multa detestabilia (inquit Matthæus Parisius) à fonte sulphureo Rom. ecclesiæ, prob dolor, imò prob pudor, tunc temporis emanarunt ad multorum perniciem. Infinitam enim, post crucis prædicationem per Mendicantes, Rustandus pecuniam exigebat. Inaudita erat exactio, quam Pontifex petebat. Vnde Fulco Londinensis episcopus dolenter dicebat: Antequam tantæ ecclesiarum iniuriæ, seruituti[?], & intolerabili oppressioni consentiam, pro Christo[?] caput amittam. Nam etsi illa curia, fideles Christi multoties usq; ad amaritudinē spiritus excruciauerit: nunquam tamen sicut hoc & sequentia te anno, tam lethaliter uniuersos & singulos Christi seruos sauciauit. Cogebantur enim insontes ido-lolatrare: & quasi apostatae, ueritati, quae Deus est, abrenunciare. Papa operatur omnia, nō in æ-dificationem, sed ruinam. Concessa fuit decima in subsidium terrae sanctae: sed cogimur eam in Apu-liam transferre contra Christianos. Et sequitur: Datur potestas personis prorsus indignis, super nobiles ecclesias. Venduntur praelati ut boues & asini. Haec est ultimae seruitutis conditio. Ecce uen-ditores, eijciendi profcti[?] à templo, ac flagellandi. Sed quia ignobilius est, facere iniuriam uiolenter, quam pati cum innocentia: credendum est, quod si per hoc clamor ascendat querulus ad Deum Dominum ultionum, &c.
units.tr: The legate of this Alexander, Rustand, came to England in the year of the Lord 1255, to collect tithes in England, Scotland and Ireland against Manfred. And (says Matthew Paris) many detestable things, alas, and indeed alas for shame, then flowed from the sulphurous fountain of the Roman Church to the ruin of many. For after the preaching of the cross by the Mendicants, Rustand demanded an infinite sum of money. The exaction the Pontiff sought was unheard of. Hence Fulk, bishop of London, said sorrowfully: "Before I consent to such great injuries to the churches, to servitude and intolerable oppression, I will lose my head for Christ. For although that court has often tormented the faithful of Christ even to the bitterness of spirit, yet it has never so deadly wounded all and each of the servants of Christ as it has this year and the following ones. For the innocent were compelled to worship idols, and, like apostates, to renounce the truth, which is God. The Pope works everything not for building up but for ruin. A tithe was granted for aid to the Holy Land, but we are forced to transfer it into Apulia against Christians." And he goes on: "Power is given to persons utterly unworthy over noble churches. Prelates are sold like oxen and asses. This is the condition of the last servitude. Behold the sellers, to be cast out of the temple and scourged. But since it is more disgraceful to do injury by violence than to suffer it with innocence, it must be believed that if by this a plaintive cry rises up to God, the Lord of vengeance, etc."

units.la: In concionatione Londinensi, cum Ruffandus[?] diceret, Ecclesias omnes esse domini Papae, modeste respondit Leonardus quidam Anglus: Verum est tutione, non fruitione: defensione, non dissipatione. Seuallus Eboracensis archiepiscopus, Roberti Lincolniensis exemplo, Papae Alexandro re-stitit, rogans per literas, ut à consuetis uiolentiis cessaret: ut Petri exemplo ouiculas pascat, non ton-deat, non excoriet, non euisceret, aut ut famelicus lupus deuorando corsumat[?]. Et sequitur in Mat-theo: Misit adhuc alios in Angliam legatos, praeùpuè Arlotum & Mansuetum, Minoritas: qui au-thoritatem habebant absoluendi pro pecuniis quoscunq; falsidicos, periuros, uotorum transgressores, adulteros, homicidas, proditores, ueneficos, Sodomitas, & omnes. Vnde mulier quaedam reclu-sa apud sinum D. Albani, terribilem uisionem habens, audiuit senem multu uenerabilem, seuerites clamasse: Vae, uae, omnibus terram inhabitantibus. Et illud ter iterauit, ac recessit. Anno Domini 1258.
