units.tr: In a sermon in London, when Rustand said that all churches belonged to the Lord Pope, a certain Englishman, Leonard, replied with moderation: "It is true of their guardianship, not of their enjoyment; of their defence, not their destruction." Sewal, archbishop of York, following the example of Robert of Lincoln, resisted Pope Alexander, asking by letter that he cease from his customary violence, so that, following Peter's example, he would feed the little sheep, not shear them, flay them, or disembowel them, nor devour them like a hungry wolf. And in Matthew it goes on: He sent further legates into England, especially Arlotus and Mansuetus, Minorites, who had authority to absolve for money whoever they were, whether false-swearers, perjurers, breakers of vows, adulterers, murderers, traitors, poisoners, sodomites, and all. Hence a certain enclosed woman near the church of St Albans, having a terrible vision, heard a very venerable old man cry out sternly: "Woe, woe, to all who dwell on the earth." And he repeated this three times and withdrew. In the year of the Lord 1258.

units.la: Ricardus Cornubiae comes, Ioannis olim Anglo-rum regis filius, in Alemaniae regem eligebatur, propter thesauri sui abundantiam. Illiq; Papa Im-perium procurabat, sed callide & silenter, ne Hi-spaniae regi Alphonso (à quo etiam aureos accepe-rat nummos) aduersarius & impostor uideretur. Thesauris enim abundabat Ricardus. Vnde Saty-ricum quidam,
units.tr: Richard, earl of Cornwall, son of John, once king of the English, was elected king of Germany on account of the abundance of his treasure. The Pope promoted the empire for him, but cunningly and quietly, lest he should seem an adversary and impostor to Alfonso, king of Spain (from whom he had also received gold coins). For Richard abounded in treasure. Hence a certain satirist:

units.la: Nummus, ait, pro me: nubit Cornubia Romae.
units.tr: "Money," he says, "for me: Cornwall marries at Rome."

units.la: Alexander quoq; ubi ab externis negotijs uaca-[?] cum erat, Decretales epistolas edidit. Assutis Ae-gyptijs, fraterculis & decretistis fuit, eorumq; plures ad Cardinalatum & episcopatus usq; pro-mouit. Templum testudineum S. Agnetis ædifica-uit: & quod antea Baccho dicatum fuerat, D. Constantiæ dedicauit, nouum deorum erector: al-treq; suis manibus consecrauit. Mendicantium ordines literis celebravit: interdixit tamen, ne què ante finitum probationis annum (insigni fulticia) ad ordinis professionem admitterent. Sedecim bullas (Palæonyloro teste) Carmelitis concessit, & Claram Franciscæ discipulam ac sororem, infan-tes retulit. Cum demum insuper Viterbium con-secrasset anno Domini 1262. pacem inter Genuen-ses & Venetos ad suam voluptatem compositu-rus, & non omnia sibi ad votum succederent: ex animi tædio, eo loci mortuus est, & in D. Laurentii templo sepultus. Mirabilem à Christo defi-dionem[?] per fraterculos mendicantes, sub hoc Pomi-fice postea notabis.
units.tr: Alexander too, when he was free of foreign business, published the Decretal letters. He favoured the Egyptians, the little brothers and the decretists, and promoted many of them as far as the cardinalate and bishoprics. He built the vaulted temple of St Agnes, and dedicated to St Constance what had earlier been dedicated to Bacchus, a new erector of gods; and he consecrated another with his own hands. He honoured the orders of the Mendicants with letters; yet he forbade them to admit anyone to the profession of the order before the year of probation was finished (a remarkable folly). He granted sixteen bulls to the Carmelites, and reported Clare as a disciple and sister of Francis, and as an infant. When at last he had consecrated Viterbo in the year of the Lord 1262, intending to settle peace between the Genoese and the Venetians to his own liking, and things did not all turn out to his wish, he died there out of weariness of spirit, and was buried in the church of St Lawrence. You will note later the wonderful apostasy from Christ through the little brothers, the mendicants, under this Pontiff.
123. Urban IV.

units.la: VRbanus quartus, natione Gallus, ex urbe Tres-censi oriundus, & Pantaleo (ut fertur) ante Pa-triarcha Hierosolymitanus, ad Pontificatu, statim è Gallia milites conuocavit, ut hostem ecclesiæ Manfredum subigeret. Et quo citius id fieret, Ludovicum Francorum regem exorauit, ut Carolum fratrem, Provinciæ & Ald-degauorum comitem, cum exercitu in Italiam mit-teret: eumq; utriusq; Siciliæ regem dixit. Carolus autem post varias conflictationes, Manfredum ad Beneventum urbem vicit & occidit: regnaq; Sici-liæ. [?]lizà Papa contra ius & fas in feudum accepit, cū Calabriæ & Apuliæ ducatu: ex quo furto manifestò patratæ sunt multæ cædes. Abeunte hoc Pontifice (Perusij namq; erat) Romani iterum libertatem studentes, Banderesios creabant, magistratus nouos, qui uitæ necisq; potestatem haberent. Senatorem, priuatum hominem quendam Brancaleonem Bononiensem elegerunt: quem paulo post su-gatum, iterum revocarunt. Pauca præter ea, quæ iam dicta sunt, Vrbanus fecit: nisi quòd cuiusdam fœminæ instinctu, festum Eucharistici panis, seu triticei Dei, quod Corporis Christi uocant, quintā feriā post Trinitatis festum instituerit, cum processionibus, facibus, uexillis, conopæis, Missarum solennitatibus, & octauis. Quibus maximas indulgentias didit indulgentias, ut præ cæteris diis omnibus coleretur deus Mauzim. Eiusq; efficium ex veteris Testamenti figuris & umbris, per Thomam Aquinatem Dominicanorum doctorem sanctum fabri-cari iussit.
units.tr: Urban IV, a Frenchman born in the city of Troyes, was (as it is said) formerly Patriarch of Jerusalem under the name Pantaleon. As soon as he became Pope, he summoned soldiers from France to subdue Manfred, the enemy of the Church. To make this happen the sooner, he begged Louis, king of the Franks, to send his brother Charles, Count of Provence and Anjou, into Italy with an army, and he named Charles king of both Sicilies. After various struggles, Charles defeated and killed Manfred at the city of Benevento, and the Pope, contrary to law and right, granted himself the kingdom of Sicily as a fief, together with the duchy of Calabria and Apulia. From this theft many killings were openly committed. When this Pope left (for he was at Perugia), the Romans, again striving for liberty, created Banderesi, new magistrates who were to have power of life and death. They chose as senator a private citizen, one Brancaleone of Bologna, who was soon driven out and then recalled. Urban did little beyond what has already been said, except that at the urging of a certain woman he instituted the feast of the Eucharistic bread, or wheaten God, which they call the Body of Christ, to be kept on the Thursday after the feast of the Trinity, with processions, torches, banners, canopies, solemn Masses and octaves. He granted very great indulgences for it, so that the god Mauzim might be worshipped above all other gods. He ordered its office to be fashioned out of the figures and shadows of the Old Testament by Thomas Aquinas, the holy teacher of the Dominicans.

units.la: Multæ sunt opiniones, super prima huius festi origine: sed hanc accipe certiorem esse, ex Arnoldo Bostio, ac Petro Præmonstratensi. Anno Domini 1264. revelatio sanè diabolica, super hoc sacramenti festo celebrando, cuidam Euæ fœminæ Leodiensi, in otia superstitioso reclusæ. Pontifici ante Papatum familiariter notæ, fista esse. Quam per suas literas ei significauit, rogans, ut festum illud Papali authoritate solennizandum ordinaret: cui has literas remisit sanctissimus pater.
units.tr: There are many opinions about the first origin of this feast, but take this account as the more certain one, from Arnold Bostius and Peter of Premontré. In the year 1264 there was indeed a diabolical revelation concerning the celebration of this sacramental feast, made to a certain woman, Eve of Liège, shut up in a superstitious seclusion, who was intimately known to the Pope before he became Pope. She signified it to him by letter, asking him to order that the feast be solemnized by papal authority. The holy father sent this letter back to her.

units.la: Bulla Vrbani Papæ ad Euam re-clusam.
units.tr: Bull of Pope Urban to Eve the Anchoress.

units.la: Vrbanus episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei, di-lectæ in Christo filiæ Euæ, salutem & Apostoli-cam benedictionem. Scimus o filia, quod magno de-fiderio desiderauit anima tua, ut solenne festum corporis Domini nostri Iesu Christi institueretur in ecclesia Dei, à Christi fidelibus perpetuis tem-poribus celebrandum. Et ideo tibi significamus ad gaudium, quod nos ad corroborationem catholicæ fidei, dignum diximus statuendum, ut de tam mi-rabili sacramento præter quotidianam commemorationem, quam de ipso facit ecclesia, speciali-or & solennior memoria celebretur, certum ad hoc designantes diem, videlicet feriam quintam proximam post Dominicam festi Pentecostes proximè sequentem, ut ipsa feria quinta deuote, turbæ fidelium, propter hoc ad ecclesias affectuose concurrant. Sitq; dies illa uniuersis Christicolis no-ua festiuitate iucundus, & ampla iucunditate fe-stiuus, prout in literis Apostolicis, quas per uniuersum mundum super hoc direximus, ad plenius continetur. Et scias quod nos huiusmodi sestum[?], ut omnibus nostris fratribus, Romanae videlicet ecclesiae Cardinalibus, nec non cum omnibus archiepiscopis, episcopis, caeterisque ecclesiarum praelatis, tunc apud sedem Apostolicam commorantibus ad hoc, ut videntibus et audientibus de tanti festi celebritate, praeberetur exemplum, duximus celebrandum.Magnificet igitur anima tua Dominum, et exultet spiritus tuus, in Deo salutari tuo. Quia viderunt oculi tui salutare tuum (horrendum idolum quod parauimus (o execrabilis Antichriste & Abadon) ante faciem omnium populorum. Laetare insuper, quia omnipotens Dominus tribuit tibi desiderium cordis tui, et voluntate labiorum non fraudauit te caelestis gratiae plenitudo. Et quia quaternum, in quo totum ipsius festi habetur effectum, tibi sub bulla nostra per latorem praesentium destinamus, volumus, et per apostolica scripta tibi mandamus, quatenus quaternum ipsum cum devotione recipias, et eius copiam personis illam petentibus exhibeas liberaliter. Et libenter infles devotis supplicationibus apud illum, qui memoriale tam salutiferum de seipso reliquit in terris, ut nobis tribuat ex alto gratiam, commissam nostro regimini Ecclesiam suam regendi utiliter, ad laudem et gloriam sui nominis, et salubriter gubergubernandam. Datum apud urbem ueterem, sex to idus Septembris, Pontificatus nostri anno tertio.
units.tr: Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Eve, greeting and apostolic blessing. We know, daughter, that your soul has longed with great desire that a solemn feast of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ be instituted in the Church of God, to be celebrated by the faithful of Christ in perpetual times. And so we signify to you, with joy, that we have judged it fitting, for the strengthening of the Catholic faith, to decree that concerning so wonderful a sacrament, besides the daily remembrance which the Church makes of it, a more special and solemn remembrance be celebrated. We have designated a certain day for this, namely the Thursday next following the Sunday immediately after the feast of Pentecost, so that on that Thursday crowds of the faithful may devoutly and lovingly gather at the churches. Let that day be joyful to all Christians with a new festivity, and festive with ample joy, as is more fully set out in the apostolic letters which we have sent throughout the whole world concerning this. And know that we have decided to celebrate such a feast in the presence of all our brothers, namely the cardinals of the Roman Church, together with all archbishops, bishops and other prelates of the churches who were then staying at the Apostolic See, so that an example might be given to those who see and hear of the celebration of so great a feast. Let your soul therefore magnify the Lord, and let your spirit exult in God your Saviour. For your eyes have seen your salvation (the horrible idol which we have prepared, O execrable Antichrist and Abaddon) before the face of all peoples. Rejoice moreover, because almighty God has granted you the desire of your heart, and the fullness of heavenly grace has not denied you the wish of your lips. And since we send you, under our seal and by the bearer of these presents, the quire in which the whole effect of this feast is set out, we will, and command you by apostolic writ, that you receive that quire with devotion and freely give copies of it to those persons who ask for them. And gladly pour out devout supplications to him who left so saving a memorial of himself on earth, that he may grant us grace from on high to govern usefully the Church committed to our rule, to the praise and glory of his name, and to govern it healthfully. Given at Orvieto, on the sixth day before the ides of September, in the third year of our pontificate.

units.la: Ex hoc Tartareo fonte effluxit innumerabilium idololatriarum ac superstitionum pelagus, quod uniuersum fere Christiani orbis populum horribiliter inquinauit. Thomas Cantipratensis: A procumbentibus, inquit, adoratur et honoratur. Sed et antea sub Honorio parabantur tabernacula. Hic sanguinis sitibundus Papa, inter Guelphos et Gibellinos plusquam triennio sedit, et eorum factiones ad ruinam et exitium multorum per Italiam certare prouocauit. Ludouicum Francorum regem, sed suo malo, in Saracenos armauit: et Mendicantium sectas, locustarum rex, fauoribus auxit, ac priuilegiis ornauit. Qui aliquando lacessitus, quod esset obscuro genere natus, respondit: Nobilem virum non nasci, sed uirtute fieri, nobilitatis est. Vnde Perusij demum in maximarum rerum conatu, anno Domini 1265. cum omnia ex voto non succederent, animam in moerore exhauit. Cometes mirae magnitudinis (inquit Matthaeus) apparuit tribus circiter mensibus ante huius Pontificis mortem: et ipsa nocte qua defunctus est, apparere desiit.
units.tr: From this Tartarean fountain flowed a flood of countless idolatries and superstitions, which horribly polluted almost the whole people of the Christian world. Thomas of Cantimpré says: "It is adored and honoured by those who fall prostrate." But even earlier, under Honorius, tabernacles were being prepared. This Pope, thirsty for blood, sat for more than three years between the Guelphs and the Ghibellines, and he stirred up their factions to struggle to the ruin and destruction of many throughout Italy. He armed Louis, king of the Franks, against the Saracens, but to his own harm. As king of the locusts, he increased the favours of the mendicant orders and adorned them with privileges. When once he was taunted because he was of obscure birth, he replied: "It is nobility not to be born noble, but to become so through virtue." At last, at Perugia in the year 1265, in an attempt at the greatest affairs, when not everything went according to his wish, he breathed out his soul in grief. A comet of wondrous size (says Matthew) appeared about three months before the death of this Pope, and it ceased to appear on the very night on which he died.
124. CLEMENT IV.

units.la: Clemens quartus, patria Narbonensis, Guido Fulcodius antea uocatus, aduocatus in Francia consistorialis episcopus Podiensis, archiepiscopus Narbonensis, ac Sabinensis Cardinalis fuit, qui duas filias & filium unum ex uxore ante Papatum suscepit. Christiani sanguinis effusiones necisse perhorrescens, praedecessoris Vrbani caepta prosecutus, Pontificiam hanc abominationis sedem solita Antichristorum tyrannide occupabat. Caroli Andegauiae comitem praedictum, magno cum exercitu in Italiam uocabat, ubi occiso Manfredo, rex Siciliae ac Hierosolymae declarabatur: hac tamen lege, ut quotannis quadraginta millia aureorum summum Romanae culinae persoluerat. Qua intereos peracta conuentione, uarijs in locis bella crudelissima atq; hominum caedes perhorrenda pullularunt. Prodidit namq; idem Pontifex Conradinum, Conradi Siciliae regis filium, regnorum heredem praedicto Carolo, ita quod eo cum Germanorum exercitu per Viterbiensis agros transeunte, ubi tum ille degebat, Pontifex dixisse fertur: Conradinum illum tanquam agnum ad occisionem duci, quo se proditionis conscium esse non dissimulauit. Deinde cum circa Neapolim cum Carolo confligeret, & initio fatis habaret uictoriam, ria, proditione sese aperiente, Conradinus & Fri-dericus dux Austriæ capiebantur. Qui in capti-uitate miserè tractati & irrisi, tandem iussu pa-pæ Clementis, etiam decollati sunt, quum pater-num & auitum Conradinus peteret regnum. Sic Neapolis regnum ad Gallos quoq; deuenit, & du-catus Sueuiæ Romanæ pontificis improbitate ces-sauit. Quis hæc audire non perhorresceat? Ponti-sex, qui se Christi uicarium, ac Petri successorem iactat, regiam maiestatem uiolauit, cuius tamen rationem summam habere ex Christi ac Petri præ-cepto teneretur. Qualiter hic Pontifex, cum diuer-sis mundi principibus circa Imperium tum uacant, pro pecuniis luserit: & quomodo Mendicantes fra-terculos, ut suis prædicationibus ipsum flecterent regem, ad Ecclesiarum dignitates prouexerit, per longum esset hic narrare. Viterbij mortem oppe-rit Clemens anno Christi 1270. apud Dominicanos sepultus. Vacabatq; Pontificia sedes duobus an-nis, cum tam scelestus inveniri non posset, qui su-perioribus bene succederet. Heguuidam uiduam, Poloniæ olim ducissam, ille canonizauit. Est
units.tr: Clement IV, a native of Narbonne, formerly called Guy Foulques, served as an advocate in the consistory in France, then as bishop of Le Puy, archbishop of Narbonne, and cardinal of Sabina. Before he became pope he had a wife, by whom he had two daughters and one son. Shrinking from the shedding of Christian blood, he carried on what his predecessor Urban had begun, and he occupied this papal seat of abomination with the usual tyranny of Antichrist. He summoned Charles, count of Anjou, into Italy with a great army. After Manfred was killed, Charles was declared king of Sicily and Jerusalem, on the condition that he pay the Roman court forty thousand gold pieces every year. Once this agreement had been concluded, the most cruel wars and horrifying slaughters of men broke out in various places. This same pope betrayed Conradin, son of King Conrad of Sicily and heir to the kingdoms, to the said Charles. When the German army was passing through the fields of Viterbo, where the pope was then living, he is said to have remarked that Conradin was being led to slaughter like a lamb, and he did not conceal that he was privy to the betrayal. Then, when Charles was fighting near Naples and at first thought he had won, the battle was lost through treachery, and Conradin and Frederick, duke of Austria, were captured. Though they were miserably treated and mocked in captivity, they were at last beheaded by order of Pope Clement, even though Conradin was claiming his paternal and ancestral kingdom. So the kingdom of Naples came also to the French, and the duchy of Swabia was lost through the wickedness of the Roman pontiff. Who could hear these things without horror? The pope, who boasts that he is Christ's vicar and the successor of Peter, violated royal majesty, although by the precept of Christ and Peter he was bound to give a full account of it. How this pope, when various princes of the world were vacant of the empire, made money from them, and how he raised the friars of the mendicant orders to the dignities of the churches, so that they might win the king over by their preaching, would take too long to relate here. Clement died at Viterbo in the year of Christ 1270 and was buried among the Dominicans. The papal see stood vacant for two years, because no one as wicked as he could be found who would succeed his predecessors well. He canonized Hedwig, a widow, once duchess of Poland.

units.la: eodem tempore & D. Ludouicus Fran-corum rex Sanctorum adscri-ptus numero.
units.tr: At the same time, Lewis, king of the French, was also enrolled in the number of the saints.
125. GREGORY X.

units.la: GRegorius decimus, natione Lombardus, patria Placentinus, de familia Mediolanensium Vi-cecomitum, Theobaldus antea dictus, ex Laudensi archidiacono post Asianam peregrinationem, finitis Cardinalium discordiis fere biennalibus, dignus tandem successor inventus est. De cuius cle-ctione[?], Ioannes Portuensis Cardinalis hos versus recinit:
units.tr: Gregory X, a Lombard by birth, a native of Piacenza, of the family of the Visconti of Milan, formerly called Theobald, archdeacon of Liège, was found at last to be a worthy successor after the Asian journey and after the cardinals' quarrels, which lasted nearly two years. Concerning his election, John, cardinal of Porto, sang these verses:

units.la: Papatus munus tulit archidiaconus unus, Quem patrem patrum fecit discordia fratrum.
units.tr: The office of the papacy was taken by a single archdeacon, whom the discord of the brothers made the father of fathers.

units.la: Hic inter caetera, pacem inter Genuenses & Venetos diu, non sine sacrae sedis incommodo, concertantes, constituit: deinde Florentinis, eiusdem sedis invadentibus oppida, sacris interdixit. Postea proficiscens in Galliam, anno Domini 1273. Lugduni concilium celebravit, in quo Michael Pa-leologus Imperator Constantinopolitanus, cum Romano dogmate rursus convenit, cum eius antecessores duodecies antea convenissent, semperq; desivissent. Interfuit & Philippus Francorum rex, cum multis Gallorum & Anglorum, aliarumq; nationum viris nobilibus atq; eruditis. In eo Concilio statuit, ut defuncto Pontifice, Cardinales in con-clave[?] quodam clauderentur, sine cibo ac potu, donec unanimi consensu alium elegissent Papa. Fecit ordinationem quinq; episcoporum Cardinalium, & ut laudabiles atq; honestae personae (sunt ergo tunc maior eorum pars inhonesta) ad talia assumerentur officia, sanciuit. Pro terrae sanctae subsidio (uetus haec erat Pontificum ars) & pro statu rerum ecclesiae multa versutus constituit. Ex nc[?] bi-libus multi, tam reges quam comites, ad iter Hierosolymitanum se cruce signabant: quos personaliter illic se visitaturum, callide pollicebatur.
units.tr: Among other things, he settled the long-standing dispute between the Genoese and the Venetians, which was not without harm to the holy see. Then, when the Florentines invaded the towns of the same see, he laid their city under interdict. Afterwards, setting out for France, he held a council at Lyons in the year of the Lord 1273. At this council Michael Palaeologus, emperor of Constantinople, came back into agreement with the Roman doctrine, although his predecessors had agreed to it twelve times before and had always fallen away again. Philip, king of the French, was present, together with many noble and learned men of the French, English and other nations. At this council he decreed that when a pope died, the cardinals should be shut up in a conclave without food or drink until they chose another pope by unanimous consent. He laid down an ordinance that five cardinal bishops should be chosen, and that men of praiseworthy and honourable character should be appointed to such offices (for most of them were then dishonourable). For the aid of the Holy Land, which was an old trick of the popes, and for the state of the affairs of the Church, he devised many cunning schemes. From these, many people, both kings and counts, took the cross for the journey to Jerusalem, and he cunningly promised that he would visit them there in person.

units.la: Mendicantium ordinum fraterculos (ne suis locis deesse videretur Abadon) ad varias praelaturas assumpsit: Bonaventuram Franciscanū Cardinalem Albanensem fecit, & Petrum de Tarantasia Dominicanum, archiepiscopum Lugdunensem ac Hostiensem cardinalem, cum aliis multis. Florentinis omne ium[?] belli interdixit: Rodulphum Habsburgensem comitem, post longam imperii vacationem & bella civilia, imperatorem approbabat: & Alphonsum Castellae regem post expertas circa imperium gravissimas, defuncto Ricardo Cornubiensi, verbis, non nummis placabat. Et quamquam Radulpho iniunctum ab electoribus esset, ut Romam intra annum proficisceretur, diadematis causa: ille tamen nunquam hoc fecit, publicas pretendens occupationes. Privatim princeps sapiens apud se dicere solebat: Casarum vestigia laeta ac magnifica uideri in Italiæ introitu, sed in exitu tristia, misera & luctuosa, alludens ad illud Æsopicum de vulpe & leone: vbi vulpecula dicebat, se quidem videre multa introeuntium vestigia (in spelunca leonis scilicet, ad quam inuitabatur) sed exeuntium paucissima. Misit tamen Rodulphus Vicepræsidem, seu Locumtenentem in Italiam, quem urbes magna parte susceperunt. Papa vero Romam revertens, ac iter prope Florentinorum mœnia faciens, eos interdicto iam fere trien-nali, soluere noluit, ut Volaterranus scribit: huius Paulini dicti immemor, Sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram, Nolite locum date diabolo, E- Aretium perueniens demum, anno Domini 1275. in itinere fato decubuit, quinto sui Pontificatus anno: & ibidem sepelitur, nec unquam pervenit aut vidit Romam.
units.tr: He raised friars of the mendicant orders (lest Abaddon seem to lack a place of his own) to various prelacies: he made the Franciscan Bonaventure cardinal of Albano, and Peter of Tarentaise, a Dominican, archbishop of Lyons and cardinal of Ostia, along with many others. He forbade the Florentines all war. He approved Rudolf of Habsburg, count, as emperor, after a long vacancy of the empire and civil wars; and he appeased Alfonso, king of Castile, who had suffered grievous troubles over the empire, after the death of Richard of Cornwall, not with money but with words. And although the electors had enjoined on Rudolf that he should go to Rome within a year for the crown, he never did so, pretending public business. Privately the wise prince used to say among his own people that the footprints of the Caesars look happy and splendid on entering Italy, but on leaving are sad, wretched and mournful, alluding to Aesop's fable of the fox and the lion, where the little fox said that he saw many footprints of those going in (into the lion's cave, to which he was invited) but very few of those coming out. Nevertheless Rudolf sent a vice-president, or deputy, into Italy, and most of the cities received him. But the pope, returning to Rome and making his way near the walls of Florence, would not lift the interdict, which had by then lasted almost three years, as Volaterranus writes, forgetting that saying of Paul: Let not the sun go down upon your wrath, and give no place to the devil. Arriving at Arezzo at last, in the year of the Lord 1275, he succumbed to fate on the journey, in the fifth year of his pontificate; he is buried there and never reached or saw Rome.
126. Innocent the Fifth.

units.la: Innocentius quintus, patria Burgundus, professione Dominicanus, & Petrus de Tarantasia prius appellatus: Aretij à Cardinalibus electus, cum adhuc duraret vetus simultas, primus ex locustis seu famelicis fraterculis ad Papatum pervenit. Post sui ordinis in Gallia præfecturam, cognito eius callido atq; arroganti ingenio, Gregorius ex archiepiscopo Lugdunensi, ut dictum est, inter Ecclesiæ Romanæ cardines ipsum adscripsit, episcopum Hostiensem ac summum pœnitentiarium creans. Ita[?] potestatem habebant locusta, creandi super se regem Abadonem, Apoc 9. dum iste esset Hostiensis episcopus, ante Papatum Cardinalis factus, cuius officium erat, Papam præ aliis consecrare: & Bonaventura{4} Franciscanus, Cardinalis episcopus Albanensis. Qui Petrus ipse, uel Innocentius, in Pa-pam electus, Romam paulo post abiens, & in D. Petri templo coronatus, animum statim, ut in amœ-na quiete ad carnem uiueret, ad res Italiæ pacan-das adiecit. Quare legatos, non infimæ authori-tatis uiros, misit, qui & Hetruscos in perniciem Pi-sanorum conspirantes, & Genuenses ac Venetos de uita & sanguine inter se certantes, ab armis di-scedere sub anathematis pœna cogerent. Aderant & oratores Caroli Siculorum regis, cuius etiam authoritate rem magis ex sententia conficí[?] posse sperabat. Fecere mandata Hetrusci, maximè ue-rò Florentini: quos ob eam rem Pontifex à Grego-rij prædecessoris interdicto absoluit. Genuenses au-tem & Veneti, quorum odia magis inoleuerant, se se inuicem mutuis cladibus conficiebant: quos ta-men Innocentius in suam traxisset sententiam, si ei diutius uixisse licuisset, adeò ad rem illam animā-tus erat. Moriebatur autem secundo die post sex mensēs meses fui Pōtificatus, eo anno quo Gregorius prædictus, in Lateranensi basilica terræ commendatus est. Hic licet multa facere proposuisset, inquit Carsulanus, morte præuentus tamen, nil nobile fecit. Presbyteris secularibus (ut narrat Platina) non parum displicuit hic Pontifex, quod Viterbii post lites inter illos & Dominicanos, super Clementis quarti sepultura, corpus eius sepeliendum Dominicanis tandem adiudicauerit.
units.tr: Innocent the Fifth, a Burgundian by birth and a Dominican by profession, was previously called Peter of Tarentaise. He was elected at Arezzo by the cardinals while the old quarrel was still going on, and he was the first of the locusts, or hungry little friars, to reach the papacy. After he had governed his order in France, Gregory, as has been said, enrolled him among the pillars of the Roman Church, for his crafty and arrogant character was known. Gregory was then archbishop of Lyons, and he made him bishop of Ostia and chief penitentiary. The locusts thus had the power, Rev. 9, to make Abaddon their king over themselves, since he was bishop of Ostia. Before his papacy he had been made a cardinal, and his office was to consecrate the pope above the others. Bonaventure the Franciscan was cardinal bishop of Albano. Peter, or Innocent, once elected pope, went to Rome shortly afterwards and was crowned in the temple of St Peter. He at once turned his mind, instead of living in pleasant ease, to the pacification of Italy. He therefore sent legates, men of no small authority, who were to compel the Tuscans, who were conspiring to the ruin of the Pisans, and the Genoese and Venetians, who were fighting one another to the death, to lay down their arms under pain of anathema. Envoys of Charles, king of Sicily, were also present, and he hoped the matter could be settled more to his liking by Charles's authority. The Tuscans complied with the orders, above all the Florentines, and the pope absolved them from the interdict of his predecessor Gregory on this account. The Genoese and Venetians, however, whose hatreds had grown stronger, went on destroying each other with mutual disasters. Innocent would still have brought them round to his opinion, had he been allowed to live longer, so eager was he for that business. He died, however, on the second day after six months of his pontificate, in the same year in which Gregory, mentioned above, was committed to the earth in the Lateran basilica. Although he had proposed to do many things, says Carsulanus, he was forestalled by death and did nothing noble. The secular priests (as Platina relates) were not a little displeased with this pope, because at Viterbo, after disputes between them and the Dominicans over the burial of Clement the Fourth, he finally awarded the body to be buried by the Dominicans.
127. Hadrian the Fifth.

units.la: HAdrianus quintus, patria Genuensis, è Fliscâ familia ortus, Othobonus antea uocatus, Romæ post Innocentium, in atrio Lateranensi Pontifex creabatur. Fuit hic Innocentii quarti olim nepos (nescio num filius) diuiq; Hadriani diaconus Cardinalis ab eodem ordinatus, & in Angliam legatus, pro colligendis pecuniis cum summa potestate missus. Sed dum controuersias inter regem & barones sedare laboraret, quo quietius res suas ageret, à ciuibus Londinensibus in carcerem est coniectus, demumque liberatus. Anno Domini 1266 magna episcoporum & sacerdotum frequentia, Nor-thamptonæ unū, & Londini alterum concilium celebrauit: ubi posteaquam res, quæ ad Papismu[?] pertinebant, ad statum sibi placentè perduxisset: leges tulit, quibus Anglia longis in posterū temporibus ad papismum utebatur. Denunciauitq; impios ef-se episcopos omnes, qui principum partes contra regem Henricum tertium, temere secuti fuissent, quos ipse tamen muneribus partim absoluit, par-tim Romanum adire Pontificem coegit. Creatus i-taq; pontifex, Viterbium statim profiscebatur, Rodulphumq; Imperatorem ad comminuendā Ca-roli Siciliæ regis potentiam (is ille est, quem con-tra fas iusq; prius euexerant) qui tum Romæ om-nia pro arbitrio agebat, in Italiam uocauit. Verū Rodulphus Bohemico bello implicitus, Hadriani desiderijs satis facere non potuit. Carolus autē ad declinandam inuidiam intentus, omnem uim belli in Achaiam transtulit, uiam sibi ad imperium Con-stantinopolitanum facturus. Hadriano, inquit Pla-tina, in animo fuerat, & ditionem ecclesiæ tutio-rem ab oppressoribus reddere, & constitutionem Gregorii prædecessoris, de restrictione Cardinali-um in eligendo Pontifice, in aliam redigere formā. Sed eius conatibus & animi magnitudini mors ob-stitit. Quid, inquit Vuicelius, faceret Papa quadra-ginta dierum? Viterbij enim decessit anno Domini 1276. ante suæ consecrationis munus, & in Fran-ciscanorum cœnobio sepulturam solennem accepit, quadragesimo die sui Pontificatus, uacabatq; sedes illa 28. diebus.
units.tr: Hadrian the Fifth, a Genoese by birth, sprang from the Fieschi family, and was formerly called Ottobuono. He was created pope after Innocent at Rome, in the atrium of the Lateran. He was once the nephew (I do not know whether he was a son) of Innocent the Fourth, and for a long time a deacon cardinal, ordained by the same pope, and sent to England as legate with the fullest powers to collect money. But while he was labouring to settle the disputes between the king and the barons, the citizens of London threw him into prison, and he was released only later. In the year of the Lord 1266 he held a great gathering of bishops and priests, one council at Northampton and another at London. There, after he had brought matters touching on papism to a state that pleased him, he passed laws by which England for a long time afterwards was governed by papism. He also declared that all those bishops were wicked who had rashly followed the side of the princes against King Henry the Third; some of these he absolved with gifts, and others he compelled to go to the Roman pontiff. Having thus been made pope, he at once set out for Viterbo, and summoned Rudolf the emperor into Italy to curb the power of Charles, king of Sicily (the very man whom they had earlier raised up contrary to right and law), who then ruled everything at Rome as he pleased. But Rudolf, entangled in the Bohemian war, could not satisfy Hadrian's wishes. Charles, intent on avoiding odium, turned all the force of his war to Achaea, intending to make a way for himself to the empire of Constantinople. Hadrian, says Platina, had in mind both to free the Church's territory more securely from its oppressors and to change the constitution of his predecessor Gregory concerning the restriction of cardinals in electing a pope into another form. But his efforts and greatness of spirit were thwarted by death. "What," says Wicelius, "could a pope of forty days do?" For he died at Viterbo in the year of the Lord 1276, before the ceremony of his consecration, and received a solemn burial in the Franciscan monastery on the fortieth day of his pontificate; that see then stood vacant for twenty-eight days.
128. John the Twenty-second.

units.la: Ioannes vicesimus secundus, natione Lusitanus, patria Ulixponensis, professione medicus, Petrus Portugalis antea dictus, ex Cardinale et episcopo Tusculano Pontifex creabatur. Hic etsi doctissimus haberetur, ignoratione tamen rerum gerendarum, et morum inaequalitate (sic habet Platina) plus detrimenti quàm honoris et emolumenti, Pontificatui attulit. Multa enim stoliditatem et levitatem prae se ferentia egit, in hoc uno tantum commendatione dignus, quod adolescentes litterarum studiosos, inopes maximè, beneficijs ecclesiasticis et pecunia iuvit. Vexabant tunc Veneti Anconitanos, quòd in Dalmatia mercaturam exercerent, nullo persoluto Venetis portorio: neq; eos (ut par erat) vectigales ecclesiae, Pontifex ipse tuebatur: in verbis tantummodo promptus, in rebus agendis timidi et infracti animi. Anconitani autem Pontificis auxilio destituti, seipsos colligen-tes, eruptione facta, Venetos urbem obsidentes, magno illato incommodo, propellebant. Usus tamen consilio Ioannis Caietani, cuius nutu tum omnia gerebantur, quod ipsius auxilio et suffragijs pontifex creatus esset, legatos tum ad Michaelem Palaeologum, tum ad reges occidentales misit, qui suo nomine cohortarentur, ut pace inter se iinita, armis in Saracenos & hostes Christiani nomĩs minus parārent. Quod nisi fecisset Palæologus, & promissum seruaret unionem, Carolo Siciliæ regi imperium Ioannis assignaret. Pollicebatur, & ex stella præsago ebat sibi longam vitam homo stolidus, & diu se victurum omnibus prædicabat: quippe cuius vita & mores omnibus patebant, adeoque erat inuerecundi & socordiæ ingenii. Sed ecce, dum hanc stultitiam coram suis iactaret, camera quaedam nova (aulam luxoriam Valerius vocat, stellatum preciosum thalamum) quam in palatio Viterbiensi ad delicias extruxerat, post quartum diem anno Domini 1277. subito corruit. Atque inter ligna & lapides soluti inuentus, septimo die post ruinam, & Pontifi-catus sui mense octauo, mi- serè interiit, in minori templo sepultus. Siceli prae-sagij uanitatem nunquam expertus: uacauit sedes per contentionem sex mensibus. Scripsit de problematibus quaedam, Aristotelem imitatus: Canones medicinæ, Thesaurum pauperum, & Epistolas.
units.tr: John the Twenty-second, a Lusitanian by nation, a native of Lisbon, a physician by profession, previously called Peter of Portugal, was created pope from being cardinal and bishop of Tusculum. Although he was thought very learned, his ignorance of affairs and the inconsistency of his conduct (so Platina says) brought more harm than honour and advantage to the papacy. For he did many things that showed foolishness and levity; he deserved praise in this one respect only, that he helped young men devoted to letters, especially the very poor, with church benefices and money. At that time the Venetians were harassing the Ancona men, because they carried on trade in Dalmatia without paying the Venetian tolls; and the pope himself, as was fitting, did not protect them as tributaries of the Church. He was ready only with words, and in carrying things out he was timid and of broken spirit. The Ancona men, however, deprived of papal help, gathered themselves together, made a sally, and drove back the Venetians who were besieging the city, inflicting heavy loss. Yet John, relying on the counsel of John Caietanus, by whose nod everything was then managed, and because he had been made pope through his help and votes, sent legates both to Michael Palaeologus and to the western kings, who were to exhort them in his name to make peace among themselves and to prepare less for arms against the Saracens and the enemies of the Christian name. Unless Palaeologus did this and kept his promised union, he would assign the empire to Charles, king of Sicily. He promised this, and as a fool he foretold from the stars that he would have a long life, and he proclaimed to everyone that he would live long; indeed his life and morals were open to all, so shameless and dull was his nature. But behold, while he was boasting of this folly before his people, a new chamber (Valerius calls it a luxurious hall, a starred and precious bedchamber), which he had built for his pleasures in the palace at Viterbo, suddenly collapsed four days later, in the year of the Lord 1277. He was found crushed between the timbers and stones, and seven days after the fall, in the eighth month of his pontificate, he miserably perished, and was buried in the lesser temple. He never experienced the falsehood of the Sicilian prophecy; the see stood vacant for six months through contention. He wrote some things on problems, imitating Aristotle, the Canons of Medicine, the Treasure of the Poor, and Letters.
129 NICHOLAS THE THIRD.

units.la: Nicolaus tertius, patria Romanus, de gente Ursina, Ioannes Caietanus, ante appellatus, protractus in sex menses electione, non sine magno puratorum patrum litibus, Papalem sedem occupabat. pabit.[?] Horum concluui, senator, Siciliae rex Caroli praefuit, qui admodum infestabat[?], ut unus aliquis ex Gallica natione eligeretur. Nicolaus ergo, mita Pontificatu, Caroli potentiam comminuturus: Hetruria vicariatum ei abstulit, Italiamq; bellicis tumultibus implevit. Et ut suis consuleret commodus, Petro Arragonum regi persuadebat (uetus ars pōtificum) ut Siciliae regnum repeteret, dicens: Hoc hereditario iure Constantiae uxoris suae ad se pertinere. Quod consilium Petro admodum placuit. Sed quosnam fructus huius sanctissimi patris consilium hoc peperit? Petrus, magna instructa classe, Sardiniam petiit, ibi q; expectabat, ut in Sicilia motus orirentur. Nam Siculi, contra Carolum et Gallos coniuratione facta, diem dederunt, ut cum primum vesperi campana audiretur, Galli ab q; ullo sexus discrimine caederentur. Quae in re adeo situm est, ut etiam mulieres praegnantes casu fuerint. At facinus hoc perhorrendum, non sub Nicolao, sed sub Martino quarto, cum successore, perpetratum est. Nicolaus praeterea, senatoriam urbis Romanae dignitatem, quam Clemens quartus praedicto regi Carolo dederat, ad se transtulit: perpetuoq; edicto vetuit, ne in posterum quis aut rex aut princeps, magistratum ipsum petere, aut obire, auderet. Huius perfidia factum est, ut Flaminia tota cum ipsa Bononia, & Rauennæ exarchatus, quæ Imperatoribus diu suberat,in Rom. synagoge potestatem redactæ sint.Sed & senatorum munus (inquit Stella) quod principibus & regibus eccle-sia demandare consueuerat,ipse solus obiuit.
units.tr: Nicholas the Third, a Roman by birth, of the Orsini family, formerly called John Caetani, was elected after a delay of six months, not without great quarrels among the cardinals, and occupied the Papal see. Charles, king of Sicily, who had been senator, was very hostile to this and wanted some one man of the French nation to be elected. Nicholas therefore, as soon as he took up the Pontificate, set out to curb Charles's power. He took away from him the vicariate of Tuscany and filled Italy with the tumults of war. And to look after his own interests conveniently, he urged Peter, king of Aragon (an old trick of the popes), to reclaim the kingdom of Sicily, saying that it belonged to him by hereditary right through his wife Constance. This counsel pleased Peter greatly. But what fruit did this most holy father's counsel bear? Peter, with a large fleet made ready, made for Sardinia, and there waited for disturbances to arise in Sicily. For the Sicilians, having formed a conspiracy against Charles and the French, set a day, so that as soon as the evening bell was heard, the French should be slaughtered without regard to age or sex. In this affair it went so far that even pregnant women were killed by chance. But this abominable deed was carried out not under Nicholas but under Martin the Fourth, his successor. Moreover, Nicholas transferred to himself the senatorial dignity of the city of Rome, which Clement the Fourth had given to the said king Charles, and by a perpetual edict he forbade that anyone, whether king or prince, should dare to seek or hold that magistracy. By his treachery it came about that all Flaminia, together with Bologna itself, and the exarchate of Ravenna, which had long been subject to the Emperors, were brought under the power of the Roman synagogue. But also the office of senator (says Stella), which the Church had customarily entrusted to princes and kings, he alone held.

units.la: Aedificijs nouis Romam ornauit: & intercetera apud S. Petrum æde s percommodas ac lepo-rarium muris altissimis cinxit:in quo & ipse (Papale officium)sæpius uenationes occupabat: basilicas Petri ac Pauli,uetustate collabentes,restitu-it: & quasdam ædes in Laterano iam diu inchoa-tas, ipse perfecit. Condidit à fundamentis Sanctæ sanctorum, & Apostolorum capita argentea cap-sulis imposuit.In Missis hypocrita lachrymas fidi-& adeò Franciscanis suit,ut & Decretali episto-la,quædam ipsius factionis ambigua declarauerit. Multa ad cleri(non Christiani populi) utilitatem constituit: & ex Mendicantium ordinum fratrum lis,Cardinales plures ad Abadonis regni commo-dum secit.Notarios ac tabelliones quosdam à se-iecit:et ne magistratus ultra annum gererentur lo in loco,sub anathemate præcepit. Reprehende-batur à multis,quòd Bertholdum nepotem (spuri-um sortasis)Romandiolæ constituisset comitem:et Latinum Cardinalem,Dominicanum, nepotem sa-lium,aut nothum potius,legatum in Hetruriam mi-sset. fisset. Suos enim à Platina, Stella, & alijs nimium amasse dicitur, ita ut ea quae aliunde rapuisset, illis sine lege condonaret. Nam quibusdam nobilibus Romanis castella ui abstulit, ac suis dono dedit, & inter alia Surianum castrum. Gibellinus, fa-[?]tiofis[?] hominibus ad suas tyrannides defendendas, ubiq; restitutis, Florentiae & alibi pro suo libito magistratus posuit, & alia incommoda gessit. Proposuerat quoq; hic Pontifex, duos reges ex domo Vrsina, unum in Hetruria, & alterum in Lombardia creare. Sed dum haec perficere cogitasset, in Sutrio oppido existens, apoplexia correptus, anno Domini 1281, & quarto sui Pontificatus anno, subita morte sine loquela expirauit: cum tamen ex bona complexione, multo diutius uicturus crederetur. Quam mortem praedixisse quendam ferunt, per exundationem maximam Tiberis, quae tunc fe-bat. Hunc dicunt ex concubina filium generasse, crinibus & unguibus similem ursae. Vide Ioannem Noviomagum, in illustrationibus Bedae.
units.tr: He adorned Rome with new buildings, and among other things he surrounded the very convenient houses beside St Peter's with a game park and very high walls, in which he himself, though a Papal officer, often occupied himself with hunting. He restored the basilicas of Peter and Paul, which were collapsing with age, and he himself completed certain buildings in the Lateran that had been begun long before. He built the Holy of Holies from the foundations and placed the silver heads of the apostles in reliquaries. In Masses he shed hypocritical tears, and he so favoured the Franciscans that in a decretal letter he declared certain ambiguous points of their faction. He made many regulations for the benefit of the clergy (not of the Christian people). And from the quarrels of the mendicant friars he made several cardinals, for the advantage of the kingdom of Abadon. He dismissed certain notaries and notaries public, and under pain of anathema he ordered that magistracies should not be held in the same place beyond a year. He was criticised by many because he had appointed his nephew Berthold (a bastard, as is said of him) count of Romagna, and had sent Latinus, a Dominican cardinal and nephew of his, or rather a bastard, as legate into Tuscany. For he is said to have loved his own people excessively, by Platina, Stella and others, so that he gave them without any law whatever he had seized elsewhere. For he took castles from some Roman nobles by force and gave them as gifts to his own people, and among other things the castle of Suriano. He restored the Ghibellines, factious men, wherever they were, to defend their tyrannies, and he installed magistrates at Florence and elsewhere at his own pleasure, and committed other mischiefs. This Pontiff had also proposed to create two kings from the house of Orsini, one in Tuscany and the other in Lombardy. But while he was thinking of carrying this out, staying in the town of Sutri, he was seized by apoplexy, and in the year of the Lord 1281, in the fourth year of his Pontificate, he expired by a sudden death without speech, although, on account of his good constitution, he was thought likely to live much longer. They say that someone had foretold this death from the very great flood of the Tiber that was then occurring. They say he begot a son by a concubine, who was like a bear in hair and nails. See John Noviomagus, in the illustrations to Bede.
130. MARTIN THE FOURTH.

units.la: Martinus quartus, natione Gallicus, patria Turonensis, Simon antea vocatus, & S. Ceciliae Cardinalis presbyter in Pontificem à Gallicis Cardinalibus, qui numero tunc superiores erant, electus, Viterbij coronari noluit, quòd illi civitati ob impetum in patres factum[?], sacris interdictum esse putaret. Viterbienses enim, Italiæ factionis primarium Ricardum Hannibalem secuti, & conclave ingressi, Cardinales capiebant, atq; in vincula coniiciebant, contemptis ac præst gatu[?] Ursinis. Ut bem[?] itaq; veterem petens Martinus, quod Oruietum vocant, eo loci omnia solennia peregit: & officio Cardinales eodem die creauit, ut sortior ad pugnam fieret. Regem vero Carolum ad se venien-tem, non modo perbenignè suscepit: verum & eidem senatoriam dignitatem, quæ fuerat à Nicolao priuatus, restituit. Quod non ita ab omnibus probatum fuit, cum ea res excitatura videretur magnas in urbe seditiones, reuersis iam Ursinis, ac pulsis Hannibalibus. Ursinis enim ob odium in Nicolaum tertium conceptum, Carolus mirificè adversabatur: Martinus tamen res suas cautelis curaturus, Matthæum de Aquasporta Franciscanum, ex gente Ursina cardinalem & episcopum Portuensem plurimum coluit. Petrum Arragonum regem, classem contra Carolum in Siciliam parantem, anathemate Martinus notauit, regnum eius in prædam id occupare volenti exposuit: subditos ab eius iuramento absoluit bonorum ecclesiasticorum usurpatorem dicebat, & cruce signatos in illum concitabat. Petrus tamen hæc nihil curans, Siciliæ regnum tuuante Palæologo obtinuit. Siculi etiam Gallorum superbias ac libidines amplius ferre nequeun-tes, suadente Ioanne Prochita, in Carolum coniurationem inierunt: & omnes simul, nullo habito sexus discrimine, pulsatis campanis occiderunt. Praeterea Martinus inter acta Papalia Romanis concessit, ut ex nobilibus duos senatores eligerent: & Palæologum Græcorum Imperatorem excommunicauit. Bellum contra Foroliuiános[?] gessit, et Mendicantes fraterculos (locusta Apocalypticas[?], quas sciebat esse similes equis ad prælium paratis) pro muniendo Abadonis regno, privilegiis fouit. Et cum solitam refectionem cum suis Capellanis (teste Carsulano) tandem sumpsisset, anno Domini 1285 arripuit eum infirmitas occulta: de qua postquam dixisset, se nimium pati, fato succubuit: licet mendici nullum mortis indicium in ipso reperissent: Perusiq; sepultus fuit. Hunc scribunt authores, quos sequitur doctissimus vir Thomas Coprum[?] in Chronicorum Epitome, primo sui pontificatus an-no Nicolai prædecessoris concubinam in suam familiarem accepisse. Sed ne similis illi casus accideret, ut futura proles fiturfo[?] similis, præcepit ursos omnes, in palatio per Vrsinæ factionis Pontificem olim depictos, auferri, vel deleri: persuasus, quòd firmæ in ipso coitu à fœminis concep-ptæ, in productis infantibus expressæ non raro ma-neant. Peritus ea in arte, ut apparet, hic Pontifex erat. Sed non animaduertit bestia, portendere hoc monstrum, qualis sit ex ciusmodi factis, Papalis cœ-libatus ac sanctitas.
units.tr: Martin the Fourth, a Frenchman by nation, a native of Tours, formerly called Simon, and cardinal priest of St Cecilia, was elected Pontiff by the French cardinals, who were then the more numerous. He was unwilling to be crowned at Viterbo, because he thought that city had been placed under an interdict for its attack on the fathers. For the Viterbans, following Richard Annibaldi, the leader of the Italian faction, entered the conclave, seized the cardinals, and cast them into chains, showing contempt for the Orsini. So Martin, seeking the old town, which they call Orvieto, there performed all the solemn rites, and on the same day he created cardinals so that the contest might be more fair. But he received king Charles, who came to him, not only very kindly, but also restored to him the senatorial dignity, which Nicholas had taken away. This was not approved by everyone, since the matter seemed likely to stir up great seditions in the city, now that the Orsini had returned and the Annibaldi had been driven out. For Charles strongly opposed the Orsini on account of the hatred conceived against Nicholas the Third. Yet Martin, intending to look after his affairs with caution, greatly honoured Matthew of Acquasparta, a Franciscan of the Orsini family, cardinal and bishop of Porto. Martin branded Peter, king of Aragon, who was preparing a fleet against Charles in Sicily, with anathema, and exposed his kingdom to plunder by anyone who wished to seize it; he absolved his subjects from their oath to him, called him a usurper of ecclesiastical goods, and stirred up those marked with the cross against him. Peter, however, caring nothing for these things, obtained the kingdom of Sicily with the help of Palaeologus. The Sicilians too, no longer able to bear the arrogance and lusts of the French, at the urging of John Procida, entered into a conspiracy against Charles, and all together, without regard to sex, at the ringing of the bells, they killed them. Besides, Martin granted to the Romans, among the Papal acts, that they might choose two senators from the nobles. And he excommunicated Palaeologus, emperor of the Greeks. He waged war against the people of Forlì, and he fostered the mendicant little friars (the apocalyptic locusts, which he knew to be like horses prepared for battle) with privileges, to fortify the kingdom of Abadon. And when he had at last taken his usual meal with his chaplains (according to Carsulanus), in the year of the Lord 1285 a hidden sickness seized him; and after he had said that he was suffering too much, he succumbed to fate, although the physicians found no sign of death in him. He was buried at Perugia. Authors whom the most learned man Thomas Coprus follows in his Epitome of the Chronicles write that in the first year of his Pontificate he had taken into his household the concubine of his predecessor Nicholas. But lest a similar accident should happen, so that the offspring that was to be born might resemble him, he ordered all the bears that had been painted long ago in the palace by a Pontiff of the Orsini faction to be removed or destroyed, being persuaded that the marks conceived by women in the very act of coition often remain visible in the infants when they are born. This Pontiff was evidently skilled in that art. But the beast did not notice that this monster portends what sort of thing Papal celibacy and holiness are, judging from such deeds.
131. HONORIUS quartus.

units.la: HOnorius quartus, patria Romanus, è gente Sa-bella, familia nobilissima, Iacobus antea nuncu-patus, ac diaconus Cardinalis, Perusij finita Car-dinalium electione Papatum sublimiter init, fra-trem ille habuit Pandulphum quendam, proba-tum uirum, senatoriam dignitatem in urbe tum ge-rentem: qui in sicarios, fures, & parricidas seuer-iter animaduertebat. Habitauit Honorius in mon-te Auentino, ubi nouas ædes extruxit, & alios ad id faciendum multos incitauit. Petrum Aragoniæ regem, qui Siciliæ regnum contra Carolum tunc occupauerat, anathemate percussit: & Martini prædecessoris interdicta aduersus illum confirma-uit, quòd Papali auaritiæ eam non relinqueret re-ligionem. Nec non & in Guidonem Feltronum, Fla-minæ urbes occupantem, terribile bellum mouit: atq; eo statim superato, Romanæ ditioni prouin-ciam illam totam præter ius fasq; per tyrannidem adiecit. Et ne pro Abadonis regno nihil uideretur scisse, Augustinianorum fraterculorum sectam, Parisijs non receptam, sed a multis impugnatam, quòd in Lateranensi concilio non satis esset pro-bata, roborauit, confirmauit, ac multis priuilegijs communiuit: Carmelitanis quoq; fraterculis, sepositis uestibus stragulatis seu pallijs barratus, alium assignauit amictum, decreuitq; dici uirginis fratres. Quibus gestis, non diu superuixit, sed anno Domini 1288. & secundo sui Pontificatus anno moriens, ex S. Sabina in Aucentino monte, ad D. Petri basilicam delatus, magna cum pompa sepe-liebatur. Decem mensibus uacabat sedes, ob aegri-tudines & terraemotus. Podagra ac chiragra ue-hementer hic Pontifex interdum laborabat, ita ut, instrumentis quibusdam (ut Platina scribit) ad id apte fabrefactis, Missas sacrificare necesse esset. Sub eo Græci, relicto Papismo, solitam fidem se-[?]abantur.
units.tr: Honorius IV, a Roman by birth, of the noble Savelli family and a most distinguished house, previously called James, and a deacon cardinal, was raised to the papacy at Perugia once the election of the cardinals was complete. He had a brother named Pandulf, an upright man who then held the dignity of senator in the city. Pandulf punished assassins, thieves and parricides severely. Honorius lived on the Aventine hill, where he built new houses and urged many others to do the same. He struck Peter, king of Aragon, who had then seized the kingdom of Sicily from Charles, with anathema, and confirmed the interdicts that his predecessor Martin had laid against him, because he would not leave that religion to Papal greed. He also waged a terrible war against Guido Feltrano, who was occupying the cities of Flaminia. When Guido was quickly defeated, Honorius added that whole province to the Roman dominion by tyranny, against right and law. And lest he seem to have done nothing for the kingdom of Abaddon, he confirmed and strengthened the sect of the Augustinian friars, which had not been received at Paris and was much opposed, because it had not been sufficiently approved at the Lateran council, and he furnished it with many privileges. He also took from the Carmelite friars their striped robes or mantles, assigned them another garment, and decreed that they be called brothers of the Virgin. After these deeds he did not live long. He died in the year of the Lord 1288, in the second year of his pontificate, and was carried from St Sabina on the Aventine hill to the basilica of St Peter and buried with great pomp. The see was vacant for ten months, owing to illnesses and earthquakes. This pope was sometimes severely afflicted with gout in his feet and hands, so that, with certain instruments (as Platina writes) made specially for the purpose, he had to offer Masses. Under him the Greeks, abandoning Papism, followed their customary faith.
132. NICOLAUS quartus.

units.la: Nicolaus quartus, patria Picenus, professione Fran-ciscanus, ex urbe Aesculana, Hieronymus antea dictus, & ad S. Sabinam presbyter Cardinalis, post decimum mensem Honorio prædicto Papa suc-cessit, cum iterum Cardinales non unum sentirent. Apud S. Mariam maiorem, seu ad præsepe Christi, stipare uirgini superstitiose deuotus habitauit, cu[?] ius apsidem ædificijs & picturis exornauit. Ex [?] ni locustarum genere, seu monachorum fact[?] one, ad Abadonis usum Cardinales creauit, ut essent e-quis similes in prelium paratis, & haberent leo-num dentes ac caudas tanquam scorpionum, qui-bus nocerent: Apoc.9. Nam omnes (inquit Platina) pariter amabat, nec plus se debere affinibus & co-gnatis, quam eorum cuilibet arbitrabatur. Sed quæ erga Dei populum amorem gesserit, ut Euangelij pabulo aut Dei promissionibus nutrirentur, certè non lego. Petrum Columnam (inquit Funccius) in patrum collegium adeptus, caeterum nihil egit memoria dignum. Anteriorem nihilominus, posseriorem[?]que Lateranensis basilicae partem restituit, ac uermiculato opere poliuit. Pro tuenda Ptolemaide Palestinae urbe, milites mult[?]s, sed are a-lieнo conducto[?]s, misit: & Ludouicum Tolosanum Minoritam, in papisticos sanctos retulit. Augusti-niani fraterculis immunitatem concessit, & Car-melius (quis non credat res esse magnas?) albi pal-lij sumptuosem per bellam plumbeam ratam fecit. Den[?]q; cum urbem Romanam cum libus dissidijs a-gitari, & incendia caedesq; plurimas perferre cer-neret (nulla arim irum habita ratione) ar imi tæ-dio, quod male sibi omnia ad sudum Pontificium succederent, anno Domini 1291[?]. in sua habitatione ad ad Mariam maiorem ex hac uita migrauit, eoque loci sepelitur. Quo mortuo, Cardinales Perusium sunt profecti, quo ei liberum Pontificem eligere liceret. Duobus annis tamen, & tribus mensibus, dissidijs intestinis adeo laborabant (mostrum ual de horrendum) ut in ea electione concordare nunquam potuerint.
units.tr: Nicholas IV, a Piceni by birth, a Franciscan by profession, from the city of Ascoli, previously called Jerome, and a presbyter cardinal of St Sabina, succeeded the aforesaid Pope Honorius ten months later, when the cardinals again disagreed. He lived at St Mary Major, or at the crib of Christ, devoutly and superstitiously devoted to the Virgin, and he adorned its apse with buildings and paintings. From a kind of locusts, or from the making of monks, he created cardinals for the use of Abaddon, so that they would be like horses prepared for battle, and would have lions' teeth and tails like scorpions, with which to harm people (Rev. 9). For (as Platina says) he loved them all equally, and thought he owed no more to his relatives and kinsmen than to any one of the others. But what love he showed towards the people of God, that they might be nourished on the food of the gospel or the promises of God, I certainly do not read. He obtained Peter Colonna (as Funccius says) into the college of the fathers, but otherwise he accomplished nothing worth remembering. Nevertheless he restored the front and back parts of the Lateran basilica and polished them with mosaic work. To defend the city of Ptolemais in Palestine he sent many soldiers, but hired from foreign lands; and he counted Louis of Toulouse, a Minorite, among the Papistical saints. He granted immunity to the Augustinian friars, and (who would believe it was a great matter?) he confirmed by a leaden bull the costly white mantle of the Carmelites. Finally, when he saw the city of Rome being troubled by civil strife and suffering fires and very many slaughters (no regard being had for anyone), weary of soul because everything went badly for him in his Papal office, he died in the year of the Lord 1291 in his residence at St Mary Major, and is buried there. After his death the cardinals went to Perugia, so that they might be free to choose a pope. Yet for two years and three months they were so troubled by internal dissensions (a horrible monstrous thing) that they could never agree in that election.
133. COELESTINUS quintus.

units.la: Coelestinus quintus, patria Efernienfis, prope Sulmonem, Ouidij natalem locum, natus, profes-sione anachoreta, & Petrus Moronem antea uocatus, transfacta biennali Cardinalium ambitione, Caroli secundi regis Neapolitani & Latini Cardinalis fauore Pontifex declarabatur. Qui post su-am [?] creationem Aquilam profectus, eo statim Cardinales omnes ad se uocabat: & 12 nouos creauit, de quorum numero duo Eremitae erat. Eius autem coronationi interfuisse ducenta hominum millia, Ptolemaeus Lucensis scribit. In primo consistorio (inquit Christianus Massaeus) dum stricte reformare uellet Romanam ecclesiam, ut alijs esset in exemplum clerus illius, tantum incurrit indignationis, ut delirum ac fatuum susurrarent. Quorum unus non re, sed nomine Benedictus appellatus, apposuit quendam cubiculo Papae, qui facto foramine per fistulam multis nobilibus insonabat, ac si esseт angelus quispiám: Cœlestine Cœlestine, ce-de, negotium enim supra vires est. Perdiu quoq; sua debant quidam, ut cedendo saluti suæ consuleret. Intellexit ista rex Carolus: vocauit ad se Pontifi-cem, & quàm maximè potuit, obsecrabat, ne dignitatem cœlitus datam abijceret. At ille: Faciam, inquit, quod Deus voluerit. Reuersus à Neapoli, cū requiem non haberet, abdicauit se magistratu, in vigilia S. Luciæ, & ad eremum ire festinabat. Tantum Massæus. Prius tamen omnium consensu con-stitutionem fecit, licere Pontifici abdicare se ma-gistratu. Quam quidem constitutionem Bonifacius octauus, eius successor, homo callidus, postea con-firmauit, ac sexto Decretalium addidit. Cæterum, successor eius Bonifacius ille, metuens, ne populus se contempto, illum sequeretur, in arctissima cu-stodia eum clausit usq; ad mortem. Defunctus est igitur anno Domini 1295. in carcere, decimo nono die Maij, post annum unum & quinq; menses initi Pontificatus. Ab eo processit Cœlestinorum mona-chorum secta.
units.tr: Celestine V, a native of Isernia, near Sulmona, the birthplace of Ovid, and by profession a hermit, previously called Peter of Morrone, was declared pope with the favour of Charles II, king of Naples, and a Latin cardinal, after a two-year ambition among the cardinals. After his creation he set out for Aquila, and at once summoned all the cardinals to himself, and created twelve new ones, two of whom were hermits. Ptolemy of Lucca writes that two hundred thousand people were present at his coronation. At his first consistory (says Christian Massaeus), when he wished to reform the Roman Church strictly, so that its clergy might be an example to others, he incurred such great indignation that they whispered that he was mad and foolish. One of them, called Benedict not in reality but in name, placed someone in the pope's bedchamber, who, having made a hole through a pipe, boomed out to many nobles as if he were some angel: "Celestine, Celestine, give way, for the business is beyond your strength." For a long time some people kept saying such things, that he might consult his own welfare by yielding. King Charles heard of these things. He summoned the pope to himself and begged him as earnestly as he could not to cast away the dignity given him from heaven. But he said: "I shall do what God wills." On returning from Naples, since he had no rest, he resigned his office on the eve of St Lucy and hastened to go into the wilderness. So far Massaeus. However, first, with the consent of all, he made a constitution that it was lawful for a pope to resign his office. Boniface VIII, his successor, a crafty man, afterwards confirmed that constitution and added it to the Sixth Book of the Decretals. But Boniface, fearing that the people, if he were despised, would follow Celestine, shut him up in the closest custody until his death. Therefore he died in the year of the Lord 1295, in prison, on the nineteenth day of May, after one year and five months of his pontificate. From him came the sect of the Celestine monks.
134. BONIFACE VIII.

units.la: Bonifacius octauus, natione Campanus, patria Anagninus, Benedictus Caietanus antea nun-cupatus, Cœlestini prædecessoris consiliarius sum-mus, Neapoli mira proditione in eius est suffe-ctus[?]. stus locum. Qui dum esset S. Martini in monti-bus presbyter Cardinalis, adeo Pontificiam hanc dignitatem exoptauit, ut nil ambitione & fraude praetermiserit, quod ad eam rem consequendam pertinere arbitraretur. Tantae praeterea arrogan-tiae fuit, ut & omnes fere contemneret. Ambitione enim exaestuans, subornatores quosdam, ut dictum est, immisit, qui noctu demissa uoce, quasi cælitus in cubiculum Cælestini pontificis, alioqui simpli-cis, ei persuaderent, ut Pontificatum deponeret, si saluus fieri uellet. Quod & factum fuit. Bonifacius uero contra ius fasq; fede Pontificia occupata, simplicem uirum, qui Roma exibat, ut solitudinem aliquam petens, ibi uitam suam degeret, captum perpetuo carceri mancipauit. Dicebatq; (teste Mario) se id facere, non alicuius odij in Cælestinum causa: sed ne authores seditionum Cælestino duce, calamitatem aliquam ecclesiae Romanae inferre possent. Quis Bonifacium istum, teterrimum monstrum, ac hominum cunctorum ingratissimum non appellet? cum simplicem uirum suis artibus delusum, e Pontificatu non solum deie-cerit, sed & illum tanquam facinorosum aliquem perpetuo carceri mancipatum, ante tempus prae animi dolore mori coegerit? Tantam Bonifacius coepit exercere tyrannidem, ut octauus Nero potius dici mererctur. Cardinales quosdam ad je uocabat Bonifacius ille. Sed huius perfidia ac furore perterriti, ad illum accedere non audebant. Schismatici ergo declarabantur. Et non solum beneficijs ac dignitatibus, quae a Pontificibus acceperant, eos priuabat: sed fundus paternus, oppidum, ac bona omnibus eos spoliabat.
units.tr: Boniface VIII, a Campanian by birth, from Anagni, formerly named Benedict Caietanus, was the chief counsellor of his predecessor Celestine. Through a remarkable act of treachery at Naples he was put in Celestine's place. While he was still a cardinal-presbyter of St Martin in the Mountains, he so longed for the papal dignity that he left nothing undone through ambition and fraud that he thought would help him obtain it. He was also so arrogant that he despised almost everyone. Burning with ambition, he sent in certain suborners, as has been said, who at night, in lowered voices, as if from heaven, persuaded the simple Celestine in his bedchamber to give up the papacy if he wished to be saved. And this was done. Boniface then seized the papal see against right and law. He had the simple man, who was leaving Rome intending to seek some solitude and live out his life there, seized and consigned to perpetual imprisonment. He said (according to Marius) that he did this not out of any hatred of Celestine, but so that the authors of sedition might not, with Celestine as their leader, bring some calamity upon the Roman Church. Who would not call this Boniface a most foul monster, the most ungrateful of all men? He had deceived the simple man by his tricks, not only cast him down from the papacy but also, treating him as a criminal, had him consigned to perpetual prison, and forced him to die before his time from grief of mind. Boniface began to exercise such tyranny that he deserved to be called rather an eighth Nero. He summoned certain cardinals to himself, but they, terrified by his treachery and fury, did not dare approach him. They were therefore declared schismatics. He not only stripped them of the benefits and dignities they had received from the popes, but also despoiled them of their paternal estates, towns and all their goods.

units.la: Collectis praeterea copijs, illos una cum Co-lumnensibus, & quotquot Gibellinae factionis ex-tabant, quocunque se conferrebant, infequtebatur [?] loca omnium, ad quae se recipiebant, uastabat ac populabatur.
units.tr: Moreover, after gathering forces, he pursued them together with the Colonna family and all who remained of the Ghibelline faction, wherever they went, and he laid waste and plundered all the places to which they retreated.

units.la: Vnde quidam eorum, nullum locum sibi ab eo tutum uidentes, memoria ac fakus [?] incolebant: quidam ex nobilissimis Italiae familiis, cum litora maris aliquandiu veluti ferae [?] inhabitassent, cum piratis tandem humanitatis expertibus, ex Italia abierunt. Mitius enim se a piratis tractan-dos nouerant, quam a sanctissimo hoc patre Boni-facio, si forte in eius incidissent manus. Tanto odio Gibellinos persecutus est, ut eorum quosdam Genuam concessisse audiens, illuc & ipse se con-tulerit [?]: ut eos omnino deleuerit, eorumq; nomen ex hominum memoria ac orbe terrarum tol-leret. Et quum in die quem illi Cinerum uocant, cineres pro more populo ministraret, archiepi-scopus urbis Porchetus (hunc Gibellinae factionis esse à multis audierat) accessit, ac genibus flexis, aperto capite stabat, ut [?]ineres acciperet. Quem cum Bonifacius intuitus esset, nullam loci, nullam populi qui astabat, nullam religionis ratio-nem habens: ira in archiepiscopum succensus est, ac cineris magnam quantitatem in eius oculos conicit, dicens, Memento homo quia Gibellinus es, & cum G bellinis in cinerem redigerit. Eundemque archiepiscopum dignitate priuauit, licet postea i-terum restituerit.
units.tr: So some of them, seeing no place safe from him, lived in caves and woods. Some of the most noble families of Italy, after living for a while like wild beasts on the seashore, finally left Italy with pirates who had no part in humanity. For they knew they would be treated more gently by the pirates than by that most holy father Boniface, should they chance to fall into his hands. He pursued the Ghibellines with such hatred that, hearing that some of them had withdrawn to Genoa, he went there himself, intending to wipe them out completely and to erase their name from the memory of men and from the world. And when, on the day they call Ash Wednesday, he was distributing ashes to the people as was customary, the archbishop of the city, Porchetus (whom many had heard to be of the Ghibelline faction), came forward, knelt, and stood with his head bare to receive the ashes. Boniface, regarding no place, no people standing by, and no reason of religion, looked at him, flew into a rage against the archbishop, flung a great quantity of ashes into his eyes, saying, "Remember, man, that you are a Ghibelline, and with the Ghibellines you will return to ashes." He also deprived the same archbishop of his dignity, although he later restored him.

units.la: Hic Alberto ducì Austriæ, Imperij confirma-tionem bis terq; petenti, semper negauit. Hic, cum tota Italia sæuissimum bellum, ortis inter Siculos Aragonensibus sæuientes, ac Robertum Calabriæ ducem, strueret: nunquam (etsi à multis ad id hor-taretur) auctoritatem suam pro ineunda pace in-terponere voluit. Sed diuino iudicio factum est, ut hi qui Italiam deferentes, cum piratis fugerant: rursus in Italiam à Deo uberrentur, ac collectis paucis aliquot, qui Bonifacij rabiem fugientes, modo illic delituerant, Anagniæ Pontificem nihil tale metuentem, refractis ualuis caperent, atq; Romam ducerent, ubi triginta quinq; dierum spacio, præ dolore ac rabiei magnitudine de-sperabundus, anno Domini 1304. infælicem a-nimam, innumeris malefactis onustam, emisit.
units.tr: He repeatedly and thrice refused to confirm Albert, Duke of Austria, in the empire, though Albert kept asking. While the whole of Italy was preparing the most savage war, with the Aragonese Sicilians raging and Robert, Duke of Calabria, in arms, Boniface never wished to interpose his authority to secure peace, although many urged him to do so. But by divine judgment it came about that those who had fled from Italy with the pirates were brought back to Italy by God again. Gathering a few who, fleeing Boniface's fury, had lately hidden there, they seized the Pontiff at Anagni, who feared nothing of the kind, by breaking down the doors, and led him to Rome. There, in the space of thirty-five days, despairing from grief and the greatness of his rage, he breathed out his unhappy soul in the year of the Lord 1304, laden with countless wicked deeds.

units.la: Hic ille Pontifex fuit, de quo dictum est vulgo: Intrauit ut vulpes, vixit ut leo, mortuus est ut canis. Ille regna & imperia in sua esse manu arbitratus, utrumque gladium usurpauit, & totius mundi dominum haberi se voluit. Reges terrarum arrogantissimus & improbus, nisi a sua sanctitate (tyrannide) regna accipere vellent, execrandos ac deponendos esse censuit. Francorum regem Philippum excommunicauit, quia extra suum regnum pecunias ferri non permisit: eique atque suis maledixit usque ad quartam generationem, porrectis etiam reliquiis & cruce. Ac Imperatorem Albertum, biennio ante reiectum, non aliter in imperio confirmauit, quam ut Franciam occuparet, Philippo deposito. Alphonsum Aragonum absoluit, & regni Sardiniæ illi certis pactis concessit. Discordias inter Italicas factiones fouit, ac semper alere studuit, et tributa a clero, sine sua concessione principibus dari vetuit.
units.tr: He was the pontiff of whom the common saying is: He entered like a fox, he reigned like a lion, he died like a dog. He believed that kingdoms and empires were in his hand, claimed both swords, and wished to be regarded as lord of the whole world. He was the most arrogant and wicked of the kings of the earth. He judged that unless kings were willing to receive their kingdoms from his holiness (tyranny), they should be cursed and deposed. He excommunicated Philip, King of the Franks, because he did not allow money to be carried out of his kingdom, and cursed him and his people down to the fourth generation, even holding up relics and the cross against them. And he confirmed the Emperor Albert, rejected two years before, in the empire only on the condition that he should seize France by deposing Philip. He absolved Alphonso of Aragon and granted him the kingdom of Sardinia on certain terms. He fostered discord among the Italian factions and always strove to keep it alive, and he forbade that tributes be given to princes from the clergy without his consent.

units.la: Cœli se clavigerum esse in superbia gloriabatur: & a nemine iudicari debere promulgauit, quamuis innumeras ad inferos animas secum duceret, tanquam licite commissurus omnia. Vt bileum Iudaico more primus instituit, & Romam adeuntibus indulgentias plenarias ac peccatorum remissiones sufflauit, ut eo orbis confluat.
units.tr: He boasted in his pride that he was the key-bearer of heaven, and he declared that he ought to be judged by no one, although he would lead countless souls with him to hell, as if he would be permitted to do everything. He was the first to institute the jubilee in the Jewish manner, and he blew up plenary indulgences and remissions of sins for those coming to Rome, so that the world might flock there.

units.la: magnatos & amicas nocturnas ditaret. Basilicam Petri tintinnabulis[?] aereis, quibus nil dulcius auditur, ornauit: eiusq; vectigalia longe adauxit. Mendicantium sectas, Abadon magnus, priuilegijs & immunitatibus mirum in modum adjuvit: ac Fraticellos, qui dicebant Apostolos à clero imitandos, damnauit. Sextum decretalium composuit, et per omnes academias publicari mandauit. Apostolis, Euangelistis, & quatuor ecclesiae doctoribus honores idolatricos duplicauit: atq; Anglorum ecclesiis, excommunicandi populum bis in anno, authoritatem generaliter dedit. Diuum Ludouicum Francorum regem canonizauit: & Hermannum Ferrariensem in sanctos relatum, post triginta annos à sepultura, exhumari comburiq; fecit. Inquisitiones confirmauit, degradationes ordinauit, rationes ampliauit: Cardinales Columnenses & Vrsinos deposuit, reges regnis deiecit, meretrices nutriuit, bastardos ac spurios generauit, & alia portenta Papalia fecit, donec Othomannum Dominus aduersus nos excitaret, quum nullus esset malorum finis.
units.tr: He enriched magnates and nocturnal mistresses. He adorned the basilica of St Peter with bronze bells, than which nothing sweeter is heard, and greatly increased its revenues. Abaddon the Great, he assisted the orders of mendicants in a wonderful way with privileges and immunities. He condemned the Fraticelli, who said that the clergy should imitate the Apostles. He composed the Sixth Book of the Decretals and ordered it to be published in all the universities. He doubled idolatrous honours to the Apostles, the Evangelists and the four doctors of the Church, and he gave the churches of the English general authority to excommunicate the people twice a year. He canonized Louis, the divine King of the Franks. He also had Hermann of Ferrara, who had been raised to the saints after thirty years from his burial, exhumed and burned. He confirmed the inquisitions, ordained degradations, and extended the accounts. He deposed the Colonna and Orsini cardinals, cast kings from their kingdoms, nourished prostitutes, begat bastards and sons born out of wedlock, and performed other Papal monstrosities, until the Lord stirred up the Ottoman against us, since there was no end to evils.

units.la: PETRI CASSIODORI AD ANGLOS EPISTOLA, SUPER EXTREMA ANGLIÆ EXPILATIONE AC SERVITUTE PER PAPAS CIRCA ANNUM DOMINI 1302, UT ROM. TYRANNIDIS IUGUM EXCUTERENT.
