units.tr: PETER CASSIODORUS'S LETTER TO THE ENGLISH, ON ENGLAND'S EXTREME PLUNDERING AND SLAVERY UNDER THE POPES AROUND THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1302, THAT THEY MIGHT SHAKE OFF THE YOKE OF ROMAN TYRANNY.

units.la: Exemplo codice ad sanctum Albani descripta.
units.tr: Copied from an exemplar transcribed at St Albans.

units.la: Ecclesiæ nobili Anglicanæ, in luto et latere ancillatæ, Petrus filius Cassiodori, miles catholicus, pugil Iesu Christi devotus, salutem, et captiuitatis iugum abiicere, et brauium accipere libertatis. Super cathedram Moysi sederunt Scribæ et Pharisæi, etc.
units.tr: To the noble Church of England, enslaved in mud and brick, from Peter son of Cassiodorus, a Catholic knight and devoted fighter of Jesus Christ: greeting, and may you throw off the yoke of captivity and receive the prize of liberty. "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat," etc.

units.la: Sequitur: Cui comparabo te, vel cui assimilabo te Hierusalem filia? cui exæquabo te, uirgo filia Syon? magna enim est tua contritio, velut mare fracta; est sine solatio, tota die mærore fracta.
units.tr: It follows: To what shall I liken you, or to what shall I compare you, daughter Jerusalem? To what shall I equal you, virgin daughter of Zion? For your breach is great like the sea; there is no comfort for you, and you are broken with sorrow all the day.

units.la: Data es in manus eius, de quo non potes surgere absque auxilio subleuantis. Nam scribæ et pharisæi super cathedram Moysi sedentes, principes Romani hostes tibi in capite fixi, sua phylacteria dilatantes, ambientes locupletari tuorum ossium ex medullis, grauia et importabilia in tuis et tuorum ministrorum imponunt humeris onera: et ultra quam decet, te constituunt sub tributo, quæ liberæ fueras ab antiquo. Recedat ab hinc omnis admirationis materia: quia mater tua domina gentium, viduarum more suo subdito desponsata tibi, ipsum in patrem constituit, et Romanæ urbis ponti-
units.tr: You are delivered into the hands of one from whom you cannot rise without the help of the one who lifts you up. For the scribes and Pharisees, sitting on the chair of Moses, the Roman princes, enemies fixed upon your head, widening their phylacteries, seeking to be enriched from the marrow of your bones, lay heavy and unbearable burdens on your shoulders and on the shoulders of your ministers; and beyond what is fitting they place you under tribute, you who were free from of old. Let all matter for wonder depart from here: because your mother, the lady of the nations, betrothed to you after the manner of a widow, has made him a father in place of a husband, and has chosen the Roman pontiff, the bishop of the city of Rome,

units.la: ficem tificem summum praelegit: qui quod ita fit, tibi in nullo paternitatis genere hoc ostendit. Super te quidem suas magnificat fimbrias, & experimento edocet se tuae matris esse maritum. Commemorat enim apud se propheticum saepe uerbum, quod est infirmio[?] pectoris sui sic digestum: Sume tibi librum grandem, & scribe in eo stylo hominis uelociter, Spolia detrahe, cito praedare. Nunquid cum Apo-stolus, ad hoc constituendum, sic scribit: Omnis Pô-tifex ex hominibus assumptus, pro hominibus con-stituitur in his quae sunt ad Deum? non ad spolia & rapinas, non pro annuis censibus imponendis, nec pro necandis hominibus, sed ut offerat dona & sa-crificia pro peccatis, qui etiam his condolere pos-sit qui ignorant & errant? Et de Petro legitur pi-scatore, cuius se esse commemorat successorem, quod post Christi resurrectionem cum caeteris A-postolis ad piscandi officium est reuersus: qui cum nihil in sinistra navigij parte caperet, Christo iu-bente ad dexteram se converti, & in terram ple-num magnis piscibus rete traxit. Est igitur mini-sterium Ecclesiae utile in parte dextera exercen-dum, per quod & diabolus uincitur, & eidem Christo copia animarum adducitur. Certe sic labor si-nistrae partis navigij non se habet: quia in eo si-des titubat, dominatur tristitia, cum quod inqui-rendo rendo appetitur, minimè inuenitur. Quis enim cre-dat, simul & semel posse ieruire Mammonæ atq; Deo? ac suæ uoluntati placere, & carnis ac sangui-nis reuelationibus inhærere, & offerre Christo mu-nera digna? Et dubio procul pastor qui supra gre-gis ædificationem non uigilat, aliunde rugienti leo-ni, quærenti quam deuoret, parat uiam. Vide in-quam, facta inaudita nuncupatiui filia patris tui, qui bonos pastores à caulis ouium amouet, & suos nepotes consanguineos, & parentes, aliosq; non-nullos, literas ignorantes, & uelut mutos & fur-dos, ouium earundem non intelligentes balatum, nec de morsibus luporum curantes, uelut mercen-rios uellera auferentes, & metentes semina alio-rum in ipsis, non ut prosint, sed ut præsint, constituit pro eisdem, quorumq; manus in cophinis serui-unt, & ipsorum dorsa ab oneribus diuertuntur. Ex quibus liquet, quòd sacerdotium prætermittitur his diebus, obsequium diuinum subtrahitur, & eleemo-synarum largitio adnullatur, per quod Regum, Principum & Christianorum sancta deuotio eua-cuatur.
units.tr: as supreme pontiff. He, that it is so, shows you in no kind of fatherly care. Over you indeed he magnifies his fringes, and by experience teaches that he is the husband of your mother. For he often recalls to himself a prophetic word, which is thus fixed in the weakness of his breast: "Take to yourself a great book, and write in it with a man's pen; hasten to spoil, make haste to the prey" (Isa. 8.). Has not the Apostle, in establishing this office, written thus: "Every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in the things that pertain to God, not for spoils and plunder, not for imposing yearly taxes, nor for killing men, but that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and may be able to have compassion on those who are ignorant and go astray" (Heb. 5.)? And of Peter, the fisherman, whose successor he claims to be, it is read that after Christ's resurrection he returned with the other apostles to the work of fishing; and when he caught nothing on the left side of the boat, at Christ's command he cast the net to the right and drew it full of great fishes to land. So the ministry of the Church must be exercised on the right side, by which the devil is conquered and a multitude of souls is brought to Christ. Certainly the labour of the left side of the boat is not like this, for in it faith wavers and sadness rules, since what is sought with effort is least of all found. For who would believe that one can serve Mammon and God at the same time, please his own will, cling to the revelations of flesh and blood, and offer worthy gifts to Christ? And without doubt the minister who does not watch over the building up of the flock makes a way for the roaring lion, who seeks whom he may devour. See, I say, the unheard-of deeds of the namesake of your father, who removes good shepherds from the folds of the sheep, and sets up in their place, for those same sheep, his nephews, kinsmen, relatives, and some others who are ignorant of letters, and like dumb and deaf men do not understand the bleating of the sheep nor care about the bites of wolves; they carry off the fleeces like hired men, and reap the seed of others in them, not that they may profit but that they may rule, and whose hands serve in the baskets while their backs are relieved of burdens. From these things it is clear that the priesthood is neglected in these days, divine worship is withdrawn, and the giving of alms is brought to nothing, by which the holy devotion of kings, princes and Christians is emptied.

units.la: Nonne debet in oculis omnium mirabile re-putari, quod ubi Christus pro se & Petro regibus solui iußit tributum, ipse regna & regnorum principes contra uoluntatem illius, cuius dicit se esse uicariuitarium, qui ab fe regna & mundi iudicia abdi= tauit, suae subiicere nititur ditioni, dominio fui sty= li, quia totum sibi uendicat, quòd scripserat esse suum? De te, filia, quid plus agit? Ecce à te trahit, quodlibet: nec tamen reputat se contentum, si par tem rerum tuarum decimam à te sumat, nisi priꝰ mos fructus beneficiorum tuorum habeat ministro rum, ut tam pro se quàm pro suo sanguine nouum constituatur patrimonium, de eisdem abiectis pis= simis uoluntatibus fundatorum: & alia etiam exe= crabili pro cursorum fuorū stipendijs, quos trans mittit in Angliam, iam imponit, qui non tantum tu um actuorum uictum auferant et uesturas, sed eo= rum pelles ac carnes lacerent uelut canes. Nun= quid Nabuchodonosor regi debeat comparari, qui templum Domini deuastauit, & uasis suis argen= teis & aureis spoliauit? quod egerat enim ille, a= iste, & ille domus Dei spoliauit ministros, ipsam debito destituebat auxilio: hæc & hic sa= cit. Certè melius est occisis gladio, quàm same a= liquiter interfectis: quia illi sunt mortui statim, isti sunt à terra sterilitate consumpti. Compa= rantur tibi filia, omnes tráseuntes per uiam, quia est dolor similis sicut tuus, iam enim pro dolo simio atq; effusione tua nimia lachrymarum su= per carbones, ò facies tua denigrata ita, quòd non es cognita amplius in plateis, in tenebrosis te tu-us præfitus superior collocauit, inebriauit te ab-finthio & filie. Afflictionem populi tui, eiusq; ge-mitum audi. Vide Domine, & defende: quia cor dicti uiri super cor Pharaonis est nimium indura-tum, quem populum abire liberum non dimittit, nisi in fortitudine manus tuae. Non enim super ter-ram flagitat[?] miserabiliter, sed post mortem: quia quorumcunq; Christianorum bona sub nomine ti-tuli de intestatis confiscant omnia, post decessum omnia devorat. Etenim ecclesia Anglicana, quae liter à retroactis temporibus Franciae in regnum Angliae suos concupiscentiae oculos dirigentes ma-chinabantur, illud suae subiecere potestati: sed quod in ipsis hactenus defuit, est timendum, ne sup-pleat prædicti uiri noua coniecturatio novi ho-stis: quia regni deficiente thesauro, & eius destru-ctio sacerdotio, efficietur vere regnum impoten-tius contra hostes. Ne igitur tua filia, tuiq; sacer-dotes in miseriam deducamini longiorem, expe-ditut pro tua & tuorum salute, quod Rex tuus Christianissimus & regni potentes, qui amplifi-mis beneficijs te ornauerunt, quiq; uos & bene-ficia huiusmodi haberent in hoc casu tueri, resi-stant coniecturationibus, conspirationibus, arro-gantia ac superbia dicti uiri, qui non Dei contem-platioplatione, [?]ed pro præmissis & pro suis ditando pa-rentibus, ac pro nido suo, quia Aquilam exaltans doper præmissa & alia imposita per eundem, to-talem pecuniam Anglicanam nouï domini genere iam compellit, ne dissimulata in hac parte simplici tas regni huius subuersionem auferat, uelut tuam, & adhibeatur seró remedij tunc cautela. Auertat hempe Dominus uirtutum de corde uiri illius ue-lamen, fibiq; cor contritum & humile largiatur: & agnoscere cum faciat uestigia ueri Dei, per quæ à suis tenebris eruatur, & præmissos labores si-nistros dimittere compellatur: nec non & uineam quam plantauit Dei dextra, sacræ fidei cultoribus repleatur. Animaduerte enim uerba Domini, & prophetiam Ieremiæ, ad propulsandum huiusmo-di incboata, quæ dicunt: Tu pastor, qui populum meum differfisti, & cum de suis habitationibus e-iectisti, ecce uisitabo super te tuorum maliciam slu-diorum, nec erit uir qui super solium Dauid de tuo semine sedeat, nec qui in luda ultrà habeat potestà tem, fiat nidus tuus desertus, & sicut Sodoma & Gomorra, taliter fit subuersus: qui si perterritus ex his dictis non desiterit ab inceptis, & restitu-tionem non ferent de perceptis, psal'ent pro eo extunc nequiter corde indurato psalmum centesi-mumoctauū, illi cui omnia seruiunt, aperte singulí [?] singulis diebus in Christo deuotissimi dicimus lau-dem.
units.tr: Ought it not to be regarded as a marvel in the eyes of all that, where Christ bade kings to be released from tribute for himself and for Peter, he himself strives to bring kingdoms and the princes of kingdoms under his lordship, against the will of him whose vicar he says he is, who withdrew himself from kingdoms and the judgments of the world; and that he claims for himself everything which he had written was his own, by the power of his pen? What more does he do to you, daughter? Behold, he takes whatever he pleases from you; yet he does not think himself content if he takes a tenth part of your goods, unless first the fruits of your benefices go to his ministers, so that a new patrimony is established for himself and for his own blood, from those most wicked wills of the founders thrown aside; and now he also imposes another detestable tax for the wages of his couriers, whom he sends into England, who not only carry off the food and clothing of your ministers, but tear their skins and flesh like dogs. Should he be compared to King Nebuchadnezzar, who laid waste the temple of the Lord and despoiled it of its silver and golden vessels? For what that one did, this one does too: that one despoiled the ministers of God's house, and left it destitute of due help; this one does the same. Certainly it is better to be slain by the sword than to be killed slowly by famine, for those die at once, but these are consumed by the barrenness of the land. All who pass by the way are made to look at you, daughter, because there is no sorrow like yours; for now, because of your deceit and your excessive shedding of tears, your face is blackened like coals, so that you are no longer known in the streets. In darkness your superior placed you; he made you drink wormwood and gall. Hear the affliction of your people and their groaning. See, O Lord, and defend them; for the heart of that man is hardened beyond measure, like the heart of Pharaoh, and he does not let the people go free unless by a strong hand. For he does not plunder wretchedly only while they live, but after death; for under the name of title he seizes all the goods of any Christians who die intestate, and devours everything after their decease. Indeed the English Church, which for some time past had directed the eyes of their desire towards the kingdom of England from France, and laid their plots, has now subjected it to their own power. But what has hitherto been lacking in them must be feared: lest the new scheming of that man and the new enemy supply what is missing, for when the treasury of the kingdom fails, and its priesthood is destroyed, it will truly become a kingdom weaker against its enemies. Therefore, lest you, daughter, and your priests be led into a longer misery, it is expedient for your welfare and for theirs that your most Christian King and the powerful men of the kingdom, who have adorned you with the greatest benefits, and who ought to protect you and such benefits in this case, resist his schemes, conspiracies, arrogance and pride, that man who does not contemplate God, but enriches himself and his relatives by the aforesaid and other burdens imposed by the same man, and for his own nest; for, lifting up the eagle, by the aforesaid things and others imposed by him, he now compels the whole English money to go to a new lord of a kind. Lest the simplicity of this kingdom, if it is disregarded in this part, bring about its overthrow as it did yours, let caution be applied, though late, as a remedy. May the Lord of hosts indeed take the veil from the heart of that man, and give him a heart contrite and humble; and may he compel him to acknowledge the footprints of the true God, by which he may be rescued from his darkness, and to abandon those wicked labours; and may the vineyard that the right hand of God planted be filled with cultivators of the holy faith. For consider the words of the Lord, and the prophecy of Jeremiah, for repelling such beginnings as these: "You shepherd who have scattered my people, and have driven them out of their dwellings, behold I will visit upon you the wickedness of your devices; and there shall be no man to sit upon the throne of David from your seed, nor any who shall have power any more in Judah; let your nest be made desolate, and let it be overthrown as Sodom and Gomorrah." If he, terrified by these words, does not cease from his undertakings, and does not restore what he has received, then let us, who are most devoted to Christ, daily openly recite for him, with a heart hardened in wickedness, the hundred and eighth psalm, to him to whom all things serve, as praise.
135. Benedictus XI.

units.la: Benedictus undecimus, natione Lombardus, patria Taruisinus, Nicolaus nominatus, professione Dominicanus, parentibus obscuris, patre uide-licet opilione, post Cardinalatum & episcopatum Hostiensem, ad Papatus apicem tandem peruenit.
units.tr: Benedict XI, a Lombard by birth, of Treviso by country, named Nicholas, a Dominican by profession, of obscure parents (his father, namely, being a shepherd), at length rose to the summit of the papacy after being made cardinal and bishop of Ostia.

units.la: Fuit ille statura breuis, ac procedente ætate cal-vus, ingenio uersutus & eloquens, ac Bonifacio pro-pterea acceptus: qui mox suscepto Pontificio sa-stu, ad Italiam pacandam, & augendam rem Pa-pisticam, quam intestinis odiis agitatam cognoue-rat, animum impense adiecit.
units.tr: He was short in stature and, as he grew older, bald. He was crafty and eloquent in mind, and for that reason was welcome to Boniface. As soon as he had taken up the papal office, he applied himself zealously to pacifying Italy and to enlarging the papal cause, which he had found torn by internal hatreds.

units.la: Narrat Leander Al-bertus, cum Pontifex esset creatus, matrem eius Pe-rufium veniesse, visendi filium gratia, ad tantam prouectum dignitatem: & à senatu vestibus orna-tam, ut eum salutatura decenter adiret. Sed illam ignominiose repulit, nec pro matre agnouit, do-nec esset priore vestimento induta. Hanc (inquit) matronam agnosco, porro mater est.
units.tr: Leander Albertus relates that when he had been made pope, his mother came to Perugia to see her son on account of his having risen to such dignity. The senate had dressed her in fine clothes so that she might approach and greet him becomingly. But he shamefully rejected her and would not acknowledge her as his mother until she had put on her former clothing. "I recognise this lady," he said, "but she is indeed my mother."

units.la: Obtulit ille templo D. Eustorgij, urbis Mediolanensis, pocu-lum argenteum ingentis ponderis, quem calicem uocant: thuribulum cum acerra, seu arcula thuris: candelabra argentea: & cortinam sericeam ma-gnam, precij aureorum centum: & trecētas libras, quæ que[?] ad ærarium Pontificium pertinebant, pro al-tera cortina facienda circa sepulcrum Petri Ve-ronensis, Papistici martyris suæ sectæ Dominica-ne. Omnia data fuere precij octo millium libra-rum Mediolanensium. Valde liberalis erat, ex pan-nosò fraterculo magnus hic Pontifex, in idolola-tris ad diaboli pompam alendis: sed in diuini uer-bi ministerio ad Christi gloriam, nihil attulit. Bo-nifacij captores, Anagninos omnes, Nogaretumq; & Sarram, quousq; soluissent, anathemate nota-uit: sed Philippum Francorum regem censuris ir-retitum, absoluit. Columnenses Cardinales, Ioan-nem & Iacobum, in gratiam recepit, quos ingenti odio Bonifacius fuerat prosecutus. Cardinales ex sua factione, Nicolaü Pratensem Hetrusrum, Guil-helmum Makles feldum antea defunctum, & Gual-terum Vuinterburnum, Anglos, fecit. Perasis ita-que aliquantulum dissidijs, ab antecessore inchoa-tis, quarum gratia Perusium erat profectus, anno Domini 1305. nono sui pontificatus mense, abba-tissæ cuiusdam ficuum obsonio, è uita sublatum su-it, & apud Dominicanos magna pompa fe-pultus. Afferunt eum (ait Leander) ueneno in ficu præparato im-terrisse.
units.tr: He presented to the church of St Eustorgius in the city of Milan a silver cup of enormous weight, which they call a chalice; a censer with its incense box; silver candlesticks; and a large silk hanging worth a hundred gold florins, together with three hundred pounds, which belonged to the papal treasury, for making another hanging around the tomb of Peter of Verona, the Papist martyr of his Dominican sect. All these gifts were valued at eight thousand pounds of Milanese money. This great pontiff was very generous, though he was once a ragged little friar: he fed the idolaters for the pomp of the devil, but for the ministry of the divine Word he brought nothing to the glory of Christ. He marked with anathema, until they should pay, all the captors of Boniface, namely the Anagnines, Nogaret and Sciarra; but he absolved Philip, king of the French, who was entangled in censures. He received back into favour the Colonna cardinals, John and James, whom Boniface had pursued with great hatred. From his own faction he made cardinals Nicolas of Prato, a Tuscan; William of Macclesfield, an Englishman who had died earlier; and Walter Winterburn, also an Englishman. Thus, after some quarrels that had begun under his predecessor, for the sake of which he had gone to Perugia, he was taken out of life in the year of the Lord 1305, in the ninth month of his pontificate, by a dish of figs prepared by some abbess, and was buried with great pomp among the Dominicans. Leander says that they report he was killed by poison prepared in a fig.
136. Clement V.

units.la: Clemens quintus, patria Vasco, ex genitore Bernardo nobili milite, Bertrandus Gothus antea dictus, episcopus Conuenarum, & archiepiscopus Burdegalensis: Perusij à collegio Cardinalium absens, post contentionem longam Pontifex constituebatur. Is autem electioni consentiens, ex Burdegala Lugdunum profectus, eò Cardinales omnes ad se uocabat. Qui sine mora Pontifici obtemperarunt, & curia Romana in Galliae translata anno Domini 1305. ad septuaginta quatuor annos ibi remansit, cum magno Romanorum incommodo. Coronationi huius Clementis, interfuere rex Franciae Philippus, Carolus eius frater, & Ioannes dux Britanniae: qui ruina muri oppressus, cum duodecim aliis statim moriebatur, dum solennitatis pompa per urbem duceretur. Philippusque rex ea ruina aliqua ex parte debilitatus fuit. Pontifex autem, in tanta trepidatione, ex equo turbatus, carbunculum ex tiara amisit, [?]pretii flo-renorum sex millium. Peracta deinde solenni pompa, pacatisque[?] rebus omnibus, plures Cardinales ex Gallis creabat, ex Italia nullum: licet Ioanni & Iacobo Columnensibus, dignitatem Cardinalatus integram restituerit. Tres praeterea Cardinales cum senatoria potestate Romam misit, quorum au sicilis [?] urbs ipsa atq; Italia gubernaretur. Sardi-niam [?] insulam Saracenis occupatam, ea conditio-ne Friderico Siciliæ regi concesit, ut eam quam-primum, pulsis hostibus (sed ad suum tandem un-de recuperaret. His Platinæ verbis, hæc ad-didit Hieronymus Marius: Clemens quintus, in-quit, quoniam nō aliis seruire ac ministrare, quem admodum Christus Apostolis suis mandauit, sed ut & illi ab Imperatoribus ministraretur optabat. decreto statuit, ut designati in Germania Cæsa-res, quamuis Romanorum regis appellatione for-tentur, à summo tamen Pontifice Imperij iura ac nomen acciperent. Atq; ut mortuo Imperatore, per omne interregni tempus, Italicarum urbium, quæ Cæsari stipendiariæ essent, arbitrium & po-testas penes Romanum pontificem esset. Hæc ille Clemens Papalem sedem, scortator publicus, ad meretricum patronus, in Auenione ad volupta-tem constituit. Viennense generale concilium an-no Domini 1311. celebrauit. In quo Templarios, rege ipso ditiores, pro publicandis eorum bonis atrociter extinxit: & Ioannitas, Hospitalarios mi-lites, qui Rhodum à Saracenis obtinuerant, eo-rum spoliis atq; indulgentijs magnifice prouexit. Fratricellos unà cum Dulcino quodam Nouarien-si, qui Ecclesiasticos impugnabat, prædicata cruccruce atq; indulgentijs datis, per Dominicanos op-pressit: & Beghardos ac Beguuinas, qui panem Eu-charisticum honorare nolebant, improbabat. Ma-gistrum Templariorum cum uno socio, Parisijs co-buri iussit, in præsentia dominorum Cardinalium: & contra ludæorum insolentias quasdam, ordina-tiones fecit, confiscatis eorum bonis. Iuramenta à principibus præstita, non subiectionis, sed fidelita-tis esse decreuit: & ecclesiæ bona non esse ab ea-dem alienanda, mandauit. Secularibus commerciis occupatos, & sumptuosis uestibus ornatos cleri-cos puniri voluit: ac monachis aucupationes & ue-nationes abstulit.
units.tr: Clement V, a Gascon by birth, son of Bernard, a noble soldier, formerly called Bertrand de Got, bishop of Comminges and archbishop of Bordeaux, was made pope after a long contest while he was absent from Perugia, by the college of cardinals. He, consenting to the election, set out from Bordeaux to Lyons and there summoned all the cardinals to himself. They obeyed the pontiff without delay, and the Roman curia, transferred into Gaul in the year of the Lord 1305, remained there for seventy-four years, to the great disadvantage of the Romans. At the coronation of this Clement were present King Philip of France, his brother Charles, and John, duke of Brittany. As the solemn procession was being led through the city, a wall collapsed; John was crushed by the ruin and died at once with twelve others. King Philip was partly weakened by that disaster. The pontiff, in such great alarm, was thrown from his horse and lost a carbuncle from his tiara, worth six thousand florins. Then, when the solemn pomp was finished and all affairs were settled, he created several cardinals from the French, but none from Italy, although he restored the full dignity of cardinal to John and James Colonna. Moreover he sent three cardinals to Rome with senatorial power, by whom the city itself and Italy were to be governed. Sardinia, occupied by the Saracens, he granted to Frederick, king of Sicily, on condition that he should recover it for himself as soon as possible, driving out the enemies. To Platina's words Hieronymus Marius added these: "Clement V," he says, "since he wished not to serve and minister to others, as Christ commanded his apostles, but that he himself should be ministered to by emperors, decreed that the emperors designated in Germany, although they bear the title of king of the Romans, should receive from the supreme pontiff the rights and the name of emperor. And that, when an emperor died, throughout the whole interregnum the authority and power over the Italian cities that were tributary to the emperor should lie with the Roman pontiff." Thus this Clement, a public whoremonger and patron of harlots, established the papal see at Avignon for his pleasure. He celebrated the general council of Vienne in the year of the Lord 1311. In it he savagely destroyed the Templars, who were richer than the king himself, in order to seize their goods; and he magnificently enriched the Johannites, the Hospitaller knights who had taken Rhodes from the Saracens, with their spoils and with indulgences. He suppressed the Fraticelli, together with a certain Dolcino of Novara, who attacked churchmen, by preaching the cross against them and granting indulgences, through the Dominicans. He condemned the Beghards and Beguines, who refused to honour the Eucharistic bread. He ordered the master of the Templars, together with one companion, to be burned at Paris in the presence of the lord cardinals. Against certain insolences of the Jews he made ordinances, and their goods were confiscated. He decreed that the oaths sworn by princes were oaths not of subjection but of fidelity, and he ordered that church property must not be alienated. He wished clerics who were occupied with secular trade and adorned with sumptuous clothing to be punished, and he took from monks their fowling and hunting.

units.la: Venetos, Florentinos ac Lucenses, sacris interdixit: & Eucharisticî panis festum confirmauit. Clementinas constitutiones congessit, et sanctorum reliquias summe uenerandas esse pronunciauit. Per Neapolionem & Pelaguram Cardinales legatos, Italicas res curabat: ac Cœlestinum quintum cons-fsoribus Papisticis adiunxit. Constitutiones monachorum ordinauit, & Franciscanorum regulam tum denuò declarauit. Nouissime Clemens, nunc dysenteria, nunc stomachi ac laterum dolore cruciatus, apud Roccam Mauram, castrum supra Rodanum, anno Domini 1314. naturæ cessit. Et Carpentoratum usq; in Vasconiam transuectum est ea ius corpus:uacauitq; sedes usq; in tertium annum. Huius temporee,[?] & eodem quo obijt anno, Henri-cus Lutzemburgus Imperator, quum Siciliæ reg-num, ad quod à Siculis uocabatur, armis iam ad se pertrahere instituieret, à pseudomonacho Bernardo de monte Politiano, Dominicastro, ex Guelpho-rum conspiratione, qui se amicum Imperatori diu simulauerat, intoxicata hostia, quam bono princi-pi dum Eucharistia sese confirmaret, dederat, per fidiose perimebatur. Pius uero princeps, cum sen-tiret uenenum sibi datum, proditorem illum mo-nachum, ut fugeret, admonuisse fertur his uerbis: Domine, recedatis. Nam si percipiunt Teutonici, & nostri deuoti, morte moriemini. Qui Senas re-cedens, aurum quod ei in mercedem impietatis e-rat promissum, accepit, scelestissimus Iudas. Sed confratres suos Dominicanos non liberauit. Nam multi eorum in Thuscia, Lombardia, & aliis lo-cis, una cum domibus, igne, gladi oue[?] perierunt.
units.tr: He interdicted the Venetians, Florentines and Lucchese from the sacred rites: and he confirmed the feast of the Eucharistic bread. He gathered together the Clementine constitutions and declared the relics of the saints to be most worthy of veneration. Through the cardinals Napoleon and Pelagrua, as legates, he managed Italian affairs, and he joined Celestine V to the Papist confessors. He ordained constitutions for the monks and again declared the rule of the Franciscans. Finally Clement, tormented now by dysentery and now by pain in the stomach and sides, died a natural death at Roquemaure, a castle above the Rhône, in the year of the Lord 1314. His body was carried as far as Carpentras and thence into Gascony, and the see was vacant until the third year. At this time, and in the same year in which he died, the emperor Henry of Luxembourg, when he was about to bring the kingdom of Sicily under his control by arms, to which he had been summoned by the Sicilians, was treacherously killed by a poisoned host. The pseudo-monk Bernard of Montepulciano, a little Dominican, had given it to the good prince while he was strengthening himself with the Eucharist; he was acting from a conspiracy of the Guelphs, having long pretended to be the emperor's friend. The pious prince, when he perceived that poison had been given to him, is said to have urged that monk to flee with these words: "Lord, withdraw. For if the Germans and our devoted followers perceive it, you will die the death." Withdrawing to Siena, he received the gold that had been promised him as the wages of his impiety, the most wicked Judas. But he did not free his fellow Dominicans, for many of them in Tuscany, Lombardy and other places perished by fire and sword, along with their houses.
137. John the twenty-third.

units.la: Ioannes uicesimus tertius, natione Gallus, patre Arnoldo de Offa, Iacobus Caturcensis antea nominatus, Cardinalis episcopus Portuensis, post biennij spacium, quo sedes ob 23. Cardinalium al-tercationes vacasset, Lugduni Papa renunciaba-tur. tur. Inde uero Auenionem cum curia professus, osto[?] Cardinales creauit: quorum de numero fuere Iaco-bus Caturcensis iunior, eius ex sorore nepos, & 10 annes Caietanus e gente Vrsina. Hugonem Geral-dum Caturcensem episcopum, Pontificalibus infi-gnibus priuatum ac degradatu, curiae secularibus ru-[?]ciandum, excoriandum, & exurendum donec expi-raret, tradidit: quod in eius personam (ut dicebat) coniurasset. Ecclesiam Tolosanam, quam unice di-lexit, ad archiepiscopatum transtulit: cuius castel-la sex in urbes erexit, ut haberet quibus dignitate praeesset. Dioeceses quoq; archiepiscopatui Narbo-nensi adscripsit, Limosam, & abbatiam S. Pontij. Adeo praeterea rebus novis Pontifex ille studuit, ut & simplices episcopatus bifariam diviserit, ac divisos in unum redegerit, atq; abbatias in episco-patus, & episcopatus in abbatias vicissim transtu-lerit. Novas etiam dignitates, & nova collegia in ecclesijs constituit, ac prius constituta in aliam for-mam transtulit. Clementinarum editionem confir-mauit, & publicandam gymnasiorum doctoribus ac magistris mandauit. Ordinem Grandimontensem (desidiosorum monachorum) additis quibusdam con-stitutionibus reformauit, et Cæsar augustana eccle-siam in metropolim sublimauit, assignatis ei quinque cathedralibus templis, ex unde[?]um quae Terraco-nensi subessent. Militum inanium,seu ocioforum nebulonum novam sectam in Lufitania institui, quæ & Christi militia subdolè dicebatur, ut Saracenis (ceu dicūt) resisterent: ac Templariorum bona, annuente Al-phonso Portugaliæ rege illis delegauit, quo liberi milites [?]ut illi militiæ vacarent. Duos Thomas in Papisti-cos sanctos retulit: unum Herefordensem episcopum Anglum, & alterum Aquinatem Dominicanum: atq; unum tertium, Ludouicum episcopum Tolo-sanum, Caroli quondam Siciliæ regis filium, Mino-ritam, à Nicolao quarto prius admissum, illis addidit. Ordinauit, ut ter in die tintinnabula pulsa-rentur, quo populus in genua flectens, salutationem angelicam D. virgini idololatricè recitaret. Creatis deinde in secunda ordinatione Cardinalibus, eos declarauit pertinaces hæreticos, qui affirmarent Christum & Apostolos nihil bilhabuisse proprij. Misit diplomata ad Academias publicas, ne scholastici ea de re disputare auderent. Damnauit præterea Petri cuiusdam Franciscani glossulam, qui ad Christi paupertatem [?]tandam quodam animum erat: quorum de numero multi damnati & exusti sunt. Habita insuper ordinatione tertia, decem Cardinales creauit: inter quos fuere Ioannes Columna, & Matthæus de gente Vrsina Dominicanus. Carmelitas [?]assumpsit in ius & proprietatem S. Petri, ab omni ordinariorum domino, ut soli sanctissimo subijciantur tanquam filij dilectissimi: pluresq; eorum episcopos fecit, Guidonem Perpinianum, Ioannem Claranum, Catalanos, atq; aliarum nationum alios. Nam mirabilem ante Papatum (authore diabolo) uisionem habebat, ut in bulla testatur: quod Maria uirgo, in magna Cardinalium contentione, ab aduersarijs illum liberaret, ac Papam faceret: hac tamen seruata pactioe, ut hos suos fratres à purgatorio seruaret immunes.
units.tr: John the twenty-third, a Frenchman by birth, son of Arnold de Offa, formerly called Jacques of Cahors and cardinal bishop of Porto, was declared pope at Lyons after the see had stood vacant for two years because of the quarrels of the 23 cardinals. Then, having moved the court to Avignon, he created eight cardinals. Among them were Jacques of Cahors the younger, his nephew through his sister, and Gaetano of the Ursini family. He handed over Hugh Géraud, bishop of Cahors, stripped of his pontifical insignia and degraded, to the secular arm of the court, to be flayed, skinned and burned until he died, because (as he said) he had conspired against his person. He raised the church of Toulouse, which he loved above all others, to an archbishopric, and erected six of its towns into cities, so that he would have places over which to preside in dignity. He also assigned dioceses to the archbishopric of Narbonne: Limoux and the abbey of St Pons. That pontiff was so eager for novelties that he divided simple bishoprics into two, joined the divided ones back into one, and in turn transferred abbeys into bishoprics and bishoprics into abbeys. He also established new dignities and new colleges in the churches, and changed the form of those previously established. He confirmed the edition of the Clementines and ordered that it be published to the teachers and masters of the schools. He reformed the Order of Grandmont (of idle monks) by adding certain constitutions, and he raised the church of Saragossa to be a metropolis, assigning to it five cathedral churches that had been subject to Tarragona. He instituted in Portugal a new sect of empty soldiers, idle good-for-nothings, which was also deceitfully called the soldiery of Christ, so that they might resist the Saracens (so they say). With the assent of Alfonso, king of Portugal, he assigned to them the goods of the Templars, so that free soldiers might devote themselves to that service. He added to the Papist saints two Thomases: one, Thomas of Hereford, an English bishop, and the other, Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican. To them he also added a third, Louis, bishop of Toulouse, son of the former king of Sicily Charles, a Franciscan who had previously been admitted by Nicholas IV. He ordered that the bells be rung three times a day, so that the people, bending their knees, should idolatrously recite the angelic salutation to the Virgin. Then, having created cardinals in a second ordination, he declared pertinacious heretics those who affirmed that Christ and the apostles had possessed nothing of their own. He sent letters to the public academies so that the scholars would not dare to dispute this matter. He also condemned the little gloss of a certain Franciscan, Peter, who had been minded to defend the poverty of Christ; of those who followed him, many were condemned and burned. Moreover, after a third ordination, he created ten cardinals, among them John Colonna and Matthew of the Ursini family, a Dominican. He took the Carmelites into the right and property of St Peter, free from the lordship of all ordinaries, so that they would be subject to the most holy one alone as his most beloved sons; and he made several of them bishops: Guido Perpignan, John Clarano, Catalans, and others of other nations. For before his papacy, by the devil's authorship, he had a wondrous vision, as he attests in a bull: that the Virgin Mary, in a great contention of the cardinals, freed him from his adversaries and made him pope; but on this condition kept, that he would keep these her brothers free from purgatory.

units.la: Docuit errores quosdam Ioannes, præsertim animas corpore exutas, Deum non uidere ante extremum diem. Sic enim (teste Maffæo) pater suus docuerat, seductus uisionibus cuiusdam Hyberni. Misitq; Parisium duos, alterum Dominicanum, alterum Franciscanum, qui eandem hæresim prædicarent. Sed Pontifici resisterunt Thomas Vualleys Dominicanus Anglus, quem Papa in carcerem misit: Durandus de S. Porciano, Guilhelmus Calethus, & alij. Pro suo arbitrio ecclesiarum ordines correxit, ac inuenit: & collegia scribarum Apostolorum numero distinxit, qui accepto precio, literas à se destinatas conscriberent. Multas constitutiones, quæ Ioanninæ dicuntur, fecit: & Ioannem de Poliaco[?] theologum damnauit, quia docebat, fratri-bus Mendicantibus non esse confitendum: monas-chas tamen, quas Beginas uocant (Auentino teste) ad coniugia compulit, & picturas detestabatur. Profolidis[?] articulis etiam tenebat, quod Christus aliam pietatis regulam Apostolis non dedisset, quàm cæteris Christianis: quod Apostoli uotu pau-pertatis nunquam uouerunt, & quod uota nihil facient ad perfectionem. Ioannes M indeuilla[?] lib. 1, cap. 7. refert, hunc Papam prolixè scripsisse ad Græcos, unicam tantum esse Christianam ecclesiam, seq; eius esse caput, ac Christi uicarium. Cui Græci breuiter responderunt: Potentiam tuam summam ergà tuos subditos, firmiter credimus: superbiam tuam summam tolerare non possumus, auaritiam satiare non valemus. Diabolus tecum, quia Dominus nobiscum. Quo[?] Laconismo seu breui loquio, totam rationem & statum Papæ indicabant.
units.tr: John taught certain errors, chiefly that souls stripped of the body do not see God before the last day. For so (according to Maffeo) his father had taught, seduced by the visions of a certain Irishman. He sent two men to Paris, one a Dominican and one a Franciscan, to preach the same heresy. But they were resisted by Thomas Waleys, an English Dominican, whom the pope put into prison, and by Durand of St Pourçain, Guillaume Calet and others. At his own discretion he corrected and devised the orders of the churches, and he divided the colleges of scribes according to the number of the Apostles; these, having received a fee, would write the letters sent out by him. He made many constitutions, which are called Johannine. He condemned John of Pouilly, a theologian, because he taught that confession should not be made to the friars of the mendicant orders. Yet he compelled the nuns called Beguines to marriage (according to Aventinus), and he detested pictures. He also held certain articles: that Christ had not given the apostles a different rule of piety from the other Christians; that the apostles never vowed the vow of poverty; and that vows contribute nothing to perfection. John Mindeuilla, book 1, chapter 7, reports that this pope wrote at length to the Greeks that there is only one Christian Church, that he himself is its head and the vicar of Christ. The Greeks replied briefly: "We firmly believe in your great power over your subjects; we cannot tolerate your great pride; we cannot satisfy your avarice. The devil is with you, because the Lord is with us." By this laconic or brief speech they revealed the whole reasoning and condition of the pope.

units.la: Ludouicum Bauarum, imperatorem optimum, ecclesiæ rebellem, schismaticum & hereticum, hic Papa declarauit, quod à principibus electus, admi-nistrationem imperij suscepisset, nullo sibi præsti-to subiectionis iuramento. Accedit Hieronymi Ma-rij de Ludouico testimonium: Ioannes, inquit, Lu-douicum Bauarum acerrimo odio prosecutus est, tum quia à Germaniæ principibus in regem Romanorum electus, nomen ac titulum Imperatori-um (ut Clemens quintus decreuerat) de manu Pon-tificis accipere dedignabatur: tum quoq; quoniam monachos quosdam, quos tanquam hereticos ipse damnauerat, aduersus illum defendebat. Ideo Io-annes Lulouicum hereticum asseruit. Ludouicus in Italiam ueniens, uicarios singulis Imperij ciuita-tibus, ut par erat, imposuit, ac Mediolanum uenit. Cumq; Pontificis rabiem delinere optaret, ad il-lum qui Auenioni in Gallia tum sedem habebat, o-ratores misit, qui Imperialia insignia peterent sibi more maiorum benigne ac amico animo conferri. Pontifex non modo id facere recusabat, sed & o-ratores summa cum ignominia repulit: Imperato-remq; ipsum peremptorie (ut dicunt) citabat, ut Auenionem ueniret, ac statutis ecclesiae se subice-ret. Imperator Pontificiam in ecclesia tyrannidem agnoscens, seq; a Deo imperatoriam maiestatem habuisse sciens, eandem pariter sanctam ac inuio-latam seruare studebat. Ideo nec Pontificibus se tanquam seruum subiicere uolebat. Ideo Auenio-nem petere denegabat. Pacis tamen cum esset avi-dus, rursus per nuncios obsecrabat, ut Imperialia signa ei benigne conferrentur. Pontifex in sua per-stabat sententia: Vicecomites, quibus tum Impe-rator Mediolani dominium permittebat, in Ludoici odium excommunicabat.
units.tr: This pope declared Ludwig of Bavaria, an excellent emperor, a rebel against the Church, a schismatic and a heretic, because, after being elected by the princes, he had taken up the administration of the empire without having sworn any oath of submission to him. To this is added the testimony of Girolamo Mario about Ludwig: "John," he says, "pursued Ludwig of Bavaria with the bitterest hatred, both because, elected king of the Romans by the princes of Germany, he disdained to receive the name and title of Emperor from the hand of the pope (as Clement V had decreed), and also because he defended against him certain monks whom the pope himself had condemned as heretics. Therefore John declared <hi>Ludwig</hi> a heretic." Ludwig, coming into Italy, appointed vicars in the individual cities of the empire, as was fitting, and came to Milan. Wishing to soothe the pope's rage, he sent envoys to him who then had his seat at Avignon in Gaul, to ask that the imperial insignia be bestowed upon him kindly and in a friendly spirit, as was the custom of his ancestors. The pope not only refused to do this, but also dismissed the envoys with great contempt, and summoned the emperor himself, in peremptory terms (as they say), to come to Avignon and submit himself to the statutes of the Church. The emperor, recognising the papal tyranny in the Church, and knowing that he held imperial majesty from God, was eager to keep that majesty equally holy and inviolate. Therefore he would not submit himself to the pontiffs as a slave, and so he refused to go to Avignon. Nevertheless, since he was eager for peace, he again begged through messengers that the imperial signs be bestowed upon him kindly. The pope persisted in his opinion, and excommunicated the Visconti, to whom the emperor then granted the lordship of Milan, out of hatred for Ludwig.

units.la: Imperator cum Pharaonis cor induratum con-spiceret, Romam, multis secum adscitis Italorum principibus, pervenit, ac honorificè ab universo populo est susceptus: imperialiaque insignia pro mo-re sibi concedi petijt. Romanorum proceres ac to-tius populus, oratores ad Ioannem in Galliam mit-tebant, eumque obsecrabant supplices, ut urbem su-am inuisere vellet, ac regi Romanorum imperia-lia insignia conferre. Quod si ipse hoc facere re-ueret[?], se antiquam populi Romani legem ac iura seruaturos asserebant. Ioannes, oratoribus audi-tis, summa cum ignominia, terroribus ac minis eos a se repulit. Quae videns populus Romanus, de-creuit optimo Ludouico concedere quod petebat. Et ita a senatoribus Stephano & Nicolao, iussit totius cleri ac populi, cum coniuge una coronatus fuit, omnibus nobilibus qui astabant acclamanti-bus, Ludouicum Augustum, Romanorum Impera-torem. Quid quaeso hactenus Ludouicus egit, quod optimum ac magnanimum Imperatorem non de-ceret? Attamen Ioannes hoc audiens, cum lesa maiestatis reum ac haereticum incusabat, durif-simos processus contra illum publicabat, impe-riali dignitate deiiciebat, regno priuabat, ex-communicatione crudelissima, tanquam Eccle-fia[?] fiæ Romanæ rebellem ac hæresiarcham condem-nabat. Hæc Marius. Aliamq; rationem non habe-bat, quasuam potestatem, fictumq; ac furtiuum ium suum defenderet, quàm commentita execratio-num fulmina. Sed quidam erant his diebus tam theo-logi quàm juristæ, qui docebant Christum & Apostolos nihil habuisse proprij, & Imperatorem non esse in temporalibus Papæ subiectum. Ex ho-rum numero fuerunt Michael Cæsenus & Guil-helmus Ockam Minoritæ, Marsilius Paduanus, & Joannes de landuno jurisperiti, cum aliis multis. Per hos Ludovicus Imperator ita confortatus est, ut Papæ se conatibus viriliter opponeret, tali ap-pellatione in omnes Imperij fines publicata.
units.tr: When the emperor saw that the heart of Pharaoh had been hardened, he came to Rome with many Italian princes attached to him, and was received with honour by the whole people; and, as was the custom, he sought that the imperial insignia be granted to him. The chief men of the Romans and the whole people sent envoys to John in Gaul, and begged him as suppliants that he would be willing to visit their city and confer the imperial insignia on the king of the Romans. They asserted that if he were to refuse to do this, they would keep the ancient law and rights of the Roman people. John, having heard the envoys, dismissed them from himself with great contempt, with terrors and threats. When the Roman people saw this, they decided to grant the excellent Ludwig what he sought. And so, at the command of the senators Stephen and Nicholas, he was crowned with his wife, while all the nobles who stood by, and the whole clergy and people, acclaimed Ludwig as Augustus, Emperor of the Romans. What, I ask, had Ludwig done up to this point that would not befit an excellent and magnanimous emperor? Nevertheless John, hearing this, accused him as a defendant of treason and as a heretic; he published the harshest processes against him, deprived him of imperial dignity, stripped him of his kingdom, and condemned him with the most cruel excommunication as a rebel against the Roman Church and a leader of heresy. So Mario. The pope had no other means of defending his power and his fictitious and stolen right than the thunderbolts of invented curses. But in those days there were both theologians and jurists who taught that Christ and the apostles had possessed nothing of their own, and that the emperor was not subject to the pope in temporal matters. Among them were Michael of Cesena and William of Ockham, Franciscans, Marsilius of Padua, and John of Jandun, jurists, together with many others. Through these men Emperor Ludwig was so strengthened that he bravely opposed the pope's attempts, having published such an appeal throughout all the borders of the empire.
Letter of Louis.

units.la: Nos Ludovicus Romanorum rex, proponimus aduersus Joannem, qui se dicit esse Papam, quod Christi testamentum de pace male exequitur, pub-licam Christianitatis pacem perturbans. Nec re-miniscitur, à sancto Constantino, id quicquid nunc habet honoris, latitanti Syluestro permissum: male gratus Romano imperio, unde desumpsit omnem quo nunc abutitur splendorem, &c.
units.tr: We, Louis, King of the Romans, charge against John, who calls himself Pope, that he wickedly carries out Christ's testament concerning peace, disturbing the public peace of Christendom. Nor does he remember that all the honour he now possesses was granted, by Saint Constantine, to the hidden Sylvester. He is ungrateful to the Roman empire, from which he has taken all the splendour he now abuses, etc.

units.la: Cum ergo Ludovicus ac Romani proceres, in-qua[?] Joannis facta[?] optime cognoscerent, popu-lusq; [?]uiq; Romanus à maiori ad minimum usque ægrè ferret, quòd ab eo oratores quos miserant, uta de-lusi essent, und omnes conuenirebant, ut antiquum mos in eligendo Pontifice in ecclesiam inuehere-tur, ut uidelicet à populo Romano electus, ab Im-peratore ipso confirmationem acciperet, ideo Pe-trus quidam Corbariensis, Minorita, in Rom. Pon-tificem creabatur, ac Nicolaus quintus dicebatur: Ioannem uero hæreticum, atq; ecclesiæ tyrannum, & non pastorem, publicæq; Christianorum pacis perturbatorem declarabant, hæc quoq; omnia Im-perator, ac Romani concilij proceres, ecclesiæ ca-tholicæ submittebant. Hæc Marius. Interim Ioan-nes anno Domini 1335. & ætatis 90. Auenione vi-te finem accepit, in cathedrali ecclesia insigni su-neris pompa sepultus. Tantum ille in thesauris re-liquit, quantum nullus ante eum Pontifex unquam Romanus: aurearum scilicet drachmarū 205000. Huic Papæ, Carolus Gallorum rex, decimas de su-is ecclesiis primum permisit, ut quæstus eius parti-ceps fieret. Bulla reuocationis huius Ioannis, su-per animarum fælicitate ante diem iudicij, habe-tur in Petri Præmonstratensis chronico. Interro-gatus aliquando, quid sbret à veritate remotum? respondit: Vulgi sententia. Nam quicquid laudat (inquit) vituperio dignum est: quicquid cogitat, vanum: quicquid loquitur, falsum: quod impro-bat, bonum est: quod approbat, malum: & quicquid extollit, infame. Sed non videbat, quod ab iis quis pastoribus ac sacrificulis hæc hausissent.
units.tr: When therefore Louis and the Roman nobles had clearly understood John's deeds, and the Roman people, from greatest to least, were bitterly angry that the envoys they had sent to him had been mocked, they all gathered together so that the ancient custom of electing the Pope would be restored to the Church, namely that the one elected by the Roman people should receive confirmation from the Emperor himself. For this reason a certain Peter of Corvara, a Minorite, was made Pope and was called Nicholas V. They declared John a heretic, a tyrant of the Church and not a minister, and a disturber of the public peace of Christians. The Emperor and the Roman council's nobles also submitted all these things to the Catholic Church. So far Marius. Meanwhile John came to the end of his life at Avignon in the year of the Lord 1335, in his ninetieth year, and was buried with great funeral pomp in the cathedral church. He left in his treasury more than any Roman Pope before him: 205,000 gold florins, to be sure. King Charles of the French first granted this Pope tithes from his churches, so that he might share in the profit. The bull revoking John's teaching about the happiness of souls before the day of judgement is found in Peter of Premontré's chronicle. Once, when he was asked what was furthest from the truth, he replied: "The opinion of the common people." For, he said, whatever they praise deserves blame, whatever they think is vain, whatever they say is false, what they disapprove is good, what they approve is evil, and whatever they exalt is infamous. But he did not see that these men's pastors and little priests had drawn these things from him.
138. BENEDICT XII.

units.la: Benedictus duodecimus, patria Tolosanus, professione Cisterciensis (Carmelitam Paleonydo-rus facit) frater Iacobus de Furno antea vocatus, S. Priscæ presbyter Cardinalis, sextodecimo die post Ioannis mortem, Avenione Papalem sedem ascendit. Hic nil (inquit prædictus Marius) Ioanne benignior in Ludovicum extitit. Execrationes innovabat, illum honore regio spoliabat, ac ducatu Bavariæ sententiis privabat. Optimus Ludovicus (videte eius bonitatem ac prudentiam) Germaniam petiit. Omnes electores, duces, episcopos, comites, humanæ diuinæq; sapientiæ doctissimos quosq; convocabat. Et coram omnibus acclamatio-ne publica ac solenni, novas confirmationes antiquis legibus addidit & corroboravit: ingenueq; demonstravit, quod electores Imperij, & præter hos nemo, regem Romanorum eligere debent. Ita ut cui plura accedant principum suffragia, is verum censeatur electus, sive Rex sive Imperator: cum in essentia idem sint, licet nomina diversa cernantur. Qui imperator possit fine Romanae fe-dis confirmatione, imperij iura exercere & admi-nistrare: quiq;[?] mox post principum insinuatio-nem, à Pontifice inungi debeat, si legitime fit ele-ctus. Quòd si recuset Pontifex, possit à quocunq; catholico antisite proclamari imperator & Au-gustus, ut iam diu fieri solebat. Cum maximè in-unctiones istae, solennitates tantum quaedam sint adinuentitiæ, à Pontificibus excogitatæ, nomina tantum, & non res concedentes: in signum defensio-nis ac unionis ecclesiae & imperij Romani. Non e-nim sacramentum fidelitatis Imperator Pontifici tribuit, sed fidei defensionis: quandoquidem hoc iusiurandum, nullam in temporalibus maioritatem operatur.
units.tr: Benedict XII, a native of Toulouse, by profession a Cistercian (Palaeonydorus makes him a Carmelite), formerly called Brother James of Fourn, cardinal priest of Saint Prisca, ascended the papal see at Avignon on the sixteenth day after John's death. Marius, mentioned above, says that he was no kinder to Louis than John had been. He renewed the curses, stripped him of royal honour, and deprived him of the duchy of Bavaria by sentences. The excellent Louis (see his goodness and prudence) made for Germany. He summoned all the electors, dukes, bishops, counts, and the most learned men in human and divine wisdom. Before them all, by public and solemn acclamation, he added and strengthened new confirmations to the ancient laws, and clearly showed that the electors of the empire, and no one else, ought to elect the King of the Romans. So that the one who gains more votes of the princes is judged to be lawfully elected, whether king or emperor, since they are the same in substance, although the names seem different. That an emperor can exercise and administer the rights of the empire without confirmation from the Roman see, and that he ought, immediately after notification to the princes, to be anointed by the Pope, if he has been lawfully elected. But if the Pope refuses, he may be proclaimed emperor and Augustus by any catholic antistes, as had long been the custom. Since these anointings are mainly solemn ceremonies, invented by the Popes, granting names only and not realities, as a sign of the defence and unity of the Church and the Roman empire. For the Emperor does not grant the oath of allegiance to the Pope, but the oath of defence of the faith, since this oath brings no superiority in temporal affairs.

units.la: Praeterea bonus Imperator salsissimum esse o-stendit, per vacationem imperij ius ad Papam de-voluitidq; esse contra sacri imperij libertatem, di-gnitatem, iura ac maiestatem. Sed longa & appro-bata consuetudine, inconcusse a maiorum ordina-tione hactenus obseruata, vacante imperio, admi-nistrandi imperij iura, feuda conferrendi, & nego-tia cætera disponendi, Palatino Rheni deberi, non obstante Clementina. Deinde in sui excusationem coram omnibus rationem fidei suae clarissime ac sanctissime protulit, planeq; confessus est, se Christianum hominem, articulos fidei integrè credere, sicut in ecclesia catholica docebantur. Et de om-nibus quæ illi à Ioanne 23 & à Benedicto 12. obij-ciebantur, se optime purgauit. Quis non admire-tur, Ludouici ita à Pontificibus uexati pietatem? Quid, si armis negotium cum Pontifice transigere uoluisset? At quoniam Christianam fidem ac pie-tatem induxerat, Christiani pariter & cuiusuis hu-mani sanguinis effusionem detęstabatur. Huius op-timi Ludouici bonitas tandem, & à Benedicto Pō-tifice cognita est. Nam cum inter Benedictum & Philippum Galliæ regem simultas quædam esset or-ta, pax inita est statim inter Pontificem & Cæsa-rem: Pontifexq; tanto erga Imperatorem amore deuinctus fuit, ut eum aduersus oratores regis Gal-liæ, qui grauissimè semper in ipsum Imperatorem inuehebantur, defenderet, ac eius innocentiam in-trepidè tutaretur. Quamobrem factum fuit, ut Pontifex hæretici protector, ab ipsis oratoribus ignominiose appellaretur. Quorum uerba, etsi Be-nedictus aliquandiu non parum pertimuisset (nam illi maxima bella indicebant, si Imperatorem ab-soluéret) tamen illum demum absoluit. Et in tota Germania publico decreto publicari iussit, pro-cessus omnes quotquot à Ioanne contra Imperato-rem facti fuerant, nullos esse: nec decuisse Ioannem contra illum talia attentare, cum Pontificis & imperatoris iurisdictiones diffinctae sint. Et aperte testatus est, Ludovicum in omnibus segefsisse, quemadmodum strenuum ac Christianum imperatorem decebat. Sciendum tamen, Pontificem nihil horum ex animo, sed arte, in Ludovici suorum rem fecisse.
units.tr: Furthermore, the good Emperor showed that it was utterly foolish that, during a vacancy of the empire, the right passed to the Pope, and that this was against the freedom, dignity, rights and majesty of the holy empire. But by long and approved custom, unshaken until now by the ordinance of our ancestors, during a vacancy of the empire the Palatine of the Rhine is owed the administration of the rights of the empire, the conferring of fiefs, and the arrangement of other business, notwithstanding the Clementine decree. Then, in his own defence, before everyone he most clearly and most holily set out the account of his faith, and plainly confessed that he, a Christian man, fully believed the articles of faith as they were taught in the catholic Church. And he cleared himself thoroughly of all the charges that had been brought against him by John XXII and Benedict XII. Who would not wonder at Louis's piety, so troubled by the Popes? What if he had wished to settle the matter with the Pope by arms? But since he had adopted the Christian faith and piety, he equally abhorred the shedding of Christian blood and of any human blood. At last the goodness of this excellent Louis was also recognised by Pope Benedict. For when a certain enmity had arisen between Benedict and Philip, King of France, peace was immediately made between the Pope and the Emperor; and the Pope was so bound by love for the Emperor that he defended him against the envoys of the French king, who always attacked the Emperor most bitterly, and boldly protected his innocence. Therefore it came about that the Pope, the protector of a heretic, was shamefully called so by those same envoys. Although Benedict had been rather afraid for some time of their words (for they threatened great wars if he absolved the Emperor), he nonetheless did absolve him at last. And he ordered it to be published by public decree throughout all Germany that all the proceedings which John had brought against the Emperor were null, and that John ought not to have attempted such things against him, since the jurisdictions of the Pope and the Emperor are distinct. And he openly testified that Louis had acted in all things as a vigorous and Christian emperor ought to. Yet it should be known that the Pope did none of this from his heart, but by craft, in order to serve his own interests with respect to Louis.

units.la: Nam cum videret regem Galliae, in cuius ditione ac regno morabatur, simultate quadam secum agere: veritus est, ne si imperatorem[?] hostem haberet, nullum ei super esse auxilium, si Galliae rex in illum aliquid moliri voluisset. Hac igitur ex causa Benedictus, e re sua esse arbitratus est, si Imperatorem sui benevolum redderet: sperans ita fore futurum esse, ut nihil contra ipsum tentare auderet.
units.tr: For when he saw that the King of France, in whose dominion and kingdom he was staying, was dealing with him in some enmity, he feared that if he had the Emperor as an enemy he would have no help left, should the King of France attempt anything against him. For this reason Benedict thought it was to his advantage to make the Emperor well disposed towards him, hoping that it would turn out so that the king would not dare to attempt anything against the Pope.

units.la: Hæ sunt artes, quibus pontifices Romani tyrannidem suam in Dei ecclesia fovèrunt, ac fovent. Hæc sunt arma, quibus inferorum portæ adversus Pontifices prævalent. Hæc Marius. Sed ad instituta redeamus.
units.tr: These are the arts by which the Roman Pontiffs have fostered, and still foster, their tyranny in the Church of God. These are the weapons by which the gates of hell prevail against the Pontiffs. So far Marius. But let us return to our account.

units.la: Benedictus sententias prædecessorum suorum in Ludovicum confirmavit: in Imperialibus Italiæ oppidis vicarios constituit, & senatorum munus Romæ ab imperatore ad se traxit. Rem omnem ad Apostolicæ pœnitentiariæ curam pertinentem excogitavit, taxationes literarum ordine constituens, & divitias ingentes ex omnibus nationibus collegit.
units.tr: Benedict confirmed the sentences of his predecessors against Louis; he appointed vicars in the imperial towns of Italy, and drew to himself from the Emperor the office of senator at Rome. He devised the whole business pertaining to the care of the Apostolic Penitentiary, fixing the taxes on letters in order, and gathered enormous riches from all nations.

units.la: Omnium episcopatuum, pralaturarum ac beneficiorum collationes, sibi & successoribus primum usurpauit, & indoctos à sacerdotijs repulit.
units.tr: He first claimed for himself and his successors the collation of all bishoprics, prelacies and benefices, and drove the unlearned out of the priesthoods.

units.la: Plures monachorum festas[?] reformauit, multasq; ordinationes ac decretales fecit. Vt omnes eius canonicas horas cum nota celebrarent, ac in uno dormitorio cubarent, constituit: nec haberent alios redditus, quàm ad mensæ victum & vestitum. Auenione pontificias ædes, & quidem celebres, cum turribus & pomœrijs ædificauit: & Francisci Petrarchæ sororem pulcherrimam, ab eius fratre Gerhardo, senex adulter, muneribus magnis ad usum improbum emit. Presbyteros Cardinales sex ordinauit, & ecclesiæ beati Petri-stium[?] absens magnis impensis restituit. Theologus inexorabilis, Pontificem habere consanguineos negabat: & alla quedam, Leandro teste, contra Dominicanos edidit. Ecclesiæ, non animarum, sed auri uim multam reliquit: ac meretrices plures aluit. Dum Zotum pictorem peritissimum, pro pingendis martyrum historijs, in nouis suis ædibus conduceret, anno Domini 1342. febre correptus, mox periit, & Auenione sepelitur. De quo tale metrum scribitur:
units.tr: He reformed several monastic orders, and made many ordinances and decretals, so that all his canons would celebrate the canonical hours with a note, and that they would sleep in one dormitory; he established that they should have no other income than food and clothing at the table. At Avignon he built papal residences, and indeed famous ones, with towers and walls; and an old adulterer bought Francis Petrarch's most beautiful sister from her brother Gerard for great gifts, for a shameful purpose. He created six cardinal priests, and at great expense restored the church of Saint Peter, which he had neglected. An inexorable theologian, he denied that a Pope might have blood relations; and he published various other things against the Dominicans, according to the testimony of Leandro. He left much power to the Church, but not over souls, only over gold; and he supported many prostitutes. While he was hiring Zotus, a most skilled painter, to paint the histories of the martyrs in his new residence, in the year of the Lord 1342 he was seized by fever, soon died, and was buried at Avignon. Of him the following verse is written:

units.la: Iste fiat uero laicis mors, uipera clero: Deuius à uero, turba repleta mero. Eius erant hæ sententiæ: Talis esto filius, quales cognatos habere cupis, Malum mortem, bonum magis uitium formidat. Quæsita legendo, serua: quæ nescis, legendo disce. Acquè [?] turpe est carere amicis, atq; eos sæpe mutare. Regi turpius est uinci beneficijs, quàm armis.
units.tr: Let this be death to laymen, a viper to the clergy: straying from the truth, a crowd filled with wine. These were his sayings: Be such a son as you wish your relatives to be. Evil fears death, good fears vice more. What you have sought by reading, keep; what you do not know, learn by reading. It is equally shameful to lack friends and often to change them. It is more shameful for a king to be conquered by kindnesses than by arms.
139. Clement the Sixth.

units.la: Clemens sextus, patria Lemouicensis, professio-ne Benedictinus, Petrus Rogerius antea nuncupatus, & abbas Fiscanensis ex Rhotomagensi archi-episcopo, Avenione pontifex Benedicto surrogatus fuit. Hic sua factione supra modum Roma-num turbavit imperium. Episcopos enim omnes, & principes, cum Imperatore Ludovico Bavaro sentientes (Nauclero teste) excommunicavit, in contumeliam eius creabat Vicecomites, Imperij vicarios: & ille uicissim Ludovicus in ecclesia ditione, Imperij uicarios posuit. Hieronymus Marius in Eusebio captiuo, Clementis uiolentiam sic describit: Clemens sextus, inquit, homo mulierum, honoris ac potentiæ cupidissimus, diabolico furore percitus, literas scriptas foribus templorum affixit, quibus imperatori grauissimarum pœnarum supplicium comminabatur, nisi infra triduum suis satisfaceret cupiditatibus, & ab occupatione iu-rium [?] rium imperij abstineret. Mira istius inclementia Cle-mentis crudelitas. Imperator Fran[?]cfordium venit: & paratus omnia sibi iniuncta pro uirili facere, per oratores petijt, ut illi veniam daret, illumq; in fui gratiam reciperet. At pontifex oratoribus di-cebat, se nunquam Ludouico veniam daturum, nisi prius omnes errores ac haereses confiteretur, & imperium deponeret, & se atq; filios suos & bona omnia in manus ac voluntatem ipsius reponeret: polliceretur q; se nihil horum rursus suscepturum, nisi ex ipsius Pontificis gratia. Et horum omnium formulam quandam scripto oratoribus tradidit: quamq;, ut Ludouico offerrent, mandauit. Ubi hic Pastoris forma? Ubi patris affectus? Ubi fandi-tatis specimen? Bonus imperator, ne qua forte o-rirentur bella, aut cædes, si non se subijceret, for-mulam Pontificis accepit, eaq; inspecta, Christiano sanguini consuluit. Hunc enim plurimum effunden-dum consipiciebat, si in sententia perstitisset. Ideo il-lam non tantum sigillo corroborabat, sed & iura-mento se omnia seruaturum esse pollicebatur.
units.tr: Clement the Sixth, a native of Limoges, a Benedictine by profession, formerly named Peter Roger, and abbot of Fécamp, was appointed pope at Avignon in succession to Benedict, by the archbishop of Rouen. By his faction he disturbed the Roman empire beyond measure. For he excommunicated all the bishops and princes who sided with the emperor Louis of Bavaria (according to Naucler), and in insult to him he created viscounts, vicars of the empire; and Louis in turn appointed imperial vicars within the Church's dominion. Hieronymus Marius, in his Eusebius Captive, describes Clement's violence thus: "Clement the Sixth," he says, "a man of women, most eager for honour and power, stirred by diabolical fury, fixed to the doors of the temples letters threatening the emperor with the punishment of most grievous penalties unless within three days he satisfied his desires and abstained from usurping the rights of the empire." Wonderful is the cruelty of this Clement's harshness! The emperor came to Frankfurt and, ready to do for his part everything enjoined on him, sought through envoys that the pope would pardon him and receive him back into favour. But the pontiff told the envoys that he would never grant Louis pardon unless he first confessed all errors and heresies, laid down the empire, and placed himself, his sons and all his goods in the hands and will of the pontiff himself; and promised that he would take up none of these things again except by the pontiff's grace. He handed the envoys a written formula of all these things, which he ordered them to offer to Louis. Where is the form of a minister here? Where the affection of a father? Where the sign of holiness? The good emperor, lest wars or slaughter should arise if he did not submit, accepted the pontiff's formula and, having examined it, took thought for Christian blood, since he saw that much of it would be shed if he persisted in his opinion. So he not only confirmed it with his seal but also promised on oath that he would keep all of it.

units.la: Quod dum Pontifex audijfet, admodum mi-ratus est. Sed num Ludouicum in gratiam suam recepit? Num illi aliquod beneuoli animi signum ostendit? Audite quomodo res se habuerit. Ludo-uicus [?]ormulam illam principibus, electoribus, ac oratoribus ciuitatum imperij demostrauit. Prin-cipes articulos quosdam, quoniam in perniciem ac destructionem imperij à Pontifice concepti fue-rant, detestati sunt: Imperatoriq; firmum auxili-um polliciti sunt, si iura imperij, ut ante secerat, defensare uellet. Per oratores Clementem roga-runt, ut ab eis articulis, in lasionem sacri imperij excogitatis, abstineret. Et nihil præterea aut a-gentes aut petentes, oratores discesserunt. Clemes uero borum omnium causam in Ludouicum trans-ferens, eius ac filiorum exterminium und[?] medita-batur. In cœna Domini crudelissime illum execra-batur, Ioannis pontificis processus omnes durissi-mos innouabat, hæreticum ac scb[?] smaticum decla-rabat. Principes electores admonebat, ut alium e-ligerent imperatorem. Archiepiscopum Mogun-tinensem dignitate, ac eligendi authoritate priua-uit, eo quod, cum imperatoris innocentiam cogno-sceret, sacram eius maiestatem uiolare nolebat. Ceteri uero electores, ingenti pecuniarum largi-tione corrupti à Ioäne Bohemorum rege, Carolum ipsius filium, regem Romanorum decernebant: quem Clemens inclemens paulo post in publico con-storio approbauit. At qua horrida bella enar-rare posset, quæ ex Clementis huius beatissimi imperium admisso scelere orta sunt[?] uiginti mili-bus bus Gallorum per Eduuardum Anglum profira-tis, & Ioanne Caroli patre cum multis nobilibus oc-cifo. Ludouicus autem, dum Pontificis processus adhuc curaret, imperij administratione relicta, ex Clementis insidijs, uenenum bibit, ex quo atq; corporis collisione mortuus est. Hæc Marius.
units.tr: When the pontiff heard this, he was greatly astonished. But did he receive Louis back into his favour? Did he show him any sign of goodwill? Hear how matters stood. Louis showed that formula to the princes, electors and envoys of the cities of the empire. The princes detested certain articles, since they had been devised by the pontiff for the ruin and destruction of the empire, and they promised the emperor firm help if he wished to defend the rights of the empire as he had done before. Through envoys they asked Clement to abstain from those articles, devised to injure the holy empire. The envoys achieved nothing further, neither by acting nor by asking, and they departed. Clement, however, transferring the cause of all this onto Louis, was plotting his extermination and that of his sons. On Maundy Thursday he cursed him most cruelly, renewed all the most severe proceedings of Pope John, and declared him a heretic and schismatic. He urged the electors to choose another emperor. He deprived the archbishop of Mainz of his dignity and of his right to elect, because, knowing the emperor's innocence, he was unwilling to violate his sacred majesty. The other electors, however, corrupted by the huge largesse of money from John, king of the Bohemians, decreed Charles, John's son, king of the Romans; and Clement the merciless soon approved him in public consistory. But what horrible wars could one recount that arose from the crime committed under the empire of this most blessed Clement: twenty thousand Frenchmen struck down by Edward the Englishman, and Charles's father John killed with many nobles! Louis, meanwhile, while still attending to the pontiff's proceedings, having left the administration of the empire, drank poison through Clement's snares, and died from it and from the collapse of his body. So Marius.

units.la: Hinc agnoscant populi, quàm omnibus bonis detestandam tyrannidem, Pontifices Romani in Christi ecclesia exerceant. Optimos imperatores iniusto anathemate feriunt: eos Imperiali maiesta-te omnibus bonis, omnibusq; liberis, quæ omnia à Deo ipso acceperunt, expoliant. Electores imperij authoritate sua priuant, aliosq; quicunq; illis placuerint, substituunt. Imperatores, inuitis omnibus imperij principibus ac ciuitatibus, eligunt: seditio-num ac bellorum semina serunt, ut Christianus san-guis ferro exhauriatur optant ac moliuntur. Si fer-ro id præstare non possint, ut id contingat letali-bus potionibus procurant. Imperium ipsum deniq; ad eam deduxerunt calamitatem, in qua hodie ad-huc iacet. Is enim Carolus, quem ipsi inuitis om-nibus imperij ordinibus imperatorem creârunt, vt filium sibi successorem pararet, Electores adeo magnis pollicitationibus ac largitionibus corrum-pit, vt publica imperij uectigalia illis oppigneran-tur, quæ & hodie retinent: atq; ideo Romanum imperium sese attollere non potest. Nam tum Electores Carolum iureiurando coegerunt, ne pignora unquam revocare posset: unde tandem factum est, ut imperio prostrato, Turca ecclesias Christi invaserit, earumq; plurimas destruxerit: parumq; absit, ne ubique per totam Europam ferro, ac misserrimo Mahumetici dogmatis iugo debacchetur. Resipiscent ne aliquando Christiani principes, ut summum ecclesiae Christi hostem ac tyrannum agnoscant? Quomodo Solymanum Ottbomanum à Christi ecclesia arcebunt, si domesticum hunc Turcam non arcent? Nunquam sane. Is namq; cum inter principes Christianos discordias ac bella serere & fovere omni studio, pollicitationibus, largitionibus, proditionibus, variisq; dolis contendat, in causa est, tum ut ipse semper aliquot principum amicitiam servans, tyrannidem suam tanquam divinum quoddam numen praefervet: tum ut Christiani principes semper inter se dissidentes, nunquam adversus Turcam coëunire possint. Quis igitur non, cum tales videat esse Pontifices, dicere audeat, contra eos inferorum portas non praevalere?
units.tr: From this let the peoples recognise how detestable to all good men is the tyranny which the Roman pontiffs exercise in the Church of Christ. They strike the best emperors with unjust anathema; they strip them of imperial majesty and of all their goods and all their freedoms, which they had received from God himself. They deprive the electors of the empire by their own authority and substitute whomever they please. They choose emperors against the will of all the princes and cities of the empire; they sow the seeds of sedition and war, and they desire and contrive that Christian blood be drawn by the sword. If they cannot achieve this by the sword, they bring it about by deadly potions. Finally, they have brought the empire itself to that calamity in which it still lies today. For that Charles, whom they created emperor against the will of all the orders of the empire, in order to provide a son for himself as successor, corrupted the electors with such great promises and largesse that the public revenues of the empire were pledged to them, and they retain them even today; and therefore the Roman empire cannot raise itself up. For then the electors forced Charles by oath never to be able to redeem those pledges. Hence at last it came about that, with the empire prostrate, the Turk invaded the churches of Christ and destroyed very many of them; and it is hardly far off that he will rage everywhere throughout Europe with the sword and the most wretched yoke of the Mahumetan doctrine. Will the Christian princes ever come to their senses and acknowledge the pontiff as the chief enemy and tyrant of the Church of Christ? How will they keep Suleiman the Ottoman from the Church of Christ if they do not keep off this domestic Turk? Never, surely. For he, since he strives with every effort, by promises, largesse, betrayals and various tricks, to sow and foster discord and war among the Christian princes, is the cause of this: partly so that he himself, always keeping the friendship of some princes, may preserve his tyranny like some divine power, and partly so that the Christian princes, always at odds with one another, can never unite against the Turk. Who, then, seeing such men to be pontiffs, would not dare to say that the gates of hell do not prevail against them?

units.la: Hic Papa Clemens, ad quinquagesimum annum, auri gratia iubileum reduxit: & absens anno Domini 1350, Romae celebravit. Et erant quo-tidie[?] tidie infra dictum annum (ut Præmostratensis narrat) quinque millia peregrinorum, intrantium et exeuntium Romam, ut bene poterant computari. Duodecim Cardinales diuersis temporibus confti-tuit, ex quibus plures erant monachi, nepotes, atque affinitate sibi coniuncti: et Petrum à Casa Carmelitam, patriarchâm Hierosolymitanum fecit: ac Petrum Beretum eiusdem professionis, Vasionensem episcopum. Palatiu Auenione pro media parte ampliauit, consistoriumq; magnum ædificauit, et tyrannides in Italia per ignobiles excitauit. Hanc monem presbyterum canonizauit, ac Flagellatorum sectam diplomate damnauit. Episcopo Bambergensi potestatem dedit absoluendi eos qui Ludouico[?] adhaeserant, sed his conditionibus: primo, ut fidelitatem iurarent tanquam Dei vicario: secundo, ut crederent imperatorem non habere ius constituendi Papam, aut deponendi: tertio, ut ne-minem agnoscerent regem vel Cæsarem, non confirmatum à Papa. Dum familiares demum ac domestici prandium adijssent, relicto ei solo cubiculario, apostemate ta-stus[?], anno Domini 1352 su-bito corruit atq; ex-pirauit.
units.tr: Pope Clement, for the sake of gold, brought the jubilee back to the fiftieth year, and though absent, celebrated it at Rome in 1350. And (as the Premonstratensian narrates) within that year there were every day five thousand pilgrims entering and leaving Rome, as they could well be counted. He appointed twelve cardinals at various times, of whom many were monks, nephews and related to him by marriage; and he made Peter de Casa, a Carmelite, patriarch of Jerusalem, and Peter Bérète of the same profession bishop of Vaison. He enlarged the palace at Avignon by half and built a great consistory, and stirred up tyrannies in Italy through men of low birth. He canonized the priest Hanc monem and condemned the sect of the Flagellants by bull. He gave the bishop of Bamberg power to absolve those who had adhered to Louis, but on these conditions: first, that they swear fealty as to God's vicar; second, that they believe the emperor has no right to appoint or depose a pope; third, that they acknowledge no one as king or Caesar who has not been confirmed by the pope.
