When at last his familiars and household had gone in to dinner, leaving him alone with his chamberlain, he was seized by an abscess, and in the year of the Lord 1352 he suddenly collapsed and expired.

units.la: EX BVLLA HVIVS CLEMENTIS super anno lubileo.
units.tr: From the bull of this Clement concerning the jubilee year.

units.la: Quicunq; peregrinandi causa ad sanctam ciuitatem (Romam, malorum omnium sententiam, intelligit) accedere proposuerit, illa die qua de bono spiritu suo uiam arripere voluerit, eligere possit confessorem seu confessores, & in uia & in locis aliis quibuscunq;. Quibus quidem confessoribus auctoritate nostra concedimus plenam potestatem, absoluendi omnes casus Papales, ac si persona nostra ibi esset. Item concedimus, quòd si vere confessus in uia moriatur, quòd ab omnibus peccatis suis sit immunis penitus, & absolutus. Et nihilominus (nota scelestissimum Antichristum) prorsus mandamus angelis paradisi, quatenus animam à purgatorio penitus absolutam in paradisi gloriam introducant, &c. Atq; in alia Bulla: Nolumus, inquit, quòd poena inferni sibi aliquatenus infligatur: concedens insuper cruce signatis, ad eorum uota, tres aut quatuor animas, quas uellent, è purgatorio posse eripere. Quam erroneam intolerabilem, quæ temeritatem atq; hæresim, tunc Parisiensis schola palam detestata est, atq; corripuit. Sed fortassis poenitens hodie, quòd non hyperbolicum illum Clementis zelum pio aliquo commento interpretati sunt, ut res valeret potius quàm periret, cum propter eorum affirmare uel negare nihil mutatur in re. Centum millia pauperum clericorum circa Auenionem eo anno ex pluribus nationibus erant, pro impetrandis indulgentijs. Et fortasse ut lucri gratia confessores essent, ac diabolicis hiis la-queis simplicium hominum conscientias domi mise-rabiliter captiuarent.
units.tr: Whoever intends to go to the holy city (Rome, which he understands to be the sentence of all evils) for the sake of pilgrimage may, on the day when he wishes to set out on his way under a good spirit, choose a confessor or confessors, both on the road and in any other places whatever. To these confessors we grant, by our authority, full power to absolve all papal cases, as if our own person were present. Likewise we grant that if someone who has truly confessed dies on the way, he is wholly free and absolved from all his sins. And nevertheless (note the most wicked Antichrist), we expressly command the angels of paradise to lead the soul, completely absolved from purgatory, into the glory of paradise, etc. And in another bull: "We do not wish," he says, "that the punishment of hell be inflicted on them in any way." He further grants to those marked with the cross that, as they wish, they may snatch three or four souls, whichever they choose, out of purgatory. The Parisian school then openly condemned and rebuked this erroneous and intolerable claim, which was rashness and heresy. But perhaps today they regret not having interpreted that extravagant zeal of Clement by some pious contrivance, so that the thing would be saved rather than perish; for nothing in the matter is changed by their affirming or denying it. There were a hundred thousand poor clerics around Avignon that year, from several nations, seeking to obtain indulgences. And perhaps they were made confessors for the sake of gain, and wretchedly ensnared the consciences of simple people at home with these diabolical snares.
140. Innocent VI.

units.la: INnocentius sextus, natione Gallus, patria etiam Lemouicensis, Stephanus antea uocatus, utriusq; iuris doctor, ex aduocato Claromontanus episcopus, & ex Cardinale Hostiensi ac summo poenitentiario Pontifex factus fuit. Erat ille uir uitæ Papalis, iurisconsultissimus, superciliosus, pertinax, seuerus, & qui ecclesiastica beneficia precium[?] persoluentibus liberaliter dedit. Post initum Papatum reseruationes quasdam à Clemente praedecessore factas, ad futurum respiciens commodum, prudenter suspendit: constituitq; statim, ut praelati, quot quot habebant beneficia, ad suas ecclesias proficiscerentur, non ut Euangelium recte praedicarent, sed ut Papistica ludibria extollerent ac retinerent, & fructus earum in ocio & ad luxum colligerent. Dicebat enim, oues pascuas à proprio pastore (ton-sore, aut corrasore potius) non à mercenario custodiri debere: impensam quoq; domesticam, quæ Magna erat, parcus & auarus imminuit: familiam suam ad certum, adhuc tamen non satis honestum (uide Petrarchâm) redigens numerum. Nec domi uoluit, nisi suis affectibus & commodis seruientes, habere: & ut idem facerent carnales (Cardinales dixissem) acerrimo edicto mandauit: dignitatis, su-am atque omnium ecclesiasticorum uitam caeteris exemplo esse debere: ita ut ad suum (non Christi ser-uatoris, qui Papalem curiam non tenuit) exem-plum, plebs Christiana respiceret. Praeterea uero Papalis palatij auditoribus (magnis certe nebulo-nibus) salaria constituit, ne suis faucibus quicquam surriperent. In uita parcus erat (scriptores inqui-unt) sed in sumptu bellico largissimus, dum ablata repeteret spolia. Aegidium Hispanum, e gente Ca-rillâ, Cardinalem Sabinum è latere suo in Italiam misit, qui bello suos hostes persequeretur, ditiones ecclesiasticas in signi tyrannide partas, tutiores illi reddēret,
units.tr: Innocent VI, a Frenchman by nation and also from Limoges, formerly called Stephen, doctor of both laws, was made pope from an advocate, then bishop of Clermont, and from a cardinal of Ostia and chief penitentiary. He was a man of papal life, most learned in law, haughty, obstinate, severe, and one who generously gave ecclesiastical benefices to those paying the price. After beginning his papacy, looking to future advantage, he prudently suspended certain reservations made by his predecessor Clement. He at once ordained that the prelates, as many as held benefices, should go to their churches, not to preach the Gospel correctly, but to extol and maintain Papist mockeries, and to collect the fruits of them in idleness and luxury. For he said that sheep ought to be guarded by their own shepherd (a shearer, or rather a fleecer), not by a hireling. He also reduced the domestic expenses, which were great, being sparing and avaricious. He cut his household to a fixed number, still not respectable enough (see Petrarch). He did not wish to have at home any but those who served his own desires and interests; and so that the carnal men (I would have said Cardinals) might do the same, he ordered by a most severe edict that the dignity of their office and the life of all churchmen ought to be an example to others, so that the Christian people might look to his example, and not to that of Christ the Saviour, who did not keep a papal court. Moreover, he fixed salaries for the auditors of the papal palace (certainly great scoundrels), so that they would snatch nothing from his jaws. He was sparing in his way of life (the writers say), but most lavish in war expenses, while he sought to recover the lost spoils. He sent Giles of Spain, of the family of Carrillo, the Cardinal of Sabina, from his side into Italy, to pursue his enemies in war and to make more secure the ecclesiastical dominions acquired by tyranny.

units.la: Per Petrum Thomam Aquitanum, Carmeli-tam, huius Pontificis legatum, Bononiae in eius po-testatem venit: qui & illuc, ut Abadoni per egre-gie inseruiret, Theologiam Sorbonicam primus adduxit. Illi propterea Pattensem [?], Militensem atque Coronensem episcopatum, Cretensem archi-episcopatum, ac tandem Constantinopolitanum patripatriarchatum dedit. Huius Innocentij pontificis iussu, Carolus quartus Romae a ducibus Cardina-libus imperij coronam accepit, sed hac adiecta conditione, ut neque Romae neque in Italia diutius moraretur. Ille nihilominus, cum domum uenisset, ar-chiprefulem Moguntinensem admonuit, ut clerum in uestibus, calceis, capillis, et toto uitae habitu reformaret, sub poena amissionis omnium beneficiorum. Coram hoc Pontifice, Ricardus archiepi-[?]pus Armachanus, contra Mendicantes fraterculos nouem propositiones publicauit. In primo sui Pon-tificatu, anno, tyrannus ille Babylonicus Ioannem Rochetaylladam Franciscanum, quod aliqua in cle-rum dixisset, Auenione cremari iussit. Plura ille prophetauit (inquit Præmonstratensis) de Antichristo et de summis pontificibus futura: et ideo de hæresi suspectus habebatur. Cœpit enim prophetizare anno Domini 1345. tempore Clementis sexti, et multa ex suis uaticiniis uisa sunt eue-nisse, etc. Festum lanceæ et clauorum Christi, hic Pontifex ordinauit, ut et ea mortua idola à Christianis Dei loco adorarentur. Mœnibus et fossis Auenionem circumdedit, et extra urbem Carthu-sienses fundauit. Cumq; classem pararet in Tur-cas, anno Domini 1362. Romanis tumultuantibus, perturbati animi tædio uitam exhalauit, apud distos[?] Carthusianos extra Auenionem sepultus. Ante te huius Pontificis mortem tanta solis defectio facta est, quanta prius unquam: quasi tam tenebrosum id tempus fuerit, ut de veritatis luce nihil pene fit in ecclesia relictum, Apoc.6. Eius etiam tempore, ut Maffeus testatur, flamma quaedam post solis occasum diu visa, terribile ostentabat incendium: deinde locustarum immensitas multis in locis, erosis frugibus, etiam virgulta depasta est.
units.tr: Through Peter Thomas of Aquitaine, a Carmelite, legate of this pope, he came into his power at Bologna. There, too, to serve Abadon outstandingly, he was the first to bring the Sorbonne theology. For this reason he gave him the bishoprics of Pattensis [?], Militensis and Coronensis, the archbishopric of Crete, and at last the patriarchate of Constantinople. By the order of this pope Innocent, Charles IV received the crown at Rome from the cardinal dukes of the empire, but on this added condition, that he should not remain longer at Rome or in Italy. Nevertheless, when he had returned home, he admonished the archbishop of Mainz to reform the clergy in their garments, shoes, hair and their whole manner of life, under penalty of loss of all benefices. In the presence of this pope, Richard, archbishop of Armagh, published nine propositions against the mendicant friars. In the first year of his pontificate that Babylonian tyrant ordered John Rochetaillade, a Franciscan, to be burned at Avignon, because he had said some things against the clergy. The Premonstratensian says that he prophesied many things concerning Antichrist and the future supreme pontiffs, and for that reason he was held under suspicion of heresy. For he began to prophesy in the year of the Lord 1345, in the time of Clement VI, and many of his predictions were seen to come to pass, etc. This pope instituted the feast of the lance and nails of Christ, so that even those dead idols would be adored by Christians in God's place. He surrounded Avignon with walls and ditches, and founded the Carthusians outside the city. When he was preparing a fleet against the Turks, in the year of the Lord 1362, while the Romans were rioting, he breathed out his life, worn down by weariness of a troubled mind, and was buried among the Carthusians outside Avignon. Before the death of this pope there was an eclipse of the sun as great as any before it, as if that time had been so dark that almost nothing of the light of truth was left in the Church (Rev. 6). In his time also, as Maffei testifies, a certain flame was seen for a long time after sunset, showing a terrible conflagration; then an immense swarm of locusts, in many places, devoured the crops and even stripped the young shoots.
141. Urban the Fifth.

units.la: VRbanus quintus, patria & ipse Lemouicensis, Grimaldus Grisaunt antea nominatus, Guilhelmi medici & Angli filius, monachus Benedictinus, Antisiodorensis primum, postea Massiliensis ad S. Victorem abbas absens in legatione Pontifex creabatur. Vocatus itaque Auenionem, & Papa salutatus, magnus Papalium canonum doctor, atque arrogantissimus mente magister, mox ad tuendam malignantis ecclesiae libertatem in auaritiis, luxuriis ac pompis animum ferio adiecit. Eorumque opera in his prosequendis ille usus est, qui in eam rem toti animi essent: praecipue Aegidium Hispanum, Cardinalem Sabinensem, cum summa potestate legitum rursus misit. Qui tanquam alter Satan, ad nocendum paratus, Italiam perambulabat, & Vicecomites aliosq; rectores miris [?] calamitatibus & cladibus pressit, ac sese submittere eidē ecclesiæ omnes terrore cogit. Ipseq; pontifex Vr-banus, quarto sui Pontificatus anno, cum Caraimlibus[?] unà Romam ueniens, constituit, non Euange-lium regni Dei prædicare ad Christi gloriam, sed obsoleta restcere templa ad idololatricam pompā. Ecclesiam S. Pauli alieno sumptu reparauit: & a-postolorum caluarias diu quasitas, ac tandem in-uenias, capsis aureis & argenteis operuit, ad ualo-rem 30 millium florenorum: atq; in loco ubi nunc uisuntur, condidit. Aedes Pontificias tum Romæ tum Viterbij, & in Monte Flascone construxit, ut ei ac cæteris Pontificibus eò proficisci liceret, vi-tandi estus causa. Caroli Imperatoris uxorem Ro-mæ coronauit, & crucem contra Turcas prædica-ri iussit. Siciliæ reginæ Ioannæ in Quadragesima rosam dedit, ac de eadem quotannis danda in do-minica Lætare, constitutionem fecit, Apostolicæ cu-ria regimen tribuit, & in sesto S. Ioannis Baptistæ symbolum Nicænum cantari præcepit.
units.tr: Urban the Fifth, also a native of Limoges, formerly named Grimoald Grisaunt, was the son of William, a physician and Englishman. He was a Benedictine monk, first abbot of Auxerre and afterwards of Marseille at St Victor's. He was created pope while absent on a legation. Summoned to Avignon and greeted as pope, he was a great doctor of the papal canons and a most arrogant master of mind. Soon he applied himself, with all his heart, to defending the liberty of the wicked Church in its greed, luxury and pomp. In pursuing these aims he used those men who were wholly devoted to such work, above all Giles of Spain, Cardinal of Sabina, whom he sent again as legate with full power. Like another Satan, ready to do harm, this man roamed through Italy and oppressed the Visconti and other rulers with wonderful disasters and slaughters, forcing everyone by terror to submit to the same Church. Pope Urban himself, in the fourth year of his pontificate, came to Rome with his retinue, and resolved not to preach the gospel of the kingdom of God to the glory of Christ, but to restore old temples for idolatrous pomp. He repaired the church of St Paul at another's expense. He covered the skulls of the apostles, long sought and at last found, with golden and silver caskets worth 30,000 florins, and set them in the place where they are now shown. He built papal residences at Rome, at Viterbo and on Monte Fiascone, so that he and the other popes might go there to avoid the heat. He crowned the wife of Emperor Charles at Rome, and ordered the cross to be preached against the Turks. He gave a rose to Queen Joan of Sicily on Lent, and made a decree that it should be given every year on the Sunday Laetare. He granted government to the Apostolic court, and on the feast of St John the Baptist he ordered the Nicene Creed to be sung.

units.la: In Auenionensi palatio plura ædificauit, & in Monte Pessulano medicorum ac decretorum scho-las condidit. Ad illum uoti causa, Brigitta Suetica Romam uenit, & suorum Brigittanorum ordinem ex utroq; sexu confirmari procuravit. Breui postea in Galliam reuersus, Ioannem Haucuith[?] Anglum Aegidij Cardinalis de functi loco, copijs suis militaribus ducem praefecit, ut tandiu ditionem ecclesiasticam ab hoste tueretur, quoad ipse reuerteretur. Redire namq; ad Italiam ei in animo fuit. Verum dum in Gallias proficisceretur, spe redu-cenda in urbem curiae anno Domini 1371. apud Massiliam rebus humanis excessit, non sine veneni suspicione. Grauia ille bella (Sabellico teste) in Ita-lia gessit, cum principibus etiam, ab antecessoribus suis prius contra Imperatorem constitutis, & eorum plures occidit. Vuicelius tamen nihil de eo re-perit, quod uel magnopere laudari uel uituperari queat, sola Platinae lectione contentus. Huius Vrbani tempore, archiepiscopus Coloniensis uxoratus fuit, ut Petrus Praemonstratensis refert. Sub eo quoque Vrbano surrexerunt ordines Iesuitarũ & Sco----petinorum[?], ut author est Ioannes Paleonydorus, lib. 3. cap. 11. Tripartiti fasciculi.
units.tr: He built many things in the palace at Avignon, and founded schools of medicine and of canon law at Montpellier. Brigitta of Sweden came to Rome to him on account of a vow, and she obtained confirmation of the order of her Brigittines of both sexes. Shortly afterwards he returned to France and set John Haucuith, an Englishman, in place of the deceased Cardinal Giles, putting him in command of his military forces, so that he might guard the ecclesiastical domain from the enemy until Urban himself came back. For he intended to return to Italy. But while he was travelling to France, hoping to bring the court back into the city, he died at Marseille in the year of the Lord 1371, not without suspicion of poison. He waged grievous wars in Italy (according to Sabellicus), including against princes whom his predecessors had earlier set against the Emperor, and he killed many of them. Wicelius, however, found nothing about him that could be greatly praised or blamed, being content with the reading of Platina alone. In the time of this Urban, the archbishop of Cologne was married, as Peter of Prémontré relates. Under this same Urban the orders of the Jesuits and of the Scopetines arose, as the author John Paleonydorus says, book 3, chapter 11 of the Tripartite Bundle.
142. Gregory the Eleventh.

units.la: Gregorius undecimus, patria quoq; Lemouicen-sis, Petrus Belfertius[?] antea dictus, S. Mariae noue diaconus Cardinalis, & Clementis sexti nepos ex fratre (si non filius) Vrbano suffectus erat. Hunc adolescentem (inquit Platina) vix decimum septimum annum attingentem, praedictus Clemen
units.tr: Gregory the Eleventh, also a native of Limoges, formerly called Peter Belfertius, a cardinal deacon of Santa Maria Nova and nephew by a brother (if not a son) of Clement the Sixth, was appointed as successor to Urban. This young man (says Platina), scarcely having reached his seventeenth year, the aforesaid Clement

units.la: Hic (cum nomine praedicto) Vrbanum VI. successor fuit. Clemens eius patruus Cardinalem creauit. Et ne uideretur (mysterium intellige) carni ac sanguini magis quam ecclesiae consuluisse, eundem ad exqui-sitissimos doctores in Italiam disciplinae gratia mittere maxime ad Baldum, qui tum Perusij Papalia decreta legebat. Vbi tantum in quouis eius doctri-nae genere profecit, ut idem Baldus eius authori-tate in confirmandis rebus dubijs plerunq; utere-tur, &c. Qui mox tandem Papatu, Gebennensem Cardinalem in Italiam misit, ut res ecclesiasticas consueto more curaret. Sed cum fere omnes Italiae ciuitates ab eo deficerent, ut Volaterranus refert, monitu Catherinae Senensis sororis Dominicanae, quae postmodum adoranda fuit, & Baldi Perusi-ni, eius olim praeceptoris, cū 12. triremibus ex Gallia rediit Romam, anno Domini 1376. Florenti-nos, qui defectionis authores erant, & omnia quae Pontificis fuerant circa se oppida, occupauerant, sacris interdixit. Quibus tandem execrationum eius fulmina spernentibus, crudelia bella intulit. Alias causas reditus eius in Italiam, alij ponunt.
units.tr: This man (under the name mentioned above) was the successor of Urban the Sixth. His uncle Clement made him a cardinal. And lest he seem (understand the mystery) to have cared more for flesh and blood than for the Church, he sent him into Italy to the most exquisite doctors for the sake of learning, especially to Baldus, who was then lecturing on papal decrees at Perugia. There he made such progress in every branch of that learning that Baldus himself would often rely on his authority in settling doubtful matters, and so on. Soon after, as pope, he sent the Cardinal of Geneva into Italy to look after ecclesiastical affairs in the usual way. But when nearly all the cities of Italy revolted from him, as Volaterranus relates, he returned to Rome from Gaul with twelve triremes in the year of the Lord 1376, on the advice of Catherine of Siena, a Dominican sister who was afterwards to be worshipped, and of Baldus of Perugia, his former teacher. He forbade the sacraments to the Florentines, who were the authors of the revolt and had seized all the towns that had been papal property. When at last they scorned the thunderbolts of his curses, he waged cruel wars against them. Others give different reasons for his return to Italy.

units.la: Brigitta mulier (inquit Maffeus) ab Hierosolymis Romam ruersa, Gregorio scripsit, Dominum uelle (muliebre somnium) ut curia Romana domum reducatur. Crantzius addit cuiusdam episcopi increpationem, quod reliqua ecclesia curiam sequeretur. tur. A quo Pontifex responsum hoc accepit: Et tu (ait) Romanus Papa, caeteris exempla daturus, episcopatum tuum non repetit.
units.tr: A woman, Brigitta (says Maffeus), who had come to Rome from Jerusalem, wrote to Gregory that the Lord wished (a woman's dream) that the Roman court be brought home. Crantzius adds a rebuke from a certain bishop, that the rest of the Church followed the court. The pope received this answer from him: "And you, Roman pope, who are to give an example to the others, do not recover your bishopric."

units.la: Sedem igitur ex Gallis, duarum mulierum & unius episcopi suasu, Romam iterum transtulit; septuagesimo migrationis anno. Decimus per to-tum Romanum imperium exegit Gregorius, & moenia urbis ac privata quaedam aedificia, ruinam minantia magna ex parte, ad pompam restituit. Sed nihil dico de Christianis moribus, ubiq; tunc ad exitium usq; labefactatis. Officium de inventione S. Crucis fieri fecit, & nativitatis beatae Mariae Virginis addidit. Tandem vero, cum omnia accurate egissent (inquit Platina) quae ad Pontificem pertinerent anno Domini 1378 intolerabili dolore vexatus, ex vita migravit. In ipsa sua mortis hora, in Avenionensi palatio ignis accensus dicitur, qui nec extingui potuit, donec maior eius pars esset exusta: sequebaturq; in Papatu schisma omnium maximum. Tunc clerus (ut Matthaeus scribit) populusq; Romanus concurrentes ad Cardinales, rogaverunt ut Italum quempiam, non Gallum, eligerent: ne curia rursus migraret in Galliam. Cum autem coepissent eligere, subito[?] orta est. Erant Itali quatuor, Gallici tredecim: qui facile praevaluissent, sed non audebant. Stabant Romani in armis, & vim faciebant. Igitur nono Aprilis, feria sexta, elegerunt Vrbanum se-xtum,qui coronatus fuit 18 eiusdem mensis, in die Paschæ. Tantum ille. Sub hac Pontifice, novum genus vel secta mirabilem quorundam daemoniacorum tam virorum quàm mulierum, praeter omnem verecundiam chorizantium, Petrus Pramonstratensis fuisse describit. Et anno Domini 1375 ex Aquisgrano in Hannoniam, atque inde in Franciam venisse demonstrat, quòd papæ Gregorij ac suorum Cardinalium commigrationem Romam praediuina-[?] re poterat. His videbatur, quòd in sanguinis flumine saltarent: quamuis astantes nihil tale viderint. Vulgus interpretabatur, quòd populus ille male baptizatus esset à presbyteris tenentibus meretri-ces. Propterea (inquit) proposuerat insurgere in clerum, eos occidendo, & bona eorum diripiendo: nisi Deus de remedio providisset per con-iurationes quasdam, &c. De hac chorizatione sit rhythmus,
units.tr: Therefore, on the advice of two women and one bishop, he moved the seat from France back to Rome, in the seventieth year of the migration. Gregory exacted tithes throughout the whole Roman empire, and he restored, for show, the city walls and certain private buildings, for the most part threatening ruin. But I say nothing of Christian morals, which everywhere at that time were shaken to the point of destruction. He had the office of the finding of the Holy Cross observed, and added the nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary. At last, however, when they had carefully done (says Platina) everything that pertained to the pope, he was afflicted with intolerable pain in the year of the Lord 1378 and departed this life. At the very hour of his death a fire is said to have broken out in the palace at Avignon, which could not be put out until most of it had been burned. In the papacy there followed the greatest schism of all. Then the clergy (as Matthew writes) and the Roman people came together to the cardinals and asked them to choose some Italian, not a Frenchman, lest the court should move again into France. When they began to elect, a sudden uproar arose. There were four Italians and thirteen French: the French could easily have prevailed, but they did not dare. The Romans stood in arms and used force. So on the ninth of April, a Friday, they elected Urban the Sixth, who was crowned on the eighteenth of the same month, on Easter day. So much for him. Under this pope, Peter of Prémontré describes a new kind, or sect, of wonderful demoniacs, both men and women, who danced in ring-dances without any shame. He shows that in the year of the Lord 1375 they came from Aachen into Hainault, and from there into France, and that they could foretell the migration of Pope Gregory and his cardinals back to Rome. It seemed to them that they were dancing in a river of blood, although those standing by saw nothing of the kind. The common people interpreted it as meaning that this people had been badly baptized by priests who kept prostitutes. For this reason (he says) they had planned to rise against the clergy, killing them and plundering their goods, unless God had provided a remedy through certain conspiracies, and so on. From this dancing comes a rhythm:

units.la: Oritur in seculo novâ quadam secta, &c.
units.tr: A new kind of sect arises in the world, etc.
143. Urban the Sixth.

units.la: VRbanus sextus, patria Neapolitanus, Bartho-lomæus antea nuncupatus, archiepiscopus Ba-rensis, extra Cardinalitij senatus[?] ordinem & ab-sens, sens[?], urgentibus vi magna Romanis, in Pontifi-cem eligebatur. Qui consueto more confirmatus, ut vocant, inthronizatus, clerum eflu quodam officii admonuit, curiamq; religionis obtentu ab pciofis[?] hominibus repurgare simulabat. Commo-neficiitq;[?] Cardinales semelq; iterum, ut a si-monia cauerent (tanquam a sibi soli desponsata uxore) contenti stipendiis ac fructibus suis. Pau-cioribus equis eos uti precepit: Ut simus, inquit, forma gregis ex animo facti: quasi Christiani gre-gis exempla ab equis, & non ab hominibus sint petenda. Quòd autem mentionem fecistis, ait, de reditu in Galliam: noveritis me Romae sem-per mansurum. Tunc ocio ex illis, Gallici natio-ne, Anagniam primò abierunt: postea Fundum, eius seueritatem veriti. Ubi conspirantes inter se, illumq; affirmantes verum non esse Pontificem, sed a Romanis violenter intrusum, alium sibi delegerunt, 20. die Septembris, quem Clemen-tem septimum nominabant. Et factum est schisma, quo nullum perniciosius aut diuturnius un-quam fuit: & durauit fermè quadraginta annis. Erat Urbanus (ut Stella commemorat) vir calidus, & iniuriarum memor ac vindex. Erat, in-quit Crantzius, homo saevus, crudelis, & inexo-rabilis. Qui Pontificatu suscepto, non pacem, ut par erat, inter Christianos componere voluit: sed magis Cardinalium, & Ioannæ Siciliæ reginæ iniurias ulcisci conabatur. Propter quod Florentinos anathemate sub Gregorio notatos, ut eos in suam reduceret sententiam, absoluit: & cum ipsis Ioannem Haucuth Anglum, suarum copiarum ducem, Neapolim contra eandem reginam misit.
units.tr: Urban the Sixth, a native of Naples, formerly called Bartholomew and archbishop of Bari, was elected pope while he was outside the college of cardinals and absent, under great pressure from the Romans. Confirmed in the customary way, as they call it, and enthroned, he warned the clergy with a certain show of duty and pretended to cleanse the Curia of unworthy men under the pretext of religion. He warned the cardinals once and again that they should beware of simony, as of a wife betrothed to themselves alone, and be content with their stipends and revenues. He ordered them to use fewer horses: "Let us be," he said, "a model for the flock, made so from the heart; as examples for the Christian flock should be sought from horses, not from men." But as for their mention of a return to France, he said, "you should know that I shall remain at Rome always." Then some of them, who were French by nation, first left for Anagni and afterwards for Fondi, fearing his severity. There, conspiring together and declaring that he was not truly pope but had been forced upon them violently by the Romans, they chose another for themselves on 20 September, whom they called Clement the Seventh. And a schism arose, more pernicious and lasting than any before, and it lasted nearly forty years. Urban was (as Stella records) a hot-tempered man, mindful of injuries and avenging them. He was, says Crantzius, a savage, cruel and implacable man. Having assumed the pontificate, he did not wish to settle the peace among Christians, as was fitting; rather he tried to avenge the injuries of the cardinals and of Joanna, queen of Sicily. On account of this he absolved the Florentines, who had been marked with anathema under Gregory, in order to bring them back to his own opinion, and sent with them John Haucuth the Englishman, leader of his forces, to Naples against the same queen.

units.la: Inde cum natura inquietus esset, atque omnino inhumanus, apud Nuceriam urbem quosdam novos creans Cardinales, septem ex veteribus in[?] [illegible, ~3 letters]cerem coniecit, quod contra ipsum pro Clemente septimo coniurassent. Ex quibus quinque sacris impositos, in ipsius odium aquis submersit, vel (ut Vui[?] celius scribit) Neptuno sacrificauit. Quod genus mortis & Adamus cardinalis Anglicus tunc valde difficulter euasit. Ex novis autem, quos numero 29. fecit, tribus exceptis, omnes Neapolitani & sui sanguinis erant. Pontifex ille Carolo Hungarico Neapolitano regi bellum indixit, quod nepotem vel spurium suum Campaniæ principem creare noluisset: & per omnem seuitiam res ecclesiæ administrauit. Atque ut huius tyranni furor infa-nus aut rabies apertius videatur, historiam ab a-mico Platina sic narrata accipe. Vrbanus, inquit, terrore Gallico liberatus, & Neapolim se conserens, à rege petit, ut sibi liceat creare nepotem su-um (sic spurios appellare solent) Campanum princi-pem. Quod cum impetrare nequiuisset, homo sub specie iusti & honesti, minus urbanus, ac nulli gratus, ad minas conuersus, coiracundia regem compulit, ut custodiis adhibitis, per aliquot dies prodire in publicum nequiuerit. Verum dissimula-ta ad tempus iniuria, Nuceriā ad uitandos æstus, ut ipse simulabat, cum bona regis uenia profectus, communitaque firmis præsidiis urbe & nouos Car-dinales creat, & septem ex ueteribus in carcerem coniecit, quod diceret eos cum rege & Antipapa Clemente contra se coniurasse. Præterea uero & processum, ut iflorum forma, loquar, contra re-gem inchoauit, missa de more citatione: qui bre-ui se uenturum Nuceriam respondit, diluituru-que obiecta crimina, non uerbis modò, uerumeti-am armis.
units.tr: Then, since he was restless by nature and altogether inhuman, while creating some new cardinals at the city of Nocera, he threw seven of the old ones into prison, because they had conspired against him with Clement the Seventh. Of these, five who had been invested with the sacred dignity he drowned in the waters, in hatred of him, or (as Vuicelius more fully writes) sacrificed to Neptune. Adam, the English cardinal, then escaped such a kind of death with great difficulty. Of the new cardinals whom he made, numbering twenty-nine, all except three were Neapolitans and of his own blood. That pontiff declared war on Charles of Hungary, king of Naples, because he had been unwilling to create his nephew or bastard a prince of Campania; and he administered the affairs of the Church with every cruelty. And so that the mad fury or rage of this tyrant may appear more plainly, take the story as told by his friend Platina. Urban, he says, freed from the Gallic terror, and having betaken himself to Naples, asked the king that he be allowed to create his nephew (for so they are wont to call bastards) prince of Campania. When he could not obtain this, the man, under the guise of justice and honour, less courteous and pleasing to no one, turned to threats, and by his anger compelled the king to put guards in place, so that for some days he could not come out in public. But when the injury had been dissembled for the time, he set out for Nocera, with the king's good leave, to avoid the heat, as he himself pretended; and, the city being fortified with strong garrisons, he created new cardinals and threw seven of the old ones into prison, on the ground that they had conspired against him with the king and the antipope Clement. Moreover, to speak of their form, he began a process against the king, sending the citation as is customary; the king replied that he would shortly come to Nocera and would refute the charges brought against him, not only with words but also with arms.

units.la: Nuceriam itaque cum satis magno exercitu ue-niens, urbem obsedit. Motus autem hac indignita-te Raymundus Balcianus, è gente Ursina, princeps Tarentinus, suis copiis fretus, Urbanum cum tota curia, ad proximum litus deductum, Genua-ensium triremibus ad id instructis, paratisque impo-suit. Quibus dum Pontifex defertur, ex septem Cardinalibus Nuceriæ captis, quinq; [?]faciis [?]inuoinuolutos, in mare demersit. Et sequitur: Defuncto post annum Carolo, desiderio, ut ipse fingebat, vi-dendi Neapolim, Ferentinum usq; peruenit, ea mente reuera, ut Ladislaum admodum puerum, & Io-annem, eius filios, hereditate paterna deturbaret, &c. Vrbanus iste Mendicantium sectarum fratercu-lis concessit, quod possint sua uota in alia impie-tatis opera commutare, & bona iniusta incerta, loco restitutionis recipere: ut Palaeophydorus [?] habet, lib. 3. cap. 13. Romam reuersus demum, anno Domini 1390. post pontificatum decennio infelici-ter gestum, non absq; ueneni suspicione, sublatus est, dolentibus valde paucis: tam erat inurbanus.
units.tr: So, coming to Nocera with a fairly large army, he besieged the city. But Raymond Balzo, of the Orsini family, prince of Taranto, moved by this indignity and relying on his own forces, took Urban with his whole court, led him to the nearest shore, and placed him on the Genoese galleys that had been fitted out and prepared for this purpose. While the pope was being carried away in them, five of the seven cardinals captured at Nocera were bound in sacks and thrown into the sea. And it follows: when Charles died after a year, Urban, from a desire, as he pretended, of seeing Naples, came as far as Ferentino, with the real intention of driving out Ladislaus, a very young boy, and John, his sons, from their paternal inheritance, etc. This Urban granted to the little brothers of the mendicant orders that they might commute their vows into other impious works, and receive unjust and uncertain goods in place of restitution, as Palaeophydorus has it, book 3, chapter 13. Returning at last to Rome, in the year of the Lord 1390, after an unhappy pontificate of ten years, he was removed, not without suspicion of poison, with very few grieving; so little was he courteous.

units.la: Annum lubileum (ut Funccius habet) eo anno impo-stor auarus indixit: cum maximum exilio sibi ac Romanis prouenire lucrum praesentiret. Annatas quoq;, ut uocant, seu uectigal praediorum sacerdo-talium instituit, parandi auxilij fuco aduersus in-fideles. Huic constitutioni Anglici aduersantes, concilio congregato, Papae ius ultra Oceani limi-tes abiudicarunt. Episcopi tamen ac praelati (pro-uinciarum proditores) id uectigal dare in se posteà receperunt. Huius Papae tempore, Bertholdum Nigrum, alias Schuuartz, alchymistam, & in Septentrionali Germania satanicum monachum, æ-neum tormentum, quod Bombardam uocant, excogitasse & inuenisse, ad humani generis perniciem ferunt.
units.tr: This Avaricious impostor proclaimed a jubilee year (as Funccius has it) in that year, since he foresaw that a great profit would come to himself and the Romans from the exile. He also instituted the annates, as they call them, or the tax on priestly benefices, on the pretext of raising aid against the unbelievers. The English, opposing this decree, gathered a council and denied that the pope's right extended beyond the limits of the ocean. The bishops and prelates, however (traitors to their provinces), afterwards undertook to pay that tax. In this pope's time, they say, Berthold Schwarz, otherwise called Niger, an alchemist and a satanic monk in northern Germany, devised and invented the bronze cannon, which they call a bombard, to the destruction of the human race.
144. Clement VII.

units.la: Clemens septimus, Gallus natione, patria Gebennensis, & ex hereditate paterna eiusdem terrae comes, Robertus antea nominatus, ex Cardinale presbytero tituli Basilicæ duodecim Apostolorum, Fudis[?] per Cardinales Gallos creatus est pontifex. Hi Cardinales post tertium mensem ab Vrbani prædicti ordinatione, videntes eius tyrannidem, & quod in Galliam redire nollet, Romani latenter exierunt, ac Fundos se transstulerunt. Primùm tamen ab eo petierunt, ut sibi cum bona eius uenia Anagniam proficisci liceret, mutadi[?] aeris gratia, ætate præsertim: sed eius reuera melancholicas passiones ad mentis[?] insanias ueriti abiere. Erant simul Ioannes Prænestinus, Guilhelmus tituli S. Stephani in Celio monte, Bertrandus S. Ceciliæ, Robertus prædictus, Hugo S. quatuor Coronatorum, Guido S. Crucis in Hierusalem, Ioannes S. Marcelli Ambianensis dictus, Petrus S. Laurentii in Lucina, Gerardus S. Clementis, Petrus S. Eustachii, Guilhelmus S. Angeli, Petrus S. Mariæ inuiolatæ, & Petrus S. Mariæ Cosmedin. Hi (inquit Platina) thesauros ecclesiæ in morte pontificum expilauerant[?], & pro arbitrio animi sui omnia prius agebant. Qui mox ut Fundos confugissent, in Vrbanum ut in pseudopontificem, mutati[?] sunt, dicentes ipsum ut creatum, ut etiam pontificatus accepisse coronam: cum electio illa & coronatio in loco minime tuto esset habita. In qua tamen liberæ deberent esse hominum voluntates, & libera suffragia: quum contrà, ipsi à populo Romano coacti essent Italum potius quàm Gallum eligere.
units.tr: Clement VII, a Frenchman by birth and a native of Geneva, and by paternal inheritance count of that same land, previously named Robert, was created pope by the French cardinals, having been cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. Three months after the ordination of the aforesaid Urban, these cardinals saw his tyranny and that he was unwilling to return to France, so they secretly left Rome and moved to Fondi. First, however, they asked his permission to go to Anagni, with his good leave, for the sake of a change of air, especially on account of their age; but in truth they feared his melancholic moods and the madness of his mind, and so they departed. Together there were John of Palestrina, William of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, Bertrand of St Cecilia, the aforesaid Robert, Hugh of the Four Crowned Saints, Guy of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, John called of St Marcellus of Amiens, Peter of St Lawrence in Lucina, Gerard of St Clement, Peter of St Eustace, William of St Angelo, Peter of St Mary Inviolate, and Peter of St Mary in Cosmedin. These men (says Platina) had plundered the treasures of the Church at the deaths of popes, and before this had done everything according to their own will. As soon as they had fled to Fondi, they turned against Urban as a false pope, saying that he had been created and had received the crown of the papacy, although that election and coronation had been held in a place by no means safe. Yet in such an election the wills of men ought to be free and the votes free; whereas, on the contrary, they themselves had been forced by the Roman people to choose an Italian rather than a Frenchman.

units.la: Has autem ob causas sede nacante, ut ipsi di-cebant, & Ioanna Siciliæ regina ipsis fauente, prædictum Gebennensem Cardinalem Robertum, qui ante legatus in Italiam fuerat, Pontificem delege-runt, eiq; Clementus septimi indita appellatio su-it. Hinc magna ac diuturna in ecclesiis Christianorum orta est discordia: cum pars principum Nea-politano, pars Gebennensi fauieret. Germania, Italia & Anglia Vrbano adhærebant: Hispania, Catalonia & Gallia Clementi: erantque per orbem multi, qui neutrum susceperunt, & hi dicebantur Neutrales. Clemens verò Auenionem profectus, à gratulantibus Gallis & Hispanis adorabatur: & durauit plus annis quindecim, multa suis statuta proponens, eiq; præter Galliæ parebant reges Aragoniæ, Castellæ, & Nauarræ. Interim est concilium Gallicanum ob pontificum discordias Lu[?]tiæ celebratum: quod Clementis partes sequeba-tur, ut Ioannes Tilius refert. Legimq; [?] tulit, Gaguinus nō teste, de gratijs expectatiuis & annatis. Eius tempore quoq;, circa annum sicilicet Domini 1387. exortum est schisma inter vniuersitatem Parisien-sem & fraterculos Dominicanos, super D. Virgi-nis Mariæ conceptione. Obiit Clemens anno Domi-ni 1392. Auenioni (ut fertur) sepultus. Bullas terri-sicas bi duo pontifices ad diuersas mundi partes mi-serunt, & libellos diffamatorios sparserunt: quibus se mutuò mordebant, blasphemabant, excommuni-cabant & Antichristos, schismaticos, hæreticos, tyrannos, fures, proditores, iniquos, vizanie [?] fato-res, ac filios Belial, sese inuicem vocabant. Ioannes de Ligniaco utriusq; iuris doctor, pro Vrbano tra-[?]datum edidit & Abbas S. Vedasti Francorum regis consiliarius, pro Clemente alterum.
units.tr: For these reasons, with the see vacant (as they said), and with Joanna, queen of Sicily, favouring them, they chose as pontiff the aforesaid Robert, the Genevan cardinal who had earlier been legate in Italy, and he was given the name Clement VII. Hence a great and lasting discord arose in the churches of the Christians: some princes favoured the Neapolitan, others the Genevan. Germany, Italy and England adhered to Urban; Spain, Catalonia and France to Clement; and there were many throughout the world who accepted neither, and these were called Neutrals. Clement, however, having gone to Avignon, was adored by the rejoicing French and Spaniards, and he lasted more than fifteen years, proposing many statutes for his followers; besides France, the kings of Aragon, Castile and Navarre obeyed him. Meanwhile a Gallican council was held at Paris because of the discords of the popes; it sided with Clement, as John Tillet reports. I have also read, though Gaguin is not a witness, that it passed decrees concerning expectative graces and annates. In his time too, around the year of the Lord 1387, a dispute arose between the University of Paris and the Dominican friars over the conception of the Virgin Mary. Clement died in the year of the Lord 1392, and was buried at Avignon (so it is said). These two popes sent thundering bulls to different parts of the world and scattered defamatory pamphlets, in which they bit and blasphemed one another, excommunicated one another, and called each other Antichrists, schismatics, heretics, tyrants, thieves, traitors, wicked men, workers of mischief, and sons of Belial. John of Ligny, doctor of both laws, published a treatise on behalf of Urban, and the abbot of St Vaast, counsellor to the French king, published one on behalf of Clement.
145. Boniface IX.

units.la: Bonifacius nonus, patria Neapolitanus, Petrus Tomacellus ante dictus, iuuenis uix trigesimus annum, sed fortis & robustus, eorum qui Romæ permanebant Cardinalium consensu fiebat pontifex. Inter tos Neapolitanos numero 26. quos de suo sanguine Vrbanus creauerat Nuceriæ Cardinales, hic præcipuus erat. Qui ut Crantzius [?] In Metropoli refert, consecratus & coronatus, statim confirmauit ea-que erant ab eodē Vrbano decreta: de Iubileo in trigesimum tertium annum, de festo Visitationis Mariæ, & de indulgentiis adue-nerationem (idololatriam) corporis Christi. Do-minum Adamum Cardinalem Anglicum, Hebrai-cæ linguæ peritum, Aquenione reuertentem, in gra-tiam recepit, ac restituit. Arcem S. Angeli, magna ex parte desolatam, purgari, renouari, ac fir-mari iußit. Comitem Fundorum, qui initio schismatis[?] stabiliuit, penitus extermin iuit. Ipse Romanis, non ut episcopus, sed ut rigidus Imperator (Nero, vel Caligula) dominabatur: multosq; sibi ex illis de perfidia suspectos, occidi per iusticiarios fecit. Capitolium, Palatium Vaticanum, atq; Hadriani mo-lem fortius muniuit: nec fuit ante eum Pontifex, qui talem in Romanos potestatem exerceret. Hæc Crantzius. Scientiarum præterea minus peritus, & augendæ pompæ Pontificiæ cupidus, legem tu-lit, qua orbis dominium obtinuit: scilicet, Non licere cuiquam sacerdotij, ad quod promoueretur, beneficium adipisci, priusquam primos annii pro-ventus Apostolico fisco aut pontificiæ cameræ per-solueret.
units.tr: Boniface IX, a Neapolitan by birth, formerly called Peter Tomacelli, a young man barely thirty years old but strong and robust, was made pope with the consent of those cardinals who remained at Rome. Among the Neapolitan cardinals, twenty-six in number, whom Urban had created at Nocera from his own blood, he was the chief. As Krantz reports in his Metropolis, once consecrated and crowned, he at once confirmed the decrees that Urban himself had issued: concerning the jubilee in the thirty-third year, concerning the feast of the Visitation of Mary, and concerning indulgences for the veneration (idolatry) of the body of Christ. He received back into favour and restored Lord Adam, the English cardinal skilled in the Hebrew language, who was returning from Avignon. He ordered the castle of St Angelo, largely fallen into ruin, to be cleansed, renewed and strengthened. He utterly exterminated the count of Fondi, who had supported the schism from its beginning. He himself ruled over the Romans not as a bishop but as a harsh emperor (Nero or Caligula), and he had many of them suspected of treachery put to death by his officers of justice. He fortified the Capitol, the Vatican palace and the Mole of Hadrian more strongly; and before him there was no pope who exercised such power over the Romans. So Krantz. Less learned in the sciences, and eager to increase papal pomp, he also passed a law by which he gained dominion over the world: namely, that no one might obtain a benefice of any priesthood to which he had been promoted until he had paid the first year's revenues to the apostolic fisc or the papal chamber.

units.la: Banderesios, nobilem Romanorum magistratum, sustulit: atq; ut externum senatorem Malate Pisaurienfem [?] accersirent, Romanos ipsos cru-deli statuto compulit. Urbem ad suum usum forti-tudinis ac propugnaculis muniuit: sed cum Vicecomi-tibus bellum gerens, Bononiam amisit. Ladislaum adolescentem, Caroli Neapolitani regis filium, ad-pud Caietam, in regnum paternum per Cardina-lem Florentinum coronari fecit: ac Brigittam Sue-uiæ dominam in sanctas retulit. Studium generale fieri Ferrariæ concessit: & schola Cracouiæ instau-rari permisit. Iubilei, nouisq; annatarum lucris ap-prime deditus, donaria cognatis & affinibus (de scortis non loquuntur) contra fis iuq; profuse tri-buit. Crimina per simoniam multa commisit: & cer-tis indulgentiis assentiens, magnæ infamiæ notam incurrit. Ex Asisio post fugam reuersus, anno Do-mini 1400. Iubileum Romæ celebrauit: & indul-gentias uenales omnibus proponens, claues Papæ-les ad contemptum usq; perduxit. Post uarias ani-mi perturbationes, laterum dolore seu calculo af-flictus, anno Domini 1404. uitam cum morte tan-dem mutauit. Alborum sectam superstitiosam ex-tro quodam sacerdote, qui ex Alpibus in Italiam cum utriusq; sexus descenderat multitudine, multo superstitiosior hic Pontifex eradicauit. Timebat ille fraudem, ut historici quidam referunt: veritas, sacer doctillum Papatu appetere. Sūt tamē, ait Platina, qui dicant, nil fraudis in homine depr[?]hensum su-isse: sed id fictum à Pontifice, abolendo rumori, quo hominem per inuidiam captum & necatum affirmabant.
units.tr: He abolished the banderesi, the noble magistracy of the Romans, and, so that they might summon an outside senator from Pesaro, he forced the Romans themselves by a harsh statute. He fortified the city with strongholds and bulwarks for his own use; but while waging war with the Visconti, he lost Bologna. He had the young Ladislaus, son of Charles, king of Naples, crowned at Gaeta in his father's kingdom by the Cardinal of Florence, and he raised Bridget, lady of Sweden, to the saints. He granted that a general study be set up at Ferrara, and permitted a school to be restored at Kraków. Devoted above all to the jubilee and to the new profits from annates, he lavishly bestowed gifts on relatives and kinsmen contrary to law and right (they say nothing about prostitutes). He committed many crimes through simony, and by assenting to certain indulgences he incurred a mark of great infamy. Returning from Assisi after a flight, he celebrated the jubilee at Rome in the year of the Lord 1400, and by offering indulgences for sale to all, he brought the papal keys into utter contempt. After various disturbances of mind, afflicted by pain in the side or by stone, he finally exchanged this life for death in the year of the Lord 1404. This most superstitious pope himself uprooted the superstitious sect of the Albigenses, which had been brought by a certain priest who had come down from the Alps into Italy with a great multitude of both sexes. Some historians report that he feared fraud: the truth, they say, is that this priest was seeking the papacy. Yet, says Platina, there are some who say that no fraud was detected in the man, but that the pope invented it to put an end to the rumour by which people asserted that the man had been seized and killed out of envy.
146. Benedict the Thirteenth

units.la: PEnedictus decimus tertius, patria Catalanus, Petrus de Luna prius uocatus, ab his qui adhuc Auenione manserant in ipso schismate Cardinalibus electus, Clementi septimo in eo Papatu successit. Hic antequam esset in Papam electus, disputauit contra authoritatem Papae & suorum spiritualium: dixitq; non esse timendam. Atq; ob illam tam ueram sententiam, nihilominus est tanquam haereticus, ab eius temporis Antichristo damnatus. Voluit equidem ipse, suum suorumq; filiorum etiam iniustam sententiam timeri, ut eius iura testantur. Nec satis ei uidebatur, quod Paulus dicebat: Nempe se tantum ad aedificationem potestatem habere, ad destructionem uero non posse quicquam. In eo perdurauit officio (inquit Crantzius) usq; ad tempus concilij Constantiensis, inq; eo authorizando uariauit: finaliter obdurescebat, destitutus in eodem. Et in pertinacia sua permansit idolum cum idolis Cardinalibus: qui etiam post ipsum tentarunt schis-ma[?] continuare, sed prohibiti sunt. Haec ille. Intertera quæ fecit hic pontifex, Francorum regi Caro-lo sexto decimas ecclesiasticas (Gaguino teste) dedit: partim ut rex illum defenderet, partim ut in-gentis eius lucri particeps & ipse fieret. Cum ille Benedictus, in patria sua Catalonia, & in castro Penisculæ munitissimo se contineret, seq; verū Christi uicarium diabolicus impostor assereret, authoritate eiusdem concilij generalis multipliciter improbatus fuit. In Perpiniano tamen synodum congregauit, ac multos Cardinales fecit. Moriens tandem Penisculæ, anno Domini 1424. bis suis Cardinalibus iußit, ut alium statim sui loco eligerent: & Ægidium Munyos, Barchinonensem canonicū mox constituerunt, Clementem octauum appellantes. Qui protinus Alphonsi regis hortatu, & Cardinales creauit, & egit quæ à pontificibus fieri consueuerunt. Verum, cum Papa Martinus quintus, in gratiam cum Alphonso reduisset, Ægidius eo iu-bente, omnia pontificatus iura deposuit, Maiori-censis episcopus declaratum: & Cardinales ab eo creati, sponte se Cardinalatu abdicarunt. Cogor hoc loco diligentissimi scriptoris, Mat-thiæ Flacii Illyrici testimonium afferre, de Theo-dorico à Nyem, qui præsentis schismatis chronicon tribus edidit libris: quum ipsum opus nunc desit. Theodoricus Nyem, inquit, aliquot Paparum intimus scriba, vir bonus & doctus, descripsit bona fide historiam schismatis inter Papas, quod ante Constantiense concilium per annos 39 durauit. Deus bone, quas in ea historia technas, quas fraudes et diabolicas vafricies [?], quae scelera & facinora Papa rum & spiritualium recensetis? [?] quibus illi Deum, religionem & ecclesiam Christi ludibrio horribiliter habent, vexant, & sua tyrannidi subjiciunt.
units.tr: Benedict the Thirteenth, a Catalan by birth, formerly called Peter de Luna, was chosen during the schism by the cardinals who had remained at Avignon, and succeeded Clement the Seventh in that papacy. Before he was elected pope, he disputed against the authority of the Pope and of his spiritual subjects, and said it was not to be feared. For that very true opinion he was nonetheless condemned as a heretic by the Antichrist of his time. He himself indeed wished that his own and his sons' unjust sentence be feared, as his laws testify. Nor did it seem enough to him what Paul said: that he had power only for building up, and could do nothing for destruction. He persisted in that office (says Krantz) until the time of the Council of Constance, and varied in upholding it; in the end he grew hardened, and was deposed in the same. He remained obstinate, an idol among idol cardinals, who even after him tried to continue the schism, but were prevented. So much for that writer. Among the other things this pope did, he gave the ecclesiastical tithes (according to Gaguin) to Charles the Sixth, king of the French, partly so that the king would defend him, and partly so that he himself might share in the king's immense gain. When that Benedict kept himself in his homeland of Catalonia, in the very strongly fortified castle of Peñíscola, and asserted himself to be the true vicar of Christ, a diabolical impostor, he was condemned in many ways by the authority of the same general council. Yet at Perpignan he gathered a synod and made many cardinals. Dying at last at Peñíscola in the year of the Lord 1424, he ordered his cardinals to choose another in his place at once; and they immediately appointed Egidius Munyoz, a canon of Barcelona, calling him Clement the Eighth. At the urging of King Alfonso, he both created cardinals and did the things that popes are accustomed to do. But when Pope Martin the Fifth, reconciled with Alfonso, had restored himself to favour, Egidius, at his command, laid down all the rights of the papacy, being declared bishop of Majorca; and the cardinals created by him voluntarily renounced their cardinalate. At this point I am obliged to bring forward the testimony of the most diligent writer Matthias Flacius Illyricus, concerning Dietrich of Niem, who published a chronicle of the present schism in three books, although that work is now lost. Theodoric of Niem, he says, a close secretary of several popes, a good and learned man, faithfully described the history of the schism between the popes, which lasted thirty-nine years before the Council of Constance. Good God, what tricks, what frauds and diabolical cunning, what crimes and deeds of popes and spiritual men does he recount in that history! By these the popes horribly mock God, religion and the Church of Christ, harass them, and subject them to their tyranny.

units.la: Equidem fateor, quod etsi multa eorum scelera prius legeram, audiveram, & etiam viderat: atqui ideo non vulgarem de Antichristi, eiusque filiorum malicia opinionem conceperam: tamen lecto eo[?] libro, animadverti eos decuplo peiores esse quam antea suspicatus sum.
units.tr: I admit that although I had earlier read, heard and even seen many of their crimes, and had therefore formed no ordinary opinion of the malice of Antichrist and his sons, yet, having read that book, I noticed they were ten times worse than I had suspected.

units.la: Vere iam assentior, Papas (ut etiam ipsorum Canonistae disputant) esse neque homines neque Deos. Sunt enim incarnati di-aboli, ipsum etiam Satanam malicia & perversitate longe vincentes. Disserit quoque idem author, Papam non habere aliquod ius politicum supra Caesarem: sed contra, Caesares debere sceleratos Papas castigare.
units.tr: Now I truly agree that popes are (as their own canonists also argue) neither men nor gods. For they are incarnate devils, surpassing Satan himself in malice and perversity. The same author also argues that the Pope has no political right over the emperor; on the contrary, emperors ought to punish wicked popes.

units.la: Quinetiam dicit eos esse indignos, ut Caesares vocentur, qui ad tam foeda scelera ac tyrannidem Paparum conniuent. Extat eius authoris scriptum in tres libros divisum. Sed spirituales & devoti Antichristi, ubi potuerunt, talia scripta aboleuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, he says that those who connive at such foul crimes and the tyranny of the popes are unworthy to be called emperors. A writing of this author exists, divided into three books. But the spiritual and devoted followers of Antichrist, wherever they could, destroyed such writings.
147. Innocent the Seventh

units.la: Innocentius septimus, patria Sulmonensis, Cofa-marus de Perusio antea nuncupatus, tituli S. Cru-cis presbyter Cardinalis, tumultuante Italia tota, post Bonifacium nonum Romae pontifex creabatur. Dum adhuc Cardinalis hic effet, teste Platina, carpere negligentiam ac timiditatem priorum pontificum consueverat, dicens: eorum socordia factum esse, ne Romae ecclesiae schisma, totiusque eorum reipublicae pernicies hactenus tolleretur. Verum, ipse pontificatum adeptus, secutus que in quibusdam Urbani & Bonifacii vestigia, quos privatus carpebat: non modo quod tantopere vituperabat, effecit: verum etiam iniquo animo ferebat, si quis apud se ea de re verbum ullum faceret. Praeterea adeo tumultuose omnia gubernabat, ut cum semel Romanis restitui in libertatem, reddiq; sibi Capitolium, pontem Milvium, & arcem Hadriani peterent, instarentq; item ut schisma perniciosum ab ecclesia tolleret, bella extingueret, ac seditiones sopiret, rege Gallorum operam pollicente, & Petro Luna concordiam non abnuente: Romanos ipsos Pontifex ad Ludovicum nepotem in S. Spiritus hospitali commorantem, tanquam ad certum carnificem miserit. Qui statim undecim ex ipsis civibus, qui labenti suae reipublicae in negligentia Pon-
units.tr: Innocent the Seventh, a native of Sulmona, formerly named Cosmas of Perugia, presbyter cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross, was made pope at Rome after Boniface the Ninth, while all Italy was in tumult. While he was still a cardinal, according to Platina, he used to censure the negligence and timidity of the earlier popes, saying that through their sloth the schism of the Roman Church, and the ruin of their whole commonwealth, had not yet been removed. But when he had obtained the papacy himself, and followed in some of the footsteps of Urban and Boniface, whom he had censured as a private man, he not only did what he had so greatly condemned, but also bore it with ill temper if anyone raised a word about it to him. Moreover, he governed everything so tumultuously that when the Romans once sought to be restored to liberty, and to have the Capitol, the Milvian bridge and the citadel of Hadrian returned to them, and also urged him to remove the pernicious schism from the Church, end the wars and quell the seditions, the king of the French promising his help and Peter de Luna not refusing concord, the Pope sent the Romans themselves to his nephew Ludovicus, who was staying at the hospice of the Holy Spirit, as if to a certain executioner. Ludovicus at once killed eleven of those very citizens, who had come to consult the Pope about their commonwealth, which was collapsing through his negligence.

units.la: Note: the scan shows the first sentence and the words "Dum adhuc Cardinalis" in italic; the italic extent is a best reading. tificis confulturi uenerant, statim necabat[?], & e st nestris deijciebat: dicens, non alio modo seditiones & sibismata[?] tolli posse.
units.tr: ...the Pope's negligence; and he immediately had them put to death and thrown from the windows, saying that seditions and schisms could not be ended in any other way.

units.la: Qua sæuitia permotus populus Romanus, acªcito Ladislao Apuliæ rege, arma suscepit, supplicium de Ludouico sumpturus. Sed pontifex declinaturus populi furorem, Viterbium cum Ludouico nepote, cum populi proditore insignis proditor, citato gressu proficiscebatur. Tum uerò populus, cum seuire in authorem tanti sacinoris non posset, in aulicos iram convertit, quorum bona magna ex parte sunt inde direpta. Seruari tẽquidam[?] dam dicebantur in ædibus Cardinalium: qui adiuuantibus seruis, ægrè tamen, ad se confugientes tuti fuerant. Capto deinde Capitolio, occupatoq; ponte Miluio, arcem Hadriani oppugnare frustra conati sunt: adiuuantibus Romanos Ioanne Columna Troiæ comite, & aliis egregiis copiarum ducibus, atq; Ladislai regis auspiciis. Rebus postea compositis, Romam rediens Papa, plures Cardinales delegit: quorum de numero fuere Angelus Corrarius Venetus, Petrus Philargus Cretensis, & Otho Columna nobilis Romanus. Confirmato hoc modo pontificatu suo, Ludouicum nepotem agri Piceni marchionem creauit, eundemq; Firmanum principem exinde constituit. Mediam partem ecclesiasticorum[?] prouetuum (ut Gaguinus habet) per Galliam & Angliam petens, repulsam passus est. Quibus ita gestis, non diu superuixit, sed anno Do-mini 1407. Romae diem extremum obijt, in D. Petri templo sepultus.
units.tr: Stirred by this cruelty, the Roman people, with King Ladislaus of Apulia invited, took up arms, intending to exact punishment from Ludovicus. But the Pope, about to avoid the people's fury, hurried with quick steps to Viterbo with his nephew Ludovicus, a notorious traitor together with the traitor of the people. Then indeed the people, since they could not vent their rage on the author of so great a crime, turned their anger on the courtiers, much of whose goods were plundered. Some were said to be kept safe in the houses of the cardinals, who, with the help of their servants, had barely fled to them and were safe. Then, after the Capitol was seized and the Milvian bridge occupied, they tried in vain to assault the citadel of Hadrian, with the Romans aided by John Colonna, count of Troia, and other distinguished commanders of the forces, and under the auspices of King Ladislaus. Afterwards, with affairs settled, the Pope returned to Rome and chose several cardinals, among them Angelo Corrario of Venice, Peter Philargus of Crete, and Otto Colonna, a noble Roman. Having thus confirmed his papacy, he created his nephew Ludovicus marquis of the March of Ancona, and afterwards made him prince of Fermo. Seeking a share of the ecclesiastical revenues (as Gaguin has it) through France and England, he suffered a rebuff. With these things done, he did not survive long, but died at Rome in the year of the Lord 1407, and was buried in the church of St Peter.
148. Gregory XII.

units.la: GRegorius duodecimus, patria Venetus, Angelus Corrarius antea nominatus, patriarcha Constantinopolitanus, & tituli S. Marci presbyter Cardinalis, Romae in demortui Innocentij locum surrogatus fuit. Sed hac lege Gregorius Romae creabatur, ut si extra foret ecclesiae, pontificatu se abdicaret, ob Benedictum 13. Petrum Lunae vocatum, qui Auenione Clementi septimo successerat. Qui suscepto mox pontificatu, quod ante promiserat, scripto confirmauit, adhibitis etiam notarijs & testibus: modo Benedictus quoque idem praestaret, ac factum[?] deponeret. Sed cum Benedictus nollet, & ex Auenione in Hispanias fugeret, nec Gregorius ipse cedere voluit. Cohortantes tamen sese in principio per legatos, & abdicationem mutuam offerentes, Sauonam, in qua urbe conuenirent, ad concordiam elegerunt. At in conueniendo pernuncios & literas, seq; inuicem illudentes, maximam Christianorum incusatione, maiorem diuisionem concitaerunt[?]. Ingens ergo concilium Pisis celebrabatur anno Domini 1410, in quo collusores & fœdi-fragi, ab utroque Cardinalium conuentu sunt habiti: & utrumque uno consensu pontificatu priuarunt. Erant enim in eo concilio 124. theologi, & pene 300. iurisconsulti, qui ambos à Papatu remouerūt, Alexandrumque Cretensem eorum loco statim elegerunt. Approbatum erat hoc factum omnibus na-tionibus, præterquam citerioribus Hispanis, Sco-tis, & Armeniaco comiti, qui omnes Lunæ adhærebant. Gregorius autem & Benedictus, contempto concilio Pisano, sese Pontifices, ut antè gesserant, subueriti[?] tamen ne caperentur, alter Arimi-num cum Leonardo Aretino secretario, alter in Cataloniam cum suis, diffugerunt.
units.tr: Gregory XII, a Venetian by birth, formerly called Angelo Correr, patriarch of Constantinople and cardinal priest of the title of St Mark, was put in the place of the deceased Innocent at Rome. But Gregory was elected on this condition: if he should be outside the Church, he would resign the papacy, because of Benedict XIII, called Peter de Luna, who had succeeded Clement VII at Avignon. Once he had taken up the papacy, he confirmed in writing what he had promised before, with notaries and witnesses present, on the understanding that Benedict would do the same and renounce his office. But since Benedict would not, and fled from Avignon into Spain, Gregory himself also refused to yield. Still, urging each other at first through envoys and offering mutual abdication, they chose Savona as the city where they would meet for concord. But in arranging the meeting, sending messengers and letters and mocking one another, they stirred up, to the great shame of the Christians, a greater division. Therefore a great council was held at Pisa in the year 1410, in which the deceivers and covenant-breakers were judged by the assembly of both groups of cardinals, and they deprived both of the papacy by one common consent. For in that council there were 124 theologians and nearly 300 jurists, who removed both from the papacy and at once elected Alexander of Crete in their place. This act was approved by all nations except the Spaniards on this side of the Pyrenees, the Scots, and the Count of Armagnac, who all adhered to Luna. But Gregory and Benedict, despising the council of Pisa, still called themselves popes as before, yet fearing capture, one fled to Rimini with his secretary Leonardo Aretino, the other to Catalonia with his followers.

units.la: Atqui ita tres soles[?] (nam Papa se solem esse iactitat) in Papatu relucebant, quorum nullus in uero Papatus cælo collocatus fuit: sed omnes infrà in nubibus pallidi apparebant, ut quibus mox euanescendum esset. Gregorius autem post dictum concilium Arimini à Carolo Malatesta, eius urbis principe, perbenignè exceptus erat. Qui dum Lucam moram faceret, ex Cardinalium consensu, qui nondum ab eo discesserant, Gabrielem Condelmerium ex sorore nepotem (si non filium) creauit Cardinalem. Nicolaum de Luca, Carmelitam, doctorem theologum, dum in concione unionem ad Christianae reipublicae commodum suaderet, e pulpito violenter traxit, & in vincula ad caeterorum terrorem coniecit. Montoliuetensium monachorum ac Hieronymitarum sectas, cum congregatione Venetorum S. Georgij de Alga approbauit. Ex Constantiensi synodo generali demum ad eum miserunt patres, ut illuc uenire, aut saltem desinaret numerum, Et Carolum Malatestam oratore misit. Qui uidens eos ita uelle, ut Papatu priuaretur, ascendit pontificiam cathedram illic praeparatā, promptissimeq; cessit, quarto die Iulij anno Domini 1415 pro qua libera abdicatione, conuentum omnium illum agri Piceni legatum creauit. Quod ut resciuit, post paucos dies Recanati, prae tristitia & animi dolore defecit: ubi & honorifica pompa conditus fuit. Restabat Petrus Luna, de quo Ioannes Gerson theologus Parisiensis, toties repetiuit in ipsa synodo praesens: Non erit pax ecclesiis, donec auferatur Luna. Sed ille nullius authoritate, nullius minis aut precibus, ut resignaret, adduci potuit. De his plura refert Thomas Vualdenus in quodam sermone, coram Anglorum rege Henrico quinta.
units.tr: Thus three suns (for the Pope boasts that he is the sun) shone in the papacy, of which none was set in the true heaven of the papacy, but all appeared pale below in the clouds, as those who were soon to vanish. Gregory, after the said council, was received very kindly at Rimini by Carlo Malatesta, prince of that city. While he was staying at Lucca, by the consent of the cardinals who had not yet left him, he created Gabriele Condulmer, his nephew by his sister (if not his son), a cardinal. When Nicholas of Lucca, a Carmelite and doctor of theology, was urging union for the good of the Christian commonwealth in a sermon, Gregory violently dragged him from the pulpit and cast him into chains, to terrify the others. He approved the sects of the Olivetan monks and the Hieronymites, together with the congregation of St George of Alga at Venice. Finally, the Fathers of the general synod of Constance sent to him asking that he come there or at least resign his office, and he sent Carlo Malatesta as his envoy. Seeing that they wished him deprived of the papacy, Malatesta mounted the papal chair prepared there and most readily resigned, on the fourth day of July in the year 1415. For this free abdication Gregory made that same man legate of the whole March of Ancona. When Gregory learned of it, a few days later at Recanati he died of grief and anguish of mind, and he was buried there with honourable pomp. Peter de Luna remained, of whom John Gerson, theologian of Paris, who was present at the synod itself, said so often: "There will be no peace for the churches until Luna is removed." But he could be brought by no one's authority, no threats or prayers, to resign. Thomas Walden reports more on these matters in a certain sermon before Henry V, king of the English.
149. Alexander V.

units.la: Alexander quintus, patria Cretensis, ac professione Fræciscanus, Petrus Philargus uel de Candia prius dictus, episcopus primum Nouariensis, deinde Mediolanensis archiepiscopus, postea Cardinalis presbyter tituli basilicæ 12 Apostolorum, Gregorio prædicto in Papatu successit. In concilio Pisano (ut dictum est) abrogatis præsulibus Benedicto & Gregorio, omnium qui tum aderant Cardinalium consensu, pontifex maximus constituebatur. Quem quidem gradum, inquit Platina, aut dignitatem adeptus, merito Alexandri nomen consecutus est: cum & exuberanti profusione & animi magnitudine (mendicus olim fraterculus) cum quouis principe conferri posset. Hinc sibi comparauit in Abadonis regno, locusta quondam valde tenuis, quasi hominis vultum, dentesque quales sunt leonum, Apoc. 9. Unde per iocum interdum dicere solebat, se diutius episcopum fuisse, pauperem Cardinalem, ac (ex empto Papatu fortasse) mendicum pontificem. Tanti reuera animi Alexander hic magnus fuit, ut Ladislaum Neapolis & Apuliæ tum regem potentissimum, qui male partas ecclesiæ ditiones dextre magis occupauerat, in concilio Pisano, approbantibus qui tunc aderant sacriculis, regni paterni iure tyrannicè deiecerit: idq; Ludouico Andegauiæ ducì in qué adiudicaue-rit. Soluto concilio Pisano, pontifex iste Bononi-am proficiscebatur[?]: cui ciuitati tum præerat Bal-thafar Coffa, S. Eustachij Cardinalis (Sodomita ci nedusq; malignus) quem Alexander in legatione confirmauit, quòd eius astutia atq; præsidijs[?] concilium illud habitum fuisset: quòdq; uir effet, qui per commodè rem ecclesiasticam occupare conatibus, obijci quouis tempore posset. In eo homine (inquit Platina) plus ferociæ[?], plus què audaciæ & secularitatis (ut ita dicam) erat, quàm eius professio requirebat. Militaris prope habebatur eius uita, militares mores (in milite ra-so)adeò, ut multa etiam (in sancta cælibatu) quæ loqui fas non est, sibi licere arbitraretur. Tantum ille. Inter acta Papalia, Alexander iste de sui Fran-cisci stigmatibus bullas fecit, ut inter Christianæ fi-dei articulos haberentur: ac solenne eorum festū, ut venerarentur à fidelibus, ordinauit. Cum gra-uiter hic Papa, ex Marsilij Parmensis medici, ma-gno precio à Balthafare conducti, uenenato phar-maco ægrotare cœpisset (ut Baptista Panetius in §6. sermone declarat) nossetq; instare mortem: Cardinales ad se uenientes, ad concordiam mutu-am (pacem inter impios, ut Christus conculcetur) & ad tuendam ecclesiæ dignitatem, Papalem sci-licet licet sedem ac pompam, adhortabatur. Et iam fi-ni proximus anno Domini 1411. octauo pontifica-tus sui mense, ait: Per eam mortem, quam adesse iam uideo (periurum) testor, omnia quae in Pisano concilio gesta sunt (quaedam impiissima probantur) bene & legitime fuisse facta. Cum haec dixisset, la-chrymantibus his qui aderant sacrificis ac fratercu-lis, illud Seruatoris dictum aegre proferens, su-perbus hypocrita, ait: Pacem meam do vobis (non est pax impiis) pacem relinquo vobis. Praesumptio diabolica erat in hoc peccatore misero, quum Christi pacem mundus dare non posset. Sed talis est Antichristi superbia, qui se extollit super omne quod dicitur Deus. Et statim arrogans bestia, qui nec ma-ximorum scelerum veriam petebat, emisit spiri-tum: ac Bononiae in Franciscanorum templo cum ingenti pompa sepultus fuit. Fame ac peste hoc an-no laboratum est, post huius pontificis benedictio-nem: tanquam sit a Domino in maledictione com-mutata.
units.tr: Alexander V, a Cretan by birth and a Franciscan by profession, formerly called Peter Philarges or of Candia, first bishop of Novara, then archbishop of Milan, and afterwards cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, succeeded the aforesaid Gregory in the papacy. At the council of Pisa, with Benedict and Gregory set aside, he was declared supreme pontiff by the consent of all the cardinals then present. This rank or dignity, says Platina, he obtained, and he rightly got the name Alexander, since with lavish spending and greatness of spirit (once a beggarly little friar) he could be compared with any prince. Hence he acquired for himself in the kingdom of Abaddon the likeness of that locust which was once very thin, with the face of a man and teeth like those of lions (Rev. 9.). So he would sometimes say in jest that he had been a bishop for a long time, a poor cardinal, and (perhaps by a bought papacy) a beggar pope. Indeed this Alexander was so great in spirit that at the council of Pisa, with the approval of the priests present, he tyrannically deposed Ladislaus, then the most powerful king of Naples and Apulia, who had more skilfully seized the ill-gotten dominions of the Church, and he deprived him of his paternal kingdom by right and adjudged it to Louis, duke of Anjou. When the council of Pisa was dissolved, this pope set out for Bologna. Over that city then presided Baldassare Cossa, cardinal of St Eustace (a sodomite and not even harmless), whom Alexander confirmed in his legation, because by his cunning and protection that council had been held, and because he was a man who could at any time be charged with seizing church affairs too easily. In that man (says Platina) there was more ferocity, more boldness and worldliness, so to speak, than his profession required. His life was almost thought military, with military manners, especially in a soldier, so that he judged it lawful for himself to do many things, even within holy celibacy, which it is not right to speak of. So far Platina. Among the papal acts, this Alexander issued bulls about the stigmata of his Francis, so that they would be counted among the articles of the Christian faith, and he ordained their solemn feast, that they should be venerated by the faithful. When this pope began to fall ill from a poisoned drug, administered by Marsilio of Parma, a physician hired by Baldassare at great price (as Baptista Panetius declares in his sixth sermon), and knowing that death was at hand, the cardinals coming to him urged him to mutual concord (peace among the wicked, so that Christ is trampled underfoot) and to uphold the dignity of the Church, that is, the papal see and its pomp. And near his end, in the year 1411, in the eighth month of his papacy, he said: "By that death which I now see is at hand, I testify, perjured as I am, that all things done at the council of Pisa (some of them most impious) were done well and lawfully." When he had said this, the priests and friars present weeping, he, uttering with difficulty that saying of the Saviour, proud hypocrite that he was, said: "I give you my peace (there is no peace for the wicked); I leave you peace." It was a diabolical presumption in this wretched sinner, since the world could not give Christ's peace. But such is the pride of Antichrist, who exalts himself above everything that is called God. And at once this arrogant beast, who did not even seek pardon for his greatest crimes, breathed out his spirit, and at Bologna he was buried with great pomp in the Franciscan church. Famine and plague afflicted this year, after the blessing of this pontiff, as if the Lord had turned the blessing into a curse.

units.la: His temporibus etiam uixit Henricus de Haf-fia, Germanus, qui scripsit de Antichristo & schis-mate. Ille in lectura super Genesim, prolixius insectatur sanctorum legendas, ut vocant: & affirmat multa ibi pueriliter & inepte, multa etiam fabulose & falso esse scripta. Composuit et libellum, publi-
units.tr: Henry of Hesse, a German, also lived in these times; he wrote on Antichrist and the schism. In his lecture on Genesis he attacks the legends of the saints, as they are called, at length, and affirms that many things are written there childishly and foolishly, and many also fabulously and falsely. He also composed a small book which

units.la: publicè dudum editum (ut Illyricus habet) contra insulsas & noxias monachorum rixas: ut de conceptione D. Virginis, & similibus obscuris, ociosis ac inutilibus, & interim publicæ quieti perniciosis controversiis. Cuius sententia sic subscribit[?] nostræ ætate Baptista Mantuanus, in 12. Fastorum libro:
units.tr: was published some time ago (as Illyricus reports) against the silly and harmful quarrels of the monks: about the conception of the Virgin, and similar obscure, idle and useless controversies, which at the same time are pernicious to public peace. His opinion is endorsed in our own age by Baptista Mantuanus in the twelfth book of the Fasti:

units.la: Pullulat hac radice grauis discordia rixæ.
units.tr: From this root there springs up grievous discord and quarrel.

units.la: Sunt etenim, qui conceptus contagia in istos
units.tr: For there are some who hold that the contagion of conception has fallen upon these beings,

units.la: Lapsa uclint, magnamq; putent traxisse parentes
units.tr: and who think that the parents have drawn into them a great defect

units.la: Fomitis antiqui uitium, cui fecit Origo
units.tr: of the ancient tinder (fomes), to which Origin gave its name.

units.la: Nominis. Sunt alij, quibus hæc absurda uidentur,
units.tr: There are others to whom these things seem absurd,

units.la: Sicq; duæ ueniunt ista in certamina secta,
units.tr: and so two sects come into conflict over these matters,
sometimes filling the benches with great laughter.

units.la: Æquanimes autem uolunt ut fi uera fateri,
units.tr: But the even-minded, if they wish to confess the truth,

units.la: Vanus utrq; labor, pietas temeraria, præceps
units.tr: say that the labour of both is vain, and that their piety is rash and headlong,
a religion veiled in the cloak of learning, which is mere frivolity.

units.la: Nec natura potest illuc extendere uisum,
units.tr: Nature cannot extend its sight that far,

units.la: Nec Deus hoc docuit, nec re dependet ab ista
units.tr: nor has God taught this, nor does our salvation depend on that knowledge.

units.la: Nostra salus. Quæ nos igitur dementia torquet,
units.tr: What madness, then, torments us,
