units.la: Vt studeamus in his consumere litibus annos?
units.tr: that we should spend our years wearing ourselves out in these quarrels?
And it continues:

units.la: Quid, seu munda fuit semper, seu sorduit olim
units.tr: Whether this was ever pure, or was once defiled,

units.la: Hæc ea, Mortales, non sunt quæ numina posc unt
units.tr: these are not the divinities that demand

units.la: Obsequia à nobis, studio dominatur in isto
units.tr: service from us; ambition rules in this study,

units.la: Ambitio, & tumidis pugnans iactantia verbis. At si sancta fides operas exposceret istas, Esset opus pugnare pium, sudare sub armis, Exilium mortemq; pati. Sed salua sepultis His nugis est ipsa fides discrimine ab omni.
units.tr: and boasting fights with bombastic words. But if holy faith demanded those labours, it would be a pious work to fight, to sweat under arms, and to suffer exile and death. But faith itself, safe from these trifles, is free from every peril.
It goes on further.

units.la: Sicq; suos iuxta affectus insomnia fingunt, O miseri, nonne hæc deliramenta uidetis? Cur igitur tam ridiculi popularia corda Obscurare opus est gerrii? & scindere pacem Inter mortales, qua nil descendit ab astris Vtilius nobis? belloq; inuoluitis orbem, &c.
units.tr: And so they feign dreams according to their own feelings. O wretched men, do you not see that these are ravings? Why then must you darken the popular hearts with such quarrels, and tear apart peace among mortals, than which nothing sent down from the stars is more useful to us? And you involve the world in war, and so on.

units.la: In prolixa quadam epistola ad episcopū Vuor-maciensem, prædictus Henricus, admodum graviter de multis grauissimis vitiis, accusat spirituales omnium ordinum, atq; adeo etiam ipsum sanctissimum, Papam scilicet.
units.tr: In a lengthy letter to the bishop of Worms, the aforementioned Henry, quite severely, accuses the clergy of every rank, and indeed even the most holy Pope himself, of many very grave vices.
150. John the Twenty-Fourth.

units.la: Ioannes uicesimus quartus, patria Neapolitanus, Balthasar Cossa antea vocatus, tituli S. Eustachij cardinalis, Papistici iuris peritus, ac militaris disciplinae quàm religionis studiosior, Alexadro prædicto eius arte sublato, papatum sceleribus coparauit. Illum aut ferunt papisticæ tyrannidis approbato res aliquot, pontificiū munus violeter potius usur-passe, quàm liberis assumpsisse [?] suffragijs. Cū enim Bo-nonie (inquit Stella) potius ut dominus quamlegatus[?] esset, magnoq; exercitu imperaret, & pa-tres pro nouo Pontifice deligendo ibidem conue-nissent, multa eis interminatus est, nisi Pontificem sibi gratum elegissent. Et ea causa multi producti fuerunt, quorum neminem approbare voluit. Quæ uero obsecraretur, ut quem vellet, significare di-gnaretur: Date mihi (inquit) Petri chlamydem, & ego dabo Pontifici futuro. Quod cum factum esset, ille pallium suis humeris imponens: Papa, ait, sum ego. Quæ res quamuis patribus displicuisset, fortè tamen sententiam abscondi consultius fuit. Homi-nem videlicet terribilem atq; armatum territare, non videbatur utile. Hac igitur arte Pontificatum (ut aiunt) obtinuit. Qui in Papam coronatus, sta-tim in Germaniam misit, ut Sigismundum Hunga-riæ regem in Cæsarem solito more constituerent. Et voti compos effectus, Romæ synodum celebra-vit, ut imperiali diademate ipsum illic ornaret.
units.tr: John the Twenty-fourth, a Neapolitan by birth, formerly called Balthasar Cossa, cardinal of the title of St Eustace, well versed in Papal law and more devoted to military affairs than to religion. After his rival Alexander, the aforementioned, was removed by his craft, he bought the papacy with his crimes. Some report that, since the papal tyranny had been approved, he seized the pontifical office by violence rather than assumed it by the free votes of others. For when he was at Bologna (says Stella), acting more as lord than as legate, and commanding with a great army, and the fathers had gathered there to choose a new Pontiff, he threatened them with many penalties unless they elected a Pontiff acceptable to him. For this reason many men were put forward, but he was unwilling to approve any of them. When he was entreated to indicate whom he wished, he deigned to say: "Give me the cloak of Peter, and I will give it to the future Pontiff." When this had been done, he placed the pallium on his own shoulders and said: "I am the Pope." Although this act displeased the fathers, it seemed more prudent to hide their judgment, since it did not seem useful to alarm a man who was both formidable and armed. By this art, then (as they say), he obtained the papacy. Once crowned as Pope, he at once sent into Germany to have King Sigismund of Hungary appointed Emperor in the customary manner. And having gained his desire, he held a council at Rome so that he might adorn him there with the imperial diadem.

units.la: In cuius prima sessione, post Missam de Spiri-tu sancto, cum ipse Ioannes in sublimiore cathedra præsideret, mox aderat bubo, quæ supra templi trabem, horrifica sua voce, iniectis in Papam ocu-lis, ipsum monstrifico more salutavit. Astantes au-tem vehementer admirari cœperunt: & quidam eo-rum submissa voce dicebant, En Spiritus sanctus de-est, quem tam ardenter invocabant, ut illis expe-ratum[?] statum ferat auxilium. Cæteri se mutuo spectantes, & Papam, vix risum continere poterant. Ioannes ipse rubore suffusus, sudare, angustiari, atq; intra semetipsum æstuare cœpit. Tandemq; non inueniens qua posset alia ratione suæ tam magnæ confusioni consulere, soluto consilio, surgens abscessit. Secuta est deinde altera sessio, in qua similia rursum, sed maiori cum verecundia passus est: nec poterat bubo aut clamoribus abigi, aut fustibus terreri: ita ut in ea synodo nihil prorsus actum sit. Tales ex hoc portento spirituales columbæ, Ec-clesiam illam longo tempore rexisse, crediderunt tunc multi. In quadam epistola Nicolai Clemen-gis, archidiaconi Baiocensis, hæc invenitur historia. Cæterum, propter Italorum discordias, quarum suscitator ille extitit, Sigismundo atq; suis tutus non erat accessus ad urbem. Citatus ergo (teste Massæo) ab omnibus ferme nationibus, ut alium designaret locum, quo convenire liceret, delegit Constantiam, Moguntinæ provinciæ civitatem, diemque præfixit Calendarum Nouembrium anni 1414. Suaserunt interim quidam illi, non accedere, ne non Pontifex sortassis reverteretur. Accessit tamen cum argutissimis advocatis & causidicis, qui facile possent diluere, si quid obiici contigisset. Sed in medio itinere ex rheda præceps cecidit: quod in su-[?] In fausto omine, futurum eius casum indica-bat.
units.tr: At the first session of this synod, after the Mass of the Holy Spirit, while John himself presided in a higher chair, a horned owl was at once present on a beam above the church, and with its horrible voice, fixing its eyes upon the Pope, greeted him in a monstrous manner. The bystanders began to wonder greatly, and some of them said in a low voice: "Behold, the Holy Spirit is absent, whom they invoked so ardently, so that he might bring help to them in their desired state." The others, looking at one another and at the Pope, could scarcely contain their laughter. John himself, suffused with blushing, began to sweat, to be distressed, and to seethe within himself. At last, not finding any other way to remedy his great confusion, he dissolved the council and rose and departed. Then followed a second session, in which he again suffered similar things, but with greater shame; nor could the owl be driven away by shouts or frightened by clubs, so that nothing at all was accomplished in that synod. Many at that time believed that from this portent the spiritual doves had ruled that Church for a long time. This story is found in a letter of Nicholas Clemangis, archdeacon of Bayeux. Moreover, because of the discords of the Italians, whose instigator he had become, access to the city was not safe for Sigismund and his followers. Summoned therefore (as witnessed by Massaeus) by almost all nations to designate another place where a meeting might be held, he chose Constance, a city of the province of Mainz, and fixed the day, the Kalends of November in the year 1414. Meanwhile some advised him not to go, lest perhaps he might not return as Pope. Nevertheless he went, with very clever advocates and lawyers who could easily refute whatever objection might arise. But in the middle of the journey he fell headlong from his carriage, which, as an unlucky omen, indicated his future fall.

units.la: Cum vero Constantiam Ioannes hic Pontifex peruenisset, eius atq; Imperatoris, et aliorum Christianorum principum consensu, concilium incepit generale, anno Domini 1414. In vigilia natalis Christi illuc accessit Imperator Sigismundus: & in eius noctis prima missa, Euangelium ut diaconus cantauit, Exijt edictum à Cæsare Augusto, &c. cumq; sedissent in concilio, præsente Sigismundo, cunctisq; data libertate loquendi, plus quam quadraginta crimina, & quidem gravissima, Papæ Ioannis obiecta sunt, ac probata: & quod Alexandrum prædecessorem, conducto Marsilio Parmen-si medico, per venenum suffulisset. Coactum est igitur, dictante Concilio, Papatu se abdicare: propterea quod esset hæreticus, simoniacus, mendax, hypocrita, homicida, veneficus, aleator, adulter, sodomita, & quid non? Quamobrem mutato statim habitu, fugere clanculum cœpit 21. die Martij sequenti, ad Scaphusam Austriæ urbem, & inde Friburgum. Sed curante ipso concilio 29. Maij, ac pontificatus sui anno quinto, omni officio privatus fuit, quæsitus, inuentus, comprehensus, et in carcerem missus, in quodam Germaniæ fortissimo castro, Heidelbergae (vel ut alij volunt, Manheimi, Palatini electoris oppido) ubi triennio mansit inclu-sus, nullis ei assistentibus nisi solis Germanis, Latinæ atq; Italicæ linguæ ad suum non modicum mafilum ignaris. Christianus Maffæus: Interim synodi præsides decretum ediderunt, quo declarabatur, generale concilium legitime congregatum, esse supra Papam, & habere potestatem à Christo, qui caput est Ecclesiæ: quamuis ad illum usq; diem, pastificæ monarchiæ vindices ausi fuissent contendere, Papam esse legitimum Christi vicarium, & Ecclesiæ monarcham[?].
units.tr: When this Pope John had arrived at Constance, with the consent of himself, the Emperor, and the other Christian princes, a general council was begun in the year of the Lord 1414. On the eve of Christ's birth Emperor Sigismund came there; and at the first mass of that night, the deacon sang the Gospel: "There went out a decree from Caesar Augustus," and so on. When they had taken their seats in the council, with Sigismund present, and freedom of speech having been granted to all, more than forty crimes, and indeed most grievous ones, were charged against Pope John and proved; among them that he had secured the death of his predecessor Alexander by poison, having hired Marsilius of Parma, a physician. Therefore, at the council's bidding, he was compelled to abdicate the papacy, because he was a heretic, a simonist, a liar, a hypocrite, a murderer, a poisoner, a gambler, an adulterer, a sodomite, and what not. Wherefore, changing his dress at once, he began to flee secretly on the twenty-first day of March following, to Schaffhausen, a city of Austria, and from there to Freiburg. But by the efforts of the council itself, on the twenty-ninth of May, in the fifth year of his pontificate, he was deprived of all office, sought out, found, seized, and sent into prison in a very strong castle of Germany, at Heidelberg (or, as others will have it, at Mannheim, a town of the Elector Palatine), where he remained shut up for three years, with no attendants except Germans alone, ignorant of the Latin and Italian tongues, to his no small annoyance. Christian Massaeus says: Meanwhile the presidents of the synod issued a decree by which it was declared that a general council lawfully assembled is above the Pope and has its power from Christ, who is the head of the Church; although up to that day the champions of the papal monarchy had dared to contend that the Pope is the lawful vicar of Christ and the monarch of the Church.

units.la: In eo concilio, cum plurimi & maxima negotia pro gloria Christi, & pro publica utilitate poterant agi, si putris caro ecclesiasticorum potuisset Euangelij salem ferre: nihil tamen magis est effectum, quam quod doctrina Christi, quæ tum per multos à S. Spiritu illuminatos viros in lucem revocabatur, per idem concilium sit condemnata, atq; sub modium abscondita. Ioannis Vuicleui doctrina Christiana, est illic proscripta ac damnata. Ioannes Huffus & Hieronymus Pragensis, salvo conducto dato, ad idem concilium citabantur: ubi tamen non longe post exauthorati, igne tyrannico cremabantur, tanquam hæresiarchæ perniciosissimi. Quoniam inter cætera dixerant (ut ipse Platina scribit) ecclesiasticos ad imitationem Christi et Apostolorum(magna hæresis)pauperes esse debere: cum tamen ex tanta rerum in illis copia & luxu populi omnes scandalizarentur. Et nil mirum, si, cum hi[?] omnia scelera impune facere uelint, concilium liberum conuocare, atq; illi interesse nolint. Si enim Pontificum huius nostræ miserrimæ tempe-statis[?] sacta, sicut in libero concilio facere oportet, ad examen reuocarentur, omnes diuinis humanisq; quæ legibus, non modò carceribus ac compedibus, sed laqueo, capite, aquis, igne & aculeo plectendi essent. Quapropter satis mirari nō possum eorum opinionem, qui liberum concilium aliquando à pon-tifice conuocandum sperant, in quo ecclesia Chri-sti consulatur, & optimè prospiciatur.
units.tr: In that council, although very many and very important matters could have been transacted for the glory of Christ and for the public good, if the rotten flesh of the churchmen could have borne the salt of the Gospel, nothing was more effectually done than that the doctrine of Christ, which was then being brought back into the light by many men illumined by the Holy Spirit, was condemned by that same council and hidden under a bushel. The Christian doctrine of John Wycliffe was there proscribed and condemned. John Huss and Jerome of Prague, although a safe-conduct had been given, were cited to the same council; yet not long afterwards, deprived of their status, they were burned in a tyrannical fire, as most pernicious heresiarchs. For among other things they had said (as Platina himself writes) that churchmen ought to be poor in imitation of Christ and the Apostles (a great heresy!), whereas the whole people were scandalised by such abundance of wealth and luxury among them. And it is no wonder that, since these men wish to commit every crime with impunity, they are unwilling to convoke a free council and to be present at it. For if the deeds of the Pontiffs of this most wretched time of ours were called into examination, as ought to be done in a free council, they would deserve to be punished by divine and human laws not only with prisons and fetters, but with the noose, the axe, water, fire and the goad. Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder at the opinion of those who hope that a free council will at some time be convoked by the Pope, in which the Church of Christ may be consulted and most well provided for.

units.la: Hæc,dū esset in ipsa Antichristi sede, fecit pre-dictus Papa Ioannes, inter alia gesta Papalia, ut in diuersis authoribus uidi. Contra Ladislaum re-gem terrifica bella excitauit: & ut de regno pelle-retur, conuentum habuit Romæ. Madauit itẽ sup-plicationes cum capite S. Ioannis Baptistæ ibidem fieri, cum id Florentinis uendere subdole statuis-set. Ordinem de Camisea, seu Frisonariorum se-sam in agro Lucensi confirmauit: & congregati-onem reformationis nouæ in monasterio S.Iustinæ, per Ludouicum Barbam apud Patauium incæp-tam, admisit. Dumq; Martinus quintus, qui illi fuc cessit, apud Florentiam existeret, è carceribus libe-ratus, præter spem omnem, admirantibus cunctis qui aderant, ad ipsum illuc venit: & eius osculatum pedes, ut suum Papam agnovit, ut Petri successorem recognovit, atque ut Deum quendam terrenum salutavit. Martinus ea eius humilitate permotus, post aliquot dies ipsum in Cardinalium assumpsit numerum, Tusculanumq; episcopum creavit. Verū, post aliquot menses, animi dolore, ut credi posset, in eadem urbe Florentia, mœstam vitam pro-perè clausit, anno Domini 14.19 ubi à Cosmo Me-dico, sui semper amantissimo, honorificentissimè in D. Ioannis Baptistæ templo, magna adhibita funeris pompa, sepultus est.
units.tr: While still in the very seat of Antichrist, the aforesaid Pope John did this, among his other Papal deeds, as I have seen in various authors. He stirred up terrifying wars against King Ladislaus, and to drive him from his kingdom he held a convocation at Rome. He also ordered supplications to be made there with the head of St John the Baptist, having decided to sell it deceitfully to the Florentines. He confirmed the Order of the Camisea, or sect of the Frisonari, in the territory of Lucca, and admitted the new congregation of reform begun by Ludovico Barba at the monastery of St Justina at Padua. While Martin V, who succeeded him, was staying at Florence, John was freed from prison beyond all hope and came to him there, to the amazement of everyone present. He kissed his feet, acknowledged him as his Pope, recognised him as the successor of Peter, and greeted him as a certain earthly God. Martin, moved by this humility, after some days took him into the number of the Cardinals and created him Bishop of Tusculum. But after some months, from grief of spirit, as might be believed, he quickly ended his sorrowful life in the same city of Florence, in the year of the Lord 1419. There he was buried most honourably, with great funeral pomp, in the temple of St John the Baptist, by Cosimo de' Medici, who was always most fond of him.
Epitaph of the same John.

units.la: Balthasar in primis vocitabar, & inde Ioannes: / Depositus rursum, Balthasar ipse vocor. / Dives eram nuper, quo nullus maior in urbe: / En mihi divitiæ abstulit hora brevis. / Dum cathedram Petri lustro, paucisq; diebus / Possedi, plures procubuere mihi. / Pestis avaritiæ me cæcum reddidit: aurum / Plus iusto sitiens, munere sacra dedi. / Hei mihi quam duxi, sponsæ Christi sine ruga, / Scandala magna nimis, sordida vita dedit.
units.tr: Balthasar I was first called, and then John; / deposed again, I am called Balthasar himself. / Lately I was rich, with none greater in the city; / behold, a brief hour has taken my riches from me. / While I held Peter's chair and for a few days / possessed it, many fell prostrate before me. / The plague of avarice made me blind: thirsting for gold / beyond what was right, I gave sacred things for a bribe. / Alas, the bride of Christ, whom I took without spot, / my foul life has made into a great scandal.

units.la: Propter quæ scelera, celso synodum sacra Petri Me uelut indignum depulit e folio. Pontifices igitur moniti sint temporis huius, Exemplo nostro, ne sacra dent precio.
units.tr: For these crimes the sacred synod of Peter's successors has cast me down from the lofty throne as unworthy. Let the Popes of this time, therefore, be warned by our example not to sell sacred things for a price.
151. Martin V.

units.la: Martinus quintus, patria Romanus, Otho Columna prius nuncupatus, D. Georgij diaconus Cardinalis, concilij Constantiensis authoritate, ab rogatis tribus Papis, Benedicto, Gregorio, & Iohanne, Pontifex creabatur. Is enim à teneris annis parentum cura moribus & literis imbutus, vbi ad doleuisset, iuri Pontificio Perusij operam dedit. Vnde ad urbem rediens, & pro uulpe agnum induens, Vrbani sexti referendarius factus est: quod munus simulata mansuetudine ita gessit, ut Cardinalis ab Innocentio septimo ordinatus fit. In omni enim controuersia, aut in utramq; partem alteratione, propter diuersarum factionum studia, relicta ueritate, medium quoddam, ut omnibus pareret, adulator tenuit. Hanc ob rem & imperatori & Cardinalibus omnibus gratus, in prædicto Concilio Papa constituebatur. In cuius electione effusu gaudio Sigismundus Cæsar, omnibus gratias egit, quod talem elegissent pontificem: & eius osculatus est pedes, in eo draconè adorans, Apoc.13. Quæ[?] Pontifex tanquam fratrem amplexus (ut regem potius agnoscere debuisset) gratias ei uicissim retulit, quod ipsius labore pax tandem Ecclesiae reddita esset. Et quia in D. Martini festo electus fuit, Martinus dici voluit. Subinde tamen a stu[?] se subduxit, & (ut scribit Volaterranus) inuito ipso imperatore, in Italiam citatim redijt. Per Mediolanum, Mantuam, Ferrariam, Rauennam, & alias urbes, Florentiam demum uenit: sed pericula metuens, Bononiam euitauit. Florentia duobus annis, in omni carnis voluptate, pompa & ocio confidis, maius altare S. Mariae Nouellae apud Dominicanos dedicauit, & nihil aliud memoria digni, quod legimus, interim fecit: certe Euangelium Christi uel semel non praedicauit. Et, quod pene omiseram, dum adhuc esset Constantiae, & super clericorum moribus, nimia licentia labefactatis, metio per Caesarem atq; alios principes fieret, Martino placuit in aliud tempus remedium transferre. Dicebat enim, rem ipsam maturitate & consilio indigere (uitæ reformatione lethaliter odiunt semper) quia ex Hieronymi sententia, inquit, unaquæq; prouincia suos habet mores mores, & suos sensus, qui tolli sine rerum perturbatione (callidus impostor) subito non possunt. De conciliis ergo celebrandis (nam ea tunc valde timebant, quod essent supra Papam) talem sententiam promulgauit, ac decretum edidit, ne rursus concilium ante quinquennium con-uocaretur, & inde ad decennium usq; protrahe-retur, ac deinceps à decennio in decennium gene-rali synodus ageretur. Martinus postea, peractis in itinere (ut distum est) duobus annis, Romam tan-dem diu expectatus peruenit: & urbem in exter-nis aedificijs ac caeremonijs Papalibus reformauit. Patrimonium Ecclesiae durissimis praelijs repete-bat: & ut peregrinus nummos afferentibus iter ef-set tutum, uiarum latrones fugauit. Ludouicum A-louisij filium in Neapolitano regno confirmauit: atq; Alphonsum Arragonum eo priuauit. Schismata quaedam aduersus regnum Papisticum sustulit: ac Bononiam rebellantem, in caulam reuocauit. Germanos aduersus Bohemos ad arma ob haere-sim (ut uocant) concitauit: & Vualdenum Carme-litam Anglum ad scribendum contra Hussitas & Vuicleuistas inuitauit.
units.tr: Martin V, a Roman by birth, formerly named Otho Colonna, deacon of the Cardinal of St George, was created Pope by the authority of the Council of Constance, after the three rival Popes, Benedict, Gregory and John, had been deposed. From his tender years he was trained in morals and letters by his parents' care, and when he had grown up he devoted himself to Papal law at Perugia. Returning from there to the city, and putting on the lamb's skin in place of the fox's, he became referendary to Urban VI. He discharged this office with feigned mildness, so that Innocent VII made him a Cardinal. For in every controversy, or in any shift of sides, because of the zeal of the rival factions, he abandoned the truth and held to a kind of middle course, a flatterer who wished to please everyone. For this reason he was pleasing to the emperor and to all the Cardinals, and was made Pope at the aforesaid Council. At his election the Emperor Sigismund, overflowing with joy, thanked everyone for choosing such a pontiff, and kissed his feet, adoring in him the dragon (Apoc. 13.). The Pope embraced him as a brother, though he ought rather to have acknowledged him as king, and in turn thanked him that by his labour peace had at last been restored to the Church. And because he was elected on the feast of St Martin, he wished to be called Martin. Afterwards, however, he withdrew from that business, and (as Volaterranus writes), against the emperor's will, he hurried back into Italy. Through Milan, Mantua, Ferrara, Ravenna and other cities he at last came to Florence, but fearing dangers he avoided Bologna. For two years at Florence, given over to every carnal pleasure, pomp and idleness, he dedicated the high altar of St Mary Novella among the Dominicans. Meanwhile he did nothing else worth remembering that we read of; certainly he did not preach the Gospel of Christ even once. And, what I had nearly omitted: while he was still at Constance, and when a remedy was sought by the emperor and other princes for the excessive licence that had weakened clerical morals, Martin chose to defer the remedy to another time. He said that the matter itself needed maturity and deliberation, since reformation of life is always hated to the death, and because, as Jerome's saying goes, each province has its own customs and its own feelings, which cannot be removed suddenly without upsetting affairs (the crafty impostor). Concerning the holding of councils, therefore (for they then greatly feared them, because they would stand above the Pope), he issued such a judgment and published a decree that no council should be convened again before five years, that it should then be put off to ten years, and that thereafter a general synod should be held from decade to decade. Martin afterwards, having spent two years on the journey (as said), at last came to Rome, long awaited, and reformed the city in its external buildings and Papal ceremonies. He pursued the recovery of the Church's patrimony in the hardest battles, and so that pilgrims bringing money might travel safely, he drove off the highwaymen. He confirmed Louis, son of Louis of Anjou, in the kingdom of Naples, and deprived Alfonso of Aragon of it. He removed certain schisms against the Papal kingdom, and recalled Bologna, when it rebelled, to its fold. He stirred up the Germans to arms against the Bohemians on account of heresy, as they call it, and invited the English Carmelite Walden to write against the Hussites and Wycliffites.

units.la: Cardinales plures creauit, & decreta Ponti-ficum in ipso schismate facta damnauit. Prospe-rum Columnam nepotem (uel spurium) habuit: & in suo Cardinalatu ad D. Georgium sibi succedere paterno animo fecit. Formulam contra stuum uen-ditionis & emptionis promulgauit, thesauros con-gregauit, & alia plura praeter Euangelij regulam egit, Florentiam urbem honore metropolitano ex ornauit: eiq; Volaterranam, Pistoriensem, & Fesulanam ecclesias subiecit. Vrbem Romanam ingressus, & dirutam ac uastatam inueniens, nō modo tepla[?], domos, uicos, & plateas, sed & eius mœnia reparauit. Porticum S. Petri collabentem in primis restituit: & pauimentum Lateranensis ecclesiæ opere uermiculato perfecit, testudinemq; ligneam superinduxit. Aedes praeterea ad duodecim Apostolos uetustate diruptas, reficit: idipsum & Cardinales omnes in suis certatim facere tituli. Papiæ ac Senis synodos otiose celebrauit: & futurum concilium, finito decennio, Basileæ tenendum, decreto suo firmauit. Apoplexia tunc demum anno Domini 1431. Romæ communi decubuit fato[?], in Lateranensi templo ante Apostolorum capita aneo sepulchro tectus. Huius tempore Marcellus Minorita[?], cum hospitalario quodam S. Ioannis, plenārias indulgentias, conficiis Papalibus literis (ut Cranzius refert) Saxonibus pollicebatur, pecuniam largientibus.
units.tr: He created several Cardinals and condemned the decrees made by the Popes during the schism itself. He had a nephew, Prosper Colonna (or a bastard son), and in his own Cardinalate he paternally arranged that Cardinal St George should succeed him. He promulgated a formula against usury in buying and selling, gathered treasures, and did many other things beyond the rule of the Gospel. He adorned the city of Florence with metropolitan honour and made the churches of Volterra, Pistoia and Fiesole subject to it. Entering the city of Rome and finding it razed and wasted, he repaired not only its temples, houses, streets and squares, but also its walls. He first restored the portico of St Peter, which was collapsing, finished the pavement of the Lateran church with inlaid work, and put a wooden vault over it. Moreover, he rebuilt the church of the Twelve Apostles, which had been broken down by age, and all the Cardinals competed to do the same in their own titular churches. He held synods at Pavia and Siena to no purpose, and by his decree confirmed that the future council, once the decade was over, should be held at Basel. At last, in the year of the Lord 1431, he was struck by apoplexy and died a common death at Rome, enclosed in a bronze tomb in the Lateran church before the heads of the Apostles. In his time Marcellus, a Minorite, together with a certain Hospitaller of St John, promised plenary indulgences to the Saxons by forged Papal letters (as Krantz reports) to those who gave money.
152. EUGENIUS the fourth.

units.la: Evgenius quartus patria Venetus, habitu Cœlestinus, Gabriel Condelmerius antea nominatus & ex Angelo patre prognatus, tituli S. Clementis cara Cardinalis[?] presbyter, Pontificatum (ut Platina refert) apud Mineruam hac ratione adeptus est. Creato enim Pontifice olim Gregorio 12. e gente Cor-raria, patria Veneto, Antonius Corrarium eius nepos (sic solent Manzeres appellare) Cœlestinorum canonicus, congregationis S. Georgij in Alga, Romam iturus, Gabrielem hunc, qui eiusdem professionis erat, secum duxit. Quo delectatus Gregorius (erant fortasse eo genitore fratres: nam & Venetus fuit, ac pro confirmando mysterio, Angelus ante Papatum dictus) eum primo thesaurarium fecit, deinceps episcopum Senensem creauit, Antonio Bononiensibus in praesulem dato. Postea rebus suis diffidens, & Roma Lucam profectus, Cardinalium auctiurus[?] numerum, utrunq; nepotem Antonium & Gabrielē in Cardinales retulit. Gabrielis enim opera, magnis in rebus primum Gregorius, postea Martinus usus est, in legationibus maximè. Vnde ad Papatum, ipsis tandem mortuis, ille peruenies, diuina humanaq; omnia perturbauit. Instantibus delatoribus, qui dicerent Martinum praedecessorem congregandi auri cupidum, maximos reliquisse thesauros, eò vesania hominem pulere quidam, ut eius vicecancellarium cum familiaribus ac nepotibus coprehendi atq; spoliari iusserit. Inde Romani ad libertatem respicientes, sublato clamoclamore ad arma concurrebant: pulsisq; omnibus Eugenij magistratibus, & capto Francisco Condelmerio, eius nepote (uel notho) atq; camerario, novos ipsi magistratus creabant. Septem fuere e civibus Romanis, quos ipsi Gubernatores appellabat, penes quos vitae ac necis hominum summa potestas erat.
units.tr: Eugenius IV, a Venetian by birth and a Celestine by habit, was called Gabriel Condulmer before he became pope. He was the son of Angelo, and was a priest and cardinal of the title of St Clement. According to Platina, he obtained the papacy by the following means. When Gregory XII, of the Venetian family of Correr, had been made pope, his nephew Antonio Correr, a canon of the Celestines and of the congregation of St George in Alga (the Manzeres, as they are usually called), set out for Rome and took this Gabriel with him, since he belonged to the same order. Gregory was pleased with him. (They were perhaps brothers by the same father, since he too was a Venetian, and Angelo was his name before he became pope, to confirm the mystery.) Gregory first made him treasurer, then created him bishop of Siena, giving Antonio the see of Bologna. Later, distrusting his own position, Gregory left Rome for Lucca, and in order to increase the number of cardinals he made both his nephews, Antonio and Gabriel, cardinals. Gregory, and afterwards Martin, made great use of Gabriel's services, especially in embassies. So when the two of them had at last died, Gabriel came to the papacy, and he threw everything, divine and human, into confusion. Informers kept saying that Martin, his predecessor, had been greedy for gathering gold and had left enormous treasures behind. Some people went so far in their madness that Eugenius ordered his vice-chancellor, together with his household and nephews, to be arrested and stripped of their property. Then the Romans, looking to their liberty, raised a shout, ran to arms, drove out all Eugenius's officials, seized Francesco Condulmer, his nephew (or bastard son) and chamberlain, and set up new magistrates of their own. There were seven of them, chosen from the Roman citizens, whom they called governors, and in their hands lay the supreme power of life and death over men.

units.la: At vero Eugenius, in tanta rerum perturbatione incertus quid potissimum faceret, de fuga cogitare coepit. Mutato itaq; habitu, sumptoq; monastico cucullo, una cum Arsenio quodam monacho cymbam piscatoriam ingressus, custodibus deceptis, a Tyberi Hostiam vehebatur: quum Romani quidam cognita eius fuga, lapidibus cum sagit-tisq; incesserunt. Abiit hinc Pisas delatus Pontifex, ac deinde Florentiam, triremibus ad[?]id paratis. Ubi aliquot annos commoratus, 16 Cardinales fecit: inter quos Graecos duos, Bessarionem Nicenum & Isidorum Rutenum, ac Guilhelmum Estouteuillam Rothomagensem numerauit. Postea Bononiam se contulit, ibiq; aedes, quas nunc inhabitant legati, sumptuose extruxit. Cum negasset ad Basilienses venire concilium anno Domini 1432. quod diceretur concilium praesse Papae: & citatus, deberet super obiectis sibi criminibus respondere: Papatu depo-nebatur, subrogato Amadeo Sabaudiae duce et eremita[?]. In eo concilio damnati sunt concubinarij, annatæ, & ambulantes in templis dum fiunt sacra, Sess. 20. Communio sub utraq; specie compro-bata, Sess. 30. Pontificis & Cardinalium nepotes & cognati (manzeres[?]) à Cardinalatibus exclusi, Sess. 32. Festa conceptionis & visitationis Mariæ ordinata, Sess. 36. cum aliis. Eugenius vero, ut illud, Basiliense concilium dissiparet, alterū Fer-rariæ, postea Florentiæ convocavit. Pontificiæ enim authoritati satis erat molestum atq; aduer-sum, cum Papam, cuius pedes osculari debebat, sub iectum[?] esse concilijs decerneret. Fuerunt Florentiæ, Græcorum, Aethiopum, Asianorum[?], Armenorum, Indorum, Rhutenorum, & aliorum orientalium legati: qui cum Romana religione illic in multis consenserunt, quoniam omnes tunc erant sumptibus Romanæ pontificis (teste Stella) enu-triti. Sed domum reversi nuncij, Rhutenorum præsertim, à suis non sunt auditi, in his quæ Papæ & Cardinalibus concesserant: ut habent annales Poloniæ.
units.tr: But Eugenius, uncertain in such great upheaval what he should do above all, began to think of flight. So he changed his dress, put on a monk's hood, and with a certain monk, Arsenius, got into a fishing boat. Having deceived the guards, he was carried down the Tiber towards Ostia. But some Romans, when they learned of his flight, attacked him with stones and arrows. The pope was then taken away to Pisa, and afterwards to Florence, in galleys made ready for the purpose. Staying there for some years, he created sixteen cardinals, among whom he counted two Greeks, Bessarion of Nicaea and Isidore of Russia, and Guillaume d'Estouteville of Rouen. Afterwards he went to Bologna, and there built at great expense the palace which the legates now occupy. When he refused to come to the Council of Basel in the year of the Lord 1432, on the ground that the council was said to be superior to the pope, and when he was summoned and ought to answer the charges laid against him, he was deposed from the papacy, and Amadeus, duke of Savoy and a hermit, was put in his place. In that council the concubinaries and those who took annates were condemned, and those who walk about in the churches while sacred rites are being performed (Session 20). Communion under both kinds was approved (Session 30). The nephews and kinsmen (the manzeres) of popes and cardinals were excluded from the cardinalate (Session 32). The feasts of the Conception and the Visitation of Mary were ordained (Session 36), along with other matters. But Eugenius, in order to break up the council of Basel, summoned another at Ferrara and later at Florence. For it was very irksome and hostile to papal authority that a council should decree that the pope, whose feet he ought to kiss, is subject to councils. At Florence there were present legates of the Greeks, Ethiopians, Asians, Armenians, Indians, Ruthenians and other eastern peoples. In many matters they agreed there with the Roman religion, since all of them were at that time supported at the expense of the Roman pontiff (according to Stella). But when the envoys returned home, especially the Ruthenian ones, they were not heard by their own people in the matters that they had conceded to the pope and the cardinals, as the annals of Poland record.

units.la: Libet hic referre miserabilem Vladislai Hun-gariæ regis cladem. Eugenius hunc regem iuvenem compulit, ut Amurathi Turcarum regi fidem, qua ei inito secum fœdere dederat, non servaret. Cui tanquam patri sanctissimo, dum Vladislaus, duos &[?] viginti annos natus, incautè obedire studet, debitas pœnas violati fœderis Amurathi persoluit. Nam dum Amurathes bellum, innumeris copiis se cum adductis, committit, magnaque suorum clade accepta, tandem & ipse, ab Eugenio deceptus, ferro[?] occubuit. Ferunt hunc Eugenium, mirum in modum amasse bella: & multa indignatione permotum, Ludovicum Delphinum, Caroli septimi Francorum regis filium, cum magno comitatu in Basilienses concitasse, unde mala infinita sequebantur. Et ubi Romam postea venit, urbi multa contulit. Maximè circa Vaticanum, aerarij officinam & aream palatii instauravit: ac vias publicas multis in locis strauit. Picturam basilicæ Lateranensis, à Martino inchoatam in pariete, absoluit: porticumque, qua ad Sancta sanctorum itur, extruxit. Monasterium quod iuxta Lateranum est, refecit: ac pulsis inde canonicis secularibus, Frisona-rios regulares ex Lucensis agri loco accitos, introduxit. Basilicam S. Petri reparavit: atque eius sacristiam multa supellectili donavit. Scholas quasdam instituit: ac gymnasia sophisticis doctoribus fouit. Monachos omnes mirum in modum dilexit: & mendicantes fraterculos privilegiis & gratiis auxit.
units.tr: It is worth recording here the miserable defeat of Ladislaus, king of Hungary. Eugenius compelled this young king to break the faith that he had pledged to Murad, king of the Turks, in the treaty he had made with him. While Ladislaus, twenty-two years old, eagerly obeyed this most holy father to his own peril, Murad exacted the penalty due for the broken treaty. For when Murad joined battle with his innumerable forces, and after great slaughter of his own men, he too, deceived by Eugenius, at last fell by the sword. They say that this Eugenius loved wars in a wonderful way, and that, moved by great indignation, he stirred up Louis the Dauphin, son of Charles VII, king of the French, with a large retinue against the Basel fathers, whence infinite evils followed. And when he later came to Rome, he conferred many benefits on the city. Above all he restored the mint and the palace courtyard near the Vatican, and he paved the public roads in many places. He completed the painting on the wall of the basilica of the Lateran, begun by Martin, and built the portico through which one goes to the Holy of Holies. He rebuilt the monastery next to the Lateran, and, driving out the secular canons from it, introduced regular Augustinian canons brought from a place in the territory of Lucca. He repaired the basilica of St Peter and enriched its sacristy with much furniture. He founded certain schools and supported the academies with sophistical teachers. He loved all the monks in a remarkable way, and he increased the privileges and graces of the mendicant friars.

units.la: Thomam Rhedonensem nihilominus, qui reformandæ festæ Carmelitice gratia in Italiam vene-[?]rat, per Rothomagensem Cardinalem, Guilhelmū Estouteuillam, terribili corporis incendio post varios cruciatus suffulit. Dixerat enim Thomas, abominationes Romæ fieri (magnum piaculum certè) atq; ecclesiam egere magna reformatione. Dixerat etiam, Papæ excommunicationem, dum Christi res agitur, non esse metuendam. Sed in eius sanctissima refartionem, regulæ mitigationem in carnium esu, eius festæ fraterculis concessit: Ioannem Facium, eorum magistrum generalem, episcopum Rhedonensem fecit: et Cyrillum, doctorem illum qui visiones habuerat, in sanctos referri permisit.
units.tr: Nevertheless, Thomas of Rennes, who had come to Italy to reform the Carmelite order, was, through the cardinal of Rouen, Guillaume d'Estouteville, put to death by a dreadful burning of his body after various tortures. For Thomas had said that abominations were being committed at Rome (a great crime indeed), and that the Church needed a great reformation. He had also said that the excommunication of the pope was not to be feared while the cause of Christ was being carried on. Yet, in order to make amends for this, Eugenius granted to the friars of that order a relaxation of the rule in the eating of meat. He made John Faci, their general master, bishop of Rennes, and permitted Cyril, that teacher who had had visions, to be enrolled among the saints.

units.la: De prædicto Thoma ex Illyrici Catalogo: Thomas, inquit, Rhedonius, Carmelita, Gallus, in duo catu Britanniæ natus, celebris, Antonino teste, concionator, floruit circa annum Christi 1430. Is inter concionandum per Galliam et Italiam solitus erat dicere ac docere Romæ magnas abominationes fieri: ecclesiam magna reformatione indigere: et quod prælati depositio fastu ac luxu, deberent modestius instar Christi et Apostolorum vivere, iniustasque Papæ execrationes non esse timendas. Ob hasce gravissimas hæreses, et in Papatum blasphemias, curavit eum Antichristus Eugenius quartus, Romæ anno Domini 1436, exuri. De sacer dotum quoq; coniugio pie sensit hic Thomas, dum scripsit, in salutem esse multarum animarum, si continere non valentes, nuptiis uti Grecorum mo-re permitterentur. Cum essent tunc immundi, & illicito coitu macularentur: ubi cum uxore propria castitas effet, &c. Antonini testimonii de hoc Tho-ma, par.3 tit.22, cap.10. Quidam, inquit, Carmelitarum ordinis, magnus prædicator, natione Gallicus, quum pluribus annis per Franciam prædicasset cum maximo populorum concursu, magnas faciens commotiones in bonum, etsi non secundum scientiam, Papismum intelligit, ad urbem veniens cum oratoribus Venetorum, qui affectuose eum Po-tifici recommissum faciebant: captus ad instantiam Cardinalis Rothomagensis, Guilhelmi de Estoute-villa, tunc vicecancellarii, & procuratoris ordinis ipsius Carmelitarum fratris, Natalis Veneti, pro hæresibus prædicatis examinatus, sic divini verbi ministros duplicit er[?] honorant, et ut relapsus convictus, ac degradatus solenniter, ad ignem adiudicatus, consumptus est.
units.tr: Concerning the aforesaid Thomas, from the Catalogue of Illyricus: Thomas, he says, of Rennes, a Carmelite, a Frenchman, born in the duchy of Brittany, a famous preacher (according to Antoninus), flourished around the year of Christ 1430. While preaching through France and Italy he used to say and teach that great abominations were being committed at Rome, that the Church needed a great reformation, and that prelates, given over to pride and luxury, ought to live more modestly after the example of Christ and the apostles, and that the unjust curses of the pope were not to be feared. For these most grave heresies and blasphemies against the papacy, the Antichrist Eugenius IV had him burned at Rome in the year of the Lord 1436. Thomas also held a godly view about the marriage of priests, when he wrote that it would be for the salvation of many souls if, since those who could not contain themselves were becoming unclean and defiled by illicit intercourse, they were allowed to marry in the manner of the Greeks, so that chastity might be with their own wife, and so on. Testimony of Antoninus about this Thomas, part 3, title 22, chapter 10: "A certain man of the Carmelite order, a great preacher, a Frenchman by nation, after he had preached for many years through France with the largest crowds of people, creating great stirrings for good, though not according to knowledge, came to the city with envoys of the Venetians, who lovingly commended him to the pope. He was seized at the instance of the cardinal of Rouen, Guillaume de Estouteville, then vice-chancellor, and of Natale Veneto, the procurator of the order of Carmelite friars. He was examined about the heresies he had preached. He honoured the ministers of the divine word in a double way, and, convicted as a relapsed heretic and solemnly degraded, he was condemned to the fire and consumed."

units.la: Ex Baptistæ Mantuani libro, de Vita beata, cap. ultimo: Thomas quidam Gallus, qui pristinum fidei feruorem adhuc in pectore fouebat, cum paucis in Italiam se contulit. Sic enim Deo visum est, ut ea regio, quæ cæteris omni munere præstat, hoc etiam uirorum habeat ornamentum uerum nō solum Italiæ, sed etiam uiro sancto Deus ipse consuluit. Illi enim dedit, cuius uitam posset imitari: isti uero, purpurei diadema martyrij. Nam dum bene beateq; uiueret, à quibusdam invidis, apud summum Pontificem capitis accersitur. Et post carcerem, post tormenta, post cruciatus, tandem quum nihil damnabile reperissent, gravius investigarunt: quod iure nō potuerunt, iniuria perficere fortiter accinguntur, & comburendum scelerato rogo com-miserunt. Ah, quo prorumpis efferate liuor? Sed tamen illum non occidisti: nequit enim anima extingui. Sed illius terrenum corpus uiolando, secisti, ut citius uita donaretur æterna. Huius flammas, non Scævolæ rogo, sed Laurentii posse compara-ri, non dubito. Dicant quicquid uelint: obstrepant, clamitent, & insaniant: ille summo uiuit Olympo. Sed multa de hoc uiro, silentio praeteriui, &c.
units.tr: From the last chapter of Baptista Mantuanus's book On the Blessed Life: "A certain Frenchman, Thomas, who still kept the former fervour of faith in his breast, went into Italy with a few companions. For God so willed that this region, which excels all others in every gift, should also have this ornament of men. God himself took thought for this holy man. He gave to Italy one whose life it could imitate, and to him the purple diadem of martyrdom. For while he lived well and blessedly, he was accused before the highest Pontiff by certain envious men. After prison, after torments, after tortures, at last, when they found nothing blameworthy, they investigated more severely; and because they could not do it lawfully, they girded themselves vigorously to do it by wrong, and they committed him to the accursed pyre to be burned. Ah, to what do you rush, savage spite? Yet you did not kill him, for the soul cannot be extinguished. By violating his earthly body you caused him to be given eternal life the sooner. I do not doubt that his flames can be compared, not with the fire of Scaevola, but with that of Laurence. Let them say what they will: let them clamour, shout, and rage; he lives on the highest Olympus. But I have passed over many things about this man in silence, etc."

units.la: CARMINA QVAEDAM IN EIVS laudem, in Nicolai Harlemensis collectionibus reperta.
units.tr: POEMS IN PRAISE OF HIM, found in the collections of Nicolas of Harlem.

units.la: Claustra Thomas gallus, primus qui lapsa refor- Carmeli gregis, heu cadit immerito. (mat[?] Compulit hunc feruor, Domini conspergere femè: Exitium uitijs uita modesta dabat.
units.tr: Thomas the Frenchman, first to reform the fallen flock of Carmel, alas, falls undeservedly. Zeal drove him to spread the Lord's fame; a modest life gave destruction to vices.

units.la: Dogmata præconis, miracula concomitantur: Illum quæ doceant pectus habere pium.
units.tr: The preacher's doctrines are accompanied by miracles, which teach a pious heart to have them.

units.la: Quantum sic populum Zabuli de dentibus egit, Et vita & verbo, credere nemo potest.
units.tr: No one can believe how greatly he drew the people from the teeth of the devil, by his life and by his word.

units.la: Lippis lux oculis nocuit: non sustinuere Vivere tam sanctum fœda Romana cohors.
units.tr: Light harmed bleary eyes: the foul Roman cohort could not endure to live so holy a life.

units.la: Sistitur hæresis, fidem quod sitiq; sacerdos, Eugenio Papæ, & frivola quæq; patent.
units.tr: The heresy is checked, because the priest thirsted for the faith; to Pope Eugenius, and all frivolous things are laid open.

units.la: Instituit sacris antistes hunc Rhedonensis, Testis apud Gallos publica fama volat.
units.tr: The bishop of Rennes ordained him to sacred duties; public fame flies, a witness among the Gauls.

units.la: Sordida Roma Thomam Papa sordente petebat, Flamma sorbendum, quamq; tyrannus alit.
units.tr: Sordid Rome sought Thomas through a sordid pope; the flame is to swallow him, which the tyrant feeds.

units.la: Urget adhoc primas Guilhelmus Rothomagensis, Cardinei cœtus. Sic perit innocuus.
units.tr: Guilhelm of Rouen, the primate, presses on with the college of cardinals. Thus the harmless man perishes.

units.la: Perstitit igne Thomas, constanti pectore firmus, Quod Christi exemplo vivere clerus habet.
units.tr: Thomas persisted in the fire, firm in a constant breast, which the clergy has as Christ's example of living.

units.la: Eugenius memorans tandem, quod insidiosa Morte viri, fuerit credulus ipse malis:
units.tr: Eugenius, at last recalling that he himself had been too credulous of the evil devices behind the man's treacherous death,

units.la: Ingemuit crebro, uir quod tam sanctus obisset, Hoc quoq; præ cunctis conqueritur abiens.
units.tr: often groaned that a man so holy had died; this, too, he complains of above all others as he departs.

units.la: Non nocuit flamma ista Thomæ, sed martyriū dat, Immortalis ei parta corona manet.
units.tr: That flame did not harm Thomas but gave him martyrdom; the immortal crown prepared for him remains.
To this is added a couplet:

units.la: Post tormenta pius (sibi dant quæ carcer & ignis) Martyr ad æthereas convolat ille domos.
units.tr: After torments, which prison and fire give to themselves, the pious martyr flies up to the heavenly homes.

units.la: Præterea, ante Papatum, Eugenius S. Agnetis templum Anconæ, atq; eius urbis portu magna impensa restituit: & in ipso Papatu, Sigismundum Cæsarem imperiali diademate Romæ coronauit: annatasq; beneficiorum omnium post Bonifacium nanum, auarum & ipse, confirmauit. Romæ tandè o-bijt anno à Christi natiuitate 1446. ad S. Petrum sepultus. In quo quidem anno Nicolaum Tolentinum, Augustinianum, in sanctos retulit, ut & illi quoq; suum habérent idolum. Mitram S. Syluestri, Romam Aueniòe delatam, ipsemet è Vaticano ad Lateranum detulit, magna cum veneratione ac leta-nia: & de quibusdam sacrificulis supplicium sumpsit, qui preciosos lapides è capitibus Petri et Pauli furtim surripuerant. Huius tempore Ludouicus Cardinalis Aquilegiensis (ut testatur Volaterranus) primus fuit ordinis erat, qui de bonis Ecclesiæ canes & equos pauperum loco alere cœpit. De scorti s non loquitur, cum id sit purpuratis patribus cōmune. Fautores prædicti Eugenij illum vehementer laudant: alij econtrà uituperant eius uitam, enormia ipsi tribuentes uitia.
units.tr: Besides this, before his papacy, Eugenius restored at great expense the church of St Agnes at Ancona and the harbour of that city. And in the papacy itself he crowned Emperor Sigismund at Rome with the imperial diadem, and confirmed the annates of all benefices after Boniface the Dwarf, being himself greedy for money. He died at Rome in the year 1446 after Christ's birth, and was buried at St Peter's. In that same year he enrolled among the saints Nicholas of Tolentino, an Augustinian, so that they too might have their own idol. He himself carried the mitre of St Silvester, brought to Rome from Avignon, from the Vatican to the Lateran, with great veneration and litanies; and he exacted punishment from certain minor priests who had secretly stolen precious stones from the heads of Peter and Paul. In his time Cardinal Ludovico of Aquileia (as Volaterranus testifies) was the first of his order to begin feeding dogs and horses at the expense of the Church's goods, in place of the poor. He does not speak of whores, since that is common to the purple-clad fathers. The supporters of this Eugenius praise him greatly; others, on the contrary, censure his life, attributing to him monstrous vices.

units.la: His temporibus magna fuit in Italia fratrum Mendicantium & aliorum monachorum reformatio: quæ nouella serpentis antiqui facies erat, ac recte decipiendi fucus. Iuxta prophetarum vaticinia, Esaiæ[?] 47. & Nahum 3. Babylonis illius meretricis magna, Dominus his diebus pudenda reuelauit: nu ditatem, ignominiam, opprobrium, & fœditatem eius, gentibus ac regnis ostendit, per electos suos Io annem Vuicleuum, Ioannem Hussium, Hieronymũ Pragensem, Thomam Thedonium, & alios. Atq; ultionem de ea capiens, contumelijs magnis per ipsos illam affecit: ut omnibus est notissimum. At serpens insidiosus, qui & suam dederat potestatem bestiæ, Apoc. 13. ad ueteres artes recurrens, nouas fraudes adinuenit, & in suis practicauit creaturis. Nouam enim hanc fucatæ reformationis faciem so phisticè induit Babylonica meretrix, ecclesiæ scilicet Romana, Satanæ synagoga, ut in omni dæmoniorum doctrinis ac superstitione mundum adhuc nutriret. Addidit illi saciei quorundam mortuorum canonizationes, ut in suis reformatis augeret simulatæ sanctitatis samam, fortiusq; per illas decipe-ret mundum Nicolaum Tolētinum Eugenius quar-tus, Augustinianus sanctum dedit, anno Domini 1446. Nicolaum quintum Franciscanis Bernardinũ Senensem, anno Domini 1451. Calixtus tertiũ Vin-centium Hispanũ Dominicanũ, anno Domini 1455. & Albertum Siculum Drepanensem Carmelitã, anno Domini 1457. ita ut eodem anno, Ioanne Pa-leonydoro teste, in Letaniis diceretur, Sancte Al-berte ora pro nobis, &c. Concefsumq; illis erat, ut sorores ac sinzocherus[?] ad suas professiones trahe-re possent, & coenobia illis aedificare. Talia enim sunt Antichristi miracula, ut dum uiuos sanctos ad ignes & inferos damnaret, mortuos quosdam ad ueterum deorum admitteret cultu. Talia sunt pro digia[?] meretricis magnae, quae sedens super bestiam coccineam, ebria est ex sanguine martyrum Iesu. Concilium equidem Papae, promittens Ecclesiae reformationem, simile est illi Aesopicae fabellae, cum parturiunt montes, nascitur ridiculus mus.
units.tr: In these times there was great reform of the Mendicant friars and other monks in Italy; this was a new face of the ancient serpent and a fine pretence for deceiving rightly. According to the prophecies of the prophets (Isaiah 47 and Nahum 3), in these days the Lord has uncovered the shameful things of that great harlot of Babylon: he has shown her nakedness, disgrace, reproach and foulness to the nations and kingdoms, through his chosen ones John Wycliffe, John Hus, Jerome of Prague, Thomas Thedonius and others. Taking vengeance on her, he has inflicted great disgrace upon her through them, as is well known to all. But the crafty serpent, who had also given his power to the beast (Revelation 13), returning to his old arts, has devised new frauds and practised them on his creatures. For the Babylonian harlot, namely the Roman Church, the synagogue of Satan, has cunningly put on this new face of a painted reformation, so that she might still nourish the world in all the doctrines and superstitions of demons. She added to this appearance the canonisations of certain dead men, so that by her reformed face she might increase the fame of feigned holiness and deceive the world more strongly through them. Eugenius IV, an Augustinian, gave Nicholas of Tolentino the status of saint in the year of the Lord 1446; Nicholas V gave Bernardine of Siena, a Franciscan, the same in 1451; Callixtus III gave Vincent of Spain, a Dominican, in 1455, and Albert of Sicily of Trapani, a Carmelite, in 1457; so that in that same year, as John Paleonydorus testifies, in the litanies it was said, "St Albert, pray for us," and so on. It was also granted to them that they could draw sisters and ... to their professions, and build convents for them. Such are the miracles of Antichrist, that while he condemns living saints to fires and hell, he admits certain dead men to the worship of the old gods. Such are the prodigies of the great harlot, who, sitting upon the scarlet beast, is drunk with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. Indeed the Pope's council, which promised a reformation of the Church, is like that Aesopic fable: when the mountains are in labour, a ridiculous mouse is born.
153. FELIX the Fifth.

units.la: Felix quintus, patria Allobrox uel Sabaudus, A-madeus eremita ante Papatum uocatus: Sabau-diae dux primus (nam antea comites erant) uxora-tus, & duos habens filios, Eugenio deposito, uigin-tifex electorum suffragio, ad Pontificatum proue-hebatur. Electus tamen, & in fede Papali Bafilien-sis synodi authoritate confirmatus, Eugenij pra-dicti factione impeditus, Romanam sellam, quam Petri cathedram uocant, ascendere nunquam potuit. Nouem annis exortum inde schisma duravit, & multae seditiones in regionibus Christianorum erant: aliis Felici, aliis Eugenio obtemperantibus, multisque neutrales appellari gaudebant. In eo quo que schismate pleriq; dicebant, Papam debere sub-iectum esse concilio generali: alij contrà, unde ea-mersit[?] mersit grandis tunc altercatio & quæstio, num Pa-pa esset ecclesiæ caput? quæ nec in hunc usq; diem finitur. Vir prouectæ ætatis ac senex ante ponti-ficatum, filiorum suorum filios, regum filiabus in matrimonio coniunctos uidit: ac reliquis seculi cu-ris, cum sex equestris ordinis hominibus secedens in solitudine Deo seruire instituit.
units.tr: Felix the Fifth, a native of Savoy or of Sabaudia, was called Amadeus, a hermit before his papacy. He was the first duke of Savoy (before this they had been counts), was married and had two sons. With Eugenius deposed, he was raised to the pontificate by the votes of twenty electors. Though elected, and confirmed in the papal see by the authority of the Council of Basel, hindered by the faction of the aforesaid Eugenius, he could never ascend the Roman seat, which they call the chair of Peter. The schism that arose from this lasted nine years, and there were many seditions in the regions of the Christians: some obeyed Felix, others Eugenius, and many rejoiced to be called neutrals. In this schism too, many said that the Pope ought to be subject to a general council; others, on the contrary, asked whether the Pope was the head of the Church, and from this arose a great dispute and question at that time, which is not settled even to this day. Having been an old man of advanced age before his papacy, he had seen the sons of his sons joined in marriage to the daughters of kings; and leaving the other cares of the world, withdrew with six men of the equestrian order into solitude and began to serve God.

units.la: Cum uero se audiuisset, generalis concilii au-thoritate Pontificem creatum, rasus ac tonsus, mul-taq; stipatus nobilitate, illuc uenit. Et consecratus[?] tum demum, omnia peregit, quæ ad Papatus stabant officium: ordinabat, confirmabat, dedica-bat, consecrabat, sacrificabat, excommunicabat, Cardinales & Episcopos creabat, benedictiones atq; indulgentias dabat, seq; pro Pontifice nouem annis gerebat. Adeo munificus in pauperes fuit, ut ab oratoribus semel rogatus, si quos haberet ca-nes uenaticos, ut eos ostenderet, responderit: se al-tera die eos ostensurum. Cum uero adessent die se-quenti, ingentem mendicorum & egenorum mul-titudinem ostendit, una discumbentium. Atq; hi sunt, inquit, canes mei, quos alo quotidie: quib. spe-ro me cœlestem gloriam uenaturum. Huic tandem placuit anno Domini 1447. in fauorem unionis, Nicolao quinto, depositò Papæ nomine, tandem ce-dere. Quem ille propterea totius Germaniæ ac FranFranciæ legatum (in titulis enim gloriantur) & Sa-binensem cardinalem constituit: nec diu postea su-peruixit. Monasterium Ripalense mirificè instau-rauit: & ibi, ut fertur, anno Domini 1449. sepul-tus, in pace requiescit.
units.tr: When, however, he heard that he had been created Pontiff by the authority of a general council, he came there, shaved and tonsured, and attended by a great crowd of nobility. Then at last, having been consecrated, he performed all the duties that belong to the office of the papacy: he ordained, confirmed, dedicated, consecrated, sacrificed, excommunicated, created cardinals and bishops, gave blessings and indulgences, and bore himself as Pope for nine years. He was so generous to the poor that, when the envoys once asked him whether he had any hunting dogs, so that he might show them, he replied that he would show them the next day. But when they came the following day, he showed them a huge crowd of beggars and needy people, dining together. "These," he said, "are my dogs, which I feed daily; with them I hope to hunt heavenly glory." At last, in the year of the Lord 1447, he was pleased, for the sake of union, to yield to Nicholas V, having laid down the papal name. Nicholas then appointed him legate of all Germany and France (for they boast of titles) and cardinal of Sabina; nor did he survive long afterwards. He magnificently restored the monastery of Ripaille, and there, as is said, he was buried in the year of the Lord 1449, and rests in peace.
154. NICOLAUS the Fifth.

units.la: Nicolaus quintus, patria Genuensis, in oppido Sarzanensi ex humili genere natus patre Bartholomeo chirurgo, & Thomas Sarzanus antea dic-tus, uno & eodem anno episcopatus Bononiensis, Cardinalatus, ac romani papatus munus est adep-tus. Missus olim cum Ioanne Caruagialla cardina-le Hispano, ab Eugenio in Germaniam, neutralita-tis tollendæ gratia (instabat enim Iubileum: mysterium intellige) Aeneam Syluium, cognomine Picolhomineum, apud imperatorem Fridericum ter-tium, fautorem inuenit. Germani etenim tunc tempo-ris neutrales ideo dicebantur, quod sub schisma-te, neque Felicis neque Eugenij dictis obtemperarent. Apud hos, ut Eugenio se submitterent, mul-tis adhortationibus agens, & ut sublato schisma-te Pontificia maiestas restauraretur, serio labo-rans, omnia ex voto reportauit. Redeuntes itaque cum tam læto responso legati, succlamantibus om-nibus, Cardinales decernebatur. Eiusque Eugenius ad portam Flaminiam roseos galeros obuiam misit, ut urbem insigniores ingrederentur, atq; in sena- tus ordinem recepit. Hinc ad Pontificatum Euge- nio defuncto susceptus, Stephanum Porcarium, e- quitem Romanum, pro urbis libertate tumul- tuantem, unà cum caeteris coniuratis, ad muros ex Hadriani mole seu arce S. Angeli, Papali cha- ritate [?] suspendit. Iubileum (diu expectatum) an- no Domini 1450. pro nummis celebrauit. In quo dum semel cum crucifixo quodam idolo è Vatica- no ad urbem redirent, sista [?] obuiam mula quaedam Petri Bardi, Cardinalis S. Marci, cum nequeuni- entes neq; redeuntes ob insequentem multitudinem cedere possent, cadente uno atq; altero supermu- lam illam iam à multitudine oppressam, ad ducen- tà hominum corpora in Hadriani ponte obtrita & suffocata esse constat. Multi etiam à lateribus pon- tis in flumen cadentes, in undis periere. Sepulta in S.Celso ad centum & triginta sex suerunt: reliqua vero ad campum sanctum delata sunt. Talia iusto Dei iudicio premia meruerunt, qui relicto eius uer- bo, tam execrabilium Antichristorum idola seque bantur.
units.tr: Nicolaus the Fifth, a Genoese by birth, was born of humble stock in the town of Sarzana, the son of Bartholomew, a surgeon. Formerly called Thomas of Sarzana, he obtained in one and the same year the bishopric of Bologna, the cardinalate and the office of the Roman papacy. Once he had been sent into Germany by Eugenius, together with John Carvajal, a Spanish cardinal, to remove the neutrality (for the Jubilee was impending; understand the mystery), he found Aeneas Sylvius, surnamed Piccolomini, a supporter of the emperor Frederick the Third. The Germans of that time were called neutral for this reason: under the schism, they would obey neither the dictates of Felix nor those of Eugenius. Nicolaus, working among them with many exhortations, and labouring earnestly that the schism might be ended and papal majesty restored, brought back everything he had wished for. So the legates returned with such a happy answer, and to the acclaim of all, he was made a cardinal. Eugenius sent rose-coloured galeri to meet him at the Flaminian Gate, so that he might enter the city in greater distinction, and he received him into the order of the senate. Afterwards, when Eugenius died, he was raised to the pontificate. He hanged Stephen Porcari, a Roman knight who was stirring up tumult for the liberty of the city, together with the other conspirators, from the walls of the Mole of Hadrian, or Castel Sant'Angelo, with papal charity [?]. In the year of the Lord 1450 he celebrated the Jubilee (long awaited) for money. During it, when once the people were returning to the city from the Vatican with a certain crucified idol, a mule belonging to Peter Barbo, Cardinal of St Mark, stood in their path. Since they could neither push forward nor go back because of the crowd following behind, one and then another fell, and the mule, now overwhelmed by the crowd, was trampled upon. It is agreed that some two hundred bodies were crushed and suffocated on the bridge of Hadrian. Many also fell from the sides of the bridge into the river and perished in the waves. Of the dead, 136 were buried in St Celsus; the rest were carried to the Campo Santo. By the just judgment of God they deserved these rewards, since they had abandoned his word and worshipped the idols of such execrable Antichrists.

units.la: Sed quid secit hic pastor iniquus, uel uoracisi- mus lupus, qui potius carnes quàm animas quaesi- uit? Vices eorum (inquit Platina) qui mortui sue- rant. rant, dolens, casulas quasdam angustiorem viam ad pontem facientes, omnino sustulit (Papalis pro uisito[?] totumq; fere annum illum (pro implendis cru-menis idololatra) in celebrationibus cofumpfit: sta-tiones ipsemet (Satanæ minister) quotidie inuisens, cum Cardinalium cœtu. Cauit etiam quàm diligen-tissimè, non ut grex Dei, Euangelij pabulo pasce-retur, sed ne crescente tanta multitudine (ad suum quæstum) commeatus, & omnia ad uictum necessa-ria, in urbe non deessent. Curauit quoq; (pontifica-le officium) execrationibus ac satellitibus, ne gras-satores in peregrinos, ad urbem accedentes (& nummos afferentes) seuirent. Et hunc integerrimū Papam Vuicelius uocat, hostem auaritiæ, ac theo-logicis deditum studijs: religiosissimumq; hominē, quòd in Letanijs, quas crebras idololatra peregit, pedes iuerit. Atq; hoc sub Euangelij luce, sed ob uē-trem, facit insignis hypocrita. Sub hoc Papa, in-quit, capta & amissa nobis est Constantinopolis, to-tius orbis nostri luctu. Magna iam certè: sed cau-sam cæca bestia non addit. Nicolaus præterea, Fri-dericum tertium Cæsarem, unà cum coniuge Leo-nora, Imperiali diademate cinxit: ac bibliothecam Vaticanam (sed pro suo regno, aduersus Christum) magnificè instituit. Literarum studia tunc ferè de-leta, ut ferunt authores, summo conatu iterum ex citauit: doctis hominibus, qui eas proponeret, prae-miis inuitatis. Et in hoc facto nunc quoq; laudandus esset, si ad Christi gloriam id praestaret[?]. Sed hoc dedecorat optimos eius conatus, quod nimio bibendi studio teneretur[?], perquisitis undiq; uinorum generi-bus.
units.tr: But what did this wicked minister do, or this most ravenous wolf, who sought flesh rather than souls? He removed the altars of those who had died, as Platina says, grieving; he entirely abolished certain little cloisters that made the way narrower to the bridge (for the papal ...), and he spent nearly that whole year in idolatrous celebrations for the filling of his purse, visiting the stations himself every day as a minister of Satan, together with a company of cardinals. He also took the greatest care, not that the flock of God might be fed with the food of the gospel, but that, with so great a multitude coming in (for his own gain), supplies and everything needed for living should not be lacking in the city. He also took care, as befits the papal office, that the curses and his guards should prevent robbers from raging against the pilgrims who approached the city (and brought money). And Wycliffe calls this most upright pope an enemy of avarice, devoted to theological studies, and a most religious man, because he went barefoot in the litanies which he celebrated often in idolatry. Yet under the light of the gospel he was an outstanding hypocrite, and he did this for the sake of his belly. Under this pope, he says, Constantinople was taken and lost to us, to the grief of our whole world. Indeed it was a great loss, but the blind beast does not add the cause. Nicolaus moreover crowned Frederick the Third, the emperor, together with his wife Eleanor, with the imperial diadem, and magnificently established the Vatican library (but for his own kingdom, against Christ). The study of letters, which the authors say had then almost been destroyed, he revived again with the greatest effort, inviting learned men with rewards to set them forth. In this deed he would even now deserve praise, if he had done it for the glory of Christ. But what disgraces his best endeavours is that he was held by an excessive passion for drinking, having sought out every kind of wine from everywhere.

units.la: De eius uero aedificijs refert Platina: Portas urbis ac turres, inquit, Capitolium, & arcem S. Angeli muris firmissimis munire coepit, cum intelligeret illuc uenturum imperatorem Fridericum. Erat enim natura formidolosus. Et sequitur: Aedificauit praeterea magnificè & splendidè, tum in urbe, tu[?] in Vaticano. In urbe aedes Pontificias apud S. Mariam praesepe. Restituit & templum S. Stephani in Caelio monte. A fundamentis erexit S. Theodori templum, inter Palatinum & Capitolinum montem. Pantheon quoq; in medio urbis positum, templum uetustissimum, plumbeo tecto operuit. In Vatica-no autem pontificias aedes ad sumptuosam for-mam redegit. Muros eiusdem Vaticani praealtos & latos inchoauit, iactis maioribus fundamentis. Pontem quoq; Miluium restaurauit, & aedes egregias ad balnea Viterbiana construxit, iuuit[?] & multos pecunia, qui in urbe aedificabant. Eius item mandato, uici urbis fere omnes strati sunt[?]. Extant adhuc uasa aurea & argentea. Extant cruces gem mis ornatæ. Extant & sacerdotales uestes auro & margaritis insignitæ. Extant peripetasmata et aulæa auro & argento intertexta. Extat & mitra pontificia (uide superbia huius Abadonis) quæ omnia hominis magnificentiam nobis ostendunt. Hæc Platina. Accipe & alia miracula, quæ Nico-laus artificiose edidit. Ex prædecessore Felice Cardinalem ac legatum fecit. Oportebat enim illum Papatui tuc cedere, propter instantem iubileum, qui tantum lucri secum afferret. At quia comiter id egit (cogente tamen imperatore) ipsius acta religio se probauit: & Cardinales ab eo prius ordinatos, admisit. Monachos mirifice amauit, ac beneficijs iuuit. Carmelitis, solicitante Soretho, sorores uir-gines dedit, easq; bullis confirmauit. Bernardinum Senensem Franciscanum, sanctorum ascripsit numero rosam in Dominica Lætare, Hasiæ Landgrauio transmisit: & alia multa valde pontificaliter egit, Febri ac podagra demum uexatus, anno Domini 1455. ex hac uita decessit.
units.tr: Platina reports on his buildings: "He began," he says, "to fortify the gates and towers of the city, the Capitol and the citadel of St Angelo, with very strong walls, since he understood that the emperor Frederick would come there, for he was by nature fearful." And he goes on: "He also built magnificently and splendidly, both in the city and in the Vatican. In the city he built the papal residence by St Mary of the Manger. He restored also the church of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. From the foundations he raised the church of St Theodore, between the Palatine and the Capitoline hills. He also covered the Pantheon, placed in the middle of the city, a most ancient temple, with a leaden roof. In the Vatican he reduced the papal residence to a sumptuous form. He began the very high and broad walls of the same Vatican, laying the greater foundations. He also restored the Milvian Bridge and built splendid baths at Viterbo, and he helped with money many who were building in the city. By his command almost all the streets of the city were paved. There still exist golden and silver vessels. There still exist crosses adorned with gems, and priestly vestments distinguished with gold and pearls. There still exist hangings and curtains interwoven with gold and silver, and also the papal mitre (see the pride of this Abaddon), all of which show us the magnificence of the man." So Platina. Hear also other marvels which Nicolaus performed with artifice. He made Felix, his predecessor, a cardinal and legate. For Felix had to yield the papacy at that time, on account of the impending Jubilee, which would bring so much profit with it. But because he did this courteously (though under compulsion from the emperor), his religious life proved itself, and he admitted the cardinals previously ordained by him. He loved the monks wonderfully and aided them with benefices. At the solicitation of Sorét he gave virgin sisters to the Carmelites and confirmed them by bulls. On Laetare Sunday he enrolled among the saints Bernardine of Siena, a Franciscan, and sent a rose to the Landgrave of Hesse. He did many other things very much in the manner of a pope. Finally, troubled by fever and gout, he departed this life in the year of the Lord 1455.
155. Calixtus III.

units.la: Calixtus tertius, natione Hispanus, patria Valentinus, Alphonsus Borgia antea nuncupatus, patre Ioanne ac matre Francisca natus: Nicolao prædicto Cardinalium suffragijs, decrepitus fuc-cessit. cessit. Fuit ille (ut eius vitae scriptores referunt) vir juris pontificij scientia doctissimus: sed Evangelij filij Dei, ut ex factis apparet, plane ignarus. Fuit, inquiunt, Alphonsi Aragonum regis primus secretarius, Valentinensis episcopus a Martino quinto factus, & ab Eugenio quarto Quatuor coronato-rum Cardinalis. Hic pontificatu suscepto, ut ante devoverat bellum in Turcas statim indixit, quu pacem potius ex Apostolico officio cum omnibus hominibus habere debuisset: Rom 12. Docendae e-tenim gentes sunt, Matth. 28 non armis impeten-dae, praesertim a Christianis pastoribus. Sed, ut est a Servatore dictum, Ioan. 10. Fur non venit, nisi ut furetur, ut mactet, ut perdat. Et Antichristus ho-micida semper est, Ioan. 8. Atq; pro mox implen-do conatu tam feroci, concionatores sibi ipsi in ra-pacitate & avaritia non infimiles, cum bullis & indulgentiis statim misit: fraterculos scilicet mendicantes, potestatem habentes ut scorpiones terrae, Apoc 9 ut Christianas gentes in eandem expedi-tionem animarent. Ex horum numero praecipui no-tantur: Ioannes Capistranus & Robertus de Li-lio, Minoritanae familiae professores, ac magnae admirationis hypocritae. Qui cognita Pontificis cau-tela, quum non esset alia spes lucri colligendi, ex-tra lubileum, omnes suas artes operati sunt per fi-stas [?] Alias[?] preces, letanias, praecepta, ieiunia, merita, persuasas confessiones, reliquias, imagines, cruces, cantus, sonos, campanarum sonitus, triti-ceumq; Christum, ut omnes eius crumenas, peras ac sacculos implerent.
units.tr: Calixtus III, a Spaniard by birth and a Valencian by homeland, was earlier called Alphonsus Borgia, son of John and Francis. Decrepit, he succeeded Nicholas, the aforementioned, by the votes of the cardinals. He was, as his biographers report, a man most learned in the science of papal law, but plainly ignorant of the Gospel of the Son of God, as his deeds show. He was, they say, the first secretary of Alphonsus, king of Aragon, was made bishop of Valencia by Martin V, and was made cardinal of the Four Crowned Saints by Eugenius IV. Once he had assumed the papacy, he at once proclaimed war on the Turks, as he had vowed beforehand, although as an apostolic office-holder he ought rather to have kept peace with all men (Rom. 12). For nations are to be taught (Matt. 28), not attacked with arms, especially by Christian ministers. But, as the Saviour said, the thief comes only to steal, to kill and to destroy (John 10), and Antichrist is always a murderer (John 8). To carry out so fierce an undertaking at once, he sent out, with bulls and indulgences, preachers who were in no way inferior to themselves in rapacity and greed, namely mendicant friars, who have power like the scorpions of the earth (Rev. 9), to stir up the Christian peoples for the same expedition. Among these the most notable are John Capistrano and Robert de Lecce, professors of the Franciscan family and men of great admiration as hypocrites. When they recognised the Pontiff's caution, and since there was no other hope of gathering profit outside the jubilee, they worked all their arts: by solemn [?] and other prayers, litanies, precepts, fasts, merits, persuasive confessions, relics, images, crosses, chants, sounds, the ringing of bells, and the wheaten Christ, so that they might fill all his purses, bags and sacks.

units.la: Nec ceßabat ipse pontifex Calixtus (quem bonum pastorem Vuicelius appellat) Christianorum principes omnes, literis ac nunciis, ad eam rem tam necessariam et sanctam, per suos legatos ad hortari. Cuius rei gratia etiam, missantibus sacri-siculis mandauit, ut orationes contra Piganos in Missis quotidianis decantarent. Voluit quoque, ut in meridie sonum campanis darent, sicut & ferò, ad salutationem virginis Mariæ: ut ea oratione (inquit Stella, Papistarum theologus) eos adiuuarent, qui contra Turcas continuè dimicabant. Ea etiam de causa, ait, transfigurationis Domini nostri Iesu Christi festum & officium ordinauit: iussitq; illud cum indulgentijs ipsis celebrari, sicut in solennitate corporis Christi. Misitq; ad Armenos & Persas, ut eadem cum eo aduersus Turcas faciant: & quosdam rusticos, qui has eius dementias rise-rant, laqueis interemit. Vincentium Valentinen-sem Dominicanum, Albertum Drepanensem Carmelitam, & Eadmundum Cantuariensem Anglum, in sanctos confessores Papisticos retulit: San civit etiam, ne quis à Papa ad concilium appella-ret: plura adhuc facturus, si longior illi vita fuisset. Nimium nepotibus ac spuriis permisit, Roderi-cumq; Borgiam vicecancellarium sub sua paternitate constituit. Veniarum, inquit, Valerius, nitidae formae literas effudit, è quibus, tunc quinque ducatis redemptis, nunc minimo redimenda[?], cetum[?] mil lenos quindecimq; mille ducatos successori reliquit. Moriens demum longo confectus senio, anno Domini 1458 in Petri basilica seu templo rotundo se-peliebatur.
units.tr: Nor did Pope Calixtus himself (whom Wicelius calls the good shepherd) cease to exhort all the princes of Christendom, by letters and messengers and through his legates, to this so necessary and holy cause. For this reason too, he ordered the priests, when they said Mass each day, to chant prayers against the Pagans. He also wished that at midday the bells should sound, as is still done at the Angelus of the Virgin Mary, so that by that prayer (says Stella, a theologian of the Papists) they might help those who were constantly fighting against the Turks. For this same reason, he says, he instituted the feast and office of the Transfiguration of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he commanded that it be celebrated with indulgences, just as the solemnity of the body of Christ is. He also sent to the Armenians and Persians, so that they might act with him against the Turks, and he put to death with nooses certain country folk who had mocked his madness. He enrolled Vincent of Valencia, a Dominican, Albert of Trapani, a Carmelite, and Edmund of Canterbury, an Englishman, among the Papistical holy confessors. He also decreed that no one should appeal from the Pope to a council, and he would have done much more if his life had been longer.
