He allowed his nephews and bastards too much licence, and he set Rodrigo Borgia, his nephew, as vice-chancellor under his own paternal care. He poured out, says Valerius, letters of indulgences of elegant form, by which, when they were once redeemed for five ducats, and now for the smallest sum, he left his successor fifteen thousand ducats. At last, worn out by long old age, he died in the year of the Lord 1458 and was buried in the basilica of St Peter, in the round temple.

units.la: Ioannes Capistranus insignis hypocrita, & Ro-bertus de Licio luxuriosissimus nebulo, in diversas regiones ab hoc Pontifice ad praedicandam obedientiam romanam missi, ut fucatis doctrinis angelicam faciem adderent, ludos & alia civilia exercitia, ut sunt conviuia, saltationes, &c. probibue-runt. Tantum deniq; sibi hoc hypocrisi nomen acquisiverunt, ut à plerisq; prosanctis Dei confessoribus adorarentur: cum tamen nihil sanae doctrinae de Christo, deq; eius meritis, de reconciliatione cum patre per Christum, ac de regeneratione in Chri-sto per spiritum sanctum, & de obedientia erga Deum tenerent. Sed tales doctores (ut Funccius exprimit) merentur mudus, suo fastidio veritatis: quod & nostris nobilibus & delicatulis civibus breui e-veniet[?]. ueniet, cum Dei ueritatem ferre, præ nimia fatu-rieate[?] non possint.
units.tr: John Capistrano, a notable hypocrite, and Robert de Lecce, a most lecherous scoundrel, were sent by this Pontiff into various regions to preach obedience to Rome; so that with feigned doctrines they might give an angelic face to the Pontiff's cause, they forbade plays and other civil pastimes, such as banquets, dances, and so on. At last they so won for themselves the name of hypocrisy that they were adored by most of the holy confessors of God, although they held nothing of sound doctrine about Christ and his merits, about reconciliation with the Father through Christ, about regeneration in Christ through the Holy Spirit, or about obedience towards God. But such teachers (as Funck puts it) deserve the world, because of their own disdain for the truth; and this will soon befall our nobles and dainty citizens too, since, because of excessive satiety, they cannot bear the truth of God.
156. Pius II.

units.la: Pius Secundus, natione Hetruscus, patria Senensis, ex patre Sylvio, matreque Victoria, Aeneas Picolhomineus antea vocatus, ambitionis vitio grauiter diu laborans, ad Pontificatum tandem peruenit. Ex paupere adolescente in tantum uirum creuit, ut testantur historici omnes qui res Pontificias scribunt, ut inter doctos Papas longè doctissimus haberetur, scriptorúmque diligentissimus. In Basiliensi concilio scriba Pontificis erat, impugnabatque orationibus & epistolis Eugenij auctoritatem. Mox ab imperatore Friderico tertio, poeta laureatus factus est, & in eius aulam vocatus, primas promotiones accepit, in epistolarum magistrum atque consiliarium assumptus. Præterea legatus, hucque illuc ad diuersos mundi principes missus: à Papa Nicolao episcopus Tergestinus, postea Senensis fiebat, & à Calixto in Cardinalium numerum referebatur. Postremò Papa factus, contra Turcas, prædecessorum more, professionem indixit: sed morte præuentus, non peregit. Sunt qui scribat eum, inquit Ioannes Funccius, præ textu belli Turcici, Germaniæ, cuius diuitias non ignorabat, ut qui multos annos in ea transfegerat pecunias ad se rapere conatum esse: ut eas in lu-xum Pontificium, in nepotes & amicos pauperes effunderet. De actis concilij Basiliensis, ille olim summa etiam diligentia duos libros scripsit: quos tamen deinde Pontifex factus, supprimere conabatur. In omnibus enim quae Pontifex agebat, non extenuare maiestatem pontificiam (superbiam ac tyrannidem potius) sed in immensum augere ambitiosissimus laborabat. Pro qua (Stella Venetus inquit) neq; reges aut duces, nequepopu-los aut tyrannos ullos, omni tyranno atrocior ip-se, formidasse comperiebatur. Imo, si quos delin-quentes uidisset, & bellis & censuris tandiu per-sequebatur, donec eos ad sanitatem redijsse nouis-set.
units.tr: Pius II, a Tuscan by birth and a Sienese by homeland, the son of Sylvius and Victoria, was earlier called Aeneas Piccolomini. Long labouring severely under the vice of ambition, he at last came to the papacy. From a poor young man he grew into such a man, as all the historians who write about papal affairs testify, that he was held by far the most learned of the learned popes, and the most diligent of writers. At the Council of Basel he was the scribe of the Pope, and he attacked the authority of Eugenius by his speeches and letters. Soon he was made poet laureate by the emperor Frederick III, and summoned to his court, where he received the first promotions, being taken on as the emperor's secretary of letters and as counsellor. Besides this he was sent as legate, hither and thither, to various princes of the world; under Pope Nicholas he became bishop of Trieste, afterwards he was made bishop of Siena, and under Calixtus he was counted among the number of cardinals. Finally made Pope, he proclaimed war against the Turks in the manner of his predecessors, but, prevented by death, he did not carry it through. There are those who write, says John Funck, that under the pretext of the Turkish war he tried to snatch the wealth of Germany, whose riches he did not ignore, since he had spent many years in that country, so that he might pour out the money into papal luxury, and into his nephews and friends. He once wrote two books, with great diligence, on the acts of the Council of Basel; yet after he became Pope he tried to suppress them. For in all that the Pope did, he laboured most ambitiously not to diminish papal majesty (rather, pride and tyranny) but to increase it immeasurably. For this cause (says Stella of Venice), he was found to fear neither kings nor dukes, nor any peoples or tyrants, being himself more savage than any tyrant. Indeed, if he saw any offenders, he pursued them with wars and censures for so long until he knew they had returned to soundness.

units.la: Propterea Ludouico undecimo Gallorum regi aduersarius extitit magnus, quod pragmatica sanctione cleri libertates in suo regno minuere tenta-ret. Borsio Estensi ac Mutinae duci succensuit, & bello eum insectatus est, quod Sigismundo Malate-stae ac rebus Gallicis contra Ferdinandum fauerit[?]. Ferdinandum nanq; regis Alphonsi notha, in Nea-politanum regnū authoritate & exercitu, contra Io-anne Andegauum Renati regis filiū, violeter posu-it. Sigismundum Austriae ducem diris execrationib. persequebatur: quòd in eius creaturam, Cardina-lem Nicolaum Cusanum, ob rapacitatem arrogan-tem animaduertisset. In eius oratorem quoq; Gre-gorium Hamburgensem iuris consultissimum, ceu exagitata quaedam uipera (ut Vuolfgangus Vuif-femburgius Basilienfis theologus scribit) uirus suae maledictionis effudit, & fulminationis suae literis ita persequebatur, ut Bohemiam sibi patriam quae-rere cogeretur. Dietherum Eisemburgium Mo-guntinensem archiepiscopum, male (ut ipse inter-pretatur) de Rom.ecclesia sentientem, sede furio-se depulit, inq; eius locum alterum suffecit. Bene-ventanum item archiepiscopum, contra eius uolun-tatem res nouas molientem, archiepiscopatu sub-mouit. Georgio Bohemiae regi, Hussitis fauenti, pro fide, sub regni sui periculo, diem dixit. Multos E-piscopos lucri gratia deposuit: & duodecim Car-dinales novos ueteribus addidit. Mantuae concilium celebrauit: ac pragmaticam legem, ut Romanae ec-clesiae perniciosam pestē, in Gallijs abrogauit. Scri-barum abbreuiatores primus creauit, atq; in ordi-nem redegit. Multas Campaniae urbes suae potesta-ti subegit, & prouentus Ecclesiae mirabiliter au-xit. Nil regibus, nil populis, timore unquam con-cessit (inquiunt arrogantes Papicolae) sed cleri ini-micos, ueluti publicos hostes constanter & intre-pide pide persecutus est.
units.tr: Accordingly he was a great adversary to Louis XI, king of the French, because he tried to diminish the liberties of the clergy in his kingdom by the Pragmatic Sanction. He was angry with Borso d'Este, duke of Ferrara and Modena, and attacked him with war, because he had favoured Sigismondo Malatesta and the French cause against Ferdinand. For he placed Ferdinand, the bastard son of King Alphonsus, violently in the kingdom of Naples, with authority and an army, against John of Anjou, son of King René. He pursued Sigismund, duke of Austria, with dreadful curses, because he had noticed his arrogant rapacity against his own creature, Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa. He also poured the venom of his cursing, like an enraged viper (as Wolfgang Wissemburg, a theologian of Basel, writes), against the envoy of that duke, Gregory of Hamburg, a most learned jurist; and with his letters of excommunication and thunderbolts he so persecuted him that he was forced to seek Bohemia as his homeland. He deposed Diether of Isenburg, archbishop of Mainz, from his see with fury, because (as he himself interprets it) he thought ill of the Roman Church, and he appointed another in his place. Likewise he removed the archbishop of Benevento from his archbishopric, because he was labouring to bring about revolutions against his will. He summoned King George of Bohemia, who favoured the Hussites, to answer for his faith, under threat to his kingdom. He deposed many bishops for the sake of gain, and he added twelve new cardinals to the old ones. He held a council at Mantua, and he abrogated in France the Pragmatic Sanction, a deadly plague to the Roman Church. He first created the abbreviators of the scribes and reduced them to order. He brought many cities of Campania under his power and mightily increased the revenues of the Church. Yet, the arrogant papists say, he never yielded to kings or peoples out of fear, but constantly and fearlessly persecuted the enemies of the clergy as if they were public enemies.

units.la: Amicos autem (nepotes etiam plures habuit) humanissime & officiosissime semper adiuvit. Fodinas inuenti tum primum aluminis, apud Topham instituit. Angelum Hierosolymae natum, Carmelitam martyrem canonizauit, solicitatore Ioanne Soretho: & Catherinam Senensem Dominicanae professionis mulierem inter virgines retulit. Ex Peloponneso D. Andreae apostoli caput transferri curauit, & alia Papalia prodigia fecit. Dum aedificandi studio vehementer teneretur, (uide commendationes Papistarum) sua impensa templi scalam ad Vaticanum vetustate collapsam, instauravit. Vestibulum aedium, ad dignitatem & loci tutelam muniuit. Aram pro foribus templi ruderibus purgatam, sternere parabat. Porticum, unde populo benediceret, inchoauit. Tyburi arcem perficisse prius, quam inchoasse visus est. Senis quadrato saxo, gentilibus suis porticum sustigiatam & ornatissimam extruxit. Corsinianum, ubi natus erat, civitatem fecit, & a suo nomine pientiam appellauit: templumq; testudineum, celebre quidem, atque ornatissimas aedes extruxit, & paternis ac maternis ossibus sepulchrum marmoreum condidit De Euangelij vero praedicatione, ad plebis in Christo salutem, non unicum verbum est. Cū Anconæ esset, ad bellum profecturus, anno Domi-ni 1464. lenta febre percussus, diem clausit extremum: Romam delatus, & in D. Petri templo sepul-tus. Morbi tamen dum viueret illi familiares erāt, tussis, calculus, ac podagra. Multas viri huius la-des (inquit Volaterranus) unum ambitionis vitium commaculabat. Quum semper promotionum appetentissimus fuerit, atque gloriæ: ea de causa & labores suscepit plurimos, & amicitias principum co-luit.
units.tr: Friends (he had many nephews too) he always helped most kindly and dutifully. He first set up the alum mines, at Tolfa. He canonized the angel born at Jerusalem, the Carmelite martyr, at the urging of John Soreth, and he counted Catherine of Siena, a woman of the Dominican profession, among the virgins. He had the head of the apostle St Andrew brought from the Peloponnese, and did other Papal wonders. While he was vehemently given over to building (see the Papists' commendations), he restored at his own expense the staircase to the temple at the Vatican, which had collapsed with age. He fortified the vestibule of the building for its dignity and the security of the place. He was preparing to lay down an altar before the doors of the temple, cleared of rubble. He began a portico from which he might bless the people. He seems to have finished the citadel at Tivoli before he began it. At Siena he built, of square stone, a portico roofed and very handsomely adorned, for his kinsmen. He made Corsignano, where he was born, into a city, and named it Pienza after his own name; he built a vaulted temple, famous indeed, and very splendid buildings, and established a marble tomb in which he placed the bones of his father and mother. But of the preaching of the Gospel, for the salvation of the people in Christ, there is not a single word. When he was at Ancona, about to set out for war, in the year of the Lord 1464 he was struck by a slow fever and ended his last day. He was carried to Rome and buried in the temple of St Peter. Yet the illnesses that were familiar to him while he lived were cough, kidney stone and gout. Volaterranus says that one vice alone stained the many praises of this man: ambition. Since he was always most eager for promotions and glory, for this reason he undertook very many labours and cultivated the friendships of princes.

units.la: HUIUS PII SECUNDI EPITAPHIUM, ex vetusto quodam codice:
units.tr: Epitaph of this Pius II, from an old manuscript:

units.la: Frigida membra Pij retinet lapis iste loquacis,
units.tr: This stone holds the cold limbs of the loquacious Pius,
who, dying, brought peace to Italy.

units.la: Summe Deus, quantum mortalibus almæ dedisti,
units.tr: Highest God, how much you gave to mortals, gracious one,

units.la: Fulmine cum tetigit hoc caput æquä manus:
units.tr: when your even hand struck this head with a thunderbolt!
He had sold nations for a price, and many crimes,
under the appearance of virtue that Pius had worn.

units.la: Impius hic fuerat, quamuis sub nomine pulchro
units.tr: This man was impious, though under a fair name
he believed he could support a false faith.

units.la: Nunc fidei comites, sceleratáq; turba clientum,
units.tr: Now the comrades of his faith and the wicked crowd of his clients

units.la: Ingemuere Pium: nam scelus orbis erat.
units.tr: groaned over Pius, for he was the scandal of the world.
Conclusion:

units.la: Impius hic situs est, crudelis, raptor iniquum,
units.tr: Here lies this impious, cruel plunderer of the unjust,
Aeneas, whom the statue-makers of Siena produced.

units.la: Reliquit hic Pius secundus, ut Platina & Sabellicus referunt, inter proverbiales suas sententias, & hanc: Sacerdotibus magna ratione ademptum est coniugium, sed maiore restituendum. Eandem quoq; sententiam protulit in secundo libro de Concilio. Fortassis, inquit, non esset potius, sacerdotes quamplures uxorari, Quoniam multi salvaren tur in sacerdotio coniugato, qui in sterili presbyte ratu damnantur. Idem Pius secundus, qui & Aeneas Sylvius, Caelio secundo teste, collegia quaedam Brigidanarum & Claranarum monialium diffol-uebat, iubens eas exire, ne amplius urerentur, ne ue sub religioso habitu meretricem celarent. Ioan-nes Maria Politianus, in suo testatur Mari magno, quod his etiam diebus inter Minoritas conven-tuales & Bullistæ, non leuis erat in Italia contentio, qui eorum illas uisitarent, custodirent, gubernarent. Lites vero alias observantium & non observantium, in suo grege, Baptista Mantuanus decima Ecloga sua dirimit.
units.tr: Pius II left, as Platina and Sabellicus report, among his proverbial sayings, also this one: "Marriage was taken from priests for a great reason, but it must be restored for a greater one." He put forward the same opinion in the second book on the Council: "Perhaps," he says, "it would be better for many priests to take wives, since many would be saved in a married priesthood who are condemned in a sterile priesthood." The same Pius II, who was also Aeneas Silvius, according to the witness of Caelius Secundus, dissolved certain colleges of Bridgettine and Clarissan nuns, ordering them to leave, lest they be burned any further or hide a harlot under religious dress. Giovanni Maria Politiano testifies in his Mare magnum that even in these days there was no slight contention in Italy between the Conventual Minorites and the Bullists over which of them should visit, guard and govern those women. Other disputes between the observant and the non-observant in their own flock Baptista Mantuanus settles in his tenth Eclogue.
157. Paul II

units.la: Paulus secundus, patria Venetus, patre Nicolao & matre Polyxena genitus, Petrus Barbus antea nominatus, ac Eugenij quarti ex sorore nepos: ex Cardinale S. Marci, prædicto Pio suffectus, diaboli atque Antichristi vicarii eius sedem occupavit. Is ante Papatum diu, iturus in mercaturam, quum audisset Gabrielem aununculum creatum esse Pontificem, literis animum adiecit. Et Romam profectus, primum archidiaconus Bononiensis, inde episcopus Cerienfis[?], postea Cardinalis, ut dictum est, ac tandem Pontifex & magnus Antichristus creabatur. Vir corpore quidem specioso, sed animo elato: diligens erat in auro colligendo, diligentior in distribuendis pro lucro beneficijs. De eius apparatu pontificio (inquit Platina,) non est cur ambigas, maiores ab hoc uno superatos, regno praesertim, siue mitram uelis appellare, in quam multae opes contulit, coemptis undique, ac magnis precijs, adamantibus, sapphiris, smaragdis, chrysolithis, iaspidibus, unionibus, & quicquid gemmarum in precio est. Quibus ornatus, tanquam Aaron redimitus ac splendidus, in publicum forma humana augustiore prodibat. Inspici tum ab omnibus volebat, & adorari. Hanc ob rem nonnunquam peregrinos in urbe retinuit, intermissa offendendi sudarij consuetudine, quo a pluribus eodem tempore cernere-tur. Praeterea, ne solus differre a ceteris uideretur, publico decreto mandauit, proposita poena, ne quisquam bireta coccinea (ita appellabant capitis tegmen) praeter Cardinales ferret: quibus etiam primo sui pontificatus anno, pannum eiusdem colibris dono dedit, quo equos uel mulas sternerent, dum equitarent. Haec Platina.
units.tr: Paul II, a Venetian by birth, born of father Nicholas and mother Polyxena, formerly named Peter Barbo, and nephew through his sister of Eugene IV: from Cardinal of St Mark, he was chosen to succeed the aforesaid Pius, and occupied the seat of the vicar of the devil and Antichrist. Before the papacy he had long intended to go into trade, but when he heard that his uncle Gabriel had been created Pontiff, he applied himself to letters. Going to Rome, he was first archdeacon of Bologna, then bishop of Cervia(?), afterwards cardinal, as has been said, and at last was created Pontiff and great Antichrist. He was a man handsome in body but haughty in spirit; he was diligent in gathering gold, and more diligent in distributing benefices for profit. Concerning his papal apparel (says Platina) there is no reason to doubt that he surpassed greater men, especially in regard to the kingdom, if you wish to call it a mitre, into which he poured much wealth, buying up from everywhere at great prices adamants, sapphires, emeralds, chrysolites, jaspers, pearls, and whatever gems are precious. Adorned with these, like Aaron, decked out and splendid, he came forth in public with a more august human form. He then wished to be looked at and adored by all. For this reason he sometimes kept foreigners in the city, having dropped the custom of the handkerchief (sudarium) by which he would be seen at the same time by many. Moreover, lest he seem alone to differ from others, he ordered by public decree, under penalty, that no one but the Cardinals should wear scarlet birettas (that is what they called the head covering). To them too, in the first year of his pontificate, he gave as a gift cloth of the same colour, with which they might cover horses or mules while they rode. So Platina.

units.la: Maiestatem quoq; suam tu authoritate, tumq; armis augere conatus, toto suo pontificatu bella per insidias in Italia suscepit. Vnde Ariminum & alias urbes oppugnans suburbia earum, imo ciuitates ipsas tormentis atq; aliis instrumentis belli- cis lacerari miserabiliter fecit. Pij praedecessoris de creta & acta stomachose odiebat: & abbreuiatores omnes, quos ille in ordinem redegerat, abrogauit atq; exauctorauit. Eos etiam bonis & dignitate, indicta causa spoliauit: quos propter eruditionem ac doctrinam, ex toto terrarum orbe conquisitos, magnis pollicitationibus & premijs uocare ad se debuerat. Canonicos regulares e Lateranensi coenobio per Calixtum expulsos restituit: multaq; apud S. Marcum, & in Vaticano extruxit. Haereticos eos pronunciabat, qui nomen Academiae uel seriò uel ioco deinceps commemorarent. Tardus ille, & crassa ceruice uir erat: & ideo nec literas nec uirtutes amabat. Totus ambitioni, luxuriae ac voluptati deditus, dives totos aut gulae (ut Volater- ranus author est) aut nummis pensitandis, aut uete- rum numismatis siue gemmis siue imaginibus spe- ctandis tradebat: ac si referatis uitiorum omnium ianuis, unumquodq; scelus committere liceret, dum se iactitaret ius suum habere in seminio pectoris fui. Præcipua illi cura fuit semper, ut omnia ad vi-tum[?] necessaria ubi non deessent: sed de Christiana disciplina non unicum verbum. Denique decem Cardinalibus ab eo creatis, inter quos Franciscus Ruerius unus fuerat, cum longam sibi vitam per-suasisset, anno Domini 1471. & cum eadem nocte iucundissime cœnasset, apoplexia correptus, vitam cum morte mutauit, nemine vidente. Cui postmodum incredibilis operis sepulchrum marmoreum a suis nepotibus Cardinalibus erectum fuit. Ex hoc tempore res pontificia ad inclinationem vergere cœpit.
units.tr: He also tried to increase his majesty by authority and by arms, and throughout his pontificate waged wars by treachery in Italy. Hence, attacking Rimini and other cities, he had their suburbs, and even the cities themselves, miserably torn apart by cannon and other instruments of war. The decrees and acts of his predecessor Pius he hated bitterly, and he abrogated and dismissed all the abbreviators whom that man had put in order. He also stripped them of goods and dignity without a hearing, though he ought to have summoned them with great promises and rewards, having sought them out from the whole world for their learning and doctrine. He restored the regular canons expelled from the Lateran monastery by Callistus, and built much at St Mark's and in the Vatican. He declared heretics those who thereafter mentioned the name of the Academy, whether in earnest or in jest. He was a slow man with a thick neck, and therefore loved neither letters nor virtues. Wholly given over to ambition, luxury and pleasure, and rich, he gave all his time either to gluttony (as Volaterranus is the authority), or to weighing money, or to viewing ancient coins, whether gems or images. And as if, having opened the gates of all vices, it were permitted to commit each crime, he boasted that he had his own right in the seedbed of his breast. His chief concern was always that everything necessary for life should not be lacking, but of Christian discipline not a single word. Finally, having persuaded himself of a long life, and having ten cardinals created by him, among whom Francis Ruerius was one, and having dined most pleasantly on the same night, he was seized by apoplexy and exchanged life for death, with no one seeing. Afterwards a marble tomb of incredible workmanship was erected for him by his nephews the cardinals. From this time papal affairs began to slope towards decline.

units.la: Qui vero de hoc pontifice plura scire cupit, ad appendices oculos convertat. Unum hoc tamen non me præteribit, quod apud Stanislaum Ruthenum reperi. Cum quædam poemata Romæ legisset Paulus in se atq; filiam scripta, illacrymasse dicitur, & acerbitatem legis cœlibatus cum amicis expo-stulasse: quod is, qui non solum Ecclesiæ, sed etiam continentiæ antistes esse deberet, filia in ore atq; in oculis civitatis cum summo probro versari videret. Quæ est[?] erat eximia plebritudine, scortatione tamen ab se ortam dolebat, existimari: cū legem Dei sciret esse, qua huic in matrimonio nasci licebat, ni si idem cœlibatus obstitisset. Itaque consilium illum cœpisse de restituendo sacerdotum coniugio fe-runt: quod ille tamen morte præventus, exequi nō potuit. Præsentationis S. Mariæ festum ille approbauit: & grande palatium in S. Marco construxit.
units.tr: But whoever wishes to know more about this pontiff should turn his eyes to the appendices. Yet this one thing will not escape me, which I found in Stanislaus of Ruthenia. When Paul had read some poems written in Rome against himself and his daughter, he is said to have wept, and to have complained to his friends of the harshness of the law of celibacy: that a man who ought to be the bishop not only of the Church but also of continence should see his daughter on the lips and in the eyes of the city, to his great disgrace. She was of outstanding beauty, yet he grieved that she was thought to have been born of fornication, since he knew that the law of God would have allowed her to be born in marriage, had not this same celibacy stood in the way. So they say he began to plan the restoration of marriage for priests, which, however, he, prevented by death, could not carry out. He approved the feast of the Presentation of St Mary, and built a great palace at St Mark's.
158. Sixtus IV

units.la: Sixtus quartus, genere Ligur uel Genuensis, urbe Sauona oriundus, Franciscus Ruerius antea dictus, Francisicanorum minister generalis, & ad S. Sixtum Cardinalis presbyter, Paulo defuncto, in execrabili hac sede execrabilior bestia successit. Cum in mitra solennijs, ad basilicam Lateranen-sem lectica portaretur, orto tumultu subito, maximum uitæ subijt periculū, ut etiam lapidibus appeteretur, & a lecticarijs pene deserueretur. Liberalissimus pontifex, eadem pluribus sæpe concedebat. Suorum in primis amantissimus (eximia laus) ac indulgentissimus fuit: quorum causa pleraq; præter fas iusq; & agebat & concedebat. Petrum Ruerium, eiusdem ordinis & patriæ, quem una à puero cum Hieronymo fratre, sibi (mysterium est) educauerat, ante omnes ad Cardinalatum (ac patriarchatum) promouit, uirum alioqui natum perdendæ pecuniæ. Nam biennio, quo tantum postea uixit, ducentorum aureorum millia in luxu uictitando solum absumpsit: sexaginta millia æris alieni, argenargenteorum item 300 pondo dimisit. Decessit tabidus voluptate, annorum 28. (Seraphicus Minorita) anno Domini 1474. opificibus maxime desideratus, quorū officinas (Rom. ecclesiae columna) novis semper lucris & operibus replebat. Ioannes Ravisius Textor, in Officina: Petrus, inquit, presbyter Cardinalis, sedete in pontificatu Sixto quarto, in duobus annis trecenta aureorum millia luxu prodegit, & vanitatibus. Accedit & Ioannis Rivij testimonium, ex libello de Erroribus pontificiorū: De luxuria eiusdem, inquit, immensa & incredibili, quaedam affert libro nono similia portenti, Baptista Fulgosus: quae, ne prolixior sim, omitto. Nā minimum omnium ac leuissimum esse puto, quod au-reis domi vestibus uti, lectos aureis stragulis integere, vasis argenteis onus ventris excipere, calceo los amicae Tiresiae margaritis opertos comparare solitum scribit. Hinc de catero luxu hominis conjecturam facias licet. Illum igitur post mortem ita salutavit infernalis Jupiter, ut in Alphonsi fui libro quarto Baptista Mantuanus habet:
units.tr: Sixtus IV, of the Ligurian or Genoese stock, born at Savona and formerly called Francis Rovere, minister general of the Franciscans and cardinal priest of St Sixtus, succeeded Paul, who had died, in this execrable see, as a beast more execrable still. When he was carried in a litter, wearing his mitre, in solemn procession to the Lateran basilica, a sudden tumult broke out, and he faced the greatest danger of his life: he was even pelted with stones and was nearly abandoned by his litter-bearers. He was a most generous pontiff and often granted the same favours to many. He was most loving towards his own people (a remarkable praise) and most indulgent to them; for their sake he did and granted many things beyond what was right and lawful. Petrus Ruerius, of the same order and homeland, whom he had raised from boyhood together with his brother Hieronymus (it is a mystery why), he promoted above all others to the cardinalate and patriarchate. Otherwise this man was born to squander money. In the two years he lived afterwards he alone spent two hundred thousand gold ducats on luxurious living; he left behind sixty thousand in debts and also 300 pounds of silver. He died wasted by pleasure, at the age of 28 (a Seraphic Minorite), in the year of the Lord 1474, greatly missed by the craftsmen, whose workshops (the pillar of the Roman church) he always filled with new profits and works. John Ravisius Textor, in his Officina, says: "Petrus, a priest and cardinal, while Sixtus IV sat in the papacy, squandered in two years three hundred thousand gold pieces on luxury and vanities." To this is added the testimony of John Rivius, from his little book on the errors of the Papists: about his immense and incredible luxury, Baptista Fulgosus, in book nine, brings forward things like monsters; these I omit, lest I be too long. For I think the least and lightest of all is what he writes, that he was accustomed to wear golden clothes at home, to cover his beds with gold coverlets, to receive the burden of his belly in silver vessels, and to have shoes for his mistress Tiresias covered with pearls. From this small sample you may infer the rest of the man's luxury. Infernal Jupiter therefore greeted him after death in the manner that Baptista Mantuanus gives in book four of his Alphonsus:

units.la: At tu implume caput, cui tanta licentia quondam, Fœmineos fuit in coitus: tua furta putabas, Hic quoq; prætextu mitræ, impunita relinqui? Sic meruit tua fœda Venus: sic prodiga in omnem Nequitiam, ad virtutis opus tua auara libido.
units.tr: "But you, feather-headed, who once had such licence for women's couplings, did you think your thefts would go unpunished here too, under the pretext of the mitre? Thus your foul Venus has earned you; thus your greedy lust, lavish in every wickedness, for the work of virtue."

units.la: Illa Dioneæ Cytherea[?] munera concha, Illa pudicitiam quibus impugnare solebas, Et noctes emere, & nudæ indulgere palæstræ, Scimus, & in scriptis tua sancta redegimus acta.
units.tr: "That Cytherean shell, the gifts of Dione, with which you used to assail chastity, and buy nights, and indulge in the naked wrestling-ground: we know it, and in writings we have recorded your holy deeds."

units.la: Hieronymus vero prædicti Petri frater, Foro-liuij Forocorneliq; princeps factus, post eum rem omnem Ecclesiæ administrauit (felix illa mater) uir ingenio seueriore, ac voluptatibus præter uni-cam uenationem (præposterè uenerij) minime de-ditus. Sixtus vero post, hos (proprij fortasse hi su-erant) fratrum fororumq; filios extulit: nec quis-quam propinquis fœcundior unquam erat. Inter quos Iulianum S. Petri aduncula Cardinalem, e-iusq; fratrem Ioannem, urbis præfectum, Soræq; ac Senogalliæ principem fecit. Supra modum, inquit Platina, nepotes amauit, humana diuinaq; præter iustitiam eis tribuens. Multorum etiam iudicio, iniuste tumultu bellico totam Italiam uexauit, Romulus certè uocandus. Volaterranus: Cum igitur tot tumultibus absumpta pecunia, indigeret: noua collegia primum excogitauit, quæ licerentur. Agrippa: Inter lenones recentiorum temporum, qui lupanaria ædificabant, nobilis erat Sixtus quartus Romanus pontifex: qui Romæ nobile admodum lupanar extruxit: atq;, ut in declamatione ad Lo-uanienses fusius explicat, utriq; Veneri assignauit. Meretricum cohortes, Heliogabali exemplo, ita adluit, amicisq; & ferus exhibuit: nonnihil emolumenti etiam ex meretricio quaestu, aerario suo accumulans. Romana enim scorta, in singulas hebdomadas, lutium nummum adhuc pendent pontifici: qui census annuus, nonnunquam viginti millia (nunc quadraginta) ducatorum excedit. Adeoq; ecclesiae procerum id munus est, ut una cum ecclesiarum probentibus, etiam lenociniorum numerent mercede. Refert Vuefselus Groningensis, lux mundi dictus, in tractatu de indulgentiis papalibus, de hoc pontifice Sixto: Quod ad praedicti Petri, tunc S. Sixti Cardinalis ac patriarchae Constantinopolitani, & Hieronymi fratris sui postulationes, domesticae familiae toti, Cardinalis D. Lucae, qui Paulo secundo a venationibus fuerat (horrendum dictu) in tribus anni mensibus calidioribus, Iunio, Iulio, & Augusto, masculino coitu frui permiserit, cum hac clausula, Fiat ut petitur. Propterea Mantuanus in praedicto Alphonso, de Sixto ac Petro nepote, miranda tradit. Ad arma conuersus, Volaterrano teste, quibus magis quam religioni natus fuerat, bella per fas nefasq; gessit. Aduersus Vitelium Tipher-nate[?], Florentinos, Venetos, Columnenses, Ferdina-dū Siciliae regem, Calabriae ducē, & aliās gentes ac principes, expeditiones iniustissimas fecit, Christianos reges obsequentes semper habere gaudebat: quos pro uoto suo aut exaltauit, aut depressit. In Longobardos execratos, igne ferroq; concitauit suos tunc confaederatos Heluetios: quos diplomate ac uexillo donauit (Christiani gregis pastor) ut Christianorum sanguinem audacter effunderent. Agnatos ac spurios praeter ecclesiae Romanae dignitatem aut honestatem, quocunq; potuit, euexit, diuina humana-q; eis iniquè tribuens. Duos enim nepotes, Leonardum & Ioannem, urbis praefectos alternatim constituit. Chriftophorum & Dominicum Rueri- os, fratres, in patrum collegium cooptauit: ac Iulianum propinquum, & Raphaelem ex sorore Vio-lentina, nepotes, ambos Sauonenses, in Cardinales promouit. Quorum tamen Raphaelem cum Sal- uiato Pifano, atq; aliis multis, Laurentius Medi- ces patibulo suspendit, quòd eius fratrem intermisfent. Monachorum mendicantium omnium tutor maximus erat, ut qui eis redditus habere concessit, & uitam æternam post mortem.
units.tr: Hieronymus, indeed, the brother of the aforesaid Petrus, was made lord of Forlì and Forlicorneli, and after him he administered all the affairs of the Church (that happy mother). He was a man of a sterner temper, given to no pleasures except one, hunting (a backwards pleasure for a bishop). Afterwards Sixtus raised up the sons of these brothers and sisters (perhaps they were his own sons), and no one was ever more fruitful in relatives. Among them he made Julian, the cardinal, nephew of St Peter's aunt, and his brother John prefect of the city and prince of Sora and Senigallia. "Beyond measure," says Platina, "he loved his nephews, bestowing on them human and divine things beyond justice." By the judgment of many, he unjustly harassed all Italy with warlike tumults, and deserved to be called a Romulus. Volaterranus: "Since his money was exhausted by so many tumults and he was in need, he first devised new offices, which could be bought." Agrippa: "Among the pimps of recent times who built brothels, the noble one was Sixtus IV, Roman pontiff, who built at Rome a very noble brothel and, as he explains more fully in his declamation to the people of Louvain, assigned it to both Venuses. After the example of Heliogabalus he equipped the troops of whores, showing favour to his friends, and he gained some profit from the prostitutes' earnings, adding it to his treasury. For Roman whores still pay the pontiff a weekly coin, and this annual revenue sometimes exceeds twenty thousand ducats (now forty thousand). So much is it the custom of the Church's leaders that, together with the revenues of the churches, they also count the wages of brothels." Wessel of Groningen, called the light of the world, in his treatise on papal indulgences, reports of this pontiff Sixtus: at the requests of the aforesaid Petrus, then cardinal and patriarch of Constantinople, and of his brother Hieronymus, he allowed the whole household of Cardinal Luca, who had been of the hunting-parties of Paul II (horrible to say), to enjoy male intercourse during the three hotter months, June, July and August, with this clause: "Let it be done as asked." Therefore Mantuanus, in the aforesaid Alphonsus, relates wonderful things about Sixtus and his nephew Petrus. Turned to arms, according to Volaterranus, to which he was born more than to religion, he waged war by right and wrong. Against Vitellius of Tifernum, the Florentines, the Venetians, the Colonna, Ferdinand king of Sicily, the duke of Calabria, and other peoples and princes, he made most unjust expeditions. He rejoiced to have Christian kings compliant, and raised up or cast down whichever of them he wished. Against the accursed Lombards he roused, with fire and sword, the Swiss, his then allies, whom he rewarded with a diploma and a banner (the shepherd of the Christian flock), so that they might boldly shed Christian blood. He raised his agnates and bastards as high as he could, beyond the dignity or honour of the Roman church, unjustly bestowing divine and human things upon them. He made two nephews, Leonard and John, prefects of the city, in turn. He co-opted the brothers Christopher and Dominic Rovere into the college of fathers, and promoted Julian, a kinsman, and Raphael, a nephew through his sister Violentina, both of Savona, to the cardinalate. Of these, Lorenzo de' Medici hanged Raphael, together with Salviati of Pisa and many others, because they had plotted against his brother. He was the greatest protector of all the mendicant monks, granting them revenues, and eternal life after death.

units.la: Vrbis Romanae quasi nouum conditor habebatur: eamq; ex lutea lateritiam fecit, sicut olim Augustus ex lateritia marmoream. Vias publicas primum strauit ac muniuit, porticibus ablatis quæ illas occupabant. Vicorum curatores ordinauit, at non regni Dei denunciatores designauit. Templa omnia vetustate obsita restituit. Xenodochium S. Spiritus ædificiis ampliauit: in quo vitæ suæ ordi-nem depingi gloriofulus curauit. Templum Pacis de novo cōstruxit, impositis canonicis regularibus: templum quoq; S. Mariæ de populo, à fundamen-tis erexit. Imò ecclesias urbis omnes aut instaura-vit, aut beneficia saltem ipsis contulit: & indici ri-tus sacerdotibus fanum[?] fabricauit. Pontem Aureum penitus collapsum, suo apposito nomine, & ædes in Vaticano pontificias refecit, Prætorianisq; excubitoribus loca commoda assignauit. Ad vice-simum quintum annum, iubileum, propinquorum suorum causa, avarus mercator reduxit, primusq; celebrauit. Multa officia scribarum, breviatorum, sollicitatorum, astipulatorum, & Apostolici fisci notariorum, ad marsupium excogitauit: quæ sem-per a pontifice pecunia possent redimi. Conditio-nes fœderis Romanæ sedis & Galliarum regni (ad ecclesiastica spectantes negotia) publicè omnibus exhibuit. Conceptionis Mariæ, ac Præsentationis eiusdem, Annæ eius matris, Iosephi nutritij, Franci-sci Seraphici, & Alberti Drepanensis, festiuita-tes instituit, Bonaventuramq; Franciscanum in sanctos papisticos retulit. Triginta duos Cardinales suo tempore creauit: ac multas ordinationes ad cleri commoditatem edidit. Laurentium Medicem Flo-rentiæ[?] renuntium[?], ob suspensum Raphaelem nepotem, excommunicauit, ac diris denouit: & Florentinos omnes magnis damnis oppressit. Sedis Antichristianæ fastigium ita tuebatur, ut non facile cuiquam, quamuis maximo, perfundari pateretur. Quum pacem ab Hercule Estensi, Ferrariensium duce, praeter eius voluntatem & consensum, cum Venetis fieri conspiceret, ex animi rancore, aduersante etiä podagra, quae tunc laborabat, anno Domini 1484. in quintum diem expirauit.
units.tr: The city of Rome was regarded as a new founder. He changed it from clay to brick, as Augustus once changed it from brick to marble. He first paved and fortified the public roads, removing the porticoes that encroached upon them. He appointed overseers of the streets, but did not appoint proclaimers of the kingdom of God. He restored all the temples overgrown with age. He enlarged the hospital of the Holy Spirit with new buildings, and had the order of his own life painted there, to his glory. He rebuilt the Temple of Peace, placing regular canons in it, and erected from the foundations the church of St Mary of the People. Indeed he either restored all the churches of the city or at least conferred benefices upon them, and he built a shrine for the priests of the (indicted?) rite. He restored the Golden Bridge, which had completely collapsed, with his own name placed upon it, and he refurbished the papal residences in the Vatican, and assigned convenient quarters to the Praetorian guards. In the twenty-fifth year, the jubilee, he brought it back, as a greedy merchant, for the sake of his relatives, and was the first to celebrate it. He devised many offices for scribes, abbreviators, solicitors, assistants and notaries of the apostolic treasury, for the purse, which could always be redeemed for money from the pontiff. He publicly displayed to everyone the terms of the covenant between the Roman see and the kingdom of France, insofar as they concern ecclesiastical affairs. He instituted the festivals of the Conception of Mary, her Presentation, of Anne her mother, of Joseph the foster father, of Francis the Seraphic, and of Albert of Trapani, and he enrolled Bonaventure the Franciscan among the papist saints. In his time he created thirty-two cardinals, and he issued many ordinances for the convenience of the clergy. He excommunicated Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, on account of the hanging of his nephew Raphael, and pronounced dire curses upon him, and he crushed all the Florentines with great losses. He so defended the summit of the Antichristian see that he did not readily allow anyone, however great, to be shaken. When he saw peace being made between the Venetians and Hercules d'Este, duke of Ferrara, without his will and consent, he was consumed with anger; and though gout, which then afflicted him, was also against him, he died on the fifth day, in the year of the Lord 1484.
On whom verses were written by various authors
These verses are said:

units.la: Non potuit seuum vis ulla extinguere Sixtum:
units.tr: No force could ever extinguish cruel Sixtus;
at last, on hearing the name of peace, he died.
On the peace after the death of Sixtus:

units.la: Die unde Alecto pax ista refulsit, & unde
units.tr: On what day did this peace shine forth, and from where did Alecto's

units.la: Tam subito reticent praelia? Sixtus obit.
units.tr: battles fall so suddenly silent? Sixtus has died.
Again, against Sixtus:

units.la: Mortuus est Sixtus, gaudet nunc Roma: trahatur,
units.tr: Sixtus is dead, and Rome now rejoices. Let him be dragged,

units.la: Vt dignum est, unco mortuus in Tiberim.
units.tr: as he deserves, dead, with a hook into the Tiber.
Another on the same:

units.la: Sixtus obit, gaudent omnes: ne funere sicco
units.tr: Sixtus is dead, and everyone rejoices. Lest he pass with a dry funeral,
lament, you swine, the acorn you have lost.
Another on the same:

units.la: Extulit auratas sed postquam maxima glandes,
units.tr: But once the greatest acorns had been carried out,

units.la: Ecclesia, innumeris patefacta est ianua portis.
units.tr: the Church's gate was thrown open by countless doors.
Epitaph of the same Sixtus:

units.la: Sixte iaces tandem, fidei contemptor & aequi: Pacis ut hostis eras, pace peremptus obis[?]. Sixte iaces tandem: latatur Roma, tuo quae Passa sub imperio est funera, bella, famem. Sixte iaces tandem, nostri discordia secli: Saeuisti in superos, nunc Acheronta moue. Sixte iaces tandem, fraudum dolique minister: Et sola tantum proditione potens. Sixte iaces tandem: tibi nil nisi fata tulere Pontificis nomen, caetera Hieronymo. Sixte iaces tandem, pressa est quo sospite virtus, Leges, sacra, pium, religiosque, fides. Sixte iaces tandem, deflent tua busta cinedi, Scortaque, lenones, alea, vina, Venus. Sixte iaces tandem, summorum infamia, sexque[?] Pontificum, tandem perfide Sixte iaces. Sixte iaces tandem, vos hunc lacerate Quirites, Dentur & impastis membra scelesta feris. Quid pia profuerint functo[?] solennia Sixto? Tradita sunt celeri vota precesque noto, Riserat[?] ut vivens caelestia numina Sixtus, Sic moriens nullos credidit esse Deos[?]. Sixte iaces tandem, superis invisus & inimis: Inclusus gravido ventre necandus eras. Stupra, famem, strages, usuras, furta, rapinas,
units.tr: At last you lie here, Sixtus, despiser of faith and justice; as you were an enemy of peace, you were destroyed by peace. At last you lie here: Rome, which under your rule suffered funerals, wars and famine, rejoices. At last you lie here, Sixtus, discord of our age: you raged against the gods above, now stir up Acheron. At last you lie here, Sixtus, minister of frauds and deceit, powerful only through betrayal. At last you lie here: nothing but fate gave you the name of Pontiff, and the rest went to Hieronymus. At last you lie here, Sixtus, under whose protection virtue, laws, sacred things, piety, religion and good faith were crushed. At last you lie here, Sixtus: your tomb is mourned by catamites, prostitutes, pimps, gambling, wine and Venus. At last you lie here, Sixtus, disgrace of the highest, and of the six pontiffs; at last, treacherous Sixtus, you lie here. At last you lie here, Sixtus: you, Quirites, tear him apart, and let his wicked limbs be given to unfed wild beasts. What good did the solemn pious rites do for Sixtus when dead? Vows and prayers were handed over to the swift south wind. As Sixtus, while living, mocked the heavenly powers, so dying he believed there were no gods at all. At last you lie here, Sixtus, hated by the gods above and by enemies: you were shut in a pregnant womb, destined to be killed. Rapes, famine, slaughters, usuries, thefts, robberies,

units.la: Et quodcunq; nefas, te duce Roma tulit. Magna licet tardæ soluenda est gratia morti: Omne scelus tecum, Sixte cruente, jacet. Aliud in eundem: Pædico insignis, prædo, fucosus, adulter, Exitiumq; urbis, perniciesq; Dei. Gaude prisce Nero: vincit te crimine Sixtus, Hic scelus omne simul clauditur, & vitium.
units.tr: and whatever wickedness Rome bore under your leadership. Great thanks, though late, are owed to death: every crime lies buried with you, bloody Sixtus. Another on the same: notorious pederast, robber, deceiver, adulterer, ruin of the city and destruction of God. Rejoice, old Nero: Sixtus surpasses you in crime; in him every wickedness and vice is shut up together.

units.la: Ex Leandro & Tritemio: Circa annum Domini 1470. Alanus de Rupe, Dominicanus, postquam malorum dæmonum illusiones, ex Mariæ psalterio Rosarium fabricauit, Euangelij loco prædicauit, atq; fraternitatem tum demum instituit. Et ut inde diminueretur Dei gloria, ac periclitaretur animarum salus, Iacobus Sprenger, Teutonia pro uincialis (nam & suas habent provincias ambitiosi nebulones) confictis miraculis hæc sublimauit, ac tandem Sixtus Papa bullis & indulgentijs approbauit. Super quo negotio liber editus est, in cuius principio legitur, beatam Virginem ingressam fuisse aliquando in cellulam clausam eiusdem Alani, concinnasseq; ei ex suis capillis annulum, et monachum sibi desponsasse, osculatam fuisse, dedisse contrectandas & lactandas papillas: ac denique fuisse illi tam familiarem, ut sponsa solet esse sponso, &c. Et hæc detestanda monachorum mendacia, à papaPapatu diabolico hucusq; foüentur ac defendun-tur. Huius fraternitatis, in Alphonso Baptista me-minisse videtur:
units.tr: From Leandro and Trithemius: Around the year of the Lord 1470, Alanus de Rupe, a Dominican, after he had fabricated the Rosary out of the Psalter of Mary, on the pretext of the illusions of evil demons, preached it in place of the Gospel, and then at last founded a brotherhood. And so that God's glory might be diminished and the salvation of souls put in danger, Jacob Sprenger, provincial of Germany (for ambitious scoundrels have their provinces too), exalted these things with invented miracles, and at last Pope Sixtus approved them with bulls and indulgences. A book was published on this business, at the beginning of which it is read that the blessed Virgin once entered the closed cell of this same Alanus, made a ring for him from her own hair, betrothed herself to the monk, allowed herself to be kissed, offered her breasts to be handled and suckled, and finally became so familiar with him as a bride is wont to be with her bridegroom, etc. And these detestable lies of the monks have been fostered and defended up to now by the diabolical papacy. Alphonsus Baptista seems to have made mention of this brotherhood:

units.la: Hi filo insertis numerant sua murmura baccis,
units.tr: These, with beads strung on thread, count their murmurings.

units.la: Ex Mari magno Ioannis Mariæ Polutiani: Anno Domini 1474. quosdam Carmelitas theologos, in causis fidei, inquisitores (ut vocant) haeretica prauitatis, Dominicani, insidijs ac variis molestationibus per Italiam vexabant: quorum unum legi fuisse Iulianum de Brixia, eximium diuini verbi praeconem: alium, Petrum Neuolarium, pro quo Mantuanus scripsit Apologiam in tribus libris. Sed id totum, per pontificem Sixtu, Christophori Mar-tignoni cura consopitum est. Qui Sixtum monachorum tutor, ut in Pontificum vitis testatur Ioannes Stella, omnes mendicantes ad æmulationes cui-tandas[?], in priuilegijs & gratijs censuit æquales esse.
units.tr: From the Mare Magnum of Giovanni Maria Polutiano: In the year of the Lord 1474, Dominican inquisitors of heretical depravity (as they are called) harassed through Italy with snares and various vexations some Carmelite theologians in matters of faith. Of these, one was Julian of Brescia, an outstanding herald of the divine word; the other, Pietro Nevolari, for whom Mantuanus wrote an Apology in three books. But all this was quieted by Pope Sixtus, through the care of Christophorus Martinonus. Sixtus, the guardian of the monks, as John Stella testifies in his Lives of the Popes, judged that all the mendicants should be equal in privileges and graces, so as to avoid rivalries.
159. INNOCENT VIII.

units.la: Innocentius octauus, patria Genuensis, ex patre Arone, Ioannes Baptista Cibo antea nuncupatus, ex D. Ceciliæ presbytero Cardinale, rex locusta-rum[?], monachorum ac sacrificulorum, Papa videli-cet, post Sixtum creabatur. Pauper olim puer erat (ut Volaterranus scribit) præstanti forma tamen: & inter Alphonsi Siciliarum regis ministros nutritus, aulicos mores perdidicit. Inde Romam veniens, in contubernio Philippi Cardinalis Bononiensis longo tempore mansit. Praesul deinde Sauonensis, postea Melphitensis, & à Sixto Datarius factus: postremò Cardinalis, ut dictum est, ac pontifex constituebatur. Fuit corpore excelso & candido, de-coroq;: sed ingenio tardo, & à literis procul, itaut inter officia publica quandoq; dormitare videretur. Quum à prædicto Sixto plurimum amatus esset, ob dulces mores & humanitatem, quà omnes (inquit) usq; ad vitium superauit: verum quum nemini tamen benignus esset, om-nibus blandus fi[?] ffet, (egre-gia laus) innatam auaritiam iocis ac dicteriis[?] transfigebat. Initio fere pontificatus contra Ferdinandum Siciliæ regem, cum eius regni proceribus conspirauit (sic sibi veteres rependit amicitias) expedi-tionis duce Roberto Seuerinate accersito. Dicebat sanctus homo ac pacis amator, pro Ecclesiae dignitate ac subditorum tutela, arma esse sumenda, ut pax inde sequatur. Ac si mala facienda sint, contra doctrinam D. Pauli, ut inde veniant bona. De-ceptum nihilominus tandem se videns, necessariò pacem fecit his conditionibus: ut sibi census debitus penderetur, & rebelles manerent incolumes. Sed neutrum eorum Ferdinandus rex sapiens praesti-tit: quam tamen ad id exigendum, Petrus Vicentium, audacissimus satelles & auditor eius camerae, cum Apostolico secretario mitteretur.
units.tr: Innocent VIII, a native of Genoa, formerly named Giovanni Battista Cibo, son of the father Arone, was created pope after Sixtus, from being cardinal priest of St Cecilia, king of locusts, of monks and of sacrificing priests, that is, the Pope. As a boy he was once poor (as Volaterranus writes), yet of outstanding appearance; and being brought up among the servants of Alfonso, king of Sicily, he learned courtly manners. Then coming to Rome, he stayed for a long time in the household of Cardinal Filippo of Bologna. Then bishop of Savona, afterwards of Melfi, and made datary by Sixtus, at last he was created cardinal and, as has been said, pope. He was tall and fair of body and handsome, but slow of wit and far from letters, so that among public duties he sometimes seemed to be dozing. Since he was very much loved by the said Sixtus on account of his sweet manners and humanity, in which (he says) he surpassed everyone to the point of vice; yet since he was kind to nobody but flattering to everyone (an excellent praise), he veiled his innate avarice with jokes and witticisms. Near the beginning of his pontificate he conspired against Ferdinand, king of Sicily, with the nobles of that kingdom (so he repaid old friendships), summoning Roberto Sanseverino as leader of the expedition. The holy man, a lover of peace, said that arms must be taken up for the dignity of the Church and the protection of its subjects, so that peace might follow; and that if evils must be done, then, contrary to the teaching of St Paul, good may come of them. Yet seeing himself deceived, he at last made peace on these conditions: that the customary tribute be paid to him and that the rebels remain unharmed. But King Ferdinand, being wise, performed neither of these; to exact them, Peter Vicentium, the most audacious henchman and auditor of his chamber, was sent together with the apostolic secretary.

units.la: Post hæc Innocentius, bellorum pertæsus, & ad simulatæ pacis concordiam conuersus, nihil prius habuit, quàm quieti, inerti scilicet, studere: quæ diuersas cupiditates, concupiscentias, fraudes, ignauias, voluptates, pōpas, gulas, luxurias, libidines, & idolomaniâs secum affert. Sixti deinde secutus exemplum, quæstus gratiâ, secretariorum collegium instituit, pristinum numerum augendo. Noua palatio papatum ornauit: & domum solatij mirabili modo instruxit. Pontificum primus, inaudito exemplo, palam suos spurios, & citra pudorem, dignitiis atq; honoribus auxit. Nam Francisco suo notho oppida nonnulla urbi vicina dedit: ac Theodorinam eius generis filiam, ditissimo Genuensi lacatam, opibus magnis ornauit. In his nihil videt Vuicelius pontificius, qui tam libidinosam bestiam[?] à vitae innocentia, doctrinâ, facundiâ, & pace commendat. Genitor, inquit, erat filij filiæq; : qui bus affatim prospexit. Nothos, cubicularios, & contubernales, Cardinales creauit: & Heliopolitanum Austriæ olim ducem, sanctorum catalogo aggregauit: Venetos Sixti censura damnatos absolutos: & indulgentiis vniuersi ac mortuis vendidit. Quam plura Italiæ templa magnis ditauit donis: cœnobio Augustinianorum Bergomensium ecclesiam argen-team mirifici operis dedit: & Norvvegijs, ut ab-uinomissire[?] possent, bullis suis concessit. Novam-que adhuc artem procumulandi nummis quaeres, cum nec indulgentiae plenariae, nec lubileum, nec Tur-cicum bellum iuuarent, crucis Christi titulum, tri-plici lingua scriptum, Iesus Nazarenus, & c in quo-dam pariete occlusum invenit, cum hastae ferro quod latus Domini perfo-lit[?]. Lorga infirmitate im-peditus, alia multa quae conceperat, implere non potuit: sed anno Domini 1492. naturæ exoluit de-bitum. Qui plura adhuc de hoc Pontifice deside-rat scire, haec ex diversis authoribus colle&a le-gat.
units.tr: After this, Innocent, weary of wars and turned to a feigned concord of peace, had nothing more at heart than to study quiet, that is, idleness, which brings with it diverse desires, lusts, frauds, sloth, pleasures, pomps, gluttonies, luxuries, lusts and idolatries. Then, following the example of Sixtus, for the sake of profit he established a college of secretaries, increasing their former number. He adorned the palace with new things and furnished a house of leisure in a wonderful way. He was the first of the popes who, to an unheard-of example, openly and without shame enriched his bastards with dignities and honours. For he gave some towns near the city to his bastard son Francesco, and he lavished great wealth on his daughter of the same kind, Theodorina, who was married to a very rich Genoese. The papist Wicelius sees nothing wrong in these things; he commends so lustful a beast for innocence of life, learning, eloquence and peace. "He had," he says, "a son and a daughter, for whom he provided amply." He created as cardinals his bastards, chamberlains and companions; and he enrolled in the catalogue of saints Heliopolitanus, formerly duke of Austria; the Venetians, condemned under the censure of Sixtus, he absolved; and he sold indulgences for the living and the dead. He enriched many Italian churches with great gifts: to the Augustinian monastery at Bergamo he gave a silver church of wonderful workmanship; and by his bulls he granted to the Norwegians that they might be dispensed from wine. And, as a new art of heaping up money, when neither plenary indulgences, nor the jubilee, nor the Turkish war helped, he found the title of Christ's cross, written in three languages, "Jesus of Nazareth," etc., enclosed in some wall, together with the iron of the spear that pierced the side of the Lord. Hindered by a long illness, he could not carry out many other things he had conceived; but in the year of the Lord 1492 he paid the debt of nature. Whoever wishes to know more about this Pope, let him read these things gathered from various authors.

units.la: Valerius Anselmus ex Platina: Paulus Secun-dus, Venetus, imperiosus & arrogans, ecclesiasti-corum, praecipuè Cardinalium pompam, etiam-num decretis augere conatur. Ad idq; apprime pe-cuniarum undiquaq; studiosus, officia, beneficiaq; venalia[?] fecit[?]. Homo corporis forma adeo sibi pla-cens fuit, ut, nisi eius pontificatus nota diffuafiffet, Formosus appellari voluisset. Fuere etiam (inquit Platina) qui dicerent, eum, dum in publicum pro-diret, faciem sibi suis concinnare solitum. Animo erat adeo rudis, ut academiae Platonicae cultores, necnon & humanitatis artium cultores, tanquam haeretihæreticos execraretur: doctos ab antecessore præ-sectos, officijs, honoribus, bonisq; spoliaret. [?]Ut Ge-orgius Vuicelius in Epitome Rom. pontificum: Et quia ab omni bona doctrina fuit alienissimus, omnes bonos doctosq; viros odijs ac iniurijs persecutus est, solitus hæreticos appellare, quotquot hu-manioribus studijs Romæ vacabant: debortans Romanorum filios, à literis politioribus. Multos erun-ditos non possessione sua tantum priuauit, verum in carceres etiam coniectos, tormentis acerbissi-mis subiecit. Inter quos fuerunt Baptista Platina & Mylaertonus Anglus, Carmelitarum provinci-alij: Phalaridemq; Agrigentinorum tyrannum potius egit quàm Paulum. Pro se causam dicentibus, respondere solebat, se ius fasq; gerere in scrinio sui pectoris, &c. Idem ornatu Neroniano, seu foemi-neo potius, magnopere delectatus, venum expofu-it nihil non. Bibacissimus quidem fuit, omniaq; of-ficia suo tempore venalia erant. In Poli oppido a-pud Aequicolos, viros octo ac foeminas sex, cum domino loci cõprehensos, hæreticos iudicauit: quia dicebant, nullum verum Christi vicarium esse, eo-rum qui post Petrum fuere, nisi qui paupertatem Christi essent imitati. Georgium Bohemiæ regem hæreseos damnauit: dignitate etiam & regno pri-uauit, stirpemq; eius funditus deleri procurauit. sceptro Mathiæ Pannoniæ regi dato. Venationem demum miro apparatu edidit in campo Merulæ: cui præfuit eius ex sorore nepos, S. Luciæ Cardinalis: de quo postea. Huius Pauli cœlibatum Ianus Pannonius his versibus commendat:
units.tr: Valerius Anselmus, from Platina: Paul the Second, a Venetian, was imperious and arrogant. He even tried by decrees to increase the pomp of churchmen, especially the cardinals. Being above all eager for money from every quarter, he made offices and benefices saleable. He was so pleased with his bodily appearance that, had the fame of his pontificate not spread abroad, he would have wished to be called the Handsome. There were also (says Platina) those who said he used to adjust his face with cosmetics whenever he went out in public. In mind he was so crude that he cursed the devotees of the Platonic academy, and likewise the cultivators of the liberal arts, as heretics. He stripped of offices, honours and goods the learned men whom his predecessor had appointed. As George Wicel says in his Epitome of the Roman Pontiffs: "Because he was most alien to all sound learning, he persecuted all good and learned men with hatred and injuries. He was accustomed to call heretics whoever devoted themselves to the humane studies at Rome, and he dissuaded the sons of the Romans from the more refined letters. He not only deprived many learned men of their property, but also threw them into prison and subjected them to the most savage tortures. Among them were Baptista Platina and Mylaert the Englishman, provincial of the Carmelites. He acted more like Phalaris, tyrant of Agrigentum, than like Paul. To those who pleaded their cause before him he used to reply that he carried law and right in the chest of his heart, and so on." The same man, greatly delighting in Neronian, or rather womanish, finery, put up almost everything for sale. He was indeed very given to drink, and all offices were saleable in his time. At the town of Poli among the Aequicoli, he judged eight men and six women, seized along with the lord of the place, to be heretics, because they said there was no true vicar of Christ among those who came after Peter except those who imitated the poverty of Christ. He condemned George, king of Bohemia, as a heretic; he also deprived him of his dignity and kingdom, and took care that his line be utterly destroyed. The sceptre having been given to Matthias, king of Pannonia. Finally he gave a hunt with wonderful display in the field of Merula, over which presided his nephew by his sister, Cardinal of St Lucy, of whom more later. Janus Pannonius commends this Paul's celibacy in these verses:

units.la: Pontificis Pauli testes ne Roma requiras: Filia quam genuit, sat docet esse marem. Sanctum non possum, patrem te dicere possum, Cum video natam Paule Secunde tuam.
units.tr: Do not look for witnesses of Pope Paul in Rome: the daughter he begot is proof enough that he is a male. I cannot call you holy, but I can call you father, Paul the Second, when I see your daughter.
Another poem about the same man, by the author Marullus.

units.la: Quid quæris testes, sit mas aut fœmina, Cibo[?] Respice natorum, pignora certa gregem. Octo recens pueros genuit, totidemq; puellas: Hunc merito poterit dicere Roma patrem. Spurcities, gula, auaritia, atq; ignauia deses[?], Hoc, Octaue, iacent, quo tegeris tumulo.
units.tr: Why do you seek witnesses, whether male or female? Look at his children, the sure pledges of his flock. He recently begot eight boys and as many girls; Rome may rightly call him their father. Filth, gluttony, avarice and idle sloth lie here, Octavius, under the tomb that covers you.

units.la: Circa annum Domini 1464. qui fuit à sua nativitate decimus octauus, Baptista Mantuanus scri-psit, post religionem ingressum, ut vocat, Eclogam nonam, de corruptis moribus curiæ Romanæ: & decimam, de fratrum Observantium & non obser-uantium controuersia: ac soluta oratione, de vita beata dialogum, ad genitorem Petrum. In Eclogâ nona docet, omne vitiosorum hominum genus Ro-mæ in honore esse ac precio: & non nisi flagitiofos, exilio & carcere dignos, illic sublimari: Quo magis appropriàs, tanto magis omnia sordet. Et sequitur: Fama est Aegyptum coluisse animalia quaedam, Et pro numinibus multas babuisse ferarum. Ista superstitione minor est quàm nostra: ferarum Hic aras habet omne genus, contraria certè Natura res atq; Deo, qui dicitur olim Praeposuisse homine cunctis animantibus unū, & c.
units.tr: Around the year of the Lord 1464, when he was in his eighteenth year from birth, Baptista Mantuanus wrote, after entering religion, as he calls it, the ninth Eclogue on the corrupt morals of the Roman court, and the tenth on the controversy between the Observant and non-Observant friars; and, in prose, a dialogue on the blessed life, addressed to his father Pietro. In the ninth Eclogue he teaches that every kind of vicious man is held in honour and esteem at Rome, and that only the disgraceful are raised up there, deserving exile and prison. The more fitting a man is for it, the more everything there is despised. And he goes on: "It is said that Egypt worshipped certain animals and held many wild beasts as gods. That superstition is smaller than ours: here every kind of wild creature has its altars, a thing surely contrary to nature and to God, who is said once to have set man above all living creatures..."
160. Alexander the Sixth.

units.la: Alexander sextus, natione Hispanus, patria Valentinus, Rodericus Borgia ante nominatus, Calixti Papae tertij quondam ex sorore nepos (si non spurius) nonnullorum Cardinalium opera Satanae sedem in ipso est adeptus Papatu. Quid huius sce-[?]lestissimi nebulonis inaudita, obscæna, & opprobriosa facta enarrent? Luxuriosissimus certè tyrannus fuit, & daemonibus ipsis ex fœdere iunctus, ut tandem in pontificem crearetur. Ab adolescentia sua in Cardinalatu diu vicecancellarium existens, omnem Romanæ curiæ statum, procur-sum [?], ac totius Italiae principum & communitatum consilia callebat. Omnes igitur Pontifex factus, per Valentinum spurium, quem ex Cardinale ducem constituit, ac Caesarium cognominatus, pene depriacp; [?]imebat: & potentes in urbe familias extermi-nabat, ita ut eos deinceps non pertimesceret. Quo certamine (inquit Valerius) Gallorum Helvetiorum præsidio, cruente admodum, in utrunq; se-xum confictio, superbus ille sacrificulus, Gallicæ coniuge Valentiæ dux, nummos aucupaturus, acco-nito Cardinalibus aliquot adparato, gloriantem tanto filio patrem consopiuit, ac subinde teli [?]ista indignam utriusq; gloriam extinxit. Iubileum anno Christi millesimo quingentesimo Romæ Alexander celebrauit: in quo his qui venire neglexerant, aut minime venire poterant, per diplomata Iubilei gratiam concessit: sed non gratis. Omnes excogitabat vias ad pecuniam, quæ suis cupiditatibus suppeteret.
units.tr: Alexander the Sixth, a Spaniard by nation, a native of Valencia, formerly named Rodrigo Borgia, the nephew (if not the bastard) of Pope Calixtus the Third through his sister, obtained the seat of Satan in the papacy through the work of some cardinals. What shall I say of the unheard-of, obscene and shameful deeds of this most wicked scoundrel? He was certainly a most lustful tyrant, and joined in covenant with the very demons, so that at last he was created pontiff. From his youth he had long been vice-chancellor while a cardinal, and he knew well the whole state of the Roman court and the counsels of all the princes and communities of Italy. Therefore, once made pope, he sought to crush almost everyone through his supposed son Valentinus, whom he made a duke from a cardinal and surnamed Caesar. He exterminated the powerful families in the city so that he would no longer fear them. In this struggle (says Valerius), bloody indeed, with a garrison of Gauls and Swiss, that proud little priest, having arranged a French wife for the Duke of Valencia in order to grab money, and having prepared poison for several cardinals, lulled to sleep the father who was boasting of so great a son, and soon after, with the same poison, extinguished the glory of both. Alexander celebrated a jubilee at Rome in the year of Christ 1500, in which he granted grace by jubilee documents to those who had neglected to come or could not come at all. But not freely. He devised every way to get the money that would satisfy his desires.

units.la: Quapropter nouum scriptorum breuium collegium instituit, numero octoginta: quorum loca singula 750 aureis venere. Principes per bullas ad dictum Iubileum inuitauit, & stationes ubiq; gentium vicatim constituit: quo absentes etiam aureos mitterent. Cardinales triginta sex suo tempore creauit, in quibus octodecim fuerunt Hispani: de suis autem, Ioannes Borgia, Valentinus Borgia, & Franciscus Borgia. Per Ioannem ab Alphonso nono rege Neapolitano iuramentum accepit, super fide Abadoni seruanda, & tributis annuis soluen-di. dit. Arcem S. Angeli ingenti impensa munitissimā reddidit. Templum Mariæ maioris incredibili pulchritudine exornauit. Vias publicas Leonina[?] ur-bis constrauit, aliaq; in urbe ædificia instauravit: sed de cælesti Hierusalem nihil cogitauit. Plures animi dotes, inquit Volaterranus, magnis obrue-rat vitijs, quæ narrare non attinet: tantum reserā quæ vulgus aspexit. Si quando rerum fisce, ait, nō premeretur, omni remissionis generi (sanctus Pon-tifex) sine discrimine se dedidit. Quapropter co-mœdias Plautinas, cæteraq; ludicra (Papale exer-citium) libenter spectauit. Frequenterq; in Hadria-ni molem ventitabat, ut palam personatos per eo-rum ferias atq; omnes dies festos, si quid elegantius in hominum genere, scortis vel Ganymedibus, per viam præteriret, propius aspiceret. In nuptijs filiæ quæ ad virum Ferrariam erat profectura, eque-stres ludos & venationes in Vaticano extra ordi-nem dedit. In urbe gladiatorum nunquam licentia maior, nunquam populo Romano libertas minor.
units.tr: Accordingly he established a new college of scriveners, eighty in number, each place of which sold for 750 gold pieces. He invited princes to the said jubilee by bulls, and set up booths everywhere among the nations, street by street, so that even the absent might send gold. In his time he created thirty-six cardinals, of whom eighteen were Spaniards; of his own family, John Borgia, Valentinus Borgia and Francis Borgia. Through John he received from Alfonso the Ninth, king of Naples, an oath to keep faith with Abadon and to pay annual tributes. He made the citadel of St Angelo most strongly fortified at great expense. He adorned the church of St Mary Major with incredible beauty. He built public roads in the Leonine city and restored other buildings in the city, but he thought nothing of the heavenly Jerusalem. Volaterranus says that he had overwhelmed his many gifts of mind with great vices, which it is not worth recounting, only those things the common people saw. Whenever he was not pressed by the affairs of the treasury, he gave himself without restraint to every kind of licence (the holy pontiff). Accordingly he gladly watched the comedies of Plautus and other plays (the papal exercise). He often went up to the mole of Hadrian, so that he could see more closely, openly, among masked men, on their holidays and all festival days, anything rather elegant in the human race that passed by the road, whether prostitutes or catamites. At the wedding of his daughter, who was about to set out for her husband at Ferrara, he gave extraordinary equestrian games and hunts in the Vatican. In the city the licence of gladiators was never greater, nor the liberty of the Roman people less.

units.la: Delatorum magna frequentia, breuissimo male-dicto pœna mortis erat. Grassatorum insuper omnia plena: nec noctu tutum per urbem iter, nec in-terdiu extra urbem. Roma gentium refugium & arx populorum omnibus seculis, nobilis iam car-nifficima[?] facta erat. Quæ quidem omnia, furiorū[?] suorum causa, quibus omnia indulserat, permittebat, &c.
units.tr: There was a great crowd of informers, and for the briefest slander the penalty was death. Moreover, all was full of robbers: no road through the city was safe by night, nor outside the city by day. Rome, the refuge of the nations and the citadel of peoples in every age, had already become a notorious shambles. All of this he allowed and permitted for the sake of his rages, to which he had given himself over entirely, and so on.

units.la: Quàm sint hæc contraria Vuicelij scriptis, prudens Lector videat, ac adulatores Papisticos detegetur. Nunquam fere reperiri potuit, quin aut libros legerit Alexander, aut sacris operaretur. Iudæq; sategit[?], ut principes à bellis intestinis vel ad pacem revocaret, vel ad resistendum Turcis inflammaret. Sic habet Vuicelius. Cumq; Alexander animo adhuc maiora, quàm quæ dicta sunt, de suis conciperet, diuturnioremq; vitam sibi polliceretur, anno Domini 1503. subitò in mortem (veneno, quod aliis parauerat) incidit, ex quo absumptus est. Plura adhuc vide in nostris Appendicibus, & apud Volaterranum, qui & filij bella, et patris fraudes graphicè depinxit. Huius Papæ tempore, Angelus apud Hadriani molem, in supremo loco positus, terrifico fulmine deiectus in terram fuit: quod in papatu casum prænunciabat. Parisiisque fiebat meretricum ordo per Minoritam, Ioannem Tissranum[?], ac si Christiana religio meretricibus etiam indigeret. De hoc Alexandro sunt hæc carmina.
units.tr: Let the prudent reader see how far these things are contrary to the writings of Wicel, and how the Papistical flatterers are exposed. It could hardly ever be found that Alexander did not either read books or busy himself with sacred things. He strove, too, to call the princes back from civil wars to peace, or to rouse them to resist the Turks. So Wicel writes. And while Alexander was still conceiving greater things in his mind than those spoken of, and promising himself a longer life, in the year of the Lord 1503 he suddenly fell into death, having been consumed by poison which he had prepared for others. Read more about him in our Appendices, and in Volaterranus, who also vividly depicted the wars of the son and the frauds of the father. In the time of this pope, an angel standing at the highest place above the mole of Hadrian was cast down to the ground by a terrifying thunderbolt, which foretold his fall in the papacy. And at Paris an order of prostitutes was instituted by a Minorite, John Tissranus, as if the Christian religion also needed prostitutes. There are these verses about this Alexander.
Epitaph of the same man.

units.la: Fortasse nescis cuius hic tumulus fiet, Adsta uiator, ut pigebit[?].
units.tr: Perhaps you do not know whose tomb this will be. Stand still, traveller, lest you regret it.

units.la: Titulum quem Alexandri uides, haud illius Magni est: sed huius, qui modo Libidinosa sanguinis captus siti, Tot ciuitates inclytas, Tot regna uertit, totq; duces letho dedit, Natos ut impleat suos: Orbem rapinis, ferro & igne funditus Vastauit, hausit, eruit: Humana iura, nec minus caelestia, Ipsosq; sustulit deos: Vt scilicet liceret (heu scelus) patri Nata sinum permingere: Nec execrandis abstinere nuptiis, Timore sublato semel. Et tamen in urbe Romuli uel undecim Praesidet hic annis Pontifex. Nunc, Nerones uel Caligulas nomina, Turpeis uel Heliogabalos. Hoc sat[?] uiator, reliqua non finit pudor: Tu suspicare, & ambula.
units.tr: The inscription you see is not that of the Great Alexander, but of this man, who, burning with a lustful thirst for blood, overturned so many famous cities and kingdoms and gave so many leaders to death, so that he might enrich his own children. He ravaged, drained and tore the world apart with plunder, sword and fire. He abolished human laws, and no less the divine ones, and even the gods themselves. All this so that (alas, the crime!) a daughter might be permitted to lie in her father's bosom, and so that he might not shrink from accursed marriages, once fear had been removed. Yet this Pontiff presided in the city of Romulus for eleven years. Now let the names of Nero or Caligula be spoken, or those of the vile Heliogabalus. Here, traveller, shame does not allow me to say more. Make your own guess, and move on.
Another epitaph on Alexander:

units.la: Hic iacet Hispanus, famae contemptor honestae: Vis breuium lapis hic contegit omne scelus.
units.tr: Here lies a Spaniard, a despiser of honourable repute. This stone, a short but mighty one, covers every crime.
Another on the same:

units.la: Nomen Alexandri ne te fortasse moretur, Hspes[?] abiiacet[?] hic & scelus & vitium.
units.tr: Let not the name of Alexander delay you, stranger. Here lie both crime and vice.
On the same Alexander:

units.la: Mirum si vomuit nigrum post fata cruorem Borgia quem biberat, concoquere haud potuit.
units.tr: It is no wonder that Borgia, after death, vomited black blood, since he could not digest the poison he had drunk.
Another on the same:

units.la: Sub quo bella diu viguerunt, pestis in urbe, Diluvium populo, semper amara fames: Mille hominum caedes, & furta incesta fuerunt: Causa mali tanti proditor ipse fuit.
units.tr: Under him wars raged for a long time, plague in the city, a flood of misery for the people, and ever bitter famine. There were a thousand murders, and incestuous thefts. The betrayer himself was the cause of such great evil.

units.la: Sacrilegus praedo, sacra qui venalia cunsta Fecerat, & tumquo polluit omne nephas.
units.tr: A sacrilegious robber, who had made everything sacred up for sale, and who polluted all things with every wickedness.
Another on the same:

units.la: Visuram se iterum Sixtum cum Roma putaret, Pro Sixto Sextum vidit, & ingemuit.
units.tr: Thinking that he would see Sixtus again when he came to Rome, he saw Sextus in place of Sixtus, and groaned.
Another on the same:

units.la: Bello, inimicitiis, furtisq; & caedibus baustam Italiam cernis Sexte, & obire potes?
units.tr: Sextus, do you look upon Italy drained by war, enmities, thefts and slaughter, and can you bear to die?
Another on the same:

units.la: Dic, in amicitiam coeant, & foedera iungant Mortales: dixit Sextus, & occubuit.
units.tr: Tell them to come together in friendship and join in covenants, mortals. Sextus has spoken, and he has died.
Another on the same:

units.la: Piscatorem hominum ne te non Sexte putemus, Piscaris natum retibus ecce tuum.
units.tr: Sextus, we would not think you a fisher of men, but see, your son is caught in the nets of a fisher.
Another on the same:

units.la: Europam Tyrio quondam sedisse iuvenco Quis negat? Hspano[?] Iulia vecta bove est. Ille sed astrigeri partem vix occupat orbis: Hic cælum atq; deos sub ditione tenet. Unde igitur, si par meritum, non par quoq; fatu, Romanam amplexu plus tenuisse fuit? Ioannes Funccius ex Volaterrano: Cardinales, qui eum elegerant, primi ingratum illum senserunt. Omnes enim varia calamitate pressit, quosdam exilio, quosdam vero carcere multans. Bellum cum Ursinis gessit, quos & per filium nothum victos cepit, ac domuit. Hinc nihil prius habuit, quàm innocentij exemplo, spurios suos honoribus, verum longe maioribus extollere: quando iam res haec honori & gloriae esse coepit inter patres. Tanta sanctitate fuerunt tunc praediti, sanctissimi illi. Ex filijs unum minorem natu Siciliae principem fecit: alterum Caesarium Valentinum nomine, Cardinalem: maiorem quoq; in Hispania ducem. Qui breui tempore postea nocte quadam trucidatus, & in Tyberim proiectus fuit. Caesarius Cardinalis, spreto sacerdotio, post eius mortem in Galliam se contulit, magna ui auri secum ablata. Ubi Ludouici regis propinquam de Lebreto in uxorem, unà cū opido Valentia accepit. Regis deinde auxilio, perpetuoq;[?] fœlere, multum in Italia sibi ditionis parauit: uiuante etiam Alexandro patre, qui nil magis optabat, quàm filium maximum fieri principem. Filia Alexandri Lucretia, ab eo prius cognita (facinus horrendum) tribus principibus successione collocata fuit. Primum Ioanni Sforziae, Pisaurien si du-ci: deinde abdicata, Aloisio Aragoni, Alphonsi regis filio notho. Quo demum interfecto, Alphonso Estensi Ferrariae duci nupsit. Ex eius epitaphio, a Ioanne Louiano Pontano eleganter edito, patet, qua-lis fuerit eius in papatu pudicitia, sanctitas, castitas, caelibatus, & religio.
