Monstrum illud erat, seu bellua partum Virginis extento cupiens extinguere collo: Cuius ab aspectu, sumptis diuinitus alis, Vt sacer Aegeae uates canit incola Patmi, Fugit ad extremae loca uirgo incognita terrae, Virgo fuit primo fruticans Ecclesia seclo, Christigenae soboles eius, quos bellua adegit Quaerere defertis aliena penatibus arua.
units.tr: A monstrous beast, powerful enough to swallow up as many thousands of men as its bloody gullet desired. That monster was either a dragon, desiring to extinguish the Virgin's child with its outstretched neck; at whose sight, with wings divinely given, as the sacred seer of Aegean Patmos sings, she fled to the far-off places of the earth, an unknown virgin. She was a virgin, the Church, flourishing at first in the age, and her offspring, the children of Christ, whom the beast drove to seek foreign fields away from their homes.

units.la: Hierosolymorum excidij causa, fuere sacerdotum scelera.
units.tr: The cause of the destruction of Jerusalem was the crimes of the priests.

units.la: Quid Solymos ritus, quid montib. æmula templa, Aequatamq; iugis molem, longumq; per æuum Limina solenni late celeberrima cultu, Antiquasq; Dei sedes cum mœnibus altis Eruit, & pulchram ex imis radicibus urbem: Sacrificæ gentis scelus & contagia passim In patrias prolapsa domos mouere tonantem. Qui romana uocans ad opes & regna suorum Castra, secundabat cursus, classemq; regebat Ausoniam: stimulosq; animis addebat & ignes. Ipse acies inter tenui circundatus aura,
units.tr: Why do the Solymi's rites, why the temples rivaling the mountains, and the mass built level with the hills, and the long-lasting thresholds widely famed for solemn worship, and the ancient seats of God with their high walls, and the beautiful city from its very foundations, drive the thunderer to tear down? The crime of a sacrificing nation, and its pollutions scattered everywhere, having slipped into their ancestral homes, roused the Thunderer. He who, calling the camps of his own people to the power and kingdom of Rome, gave their course favourable winds, and governed the Ausonian fleet, and added goads and fires to their spirits. He himself, surrounded by a thin breeze, moved among the battle lines, driving on the spirited nation to fight.

units.la: Versabatur agens animosam in prælia gentem. Oppugnansq; altas arces, scelerata ruebat Mœnia Cœlicolum post longa silentia tandem Evigilans furor imperijs regnusq; ruinam Ingerit, & celeri pessum[?] trahit omnia cæde: Sicut in antiquas flammis volitantibus ædes Quum sævit Vulcanus, eunt laquearia iunctis Cum trabibus tabulæq; leues, atq; ardua tecta In cineres: longosq; rapit brevis hora labores.
units.tr: Attacking the high citadels, the accursed fury rushed upon the walls; at last, awakening after long silence of the heavenly dwellers, it brought ruin upon empires and kingdoms, and with swift slaughter dragged everything to destruction. Just as when Vulcan rages with flying flames against ancient houses, the panelled ceilings, with their joined beams and light boards and lofty roofs, turn to ashes, and a brief hour seizes long labours.

units.la: Ex sexto Alphonsi libro, de sceleribus romæ.
units.tr: From the sixth book of Alfonsus, on the crimes of Rome.

units.la: Namq; meas pridem obscænum peruenit ad aures Rumor, & horribilis scelerata infamia romæ: Et quanta Stygis alluvie incestata nitorem Polluerit romana fides: quo verbere Ditis Spes hominum luxata cadat: quàm debilis æstu Frigeat extincto pietas: quæ grandia cete Piscari, prædaq; hominum graui ire solebat: Syrtibus in Stygijs hæret sine remige cymba. Heu scelus infandum. plures in puppe magistri Dr[?] clavo certamen habent: marcore palustri sordet inops: limo infixam turpiquæ latentem Gurgite cæci onerant omni farragine nautæ.
units.tr: For a rumour and a horrible infamy of Rome long ago reached my ears, a foul thing: and how Roman faith, defiled by the filth of the Styx, has polluted its brightness; by what blow the hopes of men, dislocated by Dis, fall; how piety grows cold, its strength extinguished; how the fishermen used to fish for great whales and the spoil of men, but now a boat sticks without an oarsman in the Stygian quicksands. Alas, the unspeakable crime! Many masters in the stern vie for the rudder; the helpless man is fouled by marsh rot; the blind sailors load with every kind of rubbish the foul thing sunk in the mud and lying hidden in the gulf.

units.la: Pastores odere pecus: nec pascere curant, Sed tondere greges, pecoriquè illudere tonso.
units.tr: The shepherds hate the flock; they take no care to feed it, but to shear the flocks and to mock the sheep once shorn.
From the third book of the Calamities.
Meanwhile the furies, with burning hatreds, harass our cities.

units.la: Exercent furiæ:per rura per oppida sæuit Martis opus. Petriq; domus polluta fluenti Marcescit fluxu: nulla hic arcana revelo. Non ignota loquor, liceat vulgata referre. Sic urbes populiq; ferunt: ea fama per omnem jam vetus Europam mores extirpat honestos. Sanctus ager scurris, venerabilis ara cinædis Seruit, honoranda diuum Ganymedibus ædes. Quid miramur opes recidiuaq; surgere tectâ[?] Turis odorati globulos & cinnama vendit Molli[?] Arabs, Tyrii vestes et muricis imbrem, Indus ebur, croceum Cilices & Tmolus odorum, Mel Siculi, ferrum Chalybes, tenuissima Seres Vellera, Cretenses mollissima vina: Tanager Pernices mercatur equos: venalia nobis Templa, sacerdotes, altaria, sacra, coronæ, Ignes, tura, preces: cælum est urnale, Deuq;.
units.tr: Through fields and towns the work of Mars rages. The house of Peter, defiled, wastes away with its flowing stream. I reveal no secrets here; I speak of nothing unknown, and it is allowed to repeat what is commonly said. Thus cities and peoples report it; this fame, now old, through all Europe, is uprooting honest morals. The holy field serves buffoons, the venerable altar serves catamites, the temple to be honoured by the gods serves Ganymedes. Why do we wonder at the riches and the rising of the roofs again? The Arab sells balls of fragrant incense and cinnamon, the Tyrian sells robes and a shower of purple, the Indian ivory, the Cilicians saffron, Tmolus fragrant things, the Sicilians honey, the Chalybes iron, the Seres the finest fleeces, the Cretans the softest wines; Tanager trades in fine horses. Temples, priests, altars, sacred things, crowns, fires, incense, prayers are for sale to us; heaven is for sale, and God too.
It follows concerning the monks.

units.la: Hi quoq; qui nomen de religione superbum Usurpant, quamquam sanctis à patribus ortos Se iactent, ovium molli sub vellere fraudes Mente Lycaonias servant, & crimine sordent. Quod speciem virtutis habens scelus omne colorat.
units.tr: Those too who, proud of the name of religion, take it up, and though they boast that they are descended from holy fathers, keep Lycaonian frauds in their minds under the soft fleece of sheep, and are fouled with crime. Crime that has the appearance of virtue colours everything.
Concerning the sacrificing priests too.

units.la: Invisi superis, fœdaq; libidine olentes, Heu frustra incestis iterat sacra orgia dextris:
units.tr: Hateful to the gods above, and reeking with foul lust, alas, in vain they repeat the sacred rites with unchaste hands:

units.la: Polluti circum quoties altaria multus Conueniunt, celebrantq; choros, et carmine mixto Sancta Deum uanis penetralia uocibus implet. Irritant, irasq; mouent, non numina flectunt. Haec prece nil opus est: nil adiutoribus istis Auxilij sperate: nouis date templa ministris. Sacrilegum genus ex adytis templisq; deorum Pellite, nec longos scelera haec uertantur in usus.
units.tr: Whenever crowds of the polluted gather about the altars, celebrate their choirs, and with mingled song fill the holy inner sanctuary of God with empty voices. They provoke and stir up anger; they do not bend the divine powers. There is no need for such prayer: hope for no help from these helpers. Give the temples to new ministers. Drive this sacrilegious race from the shrines and temples of the gods, and do not let these crimes be turned to long use.

units.la: In Calamitatum libris, in Nicolao Tolentino, in Eclogis, Syluis, Fastis, et in aliis adhuc libris, corruptissimum Romanae synagogae statum describit: in quibus Babylonicae illius meretricis impuritates ac turpitudines, sicut & alij pij ante sua tempora viri, ad liquidum detestatus est. Scripsisset quae multo plura, si per praedicti Antichristi tyrannidem, quae veritatem ipsam oppressérat, ac sepultam tenuerat, licuisset.
units.tr: In his books of Calamities, on Nicholas of Tolentino, in the Eclogues, the Silvae, the Fasti, and in other books besides, he describes the very corrupt state of the Roman synagogue. In these he has laid bare, as other pious men did before his time, the impurities and filthy practices of that Babylonian harlot. He would have written much more, had it been permitted under the tyranny of the Antichrist mentioned, who had oppressed the truth itself and kept it buried.
164. HADRIAN the sixth.

units.la: HAdrianus sextus, natione Germanus, patria Hollandus uel Batauus, Hadrianus de Traiecto antea dictus, atq; humili domo natus, ex Caroli Caesaris praeceptore, & Cardinale presbytero, tituli S. Ioannis & Pauli, Papa constitutus : idem seruauit nomen quod habuerat ex baptismo. Promittebat ille Principibus per literas, daturum se operam, ut Romana respublica, quae multis malis occasione dedit,omniu prima fcuere[?] corrigeretur: ut quae dã ni causam dedijset, medicina præberet & salutis initiu.Sed ficus hypocriticus tantu erat. More nam que præcedeffori Antichristorum,Christi puriore doctrinam est acriter infe&atus in Luthero, Oeco lampadio, & aliis piis ecclesiæ doctoribus,necali-ud in ipso Papatu fecitulla memoria dignu. Decef fit fufpe&a morte Hadrianus,anno Domini 1523. fe cundu ingressus fui pontificatus annum,quartode-cimo die Septembris. Vnde Aclius Sannazarius:
units.tr: Hadrian the sixth, German by birth, a Hollander or Batavian by homeland, formerly called Hadrian of Utrecht, born of a humble house, once tutor of Charles Caesar and priest cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, was made pope. He kept the name he had from baptism. He promised princes by letter that he would take care that the Roman commonwealth, which had given occasion for many evils, would be corrected; that the remedy and the beginning of salvation would be offered where it had given the cause. But that was merely a hypocritical fig. For, following the custom of his Antichrist predecessors, he fiercely attacked the purer doctrine of Christ in Luther, Oecolampadius and other pious teachers of the Church, and did nothing else worth mentioning in the Papacy itself. Hadrian died a suspicious death in the year of the Lord 1523, in the second year of his pontificate, on the fourteenth day of September. Hence Actius Sannazarius:

units.la: Classe,uirunque potes,demitoque oriete superbus, Barbarus in Latias dux quatit arma demes. In Vaticano noster latet.Hunc tamen alto Christe uides cælo(proh dolor) & pateris?
units.tr: You, proud one, can command both fleet and man, and cast down the East; a barbarian leader shakes arms in Latium. Our man lies hidden in the Vatican. Yet, Christ, do you see this from high heaven (alas!) and allow it?
164. CLEMENS octavus.

units.la: Clemens octauus,patria Florentinus, Leonis de cimi Papæ nothus(dixissem nepos) & Iulius antea uocatus,tituli S. Laurentij in Damafo presbyter Cardinalis,scelerato patri[?] filius, in impio Papatu successit. Peftilentiffimam sedem illam Antichristi ac Diaboli,uiolenter istum imua-fisse Valerius scribit: uix ulli superiorum,inquit,seculorum , & romanæ urbi & pontificiæ curiamagis infælicem. Porro dum armatus hic pontifex, inter Cafareanos in Gallicanos, pro Italiæ imperio dimicates,fluctuaret: roma ui capta, ac mife rabili prœda à Germanis & Hispanis militibus sa-ta[?], Pontifex ipse multis probris adfectus, in eorū incidit manus. Inde Germanorum ecclesias maiores, Papatum uelut Antichristi regnum uerbo sanguinē[?] detestatas, amisit. Subinde tamen astutus & audax lupus iam potentissimis regum populorumq; retibus instructus, Christi oues Lutherismi praetextu ad necem uenaturus, mense septembri anno Domini 1534. insulito[?] ueneficio, nempe funalis fumo, cum aliquot Cardinalium & amicis fa-miliaribus, in acerbae necis retia incidit. De hoc Clemente sic habet Vulteius:
units.tr: Clement the eighth, Florentine by country, the bastard (I would have said grandson) of Pope Leo, and formerly called Giulio, priest cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, a son of a wicked father, succeeded in the impious Papacy. Valerius writes that this man violently assailed that most pestilential seat of Antichrist and the Devil; scarcely any of the preceding ages, he says, has been more unhappy for the city of Rome and the papal court. Moreover, while this armed pontiff wavered between the Caesareans and the Gallicans, fighting for mastery of Italy, Rome was taken by force and given over to wretched plunder by German and Spanish soldiers; the pontiff himself, beset with many insults, fell into their hands. Thereafter he lost the greater churches of Germany, which had detested the Papacy as the kingdom of Antichrist by word and by blood. Afterwards, however, the crafty and bold wolf, now equipped with the nets of the most powerful kings and peoples, was hunting Christ's sheep for slaughter under the pretext of Lutheranism. In September of the year of the Lord 1534, by an unheard-of poisoning, namely the smoke of a torch, he fell with some of his cardinals and familiar friends into the nets of bitter death. Concerning this Clement, Vulteius says:

units.la: De Clemente, quod est conscriptu cirmine crimen,Id uerum, aut falsum protinus esse scio.
units.tr: About Clement, whatever is written as a crime, I know at once whether it is true or false.

units.la: Si uerum est, uerè iam possum dicere, mundiVrna breuis uitium claudit, & anne scelus.
units.tr: If it is true, I can truly say that a brief urn encloses the vice and crime of the world.

units.la: Si falsum est, uerè iam possum scribere, mundiDux, pax, lux, paruo contegitur tumulo.
units.tr: If it is false, I can truly write that the leader, the peace and the light of the world is covered by a small tomb.

units.la: At falsum esse reor. Quis enim committere summūPontificem Romæ talia monstra putet?
units.tr: But I think it false. For who would think the highest pontiff at Rome could commit such monstrous deeds?

units.la: Ex Commentarijs Ioannis Fuccij, & quorundam aliorum: Anno Domini 152[?] Clemens septimus Rom. pontifex, sed olim Hierosolymitanus miles, et Prior Capuensis, Hadriano quinto successit, cui Iulius antea nomē erat, quod & in Papatu fernare decreuerat. Sed Cardinalium monitu, Clementis mentis nomen accepit: quum moribus eius (nouit enim vulpes ad tempus dissimulare) tunc aptius id esse videretur. Hic, quum Galli contra Caesarem faceret, Roma à Caesarianis vi occupata, ad S. Angeli castrum confugit: illis tamen, quum arctius premeretur, coactum se dedidit. Carolus vero nimis obseruans Pontificis, priscis eum luxurijs mox restituit. Quae vero militum, in ea urbis occupatione, virtutes fuerint, quomodo Cardinales tractauerint, & thesauros expilauerint, longa narratione vix comprehendi posset. Quare in aliud tempus ea Funccius ille reseruat. Ex Henrico Pantaleone: Clemens pontifex, cum rege Gallorum contra Imperatorem conspirans, à ducibus Caroli, cum Cardinalibus & urbe capitur: ac ciuibus occisis, miru in modum à Germanis militibus ludificatur, anno Domini 1527. Ex Ioannis Tilij Chronico: Redimi-tur postea Clemens captiuus, 4oooo[?] florenis. De isto Clemente, in quodam commentario super articulis magistrorum Parisiensium legitur, quod fuerit nothus, veneficus, homicida, leno, Simoniacus, Sodomita, periurus, stuprator, raptor, geomanticus, sacrilegus, & omnium scelerum artifex. De quo poeta quidam cecinit:
units.tr: From the Commentaries of John Fuccius and some others: In the year of the Lord 152[?] Clement the seventh, Roman pontiff, formerly a Hierosolymitan knight and Prior of Capua, succeeded Hadrian the fifth. His earlier name was Giulio, which he had decided to keep in the Papacy. But at the advice of the cardinals he took the name Clement, since his character (for the fox knows how to dissemble for a time) then seemed more suited to it. When he sided with the French against Caesar, Rome was forcibly occupied by the Caesareans, and he fled to the castle of Saint Angelo. Yet when they pressed him more tightly, he was forced to surrender. Charles, however, who was too deferential to the pontiff, soon restored him to his old luxuries. What the virtues of the soldiers were in that occupation of the city, how they treated the cardinals and plundered the treasuries, could scarcely be comprehended in a long narrative; therefore that Fuccius reserves these matters for another time. From Henricus Pantaleon: Pope Clement, conspiring with the king of the French against the Emperor, was captured by Charles's commanders along with the cardinals and the city; the citizens were killed, and he was mocked in a remarkable manner by German soldiers, in the year of the Lord 1527. From the Chronicle of John Tilius: Clement, afterwards a captive, was ransomed for 40,000 florins. In a certain commentary on the articles of the Parisian masters it is read concerning this Clement that he was a bastard, poisoner, murderer, pimp, simoniac, sodomite, perjurer, rapist, robber, geomancer, sacrilegious, and a craftsman of every crime. Of him a certain poet sang:

units.la: Clementi nomen dedit inclementia fati, Bellorum hic fomes, sanctorum lerna malorum.
units.tr: The unmercifulness of fate gave him the name Clement; here is the firebrand of wars, the Lernaean hydra of holy evils.

units.la: Ex Valerio Anselmo: Clemens ultimo sui pontificatus anno, simulata prudentia, Francorum regem apud Massiliam adijt. Vbi adeò inter eos conuenit, ut rex pontifici neptem Catharinam, cum ampla ecclesiastici principatus dote, filio suo Henrico Aurelianensium duci, in uxorem reciperet. Subinde astutus & audax lupus, iam potentissimus regum populorumque retibus instructus, Christi oues Lutherismi [?] praetextu, ad necem uenabatur. Sed mense septembri, inaudito ueneficio, scilicet toxicati funalis fumo, cum aliquot aulae suae Cardinalib. ac familiaribus in acerbae necis retia incidit.
units.tr: From Valerius Anselmus: Clement, in the last year of his pontificate, with feigned prudence, approached the king of the French at Marseilles. There it was so agreed between them that the king should take the pontiff's niece Catherine as wife for his son Henry, duke of Orléans, together with a large dowry of ecclesiastical principality. Thereupon the crafty and bold wolf, now most powerful, equipped with the nets of kings and peoples, was hunting Christ's sheep for slaughter under the pretext of Lutheranism. But in September, by an unheard-of poisoning, namely the smoke of a poisoned torch, he fell with some of his court's cardinals and familiars into the nets of bitter death.

units.la: Ex Ioanne Baptista Folengio, in commentario Psalmi 105: Aiunt enim nostra etiam aetate, morbo pediculari, qui morborum est turpissimus & infamis, interiisse Clementem septimum pontificem maximum nonnulli ueneno censent. Mortalis erat, atque propterea sexcentis [?], ut caeteri quoque ex ulla homines, obnoxius miseriis & aegritudinibus, &c. Hoc epitaphio à Pasquillo deploratus est, qui & eius statum in inferno post mortem aliquando descripsit quoque:
units.tr: From John Baptist Folengius, in his commentary on Psalm 105: They say that in our own age Clement the seventh, greatest pontiff, died of the lice disease, which is the most shameful and infamous of diseases; some think he died by poison. He was mortal, and therefore, like other men, subject to troubles and sicknesses, etc. He was lamented with this epitaph by Pasquillus, who at some point also described his state in hell after death:

units.la: Clementem eripuit nobis clementia fati, Humanum toto gaudeat orbe genus [?]. Hic est qui fuerat iam dedecus urbis & orbis, Et fuit aetatis magna ruina suae [?].
units.tr: The clemency of fate snatched Clement from us; let the human race rejoice throughout the whole world. This is the man who had already become the disgrace of the city and the world, and was the great ruin of his age.

units.la: Hic est, si nescis, qui iam tibi, Roma, parauit Excidium, pestem, funera, bella, famem.
units.tr: This is he, if you do not know, who has prepared for you, Rome, destruction, plague, deaths, wars and famine.

units.la: Hic est, per quem tot prostant & in urbe puellæ, Per quem pulsus honos, virgineumq; decus.
units.tr: This is he, through whom so many girls prostitute themselves in the city, through whom honour is driven out and virginal dignity.

units.la: Hic est, qui molles eucxit ad astra cinædos, Formosum à tergo munere iuuit Hylam.
units.tr: This is he who raised effeminate catamites to the stars, and gave a gift from behind to beautiful Hylas.

units.la: Hic est, qui fuerat unus infamia mundi, Imperij labes, spurcities q; sui.
units.tr: This is he who was the one infamy of the world, the stain of the empire and the filth of his own people.

units.la: Contemptor diuum, sceleru[?]m uir, publicum hostis, Perfidus, ingratus, raptor, iniquus, atrox.
units.tr: Despiser of the gods, man of crimes, public enemy, faithless, ungrateful, robber, unjust, savage.

units.la: Exosus uitam, & morbo tenuatus amaro, Stabat Paeonia non reuocandus ope.
units.tr: Hating life, and worn down by a bitter disease, he stood, not to be recalled by the help of Paeon.

units.la: Mortem implorabat, nec mortem fata sinebant, Gaudebant longa sed cruciare mora.
units.tr: He implored death, and fate would not allow him to die; they rejoiced to torment him with long delay.

units.la: Hic uidit mortis centum tormenta futura, Poena tamen mortis non fuit aequa suae.
units.tr: He saw the hundred torments of death to come; yet the punishment of death was not equal to his deserts.

units.la: Ex ista tandem migrauit luce tyrannus, Quo nullus toto peior in orbe fuit.
units.tr: At last the tyrant departed from this light, than whom none in the whole world was worse.
Pasquillus to Rome.

units.la: Roma uale, uidi, satis est uidisse: reuertar, Quum leno, aut meretrix, scurra, cinædus erat.
units.tr: Farewell, Rome. I have seen you, and it is enough to have seen you. I shall return, when you were a pimp or a whore, a jester or a catamite.

units.la: Sub prædicto Clemente pontifice claruisse dicitur Nicolaus Machiauellus, historicus & secretarius Florentinus. Qui in historia sua clarè ostendit, ex ambitione pontificum pleraque Christianorum prouenisse mala. Ante Theodoritum Longobardorum rum regem, id est, ante annum Christi 500. in re-bus politicis, suis semper paruisse regibus pontifi-ces narrat: & Cardinales nihil aliud mitio fuisse, quam parochos. Sed deinceps politicam potestatem, paulatim sibi rapuisse illos dicit, ac super Caesares ipsos dominium usurpasse. Tribus artibus, in ipsis creuisse pontificem demonstrat: excommunicatio-nibus, indulgentijs, & armis: quibus tamen (inquit) scelerate sunt usi. Ab hoc Nicolao longe dissentie-bat alius eius temporis Nicolaus, cognomine Eg-mudanus, magister Louanensis & Carmelita. Qui sub ipsa Euangelij luce, talpa caecior, credidit, do-cuit ac scripsit, Pontificem Rom. esse omnium re-rum caelestium, terrestrium, et subterranearum do-minum: omnesque principes Christianos ab eius nu-tu pendere, & habere imperium in angelos ac dae-mones: uidi eius uitam cum epistola ad H. Zuinglii[?] de magistris Louanensibus.
units.tr: Under the aforementioned Pope Clement, Niccolò Machiavelli, the Florentine historian and secretary, is said to have flourished. In his history he shows clearly that most of the evils among Christians arose from the ambition of the popes. Before Theodoric, king of the Lombards, that is, before the year of Christ 500, he relates that the popes always obeyed their kings in political affairs, and that the cardinals were then nothing more than parish priests. But afterwards, he says, they gradually seized political power for themselves and usurped dominion over the emperors themselves. He demonstrates that the pope grew in power by three arts: excommunications, indulgences and arms. Yet (he says) they used these wickedly. Far different from this Niccolò was another Nicolaus of that time, surnamed Egmudanus, master at Louvain and a Carmelite. Under the very light of the Gospel, blinder than a mole, he believed, taught and wrote that the Roman Pontiff is lord of all things heavenly, earthly and subterranean, that all Christian princes hang upon his nod and that he has dominion over angels and demons. I have seen his life, together with his letter to H. Zwingli on the Louvain masters.
166. PAUL III.

units.la: PAulus tertius, patria Romanus, Alexander Farnesius antea nuncupatus, & Cardinalis episcopus Hostiensis senio fere confectus, eodem anno post Clementis mortem, duodecimo die Octobris ad hoc Satanici regni fastigiū ascendit, in eoq; sedit quin-decim annis. Hic pontifex sanctus (inquit Valerius) liberos suos à Pasquillo nobilitatos, Papali more ualde exaltare, Lutherumque & alios Christianæ ueritatis professores opprimere studuit. In astrolo-gia ac diuinatione, illa præcipuè quæ malorum de-monum adiutorio fit, primas obtinens, multa mirá-cula iuuenis fecit: & sororem suam, Iuliam Farne-siam, Alexandro sexto pontifici ad usum uenereū pro rubro gilero dedit. In ipso Papatu uero, nouü religionis genus senex adinuenit, ad diuini cultum augmentum ut cuidam matronæ nobili gratificaretur, globulum quendam ligneum Papali benedictio-ne consecrauit, & ut contra molestationes varias collo appensum ferret, paternis consiliis admonuit.
units.tr: Paul III, a Roman by birth, formerly called Alexander Farnese, and cardinal bishop of Ostia, worn out with old age, ascended to this summit of the Satanic kingdom on the twelfth day of October in the same year after the death of Clement, and sat in it for fifteen years. This holy pontiff (says Valerius) took care to exalt his children, ennobled by Pasquillus, in the Papal manner, and to oppress Luther and the other professors of Christian truth. Holding the first place in astrology and divination, especially that which is done with the help of evil demons, he performed many wonders while still young. He also gave his sister, Giulia Farnese, to Pope Alexander VI for venereal use in exchange for a red hat. Indeed, in the Papacy itself, as an old man, he devised a new kind of religion: to gratify a certain noble matron, and to increase the worship of God, he consecrated a wooden ball with the Papal blessing, and advised her, by his paternal counsel, to wear it hung about her neck against various troubles.

units.la: Mysterium magnum est. Romanæ synagogæ, sanctissimæ matris, res compositurus, concilium uniuersale Mantuan indixerat, sed frustra: nec posteriore Tridentino quicquam effecit. Supra cæteris eius actis sanctissimis Appendices quære. Anno Domini 1549. è uiuis excessit, decimo die Nouembris: uacabatque sedes illa mensibus tribus, ac diebus totidem.
units.tr: It is a great mystery. Intending to settle the affairs of the Roman synagogue, the most holy mother, he had summoned a universal council to Mantua, but in vain; nor did he accomplish anything at the later council of Trent. For his most holy acts beyond the rest, look in the appendices. He passed from this life in the year of the Lord 1549, on the tenth day of November, and that see stood vacant for three months and as many days.
Epitaph of this Paul:

units.la: Puluis eram terra, tenuisque in puluere uentus, Fœmineo suetus[?] uiuere lacte senex.
units.tr: I was dust and earth, and a thin wind in the dust, an old man accustomed to live on woman's milk.

units.la: Attamen italicis non doctior artibus alter, Quiq; Deum uberius ludere posset, erat.
units.tr: Yet there was no other more learned in Italian arts, and he could mock God more richly.

units.la: Nemq; uno summi fatuati numine Reges, Cæperunt ipsi bella mouere Deo.
units.tr: And kings, fooled by no single power of the highest, began to make war upon God himself.

units.la: Non satis aequa meae nuper Germanus Romae, Ingenij sensit subdola vota mei. Quicquid id est, inter felices gaudeo manes: Quam volui, auspicio est alea iacta meo, Nunc gratare mihi partos post funus honores, Roma mea, Stygios dum vagor umbra lacus, In culicem versus segnes affligo tyrannos, Qui furere in summum non potuere Deum. Haec mea nunc merces, hoc grato laetor honore: Pro meritis vitae praemia quisque capit.
units.tr: Lately my German soul, not quite fair, felt the deceitful wishes of my mind in Rome. Whatever it is, I rejoice among the blessed shades. The die is cast under my auspices, as I wished. Now, Rome, congratulate me on the honours won after my death, while I wander as a shade over the Stygian lake. Changed into a gnat, I afflict the sluggish tyrants, who could not rage against God on high. This is my reward now; with this welcome honour I rejoice. Each man receives the rewards of life according to his deserts.

units.la: Ex Valerio Anselmo, Paulo Vergerio, Ioan-ne Sleidano & aliis nostri temporis scriptoribus: Anno Domini 1534. Paulum tertium Romanum pontificem, Alexander Farnesius antea dictus, Clementi septimo senex admodum successit, qui liberos suos (potius nothos) Papali more valde exaltare, Lutherumque opprimere studuit. Res ecclesiae compositurus, concilium universale Mantuam indixerat, sed frustra: qui nec posteriori Tridentino concilio effecit quicquam. Perlongum esset huius sanctissimi Satanae vicarij, facinora insigniora omnia referre, parricidia, furta, veneficia, proditiones, tyrannides, incestus ac stupra nefanda. Pauca haec tamen ex multis recensebo, ut sciat mundum, qualis sit eorum in sanctissimo genere caelibatus ac sanctitas, quos Papistae tā altis vocibus iactitat Petri successores[?]. res & Christi vicarios. Astrologus, magus, & haariolus erat hic Paulus: Dionysium & Seruitâ, Geomanticum, quem ob id postea Cardinalem fecit, & Gaurium Lusitanum, Cecium & Marcellum necromanticos, insignes nebulones, socios semper ac familiares habuit, ut eius ac filiorum nothorum fata, in horoscopis, in aspectibus, & in siderum domicilijs inquirerent. Rubrum galerum, consuetis locis nocentijs & dolis instructum, sic meruit primum. Roderico à Borgia, Hispano, seu Alexandro sexto Romani pontifici, sororem suam Iuliam Farnesiâ stuprandam tradidit, ut Cardinalis & episcopus Hostiensis fieret, ac se aere alieno liberaret. Sic enim solent Papae tetterrimis libidinibus æstuare, ut mitras & galerosillus promittant, qui ad se sororem violandas, aut, quod dictu horribilius est, fratres iuniores, adducant. His artibus multi perpinguia venantur beneficia. Nec est (inquit Agrippa) via ulla compendiosior. Matrem suam ac nepotem, impudens parricidia, veneno sustulit, ut omnis ad illum conflueret Farnesiorum hereditas. Alteram deinde sororem suam, cum qua rem habuerat, videns quod nimis aperte Farnesiorum sequeretur mores, atque alios ardentius, ad actum venereum, quam ipsum amaret, toxico etiam interemit.
units.tr: From Valerius Anselmus, Paulus Vergerius, Johannes Sleidanus and other writers of our time: in the year of the Lord 1534, Paul III, the Roman pontiff, formerly called Alexander Farnese, succeeded Clement VII as a very old man. He took care to exalt his children (or rather his bastards) in the Papal manner, and to oppress Luther. He had summoned a universal council to Mantua to settle the affairs of the Church, but in vain; nor did he accomplish anything at the later council of Trent. It would take too long to recount all the more notable crimes of this most holy vicar of Satan: parricides, thefts, poisonings, betrayals, tyrannies, incests and unspeakable debaucheries. I will recount a few of the many, so that the world may know what sort of celibacy and holiness they have in that most holy line, those whom the Papists boast of in such loud voices as the successors of Peter, the vicars of Christ and of the Church. This Paul was an astrologer, a magician and a soothsayer. He always kept as companions and intimates Dionysius and Servita, geomancers (whom he afterwards made a cardinal for this reason), and Gaurus the Portuguese, and Cecius and Marcellus, necromancers, notorious scoundrels, so that they might inquire into his fate and that of his bastard sons, from horoscopes, aspects and the houses of the stars. He first earned the red hat by the usual harmful devices and tricks. He handed over his sister Giulia Farnese to be ravished by Roderic Borgia, the Spaniard, or Pope Alexander VI, so that he might become a cardinal and bishop of Ostia and free himself from debt. For the Popes are wont to burn with the foulest lusts in this way, promising mitres and hats to those who bring to them their sisters to be violated or, what is more horrible to say, their younger brothers. By these arts many hunt down fat benefices. Nor (says Agrippa) is there any shorter way. He killed his mother and his nephew by poison, shamelessly, so that the whole inheritance of the Farnese might flow to him. Then, seeing that his other sister, with whom he had had relations, was following too openly the manners of the Farnese, and that others loved her more ardently for sexual intercourse than he did himself, he also killed her with poison.

units.la: Per Anconitanam provinciam cum esset legatus, lega-tus, tus,sub Iulio secundo pontifice, puellam eius ciui-tatis nobilem nefarie circumuenit. Dissimulauit enim quis esset, ieq[?] pro nobili quopiam gerens ex legati familiaribus, sub pacti matrimonij colore il-lam uitiauit. Quæ posteaquàm cum esse, qui erat, cognouisset, sciq; non legitimam uxorem, sed concu-bimam[?] (quod ex iure Pontificio notum est) satis re-sciret, in insaniam ferè incidit. Ex eo tamen con-nubio fucato Petrum Aloysium, Sodomitarum primipilum post patrem, sustulit. Quum Nicolaus Quercæus, congredientem illum semel cum Laura Farnesia uxore sua, sed eius nepte, deprehendissit, tale ei vulnus pugione incußit, ut eius cicatrix ad mortem usq; cum ipso maneret. Vt filia sua Cōstantia, cum qua sæpiuscule rem habuerat, potiri liberius posset, maritum eius Bosium Sforziam[?] ve-neno necauit. Libidine Helicgabalum & Commo-dum longè superabat: idq; tot spurijs ac nothis do-ceri[?] poterat, filias suas Lothus uitiauit, ignarus & ebrius. Hic autem sobrius ac sciens, non modo cum nepte, sed etiam cum sorore atq; filia congressus fuit. Hic Paulus itidem statim post assumptum Pa-patum[?], Alexandrum ex filio notho Petro Aloysio, ualde adolescentem, & Ascanium ex filia notha Constantia nepotem, fortassis filium, Cardinales creauit. Perusinos oppressione tyrannica luxuriosus subegit: & Ascanium Columnam princi-pem iustissimum, in rabie uesana, e suo regno filii-cernium pellebat. Camerium urbem pessimo do-lo, pulsa eius principe foemina, singulari sapientia ac religione praedita, sibi capiebat, scelerosus la-tro ac proditor. Mirisq; artibus collegium Cardi-nalium in suam pertraxit sententiam, ut facta per mutatione Camerij non sui, in Parmam & Placen-tiam, urbes clarissimas non suas, Petrum Alcysi-um, suum spurium, perditissimumque nebulonem, dominum ac principem in eas tyrannum intruderet. Quod factum postea iustissimo Dei iudicio, meri-tam illi Petro mortem attulit. Cum suis quoq; Car-dinalibus saepe deliberabat, quomodo impediendum esset nationale in Germania concilium: praecepitq; suo legatis, ut Principum animos in Angliae regem accenderent: eiusque ditionem omnem in praedam dare cogitabat.
units.tr: While he was legate in the province of Ancona, under Pope Julius II, he wickedly deceived a noble girl of that city. Concealing who he was, and posing as some noble man of the legate's household, he ruined her under the pretence of a marriage contract. When she afterwards learned who he really was, and knew well that he was not a lawful husband but a concubine (as is known from Papal law), she nearly fell into madness. Yet from that feigned union he begot Pietro Luigi, who after his father became the chief of the sodomites. When Niccolò Querceo caught him once in the act with Laura Farnese, his wife but also his niece, he gave him such a wound with a dagger that the scar remained with him until death. In order that he might more freely possess his daughter Costanza, with whom he had often had relations, he poisoned her husband, Bosio Sforza. In lust he far surpassed Heliogabalus and Commodus, and this could be shown by so many bastards and illegitimate children. He ravished his daughters, as Lot did, ignorant and drunk; but he, sober and knowing what he did, had intercourse not only with his niece but also with his sister and daughter. Likewise this Paul, immediately after assuming the Papacy, created as cardinals Alessandro, a very young man, the son of his bastard Pietro Luigi, and Ascanio, the grandson of his bastard daughter Costanza, perhaps her son. Given to luxury, he subdued the people of Perugia by tyrannical oppression, and in mad fury he drove Ascanio Colonna, a most just prince, out of his kingdom. By a most wicked trick he seized the city of Camerino, its ruler, a woman endowed with singular wisdom and piety, being driven out; a wicked thief and traitor. By wonderful arts he drew the college of cardinals to his own opinion, so that, with Camerino changed hands, he might thrust into Parma and Piacenza, cities most famous and not his own, Pietro Luigi, his bastard and most abandoned scoundrel, as lord and tyrant over them. This deed was afterwards, by the most just judgement of God, brought upon Pietro himself, and he received a deserved death. He often deliberated with his cardinals how the national council in Germany might be hindered; and he instructed his legates to stir up the minds of the princes against the king of England, and he planned to give all his dominions over to plunder.

units.la: Non sanandae reipublicae causa, ad conscientiarum tranquillitatem, aut instaurandae religionis gratia, ad Dei gloriam: sed pro conculcanda eius veritate, opprimendisque eius verbi ministris, Tridenti anno Domini 1542 generale indixit concilium. Vbi cum non omnia illi ad voluntatem succederent, Bononiam tandem anno Domini 1546 corrupti aeris ludibrio plane transfulit: ut inde Christianis profua[?] tyrannide omnia suffragia au-ferret. Aduersus Dei sanctos horrida bella, cruentasque pugnas, Antichristus iste parauit, irrumpentibus nouo pugnandi genere in Christi gregem tigridibus ac lupis. hos ut omnino sub cælo deleret hic Pharao, cum districtis gladijs, facibus accensis, poculisque toxicatis accurrebat. Nec à suis Cardinalibus, Fulgosio & Contareno, postquam Christi dulcedinem aliquantulum gustassent, manus abstinebat tyrannus: nec à Polensi episcopo Ioanne Baptista Vergerio, quos clàm veneno sustulit: nec ab eius fratre Paulo Vergerio, Iustinopolitano episcopo, nisi Dominus illum ad maiora ac meliora seruasset. In prouincijs Christianorum, sub hac immani bestia, ubique ferociebant Neronés & Maxentij, in ueritatis Dei professores: igne, ense, laqueis, remis, rogis, flammis, aquis, exilijs, carceribus, inedia, proscriptione, & similibus malorum diabolorum afflictionibus, ad mortes usque eos insequentes. Horum principes erant, Alexander Farnesius Cardinalis, & Octauius eius frater dux Parmensis, filij prædicti Petri, ac pontificis nepotes: qui inanes spirantes glorias, quum anno Domini 1546. ex Italia Germaniam essent ingressi, superbo comminabantur ore, se tantū Lutheranorum Germanicorum sanguinis fusuros, ut in eo possent natare eorum rum equi. Paulus interim sanctissimus nebulo, cum Constantia filia solito iucundior fuit: neptemq; ad huc aliam, puellam lectissimam, non minus virgi-nali pudore quam forma praestantem, hircosus se-nex ad incestum & nefandum stuprum sollicitabat. In tabellis etiam habebat numerata 45 meretri-cum millia: ex quarum fornicatione singulis mensibus censum exegit. hæ à Papa (inquit Eusebius Captiuus) in summo honore habentur, hæ Papæ pedes exosculantur, hæ Papam familiarissime alloquuntur, hæ cum Papa die nec[?]tuq; consuetudinem habent. Qui vero unico Christo fidunt, eiusq; doctrinam amplectuntur, à Papa haeretici habentur, à Papa exulant, à Papa proscribuntur, à Papa carceribus mancipantur, compedibusq; astringuntur: triremibus, aquis, laqueo, securi, igneq; plectuntur.
units.tr: Not for the sake of mending the commonwealth, nor to quiet consciences, nor to restore religion for the glory of God, but to trample underfoot the truth of God and to crush its ministers, he called a general council at Trent in the year of the Lord 1542. When not everything went to his liking there, he finally transferred it to Bologna in the year of the Lord 1546, as a mockery of the unhealthy air, so that from there he might strip the Christians of all support by tyranny. Against the saints of God this Antichrist prepared horrible wars and bloody battles, with tigers and wolves rushing upon the flock of Christ in a new kind of fighting. This Pharaoh, to destroy them utterly under heaven, ran about with drawn swords, lit torches and poisoned cups. The tyrant did not keep his hands off his own Cardinals, Fulgosio and Contareno, once they had tasted the sweetness of Christ for a little while; nor off the bishop of Pola, John Baptist Vergerio, whom he secretly removed by poison; nor off his brother Paul Vergerio, bishop of Capodistria, had not the Lord preserved him for greater and better things. In the provinces of the Christians, under this monstrous beast, Neros and Maxentiuses raged everywhere against the professors of the truth of God, pursuing them to death with fire, sword, nooses, oars, pyres, flames, water, exile, prisons, starvation, proscription and similar afflictions of devilish evils. Their leaders were Alexander Farnese, the Cardinal, and his brother Octavius, duke of Parma, sons of the aforesaid Pietro and nephews of the pope. Breathing empty glories, when they entered Germany from Italy in the year of the Lord 1546, they threatened with proud mouths that they would shed so much blood of the German Lutherans that their horses could swim in it. Meanwhile Paul, that most holy scoundrel, was more cheerful than usual with his daughter Constance; and the old goat was still enticing another granddaughter, a most choice girl, excelling no less in virginal modesty than in beauty, to incest and unspeakable debauchery. He even kept in his ledgers 45,000 numbered prostitutes, from whose fornication he collected a tax every month. These women, says Eusebius Captivus, are held in the highest honour by the Pope; these women kiss the Pope's feet; these women address the Pope most familiarly; these women keep company with the Pope day and night. But those who trust in the one Christ alone and embrace his teaching are held as heretics by the Pope, are exiled by the Pope, are proscribed by the Pope, are consigned to prisons by the Pope and bound in fetters; they are punished with galleys, water, the noose, the axe and fire.

units.la: Sub hoc pontifice Paulo, anno Domini 1534.
units.tr: Under this Pope Paul, in the year of the Lord 1534.

units.la: Franciscani monachi cruentum ac funestum edide-runt ludum in Gallijs Aureliae, super praetoris uxore mortua, quae sine funeris pompa sepeliri se uiuens iusserat. Cum dicti Franciscani, quorum in templo iuxta patrem & auum sepulta fuit, muneris loco sex aureos tantum a marito eius accepissent, valde graviter tulerunt, quod non plus essent inde accepturi.
units.tr: The Franciscan monks staged a bloody and deadly spectacle in Orléans in France, over the wife of the provost, who had died; she had ordered while still alive that she be buried without any funeral pomp. Since the said Franciscans, in whose church she was buried beside her father and grandfather, had received from her husband only six gold coins as a fee, they took it very badly that they were not going to receive more from him.

units.la: Unde neuicium[?] quendam adoleftentem, supra testudinem templi constituebant, ut intempesta nocte se animam eius esse simularet, atq; ob Lutheranismum perpetuo damnatam dice-ret. Res est tandem Lutetiam ad regium senatum delata. Ubi coram cancellario, Antonio Praten-se, Colimannus & Stephanus Atrebatensis, ambo eius sectae theologi, in maleficio deprehensi & con-victi sunt, ac de communi consilio lata sententia ad publicam ignominiam damnati. In hos impostores, Vulteius Remensis hoc edidit carmen:
units.tr: So they set a certain young novice on the roof of the church, so that in the dead of night he would pretend to be her soul, and declare that she was eternally damned on account of Lutheranism. The matter was at length brought to Paris before the royal council. There, before the chancellor Antoine Prat, Colimannus and Stephanus of Arras, both theologians of that sect, were caught in the deception and convicted, and by common counsel a sentence was passed condemning them to public infamy. Against these impostors Vulteius of Reims published this poem:

units.la: Cum clamat larvas, furiosa caterva leonum, Infestare suam nocte dicq; domum: Res vera est, falsi, larvati deniq; fratres, Quos vestis sanctos prodigiosa ficit, Sunt lemures, larvae, furiae, vulpesq;, lupiq;, Qui infestant nitiys[?] sequé suamqué domum.
units.tr: When a furious troop of lions cries out with ghosts, to disturb their house by night and day, it is a true thing: the brothers, false and at last masked, whom a prodigious garb has made into holy men, are lemures, larvae, furies, foxes and wolves, who disturb their own house and those who follow them.

units.la: Nunc de Pauli tertij filio notho, Petro Aloysio, Parmae ac Placentiae duce, aliquid dicendum oc-currit: qui, quia superbia ferox & libidinosissimus tyrannus erat, anno Domini 1548 & decimo die Augusti, à suis nobilibus occidebatur. Quum hic sceleratissimus nebulo ( ut ex quibusdam Italicis li-bris, Vergerius ac Sleidanus referūt (exercitus Ro-mani primarium ducem agens, Fanum appulisset: ibiq; Cosmum Cherium, eiusdem urbis episcopum, qui tricesimum annum excesserat, summa pruden-tia, tia, summa eruditione, summaque pietate uirum inuenisset: illi per uim, prima quaedam, imo diabo-lica rabie, stuprum intulit hoc modo. Vsus est opera suorum, qui illum distinerent, donec perpetra-ret hoc nefandissimum ac teterrimum post orbem conditum scelus. Quod quidem facinus miserrimo illi sic doluisse ac displicuisse ferunt, ut prae maerore et indignitate rei fit triduo post extinctus. Non de-sunt tamen, qui uenenum ei datum ab illo fuisse pu-tent, ne flagitium illud tam impetuosum ad Caesa-rem deferret. Quoniam in acerbissimo suo dolore, imprudenter effutiuerat, se ad ipsum Caesarem i-turum, conquestum de tam atroci iniuria. Cum so-rore sua et nouerca Constantia, quoniam et pa-ter ab illa non abstinebat, consuetudinem habuisse frequentem hic Petrus dicitur. Omnia enim sibi li-cere putabat, dum pater esset pontifex summus, potestatem habens in coelis atque inferis. Hinc tot cum maribus et foeminis stupra commisit, hinc tot caedes et rapinas fecit: hinc tot sacrilegia et ne-fanda conuicia in Deum, ac eius Christum euomu-it. Hinc innumera alia, genitorem Papam imita-tus, omnis generis scelera patrauit. Paulus etiam pontifex nihilo secius impense filium amabat, et ad ipsius amplificationem omne studium conuer-tit, et quum de flagitijs nonnunquam audiret, non admodum ægrè tulisse ferunt, sed quasi subridendo confuesse dicere, hæc illum vitia non se commonstratore didicisse. Unde qui illum tum demum interfecerant, corpus exanime cathena religatum, cum maxima ignominia ex muro suspendebant, & agitatum aliquandiu præcipitabant in foßam. Accurrebat populus, & pugionibus ac pedibus ipsum petebant. tanta erat acerbitas odij.
units.tr: Now something must be said about Pietro Luigi, the bastard son of Pope Paul III, duke of Parma and Piacenza, who because he was a fierce proud and most lustful tyrant, was killed by his own nobles on the tenth day of August in the year of the Lord 1548. When this most wicked scoundrel, as Vergerius and Sleidanus report from certain Italian books, was leading the chief command of the Roman army and had landed at Fano, he found there Cosimo Cheri, bishop of that city, a man past thirty years of age, of the greatest prudence, the greatest learning and the greatest piety. By force, and with a certain initial and even diabolical rage, he committed rape upon him in this way. He made use of his men, who held him down, until he perpetrated this most unspeakable and most hideous crime since the world was made. They say that the most wretched man was so grieved and displeased by this deed that, from sorrow and indignation at the affair, he died three days later. Yet there are those who think he was given poison by Pietro, lest that so outrageous a disgrace be reported to the Emperor, since in his bitter grief he had carelessly let slip that he would go to the Emperor himself to complain of so atrocious an injury. Pietro is said to have kept up a frequent relationship with his sister and stepmother Constance, since his father also did not abstain from her. For he thought everything was permitted to him, while his father was the supreme pontiff, holding power in heaven and hell. Hence he committed fornications with so many men and women; hence he carried out so many murders and robberies; hence he vomited out so many sacrileges and unspeakable insults against God and his Christ. Hence, imitating his begetter the Pope, he perpetrated countless other crimes of every kind. Pope Paul also loved his son no less intensely, and turned all his zeal to his advancement; and when he occasionally heard of his disgraceful conduct, they say he did not take it very badly, but used to say, half laughing, that he had not learned these vices from him. Therefore those who finally killed him hung his lifeless body, bound with a chain, from the wall with the greatest dishonour, and after dragging it about for some time they threw it into a ditch. The people ran up and attacked it with daggers and feet; so great was the bitterness of their hatred.
167. Julius the Third.

units.la: Iulius tertius, patria Aretinus, Ioannes Maria de Monte ante Papatum nominatus, post diuturnam Cardinalium in conclaui disceptationem, anno Domini 1550. septimo idus Februarij, ex Praneftino episcopo pontifex designabatur. Cardinalium collegio à prædicto Paulo tertio, ob melancholiam et veritatis odiū ascriptus: eiusq; nomine synodo Tridentinensi cōtra Lutheranos (sic pios appellant) Sodomitae legatus præsedit. Pontifex mox factum, lubileum lucri gratia celebrat, utpote qui in annum quinquagesimum incidisset. Venerunt quæ Roma, Amphiones, tibicines, auletæ, lyricines, fidicines, histriones, ganeones, lenones, scurræ, cinædi, meretrices, pædicones, & omnium malorum colluuies. Sic magnam spem[?] Iulius emendandæ religionis (ea-ius quam papistæ cupiunt) præbuit, ac reformandi cleri. cieri. Porcellis & pauonibus libenter uescebatur podagricus senex, qui porcinam uitā duxit. Nullos prius ad ecclesiasticas dignitates promouit, quàm adolescentes lasciuos, quos Ganymedes uocare solent: ut in quodam patebat Innocentio, ad nullas uirtutes nato. In quotidiano sermone, sanctus hic Pontifex obscœnioribus utebatur verbis ac blasphemijs, quàm quisquam alius ex lenonum aut aliorum per Italiam nebulonum sece. Pro cæteris eius virtutibus pontificijs, Appendices vide. Abijt hinc Iulius, sua podagra atque aliis adhuc vexatus malis, anno Domini 1555 vicesimo tertio die Martij: & ad patrem infernalem non lætus descendit. Valedicebantq; illi Anglorum Papicolæ per funebres cantiones, monitore Polo.
units.tr: Julius the Third, a native of Arezzo, named Giovanni Maria de Monte before his papacy, was designated pope on 7 February 1550, as bishop of Palestrina, after a long dispute among the cardinals in conclave. He had been enrolled in the college of cardinals by the aforesaid Paul the Third, because of his melancholy and hatred of the truth. In Paul's name, the Sodomite legate presided over the Council of Trent against the Lutherans (as they call those pious men). As soon as he became pope, he celebrated a jubilee for profit, since it fell in the fiftieth year. From Rome came Amphions, flute-players, pipers, lyre-players, harpists, actors, catamites, pimps, buffoons, pederasts, prostitutes, and a sewer of every kind of evil. In this way Julius gave great hope of reforming religion (that reformation which the Papists desire) and of reforming the clergy. The gouty old man gladly fed on pork and peacocks, and lived a swinish life. Before anyone else he promoted to ecclesiastical dignities wanton young men, whom they are accustomed to call Ganymedes, as was plain in the case of a certain Innocent, born to no virtue. In everyday speech this holy pontiff used more obscene words and blasphemies than any pimp or other scoundrel in Italy. For his other papistical virtues, see the Appendices. Julius departed hence, still troubled by his gout and other ills, on 23 March 1555, and went down, not gladly, to his infernal father. The English Papists bade him farewell with funeral songs, at the prompting of Pole.
Luxury at Rome. L. Bigi.

units.la: Quò uentum est superi? quo uis progressa Dionesi? Quò gula? quò luxus? quæ genus omne malis? Ambrosiæ fætent epulæ, mareotica sordent Vina, nisi Iliacus porrigat illa puer. Cætera mens horret meminisse: ea discat ab uno Crimine, me quisquis legerit, atque gemat.
units.tr: To what heights, O gods, has the progress of Dionysus come? Where are gluttony and luxury, and every kind of evil? The Ambrosian feasts stink, the Mareotic wines are foul, unless a Trojan boy pours them out. My mind shudders to recall the rest. Let whoever reads me learn from this one crime, and groan.

units.la: Ex Pantaleone, Vergerio, Sleidano, & aliis ætatis nostræ scriptoribus: Anno Domini 1550. Iulius tertius, Romanus Pontifex, Ioannes Mariæ de Monte ante Papatum dictus, & patria Aretinus, nus, post Cardinalium multas ac diuturnas disceptationes, septimo die Februarij, Romae maximo triumpho salutabatur. Et quia nouum Pontifex, gale-rum suum Cardinalitium, cuicunq; voluerit, ex antiqua consuetudine largiri poterit, Innocentium quendam adolescentem, quem olim in deliciis habuerat, dum esset Bononiae legatus, in Cardinalium numerum adoptauit (quamuis reliqui illud factum improbarent, imo reclamarent) et in domesticam con-suetudinem (tam caelibes sunt rasi) rursus admisit.
units.tr: From Pantaleone, Vergerio, Sleidan, and other writers of our age: in the year of the Lord 1550, Julius the Third, Roman pontiff, called Giovanni Maria de Monte before his papacy, and a native of Arezzo, after many long disputes among the cardinals, was hailed at Rome with great triumph on 7 February. And since a new pope may, by ancient custom, bestow his cardinal's hat on whomever he wishes, he admitted to the number of cardinals a certain young man named Innocent, whom he had once cherished while he was legate at Bologna (although the others disapproved of that deed, indeed protested against it), and he took him back into his household (so unmarried are they all!).

units.la: Romae fama erat, et libellis quoque perscriptum fuit, a Ioue Ganymedem foueri, licet deformem. Atque hoc nec ipse pontifex dissimulare (prob nefas) sed per iocum fertur aliquando commemorare solitus, quàm fuisset lasciuus adolescens et importunus, Praenestinus (ut dicunt) episcopus Cardinalis, et suus Innocentius. Historiam sic accipe a Vergerio descriptam. Constituerat Iulius, inquit, creare Cardinalem nescio quem Innocentium nomine, adolescentem non modo obscurissimis parentibus, sed nulla virtute, sed vita et moribus prauis: quare cum ad Senatum Cardinalium id deferret, et nemo esset qui non resisteret, imo cum ex Cardinalibus quidam paulo liberius dixisset, Quid, obsecro, vides in hoc adolescente quod tanto hoc purpurae splendore debeas exornare? Tum Iulius: Quid, obsecro, uos in me uidistis, quod Pontificia dignitate ornā-retis? Quemadmodum ergo cum iste fit fortunæ ludus, ut quos ipsa uelit euehat, me immeritum euexistis[?] euehamus hunc puerum quoq;, & Cardinalem creemus[?]. Dum in conclaui res ageretur de hoc Iulio creando, intercepte fuerunt literæ, quas ex Cardinalis Mantuani familiaribus quidam, Camillus Oliuus, ad quendam suum Hannibalem Continum, Ianuarij die uigesimasexta scripsisse ferebatur: & simul carmen lingua populari scriptum, ubi de sua locutus affectione, & absentis desiderio, tam pudendis utebatur uerbis, ut sine flagitio uix ea recitare liceat. Hinc iocum illorum, qui Pontificem dicebant aliquem obscœnum prænunciari, qui proditurus esset ex eo conclaui, quod eiusmodi literas daret. His quidem literis se nulla memoriæ unquam uidisse obscœniores, sceleratiores, aut horridiores, dicebant illi, qui in Italia & Germania e-as legerunt. Nudis enim ac nefandissimis uerbis illic agitur (salvo honore) cum cinædo. Ex his uidere potes, optime lector, qualis sit ille spiritus, quem Papicolæ iactitant ex misis se habere in e-lectionibus suorum pontificum. Spiritus quidem ille est: at non sanctus, sed Sodomiticus. Ita ut uerissimum sit, quod Vulteius de Roma scripsit: Roma quid est? Quod te docuit praeposterum orda Quid docuit? Iungas uersa elementa, scies. Roma amor est. Amor est? qualis? Praeposterum. Vt Roma mares. Noli dicere plura, scio. (de hoc? Cum aliqui (quales sunt Paulus Vergerius, Bernardinus Ochinus, ac Hieronymus Marius) ingetes huius Iulij tertij blasphemias & horrenda scelera stylo insectarentur, subornauit sibi similem, Sodo-mitam, Hieronymum uidelicet Mutium, qui haec o-mnia editis libris tueretur atq; defenderet. Quem & ipse suis bullis approbauit, non solum ut bos in signiter[?] doctos & pios traduceret uiros, sed etiam ut Germanorum principum ac Christianissimarum ciuitatum nomen (quantum in se est) diffamaret, aut Theonino dente roderet. Quis ergo non uidet, Papam horribilia haec uitia, & crimina plusquam diabolica, quae iam nunc recitata sunt, suis diplomatibus approbasse? De illo praeterea, praedictus Vergerius in quodam scripto, inter cetera sic habet: Cum Iulius tertius (inquit) ualde male audiat, in hoc ipso genere (pederastia scilicet) quod nunc attigi, ita ut neq; a Cardinalibus abstineat (quam sancta est haec Romana ecclesia?) tamen ego illi pe rci bucusq;, quod ad teterrimam illam libidinem attinet. Verum cum omnes affirment, eū solere sæpissime illisipsis blasphemijs uti, quibus spurcissimi lego[?] lenones & reliqui nebulones in contemptum Dei uti solent: deberent tam fœdissimum idolum ac diabolicum monstrum damnare, non Christianos. Sub hoc hircoso diabolo floruit, atq; ex illius latere sancto prodijt, eiusdem generis legatus apostaticus, nempe Ioannes à Casa, Florentinus, archiepiscopus Beneuentanus, camerae Apostolicae decanus, & in toto Venetorum dominio nuncius summus, cum plenitudine potestatis: qui & breui futurus erat Cardinalis. Magnificus ille papistici cœlibatus professor, mitratus, rasus & unctus, atq; insignis catholicae Romanae ecclesiae columna, rhythmis Italicis poema scripsit: in quo opere Sodomiae papistarum Dianae laudes celebrauit: illamq; appellauit diuinum opus, atq; affirmauit se ea plurimum delectari, immo aliam venerem non cognoscere. Prob pudor: opus est Venetijs impressum, apud Troianum Nanum. An hi non sunt egregij archiepiscopi? His iudicibus utuntur Papa & diabolus in suis consisto-riis. Nam hic potestatem habebat, Christianos doctores pro haereticis damnare.
units.tr: At Rome it was the common talk, and was also written in pamphlets, that Ganymede, though ugly, was cherished by Jove. The pontiff himself did not deny this (shameful to say) but is said to have been accustomed to mention it in jest, how wanton and importunate a youth he had been, Innocent, the cardinal of Praeneste (as they say), and his own. Take the story as Vergerio describes it. Julius, he says, had decided to create as cardinal a certain Innocent, a young man of most obscure parentage and no virtue, of wicked life and morals. When he brought this to the senate of cardinals, and no one was there who did not resist, indeed when one of the cardinals spoke rather freely, saying, "What, I beg you, do you see in this young man that you should adorn him with the splendour of the purple?" Then Julius said, "What, I beg you, did you see in me that you should adorn me with the papal dignity? Just as, then, it is the sport of fortune to raise whom it wishes, you raised me, undeserving, so let us raise this boy too, and create him a cardinal." While the business of creating Julius was being done in the conclave, letters were intercepted which a certain familiar of the cardinal of Mantua, Camillo Olivo, was said to have written on 26 January to a certain Hannibal Contius, his friend; and at the same time a poem written in the vernacular, in which he spoke of his own passion and longing for his absent friend, using words so shameful that they can hardly be recited without disgrace. Hence the joke of those who said that some obscene pontiff was being announced, who would emerge from that conclave because he gave letters of this kind. Those who read these letters in Italy and Germany said they had never seen any more obscene, more wicked, or more horrible. For they deal there, in the most naked and abominable words (saving decency), with a catamite. From these things you can see, best reader, what sort of spirit it is which the Papists boast they have from heaven in the elections of their pontiffs. It is indeed a spirit, but not a holy one; it is a Sodomitic one. So it is most true, what Vulteius wrote of Rome: "What is Rome? What has the perverse order taught you? What has it taught? Join the reversed elements, and you will know. Rome is love. Love? What kind? Perverse. Such as a man for a man. Do not say more; I know." Concerning this man: when certain men (such as Paul Vergerio, Bernardino Ochino, and Girolamo Mario) lashed the enormous blasphemies and horrible crimes of this Julius the Third with their pens, he procured for himself a like Sodomite, namely Girolamo Muzio, who defended and upheld all these things in published books. Julius himself approved these books with his bulls, not only so that the learned and pious men might be defamed, but also so that the name of the German princes and of the most Christian cities might be (as far as it lay in him) disparaged, or gnawed with a Thersites' tooth. Who therefore does not see that the pope approved by his diplomas these horrible vices and crimes, more than diabolical, which have now been recited? Moreover, the aforesaid Vergerio, in a certain writing, says among other things this: "Since Julius the Third (he says) is very badly spoken of, in this very kind of vice (pederasty, namely) which I have now touched upon, so that he does not refrain even from cardinals (how holy is this Roman church?), yet I have hitherto spared him as far as that most foul lust is concerned. But since everyone affirms that he very often uses those same blasphemies with which the most filthy pimps and other scoundrels of the rabble are accustomed to use in contempt of God, they ought to condemn such a foul idol and diabolical monster, not Christians." Under this goatish devil there flourished, and from his side as a holy man there came forth, a legate of the same kind, an apostate, namely Giovanni della Casa of Florence, archbishop of Benevento, dean of the Apostolic Chamber, and supreme nuncio throughout the dominion of the Venetians, with full power; who was also soon to be made a cardinal. That magnificent professor of papal celibacy, mitred, shaven, and anointed, and distinguished pillar of the Catholic Roman church, wrote a poem in Italian rhymes, in which work he celebrated the Sodomy of the Papists as the praises of Diana, and called it a divine work, and affirmed that he delighted greatly in it, and that he knew no other love. Shame on it! The work was printed at Venice, at the shop of Troiano Nano. Are these not excellent archbishops? These are the judges whom the Pope and the devil use in their consistories. For this man had the power to condemn as heretics Christian teachers.

units.la: Vidi ego Catalogum quem fecit in sua legatione, in quo non alios connumerat, quàm qui puritatem Euangelicæ doctrinæ profitebantur. An non te pudet (inquit Vergerius) infœlix archiepiscope! Tu ne audes prodire, & libros sanctos damnare! Tu qui poema scripsisti, qui execrandissimum So-domiae scelus extulisti tanquam diuinum opus? Fa-teor (alibi inquit) haec & longe plura me aduersus eum scripsisse, &c. Huius Babylonici carnificis tyrannidem metuens Franciscus Spiera, homo foren-sis & caussidicus, Christi veritatem abnegauit, & in summa desperatione decessit: eiusque carnificina nix Petrus Paulus Vergerius, Iustinopolitanus e-piscopus, uir multae eruditionis, euasit. Vtrarque historiam Sleidanus habet: qui & cinaedici eius libel-li mentionem facit. Longum esset hic referre, praedicti Iulij tertij caetera facta, in sui temporis iubi-leo, in synodo Tridentina, in cō-fi-mato [?] idolo Lauretano, in lite quam habuit cum Ariminensi episcopo, magistro suae domus pro uno pauone, & eiusmodi aliis.
units.tr: I have seen the catalogue which he drew up during his legation, in which he enumerates none but those who professed the purity of the evangelical doctrine. Are you not ashamed (says Vergerio), unhappy archbishop! Do you dare to come forward and condemn the holy books! You who wrote the poem, who exalted the most accursed crime of Sodom as a divine work! I confess (he says elsewhere) that I have written these things and far more against him, etc. Fearing the tyranny of this Babylonian executioner, Francesco Spiera, a lawyer and pleader, denied the truth of Christ and died in utter despair; and Pier Paolo Vergerio, bishop of Capodistria, a man of great learning, escaped the slaughter of that executioner. Sleidan gives the story of both, and also mentions that libel of his. It would be long to relate here the other deeds of the aforesaid Julius the Third: at the jubilee of his time, at the Council of Trent, at the idol of Loreto, which was made of ... (fabricated), in the lawsuit he had with the bishop of Rimini, his master of the household, over a single peacock, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Delectabatur in primis porcorum & pauonum carnibus, sed cum medicus admonuisset ne porcinis uesceretur, quod ualde inimica esset podagrae, quae Iulium subinde affligebatur, nec tamen uellet Iulius abstinere: medicus submonuit praefectum conuiuio-rum, ne porcinas carnes iuberet apponi, ergo cum semel non fuissent appositae, idque pontifex animad-uertisset, Vbi est ferculum porcinarum carnium? in quit. Cumque conuiuij praefectus respondisset, medicum imperasse ne apponeretur, Pōt sex in hac uerba prorupit: Affer meum stirculum[?] al dispetto di Dio, quod si uelis Latine uertere, sonat, in contemptum Dei. ea est cotidiana blasphemia quorundam ex lenonum & aliorum nebulonum per Italiam face, quam Iulius sæpissimè usurpabat, quemadmodū etiam obscœnissima sæpe uerba.
units.tr: He took particular delight in the flesh of pigs and peacocks. When his physician warned him not to eat pork, since it was very harmful to the gout that often afflicted Julius, and Julius would still not abstain, the physician advised the steward of the banquets not to have pork served. When pork was once left off the table and the pontiff noticed, he said, "Where is the dish of pork?" The steward replied that the physician had ordered it not to be served, whereupon Julius burst out with these words: "Affer meum stirculum al dispetto di Dio," which, if you want to render it into Latin, means "in contempt of God." This was the daily blasphemy of certain pimps and other ruffians throughout Italy, and Julius used it very often, just as he often used the most obscene words.

units.la: Cum in prandio pauonem uidisset, quem non attigerat: Serua, inquit, mihi hunc frigidum in cœna, & para mihi in horto:nam habiturus sum conuiuas aliquot. Cum igitur in cœna alios pauones calentes uidisset appositos, frigidum pauonem, quem iusserat reseruari, non iudisset, uehementer excandescens, atrocissimam in Deum euomuit[?] blasphemiam.
units.tr: When at lunch he saw a peacock, which he had not touched, he said: "Keep this cold one for me for supper, and prepare it for me in the garden, for I am going to have some guests." So when at supper he saw other hot peacocks set before him, and did not find the cold peacock he had ordered kept back, he flew into a violent rage and vomited out the most atrocious blasphemy against God.

units.la: Tunc ex Cardinalibus quisdam qui accubebat: Ne tantopere commoueatur, inquit, Sanctitas vestra pro re tantilla. Tum Iulius: Si uoluit Deus usq; adeo propter unum pomum irasci, ut eiecerit primos parentes ex paradiso:cur non liceat mihi, qui sum eius vicarius, irasci propter pauonem, cum multo maior res sit pauo quam pomum?
units.tr: Then one of the cardinals who was reclining beside him said, "Let your Holiness not be so greatly moved over such a trifle." Then Julius: "If God was willing to be angry to such a degree over one apple that he drove our first parents out of paradise, why should it not be permitted to me, who am his vicar, to be angry over a peacock, since a peacock is a much greater matter than an apple?"

units.la: Creaturus Cardinalem Petrum Betanum episcopum Fanensem, ordinis Prædicatorum, aliquot è Cardinalibus resistebant, atq; id potissimū objiciebant, Episcopum illū inficitum[?] esse Lutheri hæresi. Tum Iulius: Sit ita sane, an non consultius fuerit imposito Cardinalitio galero eū mundare ab ea maculā, cula, & nobiscum tali vinculo retinere, quàm fine re ut fugiens à nobis coniungat se hostibus quos in Germania habemus, sicuti Vergerius fecit?[?]
units.tr: When he was about to create Pietro Betano, bishop of Fano, of the Order of Preachers, Cardinal, several of the cardinals resisted, and objected above all that this bishop was tainted with Luther's heresy. Then Julius said: "So be it. But would it not be more sensible, after placing the cardinal's galero upon him, to cleanse him of that stain, and keep him with us by such a bond, than to let him flee from us and join himself to the enemies we have in Germany, as Vergerius did?"

units.la: Inter reliquas Epitaphia hoc de eo scriptum circumferebatur:
units.tr: Among the other epitaphs, the following one written about him was circulating:

units.la: O. MARAE A MONTE, FORTE-FORTUNA PAPATUM, QUEM NEQ. IPSE QUIDEM SPERARE UNQUAM AUSUS FUIT, IN MAXIMA CARDINALIUM DISCORDIA CONSECUTO, QUOD SEX ANNIS PLUS CHRISTIANI SANGUINI FUDERIT QUAM ALIUS UNQUAM ANTICHRISTUS:
units.tr: O Mara a Monte, who by lucky chance attained the papacy, which he himself never dared to hope for, in the greatest discord of the cardinals, because in six years he shed more Christian blood than any other Antichrist ever did:

units.la: Fex sacrificulorum, grex Episcoporum, armentum Cardinalium, gratitudinis ergo monumentum æternum pos.
units.tr: Dregs of priests, herd of bishops, cattle of cardinals, set up as an eternal monument of gratitude.
168. Marcellus the Second.

units.la: MArcellus secundus, natione Hetruscus, Marcellus Ceruinus ante Papatum dictus, patriam habuit Montem Politianum in agro Florentino: episcopus primum Nicastrensis erat, postea Cardinalis tituli S. crucis in Hierusalem, ac tandem omnium Cardinalium in conclavi existentium consensu Pontifex creatus. Qui nono die Aprilis anni praedicti, nomen prius in baptismo susceptum mutare noluit, Mar tellus[?] secundus appellari voluit: & postridie in basilica Lateranensi papalis muneris insignia papaliter suscepit. Cum Cæsar Carolus ac Ferdinandus rex frater, semel urgerent expeditionem fieri in Turcas, scriptis respondebat Ceruinus, eam in Lutheranos potius adornari debere, hosque multo deteriores esse (culinis[?] eorum aduersabantur) omnibus Turcis. Sed id ante Papatum fecit. In ipso vero Papatu amarissimo zelo aduersus puriorem doctrinam fuit, & in retinendis superstitionibus pertinacissimus. Verum, cum multo ante cœpisset ictero laborare: invalescente tunc eo morbo, 23 post electionem die & prima Maij, mortem obiit: Papistæ apud Anglos etiam cum suo Polo, eius uale lugubriter celebrantibus. Fama quidem erat, veneno sublatum, sed eiusmodi nihil fuit, solent enim hi patres, eos libentius in Pontifices creare, quos spe-rant non diu victuros.
units.tr: Marcellus the Second, a Tuscan by birth, who before the papacy was called Marcellus Cervinus, had his homeland at Montepulciano in the Florentine territory. He was first bishop of Nicastro, then cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and finally was created pontiff by the consent of all the cardinals in conclave. On the ninth day of April of that year he refused to change the name he had received at baptism, but wished to be called Marcellus the Second; and the next day, in the Lateran basilica, he received the insignia of the papal office in papal fashion. When Emperor Charles and King Ferdinand his brother repeatedly urged that an expedition be made against the Turks, Cervinus replied in writing that the campaign ought rather to be directed against the Lutherans, and that these were far worse than all the Turks; (they opposed his culinary tastes). But he did this before he was pope. In the papacy itself he showed the bitterest zeal against purer doctrine, and was most stubborn in retaining superstitions. Yet, since he had begun to suffer from jaundice long before, and that disease then grew severe, he died on the 23rd day after his election, on the first of May. The Papists among the English, together with their Pole, celebrated his passing with mournful rites. There was indeed a rumour that he had been removed by poison, but nothing of the kind was the case; for these fathers are wont to create those as popes more willingly whom they hope will not live long.
THEODORICUS GRESMUNDUS, on the wantonness of Rome.

units.la: Roma caput scelerum, niuei iactura pudoris, Exitium fidei, luxuriaque parens. Sola Venus dispensat opes, dispensat honores, Sola facit serua quicquid in urbe libet.
units.tr: Rome, head of crimes, loss of snowy modesty, / ruin of faith, and parent of luxury. / Venus alone dispenses wealth, Venus alone dispenses honours, / and alone makes slaves of whatever pleases in the city.

units.la: Extollit, magnosque facit sapientia turpis: Sit procul, in tenero cui sedet ore decor.
units.tr: Base wisdom raises men and makes them great; far from it be that beauty which sits upon a tender face.

units.la: Tartara sunt molli potius adeunda juventæ: Si non est alius, sit tibi barba comes.
units.tr: Rather must the underworld be entered by soft youth; if there is no other companion, let a beard be your companion.

units.la: Marcellus Ceruinus patriam habuit Montem Pulcianum in agro Florentino, cum in humaniori-bus literis nonnihil profecisset, cœpit ludi magistri agere, deinde cum Paulus tertius Alexandrum Far-nesium puerum duodecim annorum nepote ex Pe-tro Aloysio filio notho Cardinalem creasset, huic Marcellum Ceruinum pædagogum dedit, non multo post Alexandrum Cardinalis, reliquis literarum studijs, totum se dedit negocijs tractandis: quæ in re opera Marcelli, utpote Secretarij, tum ipse, tum Paulus tertius utebatur. Cum Episcopatus Nica-stri tunc vacasset, eius ecclesiæ Episcopus creatus fuit: in aula tamen vivebat, neque unquam ad Eccle-siam suam accessit. Destinauit Paulus tertius eundem Cardinalem Farnesium ad Cæsarem, & Ferdinandum, qui ambo erant in Belgico, legatum. Cum vero adhuc puer esset, adiunxit illi Ceruinum Epi-scopum, qui omnia legationis consilia moderare-tur, id tunc agebatur in primis, ut contra Turcas expeditio fieret: quod Cæsar & Ferdinandus valde urgebant. At Ceruinus scriptum, quod extat, tunc edidit, quo diceret expeditione in Lutheranos potius adornari debere: hosq; multo deteriores esse omnibus Turcis. Paulus eum absentem Cardinalis creauit, ac non multo post cum ad urbem reuocas-set, eius consiliis in omnibus grauioribus rebus utebatur. dedit titulum Sanctæ crucis in Hierusalem, creauit etiam generalem hæreticæ prauitatis (ut appellant) inquisitorem, collegam nimirum Cardinalis Theatini, & Cardinalis Burgensis, quibusdam[?] licet nihil unquam fuit durius & crudelius. Cum ad concilium Tridentinum mittenda fuisset legatio, Paulus cum Cardinali de Monte et Cardinali Polo ter-tium legatum addidit, primum quidem horum, legatum concilij creauit, utpote iureconsultum: Polum, utpote cum qui cupere videbatur reformationem Ecclesiæ: (quanquam postea apparuerit, ea-am nunquam ex animo cupiuisse) Ceruinum uero, utpote eū cui Papa magis sideret, quare huic præcipue mandauerat, ne quid pateretur in concilio di-ci quod aliquo modo contra Romanæ sedis maiesta-tem tenderet, uerum exturbaret potius omnes eos qui aliquid huiusmodi conarentur. Hanc ob causam cum Iacobus Nachiantes, Clodiæ fuisse Episcopus, dixisset, se non posse probare decretum, in quo scri-ptum erat, Traditiones pari pietatis affectu & reuerentia suscipi atq; asseruari debere, quo scrip-tum Euangelium: Ceruinus fuit autor, ut is è conci-lio pellaretur. Cum etiam quidam ordinis S. Do-minici, cui nomen Dominicus Vilhelmus Venetus, in concilio dixisset, Constantiense concilium fuisse supra Papam: hunc ad se vocatum, Cervinus gra-uissime obiurgauit, cumque monachus respondisset, rem ipsam testari, illud concilium fuisse supra Pa-pam(nam cum exautorauit) tunc Cervinus: Non est ita, inquit: imò Papa tunc spōte cessit, addebat-que, se posse id bulla plumbata testari, atq; hunc quoq; iussit confestim è cō-cilio abire. Sub idem tem-pus venerat è Mantua Tridentum P. Paulus Ver-gerius, episcopus Iustinopolitanus, qui aliquot le-gationibus functus fuerat pro sede Romana in Ger-mania: cum uero tantum suspectus esset, ne aliqui-bus in rebus cum Lutheranis consentiret, eum ta-men reliqui duo Cardinales Legati, nec non Car-dinales Polus & Monte, & cum his Tridentinus & Pacieus voluissent ferre, ne scilicet proderent concilium non esse liberum, si Vergerium in Ger-mania notissimum reiecissent: Cervinus nunquam de stitit, donec illum eiectum uidisset. Multi ex Episcopis cum intelligerent agi de Vergerio è concilio extur-bando, constituerant ad Pontificem ea de re scribe-re, ac monere ne id fieri pateretur: quòd multi ef-sent dicturi, nō esse liberum concilii, ex quo episcopi eiicerētur: Hieronymus Vida Cremonensis, Albae epi-scopus, uir eloquentiss. literas suo & reliquorum epi-scoporum nomine iam dictauerat, id postquā resciuit Marcellus, Vidam grauissimis verbis monuit, ut à mittendis ad pontificem literis omnino abstineret. mali enim exempli rem esse, ut Episcopi in concilio congregati, ad Pontificem tales literas scribāt, quasi velint illi legem dare, quod usq; adeò magnū flagitium esset, ut etiam à suspicione cauendum sit. qua oratione victus Vida cum aliis Episcopis, de mittendis literis consilium mutauit. Discessurus i-taq; è concilio Vergerius, cum Cerumum [?] accessisset, interrogassetq; ob quos potissimum articulos eum è cœtu reliquorum Episcoporum vellet eiecti: tunc Cerumus, Quia audiui te sanctorum, Georgij & Christophori legēdas negasse esse veras. At Vergerius, ita est, negaui, inquit: atq; adhuc nego: sed Pauli Papæ tertij autoritate fretus. cum enim utriusq; legendam iussisset tolli è Breuiario, narrat in ea præfatione quæ initio eius libri adscripta est, se iussisse tolli legendas non veras. Cerumus deprehensus, respondit non esse pro bonis viris habendos eos, qui vel unico nutu cum Lutheranis consentire videntur. abi igitur è nostro concilio.
