Hæc ideo referenda putaui, ut appareat cum amarissimo zelo aduersus puriorem doctrinam semper fuisse, sacrarum literarum omnino rudem, atq; in omnibus superstitionibus retinendis pertinacissimum. Cum tamen esset moderatione quadam atq; innocentiā uitæ [?] vitæ non vulgari, prudentia etiam non mediocri, magno in precio atq; existimatione habebatur, ita ut si ad Papatum eum peruenire contingeret, spes esset illum multa in curia Romana correcturum, in primis omnem luxum fugiturum. Atq; ita con-tigit. Mortuo enim Iulio tertio in Papa electus est Cervinus. Verum cum multo ante coepisset labora-re ictericia, tunc invalescente eo morbo 23. post e-lectionem die mortem obiit. Fama quidem erat ve-veno sublatum, sed nihil fiat eiusmodi. Paucis ante mortem diebus voluit coronari: sed modesto admo-dum sumptu. Cardinalis Fernesius cum suis in hūc consenserat, licet graves cum eo aliquandiu simul-tates exercuisset: quia neminem sperauit, quod Pau-lus tertius instituisset facere diligentius quàm hunc promoturum. In primis autem omni studio tutatu-rum Fernesiorum familiam, ne à Parma atq; Pla-centiæ ducatu excideret, nam hoc etiam ut polli-ceretur Iulius tertius exegit Cardinalis Fernesius, antequam vellet ei, ut in Papam euaderet, adiu-mento esse. Non defuerunt qui dixerint, Cervinũ ideo multos Cardinales voluisse Papa creare, quia viderent eum ita confectum aduersa valetudine, ut de vita diuturna nulla spes esset. sic enim solent, ea-os libentius creare, quos sperant minus esse vitiu-ros.
units.tr: Marcellus Cervinus had his homeland at Montepulciano in the Florentine territory. After he had made some progress in the humane letters, he began to act as a schoolmaster; then, when Paul the Third created the twelve-year-old Alexander Farnese, the grandson of his illegitimate son Pietro Luigi, a cardinal, he assigned Marcellus Cervinus to him as tutor. Not long after, the cardinal Alexander, having set aside his other literary studies, devoted himself wholly to the conduct of business; in this matter Paul the Third used the services of Marcellus, as secretary, and himself as well. When the bishopric of Nicastro was then vacant, Cervinus was created its bishop, yet he lived at court and never went to his church. Paul the Third sent the same Cardinal Farnese as legate to Charles and Ferdinand, who were both in the Netherlands. Since the cardinal was still a boy, he attached Cervinus to him as bishop, to direct all the counsels of the embassy. At that time the chief business was that an expedition be made against the Turks, which Charles and Ferdinand urged strongly. But Cervinus then published a written work, which survives, in which he said that the campaign ought rather to be directed against the Lutherans, and that these were far worse than all the Turks. Paul created him cardinal while he was absent, and not long after, when he had recalled him to the city, used his counsels in all weightier matters. He gave him the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and also created him inquisitor-general of heretical depravity (as they call it), as colleague of Cardinal Theatino and Cardinal Burgensis; yet nothing was ever harsher and more cruel than this. When a legation was to be sent to the Council of Trent, Paul added as third legate, along with Cardinal del Monte and Cardinal Pole, the Cardinal Cervinus. Of these, he made the first, del Monte, legate of the council, as a jurist; Pole, as one who seemed to desire a reformation of the Church (although it later appeared that he had never desired it from the heart); and Cervinus, as one in whom the Pope had more confidence, for which reason he had charged him especially that nothing be allowed to be said in the council that tended in any way against the majesty of the Roman see, but rather that he should drive out all who attempted anything of the kind. For this reason, when Jacobus Nachianus, bishop of Chioggia, said that he could not approve the decree in which it was written that traditions are to be received and preserved with the same affection of piety and reverence as the written Gospel, Cervinus was the author of his being expelled from the council. Likewise, when a certain man of the Order of St Dominic, named Dominicus Vilhelmus of Venice, said in the council that the Council of Constance was above the Pope, Cervinus summoned him and rebuked him most severely; and when the monk replied that the matter itself bore witness, that that council was above the Pope (for it deposed him), Cervinus said: "It is not so; rather the Pope then resigned of his own accord," adding that he could prove this by a leaden bull; and he ordered this man too to leave the council at once. About the same time, Paul Vergerius, bishop of Capodistria, had come to Trent from Mantua; he had performed several embassies for the Roman see in Germany. But since he was suspected of agreeing with the Lutherans on certain points, the two other cardinal legates, and also Cardinals Pole and del Monte, together with Tridentinus and Pacieus, wished to support him, lest they betray that the council was not free if they rejected Vergerius, who was very well known in Germany. Cervinus never gave way until he saw him thrown out. When many of the bishops understood that Vergerius was to be driven out of the council, they resolved to write to the Pontiff about this matter and to warn him not to allow it, since many would say that the council was not free if bishops were expelled from it. Hieronymus Vida of Cremona, bishop of Alba, a most eloquent man, had already drafted a letter in his own name and that of the other bishops; when Marcellus learned of this, he warned Vida in the gravest terms to abstain altogether from sending letters to the pontiff. It was a bad example, he said, for bishops gathered in council to write such letters to the Pontiff, as if they wished to give him laws; this was such a disgrace that it must be guarded against even as a suspicion. Vida, won over by this speech, changed his mind, along with the other bishops, about sending letters. So Vergerius, about to leave the council, approached Cervinus and asked on account of which articles in particular he wished him to be removed from the company of the other bishops. Then Cervinus said: "Because I have heard that you have said the legends of the saints George and Christopher are not true." But Vergerius said: "That is so; I did deny it, and I still deny it, but relying on the authority of Pope Paul the Third. For when he ordered both legends removed from the Breviary, he states in the preface, which is prefixed at the beginning of his book, that he ordered the untrue legends to be removed." Cervinus, caught out, replied that those who seem to agree with the Lutherans even by a single nod are not to be counted as good men; "Go away, then, from our council." I have thought these things worth reporting, so that it may appear that he always had the bitterest zeal against purer doctrine, was utterly ignorant of the sacred letters, and was most stubborn in retaining all superstitions. Yet he had a certain moderation and an uncommon innocence of life, and a considerable prudence too, and he was held in great esteem and reputation; so that if he should come to the papacy, there was hope that he would correct many things in the Roman curia, and above all would flee all luxury. And so it turned out. For after Julius the Third's death, Cervinus was elected pope. But since he had begun to suffer from jaundice long before, and that disease then grew severe, he died on the 23rd day after his election. There was indeed a rumour that he had been removed by poison, but nothing of the kind happened. A few days before his death he wished to be crowned, but with a very modest outlay. Cardinal Farnese had agreed with the others to this, although he had for some time carried on bitter quarrels with him, because he hoped that no one would promote the family of the Farnese more diligently than this man, whom Paul the Third had appointed to do so. And above all he expected that he would guard with every effort the Farnese family, lest they fall from the duchy of Parma and Piacenza; for Cardinal Farnese also demanded this of Julius the Third, before he was willing to be of help to him in becoming pope. There were not lacking those who said that Cervinus had wished to create many cardinals as pope because they saw him so worn out by ill health that there was no hope of a long life. For these fathers are wont to create more willingly those whom they hope will be less able to do harm.
169. Paul IV.

units.la: PAulus quartus, patria Neapolitanus, Ioannes Petrus Carapha antea uocatus,eodem anno Domini 1555. & uicesimotertio die Maij, à Cardinalibus concorditer electus, & per omnes caeremonias exaltatus, illam coccineam bestiae sedem, in omni tyrannide nunc occupat. Nouam iste Venetijs olim in sua hypocrisi, rasorum[?] sacrificulorum sedâ[?] instituit, quos sanctissimo nomine Iesuitas appellauit: ac si Iesus seruator ipse idolatricos Papicolas, praeter Euangelium, & in superstitione genuisset. Theatinus Cardinalis postea factus, aliis rebus studuit[?], nempe fortunis adaugendis. De emendenda ecclesia libellum ante Papatum edidit: sed nunc in ipso constitutus Papatu, nec Iesum, nec ecclesiam curat. Iam totus arma meditatur, belli quam pacis amantior. Curet quae Christi sunt Petrus: Paulus hic interim,uel potius Saulus, spirans minarum ac caedis,quae sua sunt,non sine multorum sanguine,quaerit: & lupos uoracissimos immani tyrannide per omnem Europam in Dei grege saeuire sinit, quasi lupus & ille fit, non parcens gregi: Act. 20.
units.tr: Paul IV, a Neapolitan by birth, previously called Giovanni Pietro Carafa, was chosen unanimously by the cardinals in the same year of the Lord 1555, on the twenty-third day of May, and was exalted with all ceremonies. He now occupies that scarlet seat of the beast in all tyranny. In his hypocrisy he once founded at Venice a new order of shaven priests, whom he called by the most holy name of Jesuits, as if Jesus the Saviour himself had begotten idolatrous Papists beyond the Gospel and within superstition. Later made a Theatine cardinal, he devoted himself to other things, namely to increasing his fortunes. Before his papacy he published a little book on the emending of the Church, but now that he is set in the papacy itself, he cares neither for Jesus nor for the Church. Now he plans entirely for arms, more fond of war than of peace. Let Peter attend to the things of Christ; meanwhile this Paul, or rather Saul, breathing threats and slaughter, seeks what is his own, not without the blood of many, and allows the most voracious wolves to rage with monstrous tyranny throughout all Europe in God's flock, as if he too were a wolf, not sparing the flock: Acts 20.

units.la: Exurge ergo tu Domine Deus noster, exurge in quam, & uindica sanguinem seruorum tuorum fidelium, qui in Anglia, & in aliis terris abfq; omni commiseratione humana effusus est, ob sanctissimi nominis tui confessionem. Confunde sceleratissimum Papam, tuæ veritatis aduersarium: & mitte in stagnum sulphureum, ad eiusdem tui nominis gloriam, Amen.
units.tr: Arise therefore, O Lord our God, arise and avenge the blood of your faithful servants, which in England and in other lands was poured out without any human pity, for the confession of your most holy name. Overthrow the most wicked Pope, the adversary of your truth, and cast him into the lake of brimstone, to the glory of that same name of yours. Amen.

units.la: IN TYRANNIDEM QVORVNDAM aduersus pios. C. B.
units.tr: ON A CERTAIN TYRANT, against the pious. C. B.

units.la: Vt pia conspiciens cædi sua pignora mater, Ingemit, & querulos mittit ab ore sonos: Sic pater è cœlo collustrans undique terras, Morte suos plecti vidit, & ingemuit.
units.tr: As a loving mother, seeing her children slaughtered, groans and sends forth mournful cries from her mouth, so the Father, looking down from heaven on the lands on every side, saw his own people punished with death, and groaned.

units.la: An nō(mortales) nostri sat sanguinis haustum est? Nec vestra in natos definit ira meos? Quid meruere, sui servant si iussa parentis? Et pedibus nolunt nomina nostra teri?
units.tr: Has not enough of our blood been drunk, O mortals? Does your wrath against my sons never end? What have they deserved, if they keep their parent's commands? Do they refuse that our names be trampled underfoot?

units.la: Dico equidem, vobis per me licet esse tyrannis, Infamiæ meos perdere morte licet.
units.tr: I indeed say that through me you are permitted to be tyrants; it is permitted you to destroy my sons by death for the sake of disgrace.

units.la: Sed tamen in pœnam quamvis sim tardior, ultrix Sumet nostra mali dextera supplicium.
units.tr: Yet although I am slow to punish, my avenging right hand will exact the penalty for the evil done to us.

units.la: Quid postremò mihi dicendum fuerit, ut hu-iuscemodi pontificum Catalogo finem imponam? nisi id tantummodo, quod invenerim apud Hiero-nymum Marium in Eusebio captivo: Nempe quòd cum hi, de quibus sermonem habuimus, tam horrenda scelera committere non erubuerint: nec qui post hac infœlix istud Pontificium regnum occupaturi sunt, meliores futuri expectentur: atrociora enim designare non erubescent. Nam quemadmodum Christus temporis processu, sapientia & gratia crescebat apud Deum & homines: sic Antichristus in dies deteriora ac maiora scelera in Deum & eius Ecclesiam molietur. Hac nimirum ratione futurum est, ut tandem ab omnibus homo peccati ac filius perditionis agnoscatur, ut sicut Christus ipse, ex eius operibus agnitus est filius Dei, sic Antichristus, ex eius sceleribus, Diaboli filius comprobetur. Sed nunc ad narrationis scopum reuertor, Nā ex his quae à me de pontificibus narrata sunt, omnibus conicere licet, Papam(ut iactitat) petram non esse, nec ecclesiae fundamentum, contra quod inferorum portae non praualeant. Cum huiuscemo-di homines uideamus repletos nequitiis, periurijs, homicidijs, latrocinijs, superbia & ambitione afluantes, fornicationibus atq; adulteriis conspurcatos, sedifragos, fide, misericordia ac iustitia exu-tos. Hæc Marius.
units.tr: What, finally, should I add to bring an end to this catalogue of popes of such a kind? Only this, which I found in Hieronymus Marius in Eusebius captivus: namely, that since those of whom we have spoken did not blush to commit such horrible crimes, neither should those who will hereafter unhappily occupy that Papal kingdom be expected to be better, for they do not blush to devise even more atrocious things. For just as Christ grew in wisdom and grace with God and men as time went on, so Antichrist will devise worse and greater crimes against God and his Church day by day. In this way it will at last come about that he is recognised by all as the man of sin and son of perdition, so that just as Christ himself was recognised from his works as the Son of God, so Antichrist, from his crimes, will be proved to be the son of the Devil. But now I return to the aim of my narrative. For from what I have related about the popes, everyone may conclude that the Pope, as he boasts, is not the rock nor the foundation of the Church, against which the gates of hell do not prevail. For we see such men filled with wickedness, perjuries, murders and robberies, abounding in pride and ambition, defiled by fornications and adulteries, breakers of faith, stripped of mercy and justice. Thus Marius.

units.la: Ex Cælij Secundi ac Vergerij scriptis, Paulus quartus, Romanus pontifex, patria Neapolitanus, & Ioannes Petrus Carapha, atq; Cardinalis Theatinus ante initum pontificatum nominatus, magno Cardinalium consensu, Gallorum regi Henrico gratificari studentium, Marcello secundo, paucorum dierum Papa post Iulium, in Maio, ut aiunt, suba[?] substituebatur. Hunc Cælius prædictus refert, no-uam presbyterorum sectam, in hypocrisi ac fucata sanctitate fundatam, sub Iesuitarum appellatione Venetiis instituisse. Quam sectam, inquit, po-st deseruit, quum quod venabatur accepisset. Nam proiecerat rete, quum episcopatu primum se abdicasset, ut Cardinalis captaret præda. Quod ubi contigit, Venetiis decedens, interrogantibus presbyteris, quo nam abiret? respondit: Quo ego vado, vos non potestis venire. per illud intelliges, se illos in paupertate & sordibus relinquere: se au-tem Romam ad amplissimam dignitatem, tanquam in alterum cælum ascendere: quo ipsi votis & cæ-remoniis claustralibus astricti, venire nequirent. Sic novit sanctulus homo Christi verbis suis accom-modare desideriis, & Scripturas sanctas ad suum pertrahere sensum. Multa de hoc Theatino sunt narrata, ut quod purgatorium fortiter defenderit, quarundam mentium secreta noverit, ac mirabilia multa, sed non solum fecerit. Ad Paulum tertium, ut Vergerius noster habet, de emendanda Ecclesia libellum ipse dedit, tametsi nulla ex parte prorsus illam emendaverit. In quo qui legit, inquit, omnia fere capita illum confirmasse cognoscet, quæ soliti sunt in Papistis reprehendere: nempe, ecclesiam apud eos ita collapsam esse, ut iam non Christi, sed dia-
units.tr: From the writings of Celio Secundo and Vergerius: Paul IV, Roman pontiff, a Neapolitan by birth, was named, before he took up the papacy, Giovanni Pietro Carafa, the Theatine cardinal. With the great consent of the cardinals, who were eager to gratify Henry, king of the French, he was put forward in May, as they say, to succeed Marcellus II, who had been pope for only a few days after Julius. Celio, mentioned above, reports that he founded at Venice a new sect of priests, established in hypocrisy and feigned holiness, under the name of Jesuits. This sect, he says, he afterwards deserted when he had obtained what he was hunting for. For he had cast his net when he first resigned his bishopric, so that he might catch the prey of a cardinalate. When this happened, as he was leaving Venice, and the priests asked where he was going, he replied: Where I am going, you cannot come. By this you will understand that he was leaving them in poverty and squalor, while he himself was ascending to Rome to the most exalted dignity, as if to another heaven, whither they, bound by vows and cloistral rites, could not come. Thus this holy fellow knew how to fit the words of Christ to his desires and to draw the holy Scriptures to his own meaning. Many things have been told about this Theatine: that he strongly defended purgatory, knew the secrets of certain minds, and did many marvellous things, though not only such things. To Paul III, as our Vergerius records, he himself gave a little book on the emending of the Church, although in no respect at all did he emend it. Whoever reads it, he says, will find that it confirms nearly all the faults which people are accustomed to censure in the Papists: namely, that the Church among them has so fallen into ruin that it is no longer the Church of Christ but of the devil.

units.la: f[?] diaboli ecclesia fit. Papæ enim, dicit, ad sua defi-deria coacervare sibi magistros auribus prurien-tes: per Cardinales & episcopos Christi nomen in-tergentes blasphemari, clavium potestate emungi pecunias, improbos ordinari, Simoniacas nundina-tiones exerceri, ambitione & avaritia effuare pra-latos, in monasteriis horrida fieri flagitia, Romam repleri impudicissimis scortis, atque his similia plu-ra.
units.tr: For the Popes, he says, gather to themselves teachers who tickle their ears for their own desires; through cardinals and bishops the name of Christ is mangled and blasphemed; money is wrung out by the power of the keys; wicked men are ordained; simoniacal bargains are carried on; prelates are driven wild by ambition and avarice; horrible shameful deeds are done in monasteries; Rome is filled with the most shameless harlots; and many more things like these.

units.la: Multo adhuc plura graviora quoque Romae agitur, præter ea quae Theatinus in eo attigit libello. At-tigit enim vitia tantum & abusus, qui in vita communi occurrere solent, nulla prorsus facta mentione doctrinæ quæ illic colitur, quæ Christi Evangelio tam quā ex diametro pugnat. Neque tyrannides eorum plus quam Neronicas in medium attulit, quibus aper-te saeviunt carceribus, laqueis, igne, ferro, exilio, re-mis & aquis: eos persequentes per Italiam, Galliam, Hispaniam, & Angliam, qui spiritu Dei acti, horren-das eorum contaminationes ac religionis Christia-nae profanationes ferre non possint. His addo, quae Guilhelmus Vuittyngamus docte & vere de Anglia scribit in præfatione super D. Ridlei af-fertione contra transsubstantiationis haeresim. Ex-tincta, inquit, Evangelij luce in Angliā, bonarumq[?] libertate repressa, horridae quaedam Papisticæ[?] hæreseos tenebræ, ac morum quasi uastitas quædam, imperiū nunc occupant. Postea sequitur: Nam trucidatis & abactis prophetis suis, gregisque pastoribus, monachos, fraterculos, uestales, sacrificos, Satanæ professio calones ac emissarios, quos ueris nominibus (ex Scripturis ipsis) leones, ursos, lupos, hircos, canes, porcos, apros dixerit, ouili Iesu Christi ac vineæ Dei regina præfecit. Qui ut suam ingluviem satietate expleant, in cuius possessiones atque fortunas non impudentissimos oculos spe & mente defixerunt? quot Christianorum non tantum facultates sorpserunt, sed & sanguinem quoque biberunt? Adeo teterrimi Antichristi venenum nunc grassatur, ut vel in longinquas ac maximo interuallo dissitas regiones, cantharidas suas & basiliscos diffundant: qui ut æstro & aculeo, sic halitu ipso atque conspectu, Dei filios interimant. Nihil bisce hominibus perditius aut perfidium, nihilque his temporibus perniciosius. Tanta enim crudelitas ipsorum animos peruasit, quantam ex vetere memoria, & annalium monumentis, numquam inter se hominibus fuisse constat. Fœminis quidem ac viris perinde aduersantur: in senes ac pueros, in decrepitos & adolescentes, ex æquo ceuitum est: nec sexui denique nec ætati parcitur. Carceres ad unum opplentur: nec in cruces tantum aguntur, sed & palos deligantur infinita Christianorum corpora. Quibus porro in loci, regnante Eduardo sanctissimo, Evangelica vox sonabat: in iisdem iam omnia, idololatriam, super- stitiones, incendia, foeces, caedes spirant & exhalant. Incredibile fortasse videbor dicere: sed quod verissimum esse, & litera multorum, & optimites comprobant. Duobus nempe plus minus an-nis, hominum capita supra octingenta, omnibus crudelissimae mortis generibus, verae religionis cau-sa, fuisse dedita. Uno item die, cruces magna co-pia Londini ad civium contumeliam defixas, simi-lias numerosas, splendidas ac nobiles, e praediis ac possessionibus suis deturbatas. O magnum atq; in-tolerandum dolorem: o spectaculum miserum atq; acerbum. Utq; haec tyrannis morte ulterius pro-gredi videatur, exilium luctuosissimum adiectum est. Cuius rei, praeter Italiam & Galliam, etiam Germaniam totam & Sabaudiam, quae miseros & eiectos homines, una cum liberis suis & uxori-bus, urbibus & domicilijs exceperunt, testes offer-re possem. Huius autem calamitatis flabellum, Ste-phanum quendam Gardinerum, episcopum (licet falso) Vuintoniensem cognominatum constitue-runt. Tantum ille. Et crudelissima Antichristi Rom. carnificina, seu inquisitio, ut vocant, hære-tici tice prauitatis (Vergerio teste, qui optime nouit) mix triginta annorum spacio, centum quinquaginta Christianorum millia, diuersis afflictationum generibus consumpsit, neq; adhuc definit. Exurgat ergo Deus, & dissipentur inimici eius, atq; ut fumus deficit, & illi deficiant, ac statim pereant à facie illius. Exurgat inquam, ac sanctorum suorum sanguinem vindicet, qui pro confessione sui sancti nominis & doctrinæ, crudeliter est effusus.
units.tr: Much more, and things still graver, are done at Rome beyond what the Theatine touched on in that little book. For he touched only on the vices and abuses which usually occur in ordinary life, making no mention at all of the doctrine cultivated there, which fights against the Gospel of Christ as directly as possible. Nor did he bring forward their tyrannies, more than Neronian, with which they openly rage with prisons, nooses, fire, sword, exile, oars and waters, persecuting through Italy, France, Spain and England those who, moved by the Spirit of God, cannot bear their horrible defilements and profanations of the Christian religion. To these I add what William Whittingham learnedly and truly writes about England in the preface to Dr Ridley's assertion against the heresy of transubstantiation. When the light of the Gospel, he says, was extinguished in England and good liberties were repressed, certain horrid shadows of Papistical heresy and a kind of devastation of morals now hold dominion. Afterwards he goes on: For, the prophets being slain and driven out, and the shepherds of the flock, the monks, friars, vestals, priests, professed servants and emissaries of Satan, whom he named by their true names (from the Scriptures themselves) lions, bears, wolves, goats, dogs, swine and boars, the queen has set over the fold of Jesus Christ and the vineyard of God. That they may satisfy their gluttony, into whose possessions and fortunes have they not fixed their shameless eyes in hope and mind? How many Christians have they not only swallowed up in their substance, but have also drunk their blood? So deadly is the poison of the most foul Antichrist now raging that they spread their cantharides and basilisks even into distant regions separated by the greatest intervals, who slay the sons of God by breath and sight as much as by sting and goad. Nothing is more ruinous or treacherous than these men, nothing more pernicious in these times. For such cruelty has seized their minds as is known never to have existed among men from ancient memory and the records of the annals. They are opposed alike to women and men: the attack is equal against old and young, decrepit and youths; neither sex nor age is spared at last. Prisons are filled to overflowing, and not only are infinite bodies of Christians driven to crosses, but stakes are set up as well. In those places where, under the most holy King Edward, the voice of the Gospel sounded, now all things breathe and exhale idolatry, superstitions, burnings, filth and slaughter. I may seem to say something incredible, but it is most true, as the letters of many and the best men confirm. For in about two years more or less, above eight hundred men's heads were given over to every kind of most cruel death for the cause of true religion. Likewise on one day a great number of crosses were set up at London to the shame of the citizens, and similarly numerous, splendid and noble men were thrown out of their estates and possessions. O great and intolerable grief! O wretched and bitter spectacle! And that this tyranny may seem to advance further than death, a most mournful exile was added. Of this I could offer witnesses: besides Italy and France, all Germany and Savoy too, which received the wretched and expelled men together with their children and wives, cities and homes. They appointed as the fan of this calamity a certain Stephen Gardiner, falsely called bishop of Winchester. Thus he. And the most cruel butchery of the Roman Antichrist, or inquisition as they call it, of heretical depravity (Vergerius being witness, who knows it best) has in the space of thirty years consumed a hundred and fifty thousand Christians with diverse kinds of afflictions, and it does not yet cease. Let God therefore arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and as smoke fails, so let them fail and perish at once from his face. Let him arise, I say, and avenge the blood of his saints, which was cruelly poured out for the confession of his holy name and doctrine.

units.la: Finiunt Acta Romanorum pontificum à dispersione discipulorum Christi, usq; ad obitum Pauli quarti: ex Ioannis Balei Su-douolgij Angli maiore Anglicorum scriptorum Catalogo desumpta.
units.tr: The Acts of the Roman Pontiffs from the dispersion of Christ's disciples are finished, down to the death of Paul IV. Taken from the larger catalogue of English writers by John Bale, an Englishman of Suffolk.

units.la: Haec praeter authoris voluntatem in quinto & sexto libro, variis in locis omissa, hoc loco post Operis huius finem poni placuit.
units.tr: These things, omitted in various places in the fifth and sixth books against the author's wishes, it has been decided to place here at the end of this work.

units.la: Post Prophetas in Ecclesia Iudæorum, sacerdotio regnante, sectæ originem acceperunt. Ita etiam fit in Ecclesia Christianorum. Nam post pios doctores, Antichristo regnante, sectæ mo-nachorum in ea sunt exortæ. Hæ regem sibi constituerunt[?] Abadonem, Apoc. 9. ut earum hypocri-sim defenderet. Cuius furoris confirmandi robora, ac propagandæ tyrannidis arma, post Lateranense concilium fuerunt, turgida Dominicanorū doctri-na, fucata Franciscanorū sanctitas, Carmelitanorum superstitiones, et Augustinianorū impostura, quæ suis locis habentur. Dominicani enim sub Christianæ prædicationis fuco, Franciscani sub nitæ E-vangelicæ fraude, Carmelitæ sub virgi-nitatis fallacia, Augustiniani sub dolo cœlestis doctrinæ, immo sub Christianæ paupertatis versutia, pro huius sui regis Abadonis regno propagando, omnes simul Sa-thanam induerunt. Ex prædicatione crucis contra Albigenses, Dominicani surgebant, qui statim commentarios ediderant super decreta Papistica. Franciscani sophistice disputandi rationem illis ad iunxerunt, addi is theologiae summis, atq; in Sententiis quaestionibus & glossis. Indeq; mox fiebant sacri Palatij magistri, haeretica pravitatis iudices, cardinales, metropolitae, ac legati apostolici. Interim Dominicus & Franciscus, pro pacti, at nunquam soluti (ut exitus probabat) caelibatus remedio, Sorores & Claritas instituerunt. Dominicus enim, teste Nicolao Triuetho, roma anno Domini 1217. domum Sororu fundauit. Doctores Canonici iuris, mathematicos, atque ingeniosos sophistas in ordinem suum admisit: quales fuerunt, Reginal-dus, Raymundus & Iordanes. Ex Francisci militi-bus, perpende Alexandrum Halesium, Guaronem, ac Scotum.
units.tr: After the prophets, sects arose in the Church of the Jews while the priesthood reigned. So too it happens in the Church of the Christians. For after the godly teachers, with Antichrist reigning, sects of monks arose within it. These set up for themselves a king, Abaddon (Rev. 9), to defend their hypocrisy. The strengths for confirming this madness and the weapons for spreading tyranny came after the Lateran Council: the bombastic doctrine of the Dominicans, the painted-over sanctity of the Franciscans, the superstitions of the Carmelites, and the imposture of the Augustinians, which are treated in their places. For the Dominicans, under the cloak of Christian preaching; the Franciscans, under the fraud of evangelical poverty; the Carmelites, under the deceit of virginity; and the Augustinians, under the trickery of heavenly doctrine, or rather of Christian poverty, all together put on Satan, to extend the kingdom of their king Abaddon. The Dominicans rose out of the preaching of the cross against the Albigenses, and at once they published commentaries on the Papistical decrees. The Franciscans added to these the method of disputing sophistically, joined to the highest parts of theology, in the Sentences, the questions and the glosses. And from there soon came the masters of the sacred palace, judges of heretical depravity, cardinals, metropolitans and apostolic legates. Meanwhile Dominic and Francis, as a remedy for a celibacy that was promised but never kept (as the outcome showed), established the Sisters and the Clares. For Dominic, according to Nicholas Trivet, founded a house of Sisters at Rome in the year of the Lord 1217. He admitted to his order teachers of canon law, mathematicians and clever sophists, such as Reginald, Raymund and Jordan. Among the soldiers of Francis, consider Alexander of Hales, Guaron and Scotus.

units.la: Ex Londinensi Chronico: Eo anno quo Dominicani fratres ex Italia in Angliam uenerunt, scilicet anno Domini 1224. multae pluuiae ac tonitrua fuerunt, & grandines ceciderunt instar lapidum quadrangularium, ad quorum quantitatem, quibus arbores, uineae ac segetes sunt destructae, atq; homines contriti. Aues etiam per aera uolantes, carbones ignitos in rostris deferre, ac domos incendere uidebantur. Mirabiles in Anglia (inquit Matthaeus Parisius) fuere tempestates & horrenda tonitrua, uentus furibundus & segetum suffocatio, quae aedificia diruerunt, ecclesias & arbores prostraverunt, ac naves submerserunt, &c.
units.tr: From the London Chronicle: In the year in which the Dominican friars came from Italy into England, namely in the year of the Lord 1224, there were many rains and thunderstorms, and hailstones fell like square stones, of such size that trees, vineyards and crops were destroyed and men crushed. Birds too, flying through the air, seemed to carry burning coals in their beaks and set houses on fire. Wonderful storms and dreadful thunder occurred in England (says Matthew Paris), a raging wind and the choking of crops, which threw down buildings, laid low churches and trees, and sank ships, etc.

units.la: In eodem Chronico: Eo anno quo Franciscani fratres ex Italia in Angliam venerunt, scilicet anno Domini 1226 superuenit ventus a Septentrione, quatiens domos & pomaria, nemora & turres ecclesiarum: visq;[?] sunt dracones ignei, & maligni spiritus in turbine volitare.
units.tr: In the same Chronicle: In the year in which the Franciscan friars came from Italy into England, namely in the year of the Lord 1226, a wind came from the north, shaking houses and orchards, groves and church towers; and fiery dragons and evil spirits were seen flying about in the whirlwind.

units.la: Ex eodem Chronico: Eo anno quo Carmelitae fratres ex Palestina venerunt, scilicet anno Domini 1240, magna lues animalium & hominum, maxima〈q;〉 inundatio imbrium fuit. Ex qua provenit tanta blad[i] caristia, quod quaternarium tritici pro quadraginta solidis vendebatur. Matthaeus Parisius: Transijt hic annus (inquit) regno Angliae inimicus, & toti ecclesiae adversarius, aridus per tres menses, pluvialis per reliquos. Bellua marinae eo anno pugnabant in Anglico littore, quod bellū designabat futurum inter regnum & sacerdotium.
units.tr: From the same Chronicle: In the year in which the Carmelite friars came from Palestine, namely in the year of the Lord 1240, there was a great plague of animals and men, and a very great flood of rain. From this came such a great dearth of grain that a quarter of wheat was sold for forty shillings. Matthew Paris: That year (he says) passed, hostile to the kingdom of England and adverse to the whole Church, dry for three months and rainy for the rest. That year sea monsters fought on the English shore, which signified a war to come between the kingdom and the priesthood.

units.la: Ex eodem Chronico: Eo anno, quo Augustiniani fratres ex Italia in Angliam venerunt, scilicet anno Domini 1252 incepit magna pestilentia Londini, & durauit per totum regnum, a festo Michaelis usq; ad festum D. Petri ad vincula, proxime futurum. Tartari eo anno Papisticam fidem per Dominicanos & Franciscanos suscepe-runt, ut Turcas ad Rom. ecclesiæ commodū opprimerent. Religio certè Tartarea est, ac Tartaris digna, quæ ex huiusmodi locustarū hypocrisi assurgit. At imperium Romanorū & Christianorū, penè per Antichristos deletū, ab horum laboribus auxilium non sentit, imò detrimentum maximū. Et ecce, pro amplianda religione ad Tartaros uadunt. Maledicti certè, atq; iniquissimum illusorum genus. Albertus Crantzius, His temporibus (inquit) imperiū Romanum miserè iactabatur, cum esset uenale, & sensatis principibus non ualde optabile, &c.
units.tr: From the same Chronicle: In the year in which the Augustinian friars came from Italy into England, namely in the year of the Lord 1252, a great pestilence began in London and lasted throughout the kingdom, from the feast of Michaelmas to the feast of St Peter ad Vincula next following. In that year the Tartars received the Papistical faith through the Dominicans and Franciscans, so that they might crush the Turks for the advantage of the Roman Church. The religion is certainly Tartarean, and fit for the Tartars, that rises out of such a hypocrisy of locusts. Yet the empire of the Romans and Christians, almost destroyed by the Antichrists, feels no help from their labours, but rather the greatest harm. And behold, they go to the Tartars to enlarge their religion. Surely a cursed and most unjust breed of deceivers. Albert Krantz: In these times (he says) the Roman empire was miserably tossed about, when it was for sale, and not very desirable to the sensible princes, etc.

units.la: Ioannes Palæonydorus in fasciculo tripertito, Anno Domini 1245. Innocentius quartus sub Papa li protectione Carmelitas suscepit per bullam. Ioannes Maria, Polutianus, in Mari magno, Anno Domini 1245. Eremitæ montis Carmeli, mendicitatem primo in Europa post Dominicanos & Minoritas profitebantur. Inde permissi sunt prædicare, & confessiones audire.
units.tr: John Palaeonydorus, in his tripartite bundle: In the year of the Lord 1245, Pope Innocent IV, under papal protection, received the Carmelites by a bull. John Maria Pollutianus, in Mari magno, in the year of the Lord 1245: the hermits of Mount Carmel first professed mendicancy in Europe, after the Dominicans and the Minorites. Thence they were permitted to preach and to hear confessions.

units.la: Nam multi ex eis tunc erant in theologiæ facultate instructi. Sed uix unum in quolibet cœnobio, ubi tamen multi fratres erant, sacerdotem habebant, tam rari apud illos fuere tunc sacrifici. Ex bullis præfati Innocentij hæc sunt desumpta. Guilhelmus de S. Amore, in Defensorio ecclesiæ, lib. 2, Postquam fundati efsent Prædicatores & Minores, in mendicitate ociosa, finxerunt Carmelitæ, Mariam Christi matrem mendicasse: atq; Augustini fratres, Paulum primum Eremitam idem fecisse. Hæc ille. Sub prædicationis & confessionis audiendæ colore, mendicantes fratres, pro Antichristi regno exaltando, mirabilia multa his diebus ubiq; per mundum saciebant. Et ut cum aliis eadem fruerentur ex illis officijs dulcedine lucri, quidam ex prædictis Carmelitis & Augustinianis, Pontificis indultum clanculum quæritabant, ut urbes contra primum eorum institutum inhabitare liceret. Quorum impo-sturas subolens Nicolaus Gallus, sub Sagitta i-gnea titulo, aculeatum librum aduersus illos argute scripsit. Sed de his postea.
units.tr: For many of them were then trained in the faculty of theology. But scarcely one in any convent, where there were nonetheless many friars, had a priest; so rare were priests among them at that time. These things are taken from the bulls of the aforesaid Innocent. William of Saint-Amour, in the Defence of the Church, book 2: After the Preachers and the Minors had been founded, living in idle begging, the Carmelites invented that Mary, the mother of Christ, had begged, and the Augustinian friars that the first hermit, Paul, had done the same. Thus he. Under the colour of preaching and hearing confessions, the mendicant friars, to exalt the kingdom of Antichrist, did many marvellous things everywhere through the world in these days. And so that they might share with the others the sweetness of gain from those offices, some of the aforesaid Carmelites and Augustinians secretly sought from the Pope an indult allowing them to dwell in cities, contrary to their first rule. Nicholas Gallus, sensing their impostures, wrote a cleverly stinging book against them under the title The Fiery Arrow. But of these things later.

units.la: Ex Philippo Riboto & Siberto de Beka: Anno Domini 1248 Carmelitæ fratres, paupertatis & castitatis votis irretiri primum cœperunt, ut in de habērent uirtutem draconis, & ad plenum essent Papistici ordo. Præcepit enim Pontifex Innocentius quartus Hugoni D. Sabinæ Cardinali, & Guilhelmo Anteradensi episcopo, qui Dominicani erant, ut eorum regulam ipsius authoritate disquirerent, corrigerent, atq; ad suas nequitias aptarent, ut plene tandem essent eius creaturæ. Qui ut sibi in Papismo conformes fierent, ac suarum fœditatum participes essent in regno perditionis, hanc & consimiles impostrices clausulas obedientiæ eorum uoto addiderunt, scilicet, cum castitate & abdicatione proprietatis, &c. ut eiusdem cum eis Sodomæ iurati ciues essent. Vocatur namq; spiritualis illa ciuitas, Sodoma & Aegyptus, Apoc. 11. Et ita adorantes bestiam illam magnam, atq; habentes characterem & numerum nominis eius, poterant sub ea emere ac uendere, Apoc. 12. Poterant & urbes intrare, mendacia seminare, confessiones audire: nundinas exercere, exorcismos facere, Missas murmurare, panes incantare, nouos Deos Mauzim scilicet facere, & colendos aliis exhibere: nonnas, Pinzocheras ac Beghinas confuprare, & alia edere miracula. Inde Parisijs, Londini, Coloniæ, Florentiæ, Venetijs, Tolosæ, Perpiniani, et in aliis ciuitatibus, fixerunt suos nidos. Cyrilli prophetia: Ab infantiæ suæ primordio, usq; ad tempora pubertatis, margaritis multiplicibus, parentumq; sanctitudine, excisi de petra durissi-mæ uallis uirginis nitebunt, donec pedetentim muscarum stercoribus, & uiarum pulueribus fuscabuntur, &c. De abstinentia à carnibus, mendicitate ualida, silentio nocturno, horis statutis, & aliis traditionibus papisticis, nihil hic dico.
units.tr: From Philip Ribotus and Sibert of Beka: In the year of the Lord 1248 the Carmelite friars first began to be ensnared by the vows of poverty and chastity, so that they might have the power of the dragon and be fully a Papistical order. For Pope Innocent IV ordered Hugh, cardinal of St Sabina, and William, bishop of Antibes, who were Dominicans, to examine their rule by his authority, correct it, and adapt it to his wickednesses, so that at last they might be wholly his creatures. So that they might be conformed to him in Papism, and be partakers of his foulnesses in the kingdom of perdition, they added to their vow of obedience these and similar deceitful clauses, namely "with chastity and renunciation of property," etc., so that they would be sworn citizens of the same Sodom as the others. For that spiritual city is called Sodom and Egypt (Apoc. 11). And so, worshipping that great beast and bearing the mark and number of its name, they could buy and sell under it (Apoc. 12). They could also enter cities, sow lies, hear confessions, hold markets, perform exorcisms, mutter Masses, enchant bread, make new gods, namely Mauzim, and display them to be worshipped by others, debauch nuns, Pinzocheras and Beguines, and perform other miracles. From there they fixed their nests at Paris, London, Cologne, Florence, Venice, Toulouse, Perpignan and in other cities. The prophecy of Cyril: From the beginning of their infancy, until the time of puberty, they will shine with manifold pearls and the holiness of their parents, cut from the rock of a most hard valley, a virgin; until little by little they are darkened by the dung of flies and the dust of the roads, etc. Of abstinence from meat, strong mendicancy, nocturnal silence, fixed hours and other Papistical traditions I say nothing here.

units.la: Defectio à Christo Dei filio per fratercules Mendicantes.
units.tr: Defection from Christ the Son of God by the little Mendicant brothers.

units.la: NOTA hoc loco, talem à Christo defectionem per hos Satanæ ministros hypocritas, qualis non fuit à prima plantatæ per Apostolos ecclesiæ ori-gine, Ioachimus abbas in commentario super Hieremiam, tempus æstimat esse periculosum futurum, ab anno Domini 1200, usque ad ultimos dies. In quibus apparebit (inquit) lex libertatis. Euangelium regni Christi tunc prædicabitur, & ecclesia purgabitur, ut à palea & zizaniis triticum, etc. Dum in profunda cæcitatis & ignorantiæ caligine dormirent ecclesiæ proceres, his diebus, malis uidete quid fecerit Sathan. Quosdam impostores malignos statim suscitauit, qui in humilitate & religione angelorum ambulantes, inflati tamen sensu suæ carnis, ut Paulus habet Coloss. 2. uerum Christi Euangelium auferre ab ecclesia, delere ac destruere nitebantur. Et hi Dominicani ac Franciscani uocabantur, qui circiter annum prædictum nati primum erant, Dominicani scilicet anno Domini 1204. Franciscani 1207, ut Martinus Carsulanus eorum chronographus supputat. Verumtamen uterque Matthæus noster Parisius & Vuestmonasterius, Dominicanos anno Domini 1197. origine habuisse scribit. Hi nempe uidebant se aliter ter sub patribus Dominico & Francisco, non posse sui regis Abadonis avaritias, pompas ac libidines, daemoniorum doctrinis defendere, contra Vualdenses seu pauperes de Lugduno, atq; Albigenses haereticos, infensissimos hostes, nisi sepultum vel exstinctum fuisset praenominatum Euangelium. Exprati igitur Ioachimi doctrinas ac Cyrilli visionibus, Euangelium novum, fucatae suae sanctitati accomodum conflabant, et illud vocabant Euangelium Spiritus sancti, Euangelium deinceps duraturum, atq; Euangelium aeternum.
units.tr: Note here that this defection from Christ, carried out by these hypocritical ministers of Satan, is of a kind that did not occur in the Church from its first planting by the Apostles. Joachim, abbot, in his commentary on Jeremiah, reckons that the dangerous time would run from the year of the Lord 1200 until the last days. In those days, he says, "the law of liberty will appear. Then the gospel of the kingdom of Christ will be preached, and the Church will be purged, so that the wheat is separated from the chaff and the tares." While the leaders of the Church slept in the deep darkness of blindness and ignorance in those days, see what Satan has done with evil men. He quickly raised up certain malicious impostors who, walking in humility and in the religion of angels, yet puffed up with the sense of their flesh, as Paul says in Colossians 2, strove to take the true gospel of Christ away from the Church, to erase it and to destroy it. These men were called Dominicans and Franciscans, and they were first born about the said year: the Dominicans in the year of the Lord 1204, the Franciscans in 1207, as Martin of Cosenza, their chronicler, reckons. Yet both our Matthew of Paris and the Westminster monk write that the Dominicans had their origin in the year of the Lord 1197. For these men saw that, under their founders Dominic and Francis, they could not defend the avarice, pomp and lusts of their king Abaddon with the doctrines of demons, against the Waldenses, or Poor Men of Lyons, and the Albigensian heretics, the most hostile enemies, unless the aforesaid gospel were buried or extinguished. Therefore, having extracted the doctrines of Joachim and the visions of Cyril, they forged a new gospel adapted to their feigned holiness, and they called it the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, a gospel that would last from then on, and the eternal gospel.

units.la: De quo Guilhelmus de S. Amore, in libro suo de Periculis novissimorum temporum, cap. 8. Un-decima hora (inquit) jam praeterierunt, 1254. an-ni. Sunt etiam nunc transfacti 55. anni, quod alii qui laborabant, ad mutandum Euangelium Christi in aliud Euangelium, quod dicunt perfectius, melius & dignius, quod appellant Euangelium Spiritus sancti, siue Euangelium aeternum. Quo ad-veniente evacuabitur Euangelium Christi, ut paratì sumus ostendere, ex illo Euangelio maledictione. Et sequitur: Doctrina quae praedicabitur Antichristi tempore, videlicet Euangelium aeternum, Parisijs, ubi viget sacrae scripturae studium, a suis proposita fuit, ut publicè explaneretur, anno Domini 1255. Unde certum est, quod jam praedicaretur, nisi aliquid effet quod eam detineret; &c. Et sequitur: Maledictum illud Evangelium, jam in ecclesia propalatum est: propterea timendum est de subversione eiusdem ecclesiæ. Quod cōparatum (inquiunt) ad Evangelium Christi, tanto plus perfectionis ac dignitatis habet, quantum sol ad lunam cōparatum, & ad nucleum testa, &c. Quo tendis Sathan? Ubi statuisti ponere sedem? Blasphemia enim hæc est plusquam diabolica. Et in secundo sermone eiusdem Guilhelmi: De istu[?] periculis (inquit) jam quædam habemus Parisijs, in libro qui vocatur Evangelium æternum. In eo docetur, quod Christus ipse non est Deus, quod sacramentum eius nihil est (Missam eius loco tunc sumpserant) & quod Evangelium eius non sit verum Evangelium. Neq; sunt hæc penitus novæ, immo sunt 55. anni, quod primo fuerint inboata. Et ideo dicitur, quod illi per quos hæc pericula venient, dabunt aliam legem viuendi, & aliter disponent ecclesiam: quod est valde execrabile & abominabile dictu, &c. Hæc Guil. de S. Amore.
units.tr: Concerning this, William of Saint-Amour, in his book on the Perils of the Last Times, chapter 8, says: "The eleventh hour has now passed, the year 1254. Fifty-five years have now also gone by since those who laboured to change the gospel of Christ into another gospel, which they say is more perfect, better and more worthy, and which they call the Gospel of the Holy Spirit or the eternal gospel, began. When it arrives, the gospel of Christ will be emptied out, as we have shown, and that gospel will be turned into a curse. And he continues: The doctrine which will be preached in the time of Antichrist, namely the eternal gospel, was set forth by its advocates at Paris, where the study of Holy Scripture flourishes, so that it might be expounded publicly, in the year of the Lord 1255. Hence it is certain that it would already be preached, unless something held it back; etc. And he continues: That cursed gospel has now been made public in the Church, so the subversion of the same Church is to be feared. They say that compared with the gospel of Christ it has as much more perfection and dignity as the sun compared with the moon, or the kernel compared with the shell, etc. Where are you heading, Satan? Where have you resolved to set your seat? For this blasphemy is more than diabolical. And in the second sermon of the same William: Concerning these perils (he says), we already have certain things at Paris, in a book called the eternal gospel. In it is taught that Christ himself is not God, that his sacrament is nothing (they had then taken the Mass in its place), and that his gospel is not the true gospel. Nor are these things entirely new, for they were first begun fifty-five years ago. And therefore it is said that those through whom these perils come will give another law of living and will order the Church differently, which is very detestable and abominable to speak of, etc." Thus William of Saint-Amour.

units.la: Matthæus Parisius: Anno Domini 1255. gravis dissensio Parisi durabat inter scholares & Dominicanos, qui contra Universitatis consuetudines plerasque in magna superbia & abusione fecerunt. Stetit Gallorum rex pro universitate, similiter & cives. Prævaluerunt tamen Dominicani Papæ devoti, ob multimoda eorum obsequia.
units.tr: Matthew of Paris: In the year of the Lord 1255 a grave dispute at Paris continued between the scholars and the Dominicans, who in great arrogance and abuse did many things contrary to the customs of the university. The king of the French took the side of the university, and likewise the citizens. Nevertheless, the Dominicans, devoted to the Pope, prevailed because of their manifold services.

units.la: Matthæus Parisius: Anno Domini 1256. crescentibus bescentibus[?] scandalis & odiis inter magistros Parisienses & fratres Prædicatores, seu Dominicanos, electi sunt cum magna deliberatione, celeberrimi magistri, Guilhelmus de S. Amore, Odo vel Otho de Doaco, Christianum canonicum Belvacensis, Nicolaum Barum super Albam, Ioannes Driton vel de Sicca villa Anglicum, rector universitatis Parisiensis; & Ioannes Belin Gallicum, omnes philosophi, omnes rectores in artibus, in decretis, & in theologia, ex nobilibus procreati, ut Romam adirent ad Dominum Papam, pro tranquillitate universitatis Parisiensis ac fidei redintegratione, quæ detrimentum patiebatur magnum. Nam fratres nova quaedam prædicabant, legebant & docebant deliramenta, ex libris Ioachim abbatis. Incipit eorum liber, Evangelium æternum: & quædam alia, quæ non expedit recitari. Prædicatores autem suos ex expeditos nuncios contra universitatem miserunt, ut magistris in faciem contradicerent. Subsannabat populus, eleemosynas consuetas subtrahendo: vocans eos hypocritas, Antichristi successores, pseudo-prædicatores, regum deceptores, principum adulatores, falsos cōfiliarios, ordinariorum cōtemptores, & et eorundem supplantatores, thalamorum regalium subintratores, confessionum praevaricatores, et qui ignotas provincias peruagando, peccati audaciam subministrabant. Auditis igitur hincinde querelis, praecepit Papa ut nouum ille liber quem Euangelium aeternum nominant, secreto, ac si fieri posset, si ne fratrum scandalo, comburaretur, & alia que de Ioachim scriptis emanasse dicebantur. Diligentia igitur Hugonis S. Sabinae Cardinalis, & Ioannis de Columna archiepiscopi Messanensis, qui de ordine Praedicatorum erant, caute ac tacite procuratum est, ut tumultus ad horam conquiesceret. Hæc Matthæus. O Satanæ ministros, hæc certe omnium abominationum mundi maxima est. Quis his visis, Papam negabit Antichristum, & hos eius esse praecones ac filios naturales?
units.tr: Matthew of Paris: In the year of the Lord 1256, as scandals and hatreds grew between the Parisian masters and the Friars Preachers, or Dominicans, there were chosen, after great deliberation, the most celebrated masters: William of Saint-Amour, Odo or Otto of Douai, Christian, canon of Beauvais, Nicholas Barre of Aube, John Driton or of Sicca Villa, an Englishman, rector of the University of Paris, and John Belin, a Frenchman. All were philosophers, all were regents in the arts, in canon law and in theology, born of noble families. They were to go to Rome to the Lord Pope, for the peace of the University of Paris and for the restoration of the faith, which was suffering great harm. For the friars were preaching certain new things and were reading and teaching nonsense drawn from the books of the abbot Joachim. Their book begins, The Eternal Gospel, and there are certain other things which it is not fitting to recite. The Preachers, for their part, sent their swift messengers against the university, to contradict the masters to their face. The people mocked, withdrawing their customary alms and calling them hypocrites, successors of Antichrist, false preachers, deceivers of kings, flatterers of princes, false counsellors, despisers of the ordinaries, and supplanters of the same, intruders into royal bedchambers, prevaricators of confessions, and men who, wandering through unknown provinces, supplied boldness in sin. Therefore, having heard complaints from every side, the Pope ordered that that new book which they call the Eternal Gospel, and the other writings said to have come from Joachim, be burned secretly, and, if it could be done, without scandal to the friars. Through the diligence of Hugh, Cardinal of Santa Sabina, and of John of Colonna, archbishop of Messina, who were of the Order of Preachers, it was cautiously and quietly arranged that the tumult should subside for the time being. Thus Matthew. O ministers of Satan! This is surely the greatest of all the abominations in the world. Who, having seen these things, will deny that the Pope is Antichrist, and that these men are his heralds and natural sons?

units.la: Platina in uita Alexandri: Beneficus enim Alexander, & liberalis est habitus, maxime vero erga pauperes Christi (Mendicantes fratres intelligit) & bene de religione Christiana (Papismo potius) meritos, unde libellos quosdam contra paupertatem (mendicitatem ociosam) editos, a quodam Guilhelmo de sancto Amore, perpetuo edito aboleuit. Affirmabat uir ille perniciosus (pius CHRISTI seruus) pauperes religiosi deditos (impostores pessimos) & elee-mosynis[?] mofynis viuentes, non esse in statu salutis. Combus sit etiam, uidente curia Romana, libellum pestifi-rum (cur non & libelli authores?) quo author asserebat statum gratiae non a lege Euangelij, sed a lege spiritus procedere. Quae opinio ex libris Ioannis abbatis sumpta dicebatur. Hic autem liber a sectatoribus Euangelium aeternum dicebatur. Haec Platina ex Ioannes de Parma ordinis fratrum Minorum, minister generalis, qui in gymnasio Parisiensi Sententias legerat, doctrinam abbatis Ioachimi sequebatur: haec Antoninus. Contra Guilhelmum de S. Amore, & alios pios theologos, his temporibus declamitant ac scribebant, Thomas Aquinas, Albertus Magnus, Bonaventura de Balneo regio, Humbertus Viennensis, Hugo Birchinensis, Helias Brunetus, & alij mendicantium fraterculorum plures. Ex eodem Antonino. Expar te altera Guilhelmus de S. Amore, Gallus, scriptum Defensorium scripturae & Ecclesiae contra pericula imminentia Ecclesiae generali per hypocritas ac pseudoprædicatores, penetrantes domos, ociosos & curiosos, gyrovagos, lib. 4. De periculis nouissimorum temporum, lib. 1. De quinquaginta signis pseudoprophetantium, lib. 1. Quaestiones de mendicitate, contra Bonaventuram, lib 1. Et sermones aliquot. Gerardus Sagarellus, Italus, m doctor Parisiensis, scripsit contra Minoritas lib. 2[?]. Cui per Apologiam respondit Bonaventura Franciscanorum generalis. Et hic Parmae per sanguinolentos illos dicitur esse combustus. Desiderius Longobardus de statu monachorum hoc tempore disputabit: & quod deberent de manuum suarum labore vivere, librum edidit: & istum Thomas Aquinas hæresiarchum esse dicebat; ex Bernardo Luzenburgo. Philippus, scholae Parisiensis cancellarius, ac doctor theologus, contra eosdem fra-tres praedicabat, ut habet Thomas Cantipratensis. Guido Bonatus, Italus, astrologus apud forum Livij natus, scripsit contra Minoritas lib. 1. Caba-fila quidam, contra Thomam Aquinatem, calamum quoq; strinxit. Marsfredum Sicilie regem excommunicabat Papa, quia libros habebat adver-sus fratrum mendicitatem: Fasciculus temporum. Unde Ioannes Hussius, tom. 2 suorum operum: Magistri Parisienses (inquit) spiritu Iesu plura in duobus libris praedixerunt, quam possunt in Ecclesia Iesu reperiri, etc. Anno Domini 1260 Carmelitae fratres, visis populorum odijs ac scandalis adver-sus Praedicatores & Minores, officia inquisitio-nis & exequutionis causarum cum cura Monialium á se excutiunt: Ex quadam bulla Alexandri quarti, Propterea pauciores semper erant Cafinales[?] ex his & Augustinianis, quàm ex aliorum Mendicantium sectis, ut in quadam ordinaria quaestione Ioannis Chelmestoni apud Nordouicum olim legi.
units.tr: Platina in the life of Alexander: For Alexander was reckoned generous and liberal, especially towards the poor of Christ (he means the Mendicant brothers), and one who had deserved well of the Christian religion (rather, of Papism). Hence he abolished, for ever, certain little books against poverty (idle begging) published by a certain William of Saint-Amour. That pernicious man (the pious servant of Christ) affirmed that religious poor men, given over (the worst impostors) and living by alms, were not in a state of salvation. He also burned, in view of the Roman curia, a pestilential little book (why not also the authors of the little books?) in which the author asserted that the state of grace proceeds not from the law of the gospel but from the law of the Spirit. This opinion was said to be taken from the books of the abbot John. This book was called the Eternal Gospel by its followers. So Platina. From John of Parma, of the order of the Friars Minor, minister general, who had lectured on the Sentences in the Paris school and followed the doctrine of the abbot Joachim: so Antoninus. Against William of Saint-Amour, and other godly theologians, in these times declaimed and wrote Thomas Aquinas, Albertus Magnus, Bonaventure of Bagnoregio, Humbert of Vienne, Hugh of Bicchieri, Elias Brunetus, and many other little brothers of the mendicant orders. From the same Antoninus. On the other side, William of Saint-Amour, a Frenchman, wrote a Defence of Scripture and of the Church against the perils threatening the Church generally from hypocrites and false preachers who penetrate houses, the idle and the curious, the wandering vagabonds: four books On the Perils of the Last Times, one book On the Fifty Signs of False Prophets, one book Questions on Mendicancy against Bonaventure, and some sermons. Gerard Sagarelli, an Italian, a doctor of Paris, wrote against the Minorites, two books. Bonaventure, the general of the Franciscans, answered him with an Apology. And he is said to have been burned at Parma by those bloody men. Desiderius Lombardus discussed the state of monks in this time, and published a book that they ought to live by the labour of their hands. Thomas Aquinas used to call him a heresiarch, according to Bernard of Luxemburg. Philip, chancellor of the Paris school and doctor of theology, preached against the same brothers, as Thomas of Cantimpré records. Guido Bonatti, an Italian astrologer born at Forlì, wrote one book against the Minorites. A certain Cabafila also drew his pen against Thomas Aquinas. The Pope excommunicated Manfred, king of Sicily, because he had books against the mendicancy of the friars: the Fasciculus temporum. Hence John Hus, in volume 2 of his works: The Parisian masters (he says) foretold by the Spirit of Jesus many things in two books, which can be found in the Church of Jesus, etc. In the year of the Lord 1260 the Carmelite friars, seeing the hatreds and scandals of the people against the Preachers and the Minorites, took up the offices of inquisition and the execution of cases, with the care of the nuns. From a certain bull of Alexander IV: For this reason there were always fewer Carmelites from these, and from the Augustinians, than from the other sects of the Mendicants, as I once read in a certain ordinary question of John Chelmeston at Northampton.

units.la: Et quamuis Euangelium illud diabolicum, de quo iam diximus, fuerit quorundam fratrum astutia, ac Romanum Pontificum arcano praecepto de letum: mansit tamen eadem in Deum blasphemia, ac summa à rectà fide in Christum, unicum huma-nigeneris seruatorem, defectio, ad nostra usque tempora, in Papistarum meritis de condigno & congruo, in sanctorum suffragijs, Papae largitionibus atq; indulgentijs, in bonis operibus, oblationibus, donis, votis, solutionibus, coenobiorum erectionibus, ieiunijs, vigilijs, somnijs, silentijs, horis, organis, sequentijs, hymnis, cantilenis, campanis, altaribus, simulachris, purgatorijs, missis, murmurationibus, mitris, delubris, templis, synagogis, sacrificijs, sectis, breuiarijs, bullis, lustralibus, aquis, ra-furis[?], unctionibus, coemeterijs, cineribus, palmis, calculis precarijs, candelis, calcibus, crucibus, cathedris, cappis, candelabris, cereis, thuribulis, popis, ritibus Babylonicis, Aegyptiacis cultibus spectaculis, reliquijs, regulis, monachis, mendicabulis, chordis, codicib. ocreis, bracchis, pseudodoctrinis, sententijs, summis, decretis, luminibus, picturis, caremoniis,idololatriis,incantationibus, exorcif-mus, sputis, legendis,vitis,fabulis,ocijs,ineptijs, atq; aliis innumeris apostaticarum adinuentionū impostuṙis & abominationibus. Pro his perda-moniorum doctrinas firmandis, ac per disceptā-tiones sophisticas perpetuandis, Robertus D.Lu-douici Francorum regis frater,his temporibus Pa-risiorum Sorbonam primus instituit. Et alter eius frater, Alphonsus, Pictauensium comes, minis ac terroribus pios doctores per Domicanos fuga-bat. Et ut Cantipratensis habet in opere suo de A-pibus mysticis, Albertus Magnus, Hugo Cardina-lis, Thomas Aquinas, Bonauentura, & alij eiusdē farinæ theologi, mirabilia magna et multa Parisijs tunc faciebant. Philosophiam quoq; qua deinceps in scolis utebantur magistri nostri, Erasmus dicit in quadam ep stola, his diebus esse natam. Degenerabant istis temporibus (inquit Lelandus) a sua pu-ritate artes, unā cum Latinæ linguæ elegantia: per strepebatq; in scholis nescio quæ sophistica garrulitas. Eos igitur omnes, quibus Seruator Christus cordi est, adhortor in Domino, ut hæc ob ea quæ in Ecclesiæ doctrinis ac doctoribus deinceps usq; ad annum Domini 1520. sequuntur, medullitus hoclo-co perpendant, explorent, iudicent.
units.tr: And although that diabolical gospel, of which we have already spoken, was kept hidden by the cunning of certain friars and by the secret command of the Roman pontiffs, the same blasphemy against God and the same great falling away from the true faith in Christ, the only Saviour of the human race, has persisted down to our own times. It appears in the merits of the Papists, of condign and of congruous merit; in the suffrages of the saints; in the largesses and indulgences of the Pope; in good works, oblations, gifts, vows, payments, the erection of monasteries, fasts, vigils, dreams, silences, hours, organs, sequences, hymns, chants, bells, altars, images, purgatories, masses, mutterings, mitres, shrines, temples, synagogues, sacrifices, sects, breviaries, bulls, lustral waters, tonsures, anointings, cemeteries, ashes, palms, prayer beads, candles, shoes, crosses, chairs, copes, candlesticks, wax tapers, censers, popes, Babylonian rites, Egyptian cults, spectacles, relics, rules, monks, begging-bags, cords, books, greaves, arms, false doctrines, sentences, summae, decrees, lights, pictures, ceremonies, idolatries, incantations, exorcisms, spittle, legends, lives of saints, fables, idleness, follies, and countless other impostures and abominations of apostate invention. To establish these devilish doctrines and to perpetuate them through sophistical disputations, Robert, brother of Louis, king of the French, first founded the Sorbonne of Paris in these times. And his other brother, Alphonsus, count of Poitou, drove pious teachers out by threats and terrors through the Dominicans. And as the Cantipratensis has it in his work on the mystical bees, Albert the Great, Hugh the Cardinal, Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure and other theologians of the same stamp then worked many great and manifold wonders at Paris. Erasmus says, in a certain letter, that the philosophy which our masters afterwards used in the schools was also born in these days. Arts degenerated in those times from their purity, together with the elegance of the Latin tongue (so Leland says), and some sophistical chatter resounded in the schools. I therefore exhort all of them, whom Christ the Saviour holds dear, in the Lord, to weigh, search out and judge these things thoroughly, with regard to what followed in the doctrines and teachers of the Church down to the year of the Lord 1520.

units.la: Nicolaum Gallicum, patria Narbonensis, septimus Carmelitarum magister generalis, deforma-tum sui ordinis statum piis lachrymis deplorabat, quod a pristina morum probitate ac sanctis stu-diis, sui fratres tunc essent in omnium vitiorum la-byrinthum prolapsi. Prius enim dum eremos inco-lerent, orationi, lectioni, ac manuum labori iugi-ter incumbebant. Tunc autem in urbibus commo-rantes, sub hypocrisi matre, omnia in ocium, desi-diam, inertiam, libidinem & luxum convertebant.
units.tr: Nicholas of Gaul, a native of Narbonne, the seventh master general of the Carmelites, lamented with pious tears the deformed state of his order, because his brethren had then fallen from their former uprightness of life and holy studies into a labyrinth of all vices. For formerly, while they dwelt in the wilderness, they were constantly devoted to prayer, reading and the labour of their hands. But now, living in cities, they turned everything, under the mother of hypocrisy, into idleness, sloth, inertia, lust and luxury.

units.la: Is igitur post quinq; sui regiminis annos, laboris in utiliter expensi tædio tædus, officio cessit: & edi-to in eos libro satis aculeato (igneam sagittam uo-cabat) ad eremi quietem, illis relictis, est reversus in montem Euuatrof, anno Domini 1270. Qui post quam privignos, reprobos, cauteriatos errones, fibulatores, garrulos, inutiles consiliarios, mali-gnos discurfores, Sodomæ cives, optimi testamen-ti contemptores, præsentium & futurorum sedu-ctores, Draconis caudam tertiam stellarum par-tem de cælo trahentem & in terram mittentem,
units.tr: After five years of his rule, weary of the tedium of labour spent to no purpose, he resigned from office. Having published against them a book quite sharp (he called it the fiery arrow), he returned to the quiet of the wilderness, leaving them behind, to Mount Euuatrof, in the year of the Lord 1270. After he had called them stepsons, reprobates, branded vagabonds, buckle-makers, chatterers, useless counsellors, malicious runners about, citizens of Sodom, despisers of the best testament, seducers of the present and of the future, the dragon's tail dragging the third part of the stars from heaven and casting them to earth,

units.la: & his similia vocasset, in hæc veiba[?] in quinto capite prorupit: Dicite (inquit) quæ & quæ lis est ista religio nova, in civitatibus adinventa? Per plateas civitatum, de mane usq; adversperam bini & bini discurrentes, vagis gres bus circuitis, ipsum habentes pædagogum, qui rugiendo circuit quærens quem devoret. Et sic in vobis prophetiæ, in circuitu impij ambulant, ad vestræ confusionis cumulum, veraciter est impleta. Est enim causa discursuum huiusmodi principalis ac præcipua, ut visitetis non pupillos, sed puellas: non viduas in tribulatione existentes, sed fatuas iuvenculas, beghinas, moniales, ac dominas, ubi alter in alterum iactantes lumina vultus, verba quæ naturam adamantis in se habent, & quæ bonos mores destruunt atq; corrumpunt, alternatim emittitis, cordium allectiua, &c. Non est hæc religio munda & immaculata apud Deum & patrem, in qua oportet quemlibet immaculatum ab hoc seculo utiq; custodiri, heu me fratres charissimi, dum luto seculi estis involuti, cur vos creditis minime maculari? hæc Ni-colaus.
units.tr: and other things like these, he burst out in these words in the fifth chapter: "Tell me," he says, "what is this quarrel, what is this new religion devised in the cities? Running through the squares of the cities, from morning until evening, in pairs and in pairs, wandering about with restless steps, having that tutor who roars and goes about seeking whom he may devour. And so in you the prophecy is truly fulfilled, 'the wicked walk round about' (Ps. 12), to the heap of your shame. For the cause of such running about is chiefly and above all this, that you visit not orphans but girls, not widows in affliction but foolish young women, beguines, nuns and ladies; where, throwing glances at one another and emitting words that have the nature of adamant and that destroy and corrupt good morals, you lure the hearts, etc. This is not the pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father, in which everyone must be kept unstained from this world. Alas, dearest brothers, while you are wrapped in the mire of the world, why do you believe you are in no way defiled?" So Nicholas.

units.la: Unde Guilhelmus de S. Amore, qui eodem tempore vixit, in Defensorio scripturæ & Ecclesiæ lib.2. hoc testimonium habet: Fratres mendicantes (inquit) Beghinas circumducunt, gyrouagi, super hoc: Nunquid non habemus potestatem, mulierem sororem circunducendi, &c. Thomas Cantipratensis lib.2, cap.56. de Apibus, seu Bono universali: Incubi dæmones (fratres dixisset) ita religiosas virgines illis diebus opprimebant, ut nulla eis valeret crucis signatio, nec aqua benedicta, nec ipsum Christi corporis sacramentum. Thomas Ecclestonus, in libro de aduentu Minorum ad Angliam, narrat quosdam Franciscanes, statim post primum eorum introitum, virilia sibi amputasse, non propter regnum cœleste (qui longè alius castrandi modus est) sed ut in hoc mundo sanctiores haberentur, hypocritae, ac primos eorum illic ponit, Guilhelmum quendam Etonum & Ricardum Deuonium. Sic se olim castrabat Origenes, magnus ecclesiae doctor, Hierophantas Atheniensium imitatus, ne molestam sibi uenerem experiretur: aut ut alij uolunt, ne quandoq; à suis appellaretur studiis. Propter haec & alia Guilhelmus de S. Amore, de illis hoc dicit, in libro suo de Periculis nouissimorum temporum: Qui prius uiuebant in simplicitate cordis, post ingressum sectae eorum sunt astuti hypocritae. De quibus Paulus Aemilius in Chronicis Gallorum: Anno Domini 1260.
units.tr: Hence William of Saint-Amour, who lived at the same time, in his Defence of Scripture and of the Church, book 2, gives this testimony: "The mendicant friars" (he says) "lead the beguines about, as wanderers, on this point: 'Have we not the power to lead about a woman, a sister, etc.?'" Thomas of Cantimpré, book 2, chapter 56, On the Bees, or the Universal Good: "Incubus demons" (he would have said "friars") "so oppressed the religious virgins in those days that no sign of the cross could avail them, nor holy water, nor the very sacrament of Christ's body." Thomas Eccleston, in his book on the coming of the Minorites to England, tells how certain Franciscans, straight after their first entry, cut off their own private parts. This was not for the kingdom of heaven (which is quite another mode of castration), but so that they might be thought holier in this world; he calls them hypocrites, and names first among them one William of Eton and Richard of Devon. In the same way Origen, the great doctor of the Church, once castrated himself, imitating the hierophants of Athens, so that he might not experience a venery troublesome to him; or, as others would have it, lest he should at some time be called away from his studies. On account of these and other things, William of Saint-Amour says this of them in his book On the Perils of the Last Times: "Those who before lived in simplicity of heart became crafty hypocrites after entering their sect." Of them Paulus Aemilius writes in his Chronicles of the French, in the year of the Lord 1260.

units.la: Mendicantium ordinum fratres suum genus uitae miris laudibus, ac religionis sanctitate, schismatice ac seditiose commendabant. Guilhelmus à sano Amoris, Sorbonicus doctor, alij quoque doctrina clari, mendicitatem illam in uulgus, ac uctiuam sine ceu sa paupertatem improbabant, contendentes spe ciem & praetextum religionis dari inerti ac desidiosae uitae, & mendicationi. Liber eius, qui adhuc extat in Bibliotheca Sorbonæ, damnatus est. Hæc ille. Abbas Vrspergensis Conradus Lichtenauu, claustralis fictam religionem inchoasse exclamabat, anno Domini 1201 deincepsq; rapinas, depredationes, incendia, seditiones, bella & latrocinia iustificata esse apud populum & sacerdotem.
units.tr: The friars of the mendicant orders commended their way of life with wondrous praises and the holiness of religion, in a schismatic and seditious manner. William of Saint-Amour, a doctor of the Sorbonne, and others also famous for their learning, condemned that begging which goes about among the common people, and that wandering poverty without cause, contending that the appearance and pretext of religion was being given to an idle and slothful life and to mendicancy. His book, which still survives in the library of the Sorbonne, was condemned. So far he. Conrad of Lichtenau, abbot of Ursperg, cried out that a feigned religion had begun among the monks, and that from the year 1201 onwards robberies, plunderings, burnings, seditions, wars and brigandage had been justified among the people and the priests.

units.la: In detestabili monstro ac sanguinario Sodomita, Iulio scilicet tertio, anno Domini 1554. & die 28. Nouembris, post 20 diuinæ liberationis annos, Anglia nostra, ut canis ad vomitum, & ut sus lota ad cæni volutabrum reuersa, reliquis cum ipsa veritate perennibus Dei donis, Draconem ac diabolum venerabatur denuo. Horrendum certe præsenti mundo spectaculum. Fidem, periurandum Henrico patri datam, quod Pontifex Romanæ nihil eximie iuris haberet in Anglorum ecclesiis, regina Maria, pessimo aliorum omnium exemplo, prima violabat: imo, quod adhuc magis impium est, sceleratissimæ Iefabelis[?] instar violentissime violari procurabat. Iusserat etiam idem Henricus rex pater, ut in quotidianis precibus, ab ipso Deo universa plebs peteret, ne amplius eius Antichristi hæretica doctrina, blasphemis aut tyrannide molestarentur: quod & illa, cum precibus illis sanctissimis abolerī mandauit. Et in subsequenti parliamento, duo ad regni uastitatem & excidium proposuit: ut in matrimonio iungeretur Hispano, & ut Sodomitarum parens ac Pontifex Iulius eiusdem regni primatu potiretur. Primum ab ignobilitate, dixissem nobilitate, coessum est, quod animarum salutem ad se non pertinere crederent: alterum uero non, quod suarum commoditatum ia-sturam fortassis timerent. Paulo mox Gardinero, quieius matrem incestus damnauerat, Bonero Spu-rio, Tonstallo, atque aliis regni proditoribus & papistis ex captivitate prius liberatis, religionem il-li mutauit, ac Papismum, & cum eo nihil non malorum reuocauit: electos Dei ministros ministerijs deiecit, Baalitas impudicos sublimauit prophetas sanctos occidit, & ganeones rasos euexit: scriptu-ras diuinas e templis fugauit, ac uetita a Deo simu-lachra cum missis introduxit: coniugia damnauit, prostibula restaurauit, aliaque mirabilia magna fecit.
units.tr: Under that detestable monster and bloody sodomite, Julius the Third, namely, in the year of the Lord 1554, on the 28th day of November, twenty years after the divine deliverance, our England, like a dog returned to its vomit and a washed sow to the wallowing of the mire, worshipped the dragon and the devil again, leaving aside the gifts of God which last for ever along with the truth itself. Surely a dreadful spectacle for the present world. Queen Mary was the first to violate the faith pledged to her father Henry, that the Roman Pontiff had no particular right in the churches of the English, and gave the worst example of all others; indeed, what is still more impious, like the wicked Jezebel, she procured that it should be most violently violated. The same King Henry, her father, had ordered that the whole common people should ask of God himself, in their daily prayers, that they should no longer be harassed by the heretical doctrine, blasphemies or tyranny of this Antichrist; and she ordered that these most holy prayers be abolished. And in the following parliament she put forward two things for the ruin and destruction of the kingdom: that she be married to a Spaniard, and that Julius, the parent of sodomites and pontiff, should gain the primacy of the same kingdom. The first was agreed to by the baseborn (I would have said the nobility), because they believed the salvation of souls did not concern them; the second was not, because they perhaps feared the loss of their own advantages. Soon after, she restored the religion to Gardiner, whose mother he had condemned for incest, to Bonner the bastard, to Tonstall, and to other traitors and papists of the kingdom who had previously been freed from captivity; and with it she recalled Papism, and with that everything evil. She cast the chosen ministers of God out of their ministries, raised up impudent Baalites, killed holy prophets, and lifted up shaven gluttons; she drove the divine Scriptures out of the churches, and introduced the images forbidden by God together with the masses; she condemned marriages, restored brothels, and did many other great wonders.

units.la: Aduenit interim Polus Cardinalis, Romanorum diabolorum Mercurius, ab Henrico rege pa-tre ob Papismum olim deiectus, sed a Maria filia iterum ob eundem restitutus. Qui a magno pæde-rasta Iulio missus, ut patriæ suæ tam ad corpora quam animas ruinam prorsus inferret, rogabat primum, ut cum suo Baalpeore in communionem redeant,& eius authoritati,relicto Christi Euange-lio sacrosanctio,se denuò subijciant. Quoniam[?] iu- stitiæ nullum est cum improbitate consortium, neque cum tenebris luci communitas. Promisitq; ex summæ perditionis filio, rapacissimo Antichristo suo, benignitatem & clementiam.
